The *Vālmīki-Śrīvāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, together with its commentary titled *Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The *Vāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*, edited by Vāsudeva Śarman, son of Paṇaśīkara Upāhv Lakṣmaṇa Śarman.
Edited by Vāsudeva Laxmaṇa Śarmā Paṇśīkar. Chapter Four: The Section on Stability.
The First Chapter.
Now, immediately following the section on origination, hear this, O Rāma: the section on maintenance, which, when known, brings about liberation. 1.

Established in the consciousness of His own ever-present, fearless, and perfect bliss, He who here assumes all forms by His own majesty sports within them through delusion, perceiving them as diverse selves.
I salute that Supreme Brahman, whose true nature is known through the Vedas. || 1 ||
The difference between the world-picture and a well-known painting is described;
having cleared away the doctrines of the Sāṃkhya and others, the state of being Brahman alone is established. || 1 ||

In the section on origination, by demonstrating through the door of showing the superimposition of the world upon non-dual Brahman— via the demonstration of where all the creation-proclaiming statements such as "from which indeed these beings are born" find their final purport as a circumstantial definition (taṭasthalakṣaṇa)— he refutes the distinction between the world, the individual soul, and so forth.

The identity of the inner self (*pratyag-ātman*) and Brahman has been established. Now, [it is said]: "By whom all things that are born live, by whom the sky and the earth are made firm; by the command of this very Imperishable (*akṣara*), O Gārgī, the sun and the moon stand held apart.
For who indeed could breathe? Out of fear of him the wind blows; he alone upholds [all things]."
"He who alone, as the wielder of the net, rules all worlds by his ruling powers and supreme energies;

for this Self, being authorized [by Him], sustains the self of all this"—such scriptural passages establish that He is the one who maintains the current state of the world, as in: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, O Agni."

And by dispelling the various delusions arising from the diverse imaginings of the human intellect regarding the manifold intentions [of the scriptures], [the author refutes] those scriptural passages— such as "In the beginning, indeed, this was the Self alone"— which establish that the Self is the sustainer of the existence of the world at the time of dissolution.

The venerable Vasiṣṭha, commencing the Section on Stability (Sthitiprakaraṇa) in order to consolidate the knowledge of the identity with Brahman— which was established at length by demonstrating how the ultimate purport of the "indirect definition" (taṭasthalakṣaṇa) culminates in establishing the nature of Brahman as Being-Consciousness-Bliss— now proceeds.

Demonstrating the connection, he makes a formal declaration with the words "Now" (*atha*). The intention is that the connection consists in [the previous topic] being the cause of the establishment [of the present one], since it is the cause of its arising.
With the view that there is likewise a connection through having a single purpose, he says: "It is known."

Furthermore, although the word "atha" (now/then) is primarily concerned with indicating immediate succession, it is auspicious by its very nature—like the sounds of a conch, a lute, or a drum; thus, it should be understood that an auspicious rite has been performed at the beginning of this treatise. || 1 ||
In this way, understand that this visible world is established as such;
it is formless, consisting of "I," "you," and so forth, being mere delusion and composed of unreality. (2)

He shows by way of extension that the logical arguments established to demonstrate the falsity of the world's origination are equally applicable to its continued existence, with the words: "In this way, first... and so forth. || 2 ||
A painting has arisen in the sky without an artist and without colors;
it is an experience without a witness, like seeing a dream while not asleep.

It is without an agent; it is devoid of a scribe, even though provided with causes, instruments, and accessories; it is without a stage, being devoid of the materials for painting and the coloring substances. By the word "in the sky," the absence of a supporting wall or similar surface for the painting is also indicated. This applies to the viewer as well.
Because it falls within the range of the visible, it is without a seer; yet because the Witness is not overcome even when the knower is overwhelmed by the sleep of delusion, it is sleepless.
The construction of a future city arises as if established within the mind;
though unreal, it accomplishes its purpose, like the heat from a fire made by a monkey.
The fire prepared by monkeys—consisting of a heap of *guñjā* seeds, red ochre, and so forth—has as its limit only the heat it produces;
yet, with the intention that even by such means their relief from cold is well-known through tradition (*aitihya*), it was said: "Even that which is unreal accomplishes a purpose.
Thus, Brahman is non-different [from the world], yet appears as different, abiding like a whirlpool in water.
Even though it possesses a form, that form is void, like solar radiance in the sky. || 5 ||
Solar radiance is light, while heat is its glow. || 5 ||
Like a mass of jewel-lustre seen in the sky, it is without a foundation;
like the city of the Gandharvas, it is eternally visible yet without a foundation. (6)
Without walls, without intoxication, and without support. || 6 ||
Unreal like the water of a mirage, yet producing the conviction of reality;
mature like a city of one's imagination, it is experienced though composed of non-existence.
"Prakṛṣṭa" means extensive; or it means clearly experienced. || 7 ||
Consisting of the eloquence of speech and meaning, it is neither fixed nor unfixed anywhere;
though devoid of essence, it possesses an inner essence, resembling a mountain in a dream.
Its nature is such that it manifests as the structural forms of cities, mountains, and so forth, imagined by a poet;
because it does not abide in any place or time, it is non-abiding and non-existent, yet it possesses an inner essence that is exceedingly firm. (8)
Like the elemental ether, it is radiant in its source, consisting of pure emptiness;
like an autumn cloud standing before one, it is stainless, imperishable, and unimpaired.

Resplendent with the form of a great downward-turned sapphire bowl, it is fully capable of warding off the heat and other [obstacles] as long as it remains in front; it is impossible to destroy, uninjured, and uninterrupted. || 9 ||

Like the appearance of impurity in the sky, it is perceived yet lacks substantial reality; like the enjoyment of a woman in a dream, it appears to have an objective basis but is ultimately devoid of meaning.

The color of the impurity of the sky is its glossiness; or, it is like the phrase "the head of Rāhu. In the reading *vyomatalasya*, the meaning is clear. It is grounded in the object and performs the purposeful action characterized by enjoyment (*bhoga*). || 10 ||
Though in full bloom like a variegated garden, it was devoid of nectar despite its appearance of being full of sap;
though luminous, it remained lusterless, like a painted sun or fire.
Tasteless, withered, and devoid of nectar. || 11 ||
It was experienced as unreal and unsubstantial, like a kingdom of the mind;
it was devoid of essence and fragrance, like a painted lotus pond.
It is unreal by its own nature and non-substantial even in terms of its result; "essence" refers to the nectar, pollen, and so forth. || 12 ||
Manifested within the void, consisting of various colors and forms, it is empty yet perceived as a solid mass,
arisen like a rainbow.
The grasping of a solid mass is materiality; that [grasping] is empty. || 13 ||
With the delicate sprouts of the elements withered by grasping, it has been made dull, essence-less, and as hollow as the trunk of a plantain tree. (14)

By even a slight reflection upon the Supreme Self—that is, by even a slight investigation—or by even a slight impact from another, such as wind, heat, or people; [it is like] a plantain trunk, a plantain tree. 14.
The revolving wheel of darkness seen with eyes that are flickering.
Even that which has an absolutely non-existent form stands as if it were directly perceived. || 15 ||
By means of a throbbing eye—a specific kind of ophthalmic disease—his form became a form that was impossible [to behold]. || 15 ||
It is expansive like a water bubble, empty within yet throbbing with form; it consists of essence yet is devoid of essence, characterized by uninterrupted decline and arising.

It is expansive (*ābhogi*) and possesses a conceptualized form (*kalpitākāra*). Its "flavor" (*rasa*) consists of a pleasantness upon first encounter; yet, though it appears to have such flavor, it is actually flavorless and bitter in its ultimate transformation. He elaborates on this very point with the words "uninterrupted," etc. "Arising and decay" refers to births and deaths. (16)
Like a spreading mist, it is grasped as being nothing at all;
for some, it is a void that is the locus of dullness and emptiness, like an atom. (17)
For the Sāṃkhyas, it consists solely of the insentient; for the Vedāntins, it is the insentient void which is the locus of ignorance (avidyā);
for the Mādhyamikas, it is the void. For the Yogācāras, it is like an atom in terms of time due to its momentariness;
for the Sautrāntikas and Vaibhāṣikas, it is like an atom in terms of both time and space; [and for some,] only in terms of space.

The meaning is that it has been conceptualized in many ways by proponents: as being like an atom according to the followers of Kaṇāda and Gautama; and as being like an atom of indeterminate nature according to the Ārhatas. || 17 ||
"I am somewhat composed of the elements," thus [the self] remains, though it is empty and unreal;
even while being perceived, it exists like a night-stalker, having no real form. (18)
Demonstrating that the logic stated regarding the external world applies to the internal as well, he says: "Something... (verse 18).
Śrī Rāma said:
At the end of the great kalpa, the visible world remains like a sprout within a seed; it arises again from that very source in the Supreme. Tell me, how is this so? (19)

But if, in this way, the world is devoid of intrinsic existence and the existence of Brahman does not touch the world, then how could there be consistency with such scriptural passages as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.2.1), which advocate the doctrine that the effect pre-exists in the cause (*satkāryavāda*), as well as with the corroborative works of Vyāsa, Kapila, and others that follow them?
Thinking thus, Rāma asks: "Mahākalpa. The meaning is: how is that which was stated by Vyāsa and others consistent? || 19 ||
"Are those who possess such awakening ignorant or wise?
O Blessed One, tell me clearly and according to reality for the sake of pacifying all my doubts. (20)
Thus, those such as Kapila and others are so called because their understanding is that the world exists within its cause by way of its own essence during the dissolution (pralaya).
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
This visible world exists within the great-minded one like a sprout in a seed;
he who speaks thus possesses ignorance, which is his childhood.

In the great bed of dissolution; even in this state of "childhood" to be described—which consists of the firm conviction in the reality of the world despite the discernment of the Self as being unattached—there exists this childhood characterized by such a lack of detachment. || 21 ||
Listen to this: how can it be unrelated? How can it be unreal?
This is a perverted understanding that causes delusion for both the speaker and the listener. (22)

Listen to this collection of arguments that is about to be stated. One who asserts that the effect exists in the cause prior to its production must be asked: does it exist by way of the generality of existence (*sattāsāmānya*), or by way of the existence of the seed and so forth, or by way of the existence of the sprout and so forth? In the first case, is that sprout and so forth unrelated [to the cause], or is it related to something? If it is unrelated, to what is it unrelated such that it is of such a nature?

The meaning is that because the universal *sattā* (existence) is common to all things, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that a sprout or the like arising from a seed would be related to everything. If it is argued that this is an acceptable conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*), [the reply is: in this field where a sprout has emerged from a seed, only that which is actually seen is real; whereas in the case of a seed remaining in a granary or a piece of stone, [it is not].

The meaning is: how can it be said that what is seen through delusion is unreal? Even in the second case, since no distinction can be established in terms of intrinsic nature (*svarūpataḥ*) between the existence of the seed and its relation to the sprout, or its relation to objects such as pots and cloths, there is nothing that lacks a relation (*asaṃbandham*); what, then, would be the entity that exists by means of the seed? [This applies] to seeds such as rice and so forth.

There would be the consequence that all beings in the world [would exist]. If you accept this as a desired conclusion, then how is it that when a seed has sprouted, only the sprout and so forth are real, and not jars, cloths, and the like? This is the meaning. Furthermore, even in the third case, since no distinction can be established between the seed's connection with the existence of the sprout's own nature and its connection with jars and so forth, why is there no such connection [with the latter]?

"Entity" (vastu): the meaning is that there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of the existence of the sprout everywhere. If you accept this [consequence], then how is it that the sprout and so forth exist as real entities (vāstavam) only in the seed and such, and not elsewhere? Furthermore, the specific (asādhāraṇa) entity such as the sprout exists by virtue of a common existence (sādhāraṇasattā), and the effect exists by virtue of the existence of its cause.

And since the existence of a cause is established by the existence of the effect, this understanding is indeed contrary [to reality], because it cannot be logically sustained within any of the three positions; with this intention, he says: "It is contrary. (22)
Listen now to how that deluded notion—which holds that the world exists within the seed like a sprout—is merely a false prattle. (23)
Furthermore, the analogy that the world exists during dissolution (pralaya) like a sprout in a seed is incongruous;

for the intention is that it is impossible for the Self—which is of the nature of immutable consciousness alone—to possess the status of a seed. With this in mind, he says "in the seed," etc., [referring to] that which is intended as a mere empty prattle for the purpose of proposing an analogy for the existence of the world during dissolution.
That cognition is deluded and erroneous; the meaning is that it differs from the illustrative example (dārṣṭāntika). || 23 ||

The seed itself becomes the visible object within the range of the mind and the senses; just as in the case of grains such as barley and wheat, when the conditions are met, the emergence of leaves and sprouts occurs. (24)
He clarifies this very discrepancy with the words beginning "the seed" (*bījam*). "Barley-grains" (*yavadhānāḥ*) refers to husked barley;
that is the visible seed, fit to be seen. And thus, in that case, there is the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of the sprout and so forth.

The meaning is that the state of being a seed for a sprout and so forth is logical, because it is established by direct perception, because it possesses parts, because its nature is subject to transformation, and because it possesses distinctions such as genus and configuration which account for the difference in kind between the sprout and [the seed]. || 24 ||
How could that which transcends the six senses including the mind, which is exceedingly subtle,
and which is capable of becoming the seed [of all], be the self-born creator of the worlds? (25)

But [the author] says "the mind" (*manaḥ*) to show that it is not so in the case of the subject of the illustration (the *dārṣṭāntika*). It is "self-existent" (*svayaṃbhūḥ*) because it exists by itself and indeed exists as itself; thus, it is the immutable, non-dual conscious Self (*cidātman*). And so, the point is this: since even its status as a seed is difficult to establish, let alone the existence of the world through its own being. || 25 ||
How and in what manner can there be the state of being a seed for the Supreme Self, which is subtler than even space and in which no designation whatsoever is perceived? (26)
That subtle [cause] appears as non-existent, for it is indeed non-existent since it is not of such a nature;
what kind of seedhood can there be therein? In the absence of a seed, whence could there be a sprout? (27)

Having thus stated the impossibility of its being a seed from the perspective of one who knows reality, he states its impossibility even from the perspective of the ignorant—beginning with the word "tat" (that). Although in reality it is not like that, being of the nature of a single essence (*ekarasa*), yet because of its subtlety, it appears as non-existent to the ignorant; thus the meaning is that it is indeed non-existent. [The sprout...]
The sprout of the world. || 27 ||
In that supreme state, which is clearer even than the expanse of the sky and is void, how can there exist the world, Mount Meru, the oceans, the sky, and so forth? (28)
There is not even the slightest thing whatsoever that exists as a real entity within that entity;
if it did exist there, why would it not be perceived? (29)
Nothing belongs to the self, nor does anything come from anywhere or in any way; for where, from what, or when could a mountain ever arise from the empty space within a jar? (30)
There is nothing whatsoever of the Self; for this reason, the instruction regarding that which consists of the negation of all things is "not this, not this. || 30 ||
How can anything exist within its opposite, as [darkness exists] in light?
How can darkness abide in the sun, or how can frost abide in fire? 31.

He states that the existence of the world cannot be conceived there even because the existence of the single-flavored consciousness (*cidekarasa-sattā*) is the antithesis of the existence of the manifold-flavored insentient (*jaḍānekarasa-sattā*):
"In the case of the antithesis" (verse 31).
How could Meru reside within an atom? For how could there be any unity between that which has form and that which is formless, any more than there can be between shadow and sunlight? (32)
[Objection: "Let it not be so through difference; but might it be so through identity? To this he replies: "Of that which has the nature of both that and not-that" (tadatadrūpayoḥ).
This means: of those whose natures are consciousness (cit) and non-consciousness (acit). || 32 ||
It is logical that sprouts exist within the seed, such as the *vaṭa* tree;
however, it is illogical to claim that this world, which possesses great magnitude, exists within formlessness (*ākāra*). 33.
"Not in form, not in formlessness"—this is not the negative particle *nañ*, but rather another word, the particle *na*, which, having the sense of negation, is compounded [with the following terms].
Whatever power of the intellect and all the senses is seen in another place and in another person... [33]
In the cognition that perceives such [an object], it does not exist at all; therefore, it is said to be "nothing whatsoever. || 34 ||

Furthermore, regarding this existence of the world in its cause as postulated by the Sāṃkhyas and others: does it arise from the force of worldly means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), or from the force of such scriptural passages as "In the beginning, my dear, this was indeed Being"? It is not the first case; thus he says:
"In another place," etc. That which is visible—such as jars, cloths, and so forth, which possess the power of all the senses, beginning with the intellect—is [not found there].

Whether there exists another person who perceives it directly themselves, or whether such a perceiver is absent, in any other place from the location of that substratum and at any other time from the time of that substratum,
that [object] simply does not exist and does not appear at all within the cognitive functions characterized by perception, inference, and so forth.

Due to the force of non-perception—which is appropriate for the non-observation of that which is otherwise perceptible—it is asserted by all worldly people and authoritative logicians that nothing whatsoever is non-existent. Therefore, the postulation of the existence of the world during the period of dissolution (pralaya) contradicts the non-perception accepted by all the world; this is the meaning. || 34 ||
He whose understanding is utterly deluded claims that the effect has become the cause of itself;
by what means, indeed, could that effect arise from such a source?
Together with their respective causes and so forth, which function as auxiliary conditions. || 35 ||

He states that even the second [alternative] is not tenable: "of the effect" (*kāryasya*). In such scriptural passages as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," the existence of both cause and effect is not perceived as two distinct realities. This is because it would contradict the remainder of the sentence, "One only, without a second. In this regard, let this be considered: is it the case that the effect itself is Being, and that the very existence of that effect constitutes its causality?

Does the Śruti mean that the "existent" (sat) has been superimposed upon the cause as it proceeds [into the effect], or that the cause itself—that very existence—is superimposed upon the effect? Or else, that only the existent is real, and the existence of both cause and effect is merely superimposed? In this regard, if the understanding of that Sāṃkhya follows the first alternative, then his cognition is deluded; it is an error.

Indeed, [this view] contradicts such scriptural passages as "The modification is a mere verbal handle, a name," which teach that the effect is unreal; furthermore, because it would entail the unreality of the cause, it subverts one's own established doctrine. With this intention, he asks: "By whom indeed? regarding the causes.
If the qualities themselves were unreal, by what causes could that effect consisting of Mahat and the rest arise or be produced?

The meaning is that in the absence of a cause, it is impossible for an effect to arise. For this very reason, the second alternative is also not tenable; because if the effect does not exist, it is impossible to define the causality of various things which is constituted by that effect. Therefore, by process of elimination, the third alternative remains.
He states that this alone is intended by the Śruti and is logically consistent, and should therefore be accepted, in the subsequent verse beginning with "tasmāt" (therefore).
Having utterly cast aside the notion of cause and effect imagined by those of dull intellect,
that very reality— without beginning or middle— is the truth.
Know that this very world exists in this manner. || 36 ||

Therefore, since the reality of a distinction between cause and effect is not sanctioned by the Śruti, that relationship of cause and effect or of material cause and its product imagined by the dull-witted Sāṃkhyas and others— along with their respective auxiliary forms such as causes and so forth, and their various distinctions of instrumental and purposive factors— is far removed [from truth].

The meaning is: having set aside and rejected what is false, understand that only that which remains—the reality consisting of pure existence (sanmātra), which is without beginning, middle, or end—is established as the world, like a serpent and its coils; it is nothing else. || 36 ||

Thus ends the first canto, titled "The Refutation of the Produced and the Producer," in the section on Stability within the Means to Liberation spoken by the Divine Messenger, in the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, which belongs to the *Ārṣa* (sage-authored) tradition. || 1 ||
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Refutation of the Produced and the Producer," in the *Sthitiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The Second Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Now, O best among those who know what is to be known, I shall speak regarding this acceptance.
In the stainless, great sky of consciousness, which transcends all divisions of time.
Having refuted the existence of the world through reasoning by means of its diverse essential natures, that which remains here is described: the state of pure Being, whose self is perfect bliss. (1)

The remainder of the sense is: "I shall state the defects [that follow] from the assumption that this world exists as a separate reality during its dissolution. Now, one might object: "If the world does not exist, then creation itself cannot be established; for the act of origination is accomplished by an agent, and it cannot be established when no agent exists.
Furthermore, there is no agent other than that which is being produced; Brahman alone, by virtue of its existence, is that agent."
If that [Brahman] alone were to arise, the world would not; nor can that which is immutable (kūṭastha) be joined with modifications such as arising and so forth.

Therefore, in order to establish its arising, one must admit the existence of the world even during dissolution. Having thus restated this objection, he refutes it with the verse beginning "samasta... (verse 1).
If the primordial sprout of the world exists therein, then tell me: by what auxiliary causes does it arise? (2)
The postulation of the existence of a creator would be tenable only if the act of origination were established by the creator alone;

for that act, like the creator himself, requires other causal factors—such as instruments, auxiliaries, and loci—as its concomitants for its own establishment. In their absence, the world cannot come into being, even if it is postulated as existing.

With the intention that [the Lord] is capable [of this], he says: "The beginning of the world," etc. The word "beginning" (ādi) is intended to signify the manifold diversity (vaicitrya-prapañca). The particle "iva" (as if), however, is for the purpose of highlighting the utter impossibility [of such a feat by anyone else]. || 2 ||
In the absence of auxiliary causes, however, the emergence of a sprout from that [seed] has never been seen here by anyone, just like the daughter of a barren woman. (3)
If, in the absence of auxiliary causes, the primary cause alone has arisen, my friend, it remains established in its own intrinsic nature. (4)

Therefore, just like a snake [projected] upon a rope, if you accept that [the world] has arisen—that is, become manifest—even in the absence of auxiliary causes, then it is simply the root cause itself that has assumed the state of the world through the nature of delusion;
in reality, there is no creation of a world. Thus, the conceptualization of its existence during dissolution is useless. This is the meaning. || 4 ||
At the beginning of creation, Brahman itself remains within itself in the form of creation;
as it exists without form, where is there any sequence of produced and producer?
He states that very point clearly: "At the beginning of creation," etc. (verse 5).

Now, if the earth and others, or some other factors, assist here [in the production of cognition], that would constitute their status as auxiliary causes (sahakārikāraṇa); and the refutation of that has already been stated previously.

One might object: "Since it is admitted that all the constituents of the world exist during the dissolution (pralaya), there can be no scarcity of auxiliary causes, because the earth and other elements contained therein are capable of assisting one another. Anticipating this doubt, the author refutes it with the word "atha" (now). That [dissolution] must first be described as being preceded by the production of the earth and other elements; for indeed—
That which is itself unproduced cannot serve as a cooperative cause for the production of another.

Thus, the meaning is that there is the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) here: the establishment of cooperation depends on the establishment of production, and the establishment of production depends on the establishment of cooperation.
Therefore, the world remains quiescent within its locus along with its cooperative causes.
The statement that [the mind] "spreads forth from the consciousness" belongs to the ignorant, not to the wise.

And thus he concludes that the conceptualizations of the Sāṃkhya and other schools are merely the fabrications of the ignorant, with the words "Therefore": "In the state [of equilibrium], together with its primal nature, [the world] is quiescent, hidden at the time of dissolution. (7)
Therefore, O Rāma, the world never was, does not exist, and will not be;
it is only the space of consciousness that shines forth rapidly in this manner within itself.
Having refuted the opposing views, he shows his own established doctrine as the remainder: "Therefore," etc. (8).
O Rāma, when there exists only absolute non-existence of this world, then all this is Brahman; it is not otherwise.

With the intention that even such scriptural passages as "Brahman alone is this immortal [reality] in front" have their purport in this very [point]—namely, that there is no contradiction due to grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya)—he says: "absolute non-existence.
This is the well-known purport of the scriptures. || 9 ||
That which subsides through prior non-existence, destruction, or mutual non-existence does not truly subside in the mind; yet it appears as if it has subsided. (10)

And thus, prior to the sublation by scriptural testimony (*śruti*), when a jar, cloth, or other object belonging to the world of phenomena (*jāgata*) is pacified through the stroke of a mallet or similar means— whether by way of absolute destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*), transformation into another substance, or mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*)— and it is apprehended as having the nature of non-existence,
being grasped in the form "this is not now" or "this does not exist," that which [you claim] undergoes such pacification as a form of non-existence is not [the case].
It does not indeed cease; rather, this "subsidence" (upaśama) is merely the cessation of its visibility to the eyes and other senses through concealment.

For the meaning is that it does not cease at all within the mind in the form of a latent impression (vāsanā). This same principle should also be applied to antecedent non-existence (prāgabhāva) and absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva), since [the object] exists by its own being or by the being of Brahman.

Because it is impossible for a jar or the like to be non-existent anywhere without its sublation, and because its non-perception in such places as a lump of clay or the ground can be accounted for even by its concealment. || 10 ||
Since its cessation occurs only through the absolute non-existence of entities,
and it does not cease at all while the mind exists as a reality, where indeed can the state of being an object of perception ever cease?

If the visible world were to subside along with its causal seeds—such as desires, actions, and latent impressions (vāsanās)—then there would indeed be the absolute non-existence and total eradication of this visible world. However, as long as the mind exists, desires and other such states are difficult to restrain, and thus the world does not subside at all. Therefore, where can the state of being visible exist without knowledge?
It subsides; the meaning is that its pacification is indeed difficult to attain. || 11 ||
Therefore, the absolute non-existence of the world as it is perceived is the only way;
apart from this, there is no other method whatsoever for the total destruction of suffering.

For this very reason, he states that there is no means other than the destruction of the mind along with its root—which results in the sublation [of ignorance] taught in the Śruti—to attain liberation, which consists in the total cessation of the misfortune of all that is seen: "absolute non-existence" (atyantābhāva), etc. Here, the logical proof (*yukti*) is precisely the sublation (*bādha*) through the perception of the underlying substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*). Apart from this proof—
This world appears as a manifestation of the consciousness-space (cidākāśa); that which exists is simply "this is he," "this is I," or "this is not I," like a variegated tale in the world. (13)

When, by virtue of the direct realization of the reality of the world, there arises the awakening of the space of consciousness (cidākāśa)— using the genitive case as in the expression "the head of Rāhu"— and when the established, perfected knowledge arises that the space of consciousness, whose sole essence is awakening, does not possess even an atom of insentient form, then this body, bearing names such as Devadatta, is that [very same thing].

The worldly convention of common folk— that "I," who am recognized as being born from specific parents, am indeed this [self], whereas "this" other body, wall, and so forth, are not "I"— appears in various ways, just like a painted story;
for although, in the ultimate sense, every painting drawn on a wall is nothing but the wall itself.
The meaning is as follows: on the wall of a painted palace, one thinks "this is a wall," whereas regarding the painted men, elephants, and so forth, one thinks "this is not a wall";
it is just like that. || 13 ||
This is the mountain range and so forth, this is the earth and so forth, as well as this year and so forth;
this is the kalpa, this is the moment, and these are death and birth. (14)
The "variegated discourse" (citrakathā) elaborates upon this very principle even regarding the earth and other elements, beginning with the words "this," and so forth. || 14 ||
This is the agitation at the end of a kalpa; this is the great dissolution at the end of a kalpa.
This is the commencement of creation; this is the sequence of the manifested and the unmanifested.

This process of becoming—the sequence of creation—of the elements to be produced, such as space and the rest, which is currently being observed and is well-known from the Śrutis and Purāṇas, is [the subject]. || 15 ||
These marks of the kalpas, these millions of cosmic eggs, these that have passed away and these that have come again—[all these are encompassed by you]. || 16 ||
*Lakṣmāṇi* means characteristics or marks; *parigatāḥ* means passed by or transcended; *sargāḥ* means creations or emanations. || 16 ||
These networks of cognitive faculties, these divisions of space and time, are the unobstructed and infinite supreme ether of the Great Consciousness. 17.

The networks of abodes (dhiṣṇya-jālāni) are divided fourteenfold according to the distinctions of the stations of gods, humans, and others; they are the conceptualizations (kalpanāḥ) of the divisions of places (deśānām), namely the seven continents (saptadvīpānām), and of times (kālānām), namely the Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and so forth. || 17 ||
It shines by itself as peaceful, remaining just as it was before;
these are but a thousandth part of the rays of the great consciousness.

Thus, by the logic of the analogy of a painted scene, it is meant that the Great Consciousness—the supreme space itself—shines and vibrates within its own self, and nothing else. If one asks, "Is the radiance of the Great Consciousness only this much? he says:
"The lights are limited; likewise, they are limited within the millions of universes projected by the mind."

These are indeed manifestations of consciousness. The meaning is that just as the differentiation of atoms, their movement, and so forth are perceived through the solar light diffused across the sky, so too it is within the great consciousness, the supreme ether.
18. That internal wonder which is spontaneously vomited forth by consciousness—
The manifestation of that creation appears in this form, yet it possesses no supporting wall.
And so, imagining that consciousness (cit), afflicted by the limitation of the mind, as it were vomits out the world inherent within itself, he says:
"Itself," etc. (Verse 19).
They do not arise nor do they perish; they do not come nor do they go, remaining as immovable as the carvings upon great rocks. (20)
He states with the verse beginning "They do not arise," etc., that distinct objects do not exist, being like lines perceived within a crystal slab due to a defect in the eyesight. || 20 ||
These creations flash forth from the Self within the stainless Self,
like portions of space within space— formless within the formless.
"Like in the sky," and so forth, are the examples for the absence of separate existence. || 21 ||
Like the fluidity of water, like the movements in a constant wind, like the whirlpools of the ocean, or like the qualities inherent in those who possess them. (22)

This alone exists as a single mass of consciousness, thus situated—endless, peaceful, and pervasive, including within itself arising, setting, and beginning. (Note: *manārambham* is an alternative reading for *anārambham*.)
From its beginning at sunrise until its end at sunset, this world is thus, according to the aforementioned analogy, the peaceful Brahman alone, expanded and pervasive. || 23 ||
"In the absence of causes such as auxiliary factors, the world is empty;
yet it is said that the Self-Existent One (Svayambhū) is born [from it]—this is indeed the prattle of a madman. (24)

Thus, he concludes that the Sāṃkhya hypothesis is like the behavior of a madman—since production and so forth are not established even when an agent exists if there is an absence of auxiliary causes—with the words "sahakārī" (auxiliary cause). "Svayaṃbhūḥ" means that which exists or comes into being by itself;
the meaning is: even an entity that is admitted to have an independent existence prior to its production. [This is] from the perspective of emptiness (*śūnyataḥ*).

The meaning is that [the entity] arises from a primary cause that is like a void kalpa. As for the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "and it arises," its purpose is to aggregate another fault: if existence, which occurs subsequent to being produced, were already admitted beforehand, then the conceptualization of production would also be useless. || 24 ||
With all stains of the parts of objective phenomena completely stilled, with the bed of every last conceptual construction cast away,
he has for a long time dispelled the long sleep.
Fearless of existence, the ornament of the earth, he is fully awakened. || 25 ||

Because they are the cause for seeing all objects in a dream, conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) are like a bed. Ignorance (*avidyā*), which is a long sleep, is the cause even for the construction of that [bed]; if it is dispelled by the awakening to one's true nature, then there is fearlessness, due to the sublation of the causes of fear such as birth and death arising from the construction of dream-tigers and the like.

May you become one such as he by whom the assembly ground of the knowers of Brahman was adorned and embellished, just as the floor of his own assembly hall was when the king rose from his couch—this is both the instruction and the blessing. 25.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Presentation of the Seed of Stability," in the section on Stability within the Means to Liberation, in the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, belonging to the *Ārṣa* tradition.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Presentation of the Seed of Stability," in the Sthitiprakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The Third Chapter.
Śrī Rāma said: At the beginning of creation at the end of the great kalpa, he was the first Prajāpati.
I believe that the self is born from memory; therefore, the world itself consists of nothing but memory.
Having established the nature of illusory manifestation (vivarta), the process of negation (apavāda) is here demonstrated;
for while from the perspective of enlightenment the world is said to be non-existent, from the perspective of ignorance its infinity is proclaimed. || 1 ||

Granted that in the production of external objects such as jars, there is a dependence on auxiliary causes distinct from the agent of production; however, you have stated that the world is born from the volition of the mind of Hiraṇyagarbha and is like his memory and a kingdom of the imagination, and no dependence on auxiliary causes is observed in that case. Thus, during the dissolution, [the world] remains latent within Prakṛti, its own existence having become concealed.

"Prajāpati himself, being of the nature of mind, is born as the very self of memory; and within him, the world, which is essentially real, is born as the very self of memory through the nature of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*). If this is so, what contradiction is there? With this hidden intention, Rāma asks: "At the end of the great kalpa... (verse 1).
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O scion of Raghu, at the beginning of creation following the great dissolution, this very first Prajāpati exists initially as the self consisting of memory alone.
"Let it be so; nevertheless, the existence [of the world] at the time of dissolution is not established.

For even at its own time, the existence of objects such as those in dreams, fantasies, and memories is not established, and thus the postulation of existence at the time of dissolution cannot be proven by that means.
With this hidden intention, the Teacher provides a resolution by way of a formal admission:
Regarding the term "mahāpralaya" (the great dissolution): || 2 ||
Therefore, this world, which consists of the memory of that [Brahman] whose nature is volition,
shines forth in this way as a city of volition existing from before the time of Prajāpati.
The meaning is that this world was established as nothing other than the primordial city of Prajāpati’s initial volition.
At the beginning of creation, memory is simply not possible for the Supreme Self;
since there is no prior birth, how or where could it exist, like a great tree in the sky?
"In that case, let the world not be real as an object distinct from the transformations of the mind; however, it is certainly real as a transformation of the mind itself.

Just as a painted horse is unreal as a modification of flesh, yet real as a modification of pigment and material, so it is with this"—having perceived this doubt of Rāma through his signs, [the Teacher] said:
In that regard, first of all, the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) postulated by others is not capable of being the basis for memory,
because it is insentient, like clay and other such things. Nor can it be the *puruṣas* (souls),
because according to those [opponents], they are admitted to be unattached, indifferent, and changeless.

Since difference cannot be established without accepting properties that mutually distinguish entities, memory is all the more impossible in the case of non-difference from the Supreme Self; for there is no birth [of the Self], and other modifications are preceded by that [birth],
and because its mind is denied by such scriptural passages as "He is indeed without breath, without mind, pure," memory cannot occur through that medium.
Since the status of being a rememberer is unestablished for him, his memory is like a tree in the sky. || 4 ||
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahman, why is it that memory of the past does not exist at the beginning of creation?
How is it that previous memory is destroyed by the delusions of the great dissolution?

An objection is raised with the following intention: "Is it not the case that just as there is daily deep sleep (*suṣupti*), so too is there dissolution (*pralaya*); and since the mind that was merged therein manifests at the beginning of creation just as it does at the beginning of waking, what contradiction is there in the Prajāpati—so delimited by that [mind]—or someone else, being the rememberer?
With this in mind, Rāma raises the doubt: "It is not possible," namely, prior memory.
It is the residual impression from a previous eon. || 5 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Those wise ones, Brahmā and all the others, who in former times attained liberation at the time of the great dissolution, have certainly reached the state of Brahman.
Revealing his underlying intention (*abhisaṃdhi*), Vasiṣṭha avoids the objection with the words beginning "those [who exist] at the great dissolution" (*ye mahāpralaye*).

The sense is this: does your doubt arise from the view that the single living being Hiraṇyagarbha alone wanders through transmigratory existence, having mentally imagined the distinctions of various individual souls, bodies, and so forth; or rather, [from the view that there are] multiple individual souls?

Alternatively, according to the view that [individuals] conceive of a portion of the manifold world as suitable for their own respective enjoyments, and likewise conceive of Hiraṇyagarbha as the creator of all in accordance with their own respective intellects; in that case, regarding the second [view], [the text says]:
"At the beginning of creation at the end of a great aeon (mahākalpa), there was first Prajāpati," and so forth.
Because it contradicts the commencement of your own doubt and because it is inconsistent with the scriptural accounts of creation,

the first alternative remains. In that case, since at the time of the great dissolution (mahāpralaya) the living beings and the world of the previous kalpa would have been liberated through the liberation of Hiraṇyagarbha alone, leaving no other living being remaining, there would be no one at all to remember [the past].
"This is not the proof of creation. The meaning of the words is clear. || 6 ||
"O observer of noble vows, tell me then: who was the creator of memory in the past?
For memory has become rootless, since the rememberer has attained liberation."
Therefore, in the absence of a rememberer, how or why could a Smṛti arise?
For indeed, in every great aeon (mahākalpa), all beings necessarily attain liberation alone.

Whether regarding what has not been experienced or what has been experienced, that memory which arises within the self-luminous sky of consciousness is the mature world-appearance; it exists as the very radiance of consciousness.

In this way, even the creations belonging to each preceding kalpa do not establish themselves as being of the nature of memory; therefore, that which you suspected to be "memory"—the world's origin and the world's persistence—is actually the mature radiance of the consciousness of Brahman, which exists eternally as "Being.
This is the intended meaning of the Śrutis, which maintain the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (satkāryavāda). || 9 ||
This very radiance of consciousness, shining without beginning or end, appears as that which is known as "this world" and as the "Self-existent One" (Svayambhū). || 10 ||
He states clearly the very meaning already expressed: "It appears," etc. || 10 ||
That manifestation of Brahman which is established from beginningless time and is its own innate nature— that is the subtle body (ātivāhika-deha) of Virāj, having the form of the universe.

The meaning is that Virāj—the subtle, transportive (ātivāhika) body which serves as the material cause for the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa)—is indeed the Supreme Self (paramātman). Thus, the intended sense is that Brahman alone appears in the form of the universe through the process of superimposing the states of the subtle and the gross. || 11 ||
Within the supreme atom, this triple world— complete with forests, clouds, and the sky,
and endowed with the sequences of space, time, action, substance, day, and night— shines forth.

Furthermore, because the world lacks a fixed nature, it does not exist in the form of the world, but rather only in the form of Brahman; with this intention, he establishes its lack of fixed nature by means of the passage beginning with "in the atom" (paramāṇau) and so forth. || 12 ||
The atom is expanded; yet it remains exactly as it was.
Again, that same mountain range shines forth, producing a brilliant splendor.

Between that preceding atom and [the next], another extended atom exists, and it is just like that—exactly similar to the preceding atom; furthermore, there too, such a series appears as a succession of clouds, sky, and mountain ranges—thus is the connection with what follows. 13.
Even there, the visible object appears as a continuous succession of such very forms; this nature of light, my dear, is not real. (14)
He states what has resulted from that which was established: "This," etc. (verse 14).
Thus, there is no end anywhere for either right view or wrong view;
yet, O sinless one, for this [view], the Awakened has arisen, and not the unawakened.

And so, just as the vision of pure existence (*sanmātra-dṛṣṭi*) is itself infinite for one who knows reality (*tattvajña*), even so the vision of the unreal, false world (*asad-anṛta-jagad-dṛṣṭi*) is also infinite in number for the ignorant person (*ajña*). Thus he says: "Iti" (thus).
"Abhyuditam" means having attained supreme exaltation. "Buddham" means for one who knows reality; "na ābuddham" means not for one who does not know it.
Or [it is taught] with respect to one who, because of that [reason], was not awakened—that is, ignorant. || 15 ||
For one who has awakened to the Buddha, this is indeed the absolute Brahman—peaceful and immutable;
for one who has not awakened, it appears as this radiant world-system through the power of cognition.
He clarifies that very point by showing it through the words "dependent on the Buddha," and so forth. || 16 ||
Just as this radiant universe shines forth, expanded within the cosmic egg,
so too do thousands of millions of other universes shine within every single atom.
Just as there is a figurine within a pillar, and a figurine within its own limbs,
and yet another figurine within that figurine’s limbs, so too is the figurine of the three worlds.
Just as atoms on a mountain are neither identical nor countable, so too are the atoms of the three worlds within the vast Mount Meru, which is Brahman. (19)
The light particles of the sun and other luminaries can be counted, yet the atoms of the three worlds arise within the sun of consciousness. (20)
The words "if it were possible" are to be supplied as the ellipsis; or, they should be connected with the end of the preceding verse. || 20 ||
Just as atoms move within the rays of the sun, in water, and in dust,
so do the atoms of the three worlds move within the space of consciousness.
They carry, they flow; that is to say, they whirl. || 21 ||
Just as this elemental space consists of the mere experience of emptiness,
so too does this space of consciousness consist of the mere experience of creation.

If it is asked, "How can that which is free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*) and immutable (*kūṭastha*) appear in the form of a world characterized by modification? [the author] replies with the word "śūnya": just as space, though formless and non-empty, appears as empty and possessing a form contrary to its own nature, so it is here. "Empty" (*śūnya*) means the absence of obscuration; and "non-existent" (*asat*) refers to blueness.
The meaning is that it consists merely of that experience and is experienced as such, but it does not consist of the actual, full, formless experience. || 22 ||
When "creation" (sarga) is understood as the meaning of the word *sarga*, it leads one downward;
when it is understood as the meaning of the word *brahman*, it becomes a source of supreme well-being.

"He leads downward"—this is because of such scriptural passages as, "He makes a difference within himself; then fear comes to him," and so forth. "It becomes superior"—the meaning is that this is because of such scriptural passages as, "The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow," and so forth. || 23 ||
The conscious self, the ruler, the seed of the universe, is Brahman alone— sufficient unto itself as the mere space of consciousness;
one should know that whatever is born from it is that very same thing.
The object of knowledge is merely the full awakening of one's own internal consciousness. || 24 ||
Is it not the case that even knowing Brahman as something external leads to the highest good? No, he says: "The cognizing self.

That which is the cognizing self—the inner self known as the individual soul (jīva)—and that which is the seed of the universe, its cause, and its ruler, the Lord (Īśvara): through the vision of ultimate reality, when these are purified, they are fully one's own, the single essence of the inner self.

Brahman alone is the mere space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*). For it is heard in scripture that both the external and internal dualities of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) have arisen from Brahman itself. And since whatever is born from something is non-different from that very thing—as understood from such passages as "Its non-difference [from its cause] is known from the word 'origin' and so forth"—therefore, all that is to be known is [Brahman].
Within one's own internal consciousness, there is only pure awakening; the meaning is that it is pure consciousness alone. || 24 ||

Thus ends the third canto, titled "Description of the Infinity of the World," in the Section on Stability (*sthitiprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, belonging to the Holy Sage (*ārṣa*). 3.
Thus ends the third canto, titled "The Description of the Infinity of the World," in the Sthitiprakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The Fourth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
By means of the bridge that restrains the host of the senses, the ocean of worldly existence [is crossed].
One is not crossed over by any other means here than by action (karman). || 1 ||
In this world, the mind together with the senses is said to be the root of the existence of the universe;
upon its destruction, the world becomes empty, because the non-existence of the visible is perceived.
The battle for the collection of the senses is won by means of that bridge characterized by such [virtues]. || 1 ||
Through the study of the scriptures, the company of the virtuous, and practice, one who possesses discernment and has conquered the senses realizes the absolute non-existence of this visible world.

And since seclusion is the means for the conquest of the senses, and devotion solely to virtuous people and authentic scriptures is the means for that [seclusion], he says "scriptures" with this intention: || 2 ||
O best of embodied beings, all this has been told to you regarding the nature of the successions of the ocean of worldly existence— how they come forth and how they pass away.
In order to state the connection with the subject at hand regarding the mastery of the senses that has been enjoined, he recalls what was said previously with the words "etad" (this).

O best (*vara*) among those possessing form (*rūpin*), that is, the most excellent (*śreṣṭha*). They depart (*prayānti*), meaning they go away. Even if the reading is "na yānti" (they do not go), the meaning remains the same. || 3 ||
What need is there for much speaking here? The sprout of the tree of mental action—when that is severed, the world-tree, whose body is karma, becomes severed.

The tree of the world—the tree of saṃsāra—will be cut down, it being one whose body (tanuḥ) consists of the very actions, both enjoined and prohibited, that have transformed into the forms of the enjoyer, the objects of enjoyment, and the act of enjoying. || 4 ||
O Rāma, this entire world is the mind; when that [mind] is treated internally, the entire disease of the web of the world is indeed cured. (5)
The world-web is the characteristic of the malady, which is disease. || 5 ||
Thus, this world arises, agitated by the mind's own imaginings;
apart from the mind, where indeed is a body ever seen? (6)
Now, one might object: "Even if the mind has been treated, pleasure and pain would still remain dependent upon the body. To this he says: "That very [mind]...
It is the mind's very conceiving of itself in the form of the body that arises as the body—restless and capable of action, like a dream. (6)
The demon of the mind is pacified only by the absolute non-existence of the visible world, and not by any other cause, even in hundreds of eons. (7) [The reading "kalpaśatairati" is noted.]
In that case, what is the medicine for the treatment of the mind? To this he says: "dṛśya... (the visible).
It is the absolute non-existence of the visible; [this is] the sublation (bādha). Without that—here the third case ending is Vedic (chāndasī). || 7 ||
And this is indeed possible for the treatment of the mental disease;
it is the supreme and most excellent medicine, consisting of the absolute non-existence of the perceptible world. (8)

[Objection: "Is it not the case that mental illness is internal, whereas the visible world is external? Therefore, since external objects are absolutely non-existent, how can there be a possibility of treating the internal mind? To this, he says:
"This... This supreme medicine, consisting of the absolute non-existence of this visible world, [serves] for the treatment of the disease of the mind.
The ellipsis is "the means certainly exists. In the word *cikitsite*, the suffix *kta* is used in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāve*). || 8 ||
The mind takes on delusion; the mind dies and is born.
Through the clarity of its own contemplation, it is bound and again released.

How is this possible? He says: "The mind. For neither the internality of the mind nor the externality of objects is real; rather, it is the mind alone that assumes delusion—that is, error—through such conceptualizations as duality.
The meaning is that it also conceives of birth, death, bondage, liberation, and so forth. || 9 ||
This entire world vibrates within the mind when it is swooned by conceptualization;
it is just like the city of the Gandharvas appearing in the vast emptiness of the sky.

If it is asked how this is known, he says "it is known through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka)," namely: "It flashes forth" when [the mind] is swooning through reflection and has risen up. || 10 ||
This entire expansive universe exists and vibrates within the mind; it is situated therein like fragrance is in a cluster of flowers, as if it were something other than that [mind]. (11)

And likewise, since reflection (*vimarśa*) is merely a property of the mind of the world, it cannot persist when its substratum (*dharmin*) ceases to exist; with this intention, he provides examples starting with "in the mind" (*manasi*).
The final particle *iva* is used to indicate that the distinction between properties and their substrata is not ultimately real. || 11 ||
Just as oil is in a sesame seed, or as a quality is in that which possesses qualities,
or as a property is in its substratum, so too is this world in the mind.
Just as a network of rays is in the sun, just as light is in fire,
and just as heat is in the blazing flame, so too is this world in the mind.
In Citrabhānu, that is, in Agni. || 13 ||
Just as coolness exists in frost, as emptiness exists in the sky,
and as flickering exists in the wind, so does this world exist within the mind.
The mind is the entire world, and the world is likewise the mind;
for these two are indeed always inseparable from one another. When both are constantly established within the mind, [the world arises].
The world has been destroyed, but the mind within the world has not been destroyed. || 15 ||

Although there is no difference between the mind and the world insofar as they stand in the relationship of subject and object (*dharmī-dharma-bhāva*), the destruction of the world occurs only through the destruction of the mind, which is the subject, and not conversely;
for it is observed to be so in the world. With this intention, he concludes with the verse beginning "The mind":
"Inseparable" means non-distinct (*avinābhūta*). When the one is destroyed, the other is destroyed. || 15 ||
Thus ends the fourth canto, titled "The Manifestation of the Sprout of Stability," in the Section on Stability (*sthitiprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by the sage Vālmīki. 4.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Calculation of the Sprout of Existence," in the section on "Existence" within the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa-Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The Fifth Chapter.
Śrī Rāma said:
"O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, best among those who understand what precedes and follows!"
How indeed does this vast cycle of existence reside within the mind? || 1 ||

While Bhṛgu was established here in meditative absorption on the mountain where Śukra was sporting, it is said that through delusion at the sight of an Apsaras, he became completely absorbed in her. || 1 ||

The meaning is: "Tell me by means of what kind of example this vast saṃsāra, which manifests externally, appears as if it were manifesting within the mind—how it is directly perceived through the vision of examples and the presentation of illustrations. || 1 ||
O sinless one, tell me clearly through an illustrative example how this vast saṃsāra manifests as it vibrates within the mind.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Just as the worlds of the sons of Indu, though bodiless,
remained firmly established in their minds, so too does this [universe] abide.
He states that the worlds beginning with those of Indra have already been mentioned here as examples, saying "just as" (yathā). || 3 ||
Just as King Lavaṇa, whose appearance was confounded by sorcery, attained the state of a Caṇḍāla, so too has this [state] remained fixed in my mind. || 4 ||
Of one whose appearance is agitated and whose mind is distracted. || 4 ||
For a long time, due to Bhārgava’s desire to enjoy the pleasures of heaven,
he attained the status of a lord over worldly enjoyments as well as the condition of a transmigrating being.
He introduces the story of Bhārgava here as an illustrative example with the words "of Bhārgava.

"Sovereignty over enjoyments" means the desire for the pleasures of apsarases. "Worldliness" (*saṃsāritva*) consists in going to heaven and other realms for that purpose, as well as possessing another birth. Here, the root *nāth* is used in the sense of a request. || 5 ||
"And just as [the reading is] 'sovereignty over enjoyments' (bhogeśvaratvam), so too has this remained in my mind.
Śrī Rāma said:
"O Blessed One, [this was done] by the son of Bhṛgu out of a desire to experience the enjoyments of heaven. (6)
Sovereignty over enjoyments means being an enjoyer of apsarases in heaven. The question is clear. || 6 ||
"How did the lordship over enjoyments and the state of being a transmigrating being come to be?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
"Listen, O Rāma, to an ancient account, a dialogue between Bhṛgu and Kāla. (7)
On the peak of Mount Mandara, thick with the branches of *tāla* trees;
formerly, on the peak of Mount Mandara, which was dense with blossoms.
The connection with the preceding [verse] is: "Listen to the dialogue between Bhṛgu and Kāla, which took place on a mountain ridge.
He provides an introductory statement for what has been mentioned, beginning with the words "In the city," etc. (Verse 8).
The venerable Bhṛgu performed severe penance in a certain place;
his radiant and highly intelligent young son attended upon him.
Śukra, possessing the luster of the full moon and shining like the light itself, remained absorbed in meditative concentration in that excellent forest, O Bhṛgu. || 10 ||
"Sakala" means complete. In the reading "bhāskara," it means that which shines (*prakāśate*), thus "prakāśa"; he is like the radiant sun (*sphuran bhāskara*).
Like something carved at all times from the surface of a forest stone,
Śukra remained [unmoving] upon beds of flowers and in courtyards of silver.

The phrase "established at all times" connects with what precedes. The simile of being "as if carved from the very essence of forest stone slabs by the strokes of a chisel" is a poetic conceit (*utprekṣā*) intended to express his immobility. [He dwells] in courtyards of refined gold and upon platforms of silver and gold. (11)
On the unrestrained swings of Mount Mandara, the child Śukra, through his playful sport, fell into the midst of the waves of knowledge and ignorance and encountered great calamity.

The vision of knowledge (*vidyādṛk*) is the perception of the ultimate reality of the Self; the vision of ignorance (*avidyādṛk*) is the perception of the reality of the world as established by common folk and others. Between these two [is the state]. 12.
Then, like Triśaṅku, he remained distressed within his own body;
this occurred once while his father was established in the state of nirvikalpa-samādhi.
Between the two worlds, heaven and earth—within the celestial realm fashioned by Viśvāmitra—he lived like the royal sage Triśaṅku;
for this very reason, he was agitated by passion and other such afflictions. || 13 ||
He remained undisturbed in solitude like a king who has conquered his enemies;
there he beheld an Apsaras traveling along the path of the sky.
"Undistracted" means having a mind that is not diverted toward other sense objects. || 14 ||
Like Janārdana [holding] Lakṣmī churned from the midst of the milk ocean,
she was encircled by a garland of Mandāra flowers, her tresses fluttering in the gentle breeze.
Stirred from the midst of the Ocean of Milk and produced by churning; both adjectives are used because it is well known that both Lakṣmī and the Apsarases were born from the Ocean of Milk.
Her gait was resonant with the tinkling of her necklace, she perfumed the breezes of the sky, she was like a creeper upon the tree of beauty, and her eyes were rolling with intoxication. (16)

By her, the winds of the sky were made fragrant; the mention of "the sky" [is used] even when the wind has ceased, for the purpose of indicating that the region of the sky remained fragrant for a long time. 16.
Beholding his beloved, whose very location had been rendered immortal by the radiance of the moon of his body, his mind became agitated with surging longing.
By those splendors—by those rays—the rising of the moon, which is characterized by its body, [is indicated]. || 17 ||
Just as the ocean is agitated upon seeing the stainless, full moon,
she too, beholding the face of Śukra, became utterly overwhelmed.
It has the appearance of the body of the ocean, shimmering and tremulous. || 18 ||
Having awakened his mind— which had been frustrated regarding objects of desire— to that [state], Uśanas,
by means of his own self whose other functions had dissolved away, [proceeded].
And that [place] indeed became filled with brides. || 19 ||
And Uśanas, having been struck by the arrows of the Mind-born (Kāma) immediately after seeing that Apsaras,
lay prostrate; yet, having awakened his mind— whose intention was to become deluded by sense objects— as much as possible through discernment,
and having restrained his external activities such as pursuing the beloved of his body, he attained one-pointedness of mind.
Because his other mental functions had dissolved within and he was absorbed in a state of one-pointed concentration, he became as if composed entirely of the bride;
the particle *ha* is used to indicate the well-known authority of such scriptural, traditional, and experiential evidence as the statement, "Whatever the mind is set upon, that it becomes. (19)

Thus ends the fifth canto, titled "The Stumbling of Bhārgava," within the *Bhārgavopākhyāna* (The Narrative of Bhārgava) in the *Sthitiprakaraṇa* (The Section on Stability), among the means to liberation (*mokṣopāya*) in the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki according to the ancient seers (*ārṣa*). || 5 ||
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Stumbling of Bhārgava," in the *Sthitiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The Sixth Canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, meditating upon her with his mind, he remained right there with his eyes closed.
It is said that Uśanas alone has undertaken this kingdom of the mind.
In this [chapter], the journey of Śukra to heaven by means of his mind is described;
there, due to the honor shown by Śakra, he was seated in his presence. || 1 ||

This refers to the kingdom of the mind (manorājya) that is about to be described. The particle *eva* serves to exclude other possibilities and to emphasize the extent [of the state], reaching even to the forgetting of the body. || 1 ||
For this woman is here in the sky, the abode of the thousand-eyed one;
and I have reached this heaven, which is filled with restless celestial beauties.
The ellipsis is: "This woman, proceeding before me, goes to heaven, the abode of the thousand-eyed Indra. I am following her. (2)
These gods, beautiful with crests of soft mandāraka flowers and possessing bodies that grace the world like flowing molten gold, are yours.
*Kanakaniṣyanda* means molten gold; for that is renowned as being exceedingly radiant. Their bodies were playful and beautiful, like that [gold]. || 3 ||
These are those beloved ones with gazes like blue lotuses that delight the eyes;
they possess charming smiles and playful graces, and their glances are like those of does.
These lovely apsarases, whose eyes are like blue lotuses seen directly before one's eyes through the delight of their glance. || 4 ||
These Maruts, radiant with flowers and appearing like the intoxicated Kaśas, reflect one another’s forms, resembling the universal form (Viśvarūpa).

They are called *kausumodyotāḥ* because they shine or gleam with garlands (*mālya*) fashioned from flowers such as the *pārijāta*; in the reading *kaustubhodyotāḥ*, it means "shining like the Kaustubha gem" (the reading *kaustubhavat uddyotamānāḥ* is correct).

Precisely because they are mutually reflected in one another, Hari possesses the universal form (*viśvarūpa*), that is, he has all forms; the Maruts, the gods, who possess forms resembling his, are intoxicated, joyful, and shine—that is, they gleam—having such a nature. There is no tautology here, for although the gods were described previously, they are now described by way of a different mode. || 5 ||
These are those songs of the hosts of gods, sung in falsetto tones, heard by bees who have turned away from the fragrance of Airāvaṇa’s temples.

On the temples—the two cheeks—of Airāvaṇa, that is, Airāvata, the ichor is visible. Even by the bees who are detached and unattached to its fragrance, [the sounds] were heard, listened to, sung, and uttered with a *kākali*, a sweet yet indistinct sound. || 6 ||
This is that very Mandākinī, where golden lotuses serve as the moving cranes for Brahmā,
and where the Lord of the Gods rests in the gardens upon its banks.
In which [city] there move and wander the swans and cranes belonging to Vairiñca, that is, related to Viriñci (Brahmā), amidst golden lotuses. || 7 ||
These are your world-protectors— Yama, Candra, Indra, Sūrya, Anala, Jala, and Anila— their bodies radiant with scattered flames of blazing fire.
Those by whom the flames of blazing fire were scattered and spread all around with the radiance of their bodies—that is, the splendor of their physical forms. || 8 ||
This is that Airāvaṇa, whose face was scratched by the bristling of his tusks during the course of battle, and who in combat pierced the circle of the lords of the Daityas with his teeth.
In the accounts of battles, during the occurrences of war, his face was as if scratched by weapons—that is, by arms. || 9 ||
These, having moved from their positions on the earth, have attained the state of stars in the sky;
they are celestial beings moving in chariots, with the beautiful luster of molten gold.
Moving and spreading about, their bodily splendors, palaces, and so forth were like the radiance of beautiful gold.
These are those waves of the Ganges water, strewn with Mandāra flowers, by which the deities are covered with spray scattered from their collision with the surface of Mount Meru.
These are the avenues of Indra’s grove, where rows of celestial nymphs dangle on swings, tawny with clusters of full-blown mandāra blossoms.
These are the breezes from the Pārijāta tree, fragrant with the nectar of the kunda and mandāra flowers, resembling a mass of moonbeams. (13)
Their form is pleasant to the touch like a mass of moonbeams, and their configuration is endowed with coolness, gentleness, and other such qualities. || 13 ||
That Nandana grove was filled with throngs of female creepers eager to scatter the pollen of flowers like fine camphor powder.

With flowers, filaments, frost, and drops of cold nectar, they perfume the garments; thus, "paṭavāsa" refers to the fragrant pollen. And with those [pollens], by the clusters of creepers and groups of women who were eager for and intent upon the sport of mutual striking characterized by the movement of the wind, [the place was filled].
It was filled with throngs of women characterized by creepers, or rather, with throngs of women resembling creepers. || 14 ||
These two, Nārada and Tumburu, who delight the celestial maidens with the joy of their lovely songs and possess voices as melodious as the lute, are here. (15)
Nārada and Tumburu are either two specific Gandharvas or two sages. || 15 ||
These two performers of meritorious deeds, adorned with many ornaments, are stationed within celestial chariots soaring through the sky. (16)
These celestial women, their limbs intoxicated by passion and love,
attend upon the Lord of Gods like forest creepers in a grove.
Indra, the lord of the gods. || 17 ||
These are Indra’s stone-cluster flowers, bunches of wish-fulfilling gems, and these are the kalpa-trees, bristling with clusters of ripened fruit. (18)

Their forms are like masses of sapphire, appearing as nets of Indra-stones; or, according to the reading *candrāśma*, they possess flowers resembling clusters of moonstones (*candrakānta*); their clusters of buds are like *cintāmaṇi* gems;
and they are jagged with bunches of ripe fruit, as if possessing protruding teeth.
Shining brightly. || 18 ||
Here, first of all, I salute this Śakra seated upon his throne, as if he were a second creator of the three worlds. (19)
To Brahmā, the creator of the three worlds. || 19 ||
Having reflected thus, the Lord of Śacī, by means of his mind alone,
greeted him there with that [speech], appearing like a second Bhṛgu in the sky.
Then Śukra, having been honored by Śakra, rose up respectfully;
taking him by the hand, he was brought near and seated. || 21 ||
Having been brought near, he was seated. || 21 ||
"O Lord, this heaven shines with Śukra now that you have arrived;
O Śakra, may you dwell here for a long time. Thus he spoke to him.
Then, having sat down there, that descendant of Bhṛgu, with his face radiant,
eclipsed the splendor of the entire stainless moon.
Of the whole, the complete, and the stainless, which is free from the blemish of passion (rajas). || 23 ||
Worshipped by all the hosts of gods and standing at the side of Indra, that son of Bhṛgu attained incomparable satisfaction for a very long time.
He became the cherished darling of the most excellent of kings. || 24 ||
He was the beloved of that best of kings, the supreme lord of men, Indra, cherished like a son or other offspring—meaning he was most dear to him. || 24 ||

Thus ends the sixth canto, titled "The Mental Kingdom of Bhārgava," within the *Bhārgavopākhyāna* (The Narrative of Bhārgava) of the *Sthitiprakaraṇa* (Section on Stability) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa*, the sacred work of the Seer (*ārṣa*). Canto 6.
Thus ends the sixth canto, titled "The Kingdom of Bhārgava’s Mind," in the Sthitiprakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The Seventh Canto.
Thus Śukra, having reached the city of the gods by his own splendor,
forgot his former nature and his previous misfortune, except for his addiction.
Herein, furthermore, the sight of his own beloved in heaven by Śukra, and their reunion through mutual passion, is described. (1)

Thus, in the manner of the kingdom of one's desires as described, [he reached] the city of the gods, the abode of the wise, namely heaven, by means of his own splendor—that is, through the power of his merit—even without the calamity of the suffering of death. || 1 ||
Having rested for a moment by the side of that Lord of Śacī, he,
delighted by heaven, rose up to wander through the celestial realm.

"Completely gladdened and delighted by the supreme bliss of heaven. Regarding the reading *svargābhiparimoditaḥ*, the meaning is that he was encouraged by the gods, who are accustomed to moving about in heaven. || 2 ||
Beholding the celestial splendor longed for by those with restless eyes,
he went to see that multitude of women, just as a crane goes toward a lotus pond.

Having beheld—that is, having reflected upon—the celestial splendor, the beauty of heaven, and his own loveliness, as well as the coveted desirability of women with tremulous eyes, he [approached] the *straiṇa*, the assembly of women. || 3 ||
There, in the midst of his beloved women, Bhṛgu beheld that fawn-eyed woman standing within the forest like a mango creeper.
Bhṛgu, the descendant of Bhṛgu, [beheld] that Apsaras whom he had seen before. || 4 ||
She too, upon seeing that descendant of Bhṛgu, Rāma, became subject to his power;
beholding her, whose form was graced by shimmering and restless charms.
Upon seeing her, even that descendant of Bhṛgu became subject to her power; this is the connection with what follows, or rather, the syntactical link with the subsequent verse. || 5 ||
With his limbs melting away like a moonstone in the moonlight,
he gazed upon that beloved woman as all his own limbs dissolved.
He demonstrates the transitory emotion (saṃcāribhāva) known as perspiration with the words: "with limbs melting away. || 6 ||
Just as the moonstone [draws in] the cool, playful moonlight from the sky,
she too, being gazed upon by him, became entirely devoted to him.
At the end of the night, she was surely called out to like a beloved by a cakravāka bird; having blossomed with passion, they were indeed mutually enamored.

She who throughout the night cried out in lamentation due to separation is that beloved female ruddy goose; at the end of the night, like her being gazed upon by the male ruddy goose in the morning, she has blossomed—her beauty revealed—out of *rasa*, that is, out of an excess of love.
The word "nūnam" (surely) serves to indicate a metaphorical identification (*abheda-utprekṣā*). 8.
The very same splendor that belongs to the sun and the lotus at dawn became theirs;
and because it bestowed their desired objects, that region also came to be known by that name.
Of the region, of the Nandana region. || 9 ||
Having rendered all her limbs powerless, she was surrendered entirely to desire;
the arrows of Smara fell in abundance upon her tender limbs. (10)
