Like lotuses among the leaves of the *palāśa* tree, or like streams from a rain-cloud, she— agitated by passion and crowded with the circles of wandering bees— became manifest.

"Upon the *palāśa* leaves. He shows her transitory emotion (*saṃcāribhāva*) called trembling (*kampa*) with the word "she": she was shaken—that is, made to tremble—by Smara (the God of Love). || 11 ||
She was like a flower-cluster shaken by a gentle breeze, sharing the same nature;
her eyes were like blue lotuses, and her gait was like that of a swan or a crane.
The word *saha* signifies similarity; the meaning is "possessing similar attributes. || 12 ||
Madana agitated her like an elephant agitates a lotus-pond;
then, seeing her in such a state, Śukra attained the object of his desire.
Tamas, like the Destroyer who devours all beings, began to form its resolve;
that region of heaven became overwhelmed with darkness. (14)
At the time of dissolution, during the period of universal destruction, Rudra is the devourer of beings. That region of the Nandana grove is a part of Triviṣṭapa, the heavenly realm. || 14 ||
Just as the world of mortals is [illuminated] from the edge of the Lokāloka mountain by the blinding darkness,
so too was that circle of gloom [dispelled] by him, who was like a sharp-rayed sun to the darkness of shame.

When that circle of darkness, characterized by shame, had reached a state of stability and firm establishment—like the sun, the possessor of sharp rays, dispelling a mass of gloom—in that very region of Nandana, [the following occurred]; this is to be connected with what follows. || 15 ||
When that circle had reached its firm foundation, like a pair of mating birds, and all those beings had departed toward their desired directions; (16)
When her companions among the living beings had departed from that place toward their desired direction... || 16 ||

Then, from that place, at the end of the day, she— whose long and tremulous outer corners of the eyes were like those of birds— departed for the world of mortals with her agony of love fully intensified.
She approached the son of Bhṛgu, like a peahen approaching a rain-cloud, as he sat upon a prepared couch in the middle of a white chamber. (18)
A white chamber, a crystal house, situated in the middle of that.
There Bhārgava entered like Mādhava entering the Ocean of Milk;
she, leaning upon his arms, entered with her face cast down.
And she shone like a lotus clinging to the heart of the divine elephant;
and she spoke these words in a sweet voice, imbued with passion and affection: || 20 ||
Of the divine elephant Airāvaṇa. || 20 ||
Behold his sweet speech, whose syllables are entwined with the playfulness of bliss;
behold his face, like a spotless moon, which has drawn its bow into a circle.
"This Aṅgaka is indeed pursuing me, a weak woman!
O Lord, protect me, a helpless and wretched woman who has sought refuge in you here. (22)
He who possesses limbs is not without limbs; he pursues me, a weak woman, and compels me. Therefore, protect me! 22.
O virtuous one, know that comforting the wretched is a vow of true conduct;
it is practiced only by the foolish who lack the vision of affection, O high-minded one. (23)
Lovers who know the true essence of passion never disregard their affection;
for those who are mutually enamored, love arrives unexpectedly and spontaneously. (24)

"Affections" (praṇayāḥ) mean excesses of love. "Are disregarded" means they are not highly esteemed. "Unexpectedly" (aśaṅkitam) means in such a way as to be free from suspicion—such as the suspicion regarding the transgression of shifting toward another object or the presence of external conditions—and thus it has come about or arisen. || 24 ||
She eclipses even the moon, her beloved outpouring that delights all;
for this sovereignty over the three worlds does not gladden the heart as much as she does.

It surpasses even the celestial nectar that flows as a natural outflow and revives the gods; it excels the life-restoring elixir, the moon, and even a thousand moons—meaning that the affection of one's most beloved exceeds them all. Sovereignty over the three worlds refers to lordship over the triple universe. || 25 ||
Just as there is mutual joy and affection between two people who have first fallen in love, so too,
O giver of honor, have I been comforted by the touch of your feet.
Just as the night-lotus is touched by the moon's rays at night,
so do I live, O handsome one, through the drinking of the nectar of your touch.
Just as the restless female cakora bird longs for the drinking of the moon's nectar, so do you [protect] me, who am clinging to your feet, with your sprout-like hands. (28)
"Embrace me and place me within your own lotus-heart, which is filled with nectar.
Having spoken thus, she whose limbs were as soft as flowers fell upon his chest;
her eyes rolled like those of a bee, like a flower-cluster from a fine tree.

Within the heart-mind situated inside the lotus of the heart, which is filled with nectar and brimming with the nectar of affection and compassion—[therein lies] the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa). || 29 ||
The couple, radiant with amorous playfulness,
entered those forest glades,
which were pale yellow with filaments and stirred by the breeze.
Like two red bees upon lotus plants. || 30 ||

They entered; they entered deeply. The *guṇa* (vowel strengthening) is Vedic. [The flowers] were shaken—set in motion—by a yellowish-brown wind, turbid with the filaments (*kiñjalka*), the stamens (*kesara*), and their pollen.
This is a qualifying attribute common to both the forest regions and the lotus ponds. || 30 ||
Thus ends the seventh canto, titled "The Ninth Reunion," in the Bhārgava-episode of the *Sthiti-prakaraṇa* within the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, a work of the Ṛṣis. 7.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Ninth Meeting," in the *Sthitiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The Eighth Canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus, by means of those dear things long imagined through the play of the mind, [she was delighted].
Through his entreaties, there was a very auspicious meeting for the satisfaction of Bhārgava. || 1 ||

It is proclaimed that after falling here repeatedly at the end of various enjoyments in heaven, one takes many births due to the connection with latent impressions (vāsanā), and [in this state] the nature of an ascetic (tāpasattva) arises.
By means of those things imagined and constructed. || 1 ||
Then, with her who was adorned with garlands of *mandāra* flowers and intoxicated by the nectar of the gods,
he was accompanied by that second [companion], the spotless moon.

"She who wears garlands of *mandāra* flowers on all sides" means she who holds them; thus she is so described. The reading "mandāramālālakayā" is clear. "Vibudhāsava" refers to the nectar (*amṛta*) enjoyed by the gods, or perhaps another type of divine liquor. || 2 ||
He dwelt upon the banks of the celestial river, amidst golden lotus-ponds where intoxicated swans roamed, accompanied by Cāraṇas and Kiṃnaras.
Of the Mandākinī, the river that carries the immortals. || 3 ||
The playful god, together with the deities, drank the elixir flowing from the moon’s crescent while dwelling within the bowers of the *pārijāta* creeper vines.

By the "streams" (*syandaiḥ*) of moon-fragments—that is, by the outpourings of the digits of the moon, meaning those whose bodies are composed of lunar digits—in the bowers that serve as the abodes for clusters of creepers. || 4 ||
For a long time, he sported with groups of eager Vidyādhara maidens upon a swaying, beautiful vine-swing in the Caitraratha garden.
He sported and played upon a beautiful swing fashioned from creepers for the sake of pastime. || 5 ||
The expanse of the Nandana grove was violently churned by the first of Śambhu’s attendants, just as the ocean was churned by Mount Mandara.
Let it be stirred up and thrown into confusion by the Śambhavas, the attendants of Śiva, the Pramathas. || 6 ||
And they wandered through rivers thick with masses of young golden creepers,
like intoxicated elephants roaming among the lotus-beds of Mount Meru.
By the intoxicated elephant, the rutting gaja; on the Mairavi lands, those connected with Meru. || 7 ||
In the forest groves of Kailāsa,
that lover spent nights as white as the moon with her, while the songs of the Gaṇas were sung.

By means of the moon as his crest-jewel, Hara makes [the nights] bright even during the dark fortnight; that is, they are cast aside, thrown away, or—in other words—passed over. The augment *iṭ* is for metrical reasons. || 8 ||
Having rested upon the ridges of Mount Gandhamādana,
she was adorned by him from head to foot with golden lotuses.
She is the bride. || 9 ||
O Rāma, he sported with her, laughing, upon the shores of the Lokāloka mountain, which are captivating with their various wonders.
The mountain that forms the boundary of the earth is well known as Lokāloka. || 10 ||
In the groves between the Mandara trees, together with the young fawns,
he dwelt for sixty years in that place fashioned like a celestial palace.
In marshy regions abounding in water and cool climates, together with young fawns—calves of deer—for sixty years, that is, for sixty autumns. || 11 ||
On the shores of the Ocean of Milk, as he dwelt in the company of his consort,
half of the Kṛta Yuga was spent together with the inhabitants of Śvetadvīpa.
By fashioning the playful designs of celestial cities and gardens, this creator of the infinite worlds has come to imitate Time itself. (13)

By the mere power of his will, Śukra himself, becoming the creator of the entire world through a gradual process of emanation, attained—meaning reached—the imitation, that is, the equality, of Time. || 13 ||
Then that Śukra dwelt again in the city of Purandara for eight cycles of four yugas, living happily together with the deer-eyed woman.
Then, due to the exhaustion of his merit,
he fell upon the surface of the earth with that same proud woman, his form marred by suffering.
He whose divine body had its form dissolved due to the fear of falling and being reconstituted.
With all his limbs mangled by others, his chariot and its delights stripped away,
he was overcome by anxiety and ruined, like a warrior defeated in battle.
One whose all limbs were severed by being crushed into a liquid state;

one whose chariot, celestial vehicle, the Nandana grove, and the means for the enjoyment of dwellings, ornaments, and so forth were forcibly seized and taken away by the gods; one who was shattered and fell down—[in the battle].
In battle. || 16 ||
As he fell upon the ground, his body shattered into a hundred pieces along with his long anxiety, like a mountain stream falling over a rock.
The body has a nature that is fluid. || 17 ||
When their two bodies were shattered and their minds were clouded by calamity,
they wandered through the sky like two birds deprived of their nests.
The two subtle bodies (liṅgaśarīra) are merely mental; they are turbid and impure due to calamity and suffering. 18.
There, those two entered the mass of rays within the moon’s mind;
having quickly attained the state of frost, they then became rice plants.
There, in that sky, they entered; having entered, they attained the state of frost, becoming cold water. || 19 ||
That best of the twice-born ate those cooked rice-grains in Daśārṇa;
having attained the state of Śukra, he became the son of that [king's] wife.
In the Daśārṇas, which are specific regions; [he attained] the state of semen, that is, the nature of seed. || 20 ||
Then, through association with sages, he remained established in fierce austerity;
blameless, he dwelt in the thickets of Mount Meru for the duration of a Manvantara.
In the dense forest of Meru, in the regions such as Ilāvṛta and the rest.
There, a son of the deer, possessing a human form, was born to him;
through affection for him, he again fell into a state of supreme delusion in an instant. (22)
Regarding the word "mṛgyā" (by the female deer), it is understood by implication that she was an Apsaras who had become a female deer due to a curse. || 22 ||
"May this son have wealth, virtues, and eternal life"—
with such incessant anxieties, he abandoned his abiding in truth.
He abandoned his established state, which was governed by the means of valid cognition such as scripture and rooted in asceticism, meditation, and charity;
due to the collapse of his reflection on dharma, he fell into thoughts of sensual enjoyment for the sake of a son. Death carried him away when his life was spent, just as a snake seizes the wind.
He seized; he devoured. || 24 ||
With his consciousness departed along with his singular preoccupation for enjoyments, he attained the status of the son of the Lord of Madra and became the sovereign of the Madra land. || 25 ||
The intention is that Madreśa, the King of Madra, attained the status of his son—that is, the lower womb of a Kṣatriya—relative to his previous Brāhmaṇa birth. || 25 ||
Having ruled for a long time in the land of Madra, having destroyed his enemies,
he arrived here at old age, like a thunderbolt striking a lotus.
He approached; he reached. || 26 ||
Together with his desire for asceticism, he abandoned the beautiful body of the King of Madra; by that act, he was born as this ascetic, the son of a forest-dweller.
By the latent impression of austerity, it is understood by implication that he was reflecting upon the duties of the forest-dweller stage of life. || 27 ||
O Rāma, having reached the bank of the great river Samaṅgā, that ascetic of great intelligence performed austerities, free from all distress.
Free from fever, he is one whose internal heat of passion and other afflictions has been dispelled by tranquility and the like. || 28 ||
Having experienced various states of birth and successions of bodies according to his diverse inclinations,
that son of Bhṛgu remained established in happiness.
Like a firm tree on the bank of the Varaṇā river. || 29 ||
That aforementioned son of Bhṛgu, Śukra, whose disposition was manifold and who was permeated by various latent impressions (*vāsanā*),

having undergone various states of birth according to those [impressions] and having fully experienced a succession of bodies, attained— by the grace of destiny— the means such as detachment (*vairāgya*) and so forth, and thus lived happily and without distraction.

The meaning is that he remained with an unshakable disposition even amidst thousands of disturbances, such as cutting and splitting firm trees on the level bank of the river Varaṇā, which flows together with the Samaṅgā. || 29 ||

Thus ends the eighth canto, titled "Śuka’s Experience of Various Births," in the *Bhārgava-upākhyāna* (The Narrative of Bhārgava) within the *Sthiti-prakaraṇa* (The Section on Stability) of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, a work of the Sage. 8.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "Śuka’s Experience of Various Births," in the *Sthitiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The Ninth Canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
While Śukra was thus reflecting in the presence of his father, [the following occurred].
An exceedingly long period of time, consisting of many years, passed by.
In this [chapter], the falling away and the withering of the semen-body, which remains near Bhṛgu and is as if dead, are described. (1)
Thus, while he was reflecting in the manner described above and fashioning [his thoughts] through the kingdom of his imagination, in the presence of his father Bhṛgu. || 1 ||
Then, after a long time, his body, worn out by wind and sun,
fell upon the earth like a tree whose roots have been severed.
Worn out and rendered frail by wind and sun.
But the mind, its range flickering, wandered through those various and most diverse states, like a young elephant in rows of forest trees.
In those various states, such as his imagined journey to heaven, he was a deer, a *eṇaka*. || 3 ||
His mind, wandering, reeling, and agitated as if cast into a whirlpool, found rest upon the bank of the river Saṃgaṅgā.
Deluded by the conceptualization of enjoyments, and bewildered by the conceptualization of the succession of birth and death, he found rest; that is, he attained repose. || 4 ||
Shukra remained there, bodiless, experiencing that state of worldly existence— which is both fragile and yet very firm, and dense with infinite occurrences.

Because it consists of nothing more than mental construction, it is fragile; yet, through the delusion of its reality and the forgetting of the previous body, it becomes very firm. Thus, being "bodiless" (videha), he is independent of the body of Śuka. || 5 ||
Standing upon the peak of Mount Mandara, the body of that wise one became withered by the spreading heat until it was reduced to mere skin.
On the outside, they are reduced to skin alone; on the inside, they are reduced to bone alone.
Through the whistling sound of the wind flowing through the cavities of the body,
her movement seems to sing in a sweet falsetto due to the bliss arising from the destruction of suffering.

That body, by means of a *kākālī*—a subtle, indistinct, and sweet sound resembling the whistling of air as it flows and moves through the apertures of the body like wind through the holes of a flute—due to the bliss resulting from the cessation of the suffering of ego-inflation (*abhimāna*). (Note: The phrase *tadbhūtayā* appears in some versions.)
"This is such a state"—thus she seems to sing out through her gestures; this is a poetic fancy (utprekṣā). || 7 ||
It seems to laugh, as it were, with its row of teeth white as bright clouds, at the wretched mind wallowing in the pits of the realms of existence.
He describes that very state of the body through further imaginative reflections, beginning with "the wretched mind" (*manovarākam*).

That body— in which the wretched mind has wallowed, according to the manner previously described, in the pits characterized by the hope for enjoyment within the realms of worldly existence, like a dried-up pond— with its row of teeth white as a bright cloud...
It seems as if it were laughing. || 8 ||
Displaying the natural emptiness of the world through her own form, she possessed the beauty of a pit in the shape of a withered well within the forest of her face. (9)

That body, in the form of a forest consisting of the circle of its face, with the beauty of the hollows of its nose, eyes, and mouth resembling a multitude of ancient wells, seemed to directly demonstrate before the eyes of the discerning the world’s natural, uncreated emptiness— that is, its insubstantiality— within her own physical form.
The meaning is "is established. The mention of the "body" (vapuḥ) is for the purpose of indicating other means of knowledge (pramāṇa) that depend upon it. || 9 ||
Scorched by the heat and now drenched by the weight of the rainwater,
she sheds tears as if releasing the joy of remembering her former state.

First scorched by heat and subsequently sprinkled with water; "preceded by recollection" (*prāganusmaraṇa*) refers to the recollection of the succession of one's own former bodies that were once one's kin;
the tears are said to have "the splendor of recollection" (*prāganusmaraṇollāsam*) because they well up from the sorrow or joy induced by that recollection.
Through the pun (*śleṣa*) on "tears" (*aśru*) and "the appearance of smoke" (*dhūmābhāsa*), there is a superimposition of non-difference (*abhedāropa*). || 10 ||
In the forest lands, they were tossed about by the playful movement of the moon and the wind,
and pierced by the falling showers at the onset of the rainy season.
On the bank of the mountain river, she was drenched by the form of monsoon torrents and covered with dust raised by the wind, as if defiled by her own evil deeds.
She is drenched and colored by the mineral dye in the form of a mountain torrent during the rainy season. || 12 ||
Trembling like dry wood in the winds, her form emaciated by the wind,
she remained in the forest as if performing penance amidst the whistling of the piercing gales.

A beautiful form; the making of a sword-like sound arising from churning. Because of the frequent use of the suffix *ḍāc* after an indistinct imitation of sound, there is no reduplication. The forest-goddess (*araṇyalakṣmī*) is misfortune (*alakṣmī*), for she is characterized by making a terrifying, whistling sound (*bhāṅkāra*) among living beings. [She is addressed] with an offering (*balikarmaṇā*) out of childhood innocence.

"By means of food" is the sense. Since *brāhmaṇa* and so forth belong to the class of *ākṛtigaṇa*, the suffix *ṣyañ* is applied in the sense of the object (*karman*), followed by *ṅīṣ*. "One whose belly consists of leather" means one whose belly has nothing remaining but leather. || 13 ||
Crooked and with strings of dried entrails, she produces the shrieks of spirits;
like the Fortune of the Forest in her youth, she is empty, with a belly made of skin.
Because that holy hermitage was free from passion and hatred,
and because of Bhṛgu’s great ascetic power, it was not consumed by beasts or birds.
In that case, why was that body not devoured by beasts of prey, vultures, and the like? To this he replies: "By passion," etc.
Furthermore, it should be understood that because it possessed [the power of] *pramāṇa*, it did not fall apart either. || 15 ||
With her slender frame emaciated by restraints and observances,
she practiced austerities that captivated the mind of the descendant of Bhṛgu;
then her body was drained of blood by the wind.
She had long been rolling upon those great rocks. || 16 ||

That former body of Śukra, by which the slender frame had been emaciated through restraints (yama) and observances (niyama), performed penance on the bank of the Samaṅgā river, having fashioned another body for itself; the absence of the case-ending (*vibhaktyaluk*) after *klība* is Vedic (*chāndasa*). || 16 ||

Thus ends the ninth canto, titled "The Description of the Body of Bhārgava," in the section on Stability within the Means to Liberation of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Seers.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Description of Bhārgava’s Body," in the *Sthitiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The Tenth Chapter. 10.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, after a thousand divine years, the Supreme Lord...
Bhṛgu ceased from his supreme awakening and meditative absorption.
Here, the anger of Bhṛgu toward one who had seen his son’s body is described;
then, the awakening regarding Time by means of Time through the knowledge of the Self.
Because it clearly awakens and reveals the supreme Supreme Self, it is called "Supreme Awakening" (paramasaṃbodha);
from that [arises] samādhi. || 1 ||
He did not see his son before him, whose face was bowed in humility,
who stood like the personified merit of the entire host of virtues.
The presiding lord over the vassal kings of Guṇasenā, that is, the multitude of virtues. || 2 ||
He saw before him a great skeleton, devoid of all else,
appearing as if it were a body possessed by misfortune or poverty incarnate.
The characteristic of the body is a skeleton, a corpse. || 3 ||
Its body was withered by the heat; a partridge quivered within the opening of its skin;
and a frog rested in the shadow of the hollow of its dried-out internal belly.
He describes the skeleton itself with the words beginning "tāpa" (heat) and so forth: its body is dried up by heat—that is, by the sun's glare.

The term [“rāhu-”] is a bahuvrīhi compound, like the expression “rāhu-sarpaśirāḥ” (Rāhu having the head of a serpent). Because nests have been made in the apertures of the skin—the openings in the hide—there are *tittiri* birds (a species of partridge) quivering therein. In the shadow of the cavity of the belly, where the intestines are completely parched...
The frogs and toads have come to rest upon him.
With newly hatched insects clinging within the sockets of its eyes, and swarms of silkworms threaded upon the cage of its ribs; (5)
In the hollow of whose eyes are attached new insects that have grown through successive generations of offspring;
and who are threaded upon the cage characterized by the ribs—that is, the bones of the sides—or like the *kośakāraka* silkworms, or spiders (*lūtā*) well-known in the eastern regions. 5.

With her entrails washed by the stream [of tears], she was likewise intensely emaciated, possessing only a garland of bones, as she had long since abandoned the desire for enjoyment that yields both desired and undesired fruits.
The connection with the following verse is as follows: "Mocking the desire for enjoyment and the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of pleasure by means of a necklace of dried bones.
This is because of the similarity between the bones—which serve as the structural joints for the composition of various diverse forms that initiate the body—and the latent impressions.
[He wore] a white, smooth head-vessel, radiant as the moon.
And it mocked the beauty of the top of a linga drenched in camphor.

With its skin fallen away until only the bone remained, it imitated— meaning it resembled— the splendor and beauty of the top of a Śiva-liṅga that has been bathed and anointed with camphor during a special ritual of worship, possessing a luster like that of the moon. || 7 ||
With his neck— straight, its veins withered, reduced to mere bone,
and stretching backward as if to lengthen his very form— he seemed to elongate his stature.
As if following her own self, which had been set in motion by latent impressions (vāsanā). || 8 ||

He bore the appearance of having a boundary-line drawn upon his face by the bone at the tip of his nose, which was as pale as a lotus stalk and from which the flesh had been washed away by a stream [of blood].

It had the appearance of one for whom a boundary-stake was placed in the middle of the facial circle by means of the tip of the nose-bone—which was covered with rain-showers [of blood] and whose flesh was decayed—serving as a marker to determine the center of the face.
This is because the tip of the nose-bone occupies the central position within the facial circle. (In the reading *nāsāgrasthitayā*...)
The term "skeleton" (asthikā) is to be supplied as the substantive. || 9 ||
Surely, with her long neck and upturned face,
she was looking as if for her life-breaths that had departed into the expanse of the sky.
With a long neck and throat. || 10 ||
With his shanks, thighs, knees, and staff-like arms having attained a doubled length,
he appeared like a weary traveler seeking a place of rest out of fear of the exhaustion of a long journey.
Since the word *daṇḍa* does not denote a limb of a living being, there is no formation of a singular compound (*dvandvaikavadbhāva*).

[The phrase] "with the eight [limbs], beginning with the shanks" means up to the ends of the eight directions; "establishing itself" means setting out, as if about to depart, that is to say, as if wishing to flee by separating [from its base].

The absence of the vowel *u* [in *mugdha*] is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*). "Out of fear of the fatigue of the long journey" is a poetic conjecture regarding the cause; the meaning is that it was as if out of fear, for on the long path to the other world, the exhaustion of carrying the body cannot be endured. || 11 ||
With his belly excessively emaciated until it was mere skin, he seemed to display the extreme emptiness of the heart of a fool. || 12 ||
Beholding that tethering post of a skeleton, which was the elephant of suffering,
he leaped from the cliff without reflecting on what had preceded or followed.
Ālāna is a tethering post. || 13 ||
For at the very moment the light appeared, Bhṛgu’s inspired eloquence arose;
in an instant he wondered, "Has this son of mine been dead for a long time? (14)
"Āloka" means illumination; at that same time, "pratibhāna" (inspiration) refers to the *vitarka* (initial mental application) which is about to be described—the sense being that it "arose."
Even as he was thus reflecting upon his future son,
a most terrible anger toward Time (Death) quickly arose within him.

Not reflecting upon the fact that what was destined to happen must inevitably occur—[the context implies] having seen his son dead—he became enraged, thinking, "Why has my son been taken away so prematurely?
and the Blessed One proceeded to cast a curse upon Time (Kāla). || 15-16 ||
Then Kāla, having assumed a form and swallowed all living beings,
approached the sage, taking on a physical body composed of material elements.
"Of unimagined form" means that he is indeed formless; or, it means he is one by whom form has been imagined or conceptualized. || 17 ||
The glorious one, holding a sword and a noose, adorned with earrings and clad in armor, possesses six arms and six faces; he is surrounded by a fire-like army of servants.
On each side there are six arms; the meaning is that he has twelve arms for the twelve months, and possesses the faces of the six seasons. || 18 ||
The sky, by means of the leaping mass of flames arising from his body, bore the splendor of a mountain covered with blossoming *kiṃśuka* trees. (19)
The quarters of the sky shone with the circles of fire issuing from the tips of the tridents held in his hands,
as if they were golden earrings set ablaze.
The quarters are the directions; "kānakaiḥ" means made of gold. || 20 ||
By the force of his breath, the mountains had their peaks cast down;
reeling as if mounted upon a swing, they swayed and fell. (21)
Their peaks were cast down by a powerful external wind, that is, the breath of air. || 21 ||
The dark disc of the sun, illuminated by the circles of light from his sword,
appeared as if it were obscured by the smoke from a world consumed at the end of an aeon.

At the end of the eon, during the time of dissolution, it is distorted like the face of the world, which has been consumed by fire, when it is overwhelmed by smoke; [the sense being established by the phrase "overwhelmed as it were" alone, the addition of "like a face" and so forth here appears redundant. 22.
Having approached that great sage, who was enraged and as deep as the ocean agitated at the end of an aeon, O mighty-armed one, he spoke to him with words of conciliation.
"O mighty-armed one" is an address to either Rāma or the King. || 23 ||
O Sage, those who understand the nature of the world and have seen both the higher and the lower are not deluded even by a cause; how much less so, then, by one without a cause? (24)
Even though there exists a cause, such as the occasion of an offense or the like. || 24 ||
"You are a brahmin of infinite splendor, while we are merely the upholders of destiny;
therefore, O virtuous one, you are honored as one worthy of worship, and not by the will of others. (25)
By the other [means], namely that caused by the fear of a curse and so forth. || 25 ||
O ignorant one, do not waste your asceticism with the great fires at the end of an eon;
since I am not burned by them, what can you burn me with by your curse? (26)
With the intention that, on the contrary, it would be only for you and not for me that harm would come from bestowing a curse, he says: "Do not perform penance.

By means of the pretext of reproach, the term "O ignorant one" (*abuddhe*)—meaning "O you of futile intellect"—is actually a praise, implying "O you whose intellect is non-existent because it has been sublated by knowledge. This is because the rules regarding the substitutes for *yuṣmad* and *asmad* must be applied within a single sentence.
Because it contradicts the statement of Kātyāyana, the substitution of *me* for the word *mama* occurring after a word situated within a different sentence is a Vedic (chāndasa) usage.
O Sage, we have swallowed and devoured crores of Rudras, and we have consumed multitudes of Viṣṇus; where are we not capable? (27)

Having spoken of his invincibility, he declares his own unimpeded power with the verse beginning "saṃsāra...": "In what [sphere]—that is, regarding what object—are the successions of worldly existence, the rows of cosmic eggs, not capable? Speak of such a thing. In the reading "kva nu śaptāḥ," however, the meaning is: "In what offense, by whom..."
Or, the meaning is that they are overcome by a curse. "Svayam" refers to destiny, which is the natural law (maryādā).
"Īhita" means that which is produced by other causes such as desire, aversion, and so forth. || 27 ||
"O Brahmin, we are indeed the eaters and you are the food; for this is the very law of destiny, not something intended by us. (28)
Fire ascends upward of its own accord; waters flow downward of their own accord;
food goes to the eater of its own accord; and the Ender likewise brings about the dissolution of creation of his own accord. (29)
"Creation" (sṛṣṭi) means that which is created; the meaning is the state of being produced. "Antaka" is the time of destruction.
The sense is based on the Vedic scripture: "Whatever he created, he resolved to devour. || 29 ||
O Sage, this form of mine here is thus:
the Self, by itself and within its own self, unfolds spontaneously.

Whence comes your status as the enjoyer of all, or what is your true nature? To this he says: "This... (the reading "iha" appears in the printed edition). This world, both manifest and unmanifest, is my own form—imagined within me as the Supreme Self—as having the very nature of being an object of enjoyment. For the Supreme Self, within its own self...
It unfolds by itself as the very soul of the world; therefore, the meaning is that it withdraws [the world] by itself. || 30 ||
By the vision that has destroyed all taint, there is neither an agent nor an enjoyer here;
yet by the vision that has not destroyed its taint, there are many agents here.
This has been stated from the perspective of the conventional usage of the Upaniṣads; however, from the perspective of ultimate reality, he says, "Not so" (neha).
From the perspective of the ritualist, he says, "Many. The word *anaṣṭakalaṅkayā* should be split [as *na naṣṭa-kalaṅkayā*]. || 31 ||
O Brahman, agency and non-agency are merely imagined through incorrect vision alone; they do not belong to you who possess correct vision.
For you, who possess right vision—that is, the direct realization of reality—there exist neither agency nor non-agency. || 32 ||
Flowers in groves of trees and beings in the worlds come and go here of their own accord; they are conceptualized by means of names that serve as causes.
Relying on the position shown by the Blessed One in such passages as, "The Lord creates neither agency nor actions for the world," he says:

"the flowers. The construction should be made by supplying the word "time" (*kāla*), [understanding that] "it is time alone that is conceived here in this context by means of the names of causes—that is, by words such as 'agent' and so forth.
Thus, the connection is to be understood through the supply of the term *kāla* with the words "agent" and the rest.

Regarding the reading "vidhiḥ [is] by means of a cause" (hetunā), the meaning is as follows: *vidhi* is that which is ordained (*vidhīyate*), namely the very karma of living beings; it is capable—that is, competent—of producing even a manifold effect through its own implied cause, which is the diversity of conditions (*nimitta*). || 33 ||
Just as in the case of the reflected moon, there is neither agency nor non-agency in its movement, so it is with Time regarding the creations. (34)

From the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha), it is not real because of its non-existence; yet from the perspective of conventional discourse (vyavahāra), it is not unreal. This refers to Time, which is the Supreme Self in the form of time. || 34 ||
The mind, through the engagement with false delusion, produces a conceptualization consisting of agency and non-agency, just as one with a distorted vision perceives a snake in a rope. (35)
He has deluded vision and an evil perspective. || 35 ||
Therefore, O Sage, do not give way to anger; such is the course of calamities.
Whatever has happened, see it quickly as it truly is, without agitation. (36)
Because, according to the manner described by him, no offense was possible, he became agitated and gave way to anger. || 36 ||
We do not act out of a desire for reputation, nor are we overcome by pride;
for, O father, we are naturally subject to destiny alone and abide solely within its constraints. (37)

He says, "Not we," meaning that he would have been at fault in the killing of your son due to the influence of passion, pride, and so forth, yet neither of those two exists in him. For those whose effort (īhā) consists of passion for the sake of fame, honor, and the like—conceived through the error of false appearances—he uses the plural number according to the rule *asmado dvayośca* ("for the word *asmat*, the dual and plural are used"). Furthermore, his coming into your presence was not out of fear of your anger, but rather...
With the intention that ascetics are to be honored by the power of destiny, he says: "Of their own accord" (svataḥ). || 37 ||
Wise men proceed according to the necessity of their natural conduct and destiny; they do not fall under the great darkness of pride.

With the intention of showing that, because he follows all who are wise, subjection to destiny is appropriate for me, whereas for you, the persistence of the darkness of anger and pride is inappropriate, he says: "By nature...

[The commentary continues: By the power of the Great Destiny characterized by the will of the Lord, the protector of the world's boundaries, there is the regulation of the intermediate primary elements (*prakṛti*).
The meaning is that they follow along with grace, will, and necessity. || 38 ||
Those skilled in action must certainly perform their duty;
never, however, should you let it perish by resorting to the state of deep sleep. (39)

Those skilled in duty and clever in worldly affairs must certainly perform, and must invariably perform, the observance of their respective proper boundaries; do not destroy them by resorting to a state of deep sleep or a state of darkness.
In the reading "kadācid api nāśaya," the meaning is clear. || 39 ||
Where is that vision consisting of wisdom, where is your greatness, and where is your fortitude? Even though the path is well-known to all, why do you wander like one who is blind? (40)
It is established by all the wise. || 40 ||
O Sage, why do you wish to curse me in vain like a fool, without considering this state of mine which has arisen from the ripening of the fruits of my own karma? (41)
In vain; fruitlessly. || 41 ||
"O Sage, for all embodied beings here, the body is of two kinds;
do you not know that one is the physical body and the other is called the mind? (42)

Having thus censured Bhṛgu’s delusion, he begins to awaken his dormant knowledge with the words beginning "dehinām" (of embodied beings) and so forth. "Taṃ" refers to that well-known gross [body]. || 42 ||
In this regard, the body is utterly insentient and destined for destruction, and the mind is trivial; both are inevitably subjected to suffering for your sake. (43)

"Non-destruction" (āvināśa) means destruction even by a slight cause. "Fixed" (niyatam) means remaining until liberation. "Insignificant" (tuccham) means illusory. "Is made useless" (kadarthīkriyate) means it is afflicted by anger and so forth. || 43 ||
O virtuous one, just as a chariot is driven by a skillful charioteer,
so too is this body guided by the mind out of a certain affection.
Out of affection and pride, [the Lord] performed an internal activity that cannot be specifically described as being "like this" or "like that. || 44 ||
An evil resolve is formed and the body is destroyed in an instant by the mind, just as a clay figure is destroyed by a child. 45.
A mental construction (saṃkalpa) is formed with respect to an object that does not exist within its own sphere; that which was previously established as real is destroyed.
It is like a man made of mud or a doll made of moist clay intended for play. 45.
In this world, the mind alone is the person; what it does is said to be done by him.
Bound by that [mind] due to the cause of conceptualization, one is liberated when freed from that conceptualization.
Mental construction is indeed the conceptualization of the unreal; for that reason, one is bound by its very nature.
"This body, this limb situated here, and this head—this [entirety] which undergoes manifold transformations is designated as that very mind. (47)
Demonstrating the manner in which he fashions a body, he says: "This... (verse 47).

For the mind (manas) is called the individual soul (jīva) because it is the principle of determination; the intellect (dhī) is so called due to its singularity of resolve; and the ego (ahaṅkāra) is so named because of its sense of self-identification—these indeed constitute its own manifoldness.

Just as the single mind becomes what is called another life from one preceding life to the next, so it will be explained in the *Jīvaṭopākhyāna*. When the object is conceived by the mind, the mind itself subsequently becomes the intellect (*dhī*) through its singular determination.
Because of its nature as the agent of self-identification, it is called the ego (*ahaṅkāra*); thus, the meaning is that the mind itself becomes manifoldness.
If the mind, through the latent impression of the body, desires other bodies for itself,
it perceives those earthly bodies as if they were real, even though they do not exist.
If one perceives the truth, then the mind, consisting of truth,
abandons the conception of a body and attains supreme bliss.

And he states that this capacity of the mind to conceptualize the body and so forth lasts only until the direct realization of the Self (ātmasākṣātkāra), and not thereafter, with the words: "It perceives... (50).
While you were established in meditative absorption, the mind of your son followed the path of its own desires and went further and further away.
Having thus awakened Bhṛgu, he introduces the story of his son, which was created as a mere play of the mind, with the words "That... (verse 51).
Having abandoned this body of Ośanas in a cave of Mount Mandara,
he departed for the abode of the gods, like a bird flying up from its nest.
This which is being seen by you. || 52 ||
There, among the Mandara and Guñja trees, at the foot of Pārijāta trees, in the groves of the Nandana garden, and in the cities of the world-protectors; || 53 ||
O Sage, for eight cycles of four yugas, that one of great splendor attended upon Viśvācī, the celestial beauty, just as a bee attends a lotus.
The celestial nymph Devasundarī. || 54 ||

Then, when his store of merit was exhausted, he—though fashioned by his own volition and endowed with intense spiritual urgency—vanished like the mist of a winter night. (Or, according to another reading: "like the mist of Śambara.")
With the intention that even the fall from heaven occurs merely through mental construction due to the exhaustion of merit—just as the fall from heaven does—he says: "Tīvrety... 56.
With his floral crest-flower withered and the luster of his limbs and members faded, he fell along with her like a fruit ripened by time.
The withering of the flowers on the crest-ornaments in heaven and so forth are the signs of the exhaustion of merit in heaven. (56)
Having abandoned that divine body in the sky,
he then reached the elemental ether and was born upon the earth.
He was born; he obtained birth. || 57 ||
There was a brahmin in Daśārṇa, a king in Kosala, a fisherman in the great forest, and a swan on the bank of the triple-pathed river (Ganges). (58)

He describes his many births—both those previously mentioned and those not yet mentioned—which follow various latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and karmas, beginning with the words "There was... (verse 58).
In the Solar dynasty there was King Pauṇḍra, a guide among the Sauras and Śālvas;
then the glorious and wise Vidyādhara for a kalpa, and then the son of the sage.

Pauṇḍra was the ruler of the Puṇḍra country; he was a spiritual guide (*deśika*), one perfected in mantra, and a teacher of others. Consequently, through the power of his mantra-worship, he became a Vidyādhara for an eon (*kalpa*). Then, immediately thereafter, a son was born to the sage.
Then the protector of the earth, that young ascetic,
became known as Vāsudeva and dwelt upon the bank of the Samaṅgā river.
Furthermore, by the power of his own latent impressions (vāsanā),
your son wandered through various other intermediate wombs that were indeed distressing.
He says that his births were not limited to these alone, but there were others as well: "In other [births] also" (anyāsvapi). || 61 ||
He was again a Kirāta on Mount Vindhya and among the Kaikaṭas; then he was a Sāmanta among the Sauvīras and a Gardabha among the Trigartas.

A vassal is a lord of a province (*maṇḍaleśvara*). There, by means of the sins committed, he shows even births among animals, stationary beings, and so forth, starting with the words "in Trigarta," and so on. || 62 ||
The bamboo shrub is found among the Kirātas; the deer in the forests of Cīna;
the reptile on the palm tree; and the wild cock on the tamāla tree. (63)
This very son of yours, having become the best among those who know the mantras,
formerly recited the lore that bestows the city of the Vidyādharas.
He elaborates upon what was previously stated—that he became a Vidyādhara for an eon—by means of the passage beginning with "This is he," and so forth. || 64 ||
Therefore, O Brahmin, he became a great Vidyādhara in the sky,
adorned with necklaces, earrings, armlets, and a mass of playful locks of hair.
Adorned with necklaces, armlets, and other ornaments, he is a source of delight through his manifold pastimes; he is the one who brings joy to women.
He was like a second flower-bowed god of love to the lotus-like heroines;
he was the beloved of the Vidyādharīs and the ornament of the city of the Gandharvas.
For this very reason, with the intention that he is the most beloved among them, he says: "The heroine," etc. (66).
Having reached the end of the kalpa within the splendor of the twelve suns, he was reduced to ashes like a moth in a fire. || 67 ||
In the abode of the twelve suns, at the end of the eon, when the radiance of twelve suns has risen simultaneously, [the world] is reduced to ashes.
Then, in the vast sky devoid of the creation of the world,
that latent impression of his wandered about like a bird without a nest.
Then, when time had arrived, initiating its manifold undertakings at the commencement of the construction of the world-cycle, upon the passing of Brahmā’s night; (69)
O Sage, that latent impression (vāsanā) of his, though shaken by the wind,
having attained the state of a Brahmin when [the time] was made, has today been born upon the surface of the earth.
In the Kṛta, the first age. || 70 ||
O sage, that young brahmin named Vāsudeva was born among the wise, having studied the entirety of the Vedas.
O great sage, having become a Vidyādhara for an eon,
your son is now performing austerities, stationed on the bank of the river Samaṅgā.
Driven by the persistence of latent impressions from various sense-objects,
one enters into the bellies that serve as wombs within this world— bellies as formidable as the hollows of khadira and karañja trees.
And in the most dense forest regions. || 73 ||

He summarizes: "In various ways," etc. Having entered and wandered through the various types of dwelling in the womb—maternal wombs that are like the hollows of *khadira*, *karañja*, or the thorny *girika* trees. (73)
Thus ends the tenth sarga, titled "The Words of Time," within the Bhārgava-episode of the *Sthiti-prakaraṇa* of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by Vālmīki.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Discourse on Time," in the *Sthitiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The Eleventh Canto.
Kāla said:
Today, the wind resounds with the roar of a mass of wildly surging waves.
On the very bank of the river, your son is performing austerities.
The period of Bhṛgu’s yoga is correctly described through the account of his son;
it is a play of the mind and the state of the world, in accordance with the times. (1)
Where the winds, resounding with the deep-toned gurgling of the surging waves, cause the river Samaṅgā to roar as it performs its ascetic penance. || 1 ||
Wearing matted hair and a rosary of seeds, having conquered the delusion of all his senses,
he remained there for eight hundred years, steadfast in his ascetic penance.
O Sage, if you wish to see that which is like a dream, a delusion of the mind,
then quickly open the eye of higher knowledge and behold it.

Having fully opened—that is, having properly unveiled—the eye of yoga, which is called "knowledge" (*vijñāna*) because one perceives through it that son who consists of the conduct of a son and is a mental delusion; || 3 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
When this had been spoken by the Lord of the World, who views all with equanimity,
the sage reflected upon the welfare of his son with the eye of knowledge.
The conduct of the son, which was beneficial to him. || 4 ||
And in a moment, by the power of his inspired intuition, he beheld the entire account of his son reflected upon the mirror of his intellect.
The news—the account—of his son, appearing as if reflected in the mirror of his intellect purified by the dharma born of yoga, was as if directly before his eyes. || 5 ||
Then, having emerged from the bank of the Samaṅgā river, Bhṛgu entered his own body, which was situated on the slopes of Mount Mandara, healthy and established at the tip of Time.

One should not be deluded into thinking that Bhṛgu emerged from his own body, went to those various locations on the banks of the Samaṅgā, observed the sequence of events concerning his son, and then returned to re-enter his body;
for by the power of yoga, it is possible to perceive everything while remaining in one's own place. [The word "nirgatya" (having emerged) refers to this.]

Since it is impossible to see the past and the future even while wandering, one should understand that the statement "having come from the bank of the Samaṅgā, she entered her own body" intends merely the abandonment of that anxiety and the reconnection with her own physical form. || 6 ||
Having observed Kāla with a gaze smiling with wonder, his beloved spoke these words;
and the passionless sage spoke this speech to the one free from passion.
Free from passion, he was devoid of affection for his son. || 7 ||
O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, we are but children, lacking brilliance;
O God, only those like you possess an intellect that perceives the three times with stainless clarity.
The fools are ignorant; for they are unilluminated, their minds being defiled by passion and other such stains. (8)
Abounding in various forms and transformations, appearing as unreal even while being real, this state of the world produces delusion even for the wise man. (9)

The state of the world, though unreal and formless, appears as if it were real and of the nature of ultimate truth; thus, while being real only in its appearance, it produces delusion even regarding the ultimately real entity—even for the wise and steadfast man. || 9 ||
O Lord, you alone know that form which resides within you and which acts as a magician’s trick for this mental faculty.

He says "You alone" [to show] that even the form of the mind, which has become the instrument for the existence of the world of objects, is difficult to know for those like me—[a mind] which, like a magical illusion (*indrajāla*), produces the delusion of *māyā*. || 10 ||
"O Blessed One, it is said that death does not exist for this son of mine;
therefore, seeing him dead, I have become filled with agitation. (11)
He states two reasons for his own delusion with the two verses beginning "matputrasya" (of my son). [The word] "na vidyate" (is not found) means "until the end of the eon" (ākalpam). || 11 ||
"O Lord, by the power of destiny, Time has carried away my son while his life was not yet exhausted; thus, even this trivial desire of mine has arisen. (12)
One whose life-span has not yet been exhausted is "one whose life is not spent. || 12 ||
"O Lord, surely we have understood the course of saṃsāra; yet we still fall under the sway of joy and resentment when encountering both calamities and successes. (13)
The word *nanu* indeed indicates both astonishment and a matter of fact. || 13 ||
"Anger toward one who acts improperly and favor toward one who acts properly—O Blessed One, this is the established rule in the world. (14)
He explains the second cause, which is the nature of necessity (niyati), with the words "improper" (ayuktā). Stability (sthiti) is necessity (niyati). || 14 ||
"This must be done" and "this must not be done"—as long as there is such activity, it is the delusion of the world.
O Teacher of the World, the total renunciation of this [delusion] is indeed what is to be abandoned. (15)

He states how long that [delusion] remains rooted there: "This" and so forth. As long as there is the delusion of the world—the notion that "this must certainly be done" and "this must not be done," and that the results of actions which are means to the desired or undesired are real—that [delusion] persists. If one asks, "Is that [delusion] still appropriate for you now? he says "of that" and so forth. This...

Now that this delusion has been abandoned through the realization of reality, even the restrictive rule regarding anger and favor for its sake must be discarded; thus, the meaning is that anger is simply improper. || 15 ||
O Blessed One, since we became angry with you because we did not perceive that this was merely your own thought, let it be countered by that [anger]. (16)

Even though such a transgression has occurred, anger is not appropriate; however, since anger arises through the false attribution of such a fault where none exists, on the contrary, it is the one who becomes angry who deserves punishment. With this intention, he says: "Kevalam" (merely). "Cintām" refers to the aforementioned reflection, which is intended solely for the preservation of the cosmic order (*niyati*). "Bādhyatām" means "let us be subject to your punishment. || 16 ||
"O Lord, I have now been reminded by you of what was intended for my son;
therefore, this son was seen by me on the bank of the Samaṅgā. (17)
In this world, the mind is the all-pervading second body for all living beings;
for the mind alone is indeed the body by which this universe is perceived.
For since the mind itself fashions the body composed of the elements, the meaning is that the mind alone constitutes the two bodies;
by which mind [it does so]. 18.
Kāla said:
"O Brahmin, you have spoken correctly regarding the body and the mind;
the mind creates the body through its volition, just as a potter fashions a jar. (19)

Thus, Kāla, not satisfied by Vinītavāda’s grasp of the subtle meaning taught by himself, praises his statement and confirms it with further arguments, beginning with the words "Well said," and so forth. || 19 ||

Through the delusion of the mind, by means of conceptual construction (*saṃkalpa*), one creates a form that did not exist before and destroys what was created in an instant, just as a child [fears] a ghost (*vetālaka*). (20)
And likewise, powers appearing as confusion, dreams, false cognitions, and the like, resembling the cities of Gandharvas, are seen within the mind. (21)
He states that the mind's power of non-existent creation is well-known through all experience, saying: "And so it is. (21)
Relying, however, upon this gross perspective, O great sage, it is said that a person has two bodies: the mind and the physical body. (22)

Having established the validity [of the teaching] through the statement "The mind alone is indeed the body," he now censures the former [view] in order to establish its validity even further through the statement "By which this world is conceived"; thus he says:
"The state of gross vision" (verse 22).
O Sage, these three worlds are merely a mental construction of the mind; they have arisen as a vast expanse that is neither existent nor non-existent, and nothing else.

What, then, is the subtle vision? He states that with the words "the mind," and so forth. The meaning is that this [world] has arisen as something that cannot be defined as either existent or non-existent, just like the mind. || 23 ||
Through the creeper-like limbs of the body of consciousness, fueled by the latent impression of duality,
this manifoldness has arisen from ignorance, like the appearance of two moons.
The diversity of the world's distinctions is manifested by that which is like a creeper, acting as a limb of the body of consciousness. 24.
Due to the latent impression of duality, the mind perceives the multitude of objects;
it sees everything as distinct, such as jars, huts, cloths, and so forth. (25)

"I am emaciated, I am deeply miserable, I am deluded"— cultivating these and other such notions arising from its own conceptual constructions, the mind enters the state of worldly existence (saṃsāritā).
"Thinking is an artificial form; this is not my true nature, for I am not that. Through the renunciation of that [thinking], the mind becomes peaceful—the eternal Brahman. (27)
Having established the process of transmigration, he states the means for its cessation: "reflection" (*manana*).
The underlying sense is that when artificial reflection is abandoned, abiding in one's own natural, unartificial state follows as a matter of course.
Just as in the vast ocean,
where many rivers have flowed together, the various rows of waves subside through the cessation of their movement.
Having stated the matter, he begins to describe the analogy of the ocean waves in detail with the words "Just as" (*yathā*) and so forth.
The word "just as" (*yathā*) here is to be construed with the phrase "in that very way" (*tathaiva*) found in the fourteenth verse.
[The ocean exists] in the form of water in general—that is, in the form of the ocean—and in the form of the water situated in its various locations.
Because there is an absence of the vibration in the form of movement toward a distant destination that is currently being perceived, it remains in a state where vibration has subsided;
the mention of "waves" is for the sake of its magnitude, according to the maxim of the "cow and the bull. 28.
In the Self, which is like water— equal, clear, pure, sweet, cool,
indestructible, vast, of great majesty, and manifest— (29)
A short wave, manifesting its own form through its own nature, creates the mental cultivation of itself by means of the conceptualization, "I am short. (30)

The entire passage beginning with "contemplating one's own form" (*svaṃ rūpaṃ bhāvayan*) and so forth is a discourse on the superimposition of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*). If one contemplates, the meaning is that one performs the contemplation which is about to be described. || 30 ||
A long wave, manifesting its own form through its own nature,
creates the mental cultivation "I am long" by means of conceptualization.
Thinking, "I am short and my form has fallen away," he goes to the Talātala region by means of that very mental conception.
Visualizing Talātala and Pātāla, he proceeds toward the bank of the earth, fearing the fall [into the netherworlds]. || 32 ||
Once arisen, he meditates, "I have risen above the corpse," and he shines with radiant splendor like a net of jewels emitting rays of light. (33)
Immediately after a short period of time spent as a corpse, he has arisen and attained a birth suitable for enjoyment;
thus contemplating and imagining, "I am adorned," he shines like a mountain accompanied by a network of rays from excellent jewels, meaning he rejoices, thinking, "I am adorned. || 33 ||
Residing in the orb of the cool-rayed moon, he reflects the thought, "I am cool";
yet, as a reflection of the forest fire upon the mountain slopes, his body blazes with flame.
He shows him other instances of joy and fear as well, beginning with the words "tuṣārakara" and so forth:

while the reflection (*bimba*) of the moon (*tuṣārakara*) exists there as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), it conceives the thought, "I am cool. However, when accompanied by the reflection of a forest fire on a nearby mountain, it conceives, "My body is burning."
"He fears and trembles"—this is the connection with the prefix *pra*. || 34 ||
Alas, he trembles, thinking "I am burnt," and maintains a vow of silence;
yet the trees on the mountain slopes and forest banks are reflected therein like wings.

In which [lake] the forest trees on the slopes of the coastal mountains appear as if they were wings reflected [in the water]; being thus endowed with the great ostentation of undertaking the fruits of attaining sovereignty and so forth, he shines, thinking "I have achieved my purpose"—this is the connection with the following verse. || 35 ||
He shines, thinking "I am engaged in the intense exertion of a great undertaking," even though his flickering body has been utterly destroyed by the violent gusts of wind.
Crying out as if in distress, "I am being torn to pieces," you roared;
yet those waves are not distinct from the water-bearing ocean itself.

"Having assumed a cry" means as if having begun to weep; "possessing sound" refers to the noise of crying. Having stated the superimposition (*āropa*) in the illustrative example, he shows the negation (*apavāda*) with the words beginning with "and not," etc. [The phrase] "from the ocean" refers to the ocean consisting of a mass of water in the form of a great volume of water (*payobhara*).
Not even a single form among these is either existent or composed of non-existence;
nor are qualities such as shortness or length inherent in them, yet they are not absent from them either.
The meaning of the illustration is that the qualities do not exist in those waves, nor do the waves exist in those qualities. || 38 ||
For indeed, the norms are established within the ocean, yet they are not truly established there;
they are merely rendered fragmented by the conceptual constructions of those abiding in their own respective natures. (39)

Regarding the statement "they are not established there in that ocean," the sense is this: because they exist as its substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*), yet as a transformation (*vivarta*), their non-existence cannot be established since their counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is not established. What, then, are those waves? To this he says: "Only... They are "made manifold" (*vikalīkṛtāḥ*), meaning made small; that is to say, they are conceptualized through the distinctions of delimitation (*pariccheda*). || 39 ||
Those that were lost and those not lost are born again; those already born and those yet unborn arise repeatedly.
Through their mutual interaction, they do not at all attain any state of difference.
Through mutual reflection and reciprocal union. || 40 ||
Just as they are composed solely of the commonality of water in a single form and are free from affliction,
so too is this vast, white, pure, and stainless [space].
He applies this to the case under discussion with the words "in the same way," etc.; [it refers to] the white, which is of the nature of light. || 41 ||
In Brahman, whose sole body is pure Brahman, who possesses expansive form,
who is omnipotent, and who is without beginning or end, [all things] exist as distinct yet not separate.

In that which has Brahman alone as its singular body, whose sole nature is the unrestrained Brahman—for this very reason, in Brahman—fullness itself is the "expansion" (*bṛṃhaṇa*), not the act of increasing; with this intention, its explanation is established as "having a vast form. The powers (*śaktis*) are manifold, diverse, and restless in their various modes of conduct.
For it is through various powers that [the One] attains multiplicity while remaining established within its own essence. (43)
He states the reason for the metaphorical designation of the powers (*śaktayaḥ*) as the worlds (*jaganti*) through the metaphor of non-difference: "nānā" (not manifold), etc. || 43 ||
Brahman is expanded within Brahman like a circle of waves in water;
Brahman alone revolves in the form of female, male, and neuter.
The term *vyaṅganapuṃsakaḥ* is a compound of three words (*tripada-dvandva*) in which the case-ending has not been elided (*vibhakty-aluk*), a feature characteristic of Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).
There has never been, is not, and will never be any other conceptual construction called "the world";
not even the slightest difference exists between Brahman and the world. (45)
Having established this through the logical perspective, he states it even from the perspective of ultimate reality: "Conceptual construction," etc. (45).
"Indeed, this entire universe is Brahman; the world is nothing but Brahman alone.
Contemplate this with diligence, for abandon everything else. (46)
Necessity (niyati), though manifold in form yet single in essence, and the cause of hundreds of diverse forms, presides over all things with its fixed nature.
By means of the abandonment of everything else, he explains that which is pure existence (*sanmātra*) as the sole substrate of all: "Not manifold" (*nānā*).
*Niyati* is existence (*sattā*), which is always and everywhere of one single form. (47)
The mind takes on both the insentient and the sentient, and enters into that which consists of consciousness;
it is the power in the form of latent impressions belonging to the Self established in its own true nature. (48)
Anticipating the objection— "How can existence (*sattā*), which is common to both the insentient (*jaḍa*) and the sentient (*ajaḍa*), be of a single, determinate nature?"—

the author states "insentient" (*jaḍa*) with the intention that the unity of the single form of pure existence (*sanmātraikarūpya*) is not impaired by the mental constructs of "insentient" and "sentient. When the mind enters into the conscious manifestation (*cinmaye cidābhāse*), having attained it—

Conceiving that very egoity, which is pervaded by this or that [object], as the Self, and everything else that exists as non-Self, it adopts a distinction between that which is external and insentient and that which is internal and sentient.
This power of the mind, consisting of the latent impression of duality, exists in addition to the pure Being that is its substratum.
The meaning is that since the self remains in its own true nature even when falling into delusion (mithyātva), there is no loss of its uniformity (ekarasya). || 48 ||
O sinless one, it is Brahman alone that expands in this vast form, as if filled with various manifestations and vibrations, like the ocean. (49)
And thus, since the similarity between the described example and the thing illustrated is unimpeded, he says:
"Brahman alone," and so forth. || 49 ||
Through dwelling in various forms, it assumes diversity by itself;
it is the Self alone within the Self, by means of the Self, like water in the waters of the ocean.
Just as various waves are not distinct from the water, so too all conceptual constructions are not distinct from the Lord of All. 51.
Just as there are the arrangements of branches, flowers, creepers, leaves, fruits,
and buds within a single seed, so too does every potentiality always reside therein.
In a single seed. || 52 ||
Just as a variegated color is seen in the harsh sunlight,
so too does the Lord of Gods possess a manifold power consisting of both the existent and the non-existent.

Having established [the point] by means of the illustration of the theory of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*), he establishes it further by means of the well-known illustration of the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivartavāda*) with the verse beginning "vicitra... (verse 53).
This world of manifold forms arises from the undifferentiated Śiva, just as a streak of Indra’s bow [a rainbow] emerges from a cloud of a single color. (54)
From the cloud that carries water. || 54 ||
From the non-inert, the state of inertia arises, caused by the contemplation of dullness;
just as a thread emerges from a spider, or as the state of deep sleep arises from a person. (55)
Even regarding the arising of the non-conscious from the conscious, he states two examples corresponding to the two positions, beginning with "from the non-inert":
deep sleep and the chariot and so forth in a dream. (55)
If the mind is unrefined, Śiva, by his own will,
extends for its bondage a silken cocoon, just as a silk-worm produces its cocoon.

Now, one might object: "Since consciousness (cit) is uniform, how can diversity be established in its effect, the unconscious (acit)? To this it is said: "The power of the mind. This means the diversity of latent impressions (vāsanā). || 56 ||
O Brahmin, by its own will, this self brings about forgetfulness of itself and creates a harsh bondage, just like a silkworm.
O Brahmin, by voluntarily contemplating one's own body as the Self, which is Brahman,
one attains liberation from saṃsāra, just as an elephant is freed from its tethering post.
Having assumed his own body and meditated upon his full essential nature, he experienced it directly. || 58 ||
Just as one constantly meditates upon the Self, so too does it become manifest of its own accord; even though it is great, it is swiftly filled with power.
Cultivated power brings the self to the state of the Self in an instant,
just as a great, all-encompassing mist at the onset of the rainy season [obscures] the infinite sky.
Vāsanā is the power that has been cultivated through long-term meditation and made firm. Ātmatvam is the state of conformity with oneself.
Ananta is the infinite space. Prāvṛṇihikā is well known [as a specific type of cloud]. || 60 ||
The unborn [Self], when impelled by that power, quickly attains identity with it;
just as a tree, having reached the state of a particular season, becomes one with that season.
He clarifies what has already been stated: "That power... (verse 61).
There is no liberation for the Lord, nor is there bondage for the Self;
I do not know from where these notions of bondage and liberation have arisen in the world.

This conceptualization of bondage and liberation belongs to the vision of the ignorant; however, from the perspective of the vision of reality, there is not even the possibility of such things. Thus he says: "No" (na). || 62 ||
There is no bondage, nor is there liberation; yet it appears as if one were absorbed in that [world].
Alas, this world, consisting of illusion, is eternally swallowed by the impermanent! 63.

Consisting of that [consciousness], it appears through delusion as if possessing the modifications of bondage and liberation. Why? Because its eternally full nature (ātmarūpa) has been seized and obscured by the impermanent, illusory (āvidyaka) state superimposed through latent impressions (vāsanā)—namely, the relationship between enjoyer and enjoyed. That very thing is the world consisting of māyā; such is the meaning. || 63 ||
The very moment this mind was indeed conceptualized by that which is devoid of parts (the intellect),
then this self was enveloped by it, like a silkworm in its cocoon.
In that regard, he shows the primary bondage with the words: "As soon as... (64).
But these millions of mental powers, which possess mutually distinct forms and have entirely imagined bodies, emerge from this [consciousness]. (65)
He states that other bonds are indeed produced by those [two] in the verse beginning with "anyonya" (65).
Born from that, situated in that, yet appearing as distinct forms, like waves from the ocean; born from that, situated in that, yet existing separately, like rays from the moon.

They appear as if distinct. Two examples are presented in succession with the intention of illustrating their differentiation, whether based on the distinction between the organs of action and knowledge, or the distinction between the tamasic and sāttvika modes. || 66 ||

In this vast ocean of the Supreme Self, which consists of vibration, whose waters are consciousness, whose expansive expanse is spread out, and which is garlanded by the essence of pure consciousness alone; (67)

He begins to demonstrate in detail, through the diversity of names, forms, actions, and so forth, the very distinctions of consciousness known as the individual soul (*jīva*), which arise from the limiting conditions (*upādhi*) of primary and secondary bondage—starting with the words "In this... and so on.
Some became stable as Brahmā and Viṣṇu; some attained the state of Rudra;
some reached the condition of being Puruṣas; and some attained the status of deities.
The state of being a person, the state of being human. || 68 ||
These waves,
which manifest their own nature through their inherent character, surge forth;
some among them take the forms of Yama, Mahendra, Arka, Vahni, Vaiśravaṇa, and others.
Some waves, characterized by restless longing, strike, form, and persist—
beings such as Kinnaras, Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, and gods.
Fierce waves leap up and fall, surging and tossing;
some remain somewhat steady in form, like Brahmā and the other deities.
Some have arisen and perished, such as gods, humans, and others;
some, such as worms, insects, moths, snakes, mice, and pythons, flash within that great ocean like drops of water. (69)
Maśās and maśakas—in the great ocean, in the form of aquatic creatures; this is the ellipsis. Or, it may be considered a remainder of the illustration. 69.
Some flickering beings, such as humans, deer, vultures, jackals, and so forth, dart about in the mountain thickets like [birds] on the shores of the coastal forests.
*Jambulakāḥ* means jackals. If the reading is *cañculakāḥ*, they are a species of birds. "Moving like the slopes of the coastal forests" means unstable;
for it is well known that among those [forests], trees, shrubs, creepers, and so forth are always in motion due to the intensity of the wind. (70)
Some have very long lives, while others have extremely short lives;
some possess substantial mental faculties, while others have insignificant bodies.
Those for whom there is a non-void, great conceptualization consisting of the imagination of the body's configuration. || 71 ||
In the turbulent dream of saṃsāra, some are imbued with a sense of stability, while others, struck down by false conceptualizations, imagine the world to be truly firm.

By "steadfastness" (sthairyeṇa), meaning by long duration; "struck" (hatāḥ) means deluded by firm conceptual constructions (suvikalpaiḥ dṛḍhavikalpaiḥ); they "fear" (śaṅkante) means they imagine [the world to be real]. || 72 ||
Some have very little cultivation [of the mind], being overcome by the fault of dejection;
they are dominated by sufferings such as "I am emaciated," "I am extremely miserable," and "I am deluded. (73)
He shows that cultivation itself is threefold by means of the word "emaciated" (kṛśa). || 73 ||
Some have attained the state of stationary beings, some have reached the status of deities;
some have attained manhood, and some have become the oceans.

The state of being a person is the state of possessing a body; the state of being an ocean is the state of being an ocean of delusion in which latent impressions (vāsanās) have not yet manifested, as in deep sleep or cosmic dissolution. || 74 ||
Some remain in this world for no fewer than hundreds of eons,
while others proceed to the supreme state, pure as the moon;
they have arisen from the ocean of Brahman, as restless as waves.
For consciousnesses are indeed synonymous with the act of thinking (manana). || 75 ||

Like the moon, because they are filled with the nectar of knowledge, these pure and true ones proceed to the supreme state—liberation, characterized by abiding in one's own perfect nature. Like restless waves, the flickering consciousnesses (*citaḥ*) are distinctions of conditioned perception; through the superimposition of identity with the mind (*manas*), they are designated by that name, "mind" (*manana*).

Thus ends the eleventh canto, titled "The Vision of the Evolution of Saṃsāra," within the *Bhārgavopākhyāna* (The Narrative of Bhārgava) of the *Sthitiprakaraṇa* (Section on Stability) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa*, the Great Epic of Vasiṣṭha, composed by the Sage.
Thus [ends] the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa* (The Elucidation of the Essential Meaning of the Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa), in the *Sthitiprakaraṇa*.
The eleventh canto, titled "The Vision of the Progression of Saṃsāra."
The Twelfth Chapter.
Kāla said:
"O Sage, these perceptions which take the forms of gods, asuras, and humans—"
They are non-different from the ocean of Brahman; this is the truth, and everything else is false.

Preventing [the opponent] from reaching the conclusion that the Self undergoes modification—based on the analogy of waves and the ocean—he declares that the manifold variety arising from delusion is a mere illusory transformation (*vivarta*). (1)

Therein, first, he makes a formal declaration (pratijñā) in order to establish the identity of all living beings with Brahman and the falsity of the phenomenal world which causes differentiation: "surāsura... (verse 1).
O Brahmin, those defiled by their own conceptual constructions through false meditation have fallen to lower states because of the internal conviction that "we are not Brahman. (2)

If they are non-different, then why do they not experience it as such? To this he says: "through delusion" (*mithyā*). This means: by way of the cause that is false conceptualization—the delusion of perceiving a self in what is not-self. "Fallen downward" (*adhogata*) means having reached a degraded state. || 2 ||
Even those who have entered the ocean of Brahman, conceiving themselves as distinct from Brahman,
become utterly deluded within the terrifying realms of worldly existence.
They conceive of and imagine distinctness and limitedness. || 3 ||
Know that these cognitions, though they belong to Brahman and are stained solely by the act of thinking, are indeed non-action (akarma), even though they are the seed of actions. || 4 ||
Mentation (*manana*) is the repeated contemplation of the identity of the body with the self;

that indeed is what constitutes these actions consisting of the engagement in merit and demerit. Know, however, that even such cognitions are non-action—that is, they are none other than the actionless Brahman. || 4 ||
O Sage, by this very internal process of conceptualization, which takes the form of volition,
[the world] is produced through that formidable handful of seeds— the *karañja* trees of the web of karma.

"Prāṇa, joined with fire (tejas) and together with the self (ātman), leads [the person] to the world as intended," according to the Śruti; thus he states that volition (saṃkalpa) is the cause even in the regulation of the diversity of the sprouting of the seeds of karma, saying: "by means of that which has the form of volition. || 5 ||
These vast rows of skeletons in this world stand, leap about, weep, and laugh. (6)
From Brahma down to a blade of grass, like the wind through its vibrations,
they emerge, they vanish, they wither, and they laugh.
Among these, some are exceedingly clear, such as Hari, Hara, and others;
some are the abodes of slight delusion, such as the serpents, humans, and gods.
