Now, he analyzes and illustrates the individual souls (*jīvas*), which are termed *cit-saṃvit* and correspond to the waves [of consciousness], according to the degrees of clarity of their limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), the distinctions among the stages of knowledge (*jñāna-bhūmikā*), and the various modes of transmigration (*saṃsaraṇa*) occasioned by the diversity of the course of karma—
beginning with the words "These very ones" (*tā etā*). They are exceedingly pure because they represent the ultimate limit of the excellence of knowledge and sovereignty.
Having attained the fitness for the stage of knowledge, they abide in only slight delusion. || 8 ||
Some remain in a state of extreme delusion, such as trees, grass, and the like; others, utterly bewildered by ignorance, have attained the state of worms and insects.

The meaning is that because [beings] possess the capacity for engagement with or withdrawal from the desirable and the undesirable, worms, insects, and so forth do not abide in absolute delusion as do stationary beings (sthāvara). || 9 ||
Some are carried away like blades of grass, far from the great ocean of Brahman;
these have not attained the spiritual stages (bhūmikās), just like serpents, mountains, and the like.
The meaning is that they are carried away and swept along by activities contrary to the scriptures, remaining far from liberation, which is like a great ocean of Brahman. || 10 ||
Perceiving only the presence of a living being, some have arrived in this manner;
whether already born or yet unborn, they are buried by the aged rat of Death.

Thus, having attained the state of humans and so forth through the process of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), [the yogi] perceives—having seen it through the scriptures and heard it—that the mere presence of the stages of yoga (*yogabhūmikā*) is the sole cause for resting from the fatigue of transmigration;
this is the meaning even when the reading is *taṭamātra*. Having perceived it through the scriptures and heard it...

Those who are intent upon that—whether already born or yet to be born—are buried by Kṛtānta (Death) through adverse fate (duradṛṣṭa), which acts as an obstacle and is characterized by an old mouse; that is to say, they are tormented by the spoiling of their foundation. || 11 ||
Having reached the inner essence of the great ocean of the reality of Brahman, Viṣṇu,
Brahmā, Hara, and the others have attained identity with it, together with their bodies.

The "interval" (antara) is the slight differentiator, the adjunct (*upādhi*) of pure knowledge. Through the [three] bodies, one attains that state of being the great ocean of Brahman; that is to say, liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*). || 12 ||
Some, whose nature is characterized by little delusion, remain supported by that very ocean of Brahma,
which has an unfathomable shore, ground, and flood.
Having relied upon him through meditative absorptions—he whose further shore is not seen and whose flood is thus full—[he crossed over]. || 13 ||

Some multitudes of births yet to be experienced, and crores of multitudes of births already experienced, as well as the various classes of beings—some barren and some manifesting in darkness—remain established [in this state]. (14)
Even though [the truth] has been revealed through the attainment of a body qualified [for it], those who are tamasic remain blind with passion.
Some go from above to below, like a large fruit falling from the hand;
some go further upward from above, while others go even lower from below.
From above, meaning from a superior birth, [one falls] below, meaning to an inferior birth such as that of an animal and so forth. || 15 ||
This inexhaustible mine that produces much pleasure and pain has arrived here through the non-remembrance of the supreme state;
it goes to destruction through the realization of the supreme state.
It was like the pain from poison [subsiding] through the remembrance of the Lord of Birds. || 16 ||

Having thus elaborated upon the state of being a living soul as the source of thousands of misfortunes, and reminding [the disciple] of its root cause, he states the means for its cessation, beginning with the word "bahv-": "This state of being a living soul is such that it contains many mines— that is, sources— of births that produce pleasure and pain, namely attachment and the other [afflictions]."
It has arisen from the fault of failing to reflect upon and forgetting the supreme state, which is the reality of one's own self. || 16 ||

Thus ends the twelfth canto, titled "The Description of the Extensive Arising of Saṃsāra," within the *Bhārgavopākhyāna* (The Narrative of Bhārgava) in the *Sthitiprakaraṇa* (Section on Stability) of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, a work of the Ṛṣis.
Thus ends the twelfth canto, titled "The Description of the Detailed Arising of Saṃsāra," in the *Sthitiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The Thirteenth Chapter.
Kāla said:
"Of these classes of beings, as of waves from the ocean..."
Like various and diverse creepers in the month of Mādhava.
Having thus described the mental powers of Bhṛgu and Kāla,
the rising [of Śukra] to go into the presence of Śukra is now set forth.

Among the aforementioned classes of living beings, he states that only those who are liberated while living (jīvanmukta) have achieved their purpose, and not others, with the words beginning "etāsām" (among these). The phrase "of those emerged from the ocean" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. The connection with the subsequent clause is: "among these, those who have conquered the delusion of the mind are 'bhavyāḥ'—that is, they become those who have achieved their purpose."

In the case of *bhavya*, *geya*, *pravacanīya*, and so forth, the suffix *-yat* is applied in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). The inclusion of this triad beginning with *yakṣa* is for the sake of illustration and not for the purpose of an exhaustive enumeration, since [the suffix] is also possible in the case of *manuṣya* and others. || 1 ||
Fortunate ones who have conquered mental delusion, who have perceived the higher and lower states of the world,
and who are liberated while living, roam here as yakṣas, gandharvas, and kiṃnaras.
But others, such as stationary and moving beings, are deluded like wood or walls;
others have their delusion destroyed—what need is there to deliberate upon them? (3)

With the intention that only the ignorant—those endowed with the fourfold means of accomplishment—are qualified for the investigation of the scriptures, and not those who already know the truth, he says: "What [is there] for them? (3).
In this world, for the sake of establishing the self of living beings who are awakening, various treatises have been composed and promulgated by those who have realized the Self. (4)

If it is asked, "For what purpose, then, do they maintain a body? the intention is that it is solely for the sake of uplifting the ignorant through the composition of scriptures; with this in mind, he says: "In the world... (verse 4).
But for those whose intentions are fully awakened through the exhaustion of their misdeeds,
their intellect proceeds stainlessly in the investigations of the treatises.

Based on the Smṛti passage, "Knowledge arises for a person from the destruction of sinful karma," [the author] says "saṃprabuddha... (v. 5) with the intention that even the scripture is fruitful only for those with pure minds, and not for others.
The delusion of the mind dissolves through the investigation of the true scriptures,
just as the darkness of night vanishes from the sky due to the movement of the sun.
That which arises in the night is "śārvaram."
For a mind that does not diminish leads only to delusion and not to accomplishment;
like a mist obscuring the view, it leaps about like a Vetāla spirit.
"Like mist" is an illustration for obscuration; "like a vetāla" is an illustration for distraction. It leaps and dances. || 7 ||
O Sage, in this world, for all bodies whatsoever, it is the mind alone that is the vessel for pleasure, pain, and objects; it is not the body composed of flesh.
Of bodies, that is, of living beings who have attained the nature of those [bodies]. || 8 ||
This collection of flesh and bone that is seen, composed of the five elements—know it to be a mental construction; in the ultimate sense, it is not the body.
O Sage, this son of yours has quickly obtained exactly what he performed with his mind and body; we are not at fault in this matter.
Whatever action a person performs with whatever latent impression (vāsanā), he obtains exactly that; here, there is no agency for anyone else.
Who indeed is there in this world, even a lord of the earth, who possesses the power to undo what has been internally resolved by one’s own mental impressions? 12.

With the intention that "even by the mere continuation of a mental impression (*manovāsanā*), that which is accomplished in a single moment cannot be achieved by us even with great effort over a long period; therefore, there is not even the slightest suspicion of fault in us," he says: "that which was mentally intended" (*svānusaṃhitam*). || 12 ||
Those creations which are the expanses of hell, those desires for birth and death—by means of the mentalizing of one's own mind, all this, though motionless, bestows suffering. (13)
That state, consisting of mental deliberation, is motionless; even its slight movement brings suffering. || 13 ||
What is the use of much speaking here by one who merely collects words?
Arise, O Blessed One; let us go to where your son resides.

The meaning is that "the collection of sounds" refers to hearing [them], performed by one who acts as such, and not by one who demonstrates the meaning. Regarding the word "yām" (we go), the plural number is used either according to the rule *asmado dvayośca* ("for the word *asmad*, the dual and plural are used") or because of the inclusion of the attendants. || 14 ||
Having experienced everything with his mental body as if in an instant, Śukra remained there like an ascetic, composed through contact with the rays of the moon. (15)

The meaning is that, having enjoyed every celestial pleasure with a body fashioned by the mind, he then descended to earth through the sequence of ether and the other elements; entering the herbs through contact with the moonbeams, and passing through the stages of becoming food and so forth, he reached a succession of births and now stands as an ascetic at the Samaṅgā river.
The vital breath (prāṇapavana), released from the mind, becomes like the dew-drops falling from the rays of the moon;
having become thus, it remains within as potency (vīrya). || 16 ||

He clarifies what was stated regarding "due to contact with the moon's rays" with the words *tatprāṇa* and so forth: when the vital breath (*prāṇa-pavana*) of that semen is released from the mind (*citta*), which is the power of consciousness, it becomes condensed;
through its state as dew (*avaśyāya*), by virtue of contact with the moon's rays, it takes on a similar nature and, via the medium of grain, results in that fruit, such as rice and other crops.
Having become [the seed], having entered the man, and having become virile semen, it remains within the womb of the woman; this is the meaning. || 16 ||
Having spoken thus regarding the course of the world, the Lord Kāla, as if smiling,
seized Bhṛgu with his hand from [Brahmā’s] hand, just as the sun seizes the moon.
The ablative case in "hastāt" is used in the sense of an elided *lyap* suffix (i.e., it functions as an adverbial ablative). The meaning is "having extended the hand.

In the case of the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), by means of *lakṣitalakṣaṇā* (indirect indication based on a secondary characteristic), the word "hand" (*hasta*) includes that which is denoted by the word "ray" (*kara*). || 17 ||
"Ah! How truly wondrous is the established order of destiny!"—saying this softly, the venerable Bhṛgu rose up like the sun from the mountain of sunrise.
Of necessity, fate, or karma. || 18 ||
O dear one, those two treasures of splendor, rising together at that time within the net-like clouds in the sky,
shone like two [suns] of equal emergence in a cloudless firmament, as if to sport therein.
They rose up together like two clouds, possessing both the full moon and the sun.
Śrī Vālmīki said:

The particle *ha* is used here in the sense of *kila* (indeed); *aṅga* is a vocative particle. In the Mandara grove thick with *tāla* trees, those two repositories of splendor, Bhṛgu and Kāla, rose up together, simultaneously, like two rain-bearing clouds in the expanse of the sky rising at the same time; indeed, they were complete.
The meaning is that they shine like the full moon and the sun. || 19 ||
When the sage had spoken thus, the day departed; the sun went to its setting for the performance of evening rites;
and the assembly, having offered salutations, departed to bathe.
At the end of the night, he arrived together with the rays of the sun. || 20 ||

Thus ends the thirteenth canto, titled "The Consolation of Bhṛgu," within the "Episode of Bhārgava" in the Section on Stability (*sthitiprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, belonging to the lineage of the Seers (*ārṣa*). 13.
Thus ends the thirteenth canto, titled "The Consolation of Bhṛgu," in the Sthitiprakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The eighth day.
The Fourteenth Canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Then the two gods, Kāla and Bhṛgu, [emerged] from the cave of Mount Mandara.
They set out on the earth to go to the bank of the river Samaṅgā. || 1 ||
Having gone there, the awakening of Śukra who was absorbed in meditation by those two, the reminder of his former conduct, and his desire to depart are narrated. (1)
"Having descended to the earth"—this is the ellipsis. || 1 ||
Descending from the mountain, those two of great splendor beheld sky-dwellers sleeping in bowers formed by networks of fresh golden creepers.
The hosts of gods who move through the sky and the birds.
Playing in the courtyard of the sky upon swings made of winding creepers,
they recalled blue lotuses with their gazes, as innocent and lovely as those of a doe.
By those side-long glances, so utterly charming like those of does, lotuses were called to mind;
for since the sight of a similar object is a cause for recollection, a resemblance is understood. (3)
They sat upon high stone slabs used as seats by perfected beings (siddhas);
they appeared as if their very forms were composed of vigor, having effortlessly beheld the three worlds.
Those for whom high fragments of rock served as seats upon which they sat;
who remained like personified energies, having assumed physical forms; and by whom the three worlds were surveyed with effortless ease. || 4 ||
He saw the leaders of the elephant herds, who were submerged in a continuous downpour of falling flowers and whose trunks were raised high as tall palm trees.
They both saw leaders of elephant herds—those who possess trunks as long and thick as palm trees rising high; this description applies to all instances [of the phrase]. (5)
They were as if intoxicated, drowsy with pride, and standing there like personified forms of intoxication;
their limbs were red with the filaments of flowers, and their tails were crimsoned by the wind.

He further qualifies those very [elephants] with the word "mada" (intoxication): by means of the filaments of flowers, and because they are filled with pollen by the wind colored by their reddened limbs, they have "reddish tails"—this [attribute] connects with both the preceding and the following [phrases] according to the *dehalī-dīpa* (door-lamp) maxim. || 6 ||
He saw beautiful, restless yak-tails serving as fly-whisks for the circle of kings,
which were immersed in incessant showers of falling flowers.
The *camaras* are a specific kind of deer; they were like the fly-whisks (*cāmaras*) belonging to the circle of mountains, that is, the assembly of kings of the mountains. || 7 ||
There were wild date-palms inhabited by kinnaras, their branches reaching out in straight lines, while their hollow bamboos emitted shrill whistling sounds as they struck one another's fruits.

The phrase "they saw the *kinnaras*" is to be connected with what precedes. They saw various species of the *bhūma-kharjūra* (the ground-date palm), which had reached a state of straightness and rectitude up to the very ends of their branches; they were captivated by games characterized by the mutual striking and hitting of *kharjūra* fruits.
Those monkeys by whom the hollow bamboos, having grown roots downward, were made to bear fruit. || 8 ||
[He saw] monkeys with faces as dark as red mineral ore, fiercely dancing,
whose mountain peaks and grove-dwellings were covered by canopies of spreading creepers.
Those whose faces were distorted and foul-mouthed, as red as ochre ore; those who were fierce and intoxicated in their dancing and twitching. (9)
[He saw] the perfected ones (siddhas) being struck by celestial women with mandāra flowers,
and [the mountains] covered by clouds that resembled pale-red mineral ores.

[He saw] the Siddhas, who are a particular class of divine beings, being struck with Mandāra flowers by the celestial nymphs (apsaras) to signal the time for dalliance; for this very reason, they were covered by cloud-like cloths that were pale-red like minerals and possessed of no gaps or openings. || 10 ||
The rivers, with their masses of waves covered in kunda and mandāra flowers, appeared like Buddhist renunciants who have abandoned contact with people on the banks;
they seemed to have donned the ornaments of the month of Madhu out of longing for the ocean.
The slopes and precipitous regions, devoid of human contact and unfit for the passage of people;

the example of Buddhist renunciants is cited with the intention of suggesting their fitness for falling in vain; they were seized and held fast by the lovely ocean, as if by the very cause of its longing and yearning.

The month of Caitra is the "honey-month" (*madhumāsa*); those [women] who possess adornments—such as flowers, sprouts, and other ornaments—related to that month are described by the compound. However, according to the reading *utkaṭatācāntamadhumāṃsaprasādhanāḥ*, it means those whose adornments consist of honey and meat that have been consumed (*ācāntaiḥ*) for the sake of the ocean’s intensity (*utkaṭatāyai*), that is, for the intoxication of enjoyment.
Those whose adornment [is such]. || 11 ||
The trees, their limbs laden with a weight of flowers and shaken by the wind,
seemed like drunkards reeling upon obtaining honey, with bees for their eyes.
Beholding the vast splendor of the king of mountains here and there,
the two of them reached the earth adorned with cities and towns.
In an instant, they reached there the river Samaṅgā, which had waves shimmering with flowers and was as if composed entirely of blossoms.

In the compound *puṣpalolataraṅgām*, since the possessive sense is already obtained through the *bahuvrīhi* itself, the suffix *-in* is used for the purpose of indicating an excessive and constant connection. To clarify this very point, he says: "as if consisting of all flowers" (*sarvapuṣpamayīmiva*). || 14 ||
Then, on a certain bank, Bhṛgu beheld his son,
who had undergone a transformation of body and attained another state of being.
Another state is the absence of semen. || 15 ||
With his senses stilled, established in meditative concentration, and the deer of his mind motionless,
he appeared as if long rested at last to quell his long-standing fatigue.
For the sake of pacifying that very long weariness—the weariness of beginningless saṃsāra.
He seemed to be contemplating the infinite courses of the ocean of worldly existence—long enjoyed and recently abandoned—which are incessantly filled with joy and sorrow. (17)
Long enjoyed, they were soon abandoned and cast away. || 17 ||
Surely it has attained immobility, like a wheel that has spun excessively,
as if from the extreme exhaustion of revolving through the cycles of the infinite worlds.
The simile "like a wheel that has spun excessively" is intended to illustrate that, through the process of the subsiding of passion, the mind comes to rest by itself. || 18 ||
He stood in a secluded spot, lovely and solitary, relying on his own splendor;
his laughter was stilled, and the agitation and attachment of his mind were utterly broken.
He clearly states the very intention behind the analogy of the wheel in the verse beginning with "upaśānteha" (19).
Established in non-conceptual samādhi, he was free from the fluctuations of dualities, laughing at the entire course of worldly existence with a mind that was coolly detached.
From the occurrence of dualities, such as cold and heat, pleasure and pain, and so forth. || 20 ||
Devoid of all objective phenomena, free from the state of being an enjoyer,
with the web of conceptual construction cast aside, it rests upon the supreme station.

The *vṛttāntas* are the active manifestations; their fruits are the states of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtās*). The "Great State" (*mahāpadam*) is the unlimited bliss of the Self (*ātmasukham*). || 21 ||
In that state of infinite rest, he rests within the Self,
remaining like a white jewel that does not grasp a reflection.
Bhṛgu beheld his son, whose intellect was fully awakened and steadfast, and who was completely free from the conceptual constructions of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted.
Beholding that son of Bhṛgu, Kāla spoke these words to Bhṛgu, which resembled the roar of the ocean: "This is indeed your son. (24)
With the words "Awake!", he emerged from his meditative absorption,
just as a peacock slowly rouses itself at the roar of thunderclouds.
The peacock is the wearer of a crest. || 25 ||
Opening his eyes, he beheld at the end two powerful lords, Kāla and Bhṛgu,
who had arrived together like the two gods, the Moon and the Sun.
"Near" means in close proximity; they arise together and manifest face-to-face, but not by arising separately. || 26 ||
Then, rising from her seat of *kadamba* creepers, she bowed to those two beloved Brahmins who had arrived together, appearing like Hari and Hara.
The two brahmins were disguised as brahmins. || 27 ||
Having performed their mutual greetings, they sat down upon a stone slab,
like Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara, who are worshipped by the world, seated upon the summit of Mount Meru.
O Rāma, that twice-born man, Śāntajapa, who had performed mutual social customs such as greetings and expressions of respect appropriate for the occasion on the bank of the Samaṅgā,
then spoke these peaceful words, beautiful like a flow of nectar: || 29 ||
His recitation is stilled and his meditative absorption is perfected; for it is seen from the meaning of the verbal root that "japa" refers to mental [recitation].
This half-verse, due to the greater force of the logical sequence over the sequence of recitation, should be placed before the words "kadambalatikāpīṭhāt. || 29 ||
By the sight of you two today, I have attained peace, like the world when the cool-rayed and hot-rayed ones [the moon and sun] have come together. (30)
Nirvāṇa is happiness. || 30 ||
That delusion of my mind, which could not be destroyed by scripture, nor by austerity, nor even by knowledge or learning— that very thing has been exhausted by the sight of you two.
"By knowledge, by worship, by learning, by the knowledge of Brahman"—this is an exaggeration (atiśayokti) for the sake of praise.
"Vām" means "of you two. || 31 ||
Showers of pure nectar do not gladden the inner self as much as these visions of the great ones bring supreme joy. (32)
"O you two of immense splendor, who have purified this region with your feet, as the moon and sun purify the sky? (33)
To him who had spoken thus, Bhṛgu replied:
"O scion of Raghu, remember your own self; you are awakened, you are not ignorant. (34)
Awakened by Bhṛgu, he remembered his own state in a previous birth for a mere moment, his eyes opened through meditation. (35)
He is one by whom the divine eye has been opened and unveiled through meditative absorption (dhyāna). || 35 ||
Then, with a face smiling from wonder and a joyful mind, that best of speakers uttered words slow with reflection: (36)
"From wonder" means from the sight of something marvelous. || 36 ||
The destiny of the Supreme Self has its commencement unknown in this world;
under its control, this expansive wheel of the universe revolves. (37)
Niyati is the power of illusion (māyā-śakti) which is the cause for the determination of the fruits of karma. || 37 ||
My infinite past births, though unknown,
have experienced infinite fruits of their conditions, as if they were fashioned by the end of an eon.

The fruits of the *daśās* are the results of evil periods such as death and fainting, consisting of suffering, delusion, and so forth; [this is] like [the destruction] caused by the end of the eon (*kalpānta*), that is, by dissolution (*pralaya*), resulting from rain, wind, fire, and the like. || 38 ||
We have witnessed fierce conflicts and the delusions of acquiring wealth;
we have also wandered for a long time through the sorrowless regions of Mount Meru. (39)
Those kings, whose power consists of harshness, agitation, anger, and exertion, are merely deluded by the pursuit of wealth. 39.
On the slopes of the mountain of the gods, there is the yellow, fragrant water of the Mandākinī, reddened by the filaments of mandāra flowers and filled with kahlāra lilies.
Milk or water. || 40 ||
I wandered through the groves of Mount Mandara, where golden creepers were in full bloom,
and upon the mountain peaks of Meru, beautiful with flowers and the shade of wish-fulfilling trees.
There is nothing that has not been experienced, there is nothing that has not been done,
and there is nothing that has not been seen among the various circumstances, whether pleasant or unpleasant.

"There is nothing [that remains] to be done"—this means that everything has been performed, enjoyed, and seen. "In favorable and unfavorable conditions" refers to states or circumstances that are agreeable or disagreeable. || 42 ||
That which was to be known has now been known; that which was to be seen has been seen unimpaired.
Now, long weary, I have come to rest; all my delusion has vanished.
He demonstrates that through even a single cognition, all things are known—thus: "It is known. "I have been weary for a long time;
now I am at rest. (43)
"Arise, dear father, let us go; let us behold that body situated on Mount Mandara, which has become so completely withered, like a dried-up forest creeper. (44)
In this world, there is nothing desired by me, nor is there anything undesired;
I merely wander about to observe the arrangement of destiny. (45)
"What is desired by you through that body? To this he replies: "No. (45)
Whatever is exceedingly beautiful and practiced by the noble,
that I follow with steadfastness and a single-minded resolve; may that desired wisdom be sufficient for me.
I am performing this customary legal proceeding. || 46 ||

One might object: "Surely, as you wander about to observe the fixed arrangement [of the world], because of your attachment (*abhiniveśa*) to it, you will again fall into saṃsāra—such as by following the desires of celestial nymphs—as before.
Anticipating this, [the author] replies: "No, because [that attachment] is merely a persistence [of habit] that has been sublated by the most firm knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*)."

He states that there is a risk of falling back into the same attachment as before, beginning with the word "yad" (since): because, by means of the notion of a single being— that the Self alone is the one reality, the ultimately true existence,
and nothing else— one forms a firm conviction.

I follow—that is, I pursue—exactly that conduct which is exceedingly beautiful and brings about ultimate auspiciousness, and which has been practiced by the noble ones and other liberated-in-life (jīvanmukta) beings, so that it may become firm; I do not follow my former deluded behavior as before.
Therefore, may the understanding regarding your and my previous bodies, lives, and so forth, be entirely correct and favorable.

There is no harm whatsoever in that name. By it, I mean: "I shall carry out the worldly conduct of one who experiences the remainder of what has been commenced [by past karma], but I shall not become attached like a fool."

Thus ends the fourteenth canto, titled "Description of the Remembrance of Previous Births by Bhārgava," in the Section on Stability (Sthitiprakaraṇa) of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Valmiki. 14.
Thus ends the fourteenth canto, titled "The Description of the Subsequent Birth of Bhārgava," in the Sthitiprakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
Fifteenth Canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus reflecting upon the courses of the world, those knowers of reality—
From that bank of the Samaṅgā river, those whose lives were flickering set forth. || 1 ||
In this [chapter], having observed that body of Śukra, his lamentation is presented;
through the specific description of its cause, his true nature is also taught. (1)

Thus reflecting upon the worldly courses of existence (*jāgatīḥ sāṃsārikīrgatīḥ*) in the manner previously described, they set out from the bank of the *Samaṅgā* toward the hermitage of Bhṛgu; that is, they departed. By the phrase "with flickering life-breaths" (*cañcalāsavaḥ*), it is indicated that the metaphorical movement of theirs consists solely in the activity of their vital breaths (*prāṇakriyā*), and not that there is any activity within the Self (*ātman*). || 1 ||
Gradually ascending into the sky and emerging from the hollows of the clouds,
they reached the cave of Mount Mandara in an instant by way of the path of the Siddhas.
By the hollows of the clouds, that is, by the openings in the clouds. || 2 ||
On the plateau of that mountain, the descendant of Bhṛgu beheld his own body from a previous birth, now withered but still covered by moist leaves.
On the plateau, that is, on the upper portion of the ground. || 3 ||
And he said this: "O father, this slender body is indeed that very one which was formerly cherished by you with pleasant enjoyments. (4)
This refers to the statement that will be explained below; "tanvī" means slender or emaciated. || 4 ||
This is that body of mine, whose every limb the Creator long anointed with affection using camphor, agallochum, and sandalwood.
He elaborates upon what was stated as "by means of the enjoyments of pleasure" with the verse beginning "camphor," etc. (verse 5).
This is that very body of mine, for which a cool bed was prepared with heaps of Mandāraka flowers in the groves of Mount Meru.
Behold, this very body of mine, once caressed by hosts of intoxicated celestial women,
now lies upon the surface of the earth, crushed by the mouths of crawling serpents.
"Crushed" means trampled and pulverized by reptiles and insects, such as snakes, scorpions, and the like; that is to say, it was perforated. || 7 ||
This very body of mine, by which I long sported in the groves of sandalwood gardens, has now become a withered skeleton. (8)
In the garden groves of sandalwood and yellow sandalwood trees, it shines, graced by playful sports;
this is clear if the reading is "nandanāḥ" [meaning "those who rejoice"]. || 8 ||
Today my body withers away, deprived of the mental state that, through the agitation of intense passion, sought union with the limbs of celestial nymphs.

One withers away by means of such a mental state—one that is devoid of and abandoned by those lofty waves of passion which shatter the bodiless god of love; this is expressed in the present tense (*laṭ*) in the sense of a state of being (*bhāve*). || 9 ||
Amidst those various amorous pastimes and in those various conditions, you are so bound by the contemplation of them; how then, O little body, can you remain at ease?
Now, addressing the body itself, he laments with the words beginning "in those various," and so forth:
"in those various diverse locations," such as the regions of celestial gardens; "in those various diverse stages," such as childhood, youth, and so on;
and likewise, "of those types never before experienced," namely those particular forms of beauty and ornamentation.

Having been one whose nature was connected with the contemplation of song, laughter, pleasure, amorous play, and so forth, how are you now at ease? The meaning is: why do you not grieve for that [past state]? || 10 ||
Alas! You who were once named Śavā, you have now reached a state of emaciation through asceticism;
you have become a mere skeleton, O ill-fated woman, and you terrify me. 11.
The state of being a skeleton, with nothing remaining but bones. || 11 ||
I am now terrified of that very same body by which I once rejoiced in its playful dalliances, for it has now become a mere skeleton.
Behold, those ants are now clinging to my chest, where in former times there was a necklace with the appearance of a web of stars.
A *hāra* is a string of pearls. || 13 ||
Behold: by that very body of mine, which once captivated excellent women with its luster like molten gold, I am now dragged away as a mere skeleton.
Like molten, flowing gold, it is radiant with its lovely luster;
"greed" refers to the longing for sensual enjoyments. "Is carried" means it is borne [by the wind]. "Behold! is a further address directed toward the father. || 14 ||
Behold, with my wide-open mouth, which is like the dried skin of an ascetic, and with my hideous skull-face, the deer in the forest are terrified. (15)
With a distorted face that was crooked. || 15 ||
I see that the cave of my corpse’s belly, due to its state of complete desiccation,
shines as if illuminated by the net of the sun’s rays, as if by discernment itself.
Because it has entered within, it shines by means of the light—the manifesting web of solar rays.
In the expression "I see," the meaning of the sentence is the object (karman), just as in the case of "Look! The deer is running. 16.
This slender body, withered and lying supine upon the stone of the mountain, seems to lead the hearts of the virtuous toward dispassion by means of its own insignificance. (17)
By means of [pointing out] the emptiness and worthlessness of one's own self—in other words, by demonstrating its contemptible nature—it leads [one], as it were, [to wisdom]. || 17 ||
Freed from attachment to sound, form, taste, touch, and smell,
this very [body] withers away on the mountain through non-conceptual meditative absorption alone.

My slender body, liberated from desire and longing for objects ending with fragrance, has for all this time been beyond my perception; but now, it is directly before me, and as she possesses a non-conceptual concentration (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*), she indeed withers and suffers. 18.
Having surely been freed from the demon of the mind, her body remains as if in bliss; it does not fear even the slightest injury from the gods.
Happiness is well-being [attained] through calamities and misfortunes brought about by the gods. 19.
When the vampire of the mind has been completely stilled, the body attains a fraction of that bliss which cannot be reached even by sovereignty over the entire world.
The construction is as follows: [even] by means of sovereignty over the world—that is, pertaining to the three worlds—one cannot equal even a fraction of this wonder of bliss. || 20 ||
Behold how he sleeps happily in the forest—his doubts stilled, all curiosity vanished, and the web of mental constructions cast aside. (21)
The tree of the body, agitated by the frantic agitation of the monkey-mind,
shakes with such force that it uproots itself.

Agitated by impetuosity— the restlessness of desire and so forth— he does not merely move in such a way as to destroy his own branches, twigs, and leaves, such as the presence of discernment and wholesome latent impressions; rather, he moves in such a way that he cuts them down from the very root and becomes uprooted.
The meaning is that it causes the individual soul to fall precisely into the wombs of stationary beings and others who are not qualified for discernment and the like. || 22 ||
My body, liberated from the miseries of the mind and remaining as if established in supreme bliss, no longer perceives the conflict between elephants, clouds, and lions upon the mountain. 23.
On this Mount Mandara, my body— now liberated from the misfortune characterized by the mind—
no longer perceives any conflict, enmity, or hostility with elephants, clouds, lions, or tigers, such as the desire for battle, roaring, or attacking.

The meaning is that he does not rejoice today as he did previously when he was absorbed in the joy of watching the spectacle from outside; or rather, the meaning is that he no longer sees today the reflection of the bodies, battles, or forms of the gods, demons, and men upon the crystal slabs of the mountain (*adrau*). However, in the reading "he watches the drama" (*nāṭyaṃ paśyati*), [the interpretation is as follows:]...

Just as one liberated while living (jīvanmukta), established in the Supreme Self which is supreme bliss, first beholds the drama of the self-dancer— whose bodies are like an elephant (gross), like a cloud (subtle), and like Hari (the causal)— so too does my body [behold its own].

The meaning is that, because his mind is liberated from all misfortune, he remains distinct [from the world] and observes the performance of his own self acting out various forms upon this mountain— here as clouds, there as rocks, and here as lions, monkeys, and so forth. || 23 ||
I see no other source of welfare for living beings than mindlessness (acittatva), which is like the arrival of autumn to the mist of delusion caused by the fever of all desires. (24)

It is the arrival of autumn for the seed of clouds—the mist characterized by delusion (*moha*), which is the cause of all those fevers that take the form of desires; it is the arrival of autumn for the mist of delusion, which acts as a fever in all desires or in all directions. It is the state of mindlessness, the destruction of the mind.
Without || 24 ||
Those very ones of great intellect, whose minds were once tranquil, have now reached the limit of the enjoyment of pleasure by becoming despondent. (25)
The enjoyments of pleasure, beginning with those of the world of Hiraṇyagarbha and ending with the bliss of the Creator, are the experiences of sensory objects;
their limit, their ultimate boundary, is the bliss of the Infinite (bhūmānanda). Because it is the direct realization of the undivided Brahman, it belongs to the one of great intellect;
because the mental activities of passion and the like have subsided, it belongs to the one of tranquil intellect. || 25 ||
"By good fortune, I behold this body of mine in the forest—freed from all states of suffering, established in a state free from fever, and beyond mental agitation. (26)
He rejoices, considering the equality of his own body with that of one liberated while living: "All... [etc.]. "By good fortune" means through the dawning of merit. || 26 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, it is said that at that time the descendant of Bhṛgu repeatedly took up very many bodies again and again.
The intention behind Rāma’s question is clear. || 27 ||
Since the body was produced by Bhṛgu, what further excellence has arisen in it now, or is it merely a matter of lamentation? (28)
From those bodies; in that body, what [is it] and for what reason is it "great," meaning increased? The word "excess" (*atiśaya*)—of affection (*sneha*)—is to be supplied as the remainder. || 28 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, that conceptualization of Śukra which had reached the state of a living being was born as the son of Bhṛgu, in the form of Bhārgava, consisting of the nature of karma.

At the time of his departure [from the body], the virtuous deeds performed by Śukra in previous kalpas— which serve as the cause for his enjoyment of his current position as a planet— undergo transformation into the form of a body produced from the lineage of Bhṛgu within this kalpa.

Because it persists for a long time during the dissolution (pralaya) in the form of latent impressions (vāsanā) possessing such a form, it enters that heart— following the sequence of ether and so forth during the production of Bhṛgu’s body in this current aeon— by means of food, through the flow of the prāṇa and apāna breaths, and by way of transformation into the form of semen.

Since the commencement of the body of Śuka occurred solely in accordance with the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of past desires and actions, which were solidified through long-term practice, even though he has experienced the fruits of only a few actions, many *prārabdha* karmas yet to be experienced remain; therefore, his excessive attachment toward him is appropriate, whereas it is not so toward other bodies.

With the intention that there is no remainder of those karmas to be experienced, Vasiṣṭha gives the following answer beginning with "of Śukra": *kalanā* refers to the previous formation at the time of departure [from the body], namely the formation of the shape of a future body.
The phrase "having the form of Bhārgava" means that it was the shape of a body produced by Bhṛgu which existed in a previous kalpa; this is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 29 ||
For she, having first emerged from the supreme state and reached the station of the elemental ether (bhūtākāśa), became agitated by the winds.

The connection with what follows is: "For she herself has now become this body of Uśanas. He explains the sequence by which this occurs with the words beginning "as being for the first time" (*idaṃprathamatvena*).
From the supreme state (*parātpadāt*), that is, from the Lord who is variegated by *māyā* and remains at the time of dissolution, [she arises] as being for the first time.

Having assumed the state of the first body belonging to this kalpa, and having manifested slightly— like the internal power of a sprout within a seed that has been moistened and swollen— it gradually proceeds through the stages of space and the other elements;
reaching a state of equilibrium with those respective elements, it is transformed by the vital breath (prāṇavāta) through the medium of rain into the form of food and so forth.
Being included within. || 30 ||
Entering the heart of Bhṛgu by means of the flow of the prāṇa and apāna breaths,
they gradually attained the state of semen and became the body of Uśanas.
By means of the flow of the *apāna* [wind], which consumes food and consists of the specific activity of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). || 31 ||
Having received the sacred rites of initiation according to the Brahma-vidhi, she remained there before her father;
after a long time, she attained the state of a withered skeleton.

In her, the *brāhma* sacraments—those appropriate for birth as a Brahmin, such as *garbhādhāna*, *puṃsavana*, *jātakarman*, *annaprāśana*, *caula*, *upanayana*, and so forth—were performed according to the prescribed rules. The sense is that one cannot be entitled to receive the planets or enjoy their benefits if one has not been consecrated by these rites. || 32 ||
Since this was the first time that this body of Brahmā had arrived,
Śukra then uttered that lamentation directed toward it.

Since she came from the presence of Brahmā in the manner described, for the first time and for that reason, it was at an improper time (*akāle*). The suffix *dā* is used here for the ablative case (*pañcamī*) by Vedic license (*chāndasa*). || 33 ||
Though free from passion and devoid of desire, Śukra, assuming the form of Samāṅgā, grieved for his body; for such is the nature born of the physical frame.
With the intention that even the wise do not transcend *prārabdha* (the karma already set in motion), he says: "Free from... (verse 34).
Whether for the wise or the ignorant, this process persists as long as the body exists;
this worldly activity continues always, whether through attachment or detachment.

"As long as the body lasts" means for as long as one lives, at all times; "the sequence" means the rule of restraint that never deviates. The meaning is that there is a distinction: for the knower it is through detachment (*asakti*), whereas for the ignorant it is through lack of detachment (*asakti*).
Those who have fully understood the course of existence and those who are ignorant, following the nature of cattle, remain within worldly conventions like those caught in a net.
For this very reason, he states that those two are equal even in other conventional usages with the words "ye" (those who). || 36 ||
In worldly transaction, the unlearned and the all-knowing scholar are exactly alike;
here, the difference lies solely in their latent impressions (vāsanā), which are the cause of bondage and liberation.
If that is so, since both are equal, from what source does the distinction arise that one is bound while the other is liberated? To this he says: "Vāsanā" (Verse 37).
For as long as there is a body, so long is there suffering in suffering and pleasure in pleasure;
yet the wise, whose minds are unattached, demonstrate this as if they were unawakened.
In suffering, when the cause of suffering is encountered, they show [it] and mock [it]. || 38 ||
Great-souled ones are always happy amidst pleasures and sorrowful amidst states of suffering; for they appear as if they were unawakened, even though they are clearly seen [as awakened]. (39)

In the occurrences of suffering and in the causes of suffering, they appear as if afflicted, as though they were suffering; yet, while within the sphere of empirical activity that is perceived, they conduct themselves like those who are unawakened, whereas regarding their own true nature, they remain firmly established and do not behave like the ignorant—this is the meaning. || 39 ||
The reflections of the sun are agitated, but not the sun itself; likewise, the knower of reality remains amidst the activities of the world through both movement and stillness. (40)

To ward off the contradiction of a single entity simultaneously possessing both stable and unstable states, he provides an illustration with the words "of the sun" (sūryasya). The meaning is: just as it is only the reflected forms of the sun situated in water that are agitated and move, but not its stable disc-form situated in the sky, so it is here; the word "punaḥ" is used in the sense of "tu" (but/rather). || 40 ||
Like the sun remaining steady and composed within its reflections,
he is truly awakened even while appearing as one whose intellect is unawakened, though he has completely abandoned worldly activity.
Just as the sun, though remaining established in its own state, appears in reflections to be in a non-own-state, undivided yet as if moving;
in the same way, the Buddha himself, while situated within conventional reality, appears to possess an unawakened intellect—this is the meaning. || 41 ||
For one whose faculties of intellect are liberated is liberated even if the faculties of action are bound;
likewise, one whose faculties of intellect are bound is bound even if the faculties of action are liberated. (42)

Anticipating the objection that "in that case, he too would be bound by actions prescribed or forbidden, just like one who is ignorant," [the author] says—with the intention that only those actions performed preceded by non-attachment of the intellect and senses cause bondage, and not others:
"He whose self is deluded regarding the objects of the senses is called a hypocrite," and so forth. (42)
In this world, the perception of pleasure and pain, as well as the perception of bondage and liberation,
has the intellect and the senses alone as its cause, just as light is the cause for illumination.
Of the perception of pleasure and pain, and of the experience of pleasure and pain. || 43 ||
Maintain conduct appropriate for the external world while remaining free from internal worldly conduct;
indeed, remain perfectly equanimous, with all desires completely stilled. (44)

To the question, "In that case, how should I remain? he says: "Externally... [and so forth]. Devoid of conventional conduct, firm in the realization of the immutable Self, and thus inactive; for this very reason, equanimous, being free from all partiality. (44)
Free from all desires, abiding in the Self by means of the self, perform the necessary actions; for the maintenance of the body is indeed required.

"Desire" is attachment to the fruits of action; perform actions with a mind that is liberated from that [attachment] and established in the Self—that is, abiding in Brahman. "Surely" (nūnam) is used in the sense of a reason; for actions are the functions of the body, meaning they are its very nature. Indeed, it is not possible for one who bears a body to renounce them.
"Karmas in their entirety," so it has been stated by the Blessed One as well. || 45 ||

Do not fall into this pit of worldly existence on the path of saṃsāra, which is filled with the great whirlpools of mental and physical ailments, and which is a fierce, dark well of possessiveness that brings about calamity. (46)

Mental anxieties are *ādhi*s; physical ailments are *vyādhi*s. Great whirlpools are the revolutions of birth and death, which are themselves the pits and chasms; do not fall into that pit of blind darkness called "mine-ness" on such a path of *saṃsāra*. 46.
You do not exist in things, nor do things exist in you, O lotus-eyed one;
you are of the nature of pure awakening—remain as the self, firmly established within.

He states the means for its non-falling away with the words beginning "But you are not," etc. The meaning is that you abide within "entities" (bhāveṣu), that is, within visible objects such as the body and so forth. The phrase "they exist in you" is to be understood as the ellipsis. || 47 ||
For you are indeed the stainless and pure Brahman; you are the self of all and the creator of all.
Contemplating the entire universe as peaceful and unborn, be truly happy. 48.
Cultivating it through investigation and experiencing it. || 48 ||
O Great-souled One, if you have attained the stainless state free from longing and have dispelled the great darkness of the notion of "mine," you possess mastery over the mind.
Salutations to you, who are the support for the great and eternal intellect. || 49 ||

O Great-Souled One, having attained— that is, having reached through perfect realization— that state which is free from longing, which turns back all desires, which is full bliss, stainless, and devoid of ignorance and the like;
and being one whose great darkness of "mine-ness" has vanished, if you are capable of destroying the mind— that is, the consciousness.

If you were thus capable, then homage be to You—the one of transcendent intellect, of immeasurable wisdom, the Great, the Full, the Existent, who has become Brahman, the ultimate truth! The intention is that You shall always be worthy of worship even for those such as ourselves. || 49 ||

Thus ends the fifteenth canto, titled "The Imparting of Instruction in the Context of Bhārgava’s Lamentation," within the *Bhārgavopākhyāna* of the *Sthitiprakaraṇa* in the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki according to the Ṛṣi tradition.

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Giving of Instruction in the Context of Bhārgava’s Lamentation," within the Section on Stability (*sthitiprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*. 15.
The Sixteenth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, having set aside the words of that son as well as those of Bhṛgu, [he spoke].
The Lord Kāla, with a deep resonance, spoke these words.
When the time has passed according to the statement of the period, there is again an entry into one's own body;
the state of being the preceptor of the Daityas for Śukra and liberation while living are described. || 1 ||
Likewise, having rejected—that is, having cast aside by describing its impropriety—the speech of Śukra, the son of Bhṛgu, which was a lamentation of the kind previously described; || 1 ||
Kāla said:
O Bhārgava, having cast off this body of a female ascetic, enter this [new] body, O virtuous one, just as a king enters his city. (2)
O sinless one, having performed penance with that former body at the proper time, you must once again assume the leadership of the lords of the asuras.
"At the proper time" means at the time when the presiding *prārabdha-karma* is awakened; "by the first" means by that which has occurred for the very first time.
When the end of the great aeon has arrived, you must cast off this body of Bhārgava, like a withered flower, so that it is never to be taken up again.
When, then, is that [bond] to be abandoned? To this he says: "at the end of the great aeon" (*mahākalpānte*).

At the end of the great aeon—that is, at the conclusion of a *kalpa* (the day of Brahmā), measured by a thousand yugas—for the sake of non-re-acceptance, meaning for the sake of not assuming another body again, like a flower that has been enjoyed and withered. || 4 ||
Having attained the state of liberation while living, remain, O high-minded one, performing the role of preceptor to the great lords of the asuras with this body of your former form.
By means of her former form, which was initiated by karma acquired in a previous kalpa.
May it be well with you both; we shall go to our desired direction, for there is nothing whatsoever that would not be pleasing to one's heart.

"May there be auspiciousness (*kalyāṇam*) or welfare (*śubham*) for you two. The word "we" (*vayam*)—derived from the stem *asmad*—is used in the plural despite referring to a single person, either because of the rule "and [it is used] when two are meant," or because of the intention to include one's followers. The term "desired" (*abhimatām*), which qualifies the direction, was not employed merely to exclude what is undesired.

Because that which is not desired by the complete Self is simply non-existent. For whatever mind there may be the conceptual construction that "this is desired" and "this is not desired," when that mind—which, having abandoned what is undesired, approaches what is desired—is thoroughly investigated, it is found to have no form as a real entity whatsoever. Therefore, regarding the phrase "toward the direction of the desired":

Showing that this qualification was employed to indicate his own intention—that "we shall go to the state of being the Self, which is the object of supreme love"—he says: "Nothing whatsoever... (verse 6).
Having spoken thus, as the two of them shed tears like the heaven and earth whose limbs are heated by the sun, he vanished along with his rays.

As those two, Bhṛgu and Śukra, were shedding tears out of affection, the sixth case is used in the sense of disregard; thus, there is either the sixth or the seventh case in this indication of a state. || 7 ||
When the Blessed Lord Kṛtānta had departed,
Bhārgava reflected upon destiny— the inevitable course of fate that is determined by the unbreakable laws of necessity.

"At the appointed time" means at the end; "destiny" refers to the inevitable course of karma; and "the fixed course of necessity" means the unavoidable direction of the will of the Lord—having reflected upon these is the meaning. || 8 ||

Mādhava entered that youthful body— which was withered by the cause of time yet destined for the auspicious emergence of future flowers (or fruits)— just as a spring breeze enters a beautiful creeper.
"Kāla" refers to a long period of time, specifically the seasons of Hemanta and Śiśira; for that reason and by that cause, [the ground] was completely parched.
"Mādhava" refers to the spring season. || 9 ||
That body of the Brahmin woman, with its face and limbs turned pale,
fell trembling quickly upon the ground like a creeper whose roots have been severed.
She, known by the name Vāsudevā, was the ascetic maiden Samaṅgā.
When that body containing the entered soul had been restored, the great sage performed a nourishing rite with mantras using the waters from his water-pot.
When that body called semen has entered it—that is, when the individual soul (jīva) has entered such a body—[then... || 11 ||
Then all the channels of her body shone,
filled to the brim like rivers whose hollows are overflowing with floods during the rainy season.
Then, after the nourishment [of the mantra]. || 12 ||
Like a lotus pond in the rainy season or a fresh creeper in spring, when she was full, her edges appeared as if covered in young shoots. (13)
The extremities—the fingernails, hair, and so forth—shone as they emerged like sprouts, appearing as if they were budding leaves. || 13 ||
Then Śukra rose up, his vital breaths flowing forth,
like a cloud filled with water through the union of essence and wind.
From the conjunction of moisture, water, wind, and the preceding breeze. || 14 ||
He first saluted his father, whose appearance was purifying,
just as a cloud first risen in the morning greets a mountain with its thunder.
By the force of the simile "as if by thundering," it is understood that salutation is preceded by the proclamation of one's name and lineage. || 15 ||
Then the father embraced his former body,
his heart moist with affection, just as a cloud after a long time embraces the slope of a mountain.
"Of her body, [that is,] of the body of her son"—this refers to her former form, in contrast to the appearance that was withered and decayed;
that is to say, as previously possessed of youth, beauty, and so forth. "Ākṛtim" means the physical form. 16.
The high-minded Bhṛgu beheld with affection that former body of his, and even as he laughed, he maintained the conviction, "This one was born from me."

Because of his childhood, his body was slender and delicate; that very body was "tānavī" (delicate). [The Lord], though smiling even while considering the impropriety from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattvadṛśā*), acted upon that body—the body of his son. This is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 17 ||
At that time, the affection arising from the thought "this is my son" overcame even Bhṛgu;
for the sense of "mine-ness" regarding one's own body persists as long as its physical form remains.
It will continue as long as her form lasts, for as long as she lives; the suffix *ṇini* is used here in the sense of necessity (*āvaśyaka*).
The meaning is that it is inevitable due to the power of what has already begun. || 18 ||
Then the father and son became mutually resplendent,
like the sun and a lotus-pond at dawn when night has ended.
Like a pair of ruddy geese joined after a long separation,
or like a peacock and a cloud filled with affection at the arrival of the rainy season.

The pair known as *cakrāhva*, that is, the husband and wife of the *cakra* bird; by the word "cloud" (*ghana*), that particular time [the rainy season] is indicated. The verb "became" (*babhūvatuḥ*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. || 20 ||
Having remained there for a moment with their long-standing and firm longing satisfied by that equal fitness, those two of great intelligence then arose.

Having stood for a moment, rendered motionless by the weight of an equal joy—due both to her being world-renowned and to the description of her form provided by her—and having their longing for reunion intensified by their long separation, [they remained there]. (21)
There they reduced that body of the twice-born Samaṅga to ashes;
for who indeed in this world does not follow established custom? (22)
"Conduct" means good conduct. Thus, the meaning is that the very preservation of such conduct results in [the avoidance of] burning and so forth, and there is no other fruit here. || 22 ||
Thus those two ascetics, Bhṛgu and Bhārgava, resplendent like the moon and the sun in the sky, dwelt together in that sacred forest.

They were both masters of yoga and knowers of what is to be known; liberated while living, they were teachers of the world, perfectly equanimous and steadfast amidst the floods of place, time, and circumstances. (24)

They are equal toward places and times, as well as toward the floods of auspicious and inauspicious conditions, being devoid of the imbalance of joy and sorrow; for this means they are firmly established in their own true nature. || 24 ||
Then, in the course of time, Śukra attained the status of preceptor to the Asuras,
while Bhṛgu likewise remained in his own appropriate and painless station.
The mention of "being the preceptor of the Asuras" is also an indication of his authority over the planets; "pada" refers to the office of Prajāpati.
This Śukra was first born in that sequence from that supreme state of reality; thereafter, due to his own swift wandering into the path of memory, he of noble fame—
He is thoroughly agitated among others throughout the ten states. || 26 ||

He concludes the description of Śukra’s journey in brief with the words "Śukra": by means of his own [mental state], that is, through the delusion of a mental kingdom (manorājya) induced by the apsaras who had repeatedly ascended to the path of his memory. || 26 ||

Thus ends the sixteenth canto, titled "The Rejuvenation of Śukra, the Son of Bhṛgu," in the Section on Stability within the Means to Liberation of the venerable Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa composed by Vālmīki. 16.
Thus ends the sixteenth canto, titled "The Reanimation of Śukra," in the Sthitiprakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The seventeenth canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
"O Blessed One, through the experience of the manifestation of the son of Bhṛgu..."
Just as this has become fruitful, why should it not be so for another? || 1 ||
In this context, it is said that for pure minds, there is the fulfillment of their true intentions,
as well as mutual union when their latent impressions (vāsanās) and perceptions are identical.
Rāma raises a doubt: "Surely, O Blessed One, just as Śukra’s mental kingdom of the apsarases, heaven, and so forth, became fruitful through long enjoyment, why should it not be the same for others?
He says, "O Blessed One," and so on. Just as that visionary power (*pratibhā*) belonging to the charioteer of the Sun becomes fruitful through the experience of heaven and other realms...
The logical connection (anvaya) is: "If it has arisen [in one], why should it not likewise arise for others as well? || 1 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
This body was first produced from the foot of Brahmā;
it is the pure lineage of Bhārgava, unstained by any other birth.

Regarding the fact that the fruits of [Śuka’s] eloquence correspond to the enjoyment of their results and are thus fruitful, there are two causes: the purity of mind capable of true resolve (*satya-saṃkalpa*), and the manifestation of karma that bestows future enjoyment, which has been awakened at the time of death.
Among these, he provides the solution by demonstrating the first cause in Śuka’s case, beginning with the words "This was first," and so forth. [The author then discusses] Śuka’s...
Because all defects belonging to previous kalpas have been exhausted through the performance of ritual acts and meditative worship (upāsana) carried out during his final birth,
this body of Brahmā was produced first in this kalpa; thus, there is no possibility of defects pertaining to this kalpa affecting him.
Because he was born from the mere word of his command for the sake of exercising authority and enjoyment— being produced by the resolve (*saṃkalpa*) of the Creator—
the defects inherent in being born of such a resolve do not apply to him; since he is of the Brāhmaṇa caste with purity on both paternal and maternal sides,
the defects associated with seed, womb, or caste are likewise inapplicable, and thus he does not incur the state of having false resolves, which distinguishes him from others.
The meaning is "distinction. || 2 ||
That state of the pure mind which exists when all cravings have been completely stilled is called Truth; it is described as this stainless consciousness.

With the intention that even for other knowers of Brahman (*brahmavid*), although they possess the power of true resolve (*satyasaṃkalpa*), the cause of the mind’s attainment of the state of being the True Self is precisely its purity resulting from the destruction of defects such as passion (*rāga*) and so forth, he says: "Of all desires... (Verse 3).
Whatever a being whose self is pure of mind contemplates,
that very thing quickly comes to be in that manner, just as water becomes a whirlpool.
Just as the delusion of the son of Bhṛgu arose spontaneously [the reading "sotthitaḥ" is also found],
so too is each individual case here illustrated by the example of Bhṛgu’s son.

Since others lack purity of mind, their *satya-saṃkalpa* (the power of true resolve) is not established; thus, although the first alternative is impossible, according to the second alternative, there is indeed equality with Śukra in the manifestation of the world that conforms to the experience of pleasure and pain, which accords with the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of karma awakened by previous death. With this intention, he says: "Just as... (verse 5).
Just as the seed, the sprout, the leaf, and so forth, manifest their own wonders,
even so do the fragments of delusion arise for all the multitudes of living beings.
The fragments of delusion are the divisions of duality created by error.
This entire universe that is seen is exactly like this; every single thing arises falsely and likewise sets falsely.
"It is seen by us"—this is the ellipsis. "Each" means for every individual soul. || 7 ||
Nothing whatsoever in the world sets or rises for anyone;
this is mere delusion, expanding like one bewildered by illusion. (8)
But from the perspective of ultimate reality, he says: "It does not set. She is like a deluded woman, as if insane. || 8 ||
Just as one who stands within a reflection is himself a fragment of the cycle of existence,
so indeed do thousands of such [fragments] appear falsely to them.
He says "yathā" (just as) to show that it is an established fact of experience that even for each single individual soul (*jīva*), there are many worlds.
"Bhāsasthaḥ" means situated in the manifestation—that is, in the immediate appearance (*aparokṣāvabhāsa*)—which occurs at present during the waking state; "of us" is the ellipsis.
"Of those" refers to the fragments of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*). The meaning is that they exist in dreams, delusions, and so forth. Or else, if...
If it is asked, "Since individual cycles of existence (saṃsāras) have arisen for every single living being, why then do they not appear?"—the answer is that they indeed do appear.
He says "yathā" (just as): "samyakpratibhāsaḥ" means a clear experience; "tatsthaḥ" means residing therein, with "of us" being the understood subject.
"Teṣām" refers to those thousands of other living beings, with "of cycles of existence" being the understood object. || 9 ||
Just as the activities of dream-towns and cities of imagination are not seen as distinct from one another, so too are these delusions of saṃsāra.
If that is so, why are the individual worlds of all beings not seen separately by one another?
To this he replies with the words "as in a dream" (svapne). The meaning is that just as the dream of one person is not seen by others, so it is in this case. || 10 ||
In this way, multitudes of cities exist in the sky as forms born of mental construction;
they are not seen except by those with the vision of false knowledge.
Indeed, there exist Piśācas, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas of such a nature;
their bodies consist of mere volition and are composed of pleasure and pain.
In this very same way, O delight of the Raghus, we and these others have come into being; our forms consist of our own volitions, appearing as both false and real.
In this very way, it is just like semen. || 13 ||
For such indeed is the continuity of creation found in others;
it is not real, yet the nature of reality is established thus even in that which is unreal.
Even regarding Hiraṇyagarbha, who is beyond the individual soul (vyaṣṭi), the same [error] persists through a mere blind tradition.
In this very way, the entire universe, though appearing as individual joys, is indeed delusion alone,
just as the single essence of spring manifests in the form of forests and shrubs.
He states that Brahman alone has arisen in the form of the entire world of living beings with the words "pratyekam" (each one). || 15 ||
Just as this first mental construction has come into manifestation,
so too is it thus contemplated when seen through the ultimate truth.

How is it known that the very first volition of one's own self has come to manifest in the form of the world? To this he says: "The first. The meaning is that it is known through the vision of reality (tattvadarśana). || 16 ||
The mind, which is individually delighted and situated within the belly of its own inherent nature,
perishes as it perceives this world as being engaged in such-and-such undertakings.
The meaning is that one's own nature is beginningless ignorance; seeing that the mind situated within its womb is indeed the world, one perishes by oneself. || 17 ||
By the power of appearances things exist, but by the observation of reality they do not;
the web of the world is a long dream, the tethering post for the elephant of the mind. (18)
And thus, he says—beginning with "pratibhāsa"—that the existence of the world lasts only as long as its appearance, and cannot persist once the vision of the real substratum is attained. || 18 ||
The existence of the world is nothing but the existence of consciousness; the existence of consciousness is nothing but the world.
With the absence of one, both are destroyed, and that occurs through the investigation of reality.
If so, one might ask: is the existence that previously appeared in the world absolutely non-existent? He says, "No—it is the very existence of consciousness.

In the reading "the world is indeed the existence of consciousness," he clarifies the intent of what was stated—that the mind is the tethering post for the elephant of consciousness—by saying, "it is the very existence of consciousness. He states the result of this: "because of the absence of the one [duality]. || 19 ||
For the manifestation of a pure mind becomes true, just as the impurity of a gem is removed here through the proper application of cleansing. (20)

If it is asked, "Where is the existence of the world seen to arise from the existence of the mind? [the author] says, "Of the pure one," with the intention that it is seen in the case of an object produced by the true resolve (*satyasaṃkalpa*) of those whose minds are purified. The meaning is: "from the polishing of the gem" is like the removal of poison through the light [produced] by the gem's function. "By means of reasoning" means by way of a method (*upāya*). || 20 ||
Through long and firm practice, purification of the mind occurs; for one who is not assailed by volitional constructs, intuitive insight arises in the mind. (21)
Single-minded firm practice is the practice of strengthening one-pointedness. Intuition is luminosity resulting from clarity. 21.
Just as gold does not remain [pure] when there is a soiled garment, so too a single vision does not remain stable when the mind is withered. 22.
*Suvarṇam* means gold, a substance of beautiful color, or molten gold. *Malavaty-aṃśuke* means in a soiled garment. *Ekā dṛṣṭiḥ* means non-dual knowledge of the Self. 22.
Śrī Rāma said:
In this world, which is of the nature of a reflection, how could these sequences of time and action, along with their rising and setting, arise for the mind of Śukra? (23)

It has been stated that the delusion of the world follows from latent impressions (*vāsanā*); however, regarding the sequence of various wonders such as the succession of births among celestial nymphs in heaven— which have never been experienced— since the seed in the form of a latent impression is impossible there,
Rāma asks with the intention of inquiring how Śuka’s process of superimposition came about:

Regarding the phrase "in the nature of appearance": how and by what cause have they arisen in the world, which consists of the appearance of the mind—that is, the mind of Śukra—and which is of the nature of conceptual construction (*prātibhāsika-kalpanā*)? By the expression "together with rising and setting," it is indicated that since it is impossible to grasp the rising and setting of an appearance at the very time of its appearance, [they must be grasped] at a time when there is no appearance.

And since even those two [the preceding and succeeding moments] are not established by experience, it is indicated that the latent impression (*vāsanā*) having them as its object is all the more unestablished; and if that is unestablished, the sequence itself is also unestablished—this is the intended meaning. || 23 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Just as this world was perceived by Śukra through his father’s teachings,
so too does it abide in the mind of someone else, like a peacock within a peacock’s egg.

In his mind, there arose an understanding— both pertaining to this world and the next— of whatever exists as characterized by such things as birth and destruction, derived from his father, from the eyes and other senses of his parents, from his father’s words, and from the scriptures such as the Śruti and Smṛti.

It remains in that very same way in the form of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*). Thus, the meaning is that the arising of that [impression] also occurred precisely through the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)— such as the scriptures of the ancestors— and through their fallacious counterparts (*tadābhāsa*), which appear as if they were valid cognitions.
The intention is that the mental impressions (saṃskāras) regarding the sequence of arising and destruction will be established by the witness-consciousness alone. || 24 ||
This [world] resides within the treasury of its own nature; it has arisen through this sequence, just as sprouts, leaves, and so forth, creepers, flowers, and fruits arise from a seed. (25)
The treasury of intrinsic nature is ignorance, which is presided over by consciousness and endowed with life; this is by means of the fatherly scripture. 25.
Bound by whatever latent impressions (vāsanā), the living soul perceives that very thing within;
and here, the illustration of its own nature is this long dream that is the world. (26)
One's own form is the body imagined by oneself in a dream. To the objection that "this is not a dream," he says: "prolonged," and so forth.
O Rāma, each fragment of worldly existence surely arises individually;
it appears clearly within oneself like the net of dreams of men in an army at night. (27)

The meaning is as follows: just as men stationed in an army who are permeated by the impressions (*vāsanā*) of that army during the day perceive, in their dreams at night, various armies each fashioned by their own respective impressions, yet still consider them to be one; so it is in this case.

Śrī Rāma said: This [individual soul], arising from the fragment of worldly existence, either unites with that [Supreme Soul] of its own accord or does not unite; you ought to tell me that according to the truth. (28)

But if this were so, since neither the person nor his transmigratory existence could be perceived by others, the teachers' engagement in lifting their disciples out [of suffering] and their composition of scriptures would— like a benefit for strangers directed toward oneself—
not reach the disciple; and thus, due to the lack of instruction, the disciple’s failure to attain liberation would follow by an identical logic.

With the intention that this conceptualization would be a "root-destroying" error—resulting in the fault of non-liberation due to the failure to receive instruction even from one's own guru—Rāma asks: "This... [verse]. If it does not meet [the guru], then the aforementioned fault occurs;
if it does meet him, then this transmigratory world is common to all and cannot be sublated by the knowledge of any single individual.
Thus, the intention is that this is a rope with nooses at both ends. || 28 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: A mind that is impure and lacking in vigor is not fit for mutual union;
yet when iron is heated and pure iron is heated, the latter merges into the former.
To avoid the two faults [of contradiction and impossibility], he provides the answer by way of a systematic distinction, beginning with the word "malinam" (stained). This is the meaning:

for a stained mind does not deserve mutual contact—that is, a blending—with a pure mind. Why? Because it is "avīryam," meaning it lacks the capacity for the subtlety required for union with the pure. It is "taptam" (heated).
Once purified by the digestion of the impurities (kaṣāya-pācana), it merges—as if into heated iron—and attains oneness with that which is heated;

for the intention is that, because its subtlety has been practiced through the knowledge of samādhi, it is endowed with vigor (savīrya). And thus, precisely because of this possession of vigor, there occurs, as it were, the grace of granting boons by the gods entering into the dreams of others.
The meaning is that there is no first fault, because [the Lord] is indeed capable of awakening [the disciple] by entering into the world imagined within the mind of the disciple;
nor is there the second fault, because it is not admitted that [the Lord's power] is common [to all]. || 29 ||
Pure mental principles merge with one another;
for waters that are of a single form attain unity, but not those that are turbid.
For the purity of the mind consists in being free from latent impressions (*vāsana*) and is of a single nature: the non-perception of that which has not come into being.
Through its swift purification, one becomes awakened.
By means of the reasoning of the "mere-I," one attains union with the Supreme. || 31 ||

Showing that the supreme pinnacle of mental purity is reached only through its attainment—whereby the knowledge of reality becomes firm and the highest goal is established, and not otherwise—he concludes with the words "For purity...
The meaning is that the ultimate purity of the mind consists precisely in the state of being free from latent impressions (*vāsana*), which is the absolute destruction of all tendencies. Of that...

By means of attaining through reasoning that supreme state which consists of pure consciousness alone—that is, the mind reduced to its mere essence characterized by the purification remaining as such pure consciousness—one attains union with the Supreme, which is liberation; this is the meaning. || 31 ||
Thus ends the seventeenth canto, titled "The Convergence of Mental Kingdoms," in the *Bhārgavopākhyāna* of the *Mokṣopāya-sthitiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by Vālmīki. 17.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Convergence of Mental Kingdoms," in the *Sthitiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The Eighteenth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Within all the fragments of the cycle of worldly existence, [there exists] that which has the nature of the subtle essence of the seed of beings.
The appearance of that which consists of the mere [object] is distinct from the appearance [of the cognition]. (1)

The association of the impure with the impure is described as purification through a particular state; for the wise man, however, union with the subtle elements and association with the Supreme are prescribed. (1)
