The manner of union between the pure kingdom of the mind (*manorājya*) and both the pure and the impure has been described. Now,

by means of the purification of the impure [elements] through their union with the impure, as well as the waking and other states and the seer and the seen, [the author explains] the method of the subtle elements (*tanmātra-yukti*) mentioned in the final verse.
[The reading is *yuktitayā*: By means of that [reasoning], and in order to demonstrate the attainment of union with the Supreme,
the previously mentioned differentiation of the manifold states such as waking and so forth is [sublated] by a manifestation dependent upon the unique self-manifestation of one's own Self.

He establishes this with the words "of all," etc. For all living beings (*jīva*), within the fragments or portions of the cycles of creation and re-creation that consist of their own individually imagined worlds, there is a "calculation" (*kalana*)—that is, a "portion" (*kalā*)—of the elemental self (*bhūtātman*), which is gross, and of the seed-self (*bījātman*), which is subtle; this consists in the tendency toward the state of the *liṅga* (the causal body), which is the nature of the causal self (*kāraṇātman*).

The diversity of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*) that has been described for each individual soul is merely that [pervasive reality] itself which appears; nothing else appears. Thus, "the appearance of that alone" refers to the Self, whose sole essence is self-luminous consciousness (*svaprakāśacidekarasa*).

The meaning is that this [diversity] is not established by way of the actual nature of things (*vastuvṛtti*), but rather through the conceptualization of specific forms by means of its manifestation. || 1 ||
Whether it be engagement or withdrawal, for the entire class of living beings, it is preceded by the functioning of those subtle elements immediately following the state of deep sleep. (2)

How is this understood? To this he says: "Activity" (*pravṛtti*). Because, immediately after the state of deep sleep—that is, in the very next unmediated moment—all classes of living beings experience the activity of beginningless dualistic discourse;
and because there is activity directed toward forests, rivers, and so forth in dreams and in the waking state, as well as cessation from that [activity].

Alternatively, that "parāvṛtti" (transformation) refers to the universal pervasion (*parāvṛtti* = *pari-vṛtti*) of that which consists solely of consciousness (*tanmātra-cidekarasa*); it is well-known as being preceded by such pervasion, and thus the meaning is "for this reason. || 2 ||
Those living beings who participate in phenomenal activity perceive only the subtle elements (tanmātras);
because of their oneness with those subtle elements, they see the various creations as mutually imagined.

All those living beings who engage in worldly activity and conduct their affairs are manifested by that alone—by pure consciousness (cinmātra) itself—and possess the illumination of objects through no other light. This being so, [the opponent asks: "Even if this be granted, how is the manifestation of the manifold world of another's mental construction established? To this, he replies: "By that alone" (tanmātra).

The meaning is that, through the merging of the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of those respective pure consciousnesses (*cinmātra*)—or rather, by attaining oneness through the firm realization of their identity with Brahman—they perceive each other's creations, and not otherwise. || 3 ||
Through the single channel of the subtle elements (tanmātra), the diverse reservoirs of creation mingle with one another and attain density on all sides.

By means of the single conduit of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*)—that is to say, by the single path—as previously described; [it attains] density, which is a state of compactness resulting from the firmness of the delusion of reality through the corroboration of another's worldly transactions and so forth. || 4 ||
Some exist in separate states and go to dissolution separately;
some are joined together with one another, remaining as the unimpaired humming of the world.
Without the merging of separate creations, some are mutually combined; in this manner, the world—the cosmic egg—is formed, and the *guñjā* seed is well known as its characteristic measure. || 5 ||
That in which thousands of world-jujube fruits exist within every single atom,
yet remain without touching one another— that is the forest named Brahman.
In every single atom, there is no concealment. Brahman is variegated by Māyā. Kānana means a forest. || 6 ||
Through their mutual blending, these [elements] attain density;
whatever is established in a particular place in a particular manner, that alone one perceives there, and nothing else.
These are the "gunjas" (seeds/essences) of the world; through their density—that is, their state of being compacted—they attain the fitness for common worldly transaction. [The author asks:
Are all objects suitable for the perception of everyone? No; he says "yadyat" (whatever).
To whatever extent a thing is established in a particular place according to the karma and experience of as many living beings as are capable of perceiving it, to that same extent it exists there.
He sees nothing else; that is to say, neither what belongs to another place nor what belongs to another world. || 7 ||
When the present kingdom of the mind has come to fruitionlessness,
that should be known as the cutting off of the mind's succession of lives.
For this very reason, with the intention of establishing both the differentiation of minds and the differentiation of individual souls (*jīva*) based on those limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), he says:
"The present. For one mind, the mental kingdom existing within another mind has reached futility—characterized by an incapacity for seeing or enjoying it—a state of fruitlessness.
The meaning is that whatever state exists, that itself is to be known as the cutting (kṛtti), the severance, and the cause of the differentiation of the mind.
From that very source, the succession of living beings (jīva-paramparā) and even the various distinctions among living beings are to be known; this is the sense to be supplied. || 8 ||

As successive creations merge with one another and their latent tendencies become firmly established, the existence of the body becomes deeply rooted; conversely, the absence of the body is forgetfulness.

Thus, through the convergence of individual creations—which consist of diverse mental kingdoms—tending toward their fruits simultaneously due to the similarity of their karmic impressions (*vāsanā*) and so forth, the existence of both the individual (*vyaṣṭi*) and collective (*samaṣṭi*) gross bodies is to be understood as firmly established;
however, the meaning is that upon forgetting that [divine power], the absence of the body is indeed natural. || 9 ||
Because it has assumed the state of being a body, consciousness—which is like gold—has forgotten its true nature;
thus, ignorance, though falsely experienced, is in reality pure, just as [gold] assumes the form of a bracelet.

When the state of the gross body has become firmly established, the natural abiding in the Self is forgotten and the imagined worldly condition is accepted; thus he says: "dehatve" (in the state of being a body). Consciousness itself is the gold (*ciddhema*); by that [consciousness-gold], when the Self is forgotten, it becomes pure and absolute *kaṭakatā*—that is, it assumes a state resembling that of a bracelet.
The meaning is that ignorance, characterized by saṃsāra, has been experienced as nothing but false. || 10 ||

Just as the pure vital breath (prāṇamarut) perceives the object of knowledge through the sensation of another breath and so forth, so too does it perceive the kingdom of the mind (manorājya) which rests upon other creations. 11.

Having thus established the mutual union even of those who are impure, he provides an illustration for the experience of the supreme sovereignty of the pure ones, beginning with "Just as": just as the vital breath (*prāṇamarut*), purified by the practice of *haṭhayoga*, [enters] another body and [experiences] the vital breaths of others.

The meaning is that, because he perceives his own body and senses as being under his own control—as indicated by the word "etc. (ādi)—he likewise perceives sound and other objects of those senses; similarly, the pure mind also perceives mental constructions (manorājya) based on other creations. || 11 ||
For all multitudes of living beings, the Self rests in three states known as waking, dreaming, and deep sleep; in this regard, the body is not the cause.

Now, if it be argued that the existence of the gross body is established only through the mutual convergence of mental desires (*manorājya*), then in the absence of such convergence there would be no body at all; [how then could one say]: "One should know the waking state as residing in the eyes, one should enter the dream state in the throat, the deep sleep state resides in the heart, and the fourth (*turīya*) is situated in the head"?
Anticipating the objection that even the states such as waking and so forth would not exist if they were dependent on the distinctions of bodily regions revealed by scripture, he says:
"Of all [beings]... The conceptualization of the three states arises from the very nature of being a *jīva*, and does not depend upon the body;
for if the body were not established without the conceptualization of the waking state, there would result the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). As for the scripture:

The sense is this: by way of restating the body as established through the views of others, [the scripture] intends only that the expansion of the phenomenal world (prapañca) consisting of waking and so forth is not real, because it is seen as a mere part of that [body]; it does not intend for the body to be the cause of that [world]. Thus, while the self exists as the individual soul (jīva) within the three states, [it remains unaffected].
Nor does corporeality manifest within this [consciousness] as the state of waves manifests in water. || 13 ||

Just as water alone manifests itself in the form of waves and so forth, when the reality is seen, even upon reflecting that the individual soul (jīva) alone consists of the three states—just as there is no separate entity like a wave apart from the water—it follows that no bodily state exists as a real entity other than the soul. Thus he says: "In this way" (evam). || 13 ||
Having attained the state of the power of consciousness (citkalā) and remaining in the state at the end of deep sleep,
the enlightened living being (jīva) returns [to its source], while the deluded one proceeds toward creation.

In this very way, the Buddha, the knower of reality, having reached and attained through knowledge the state of pure consciousness— the fourth state (*turya*) which is the ultimate end and final limit of deep sleep, whose nature is the single flavor of sentience— turns away from the condition of being a limited individual (*jīva*). But he who is deluded and ignorant of reality, by his own mental construction, [remains bound].
The meaning is that he again engages in creation in the form of the conceptualization of the shapes of the body and so forth. || 14 ||

Because it demonstrates its own benevolence toward the two, that which is ignorant, in deep sleep, and unawakened—the individual soul (jīva)—is indeed of one and the same nature [as the other], yet it partakes in creation. 15.

In that case, does even the deep sleep (*suṣupti*) of the knower and the ignorant differ? He says "no"—"of the two. The ellipsis is that deep sleep is of one and the same nature. This is because, in the Śruti, the profound peace (*saṃprasāda*) of the ignorant person himself is presented as an illustration of liberation, which is unsurpassed bliss. If so, is that [deep sleep] the seed of creation for one, but not for the other?
To the question "No, from what [distinction]? he says: "The ignorant one" (ajñaḥ). Between those two, the ignorant one is either in deep sleep or otherwise unawakened;
he is devoid of knowledge of the real Self and is permeated by the latent impressions of the delusion that the body and so forth are the Self.
It is precisely because of this distinction that he is the *jīva* who participates in creation—this is the meaning. || 15 ||
Because consciousness is all-pervasive, some are led away by the process of creation;
in each creation there is a distinct form, and there are indeed other creations as well. (16)
Regarding this, he states a further distinction: "because of its all-pervasiveness" (*sarvagatvāt*)—[the reading *sargagatvāt* occurs in both places].
It is "led," meaning it is brought inside. "In a separate form" (*pṛthagrūpam*) is an adverbial modifier of the action. || 16 ||
Within those as well, there are floods of internal creations, like the layers of a plantain leaf-stalk;
they are not far from all other creations and possess the thick, rounded form of leaves.
The meaning is that just as the sheaths of bark serve as the seats or supports for the plantain leaves, so too does Brahman exist within and within.
However, Brahman is present with an identical nature in all creations, like a pavilion made of plantain leaves; thus he says:
"not far away, possessing a thick circular form through its broad leaves spread outward"—[this refers to the word *bṛhat*].
The meaning is that there is a syntactical connection with the word "Brahman" occurring in the subsequent verse; [it is] connected with what follows. || 17 ||
Brahman is by nature cool, like a pavilion made of plantain leaves;
just as there is no difference between the plantain tree and its hundreds of leaves, so too there is no otherness within it. 18.
He explains the illustration with the words "in the plantain tree" (kadalyām). || 18 ||
There is no otherness within the reality of Brahman even across hundreds of creations;
just as a seed, having blossomed from its sap, becomes a seed once again. (19)

Thus, he provides an illustration for the return to its own essential nature of Brahman, which had assumed the state of the world: "As a seed," and so forth. Just as the very seed of a banyan tree or the like, having blossomed through contact with sap, water, and other factors, becomes a tree and the like, and then, by means of the spreading of its branches and the production of fruits, manifests once again in the form of its previous seed—so too [is it with Brahman].

The meaning is that even Brahmā, having become the mind through contact with the essence of desire, action, and so forth, manifests in his prior state as Brahmā upon the dawning of awakening— following the sequence of hearing, reflection, and so on— once he has attained a body qualified for such practice by means of the conceptualization of birth, death, and the like. || 19 ||
Likewise, Brahman, having become the mind through awakening, becomes the supreme Brahman;
the seed whose cause is rasa unfolds in the form of a fruit.

If you consider the seed to be a non-example because even that seed might return to the state of a living being—just as it returns to the state of a tree through contact with sap—even after it has been liberated, then let sap itself be the example; thus he says: "caused by sap" (rasakāraṇaka). || 20 ||
The individual soul, having Brahman as its cause, expands in the form of the universe;
it is not appropriate to say what the cause of that essence (rasa) might be. (21)
And this being so, he says "of the essence" (rasasya) [in verse 21], meaning that there is no room even for the doubt as to what the cause of Brahman might be.
It is not appropriate to say what the cause of Brahman might be;
nor is it appropriate to say that its nature is something else, because it is devoid of distinctions. (22)

Now, since sapidity is observed in leaves, stalks, trees, flowers, fruits, and so forth, that sapidity—which constitutes their very nature—appears to be their cause; likewise, Brahman, as the cause of the world, would also be merely a specific natural attribute of the world's qualities.
And thus, the proof for Brahman’s causality would be rendered redundant by the doctrine of natural causality (*svabhāva-kāraṇatāvāda*).
Anticipating this objection, he says: "Intrinsic nature. This is not tenable. Why?
Because the cause is devoid of distinctions;
for the intrinsic nature of that [cause] consists in specific, uncommon properties that arise simultaneously with the effect.
One should not search for causes such as "causality" in that which is causeless, nor for "substance" and so forth in that which is the ultimate reality.
For one must investigate the essence; what is the use of investigating the non-essential? (23)

If it is argued that, since the nature of insentience and so forth cannot be established in the world by means of the cause which is Brahman as pure consciousness alone, one must therefore accept that Brahman possesses the nature of insentience and suffering, and that there exist other causes and other instrumental factors for the world's diversity— [the author] says "no" to this:

The meaning is this: since even such entities as a cause, an instrumental cause, and so forth are impossible in Brahman—the primordial cause of all superimpositions of conceptual proliferation—precisely because of the contradiction with its own nature, the world, which is a transformation (*vivarta*) of that which has no [material] cause, is indeed unreal. [Objection:

In that case, it would be more appropriate for the primordial cause of the world—which is insentient, unreal, and of the nature of suffering—to be something that is itself insentient, unreal, and of the nature of suffering.
If it is asked, "Let that very thing be investigated; why investigate Brahman without a motive? he says in response: "It is to be investigated.
What is the use of investigations into that which is essence-less? The meaning is: what is the human goal (puruṣārtha) [to be gained thereby]? || 23 ||
The seed, having abandoned its form as a seed, is seen as the fruit;
yet Brahman, not abandoning His own nature, abides both as the fruit and within the seed.

To reveal the underlying intention behind the statement that the causeless is the primordial cause, he describes the distinction of Brahman by reference to the previously mentioned analogy of the seed: "The seed... In the world, a seed is seen to abandon its form as a seed—its seed-shape—and become the fruit, such as a sprout and so forth; it is not so [with Brahman].

"Brahman. Therefore, the intended meaning is that it has been stated that Brahman is not a cause because it is the material cause of its own illusory manifestation (*vivarta-upādāna*), since there is no effect possessing the same ontological status (*samasattāka*) as itself. || 24 ||
Everything possesses form, whereas the state [of Śiva] is formless;
therefore, it is not possible to equate them. Consequently, there is no analogy for Śiva. (25)

Showing yet another distinction, he says "of the seed" (*bījasya*) to indicate that the comparison presented for that which is devoid of specific qualities (*nirviśeṣa*) is based merely on figurative usage (*upacāra*) and not on actual reality (*vastuvṛtti*). Everything—its own nature as well as its parts, qualities, and so forth—is "possessing form" (*ākṛtimat*), meaning it possesses a genus (*jāti*) and configuration (*saṃsthāna*) that distinguish it from others. It is [the Brahman] that is to be "made equal to" or "balanced against" (*samīkartum*) by means of that seed. || 25 ||
That which appears as non-self is born only as itself, yet it is not born as something perceived by another;
therefore, know that Brahman—the world, like the sky—is neither born nor unborn.
Then he states what the purpose of this metaphorical designation is: "one's own self," etc. "Non-self-appearing" means appearing as something other than the Self. || 26 ||
Perceiving the visible object, one does not perceive one's own self as the seer; for whom, whose consciousness is overcome by the manifold world (prapañca), can its innate state arise? (27)

If one perceives the world-appearance as nothing but oneself, then from where would this misfortune arise, such that a scripture for its avoidance would be fruitful? To this he says: "The visible" (dṛśyam). The meaning is that because one does not perceive one's own self as it truly is, there is consequently misfortune. || 27 ||
When the delusion of water in a mirage exists, what cleverness is there? But when cleverness exists, what indeed is this mirage? (28)

With the intention that his natural, full-blown self-luminosity of bliss has become futile upon the arising of delusion, he says: "Like a mirage. *Vidagdhatā* means the state of being a wise man (*vidvatā*). || 28 ||
The seer, as clear as space, does not perceive even his own entire body; alas, what a delusion that he sees himself as if it were an object of sight, like one's own eye! 29.

Although the Self is worthy of being clearly perceived by everyone at all times—because its nature is stainless, self-luminous, and all-pervading—it is never seen in its true reality by anyone; alas, how powerful is the delusion of those whose faces are turned outward! Thus he says: "Like space," etc. Just as the eye...
Because it is directed toward the external, it does not perceive its own self; so it is in that case. || 29 ||
The seer, as clear as space, does not see even his own limbs;
he perceives them as if they were his very self, appearing as though they had become objects of sight, yet remaining free from delusion.

If it is argued that while one who is outward-turned may not perceive his own inner self, he might nevertheless perceive the selves of others who are external, the author says "no," beginning with the word *ākāśa*. Just as he does not perceive his own self, he likewise does not perceive the ultimate nature (*pāramārthika-rūpa*) of all those external beings, just as [in the following example].

The meaning is as follows: one who is free from delusion—meaning one whose error has ceased without remainder—and who is liberated, does not perceive duality that has become visible or has attained the state of being an object of sight. || 30 ||
Brahman, which is as pure as space, is not attained even with effort;
when the visible world is perceived as something merely visible, its attainment is very far off indeed.
And thus, the meaning is that the object of sight should not be viewed as an object of sight, but rather as pure vision itself.
Where [an object] is not perceived without its specific nature,
even there the visibility of a subtle observer is cast far away.
One might object: "Let the internal self of the knower not be seen by that [consciousness] when it is directed toward objects;

however, let that which serves as the substratum for objects such as jars be seen through the pervasion of the external mental modification (*vṛtti*), since inward-facing orientation (*pratyagmukhatva*) is of no use there. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "tādṛk" (such), where...
In the location where objects such as a jar are situated, because the modification (vṛtti) of the seer— delimited by that modification—

is colored by the external form of the jar and so forth, the seer itself cannot perceive the jar and so on without assuming a nature corresponding to that [form]. In that case as well, there is the "seer-ness" of the seer, meaning its fitness for being seen.
"Thrown far away" means cast away from afar. He qualifies this with a statement containing the reason: "of the subtle.

The sense is that it is because one is unable to discern the subtle pure consciousness by separating it from its own nature as colored by the conformity to the states of the objects [of perception]. || 32 ||
O Rāma, by that [consciousness], the visible is seen, but the seer is not seen;
for only the seer alone exists, while here the visible does not exist at all.
If the seer is not perceived in any way whatsoever, then how can its attainment be established through the reasoning of "that-only" (tanmātra)?

Anticipating this doubt, he states the means for it, beginning with "the seer itself exists," etc.: "If the seer, who is the self of all, resides within the seen, what indeed remains of the state of being a seer? (33)
Whatever is accomplished by a king who possesses all powers, and in whatever manner; || 34 ||

To explain why [the Self] does not exist [as such], he says: "The Seer. Since it would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) if the status of being a seer belonged to that which resides in the regions of the visible, and because of scriptural texts such as "The abode of all beings, the witness, the cognizer," it must necessarily be stated that the Seer is the Self of all and yet resides within the visible. If this is so, then with respect to the entire visible world which has become its own self...

The meaning is that, because of the contradiction of an action operating upon itself, how can there be the status of a seer? If, however, one were to argue that—due to possessing all powers—he is capable like a king, and by producing the object of vision and experiencing it as such, he will become a seer; then, since he would depend on instruments external to himself, his powers would necessarily undergo contraction, and thus he would not remain unmodified. That very [Self] remains unchanged.

With the intention that, since the alternative remains that it arises in this or that way in the form of various objects of perception, it cannot be the seer, and thus an entity distinct [from the seer] is established, he says: "possessing all powers. (34)
It experiences itself in that very way and immediately arises as such;
just as a piece of sugar, through its own sweet effulgence, becomes radiant. (35)

Having described a fitting illustration for the point already stated, he applies it to the subject at hand with the words beginning "yathā" (just as). "Madhurasasya" means of a sweet-tasting substance—either of sugarcane juice or of a well-known sweet liquid; for it is well known that even from honey (*madhu*), when in a particular region, sugar-candy (*khaṇḍa*) and granulated sugar (*śarkarā*) are produced. *Khaṇḍa* [is thus explained].
Sugar-candy. || 35 ||
Just as a tree, though lofty with its fruits, flowers, and creepers, does not abandon its state of being sap,
so too the living soul (*jīva*), which is the radiance of consciousness (*cid-ullāsa*), repeatedly becomes embodied.

Just as a forest grove rises up in the form of fruits, flowers, and creepers—whereby the word "fruits, flowers, and creepers" is used figuratively to denote their juice—or else as the sweet nectar, the essence that enters the trees during the spring season, rises up; so too is he elevated by the juices of fruits, flowers, and the like, brought forth by honey-bees. (Note: In the original, the phrase "fruits, flowers, and creepers" is understood through secondary indication [lakṣaṇā] to mean their juice. Alternatively, it is like a forest grove that rises up in the form of fruits, flowers, and creepers when the sweet nectar has entered the trees in the springtime.
It should be explained as: "it becomes like that. || 36 ||
Without ever abandoning that state of pure consciousness,
the internal self-experience perceives the world-dream as consisting of the very nature of vision.
Just as there is a sense of fragmentation within the earth due to its taste of egoism (ahaṃtā),
so too does one perceive thousands of various fragments within one's own non-dual self.
Just as saltiness exists within salt and the like, so too does the sense of "I" (ahaṃtā) and its derivatives exist within the Self;
this is the proof for the proposition stated by the passage beginning with "by means of thousands of diverse fragments" and ending with "the mind arises without agitation.
[The Self] is non-dual and non-distinct from the salt and other such things, which are its own nature. || 38 ||
Just as the taste of the earth arises, so too does it arise without agitation;
for the trees of the effulgence of the essence of consciousness shine by themselves within the Self. 39.
With the intention of showing the infinity of the universe, he says: "In the essence of consciousness... (verse 39).
The end of these [scriptures], rich with hundreds of visible branches, cannot be comprehended here;
for each of these sections possesses its own aesthetic wonder, just as this [work] does. (40)

He shows that within each of those, the wonders of enjoyment (*bhoga*) are likewise infinite— by the word "khaṇḍa. Just as this visible fragment, this forest-tract characterized by this Brahma-egg, tastes and experiences its own inherent wonder (*svarasa-camatkṛti*) in such and such a manner, even so does this Consciousness (*cit*).
"He sees" and "he experiences"—this is the connection with what follows. || 40 ||
In this way, this consciousness experiences [objects] and perceives existence as distinct;
whatever individual manifestation of its own cycle of birth arises for whichever living power (jīva-śakti), and in whatever manner it arises. (41)

The word "separately" (pṛthak) should be understood as being used distributively; the meaning is "in every Brahmāṇḍa. He states that the cause for the diversity of wonders is precisely the awakening of the various latent impressions (saṃskāra) of the respective individual souls (jīva) who fashion them, using the words "yā yā" (whichever... whichever). || 41 ||
In that very manner, she [the Goddess] exists as the world-form of her own conscious self; thus, certain streams of individual souls (jīva-saṃsṛti) meet one another. 42.

In this regard, he concludes the description of the merging of the transmigrations of individual souls—the fact that even the transmigrations of ignorant living beings meet together when there arises a latent impression (vāsanā) of a similar form—with the words: "The transmigrations of the souls" (jīvasaṃsṛtayaḥ). || 42 ||
Having wandered through saṃsāra themselves, they find peace after a long time;
behold this with a subtle, supreme vision and a mind of wisdom. 43.
If so, what is the means for me to see thousands of other transmigrations? He states this with the words beginning "by the subtle," etc.
"By the mind of knowledge" (jñānacetaseti) means by the previously mentioned means of perception belonging to those with purified minds. || 43 ||
Thousands of world-conflagrations exist even within the interior of a single atom—
in the mind, in space, in stone, in flame, in wind, and in water.
There exist hundreds of thousands of transmigrations within the entirety [of existence], like oil in sesame seeds;
when the mind attains perfection, then the individual soul (jīva) becomes pure consciousness (citi). || 45 ||
And she is pure and all-pervading; therefore, their mutual union is the form of the bee of one's own essential being for all [beings], beginning with Brahmā. (46)
He states that the perception of the world by Padmajā and others, as well as by ourselves and others, occurs solely through the power of purity—with the words "And [she is] pure" (*śuddhā ca*).

Because it has the single flavor of the all-pervading Brahman, she is all-pervading (*sarvagatā*). With the intention that even the meeting of one's own and another's dreams is, like occasional coincidences, merely of the nature of internal mental construction (*svānta-kalpanā-ātmaka*), he says:
By the words "of all," and so forth. || 46 ||
This long, great dream of the world has arisen within;
certain successions of beings pass from one dream to another dream. (47)
Therefore, this perception [of solidity] remains most firm in relation to walls and the like; whatever consciousness conceives of here, that very thing quickly becomes fully manifest there. (48)
By that constant wandering through the succession of dreams, it becomes even more firm due to the strengthening of those latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
He demonstrates that the capacity of consciousness for transformations corresponding to the arising of latent impressions is universal, stating: "Whatever [is seen] here... etc.
Whatever is seen by her even in a dream is indeed real at that time; for within the atom of consciousness (cidaṇu), all atoms of experience exist. (49)

For this very reason, he says "by that" to express the experience of the penetration of the existence of consciousness (*citsattā*) therein; "atoms of experience" (*anubhavāṇavaḥ*) refers to experiences that have become subtle, which is to say, the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the world-form. || 49 ||

(As this reading enclosed in brackets appears to be an interpolation— since it is not found in other manuscripts and is not accepted by the author of the commentary— the atoms of leaves, creepers, flowers, and fruits exist within other seeds.)
Within the world of atoms, I consider there to be only atoms of consciousness;
space is dissolved within space—abandon the delusion of duality and unity. 50.

"Into the atom. Thus, the meaning is that I consider it a marvel that the conscious principle and the world have entered into one another in their entirety. Alternatively, with the intention that this is not a marvel because the space of consciousness itself—though perceived as differentiated by the illusions of the world—is dissolved within its own self, he says: "dissolved. || 50 ||
Through its own space, time, activity, and substance, consciousness experiences atoms within itself;
it does not experience other [external] atoms, because such a thing is impossible.

He elaborates on what has already been stated with the words beginning "deśa" (place) and so forth: Through its own subtle atomic portions of consciousness (*cidaṃśa*), it experiences those which are essentially its own self as if they were others; however, in reality, there are no others, because others are impossible, being non-existent. || 51 ||
The atom of consciousness itself, manifesting as the creation within a dream, is experienced through the perception of bodies, ranging from Brahmā down to an insect. (52)

The meaning is this: from Brahmā down to the level of an insect, the fragment of consciousness—which is common to all—is delimited by the respective adjuncts of their internal organs (*antahkarana*). Although it is indistinct during the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), when creation occurs like a dream, it becomes experienced through the perception of each respective body. || 52 ||
In this world, nothing whatsoever exists as a real entity;
yet the atoms of consciousness themselves, being inherently real, experience duality as their own flavor.
To the question, "What is that which is experienced? he says: "It is *kacita*.
This means it is something indescribable (*anirvacanīya*). Then, to the question, "What is that? he says: "It is itself real (*svayaṃ satyam*).
Just as someone who is deluded might wish to climb upon his own shoulders, so too are the individual souls (*jīvas*) atoms of consciousness (*cit-paramāṇus*).
The meaning is that, through delusion, they imagine their own true nature—which is in fact reality itself—to be duality, and thus they taste it.
The minute fragment of consciousness, possessing a vast body, shines forth by itself,
emitting the fragrance of pure awareness through the flower-like gateways of the eyes and other senses.
Consciousness itself, due to the limitation of the internal organ (antahkarana), becomes a minute fragment.
Someone perceives the jar of consciousness even more clearly through its external form, because consciousness—the seed of all that is visible—is omnipresent and indestructible. (55)
A certain individual form of consciousness itself, due to its limitation by a gross body similar to a jar, is a "consciousness-jar" (cidghaṭa).
This occurs spatially and temporally through its externalized form. The reasons for this, respectively, are its omnipresence and its indestructibility. || 55 ||
Within [itself], a certain person perceives the entire world as stainless;
therein, through the passage of immense time, it emerges and submerges.
A certain collective self, whose form is the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa),
due to the passage of immense time and through long-standing practice, sinks— that is, dissolves— by means of the conceit of identity, and then emerges, manifesting once again. || 56 ||
Seeing one dream after another there again and again, he rolls about falsely among the banyan trees like a stone fallen from a mountain peak. (57)
Some were gathered together, while others remained in the cloudless void within themselves;
these fragments of bodies were submerged in the expansion of their own consciousness, yet vibrating with life.
Those who perceive within themselves the delusion of the world and living beings, by them that visible world is regarded as unreal, like a dream, though it is spread out by various means. (59)
With the intention that the specific distinction for those who perceive the internal objects of sight and the seer is the knowledge of their falsity, he says:
"By itself" (svayam). || 59 ||
Because the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is the self of all, that which is seen exists as truth within the Self;
for wherever the all-pervading [Self] is found, there indeed everything arises.

Keeping in mind the established principle of the seed—that for some, the cause of its existence is internal during the arising of the universe within them, whereas for others, upon seeing it, the cause of its existence is external—it is said: "Because it is the self of all. (60)
Furthermore, within the manifestation of every living being,
a fragment of the living soul (jīva-khaṇḍa) arises intensely, and yet another even more internal than that also emerges.

Even when various individual souls (jīvāntara), along with their respective phenomenal expansions (saprapañca) and unstable arisings, emerge here and there, the cause for the existence of each particular thing within that consciousness is that very consciousness itself accompanied by ignorance (ajñāna). However, once [reality] is known, nothing whatsoever has been, is, or will be anywhere;
with this intention, he says "jīvāntara... and so forth. || 61 ||
A living being is born within a living being, and within that too there is another living being;
for everywhere, like the layers of a plantain leaf, a living being exists indeed within another living being.

Immediately upon the transformation of the intellect regarding the visible world, this [duality] perishes once it is fully understood, just as the nature of being a bracelet and so forth vanishes from gold.

When there is a revolution of the intellect (buddhi)—having abandoned its outward orientation and attained an inward orientation—this internal and external [world], being simultaneously and equally realized in its true nature, perishes. || 63 ||
For one in whom the inquiry, "Who am I? What is this? does not arise, the long-lasting delusion of the fever of worldly existence does not cease within.
Having thus demonstrated the reasoning based on the subtle elements (*tanmātra-yukti*), which is characterized by the vision of reality (*tattva-darśana*),

he begins to explain, in reverse order, the means for attaining and establishing that [vision], starting from the conquest of the senses (*indriya-jaya*) and ending with discernment (*vicāra*): "Discernment" (verse 64).
The reflection of that person of right-mindedness should be known as fruitful, for whom the greed for enjoyments diminishes day by day. (65)
He says "saphala" (fruitful) to show that only inquiry preceded by dispassion culminates in the fruit, whereas that which is colored by passion does not.
Just as medicine administered to the body brings about health,
so too, when the conquest of the senses is practiced, discernment becomes fruitful.

He states that dispassion (*vairāgya*), preceded by the practice of mastery over the senses, is the cause of discrimination (*viveka*) and not otherwise—beginning with the words "Just as" (*yathā*). [The body] is utilized through the body and served by rules such as the consumption of wholesome food (*pathya*). (66)
Discernment exists only in words, brilliant like fire in a painting;
for one who possesses it, non-discernment is never abandoned and leads only to suffering. (67)
He shows that even discrimination (viveka), by generating dispassion (vairāgya) and the longing for liberation (mumukṣā),
culminates in the fruits of renunciation (saṃnyāsa), hearing [the scriptures] (śravaṇa), and so forth;
it is employed only for the establishment of the birth of those endowed with that [discrimination], and is not merely a sprout of words— thus he demonstrates:

By the words "discrimination" (viveka) and so forth: the meaning is that for one who possesses discrimination only in speech and not in the mind, that lack of discrimination has not been abandoned; thus, it leads only to suffering. || 67 ||
Just as the wind makes its presence known through touch and not by speech,
so too is his discernment awakened solely through the attenuation of desire.

If it is asked what the sign is when this discrimination is established in the mind, he says that it is precisely the firmness of dispassion—meaning "in the same way. *Tānava* means destruction through the process of gradual diminution. || 68 ||
Know that the nectar of a painting is not truly nectar; know that the fire of a painting is not truly fire;
and surely, a woman in a painting is not truly a bodiless goddess.
But verbal discrimination is actually non-discrimination.

He shows by way of a parallel statement that the discrimination shown by one who is still subject to passion is actually non-discrimination itself, because it consists of the branches and sub-branches of non-discrimination: "It is painted nectar. This means nectar, ambrosia, or water depicted in a painting. (69)
First, through solitude, passion and enmity are thinned out along with their very roots;
thereafter, even effort itself completely perishes.
That place is purifying where there is discernment.

Exertion, which is activity conducive to the attainment of the desired and the avoidance of the undesired, is indeed completely exhausted through the uprooting of its cause by the arising of knowledge. Therefore, he alone in whom discernment exists is a true person; the meaning is that he is pure and fit for being established in the reasoning of the *tanmātras*. || 70 ||
Thus ends the eighteenth canto, titled "The Introduction of the Section on Living Beings," in the *Sthitiprakaraṇa* of the *Mokṣopāya*, within the *Vāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa*, a work of the Sage. 18.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Introduction of the Section on Living Beings," in the *Sthitiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The Nineteenth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
The seed of the living soul is the Supreme Brahman, existing everywhere like space.
Therefore, even within the world that is the belly of a living being, there exists a soul in manifold ways. || 1 ||
Just as the attainment of the fruit of worship arises from awakening, so too is established the true Self;
and the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, as well as the fourth state (turiya), are described. || 1 ||

Now, if one were to postulate a succession of inner and inner living beings within the individual soul (*jīva*), then the outermost living beings would be the seeds of the innermost worlds of living beings, because they serve as their substratum; and likewise,

through the awakening to the nature of the outermost living beings within each successive inner level, by the process of attaining those respective states, [the realization culminates] in the outermost living being.

One might raise this objection: liberation is logically possible only upon the dawning of the realization of Brahman, not for other [entities] in the interim; for if Brahman were not directly present here and there, it could not function as the seed characterized by being the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*). And if that were possible, then since [Brahman] would be equally present in all things, the conceptualization of various internal sentient beings would be rendered rootless. Anticipating this doubt:

He establishes that Brahman alone is the seed, because it is the substratum even for the living beings within the world of living beings—stating "the seed of the living" (jīvabīja). This is by reason of its being present everywhere. || 1 ||

Because they consist of the single, solid mass of consciousness, the various classes of living beings exist within the individual soul like the layers of a plantain tree, or like insects within the belly of the earth.

In the conceptualization of a succession where one follows another with a single interval, there are many [beings] at each single interval, like the layers of a plantain tree; however, in the conceptualization of a succession where even within that interval there is only one, they are like insects in the belly of the earth—such is the distinction. || 2 ||
Whatever indeed, just as a worm might arise from the heat of the body in summer,
whatever is perceived in the pure space of consciousness, that becomes a living being by itself.
If it is asked, "Since the locus is identical, what is the solution to the argument that the conception of internality is groundless? he says this in response:
"He exists within each of those very things; likewise, pure consciousness is also internal or external.
Whatever is perceived anywhere, the individual soul (jīva) becomes the enjoyer of that very thing in that very place. This is the meaning. || 3 ||
In whatever manner those seekers of life strive for the perfection of their own inner selves,
in that very way they quickly become [perfected] through various methods of worship.
With the intention that the establishment of all order is due to the power of karma, which consists of the efforts of previous persons, he says:
"Those who sacrifice to the gods go to the gods; indeed, the Yakṣas go to the Yakṣas;
those who sacrifice to Brahman go to Brahman. One should take refuge in that which is not trivial. (5)

With the intention that even in the case of union (*sāyujya*) with deities or individual souls (*jīva*), which correspond to the gradations of ritual action and worship, the attainment of enjoyment is established according to the respective gradations within those deities—as proven by the authority of the scriptures—he says: "the gods. *Brahman* refers both to the one named Hiraṇyagarbha and to the Supreme. Regarding these, he states what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted: "that which... [and so forth].
For that son of Bhṛgu was indeed liberated by the purity of his own consciousness,
yet he was swiftly bound again by nature through the object of perception seen for the first time.
He states that the *Bhārgava-upākhyāna* (the story of Śukra) is also consistent with the point already stated: "He," etc.
The meaning is that Śukra became bound by the form of an Apsaras seen for the first time. || 6 ||
Just as a young girl born on earth who has withered away is first instructed before her very eyes while still unenlightened,
and is subsequently educated in exactly that same way,
so too must she be educated through the very nature of the Real Self, which is Brahman; it is not otherwise.
With the intention that [the world] exists through states such as wrong livelihood and so forth, he concludes with the word "on earth" (bhuvi).
The meaning is: as long as it is not withered by the afflictions of worldly calamities. || 7 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
O Blessed One, you should explain the distinction between the states of waking and dreaming;
how is there waking-within-waking, and how is a dream a delusion within waking?

Śrī Rāma asks— beginning with the words "jāgrad" (waking)— in order to know the distinction between when consciousness is "childlike" and when it is "mature," and the cause for the difference between the states of waking and dreaming:
"Even though there is no difference in the nature of direct manifestation, by what cause is it the waking state?"

The meaning is: how can it be that the waking state is the cause for the conventional usage of "truth," while the dream state is merely an illusion having the form of the waking state? Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
That which is accompanied by a stable conviction is called "waking."
That which has unstable conditions is declared to be a dream.

Vasiṣṭha provides the resolution: "The very capacity for stable cognition, brought forth by repeatedly verified recognition, is the cause for the conventional usage of 'truth' regarding objects in the waking state"—thus [he says] with the verse beginning "sthirā" (9).
In the state of waking, what is seen for a moment becomes a dream when it persists through a later time;
thus that which was waking attains the state of dreaming, and the dream reaches the state of waking.

If even a dream were to persist until another time, then it would certainly be perceived through direct experience in the waking state as "this is indeed waking" in that very moment; likewise, if waking were not to persist until another time,
then it would simply be a dream— thus, the waking state attains the nature of a dream, and the dream attains the nature of waking.
The meaning is "he goes. || 10 ||
The distinction between the states of waking and dreaming does not exist without stability and instability;
yet, the entire experience of both is always equal in every respect.
The experience, however, as well as the aspect of experiencing, is the same for both of these. || 11 ||
Even a dream attains the state of waking during the time of dreaming due to its stability;
whereas that which is unstable remains as waking, because it is perceived as such.
"Because of instability," as, for example, the mental constructions of one who is awake. 12.
Even a dream follows the state of waking through the aspect of waking-consciousness;
however, its dream-nature remains established according to the perception of dream-consciousness.

The waking-cognition-portion is the portion of instability grasped by waking cognition, such as the twelve-year [reign] of Hariścandra. If so, how can it have the nature of a dream? To this he says: "It is called a dream... (verse 13).
That which is perceived as stable for as long as it persists is called the waking state;
however, because of its momentary destruction, it is like a dream—listen now to how this occurs. (14)
He clarifies this point—that [the object] is stable according to its perception—with the words beginning "yattu" (but as for that), etc. || 14 ||
The life-element exists within the body by which one lives;
it is designated by such names as "vitality," "prowess," and "life-element," O dear one. (15)
By way of an introductory explanation of the description of what was promised, he establishes its nature as the living being (*jīva*) with the words "the element of life" (*jīvadhātu*).

By the phrase "that by which one lives," he shows that the very act of living is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) proving its existence. That which is called "heat" (*tejas*) is the warmth of the body, and that which is called "vitality" (*vīrya*) is the strength that is the cause of bodily movement.

That characteristic has been stated. By the term "vital element" (*jīvadhātu*), it is shown that the cause of life—the essence consisting of unconditional love—is its characteristic. From the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), it should be understood that other well-known factors such as knowledge, which serve as the basis for the conceit "I am," are likewise indicated. || 15 ||
When the body engages in worldly activity through mind, action, or speech,
then the vital element (jīvadhātu), impelled by the wind, flows forth.
Let it be that the individual soul (jīva) resides in the body; what is the cause for its engagement in perceiving forms and other objects? To this he says:
"The agent of worldly activity" (vyavahārī). The meaning is that it proceeds forth from the heart and moves about after having emerged, like water flowing from a canal into a lake. || 16 ||
As that [consciousness] spreads through the limbs, all cognition indeed arises;
for it is observed that the thing called "mind" (citta), which contains the delusion of the world within it, moves forward. (17)

Regarding this, he says "in that" (tasmin) to explain that the seeing of dreams occurs there due to the arising of latent impressions (*vāsanā*); "in the limbs" refers to the channels (*nāḍī*) within the limbs. || 17 ||
Flowing outward through the apertures such as the eyes,
she perceives within herself a form rich with various shapes and transformations that consists of the external world.
He states the waking state of that [consciousness] with the words "in the acts of seeing, etc.

The meaning is that although at the time of experience the cognition is not distinct from dream, yet after the occurrence of daily recognition, the conceptualization of stability is understood as being the waking state. || 18 ||
Because of its stability, that state is understood to be exactly as it is; thus, it is called the "sequence of waking. Now, hear the sequence beginning with deep sleep.
By the phrase "suṣuptādi," the sequence beginning with the fourth state (turiya) is also included. || 19 ||
When one's body is not agitated by mind, action, or speech,
then this constituent element of life remains established in itself, with a peaceful soul.

With the intention that the emergence of dreams occurs when vocal and physical distractions have ceased, whereas deep sleep occurs when even mental distraction has ceased, he says "by the mind," and so forth. || 20 ||
When the winds have attained equilibrium, the heart-sky is no longer agitated, just as a lamp in a windless chamber produces nothing but light. (21)
It is the sole producer of light, the cause of mere undistracted illumination. || 21 ||
Consequently, consciousness does not move through the limbs, and for that reason it is not agitated;
it does not enter the eyes and other [senses], nor does it go outside through the apertures.
By the first half [of the verse], the absence of the cause for dreaming is stated; by the second half, the absence of the cause for waking is stated. || 22 ||
The living soul vibrates within itself, just as the consciousness of oil is in the sesame seed;
just as the consciousness of cold is in frost, and the consciousness of oiliness is in clarified butter.

[Objection: But surely, by the Śruti text, "Then, my dear, he becomes merged in Being; he has gone to his own Self," it is heard that at the time of deep sleep the individual soul (jīva) merges into Brahman; how then can it be said that at that time the soul's location is like that of a lamp? To this, he says: "The soul... [The soul] merges into Brahman accompanied precisely by the latent impression (saṃskāra) of "I am the soul," and not as liberated from that [impression], just as in the case of sesame seeds.
The meaning is that, having attained that state, it shines forth like the consciousness of oil. || 23 ||

A certain subtle power (kalā) in the form of the individual soul (jīva), being consciousness itself, attains within itself the state of deep sleep—a state that is tranquil, windless, and devoid of objective cognition—by virtue of its own transparency. (24)

[Objection: "But then, what is the status of such scriptural statements as, 'For then one has crossed over all the sorrows of the heart,' and 'He becomes the one seer, non-dual, like water'? To this, he says: "In the form of the individual soul" (*jīvākāra*).

Any consciousness (*cit*) that previously possessed the form of the individual soul is a "part" (*kalā*); through the dissolution of its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), by virtue of its transparency, it [merges] into the Self that is Brahman.

The meaning is that those scriptural passages proceed by taking up a state that is unconscious and devoid of separate consciousness, and not with the intention of dissolving the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of duality.
Anticipating the objection that there might be distraction caused by the vital breath (*prāṇavāta*), he qualifies it as "tranquil" (*saumya*). || 24 ||

Having known the cessation of diversity and abiding in equanimity even while engaged in worldly activity, one who is fully awakened throughout the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep is said to possess the fourth state (turya). || 25 ||

In this context, he shows his fourth state with the words "having known" (*jñātvā*). When the mind (*citta*)— or according to another reading, "when the consciousness (*cetasi*) has ceased"— has ceased,

meaning when all worldly activity has subsided, the yogi, having understood from the scriptures the equanimity (*sāmya*), which is the absence of fluctuation (*avaiṣamya*) within that consciousness, becomes fully awakened through his own efforts consisting of inquiry and one-pointed concentration, thereby attaining direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*).

Whether engaged in the activities of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep—these well-known states—or even in the previously mentioned distinctions of the stages (bhūmikās), and by the force of the word "api" (even/also), even while established in samādhi, one who does not fall away from the essential nature of the Fourth State (turyātman) due to the strength of firm realization is always considered to possess the state of Turya. This is the meaning. || 25 ||
When that vital element, the life-force, is set in motion by the breaths which have attained a state of serenity during deep sleep, it arises as consciousness; therefore, it is designated as "citta."

Having restated the present state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), he speaks of the arising of the mind (*cittotpatti*) in order to elaborate upon the previously mentioned descent into the dream state— beginning with the words "In deep sleep. When that constituent of the living being (*jīvadhātu*), characterized by vital breaths (*prāṇa*) that have attained a state of tranquility (*saumyatā*), is moved by those very same breaths which have acquired an imbalance produced by the ripening of the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) of the experiencer, then that [state arises].

The meaning is that [the body] comes into being as something manifested, having arisen as consciousness due to the awakening of prior latent impressions (saṃskāra) conducive to the experience of that living consciousness. || 26 ||
Within its own interior, it quickly perceives the entire web of worlds— along with their existence and non-existence and their sequential delusions— as expansive as a tree within a seed.

Then he describes the vision in a dream with the words "svāntaḥsaṃsthā" (abiding within oneself). Just as a yogi, by the power of yoga, discerns and beholds a tree existing within a seed—endowed with expansion through its latent state—in the same way [he perceives the world]. || 27 ||
When the element of life (jīvadhātu) is slightly or intensely agitated by the vital winds (vātas), one then perceives within oneself the sensation of moving through space, thinking, "I am asleep."

Having clearly restated what has already been said, he describes the arising of the ego from the mind and the causes for various types of delusion, beginning with the word "jīva": "When a sleeping person is slightly agitated by the vital winds (vātas), then he perceives, 'I am.
But when he is intensely agitated, then he perceives movement in the sky—that is, traveling through space. This is the meaning.
When it is flooded by water, then it experiences within itself the agitation of the water and so forth,
just as a flower experiences its own fragrance.
By water, that is, by the liquid phlegm located within the channels. || 29 ||
When one is overcome by bile and other humors, then one experiences within oneself a vast delusion of summer and so forth,
as if it were entirely external.
Just as one sees external places and times filled with blood and red in color, because it is of the nature of experience, one sinks right there. (31)

Being filled—that is, drenched—with blood, meaning with the blood within the channels, he perceives regions as regions pervaded by red chalk and the like, and times as times such as the twilight pervaded by red clouds. || 31 ||
Whatever latent impression (vāsanā) he cultivates, that he perceives within while asleep, just as one agitated by the wind perceives through the apertures of the eyes and other senses. || 32 ||
Because his sensory gaps have not been overcome, he becomes agitated within;
he quickly experiences consciousness [in that state], which is called a dream. (33)
One whose sensory apertures—the locations of the eyes and so forth—are not invaded; being such as that, he is one who experiences internal objects. || 33 ||
When one whose sensory apertures have been invaded by the agitated breath perceives [objects], the best of sages call that "waking."

He states the definition of the waking state (*jāgrat*) as being characterized by attainment: "When fully pervaded," and so forth. The meaning is that when the individual soul (*jīva*), being agitated, becomes one whose sensory apertures are fully pervaded and perceives external objects such as sound and the like, they call that perception "waking. || 34 ||
Thus, by you who have realized this, whose great intelligence is now renowned within, the proclamation of reality should no longer be maintained here in this unreal world.
She who contemplates the faults of death, destruction, and dissolution. || 35 ||

In this world expanded by the distinctions of waking and so forth, the very notion of reality is an evil because it is the cause of attachment; therefore, that alone is to be abandoned. Thus he says: "iti" (thus). Here, in this unreal world, the view called "reality" must certainly not be cultivated. Why? Because that view is death—death [caused] by internal causes.

The meaning is that *hatih* is death caused by physical (ādhibhautika) factors, and *saṃhṛtiḥ* is death caused by divine (ādhidaivika) factors; it is that which brings about (*bhāvanī*) those defects which are the causes of such deaths, necessarily producing them. || 35 ||

Thus ends the nineteenth sarga, titled "An Investigation into the Nature of Waking, Dreaming, Deep Sleep, and the Fourth State," in the Section on Stability (*sthitiprakaraṇa*) of the Holy Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa, composed by Valmiki, the son of Daśaratha. 19.

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "An Investigation into the Nature of the Waking, Dreaming, Deep Sleep, and Turīya States," in the *Sthitiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The Twentieth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus has all this been told to you—the description of the nature of the mind.
O Rāghava, it was by me alone, and not by anyone else, for no other reason whatsoever. || 1 ||
For the universe is indeed the delusion of the mind when it does not rely upon the True Self;
but when the mind relies upon the True Self, the universe and the self are described as being one. || 1 ||
He demonstrates the connection of the previously described characterization of the nature of waking and so forth with the subject at hand by saying "this":
that by which the form of the mind is defined—that is, understood correctly—is such [an instrument].
The description of waking and so forth is introduced for the sake of thoroughly knowing the nature of the mind, and not by any other means.
The meaning is: "by means of a purpose. || 1 ||
Whatever the mind, possessed of firm resolve, meditates upon repeatedly, that it becomes; just as a lump of iron attains the state of fire through contact with flames. (2)

If it is asked what kind of nature of the mind has been fully understood by this [verse], he says: "The nature of firmly maintaining the form of an object that has been intensely cultivated"—thus, "firmly" (dṛḍha). || 2 ||
Views concerning the grasping of existence and non-existence, or their rejection, are fashioned by consciousness;
they are neither unreal nor real, being produced merely by the fickleness of the mind. (3)

Therefore, it is established that all objects of cognition—whether existent or non-existent, to be abandoned or to be adopted—are distinct from both existence and non-existence, because they are merely mental constructions; thus he says: "bhāva... (verse 3).
But the mind, when deluded, becomes the agent and the cause for the persistence of the world;
indeed, the defiled mind expands this [universe] through its universal form. (4)

In this regard, he states the distinction—that the mind, in its individual (vyaṣṭi) form, is the agent of delusion, while in its collective (samaṣṭi) form, it is the material cause (upādāna) of the world which is its object—by saying "the mind. This is by way of its universal form, that is, by way of its individual and collective forms. || 4 ||

For that which is called the person is indeed the mind; having directed it onto the auspicious path, one achieves all prosperities in the world, for they are accomplished solely through its conquest. (5)

In that regard, if the aspect of the agent is directed toward the auspicious path, then the powers such as *aṇimā* residing in the aspect of the instrument, as well as the realization of reality (*tattvabodha*), come under one's control; thus he says: "The mind... (verse 5).

If the person were identical with the body, how could the high-minded Śukra have gone through hundreds of wanderings in various forms throughout successive births? (Alternatively, "through hundreds of other lives," according to another reading.)
If it is argued that the body alone should be the person (puruṣa) and not the mind, he says "no"—"The person... (verse 6).
Therefore, the mind is indeed the person, and the body is the object of perception;
whatever this [mind] consists of, that it undoubtedly attains. (7)
Since it is impossible for the body to be the person, because it is like a jar or a wall, [the person] must be consciousness alone by the method of elimination;
thus he says: "Therefore," etc. This is the mind (citta). || 7 ||
Strive with effort to contemplate that which is non-empty, effortless, free from limiting conditions, and beyond delusion; you shall thereby attain that very state.
"May my mind be capable of attaining everything. To this, he says "yad" (that which), meaning: "If you exert yourself toward liberation, that attainment will be yours. || 8 ||
The mind rushes toward the body it inhabits, but the mind does not go toward a physical form that has been abandoned; therefore,
let your mind truly rush toward that here.
O fortunate one, let the mind abandon that which is unreal and other than [the truth]. || 9 ||

He summarizes the very point already stated in brief: "It flies toward. The body flies toward the place or object desired by the mind; however, the mind does not necessarily go to the place or object traversed by the body. Therefore, for the accomplishment of what the mind desires— [The original Sanskrit text continues: manaḥsthitamiti | manaḥsthitam manobhilasitam deśam viṣayam vā śarīramabhipatati vapuṣācaritam tu deśam viṣayam vā mano na niyamena prayāti ato manasaḥ svābhilaṣitasiddhau || *Note: The provided source text contains a repetition of the phrase "manaḥsthitamiti" and the subsequent commentary. The translation above reflects the core meaning of the passage as it appears.*

Since you possess the capacity to govern the body, the senses, and so forth, let your mind—which is indeed real—be directed toward the supreme reality, the truth of the Self; strive for its attainment. By that means, abandon the unreal duality consisting of the delusion of the body, senses, and so on; this is the meaning. || 9 ||
Thus ends the twentieth sarga, titled "The Description of the Form of Manas," in the Sthitiprakaraṇa of the Mokṣopāya section of the glorious Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa, a work of the Ṛṣis.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Nature of the Mind," in the Section on Stability (*sthitiprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa-tātparya-prakāśa*.
The Twenty-first Chapter.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, this great doubt which I have—"
It turns back within the heart, restless like a wave in the ocean. || 1 ||

If [the mind] were pure, the mental construction [of it] would not be tenable due to the absence of a conceptualizer; if it were impure, there would be various conceptual proliferations of different doctrines because the mind itself is established [as the basis]. (1)

"Exert yourself to pursue that which is non-empty, effortless, free from attributes, and beyond delusion," was the instruction given by the Guru. Having pursued it with such effort, Rāma, through his own intellectual skill,
perceived therein no fitness for the mental construction [of objects] as previously described.

Finding no consolation in his own mental constructions, with his mind only half-awakened and desiring to question, he turns toward the Teacher and reveals his doubt, saying, "O Blessed One. The epithet "knower of all dharmas" is a qualification intended to highlight the Teacher's skill in discerning the disciple's inner disposition. || 1 ||
In that which is unconditioned by space, time, and the like, all-pervading, eternal, and free from affliction—whence has this withered consciousness, called "mind," arisen? || 2 ||
Because it lacks spatial limitation, it is pervasive; because it lacks temporal limitation, it is eternal;
because it is devoid of the limitations imposed by objects—as indicated by the word "beginning"—it is free from affliction. [The mind] is withered and turbid with the forms of sense-objects.
Why? Because there is no possibility of a cause. Where? Because there is no possibility of its own nature. And "this" refers to the immediacy of the mind.
It has been shown. || 2 ||
Since there is no other name, no past, and none that will ever be—how, of what kind, or in what manner could any blemish exist therein? (3)

If they were to say, "Because of the influence of the stain of ignorance," he says in response to that as well: [the reading is *brūyāḥ*]—the meaning is that the existence of such a stain is not possible. || 3 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Well spoken by you, O Rāma! Your mind has become a partaker of liberation, flowing with the essence of the highest truth like a cluster of blossoms from the Nandana grove.

Being thus questioned, Vasiṣṭha first praises Rāma’s intellectual skill, which is wondrous in its familiarity with the subject matter, saying, "Excellent!"— she whose wonder at the experience of things is like the finest flow of nectar. || 4 ||
This mind of yours is intent upon investigating what precedes and what follows;
you shall attain that most exalted state which was reached by Śaṅkara and the others.
But, O Rāma, this is not the time for this question now;
this question is addressed only when the final conclusion is being stated.

The question—"The stain of ignorance is not fitting for the pure conscious Self"—would be appropriate only for one who has personally experienced the pure Self. However, we do not direct our minds toward such a person, so that he might ask in that manner. But as for one who has not experienced the pure [Self] and perceives the learned man alone as the Self—

Thinking thus, he should doubt how his own purity—which contradicts his own experience—could possibly exist; however, he should not, having accepted a purity that contradicts experience, wonder how there could be impurity within that purity.
With the intention that this is not the occasion for the inquiries of a wise person at the time of instruction for the ignorant, he says:

Regarding the phrase "of the question": in this context of Nirvāṇa, where—immediately after the establishment of the meditative absorption (samādhi) of your vision of the Self—I am stating the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), the very meaning ascended through experience, for the sake of corroboration by my own experience;
therein this question is raised. The meaning is that it is being resolved. || 6 ||
At the time of the final conclusion, you must ask me this supreme question;
by that, your final realization will become as clear as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of your hand.
He says, "I will speak," yet there is no confidence that this will be so; therefore, he says, "Or rather, I must be questioned again," adding, "at the time of the final conclusion" (*siddhāntakāle*).
By that question, when I have composed myself, the final conclusion—the Self whose reality is established through direct experience—will come to be.
This statement of yours regarding the question at the time of the final conclusion shines forth.
For the cry of the peacock is appropriate in the rainy season, while the song of the swan is fitting in autumn.

In autumn, however, the cry of the swan is appropriate, but not that of the peacock; likewise, a question suited to the level of the ignorant is proper, because the realization of the reality of the Self has not yet arisen for any of the listeners—this is the intended meaning. || 8 ||
The innate azure of the sky shines at the end of the rainy season,
whereas during the rains it arises from dense and towering masses of clouds.
Now, this question is like describing the natural deep blue color of the sky during the rainy season; thus he says:
"This supreme determination of the mind, which is the subject at hand and now commenced, is that by whose power the birth of living beings occurs; listen to it, O observer of noble vows. (10)
Having thus composed himself, he makes Rāma favorable toward listening to the matter at hand with the words "This... (verse 10).
Thus, O Rāma, this nature, characterized by the mental faculty and the act of thinking, is determined by all seekers of liberation to be karma. (11)

Thus, in the manner previously described, since Mālinī is established through the experience of the Command (ājñā), this Consciousness (cit) conditioned by her, when undergoing differentiation, becomes the form of Prakṛti. Being characterized by the faculty of thinking, she becomes the mind (manas);
as seeing, she becomes the eye; as hearing, she becomes the ear; and as seeing, she is the eye, and as hearing, she is the ear.

This is because of such scriptural passages as "thinking, [it becomes] mind" (manvāno manaḥ). Thus, the meaning is that it has been determined by the seekers of liberation through the authority of the Vedas and other sources that action, known as dharma and adharma, itself comes into being through the activity of those who have assumed the state of the organs of action. || 11 ||

Listen to its name and the forms it is conceived to have according to the different philosophical systems, as they are described by eloquent speakers through their various perspectives on the scriptures. (12)

He says "Listen" (śṛṇu) to show that it is indeed that very same [reality], though it is conceptualized otherwise by many disputants according to their own preferred names, forms, and shapes. || 12 ||
Whatever state the mind, flickering with its own thoughts, assumes, it takes on that very form, just as the wind dwelling within acquires the intense fragrance of the object it carries.

Now, under the guise of resolving the doubt—"If they have a single root, how can there be a difference in their philosophical tenets?"—it was stated that "karma" has been determined; this he demonstrates with the verse beginning "yaṃ yam," etc.: "Whatever state [of being], arising from such-and-such a latent impression (vāsanā)... as follows:
Just as the wind residing within flowers—which possess various scents such as fragrant, putrid, or pungent—attains the nature of those respective odors, so it is in this case. 13.
Then, having determined that very [object] and conceptualizing it as such, he colors his own ego with an internal passion. (14)

Having determined through reasoning that this [world] is indeed constructed solely by the latent impressions (vāsanā) of each individual, he colors his own ego with the passion for his own imagined object, as if inducing the state of being that [object]. || 14 ||
Taking that certainty as his basis, he attains aesthetic flavor (rasa) in that very state;
for [the self] consists of that [consciousness] within the body, and likewise within the faculties of cognition and action. (15)

"Rasa" refers to the aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*) arising from repeated relish. With the intention that even for those attached to sense objects, this is precisely the same state regarding the flavor of relishing sense objects, he describes the assumption of a body corresponding to that as "being composed of that" (*yanmayatvam*). || 15 ||
For that mind of which this body is composed, O Rāma, follows its lead and comes under its control;
it attains the nature of that [object], just as the wind within a fragrant substance takes on the nature of fragrance.
The wind, having entered within the fragrance—that is, within the fragrant substance—assumes, as it were, the very form of that fragrance.
When the organs of perception are active, the group of organs of action then vibrates of its own accord, like dust tossed by the wind.
When the body is sustained in accordance with the mind, the sense organs (jñānendriyas) manifest therein;
then, for the sake of performing actions that result in the attainment of objects deliberated upon by those [senses], the organs of action (karmendriyas) appear. Thus he says:
"In the sense organs. When they are "leaping," meaning when they have manifested and are leaping toward their respective objects; as the wind, restless with passion (rajas), blows.
She is like the earth, whose form consists of the *rajas* quality contained within that [universe]. || 17 ||
When the group of organs of action is agitated, it fully exerts its own power;
thus, extensive action is accomplished, like a mass of dust in the wind. (18)
He brings forth—that is, manifests—his own power, the power of action (*kriyāśakti*). || 18 ||
For thus the activity of the mind is the seed of action, and the mind is known as that very seed;
the existence of the two is non-different, just like that of a flower and its fragrance. (19)

Concluding the demonstration of how the mind attains the state of being action, he states that action and the mind are mutual seeds and possess an identical existence, saying: "In this way" (evam). || 19 ||
Whatever state the mind adopts through the power of firm habituation,
it accordingly sheds the branches of manifestation known as vibration and action.

Thus, because the impressions (*vāsanā*), karma, and the experience of their fruits are also of a uniform nature, he says "of whatever kind" in two verses to show that there is but a single reality. || 20 ||
Thus, with devotion, one brings about the action and its fruit;
then, having experienced that very relish, one is swiftly bound.
Whatever state he assumes, he perceives that very thing as the reality;
and the conviction arises within him that there is no other excellence than that. || 22 ||
Let it be so; nevertheless, how is it that living beings and disputants exhibit such partiality toward their own desired object, even though it is devoid of essence?
To this he says: "Whichever [object]... (verse 22).
For they always strive for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa;
their minds are indeed firmly divided by their very own practice.
