Indeed, having accepted the mind as the innate, pure principle of the followers of Kapila and having determined it, the philosophical perspectives of their scriptures were formulated. (24)

In that regard, for the followers of Kapila, the mind— due to its discriminative nature— is pure and stainless by virtue of its own innate apprehension of mere objects as being nothing but unattached consciousness. However, concerning those objects, because of delusion arising from a lack of reliance on scripture, they [erroneously] perceive through their own intellect that which is insentient and consists of pleasure, pain, and delusion.

The meaning is that, having accepted that the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world must be the *pradhāna*— which consists of the three *guṇas*— and having repeatedly relished this view and determined that this alone is the truth, their scriptural perspectives were thus constructed. || 24 ||

But regarding liberation, there is no other way to attain it; thus, those whose minds are so conditioned reflect their own views while remaining fixed in the delusions of their own restrictive rules. (25)

Otherwise, those whose minds are convinced that there is no attainment of liberation for anyone except through the means taught by themselves, remain fixed in the delusions of their own fabricated rules; having turned away from the views of others regarding alternative means, they manifest their own perspective through the composition of treatises and other such works, thereby reflecting it within the intellects of others.
The meaning is "they cause to transfer. || 25 ||
The proponents of Vedānta, having determined through the intellect that "this is Brahman," have conceived liberation as being endowed with tranquility and self-control. (26)
He says that the same applies to the Vedāntins as well: "the proponents of Vedānta.

According to the authority of the Śruti, by means of the method of superimposition and negation (adhyāropāpavāda), it is established through common usage that this world is indeed Brahman alone and nothing other than Brahman exists even in the slightest degree; [thus] tranquility (śama) is the cessation of all misfortune, and self-control (dama) is...

The meaning is that there is a manifestation as the nature of Brahman—which is real, unsurpassed bliss, and unlimited—attained (*itā*) in its very own place, in close proximity (*upa*), in that very form; it does not mean traveling a long distance by way of the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi*).
Alternatively, it may mean "the Vedāntins endowed with tranquility and self-control. The prefix *pari* is used here in the sense of "above" (*upari*), signifying being preeminent among all.
The meaning is "established. || 26 ||
But for those whose minds are convinced that liberation cannot be attained otherwise, they reveal their own view through their own arbitrary delusions regarding restrictive rules. (27)

By the phrase "through errors regarding the rules," it is indicated that for the Vedāntins, only the reality of the goal (upeya-tattva) is real, whereas the differences in the methods and procedures (upāya-prakriyā-bheda) are merely conceptual constructs, just as they are for Pāṇini. || 27 ||

The Vijñānavādins, having determined through their intellect—which is filled with shimmering errors—that liberation consists in being endowed with tranquility and self-control, have formulated this [view]. (28)

It is endowed with tranquility (*śama*), which is the pacification of the calamities of the cosmic dissolution, and with self-control (*dama*), which is the restraint of the doors of the senses; it is characterized by the entry into the stream of the omniscient Buddha’s wisdom.
Or, it is "endowed" in the sense that it has been attained through the means of accomplishment well-established as tranquility, self-control, and so forth. || 28 ||
But for those whose minds are convinced that liberation cannot be attained otherwise, they expound their own view through their own arbitrary delusions regarding restrictive rules. (29)
By delusions regarding observances—that is, by delusions regarding the rules of ritual procedure, or by delusions regarding the rules for ascetic practices such as climbing heated stones. || 29 ||

By the Arhats and others, as well as by various [teachers], diverse philosophical systems have been devised according to their own respective inclinations and whims, through their varied modes of conduct. (30)

"By the Ārhata and others"—by the word "others," the Kāpilas, Kaulikas, and so forth are included. For in the Ārhata doctrine, there are seven categories (padārthas), beginning with the soul (jīva) and ending with liberation (mokṣa). Among these: 1) the soul (jīva) is conscious and equal in size to the body; 2) the non-soul (ajīva) consists of stones and the like; 3) that by which the soul flows [toward objects] is the influx (āsrava), namely the group of sense organs; 4) that which covers [the soul] is restraint (saṃvara).
Others say that *viveka* consists of the restraints (*yama*), observances (*niyama*), and so forth. *Nirjara* is that by which desire and the like are worn away without remainder;
it refers to asceticism such as the plucking out of hair. *Bandha* is the repeated cycle of birth and death.
*Mokṣa* is the eternal upward movement into the non-worldly space (*alokākāśa*) resulting from the cessation of that [bondage]. These are the seven. Of these—

The practitioner [of this system] is the logic of the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅgīnyāya*). There are four types of proponents: the proponent of existence (1), the proponent of non-existence (2), the proponent of both existence and non-existence (3), and the proponent of the inexpressible (4). Even within the doctrine of the inexpressible, there are three further divisions based on existence and so forth; thus, in total, there are seven proponents. Among them, the proponent of existence [refers to] the Ārhata...

When asked, "Is liberation and so forth present according to your doctrine? he replies, "It may be (syāt) that it exists. The indeclinable *syāt* is a particle resembling a verbal form (*tiṅanta-pratirūpaka*) which signifies "somewhat" (*īpad-artha*) or "in some way" (*kathaṃcid-artha*), and is used in every instance.
Similarly, for those who maintain the doctrine of non-existence and so forth, the respective answers are "it may be that it does not exist" (*syān nāsti*) and so on. By this means, their...
"Silence is the Arhat’s desire"— this [statement], found as a marginal note in the Kashmiri manuscript, is accepted.

Through the conceptualization of the divisions of categories such as soul (jīva), non-soul (ajīva), influx (āsrava), restraint (saṃvara), shedding (nirjarā), bondage (bandha), and liberation (mokṣa), [the world] may be said to exist.

They are diverse through the conceptualizations of the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅgīnaya*), such as: "it may not exist," "it may both exist and not exist," "it may be inexpressible," "it may both exist and be inexpressible," "it may both not exist and be inexpressible," and "it may exist, not exist, and be inexpressible.
They are also diverse through their various practices, such as the conduct of going naked or the practice of begging for alms. || 30 ||
Indeed, these various styles (rīti) arise from their own certainties like a multitude of gentle water bubbles rising from a signless source; thus they are established as mature. 31.

He states in two verses beginning with "nirnimitta" that the root of all the various conceptual constructions is not the object of knowledge, but rather the mental construction itself, firmly established through long-standing habituation. || 31 ||
O mighty-armed one, the mind is the source of all these modes, just as the ocean is the source of jewels.
The neem tree and the sugarcane are not simultaneously bitter and sweet, nor are the moon and fire cold and hot;
whatever is intensely practiced and perceived in a certain way, it is experienced exactly as such.

Regarding "cold and heat": the implication is that for the gods dwelling in the lunar orb, the solar orb, the fire-orb, and so forth, there is no affliction from cold, heat, and the like. "Supremely practiced" means practiced until the point of producing the fruit of the impelling unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). || 33 ||
But that bliss which is uncreated—men striving for its sake should lead their minds to consist of it, so that it may be fully attained. (34)

If such firm practice is required even for a trivial matter, what need is there to mention that it is required for the fruit of liberation—which is uncreated bliss—when that fruit is obscured by beginningless, contrary worldly tendencies? With this intention, he says: "But he who... (verse 34).
The mind that avoids its own trivial and delusive objects of perception is not necessarily dragged away by the pleasure and pain born from them. (35)

If it is asked, "Then for whom should firm practice be performed for the sake of liberation?", the author says "the visible world" (*dṛśya*) and so forth, with the intention that it is precisely for the cleansing of the visible world.
*Saṃpariḍimbha* means one who, out of affection, completely embraces and treats [the world] like a child or an infant. Of such a nature...
One's own mind, having abandoned that which is seen, does not get dragged away by pleasure and pain arising from what is seen; "inevitably" (avaśyam) serves as an emphatic particle. || 35 ||
O sinless one, contemplate the visible world as impure, unreal in nature, delusive, a cause of fear, a mere appearance, expansive, and a bondage— do not give rise to it as a reality. (36)
This is illusion, for this is ignorance; this is mental cultivation that brings fear.
The wise know that "action" (karman) is that state of consciousness which consists of being absorbed in that [cultivation]. || 37 ||
The meaning is that they know that very state of being absorbed in and dominated by the visible world becomes the binding karma through the sequence previously described. || 37 ||
Seeing that the mind is intent solely upon the objects of sight, know it to be delusive;
wipe away that false, great mire of impurity.
This state of identification with the visible world, which is experienced as one's own nature, is called the intoxicant of saṃsāra, namely ignorance (avidyā), by the wise. (39)
If it is asked, "What offense has the visible world committed that its cleansing is thus prescribed?", he says in response: "By the visible," etc. (Verse 39).
Afflicted by this, the world does not attain what is auspicious,
just as one whose eyes are blinded by a cataract cannot perceive the brilliant light of the sun.
Tapanah means the Sun; this light belongs to him, hence it is called tāpana. || 40 ||
And that [world] arises by itself from mental construction, like a tree in the sky;
O Mahāmati, it ceases through mere non-constructive thought regarding such ideation.
He states that non-mentation (*asaṃkalpana*) is the cause for the cleansing of the visible world, saying "by oneself" (*svayam*). || 41 ||
When [doubt] has been exhausted by its own inherent force through playful inquiry,
non-attachment toward all objects has attained stability.
By means of discernment and inquiry, consisting of hearing and reflection, and by means of playful absorption, characterized by the playfulness of firmness in the practice of samādhi.
When the vision of truth has been attained and the unreal has come to an end,
that Self, which is the pure essence of non-conceptual consciousness, is fully realized.

The "pure self" (acchātman) is that self which is of a transparent nature; it is the self that is ultimate reality (paramārthasatya). Whether the reading is "I am that self, I am that self," or in another version, "I am that self, the pure non-conceptual consciousness, is attained"—in both cases, the meaning is the inner self (pratyagātman). || 43 ||
He for whom there is neither existence nor non-existence, neither happiness nor suffering, in whom only the state of absolute oneness is perceived within—[he is the liberated one]. (44)

Existence is manifestation; non-existence is non-manifestation. Pleasure is a modification of the mind in the form of *sattva*; it is perceived within one's own heart through one's own direct experience alone. || 44 ||

He who is abandoned by that cultivation which is incapable [of liberation], as well as by the mind, the senses, and the views—even though these are not distinct from the self—is [truly liberated]. || 45 ||

It is understood that [the Self] is not perceived by means of the conceit of "I" regarding the body and so forth—which is unfitting and a cause of misfortune—and which, due to the superimposition of identity with the Self, have become non-different from it. (45)
Just as the sky is obscured by endless rows of clouds, so too is the reality of the rope perceived as a snake when it is shrouded by infinite latent impressions (vāsanās). 46.
Due to the attraction of the word "also" (*api*), the connection with the preceding [phrase] is: "he is also completely devoid of latent impressions" (*vāsanābhiḥ*).
All these preceding qualifiers are connected with the distant term: "that Self is attained.
Having elaborated upon the means for the removal of bondage, he speaks of the one who fashions the notion of bondage:
Regarding the phrase "when there is doubt," and so forth: *sarpatattva* means the nature of a snake. || 46 ||
Bondage, which is essentially the nature of the sky of consciousness, is imagined through non-bondage itself;
for every imagined thing is rendered otherwise by a counter-imagining.

The phrase "by means of the nature of the consciousness-ether" implies "within one's own self. With the intention that Brahman itself, due to being permeated by imagined objects, appears as if it has attained various diversities in each individual object and is perceived as the nature of suffering and saṃsāra, he says:
"The imagined, the imagined. (47)
That very [Self] assumes otherness, as it were, like its own day and night—
that which is non-vacuous, effortless, free from limiting adjuncts, and devoid of delusion.
He says that when conceptual construction is abandoned, the bliss of the supreme human goal remains as that alone:
"That which is non-trivial" (verse 48).
That which transcends all such conceptualization leads only to happiness, just as there is fear when one thinks "there is a lion" in an empty granary. (49)
Likewise, there is fear that "I am bound within this very empty body";
yet, when one looks into an empty granary, no lion is found. (50)

Regarding the perception of fear even where there is no fear due to ignorance, and its cessation through mere observation, he provides an illustration with the words beginning "In a void," etc. (Verse 50).
Likewise, when this purpose of the bondage of saṃsāra is scrutinized, it is not found;
[rather,] "this world" and "this I" have arisen as a delusion. (51)
This is the aggregate consisting of the body and so forth. || 51 ||
Just as the shadow of a palm tree appears during midday to children,
so do existence and non-existence, good and evil, arise for a living being through the power of conceptual construction.

In the intermediate period between extreme childhood and youth, at the time of three or four years of age; or in the interval between daylight and night, during the time of dim darkness; "chāyā" refers to dense darkness in places such as the foot of a tree; "vaitālikī" means having the form of a *vetāla* (vampire); "bhāva" means prosperity (*vaibhava*), while "abhāva" means poverty (*dāridrya*); [the forms] consist of these.
Phenomena are both auspicious and inauspicious. || 52 ||
In one moment they come to non-existence, and again in a moment they exist;
even a mother, once assumed the state of a wife, hangs from the neck. 53.
The meaning is that they reach non-existence, concealment, and again existence, manifestation;
for it is well known that the capacity of objects to perform causal efficiency follows their conceptual construction—this he states with the words "the Mother alone," and so forth. || 53 ||
Bestowing the bliss of amorous union, she performs the duties of a housewife;
embraced around the neck with the affection of a mother, she is truly like a beloved wife. (54)
Surely she causes one to forget even the god of love through her maternal affection,
as she gazes upon the multitude of objects that yield fruits according to one's inner disposition.
In this world, no single form is declared for objects by the wise; rather, the mind, through firm contemplation, intensely imagines each thing exactly as it conceives it.
One perceives each respective fruit, having that very form, for that duration of time.
There is nothing that is not real, and there is nothing that is not false.
In whatever manner and by whatever means something is determined, it is characterized as such;
the mind, having cultivated the image of a celestial elephant, is perceived as a sky-elephant. (58)

The connection with the following verse is as follows: by one who has cultivated the space-elephant (*ākāśamātaṅga*)—that is, a mind of such a kind—the mind, being afflicted by desire through the imagined state of being a sky-elephant, pursues and follows its own imagined female elephant (*mātaṅgī*), a she-elephant wandering in a forest imagined within that very space. 58.
He pursues the female elephant of the forest of the sky who stands within the sky;
therefore, you must [subdue] that very volition which consists of the nature of all things. (59)

Therefore, concluding that one's state of being consists in abiding in the natural self-nature precisely through the renunciation of volitional constructs (*saṃkalpa*), he teaches with the words "therefore" (verse 59).
O Rāma, remaining in the state of deep sleep, become the Self of the self by means of your own self;
for a gem is indifferent toward the act of rejecting reflections.

The meaning is: "Be as your own self through its ultimate nature of non-dual bliss, and not as a self whose nature is non-ultimate suffering. Now, one might raise this objection: "Even though dualistic states have been abandoned by me through my resolve, they may still be unavoidable within me—despite my lack of desire for them—just as reflections appear in a jewel even when one does not wish for them. Anticipating this doubt:
He states the distinction: "The jewel," etc. (verse 60).
It is incapable due to its insentient nature, O Rāma, but not so for one like you;
for here, O Rāma, the entire world is reflected within your own self.

He says "when" (yadā) to show that even if, by chance, a reflection of duality should occasionally appear in the mind when it has ceased [from its usual state], one must abandon the coloring of that reflection with the nature of reality through the contemplation of its falsity. || 61 ||
Having determined that it is a non-entity, do not allow yourself to be colored by it;
nor, on the other hand, should you regard it as real, for it is non-different from the Supreme Self.
He states that its dissolution should be effected through the contemplation of its identity with consciousness, saying: "That very [is it].
The word "eva" (very/only) is to be construed out of its place. The meaning is: "That is indeed the real Brahman. || 62 ||
Having realized within yourself that you are without beginning or end, contemplate the Self by means of the self.
O Rāghava, those objects that reflect in your mind may color it due to their attachment to others; let them not stain you, as they do a crystal.
May they not cause you to be attached. || 63 ||
Just as various colors enter a crystal without coloring it due to its transparency,
so too should they enter here without mental agitation.
Through its manifestation, this desire for the worlds seeks you. || 64 ||

Or, even if there is the appearance of duality, nevertheless, because of the realization of the changeless Self, there can be no coloring of You by those [appearances], just as there is none for a crystal; thus he says: "Like a crystal. "Free from mental reflection" (*amananam*) means devoid of the depositing of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) such as passion, which arises from the repeated contemplation (*anusaṃdhāna*) of objects reflected [in the mind]. "Worldly desires" (*bhuvaneṣaṇāḥ*).
They possess the desire for worldly activity appropriate for the enjoyment of their *prārabdha* (commenced karma). || 64 ||

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Doctrine of Consciousness," in the Section on Stability within the Means to Liberation of the venerable Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa composed by Vālmīki. || 21 ||
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Doctrine of Consciousness," in the *Sthitiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The twenty-second canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
For a living being who has practiced inquiry, whose mind’s mental fluctuations have dissolved—
For one who has known something and whose self is somewhat transformed, reflection ceases upon its abandonment. || 1 ||
In this [work], the complete destruction of all defects, serenity, and the vision of the perfectly pure Self of one whose awakening has fully blossomed are described. (1)
Desiring to elaborate upon the manner of experiencing the state of liberation-in-life (jīvanmukti), which is the fruit of knowledge,

he first demonstrates how the excellence of the destruction of defects increases in proportion to the firmness of knowledge gained through the progressive cultivation of hearing, reflection, and so forth, by means of the verse beginning with "jantoḥ" and so on.

For that qualified person whose mind has become thus— having gradually abandoned both external contemplation and self-contemplation through the practice of *samādhi*, and whose self (*ātman*) has come to rest in the form of the pure Self as it has somewhat matured—
when the dross has been worn away and unity with the water of the Self is attained, his essential nature [arises] by the power of higher knowledge (*vijñāna*).
The connection is with the word "becomes serene" (prasīdati), which occurs in the eighth verse. || 1 ||
For one who has abandoned the object of sight as something to be discarded, who has attained that which is to be accepted,
who perceives the Seer, and who no longer perceives the visible object as a seer— (2)
For one who completely abandons the distinctions of the stages of ignorance (*ajñāna-bhūmikā*), which are to be discarded;

who attains the specific excellence of the stages of knowledge (*jñāna-bhūmikā*), which are to be accepted; and who perceives both the seer—the cognizer—and the seen as knowable by the witness-consciousness (*sākṣi-cit*); or alternatively, [perceives] all that is seen as being the seer and the illuminator.
For one who perceives that there is only pure consciousness alone, and does not perceive a non-seeing seer distinct from the illuminating consciousness; || 2 ||
While one must remain awake to the supreme reality,
he lives as if wakeful yet remains asleep upon the path of saṃsāra, which consists of dense delusion.

As it is said in the words of the Blessed One: "That which is night for the sage who sees is the waking state for beings who sleep in the dense darkness of delusion, consisting of the transformations of ignorance. (Gītā 2.69) || 3 ||

For one who is free from desire and devoid of expectations, being detached even toward worldly enjoyments— whether they be flavorful or flavorless, and whether their full enjoyment is delightful— their state is one of ultimate and absolute dispassion.

For one who is detached from all objects of enjoyment and their means—such as garlands, sandalwood, and the like—which are pleasant only for the duration of their actual experience; who is indifferent toward both the flavorful, which lead to gradual liberation through extreme dispassion up to the state of Brahmā (virañcipada), and the flavorless, which lack that quality; and who is thus free from attachment even to the mere prospect of enjoyment until the end of the time of experiencing it—for such a person, [he acts] solely for the sake of maintaining the world.

The summarized meaning is as follows: one who is free from desire for the fruits of actions currently being performed and for the enjoyments brought forth by *prārabdha* karma; and who, due to dispassion (*vairāgya*), is detached from the happiness extending up to that of Brahmā (*āviriñca*), as well as from the means to that happiness—such as celestial nymphs and divine chariots—and from worldly enjoyments. || 4 ||
When the dullness of ignorance has decayed, the self attains complete oneness with the ether;
it dissolves away when attachment has vanished, like a mass of snow in the heat of the sun.

When the ancient dullness—the primordial inertia within the sky of ignorance—dissolves, what happens? It does not remain as a residue of flavor like a lump of salt in water; rather, it says: "It attains oneness with the water of the Self.
This means that, like a block of ice in the sun, it vanishes without remainder. || 5 ||
And when their inner waters were rippling and restless with surging waves,
their cravings then subsided like rivers at the end of the rainy season.

The word "taraṅgitāsu" (in those that are wavy) is an epithet for both the river and the thirst; in the case of thirst, it means "among those whose inner states are as flickering as waves of water. (6)
When the knot of the heart has been severed—like a bird’s web in the snare of worldly tendencies by a mouse—and loosened by the force of dispassion; (7)
In a net for birds, by means of the method of binding the wings; by a mouse—that is, a rat. || 7 ||
Just as water becomes clear upon reaching the kataka fruit,
so too does one's own nature become perfectly serene through the power of higher knowledge.
*Kātaka* refers to the fruit associated with the *kataka* tree; that is to say, its powder. Here, "nature" (*svabhāva*) refers to the mind (*manas*). || 8 ||
Free from disease, free from attachment, free from dualities, and free from dependence,
the mind emerges from delusion like a bird from a cage.

Passion (*rāga*) is desire (*kāma*). Attachment (*upāsaṅga*) is that which binds and fastens one to sense objects; it is the continuous pursuit of the qualities of sense objects. Duality (*dvandva*) is association with people such as wives and others. Resort (*upāśraya*) is a place where enjoyment is repeatedly obtained. From these, [the mind] has first departed.
Afterwards, he emerges from delusion and ignorance. || 9 ||
When the wickedness of doubt has been stilled and the delusions of curiosity have vanished,
the mind, its interior completely full, shines like the full moon.
He describes the state of one who has emerged [from that] with the words beginning "in the tranquil," and so forth. || 10 ||
Having produced supreme beauty and rising high from afar at the time of its setting,
it ascends everywhere with equanimity, like the wind in a calm ocean.
Equanimity is the state of equal vision. || 11 ||
Consisting of darkness, mute, and with its inner core shattered by dullness,
the latent impression of worldly existence (saṃsāra-vāsanā) reaches a state of attenuation at the time of awakening, just as the night does at sunrise.

"Mute" means devoid of the verbal expression of awakening; "on the side of night," her inner being is shattered by dullness—either by the cold of frost or, in the case of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), by ignorance. "Emaciation" refers to decline. The syntactical connection is: "like the night at the rising of the sun. 12.
The lotus-pond of wisdom, its sun of insight already seen, its shoots of merit, blossoms with stainless radiance like the personified dawn of day. (13)
The sun of consciousness has been beheld by her;

thus, the lotus of wisdom— the lotus of discernment— shines within the lake of her heart, its sprouts being the very merits consisting of service to the guru, hearing [the teachings], meditative absorption, practice, and other such virtuous deeds.
The sky is like the firmament. || 13 ||
Wisdom, captivating the heart and capable of delighting the world,
increases when attained by a being of goodness, like the rays of the full moon.
Wisdoms that captivate the heart and enchant the mind, acquired through the accumulation of the quality of goodness, continue to flourish.
What is the use of saying more here? The one of great intelligence, who has known that which is to be known, neither rises nor sets, being like the expanse of the non-existent sky. (15)
The meaning is that it is non-existent—that is, devoid of the four elements such as air—and like the hollow of space, it is delimited [the reading "unlimited" (aparicchinna) is also found]. || 15 ||
For one whose true nature is fully known and whose self has arisen through discernment, compassion arises here; such a person becomes Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and Śaṅkara. (16)
He states its great power with the words "vicāraṇā" (investigation):
"The secondary forms are to be fashioned by observing the afflictions associated with the authority over creation, descent, and so forth. (16)
Even though he manifests an outward form, conceptual constructions do not reach him whose inner mind is free from egoism, just as deer cannot reach a mirage.
Furthermore, he prevents the recurrence of distraction due to negligence, as before, by saying "in a manifest form. Here, "mirage" refers by implication to the drinking of its water. || 17 ||
Like waves, these worlds of the mind come and go;
they embrace the ignorant, but not the wise, in birth and death.
In this way, he also prevents the persistence of birth and death with the words "like waves": they come forth, that is, they are born;
they go away, that is, they die; [all] by virtue of the latent impressions (vāsanā) of one's own mind (cetas). || 18 ||
Manifestation and concealment constitute transmigratory existence (saṃsāra), and there is no other sequence; one who perceives through these two delights, and he is bound. (19)

The phrase "having known" is to be supplied [to the verse]: having known that such a sequence does not proceed toward one who knows reality—that is, one distinct from the ignorant—the latter being the opposite.
One who possesses right illumination, which is the vision of the true nature of things, is a knower of reality;
he rejoices as if by beholding the spectacle of a magical tiger and the like, whereas the ignorant person is bound. 19.
Just as the space within a jar is neither born nor dies when the jar is decorated or defiled,
so too is the possessor of the self (ātman) here, even when the body is adorned or corrupted.
When the cool light of discrimination has arisen,
the latent impression born of false delusion withers away completely, like a mirage in the desert.
"At the time of dusk (pradoṣa), when the moon has risen at its zenith" (sāgre); or there is a reading "at evening" (sāye). || 21 ||
As long as one has not investigated "Who am I? and "How is this?", the grand spectacle of saṃsāra remains like darkness. (22)
This body, born from the weight of false delusion, is the very seat of calamities;
he who perceives it as not being the self truly sees.
In what state, then, does one perceive the full Self, which is free from the darkness of saṃsāra? To this he says:
"He who perceives the pleasures and pains in the body as arising through the influence of place and time, and is free from the delusion that 'these are mine'—he truly sees. (24)

He who perceives that the physical sufferings arising from the power of other beings, the divine afflictions arising from the power of time, and the internal sufferings arising within the body— all these pleasures and pains— are not his own.
He truly sees who perceives everywhere: "I alone am that which is the boundless, limitless sky, endowed with the directions, time, and all activity. (25)

He who perceives that "I alone am" everything—from the limitless expanse of space, the directions, and time, as well as whatever therein is limited and endowed with activities such as arising and movement—[he is a knower of Brahman]. || 25 ||
He who perceives that "I am subtle" and all-pervasive, even when compared to a ten-millionth part of the tip of a hair, he truly sees.
He who, being all-pervasive, [is greater] than ten million times a hundred-thousandth part of the tip of a hair; the word "tu" has the sense of "api" (even/also). || 26 ||
He truly sees who perceives both himself and everything else through a vision that is eternal and non-differentiated, seeing all as nothing but the light of consciousness. 27.

The meaning is: he who perceives with a vision that is eternally non-different from that [consciousness]—namely, the self known as the individual soul (jīva) in its own nature, and everything else that is visible—as being the light of consciousness (cij-jyotiḥ). || 27 ||
He who perceives that which is omnipotent, infinite in nature, abiding within all beings, non-dual, and pure consciousness—that person truly sees. || 28 ||
He who, though wise, does not perceive "I am the body"— which is subject to birth, old age, and death, and is agitated by the fears of mental and physical ailments— he truly sees.
My greatness pervades horizontally, upwards, and downwards;
he who perceives that "there is no second to me" truly sees.
Mahimā means expansion. || 30 ||
All this is strung upon me like clusters of jewels on a thread;
he who perceives that "the mind is not indeed I" truly sees. 31.
Consciousness alone is the thread by which all is woven; whether as "I am indeed everything" or as "the mind, the internal organ, is not I," [it is consciousness].
"I do not exist, nor does anything else; only the stainless Brahman exists.
He who perceives thus in the midst of existence and non-existence—he truly sees.
When it is said, "one sees 'I alone,'" let it not be that the pure consciousness (*cit*) is abandoned while only the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) is grasped;

rather, having negated the world along with the ego-sense, one should see only Brahman, which is of the single essence of consciousness, as the remainder. Thus he says: "Not I. This refers to what is existent (the present), non-existent (the past), and yet-to-be (the future).
In the middle: [it is] either of that which exists as manifest or of that which does not exist as unmanifest. || 32 ||
Whatever exists in the three worlds is indeed a limb of Me;
he who perceives it as such, like a wave in the ocean, truly sees.

Regarding the term "member" (avayava): the sense is that this is supported by the Vedic scripture, "All beings are but one foot of Him," and by the words of the Blessed Lord, "Pervading this entire world, I remain with but a single fraction. || 33 ||
"She is to be pitied and protected by me alone; she is my younger sister.
He who looks upon the three worlds as fragile indeed—he truly sees. (34)

She is to be pitied because she is as good as dead due to being devoid of inherent existence; for this very reason, she must be protected by bestowing upon her the radiance of one's own being. She is a younger sister (svasā), meaning a junior or lesser [sister]; the substitution of *kan* occurs according to the rule *yuvālpayoḥ kananyatarasyām*.
She is delicate (*pelavā*) because she is afflicted even by a mere glance. (34)
He for whom the states of "self" and "other," as well as "thine" and "mine," have ceased in relation to worldly existence— surely that noble-souled one, possessing clear vision, beholds reality.
Existence refers to the worldly body and so forth; from that, having ceased means having desisted due to discernment and the destruction [of afflictions]. || 35 ||
He who perceives the body consisting of the Bhairava of Consciousness, free from the pursuit of objects of thought and filling the entire web of the universe— he truly sees.

It is free from the intrusion of objects and devoid of the confluence of the visible; for this very reason, by the unimpeded radiance of its own nature, it has filled and pervaded the entire web of the world on all sides with its splendor, like light pervading darkness. || 36 ||

Whether one perceives pleasure, pain, existence, non-existence, or whatever mental constructions of discrimination there may be—as being "I myself," one certainly does not fall away from the truth. (37)
"Bhava" refers to the body of one who holds authority; therein, "bhāva" is faith in the guru, the deity, the scriptures, and so forth;
therein, "viveka" is the discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal;
by that, "kalanās" are all the various gradations of self-realization through the sequence of hearing and so on—he who perceives all these as "I alone."

In this world, which is filled with both one's own self and others, the one who possesses excellent vision perceives that as he exists even in a partial manner, "What is there for me to abandon? What is there to be accepted? (38)

When the entire world, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, is filled by my own supreme existence— which is a mass of unsurpassed bliss— and is thus satisfied by the bestowal of a mere fragment of that bliss, what suffering could I have that ought to be abandoned, given that it exists only as a partial portion consisting of objects of enjoyment pertaining to this world or the next?
Or rather, seeing that there is no other happiness worth adopting, he is "sudṛk"—meaning one whose vision is unerring.

He for whom the notions of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted have utterly perished—this reality being merely Being, beyond reasoning and devoid of appearance—he indeed is the true person. 39.
"Inconceivable" means inaccessible to logical reasoning; "without appearance" means devoid of the reflection of the various modifications of the mind, that is to say, undisturbed. || 39 ||
He who, like space, is a single self even while pervading all beings, and who does not undergo the coloring of existence— he is the Great Self, the Great Lord.
The meaning is that Śiva is the Great Lord, capable of enjoying unsurpassed self-bliss. || 40 ||

I bow to him who has attained the state of the Absolute (pada), who is free from the conceptualization of darkness and light, who has become the very soul of time, who is gentle, perfectly equanimous, and established in his own self.

He who is free from darkness (tamas), which is deep sleep; light (prakāśa), which is waking; and ideation (kalanā), which is dreaming; who has attained the state of being the very self of both time and death, as well as the state of being the object of unsurpassed love; who is established in his own nature and grounded in the fourth state (turiya)—to him [I bow]. 41.

For him whose infinite activity is always directed toward the manifold and wondrous processes of the arising and passing away of all things throughout the world— processes that possess beautiful manifestations— he possesses the singular intellect that perceives all as one.
Salutation to that Śiva, who possesses supreme awakening. || 42 ||

Salutations to that Supreme Śiva, who possesses the realization that Brahman alone is one in the entire universe; whose mental state consists of an infinite and undifferentiated vision of the form of Brahman amidst the diverse activities of the world—characterized by its arising as creation, its setting as dissolution, and its persistence as maintenance; and who is the very embodiment of liberation while living, endowed with supreme awakening.
This is the meaning. || 42 ||

Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of Resting in the Supreme State," in the *Sthitiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis. 22.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of Resting in the Supreme State," in the Sthitiprakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The Twenty-third Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
He who rests upon the supreme state remains established like the whirling of a wheel.
Even while exercising sovereignty over the city of the body, he is not defiled. || 1 ||
In this [work], the sovereignty of the awakened one over the city of the body is described;
there, through the enjoyment of true pleasures engaged in for diversion, arises the bliss of the conquest of the mind. || 1 ||

Desiring to describe the sovereignty over the city of the body of one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), he raises Rāma’s inquiry as the motive for the question, beginning with the words "The body... Just as the rotation of a potter’s wheel continues by its own momentum even after the purpose of producing the jar has ceased, so too does [the body continue] until the exhaustion of *prārabdha* karma.

The meaning is that one who remains engaged in the worldly activities of maintaining a body is "liberated while living" (jīvanmukta). The underlying sense is that such a person is not tainted by them, due to the absence of the conceit of reality [regarding those activities]. || 1 ||
For one who knows that, this great city of his own body—resembling a pleasure grove—is for the sake of enjoyment and liberation; it leads only to happiness, not to suffering.
Because it serves as a cause for play and diversion, it is like a pleasure grove.
Śrī Rāma said:
O great sage, how indeed is the cityhood of the body [established],
and how is it that a yogi dwelling within this [body] becomes solely a partaker of royal happiness?

Dwelling within, presiding over, and protecting this city of the body as described by you, one experiences only happiness due to the natural excellence of its single foundation; the meaning is that, unlike kings, one does not experience even a fraction of its suffering. 3 Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, this city of the body is delightful and endowed with all virtues;
for the wise man, it is rich in infinite diversions and illuminated by the sun of self-perception.
He himself is the self-luminous light of the Self; he alone is the Sun. || 4 ||
The interior of the world was illuminated by the light shining from the windows of her eyes;
the wilderness of her feet was reached by the expansion of the main street of her hands.

In that [city], the intermediate worlds are illuminated by the two windows which are the eyes, by means of the two radiant lamps of the senses; its main streets are the two arms, and it possesses the "foot-firmness" characterized by reaching down to the knees, attained through the breadth of those [streets]. || 5 ||
Her creeper-like line of body hair was a thicket of vines, her skin was garlanded with a network of veins,
and the circles of her calves, thighs, and pillar-like shanks merged seamlessly into her ankles and toes.
Her feet are adorned with networks of veins appearing on the skin. The *gulpha* are the knots at the joints of the feet and shanks;
by them the *pārṣṇi* (heel) is characterized, along with the toes associated with it. The singular number is used for the class [of body parts]. 6.
Its forepart was fashioned from stone, its surface divided by lines,
and it was beautiful with the boundaries of the joints, sinews, and vital parts of skin.
Here, by the term "forefoot" (pādāgrapada), the hard skin beneath the foot is meant; that very [skin] is the foundation stone at the base of the pillar.
It was fashioned first, divided by lines and possessing various characteristics;
the meaning is that it was created by the construction of the primary foundation. The outer layer is the skin, while the inner vital points are the boundaries.
At intervals among the veins, the essential nodes are the branching sprouts; in the bones, however, the joints are the boundaries, and by means of them, they are beautiful to the mind.
The rivers of her private parts were formed from the tips of the broad and slender portions [of her body],
and she was covered by forests on mountain plateaus consisting of the shimmering rows of her hair and the petals of her skin.

The river of the city, which takes the form of the organ of generation, was fashioned at the front— the forward portion— of that junction between the two thighs, the two breasts, and the middle of the body; its head-plate,
consisting mostly of pleasure-mountains, possessed dark blue petals like glass, shimmering like a mass of hair.
And she was covered by forests of hair on her face, armpits, and other parts.
Adorned with a garden-like face featuring eyebrows, forehead,
and lips of perfect hue, her broad cheeks were strewn with the lotuses of her falling glances.

Her face was like a garden, endowed with a beautiful luster through eyebrows resembling blue lotus petals, a forehead resembling a fresh pale leaf, and lips resembling flowers; it was graced by that garden-like countenance as well as by her glances, which were like groves of plantain trees.
Where the two pleasure-grounds of the cheeks are strewn with blue lotuses characterized by her sidelong glances;
where the lake of the chest bears the bud-like lotuses of her breasts, and the mountain for her play upon the shoulders is covered by the dense line of body hair. 10.
In which [city], the very aggregates [of the body] are two pleasure-mountains.
Intent on devouring her own food cast into the cavity of her belly,
she makes a sound through the agitation of wind expelled from the long hollow of her throat.

In her whose belly— the hollow of a treasury— is filled with those very foods that are her own wealth, brought forth by her own past actions (*prārabdha*), as well as desired and beloved grains, garments, ornaments, and so forth;
she is called *Bhakṣyataḥ* because she extends the enjoyment of permitted objects of sense (*aniṣiddha-viṣaya-upabhoga*).
In this [city], the tongue, ears, and other [senses] are like prominent citizens seated at the windows of a palace on the head;
it resounds with the opening of the door-panels of the throat-gate, caused by the agitation of the vital breath (prāṇavāta) expelled through the long, upward-facing cavity of the throat. 11.
Adorned with objects obtained as they were acquired, determined at the marketplace of the heart,
it has the great serpent of the vital breath flowing incessantly through its nine gates.
By the term "marketplace of the heart" (hṛdayāpaṇa), those people characterized by inquiry who reside therein and examine jewels and such are intended.

Adorned with the commodities consisting of latent impressions (vāsanā)—namely, the objects such as sound and so forth which have been determined (nirṇīta) by them, examined, grasped, and obtained through the doors of the eyes and other senses according to their respective fitness—[the mind is thus described]. || 12 ||
With her mouth wide open, filled with fragments of bone from teeth that had been seen before,
the fierce goddess has her tongue lolling from its place in her mouth as she devours her food.
In her mouth, which is wide like a gateway,
there is an arrangement of door-panels consisting of fragments of bone scattered slightly by the appearance of tusks;
and it is chewed and tasted by the fierce Kālī, whose tongue acts as a doorkeeper, wandering all around the opening of the mouth.
In which there are four kinds of foods and grains. || 13 ||
Covered with hair-grass, it has the hollows of the ears as its deep pits;
with the chains of the buttocks situated at its edge, it has the broad back as its vast wilderness.
It was covered with long grasses resembling the feathers of peacocks and possessing the characteristics of hair.
The ground of the garden of the mind is covered with the endless mud flowing from the water-wheel of the anus; there, the noble lady of self-reflection sports.

In that garden-ground characterized by the mind, there is a self-reflection characterized by constant play, leaping about; it is a ground where, at the edge of the water-wheel— that is, the mechanism of the urinary tract— there flows a vast, far-reaching mire consisting of that very impurity which rises and emerges from the rectum.
In which [city] there is a beautiful woman as its mistress. || 15 ||
The restless monkeys of the sense-faculties are firmly bound by the ropes of wisdom;
she is delightful with the blossoming flowers of laughter from the garden of her face. (16)
In her, the restless senses are like monkeys firmly bound by the leather thongs of wisdom;
in the garden of her face, laughter itself is the blossoming of flowers, making her delightful.
To one who finds his own body pleasing, she is the most auspicious and beautiful of all women;
she leads only to happiness and not to suffering, and to the highest benefit.

One who knows his own body and mind is a knower of reality (*tattvavit*); for the sake of the happiness of such a person, there is the supreme benefit consisting of the upliftment of others through instruction and so forth, and [the teaching] is for him. 17.
For the ignorant, this is a collection of coffers for infinite sufferings;
but for the wise, it is a collection of coffers for infinite joys. || 18 ||
O subduer of enemies, when this [intellect] is lost, everything is lost for the wise man;
when it is present, everything is established. Therefore, this [intellect] brings about the happiness of the wise man.

He demonstrates what was stated regarding the infinite bliss of the Knower with the words "something" (kiṃcit) and so forth. "Something" means a small, trivial thing that has perished and is not a real entity; [the Knower knows] all the happiness of enjoyment and liberation [to be such]. || 19 ||

Since the Knower, having mounted this [intellect], dwells extensively within saṃsāra for the sake of both complete worldly enjoyment and liberation, it is therefore remembered as the "chariot of the Knower."
Like the chariot of a wise man, so is his chariot. || 20 ||
Since sound, form, taste, touch, smell, kinsmen,
and prosperity are indeed obtained through this very [wisdom], it bestows gain upon the wise man.
O Rāma, that this [intellect] itself bears the web of the activities of pleasure and pain is because it is capable of supporting the weight of all things for one who knows everything.

One who knows the Self as entirely full is the "all-knowing" (sarvajña), the knower of reality; his capacity for sustaining—that is, gathering—all things that serve as means to enjoyment and liberation is his "patience" (kṣamā). 22.
For in that city of the body,
the wise one, free from fever and devoid of agitation, dwells exercising sovereignty, just as Vāsava does in his own city.
The word *vyagra* has the abstract state (*bhāva*) as its primary meaning; thus, "one who has gone beyond agitation" means one who is composed (*svastha*). || 23 ||
He does not cast the wild horse of the mind into the pit of arrogance, nor does he hand over the daughter of wisdom to the wicked tree of greed. (24)
In the pit of the womb, which is the abyss of desire, there is swelling and prowess; regarding that object, he does not cast [the mind] nor does he impel it.

Having taken up greed itself—the evil tree of poison—as a bride-price (*śulka*), he does not give away his daughter, characterized by wisdom, to those of ill-bred lineage such as delusion and unrighteousness. Or alternatively:

By the word *durdruma* (evil tree), its fruit is indicated. One who eats—that is, experiences—the fruit of the evil tree characterized by greed is called a "greed-eating evil-tree-eater," referring to unrighteous people; he does not give his daughter, whose characteristic is wisdom (*prajñā*), that is, a discerning intellect, to such persons. The meaning is that he moves about concealing his own wisdom from them. || 24 ||
And the enemy of ignorance sees no vulnerability in him;
it merely cuts away the very roots of the fear of the cycle of existence (saṃsāra). || 25 ||
It cuts away those roots of affection which are the causes of fear for one who has the characteristics of saṃsāra as its enemy. || 25 ||
Having turned away from the core of craving, he does not sink, though overwhelmed, into the difficult-to-grasp enjoyment of sensual pleasures—that arena which bestows both pleasure and pain. (26)

He does not sink into the great whirlpool of the river of craving—the refuge and essence of which is its current—though it is filled with the wicked crocodiles characterized by the enjoyment of sensual desires; for, being turned inward, he is not drawn outward, even while [the world] wails with sufferings characterized by mere fragments of pleasure, which serve as the means for lamentation. (26)
With his mind fixed on his desire, he performs an uninterrupted bath at the confluences of rivers and sacred fords, observing both the external and the internal in due order.

By beholding this Vāsudeva, the Supreme Self, both externally and internally, one performs an uninterrupted and perpetual bath in all rivers, confluences, and sacred fords—both those pertaining to the physical world and those pertaining to the self.
Thus it has been said by the elders: "By him, a bath has been taken in the waters of all sacred fords; indeed, [all merit is attained]."
"Earth has been given away, thousands and tens of thousands of sacrifices have been performed, and the gods have been fully worshipped;

one's own ancestors have been rescued from the cycle of existence—he indeed is worthy of worship by all whose mind attains even a moment of steadiness in the inquiry into Brahman. This is the aspiration here.
The mental modification (vṛtti) having the form of Brahman, being directed toward that [Brahman], is mounted upon it. || 27 ||
Averse to the sight of pleasures invisible to all the senses,
he dwells eternally in the bliss called meditation within the inner sanctum.

Averse to the pursuit of pleasures in objects that appear attractive at first glance but are invisible to those who possess the characteristics of all-encompassing wisdom, [he remained indifferent]. || 28 ||
This city is indeed always a bringer of happiness to one who has realized the Self;
it bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, just like Amarāvatī belongs to Śakra.
Everything remains established by that which is itself established; nothing is destroyed by that which is not destroyed.
How could that most magnificent city not bring happiness?
When the city of the body has perished, nothing at all is lost for the wise man,
just as when a jar is destroyed, the space within that jar belonging to oneself remains unaffected.
How could the space within a jar, which has been occupied and made one's own by someone, belong to that very person? 31.
Just as the wind touches an existing jar but not one that is not present, so too does the embodied soul touch this city of its own body.

He states this by means of an illustration: "That which exists... (verse 32). For one who does not have even a correct perception while in the state of existence, what need is there to mention that there is no perception upon its destruction? Thus he says: "vidyamānam" (that which exists).
The person situated here, though being the all-pervading Self, experiences enjoyments created by the fashioner of the universe;
having partaken of them, he becomes a possessor of the objects attained by men.
In this context, the knower of reality (*tattvavit*), abiding here in this city of the body (*atrastha*),

having experienced the universal conceptualization (*viśvakalpa*) and the enjoyments of *prārabdha* karma produced by it, attains and enjoys the goal that is his own full nature— previously realized directly— which is liberation, the supreme human purpose (*paramapuruṣārtha*).
The remainder of the sentence is: "Thus, one becomes a partaker of the realized meaning. || 33 ||
Even while acting, he does not act; though intent upon all purposeful activity, he sometimes carries out all the duties pertaining to his nature.
Even while acting from the perspective of conventional reality, he does not act from the perspective of ultimate reality. || 34 ||
Sometimes, with a playful longing, his pure mind— unimpeded in its movement— ascends a lovely celestial chariot to wander at will.
He describes the fruits of enjoyment, such as beloved women, within that city of his body, beginning with the words "kadācit" (at one time).

The *vimāna* is the lotus of the heart (*hṛtpuṇḍarīka*), which is equal to a celestial chariot (*vimāna*). It is for the purpose of sporting—that is, to delight and amuse—the mind, which is like a lover eager for enjoyment. || 35 ||

Abiding there, he constantly delights in the company of Lokasundarī, whose limbs are ever cool; dwelling eternally within her heart, he rejoices with that Rāmā who is the very embodiment of loving-kindness.
Remaining there as before, with loving-kindness characterized by friendliness, that is, with his beloved Rāmā. || 36 ||
Two beloved ones stood properly at his two sides, Satyabhāmā and Ekata, like the two stars Viśākhā gladdening the heart of the moon. (37)
He beholds all the worlds— exhausted and split asunder by the saw of suffering—
as if from the back of the sky, like the sun looking down upon those situated in a forest of creepers.

He describes his perception of the suffering of ignorant people as being like a denizen of heaven perceiving the misery of those in hell—by the words "kṣapitān" (those who have been destroyed). They stand entwined with one another like a forest with its creepers. By the simile "standing on the back of the sky like the sun," it is understood that even for the knower of reality, there is a vast distance from the forest of saṃsāra. || 38 ||
Having long fulfilled all his hopes and being beautiful with every excellence, he shines like the full-orbed moon, never again to suffer eclipse. (39)

"Āśās" refers to the directions and mental desires. He is "beautiful" (sundara) by virtue of all those prosperities as well as the prosperity of his entire physical being. This is for the sake of non-fracture—that is, for the absence of further decay. || 39 ||
Even while enjoying a flood of worldly pleasures, no weariness arises in him;
indeed, the Kālakūṭa poison in the throat of Śiva, far from causing distress, shines forth all the more.

The flood of enjoyments—the flood of enjoyments such as garlands, sandalwood paste, and so forth—leads to weariness, that is, to the suffering of rebirth and so on. Alternatively, the flood of enjoyments is a difficult undertaking; the flood of enjoyments leads to weariness, meaning to immediate suffering. As for the word "pratyuta" (on the contrary):
the sense is that even for one who knows reality, the hardship of austerity and the like shines forth as having the great fruit of instructing ignorant people.
For enjoyment that is fully understood and then experienced leads to contentment;
a thief, once recognized and treated with friendliness, becomes a friend rather than an enemy. (41)
With the intention that, on the contrary, wealth becomes a cause of happiness for one who has fully understood it, he says: "By one who has fully understood... (verse 41).

To the wise man, the splendor of enjoyments— like a festival procession— is seen as something beautiful even during separation from men, women, and throngs of actors [or, according to another reading, rivers], who have departed for distant lands. (42)

He asks "whence" regarding that [instability] and says: "In separation," meaning when the assembly is dissolved; for the multitude of actors consisting of men and women gathered in the assembly, whose nature is to depart to distant places, their "procession" is like the assembly itself.
"The splendor of enjoyment" refers to the glory of objects of enjoyment, such as sons, wealth, and so forth. || 42 ||
Just as travelers encounter a village festival that has arrived unexpectedly and observe it,
in that very same way, the wise observe activities consisting of worldly transactions (the feminine suffix *ī* is archaic).
Just as the eye falls upon objects presented without effort with no passion for them, so too does the intellect of the steadfast fall toward its duties.

Just as, when mountains, forests, lotus ponds, and so forth— whether effortlessly presented to the eye or intentionally constructed— are perceived, there is an absence of the conceit of "mine" regarding the objects therein, such as trees, shrubs, and lotuses, even when one observes their cutting, breaking, or theft.

The meaning is that, just as one falls into a state of passionlessness due to not perceiving suffering, so too the intellect of the wise and steadfast man falls into a state of passionlessness even regarding the activities of worldly dealings with his own sons, friends, and others. || 44 ||
The senses never take away an object already attained, nor do they grasp what has not been attained; thus, the perfect Knower remains established.

How, then, does it proceed? To this he says: "Of the senses. It does not seize—that is, it does not take away—the object (viṣaya) that has been reached and presented by past karma (prārabdha); nor does it reject it. And regarding what is not yet reached, it does not acquire or bring about it through deliberate effort. The meaning is that it lives by making use of whatever is obtained as it comes. || 45 ||
Those of noble mind, who do not dwell on what has not been attained and maintain equanimity toward what has been attained,
are not shaken by fickle things, just as a mountain is not moved by blows from peacock feathers.

He asks "whence" regarding that [immovability] and says: "because they are unattained," etc. Since their thoughts are not yet attained and they are indifferent toward what has been attained, they do not shake or unsettle him through remorse, just as they would an ignorant person; this is the meaning. "Strikes with tail-feathers" means strikes with peacock plumes. || 46 ||
With all doubts completely stilled, with all curiosity dissolved, and with the body of conceptual construction utterly exhausted, the knower shines like a sovereign emperor. (47)

With all doubts completely stilled by the very destruction of the ignorance that is the cause of all doubt; with all curiosity dissolved through the perception of falsity in all enjoyments; he whose two bodies—the gross and the subtle—which are the causes for the conceptualization of those two [enjoyment and liberation], have been utterly exhausted—this is a descriptive epithet containing a reason (*hetugarbha*). He is a sovereign emperor (*samrāṭ*), the fruit of the *rājasūya* sacrifice.
He has, as it were, attained the state of self-sovereignty, according to the Vedic revelation: "He becomes a self-ruler. || 47 ||
Not contained within itself, it expands by its own self within itself;
full and boundless, like the ocean of milk expanding within the great ocean.

With the view of the ignorant, there is the illustration of self-sovereignty (*svārājya*); however, with the view of reality, there is no illustration because of the absence of any limitation—this is the intention behind saying "in the Self alone. The meaning is: "in the ocean of one's own Self.
[The Lord addresses] those beings who are wretched due to their desire for enjoyment, as well as those whose senses are miserable.
With an unmadened mind and tranquil, he laughs at those who are mad. || 49 ||
With an unmadened mind and a tranquil heart, he laughs at beings who are wretched in their desire for enjoyment, and at his own and others' miserable senses, as if they were madmen. (49)
Just as one who desires a wife abandoned by another is mocked by that other man, so too is he who desires enjoyment through his senses ridiculed by the wise. 50.
The activity of one who knows reality but abandons enjoyment while desiring it for the sake of the senses is an object of ridicule; the phrase "is ridiculed" is to be supplied in both cases.
One should bring under control with discernment the mind that has fled toward sense objects and abandoned its own gentle bliss, just as one subdues a lordly elephant with a goad. (51)
Now, one might ask: how can a person of dull intellect quickly restrain the mind from sense-objects? To this, he says: "abandoning... (verse 51).
That mental tendency which is allowed to flow toward enjoyments must be destroyed at the very outset, just like the sprouting of a poison plant.
By which thirst for enjoyment it is given—this is the ellipsis. || 52 ||
For even the honor shown after one has been struck is infinite;
like a field of rice scorched by the summer heat, even a meager watering acts as nectar.

If it is argued that a mind afflicted by such restraint would, like an angry child, fail to find delight even in itself— [the reading being *tanunigrahapīḍitam*]— to this he replies with the words "of one who has been beaten. For while such might indeed happen to one who has long been pampered by madness and is then suddenly restrained and subsequently abandoned, it is not so for one who has been brought to despair through long-term restraint.
The sense is "so it is. By the word "even" (api) in the phrase "even a poor watering," it is understood that what need be said regarding a good watering is obvious. || 53 ||
For one who is not in need, honor and great respect are not perceived;
the monsoon flood of full rivers does not shine when they are already brimming.
He elucidates the very point already stated with the words: "by one who is not distressed" (anārtena). || 54 ||
Even when full, an ordinary person desires something else;
yet the ocean takes in water that is fit to fill the entire world.

When the mind has been restrained, that very enjoyment and adornment which follows—though it has not attained expansion—is highly esteemed because of its intensity; [it is highly esteemed because of its intensity compared to that which has attained expansion, as appears to be the reading consistent with the commentary]. || 56 ||
For one who is completely restrained and held in check, "caressing" consists of providing limited objects such as enjoyments, ornaments, alms-food, and so forth.
One considers this to be much more than the previous enjoyment from which one had attained expansion. || 56 ||
A king who is free from bondage is satisfied with a mere morsel of food;
being neither bound by others nor oppressed, he does not hold sovereignty in high regard.
He provides an illustration for the stated point: "one who is liberated from bondage" (verse 57).
Pressing hand against hand and grinding tooth against tooth,
and as it were crushing limb with limb, one should conquer the enemies that are the senses.

Therefore, he says "the hand" (verse 58) to show that for the sake of uprooting the mind through long-term restraint and awakening, the conquest of the senses must first be accomplished with every effort.
By wise men here who are resolved to conquer another, the senses must first be thoroughly conquered, because they are the enemies of the heart. (59)
He states that the conquest of the senses is necessary not only for the sake of conquering the mind, but also for the sake of conquering external enemies: "To conquer... (verse 59).
On this vast expanse of earth,
those men are truly fortunate who possess virtuous intentions and are reckoned among the best of men in their various arts.
Those who have not been conquered by their own mind. || 60 ||
He praises the fruit of restraining the senses—the conquest of the mind—through both the praise of its basis and through salutation:
the meaning is that such persons are reckoned among those skilled in the arts of self-bondage and liberation. || 60 ||
The great serpent of the mind, rendered helpless by its coiling within the hollow of the heart,
has attained pacification for him—
I pay homage to that stainless, perfectly pure, and greatly joyful one. || 61 ||

The meaning is: I bow to that knower of reality (tattvavid), who has attained ultimate peace—the total destruction [of the mind]—who is free from the power of pride because his mind has become helpless through the formation of earrings within the cavity of the heart; and who, being thus liberated, has arisen and manifested in his own perfectly pure form as a great sage. || 61 ||
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Array of the City of the Body," in the Section on Stability (*sthitiprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki. 23.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Yoga of the Splendor of the City of the Body," in the *Sthitiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The twenty-fourth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
In the empire of the great hells, the elephants of one's own intoxicated evil deeds—
For the enemies that are the senses are difficult to conquer, being filled with the arrows and shafts of desire.
Here, the predominance of the senses and the means for their conquest are described;
by means of that, through serenity and awakening, the destruction of latent impressions is brought about. (1)
In this context, wishing to prescribe an abundance of effort and means for the conquest of the senses, he describes their invincibility with the words beginning "mahānaraka":
[He describes] the great hells known as Tapana, Avīci, Mahāraurava, Raurava, Saṃghāta, Kālasūtra, and so forth.
Those for whom elephants are their warders; they are rich with those very arrows and shafts which are hope and craving. || 1 ||
Those who, being ungrateful, destroy their own first refuge—the body—they are the enemies of one's own senses, difficult to conquer, and the great storehouse of evil deeds. || 2 ||
Those very evil deeds and sins are the great treasuries, the accumulations of wealth, belonging to those [fools]. (2)
Having reached the abode of the body, the vultures of the senses—greedy for the bait of sense-objects and possessing the fierce wings of what ought and ought not to be done—flit about restlessly. (3)
The body is the nest, characterized by its physical form. Greedy for the "baits" characterized by sense objects means being desirous of them;

the "greedy ones" are the eyes, that is, the senses themselves. "Kārya" is action that is fit to be performed and not prohibited, while "akārya" is prohibited action; these two constitute the fierce wings.
From those two, the fierce birds [were born]. || 3 ||
Those rogues who have been captured by the net of the threads of discernment—
his limbs they cannot mangle, just as no snares can overcome the strength of a serpent.

Those deceitful and cunning enemies, the senses, do not destroy the limbs—such as tranquility and the like—of that person by whom they have been seized and subdued. [They cannot overcome] the elephant-force, the array of elephants. || 4 ||
He who delights in sense-objects that are charming only at first sight— though he possesses the wealth of discernment— is merely a resident in this city of the wretched body.

With the intention that, in order to conquer those enemies, one must first accumulate the wealth of discernment (*viveka*), he says: "One is not helplessly overcome by the internal enemies of the senses as much as kings who dwell in formidable cities made of clay are not [overcome] by happiness. (6)
The qualification of the city as "made of clay" and "fierce" is for the purpose of demonstrating its excellence by showing that it is of a different nature from one's own body-city.

Just as those who have brought their minds under their own control are lords within the city of their own bodies—having subdued the servants that are the senses and having firmly seized the enemy that is the mind—so too [is the yogin]. (7)
He states the fruits of the restraint of the senses and so forth, beginning with the words "overcome" (ākrānta) and so on. || 7 ||
Like blossoms in springtime, those of pure intellect flourish—those whose mental pride has been destroyed and who have subdued the enemies that are the sense faculties. (8)
Like lotus ponds in winter, the latent desires for worldly enjoyments wither away; yet as long as it is midnight, those latent desires continue to prowl like vampires within the heart.
By the word "midnight," the darkness of ignorance is understood. || 9 ||
Until the mind has been conquered through firm practice on a single principle, it remains a servant because it performs desired tasks, and a minister because it accomplishes noble deeds. (10)
He says that within the empire of one's own body-city, it is the pure mind alone that carries out the affairs of servants, ministers, vassals, and so forth—thus: "The servant," etc. (10).
I consider the mind of the discerning person to be a vassal of the senses;
it is a tender woman because of its fondling, and a purifying father because of its protection. (11)
Snigdha means oily or affectionate; lalanā means a wife. || 11 ||
I consider the mind of the wise to be the supreme confidence of their best friend;
it is beheld by them with the vision of the scriptures and experienced within by their own intellect.

He states another reason for the mind being the father: "beheld by oneself" (svālokitaḥ). It is "beheld by oneself" through the vision of the deity as revealed by the scriptures—because its commands are not to be transgressed and because it is the vibration of pure consciousness (cinmātra)—and by means of the intellect (buddhi) through both the intellect of affection and the intellect of discrimination. || 12 ||
Having abandoned its own self, the father of the mind bestows supreme perfection when it is well-observed, well-examined, well-strengthened, and well-awakened. || 13 ||

Having abandoned the supreme accomplishment—characterized by wealth and such acquired by oneself, as well as that characterized by the knowledge of reality—and having abandoned the self, the body, and the form of the mind; because of the qualification "very firm," it is understood to be a diamond gem (*vajramaṇi*).
It was first well-examined with the eye of investigation shown in the scriptures, and then discovered in its place of origin through good fortune.

Then, with the assistance of teachers, fellow students, and others, it is thoroughly examined until one’s own direct experience is reached, and it is properly polished by the rubbing of a whetstone. Thereafter, through *nididhyāsana* (meditative contemplation), it becomes very firm and indestructible even by a thousand heavy blows. Finally, through the direct realization of reality (*tattva-sākṣātkāra*), [it is fully established].
It is well-awakened by the manifestation of splendor and well-awakened by the cleansing of the essence. || 13 ||
Joined with excellent virtues, this heart-pleasing jewel of the mind shines within the heart;
it is an axe for the tree of rebirth and brings about future prosperity.

Then, [the term] *suguṇe* refers to being joined with the distinctions of the fifth stage (*bhūmikā*) and so forth, as well as being joined with things of excellent quality such as golden necklaces and the like. Even in the context of the analogy of the jewel, having previously stated that "Rāma’s minister [is present] within because of the cause of the effect being pre-existent" (*satkāryakāraṇāt*), he speaks of "birth" (*janma*) etc., perceiving a desire to know the specific nature of that pre-existent effect (*satkārya-viśeṣa*) regarding auspicious action (*śubhakarma*).

The phrase "for one engaged in the scriptural [path]" is to be understood as the ellipsis. They are axes—that is, cutters—of the trees of birth, which are characterized by a succession of misfortunes; and likewise, they are such that their *udarka*—the subsequent result or arising consisting of the manifestation of unsurpassed bliss—is produced from them.
He ordains—that is, causes to be performed—all actions beginning with the attainment of the fourfold means and ending with direct realization; this is the meaning. || 14 ||
Thus the master of mind-mantras directs his actions toward auspicious deeds;
thus, O Rāma, is the jewel of the mind, though stained by much mire, [purified].
Having thus consoled Rāma, he concludes by taking up the very subject at hand, the jewel itself, with the words "evam" (thus). Alternatively,
because of the inconceivable power of jewels, mantras, and medicinal herbs, there is a variety in the accomplishment of the effects of mantras.

Since it is possible [to attain liberation] even through a [physical] jewel, the "mind-jewel" (manomaṇi) alone is called the "mantra. And its cutting down of the tree of birth and the arising of unsurpassed bliss constitute its various forms of accomplishment (siddhi); thus, this should be interpreted according to the metaphor of the jewel, with this as the intended meaning. || 15 ||
Wash yourself with the water of discernment for the sake of perfection and become possessed of light;
for you have been dwelling in the terrifying realms of worldly existence, devoid of discernment.

Having thus described how seclusion results in unsurpassed auspicious consequences, he restrains Rāma from the negligence of that very seclusion—which leads to great misfortune—with the verse beginning "In the realms of worldly existence" (bhavabhūmiṣu), etc. (16).
Do not fall, helpless like an ordinary person, into this cycle of existence that arises from illusion, teeming with hundreds of calamities, and full of falls and upheavals. (17)
"Utpātas" refers to passion and the like, which cause things to fall from the upward state; [the world] is full of these. || 17 ||
Do not disregard this mist of great delusion;
rather, relying upon supreme discernment and perceiving the truth with your intellect. (18)
"Do not disregard [it]," meaning do not treat it with indifference as if it were a great disease.
He concludes the present instruction on the means for conquering the enemy of the senses with the word "viveka" (discrimination). || 18 ||
Having fully conquered the enemies that are the senses, cross over the ocean of existence;
for this body is indeed unreal, and pleasure and pain are likewise non-existent.

[Objection: But surely, in the section on "Origination," the non-existence of the body, senses, and so forth was established; so why is the means for conquering them taught here? To this, he says: "Even though they are non-existent," etc. (19).
O Rāghava, let not the analogy of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa be yours;
through the firm abiding of Bhīma and Bhāsa, you shall attain freedom from sorrow. 20.

Although it is non-existent from the perspective of reality (*tattvadṛśā*), its existence is experienced from the perspective of delusion (*mohadṛśā*); therefore, if no remedy is applied, the attainment of misfortune is unavoidable—following the analogy of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa—due to the strengthening of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). However, if a remedy is applied through the practice of discrimination (*viveka*) and so forth, [the situation changes].
He says that there is no attainment of misfortune because of the firm logic of Bhīma and Bhāsā: "The tether... (verse 20).
O Mahāmati, having thoroughly cast aside with your own intellect that vain certainty of "this is I," rely upon that other state.
Go, drink, and eat; you are not bound, O mind.

Having thoroughly cast aside that vain conviction and false identification which holds that this very body and so forth, appearing as the object of sight, is the "I," by means of one's own intellect and the ascertainment of one's true nature; and having taken refuge in that which is other than this [body], namely the inwardly uniform essence, and being "mindless" (amanaska) because of abiding in its own nature, one carries out worldly activities such as walking and so forth.
Even while acting, you are not bound; the meaning is that you are indeed liberated. || 21 ||
