Thus ends the twenty-fourth canto, titled "The Exposition of the Non-existence of the Mind," in the *Sthitiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Valmiki, according to the ancient seers. 24.
Thus ends the twenty-third canto, titled "The Demonstration of the Non-existence of the Mind," in the Section on Stability (*sthitiprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The Twenty-fifth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
For that wise one who delights in the world and sports within this world, [the following occurs...]
For one who abides for the sake of the highest good, there is an effort directed toward expressing the supreme goal. || 1 ||
In this [chapter], the slaying of Śambara by the generals of the gods, the birth of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa, and the hope for victory through them are described. || 1 ||

If even for one who is free from latent impressions (*nirvāsana*), a succession of births and deaths occurs through the gradual accumulation of impressions that gives rise to the identification with the body and so forth— how much more so for one whose impressions are thinned by a lack of discrimination? This is shown by way of the *kaimutika-nyāya* (the principle of "how much more so") for those who have attained some slight proficiency in the Self but have not yet achieved complete steadfastness.

Vasiṣṭha, wishing to speak to Rāma the narrative known as Dāma-vyāla-kaṭa— which is intended to demonstrate the necessity of firm perseverance in the effort to eradicate latent impressions (vāsanā) for those of dull or middling faculties— said:
To generate a desire to hear that very [instruction], he restates it after having analyzed it once more with two verses beginning with "In this": "In this," etc.

"Loka-ārāma" means one in whom people (loka) find delight (āramante) and rest; of such a person who remains steadfast and practices effort, [the Lord] declares the supreme goals such as tranquility (śama) and self-restraint (dama), and reveals them within his own self.
Of one who possesses that character. || 1 ||
"O Rāghava, let the maxim of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa not be yours; through the firm abiding of Bhīma and Bhāsa, may you be free from sorrow. (2)

The phrase "let there be no recurrence of the logic of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa" and "be free from grief through the firm abiding of Bhīma and Bhāsa" were previously uttered; this is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 2 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
"O Brahmin, you who remove the torment of worldly existence, why have you cited the analogy of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa? Pray, explain this to me. (3)
Furthermore, having his curiosity aroused by this restatement, Rāma asks for a detailed explanation of both those points, beginning with the words "Dāma" and so forth. || 3 ||
"By the firm presence of Bhīma and Bhāsā, may you be free from sorrow"—O Lord, remover of the torment of worldly existence, what was it that you said? 4.
Awaken me, who am pure, with this noble speech that removes the thick heat of my suffering, as the rainy season awakens the peacock.

By means of this [work], which consists of the description of these two narratives, there is—on the side of the peacock (kalāpin)—the awakening, that is, the gladdening, of the dense cloud (ghana). || 5 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāghava, hear the analogy of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa, which is firmly established in the case of Bhīma and Bhāsa; having heard it, do whatever you desire.
In the cavern of the netherworld, which was delightful with every wonder,
there lived a lord of the Daityas named Śambara, a great ocean of the jewels of illusion.
Like a great ocean, he is a mine of jewels characterized by their illusory nature.
He had constructed Asura palaces within gardens in cities of the sky;
his own realm was adorned with artificial, excellent suns and moons.
He elaborates upon that very reality with the words beginning "ākāśa" (space) and so forth: by whom the temples of the Asuras were constructed in the gardens within a city imagined in space. || 8 ||
The mountain of the immortals (Amarācala) is filled with lotuses and other flowers produced from fragments of rock; it satisfies the dānavas by initiating displays of infinite majesty.
With the easily available gems such as rubies and others produced like fragments of stone, Padmākara became like Meru, the mountain of the immortals, which is a repository of treasures. || 9 ||
The sound of the songs sung by the women in his jewel-adorned mansions surpassed the voices of the celestial nymphs;
the trees in his pleasure groves were filled with the full orb of the moon.
In whose house the riches of song— the melodies sung by women who were like jewels— surpassed even the celestial strains of the wives of the immortals.
The abode of lovely women was made formidable by the clusters of blooming blue lotuses;
there, the cranes were summoned by the cries of jeweled swans amidst the golden lotuses.
He whose abode of love and pleasure-house is formidable with clusters of blooming blue lotuses that inspire fear in lovers; he was summoned by his voice—that very sound. || 11 ||
At the tips of the branches of the golden trees, lotus buds were formed;
it was a source of mandāra flowers falling from the thickets of karañja trees.
By means of the machine of logic, he conquered Indra, who had been defeated by the endless Daityas;
he constructed a garden pavilion fashioned from the flames of fire that were as cold as snow.
By whom Vāsava was defeated by means of the *tarku* (wooden lathe) and *kartarī* (scissors) machines through his own infinite and numerous daityas;
and by whom a garden pavilion was constructed and fashioned with fire-flames as cold as snow. 13.
Everywhere he surpassed the Nandana and Nandana gardens with his flower-groves;
he was the sandalwood of the Malaya mountains, removing the serpents that steal away all through illusion.
By him, through his illusory power, all the sandalwood trees from the Malaya mountain, together with their serpents, were carried away.
The women of his inner apartments were surpassed by the golden splendor and worldly beauty [of his city];
the courtyards of his houses reached the knees with heaps of various flowers. || 15 ||

He whose inner apartments (antaḥpura) consisted of women who had surpassed the splendor of gold and the loveliness of the world—here, the placement of the suffix *niṣṭhā* at the end of the compound is a Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). 15.
For the sake of sport, he is the wielder of the discus and mace who has conquered the Lord of the Clay (the Great Illusion);
his celestial city is filled with stars that are masses of jewels flying upward incessantly.
By him, the wielder of the discus and mace, Viṣṇu, was defeated for the sake of sport with a mere earthen image of Īśāna;
he by whom the sky and the interior of the city were made rich with stars and star-spangled by means of masses of jewels flying up incessantly like circling fireflies.
The surface of the sky was like a hundred moons for the entire underworld during the midnight hour;
it was intense with the sound of songs sung by the world’s statues as they watched him.

He whose song— a musical composition— is sung by those people characterized as "beholders of their own statues" (sva-śālabhañjikā-loka), who, at the midnight of the new moon and other such times, behold in the entire underworld the vault of heaven filled with a hundred moons as the image of a statue fashioned by himself.
One for whom battle is the highest peak and for whom martial valor is paramount. || 17 ||
By his illusory power, he put to flight the lordly elephant of Airāvaṇa, which had terrified the celestial elephants;
and the interior of his inner apartments was filled with the excellence of the splendors of the three worlds.
Regarding riches such as women, elephants, horses, and so forth, [he was distinguished] by excellences consisting of the "jewels," such as the jewel of a woman (strīratna) and others. || 18 ||
Fortunate with every prosperity, honored by all who possess sovereignty,
his formidable commands were saluted by all the vassal lords of the Daityas.
The circle of asuras rested in the shade of his great forest-like arms;
he was adorned by a mandala of jewels that served as the support for the entire assembly of wise ones. || 20 ||
From the mention of "forest" and so forth, it is understood that by his own will he possesses a thousand, ten thousand, or more illusory arms. || 20 ||
That demon, who had destroyed the gods and possessed a harsh and terrifying form, came to have a vast army of asuras capable of destroying the deities.
Of that Śambara: he whose form was hard, unbearable, wild, terrifying, and moving through the sky. || 21 ||
While that Māyābala was asleep and likewise gone to another land, the gods, having found a vulnerability, swiftly struck down his army. || 22 ||
In that illusory being, whose power is illusion (māyā).
Then, for the sake of protection, Śambaradaitya appointed Muṇḍi, Krodhadruma, and others as subordinate commanders over his own armies.
The vassal lords are the army commanders. || 23 ||
Having reached their midst, those terrifying gods struck them down,
like hawks swooping from the sky and scattering agitated sparrows.
Furthermore, that best of asuras appointed other generals,
who were restless and possessed a formidable roar, like the ocean appoints its waves.
The gods quickly struck them down as well; therefore, filled with wrath, he went to the full celestial realm of Triviṣṭapa in order to destroy the immortals. (26)
It is understood by implication that [the world] is filled with gods. || 26 ||
Therefore, terrified by her illusory power (māyā), those gods vanished,
like deer into the groves of the forest on Mount Meru when faced by Gaurī and Hara.
Like deer terrified by the lion, the vehicle of Gaurī’s consort, they fled from the lion of Gaurī and Hara. || 27 ||
He beheld heaven empty, like a world exhausted at the end of an aeon, with the hosts of minor gods wailing and the faces of the apsarases drenched in tears.
While dwelling there in anger, having seized a beautiful object he had obtained,
he burned the city of the world-protectors and went to his own abode.
There, having plundered heaven, he brought back—that is, took with him—the beautiful jewels and other treasures he had obtained. || 29 ||
When the enmity between the Dānavas and the gods had thus become more firm,
the gods abandoned heaven and vanished from sight in all directions.
Invisibility is disappearance. || 30 ||
Then, whatever army commanders were appointed with great effort by the Daitya Śambara, those gods, intent on their own exertion, slew them.
They struck down various [demons] until Śambara, having become agitated, blazed up; this is the connection with the following verse. || 31 ||
Until Śambara, overcome with agitation and filled with intense wrath,
blazed up excessively like a fire fed by straw, panting heavily.
In the phrase "socchvasan," the *s* is elided according to the rule "if *s* is elided for the sake of completing the metrical foot" (*soci lope cet pādapūraṇam*); thus, the *s* is dropped. || 32 ||
Then, even after searching throughout the three worlds, he did not find the gods,
despite his supreme effort, just as a wrongdoer fails to find a hidden treasure.
By means of his illusory power (māyā), he created three terrible and exceedingly powerful asuras,
who stood like Time itself personified, arisen for the purpose of protecting Bala.
His army and forces, for the sake of protection, were both active and inactive; and time is well known to be threefold: past, future, and present. (34)
Manifested through illusion, those terrifying beings of great power, who carried away trees by their strength,
rose up like mountains whose wings had been stirred by a great wind.
In the case of the mountains, they carry away those of that nature, just as a flood carries away trees. || 35 ||
Marked by the names Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa, they are each the sole agent of whatever occurs to them, possessing the nature of pure consciousness alone. (36)

"Dama" means one who subdues enemies; that very thing is "dāma. One who encircles others like a serpent is a "vyāla. One who protects one's own from the weapons of others by warding them off is a "kaṭa. Thus, they were distinguished and marked with these names that possess their literal meanings. || 36 ||
Because those past karmas no longer exist, there are no latent impressions (vāsanās) either;
they possess as their sole characteristic the vibration of pure, non-conceptual consciousness alone.
He states the reason for the distinction of those [beings] over the previous ones with the words beginning "due to the absence" (*abhāvāt*).

Those [beings], such as Dāma and others, are not former beings established in a prior state, nor do they possess latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Why? Because of the absence of actions (*karman*), such as merit (*dharma*) and so forth. Rather, they are free from conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), being devoid of conceptualizations such as fear, apprehension, and flight.
Those whose bodily movements are caused solely by the proximity of pure consciousness (cinmātra) possess that as their sole attribute. || 37 ||

Having reached the peak of their prosperity, they regard the slender, essence-less, and artificial distinction between "action" and "the living soul"—which is inwardly unfulfilled—as the very identity of the mind. (38)
Now, if they possess no latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of karma and desire, then, due to the absence of the seed of birth, birth itself would not occur.

And if birth were to occur even in the absence of a seed, then even liberated beings (*muktas*) would undergo rebirth. Furthermore, as will be stated later: "Wherever there exists a latent impression, there it attains nourishment. Therefore, [the objection] is inconsistent.

Anticipating the objection that this is a statement regarding the non-existence of karma and so forth, he says: "the portion of the karma-possessing soul" (*karmajīvakalām*). These souls are not independent; rather, they are "inner-impellers" (*antaścodā*), meaning the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) who impels from within. By means of that [inner controller] acting as the efficient cause, [he perceives] the "portion" (*kalā*) of Śambara—the karma-possessing soul—which consists of skill (*kauśala*), is subtle (*tanvīm*), small in dimension (*alpaparimāṇām*), and underdeveloped (*apuṣṭām*).

Having taken up this mental differentiation— the activity of the volition of creation— which is not accumulated by karmic impressions, is artificial, consists of illusory conceptualization, and is therefore insubstantial and devoid of the essence of enjoyment,
they have come into manifestation and appearance; and thus, like other men created by a magician.
The sense is that even in the absence of independent karma, birth characterized by manifestation is possible. Alternatively,
according to the principle to be explained in the narrative of Vipaścit,
the karma-jīva arises from the division— like sparks from fire— of the very jīva of Śambara, both internally and externally.

Having attained an artificial distinction consisting primarily of the mind— a portion (*kalā*) that is underdeveloped there due to the extreme paucity of karmic impressions (*vāsanā*) and the like— they have come to, or reached, birth (*udaya*), arising from the emergence of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the body. And so it is said:

Just as in the case of the dissolution of the body of a yogi, because the birth of these [beings] is established solely through the power of the seeds of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of desire, action, and *śambara* [magic], there is no separate dependence upon those [seeds]. However, this much is the distinction: since for yogis the body-dissolution is sublated by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), there is no accumulation of the seeds of birth—such as desire and so forth—in each individual body, as was the case with the bodies of Dāma, Vyāla, Kaṭa, and others.
The sense is that because of ignorance regarding you, one attains a succession of births through its accumulation; thus, there is no inconsistency whatsoever. || 38 ||
For those men, having abandoned their latent impressions (vāsanās), follow the customary action by way of a blind tradition, like the "crow-and-palm" coincidence. (39)

For this very reason, he says "te hi" (for they), stating that their worldly activity continues just like that of a yogi as long as the accumulation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) persists. || 39 ||
Just as children who are half-asleep merely move their own limbs,
so too are those [liberated ones] indeed devoid of both latent impressions (vāsanā) and the conceit of selfhood (ātmābhimāna).

If it is asked, "Where is the activity of those whose latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are not awakened observed? he says in response: "Half-asleep" (*ardhasuptāḥ*). They "stagger" (*riṅganti*), that is, they move about. || 40 ||
They knew neither retreat nor flight, nor did they know of fleeing; they knew neither life nor death, neither battle, nor victory and defeat. (41)
*Abhipāta* is the falling upon enemies face-to-face at the time of battle; *āpāta* is the sudden falling upon enemies who are resting and unsuspecting. (41)
Seeing only the soldiers standing before them intent on striking,
they rushed at their enemies in battle, their mountain-like bodies shattered by blows.
If they did not know [the truth], then how did they attack their enemies? To this he says: "Kevalam" (merely).

Because his body consisted solely of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of Śambara’s resolve that one must strike after having attacked, Śambara thought thus with a supremely satisfied mind as he faced [his enemies].
For my army, well-protected by the illusory power of the Asura, shall indeed be victorious.
It was well-guarded by asuras created through illusion. || 43 ||
Protected by the tree-like arms of the exceedingly powerful Asura, my army will attain perfect stability,
even when struck by the tusks of the celestial elephant.
Like the golden rock of Mount Meru in the world of the gods. || 44 ||

The mountain of the immortals, Meru, will attain—indeed, it will fully obtain—an extreme steadfastness even under the blows of the enemy, like a golden slab belonging to those world-elephants, the celestial tuskers, when their tusks clash together. || 44 ||

Thus ends the twenty-fifth canto, titled "The Description of the Origin of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa," in the Section on Stability (*sthitiprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, belonging to the Holy Tradition (*ārṣa*). 25.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa," in the Section on Stability (*sthitiprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The twenty-sixth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having thus resolved, the lord of the Daityas, accompanied by Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa—
He dispatched an army to the surface of the earth that was capable of destroying the gods.
Herein is described the great and fierce battle between Dāma, Vyāla, Kaṭa, and the others who had emerged from the netherworld (rasātala), together with the gods. || 1 ||
"In this manner," meaning by the previously mentioned method beginning with "he will be victorious. || 1 ||
Armed with weapons, the Daityas emerged from the groves along the ocean and from the mountain caves with a terrifying roar, like winged mountains in flight.
From the oceans, from the groves on the coastal forests, and from the mountain caves, they emerged and ascended according to their respective paths. || 2 ||
The Dānavas, emboldened by Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa, filled the hollow of the two worlds (Heaven and Earth), wherein the sun had been struck down by the blows of their hands.

The hollow space between the two worlds—heaven and earth—in which the sun was struck by blows from their hands and rendered lusterless; [this space] was nourished and increased by Dāma, Vyāla, Kaṭa, and the others. || 3 ||
Then, from the groves and the caves of the divine mountain,
the terrifying hosts of the celestial dwellers arose, as agitated as at the end of a cosmic dissolution.
"They rose up for battle"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 4 ||
Between those two armies, which bore the banners of the gods and the asuras, there occurred a battle within the world that was terrifying like a premature and violent dissolution of the kalpa.
It was like the terrifying dissolution at the end of an eon—an untimely, violent, and unbearable cataclysm. || 5 ||
Then their heads, from which the darkness was swallowed by the radiance shining from their earrings, fell like the luminous orbs of the sun and moon overturned at the time of universal dissolution.

With their heads, which had swallowed the darkness by the brilliance of their earrings, the [heads of the demons] fell from the headless trunks like the blazing splendors of the sun and moon cast down at the time of universal dissolution. || 6 ||
Resounded by the lion-roars emitted by the soldiers,
the mountains reeled like they were breaking into loud laughter under the full force of the winds of cosmic dissolution.

The bursting open by the great floods and surges of the winds of universal dissolution is clearly evident; the suffix *ka* is used here in the sense of intensity (*ghañ-arthe*). They are those whose laughter is like the brilliance of the teeth due to the wonderful internal play of the elements.
The dust was like the impact of blows from mountain rocks, and the walls were struck down by weapons; circles of lions rested fearlessly upon the slopes of the great boundary mountains.
In such places, the lion-packs— timid and therefore resting, hidden within— their walls of stone were shattered by blows from weapons resembling mountain rocks, and their ramparts broken; likewise,
the slopes of the principal mountains, such as the Himavat and others.
Reṇu and Dadhvanu; [the latter] is from the root *raṇ* in the perfect tense (*liṭ*). 8.
The flickering sparks of fire arising from the weapons struck down by their mutual blows were like the stars scattered at the end of a kalpa.
On the shores of a single vast ocean filled with floods of blood and flesh,
there were Vetālas as tall as the Tāla trees of the Kalpa age, clapping their hands in rhythm.
The eon is the period of dissolution; its calamities are as violent as the palm trees at the time of that destruction. || 10 ||
In the sky, where the clouds of dust were stilled by the downpour of gushing blood, the tips of crowns and earrings were shattered and struck down by weapons. (11)

In that sky, the dust became like calm clouds, and the tips of the crowns and earrings were distinguished by their sun-like forms; this is connected [to the preceding verse] by the analogy of the "lamp on the threshold" (dehalī-dīpa-nyāya). || 11 ||

The quarters of the sky became devoid of any gaps, filled with Daityas who resembled the sun, who bore the likeness of the wish-fulfilling trees of the kalpa age, and who had crushed the great lords of mountains with their blows.
by those who brandished uprooted world-trees for the purpose of striking [the enemy].
With their walls brought down by the wind from the edges of the blazing swords,
the mountains were reduced to a mass of fragments, as if shattered by the fire of cosmic destruction.
Their walls and ramparts were struck down by gale-force winds characterized by razor-sharp edges;
these [walls] were reduced to a mass of powder, a collection of fine dust. || 13 ||
And those gods gathered together like those invigorated by horse-sacrifices,
[driving away] the Asuras who were deprived of their weapons, just as winds scatter the clouds.
Then, attacking them, they seized them like cats seizing old mice; and they, in turn, seized those intoxicated men like trees with bears perched upon them.

Just as cats seize silver-eared old mice, those Asuras seized the gods— like men who are intoxicated and careless— as they climbed or had climbed upon the trees; [the gods] whose arms were like trees adorned with the flowers of flashing weapons and whose foliage was their blades.
The gods and asuras shone like blossoming trees swaying in a forest. || 16 ||
Their weapons themselves were the flowers, which shone upon trees characterized by a hundred thousand [points]. || 16 ||
They filled the ten directions with showers of weapons,
just as the wind fills the forests on Mount Sumeru with masses of blossoms.
A terrible battle took place between the armies of the gods and the dānavas,
like that of swarms of great gnats within the hollows of the sky and the earth, which were like the interior of an udumbara fruit.
In that region within the Udumbara tree which has the form of a hollow in the ground, there were the two armies of the gods and the Dānavas, consisting mostly of swarms of great mosquitoes. || 18 ||
Then, as the circles of world-protectors rose up with loud cries,
there arose a terrible clamor of battle, resembling the thundering of clouds at the end of an aeon.
Now, he describes the clamor of battle among the people being crushed by the world-elephants and other [beings] with seven verses beginning with "atha": || 19 ||
Like a paved courtyard on the earth, it was grasped as a single mass in the sky;
thick and heavy, with a belly as slow-moving as a great cloud, it could be seized by the fist.

By means of its mass-grasping—that is, by accepting a state of condensation—it makes the sky appear like a paved courtyard on the ground; this is the implied sense. In some places it is as if graspable by the fist, and in others its belly is thick and deep, being heavy with the slow-moving burden of water from the clouds. || 20 ||
The chariots crushed together like mountains of weapons, while the dancers shrieked;
there was a gurgling sound from the harsh lamentations of those whose hearts were shattered and their strength gone. || 21 ||
With weapons crushed by the impact of chariots, it resounds upon the rocks like a dancer following the rhythm of the beat;
it is a gurgling roar of harsh lamentations from the heartless whose hearts are breaking. || 21 ||
It was amplified by the roar of the end of the eon, surging forth from the dissolution of all things;
it was like a mountain of gold melting from the impact of the twelve suns.

It is like the sound of that golden mountain which melts through the conjunction—that is, the meeting—of the twelve suns; it is the swelling roar, consisting mostly of an echoing resonance, of the well-known cataclysm at the end of a kalpa (the day of Brahmā), which is set in motion by the causes of dissolution such as fire, wind, and so forth. || 22 ||
Emerging from the impact with the vessel of the universe through its reversal,
he was like a great torrent of water, a mine of beings as it were.

The ablative case in "saṃghaṭṭāt" is used with the elision of a gerund (*lyap*), meaning "having reached the collision. Having undergone a reversal upon reaching that collision, and having emerged from his own place by means of the letter *ca*, he was struck by beings—that is, living creatures—and thus became a "mine of beings" (*sattvākara*), like the sound of the flood of water from a great stream. || 23 ||
The sound of his wings flapped as he moved, causing the king of mountains to tremble;
the mountain caves were rent asunder by the force of his hard, filling flight.
Where the sound of the moving mountain lords, as if they were trembling with wings, vibrates like the wind from their flapping;
and by which [sound] the mountain caves—filled with harsh and grating echoes—are shaken, agitated, and seem to burst forth, reaching even to the ears. 24.
His body resembles the agitation of the Milk Ocean when churned by Mount Mandara;
he is the source of the creatures of the islands, brought together by the loud, rhythmic slapping sounds of his amorous play.

His body possesses a form resembling the tumultuous roar of the Ocean of Milk as it was churned with Mount Mandara for the sake of nectar; and at that very moment of the nectar’s emergence, the slapping of his arms— which resounded like a deep,
humming drone (*ghuṃghumā*) due to the excess of joy experienced by the gods and demons who were listening to it through their passion for it— [is described].
The sounds produced by the slapping of their arms pervaded the worlds of living beings, characterized by the seven continents, serving as the dwellings of creatures. || 25 ||
When the two armies were agitated, there occurred a battle characterized by the upheaval of dānavas,
in which cities, villages, mountains, forests, and men were crushed to pieces.
From this point until the end of the section, he describes nothing but the battle, beginning with the words "of the two armies" (senayoḥ) and so forth. || 26 ||
The quarters were filled with the mountain-like Dānavas cut down by hundreds of great weapons,
while the interior of the sky was filled with the dust of weapons and other implements struck against one another.
The hundreds of peaks of Mount Meru were shattered by the slapping of his *bhuśuṇḍī* discs,
while the lotus-faces of the Daityas and gods were severed by the wind of his arrows.
The old grass of gods and demons was whirled about by hundreds of revolving whirlpools,
while the sky was enveloped by the surging waves of the army's blows.
The multitude of celestial chariots was crushed and cast down by the fierce winds of his weapons, while the city of the sky was flooded by the surging mass of ocean waters unleashed by his missiles.

Where hosts of celestial beings fall, crushed by fierce winds acting as weapons; and where the aerial cities, such as Amarāvatī and others, are flooded by the masses of water from the ocean raised up by Varuṇa’s missiles and other weapons.
We are carrying across hundreds of rivers consisting of great missiles, swords, spears, and pikes,
while the pavilion of the universe lies shattered by the forceful blows from the wings of the mountains.
Where the pavilion of the universe trembled from the forceful slapping of arms against the flanks and sides of the mountains as they rolled about. || 31 ||
The city of the world-protectors was being overwhelmed by the flood of blows from the heels of the Daityas;
the mansions resounded with the tinkling of bracelets as women cried out in distress.
It was filled with a flood of intoxicated blood arising from the hosts of tumbling Daityas— [the reading "baloddhūta" is also found]—
and it was filled with people fleeing while emitting fierce cries as they were washed by the blood of the throngs of men.
It was filled with Yama, who was concealed by the lotus-like faces of the world-protectors,
and it was once again crowded with hosts of troops seen by the gods and asuras.
He was accompanied by Yama, who— like a bee among lotuses characterized by the marks of Indra and the other world-protectors (lokapālas)—

is sometimes disguised for the purpose of taking away the lives of the dead, and sometimes unmasked and manifest for the sake of battle; and who, moreover, [acts] with blows and strikes at the time of flight.
Having turned back, he was assailed by the host of soldiers who, seeing him from afar, struck out with their weapons.
It was terrifying with the loud, resonant clanging of many "śava-śava" cries as they moved back and forth between the mountain-like bodies of the Dānavas and their own side.
It was terrifying with many *bhāṅkāra* sounds in the form of imitative cries such as "śava-śava. || 35 ||
The entire earth, oceans, and mountains were reddened with blood from the cascades flowing from the fierce mountains of Daityas, shattered by the tips of weapons. || 36 ||
It was filled with the ruins of kingdoms, cities, forests, villages, and caves,
and it bore mountains of corpses of countless asuras, elephants, horses, and men.
Wherein there are mountains such as Meru and others, which bear the corpses of innumerable gods, elephants, horses, and humans.
The elephant [of Indra] was resplendent with rows of iron arrows that pierced through its armor,
while the intoxicated Airāvaṇa elephant had its shoulder crushed by a blow from [Rāma’s] fist.
It shattered mountains with torrents of rain like the clouds at the end of an eon,
and it pulverized the great boundary mountains, which were blown up by the impact of a massive thunderbolt.
The Dānava was set ablaze by the mass of flames leaping from his provoked fire,
yet he extinguished that fire by pouring out the ocean brought forth in a single hollowed palm.
"Kupitāgni" refers to the prowess of the gods; "ekāñjali" refers to the prowess of the asuras. || 40 ||
The great flames were turned to stone by the massive heap of the fierce Daitya;
the fire, with its rays like kindled forest-fuel, caused the mountains and the masses of water to melt away.
The great fire, blazing where it was turned to stone by the fierce Daityas who hurled massive loads such as mountain rocks— this is the prowess of the Daityas—
is driven back by the flames of other fires fueled by the fuel characterized by the forest-array; for this reason, they consist mostly of water.
"Wherein there is a mountain-heap, [known as] Devaparākrama. Thus, in the subsequent passages as well, it should be understood according to what is appropriate. || 41 ||
The night of the end of the aeon, created by weapons and characterized by irresistible darkness,
had its thick veil of gloom dispelled by the radiance of the multitude of illusory suns.
It rained down a mass of thick clouds whose essence had been sucked dry by a rain of illusory fire;
it rained down a clashing of weapons that vomited forth fire accompanied by hissing sounds. || 43 ||
*Kalā* is the skill of *māyā*; it is that wherein there is the raining down of wealth from the clouds employed by it. || 43 ||
It was filled with the agitation caused by the rain of mountain-like weapons dispelled by the rain of vajra-weapons;
it was rich in battles between the weapons of sleep and awakening, and it took refuge in the obstruction of mutual rivalry.

That very conflict and mutual subjugation was the obstruction previously mentioned that hindered the rain; it bore the *krakaca* tree-weapon supported by that [obstruction], accompanied by water, fire, and the *asmarana* weapon,
a battle as fierce as the *brahmāstra*, where darkness was dispelled by the *tejas* weapon.
Blinded by delusion through the failure to remember [the danger of] water and fire. || 45 ||
The entire sky was made dense by the masses of weapons vomited forth by the stars,
shattered by the weapon of the shower of rocks, and illuminated by the weapon of the shower of fire.
Where the entire sky was rendered dense by the weapons— spears, clubs, mallets, and so forth— vomited forth by the missiles of the Asuras, Piśācas, and others.
In a mere moment, with chariots whose banners touched the moon and which roared with the whirring of their wheels, they traversed both the mountain of sunrise and the mountain of sunset.
The great asura who does not die even when struck by the vajra;
the great asura whose life is sustained by the great vidyā-mantra of the immortal semen. || 48 ||
Śukra’s great lore, known as Amara, is the science of reviving the dead; it is there that the great Asuras are kept alive by means of it. || 48 ||
The hosts of gods were fleeing from it, while the gods were overawed by its victory;
here and there were the great comets of the auspicious planets.
In some places he saw masses of gods fleeing, and in others, gods exulting in victory;
here and there, with necks upraised and throats lifted, they looked about as if to observe the great auspicious planets and rows of comets with their own intellects. (49)
He who uproots the necks of the intellects of those who cause portents and misfortune;
he who is like a mountain, the earth, the ocean, the sky, and the world—a sea of blood.

In some places, however, with his neck uplifted for the purpose of perceiving the portents and floods of auspicious signs, he [beheld] the world itself as an ocean of blood, accompanied by mountains, his own sea, and the day; for the word "buddheḥ" (of perception) is used in the ablative case because perception is intended to be expressed as the cause of the result. 50.
Due to irresistible enmity, he turned the forest of *kiṃśuka* trees into a mass of full-blown blossoms,
and created a great ocean filled with corpses, as numerous as mountains.

The word "jagat" (the world) is understood to carry over [from the previous verse]. The word "kurvat" (acting) connects with both the first and second halves [of the verse]. In both cases, the word "rudhireṇa" (with blood) is to be supplied as an ellipsis.
With great corpses hanging and swaying from the tips of all the tree branches, and with the feathers of birds shining and their fruits gleaming as they were agitated by their own winds; || 52 ||
He qualifies the comparison of the multitude of arrows to a forest with the words "blazing," and so forth:

[the arrows] are those whose flowers are the very feathers of herons and other birds, which are blazing due to the reflections of the sun’s rays and are flickering because they are distressed by their own forceful wind; and their shining fruits are the iron parts themselves.
By those [trees] whose fruits [result] from their being joined together. || 52 ||
The expanse of the sky was filled with showers of arrows falling like palm trees,
while hundreds of headless trunks, resembling mountains, were seen with their many arms.
Even higher than the palm trees, they were towering. || 53 ||
With dancing [demons], they brought down clouds, celestial chariots, and the stars of the gods;
with arrows, spears, maces, darts, and battle-axes, they impaled the mountains.
Where clouds and celestial chariots were felled by hundreds of arms like headless trunks, and where the stars of the gods were struck down;
where mountains were pierced and held fast by the ends of sharp spears.
The sky was covered with fragments of walls fallen from the seven worlds,
while the firm kettledrums were struck incessantly by clouds intoxicated with constant passion.

Although there are only six worlds above, it is nevertheless called "the seven worlds" because even fragments of walls situated on the earth-world (*bhūrloka*) can fall by being carried upward. || 55 ||
Thus, [he beheld] the elephant of the netherworld, roaring with a hundred sounds,
whose long trunk was drawn by Vināyaka like a mountain of Dānavas.
Thus, it was there that the elephants of the quarters, the guardians of the netherworld, were roaring back with hundreds of sounds in the manner previously described.
The hosts of Siddhas and Sādhyas fled in every direction, as did the Gandharvas, Kinnaras, gods, and Cāraṇas. || 57 ||
Where, by chance, the sun, the moon, and other celestial bodies that normally distinguish the directions meet in a single direction;
where the hosts of Siddhas, Sādhyas, and Maruts remain motionless out of fear of the Asuras, even though they are the ones who determine the directions.
With their limbs shattered by the falling of thunderbolts and reduced to fragments of crushed rock,
they stood at the horizons like harbingers of the time of universal dissolution for the gods.
The winds are voracious, making gurgling sounds in the celestial trees. || 58 ||
Now he describes the portentous storm: "They blew," and so forth.
With the falling of thunderbolts—the descent of lightning fires—limbs of living beings were shattered and fragments of rocks were crushed.
These winds were the indicators of the time of dissolution for the gods, [and they shattered] the deep-sounding fruits of the celestial trees.

The winds—meaning the gale-force storms—blew as devourers, that is to say, as consumers or concealers, of the sounds of the bees, cuckoos, and other creatures associated with the wish-fulfilling trees (kalpavṛkṣa). || 58 ||

Thus ends the twenty-sixth canto, titled "The Description of the Battle between Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa," in the Section on Stability (*sthitiprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, a work of the Seer (*ārṣa*). Volume One, Part Two. Canto Twenty-Six. || 26 ||

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Battle between Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa," in the Section on Stability (*sthitiprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, in its exposition of the essential meaning (*tātparyaprakāśa*). || 26 ||
The twenty-seventh canto.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha said:
While that terrible tumult of battle was then taking place,
Within the bodies of the gods and asuras, which were like pits or the interiors of clouds.
The gods were defeated; to them who had sought refuge there, the Lotus-born Lord spoke of the means for slaying the Daityas and the long-accumulated increase of their latent impressions (vāsanā).

The connection with the subsequent verse is as follows: "While pits and wounds were formed in the bodies of the gods and asuras, and while streams of blood were flowing like the floods of the Gaṅgā falling from the sky;
and while there was a deep roar of shouting produced by the multitude of gods encircled by the cord. (2)
He who, having crushed all the celestial abodes by dragging them with his own hands, let out a great roar in the form of a lion’s roar that surrounded the hosts of gods; he who,
on the battlefield where the gods were destroyed in a conflict of fierce fury, [trampled] the serpents.
By whom all the abodes of the gods were crushed—that is, pulverized—by means of that attraction and drawing forth.
While Airāvata, his roar silenced, was intent on flight,
the army of the Dānavas surged forward like the sun at midday.
Afflicted by the pain of fallen limbs and with blood flowing from their wounds,
the divine armies fled like waters whose banks have been breached.
"Without embankments" means those whose embankments have collapsed. || 5 ||
Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa, who had long been hidden,
followed after them with loud shouts, like fires following after fuel.
They were hidden, concealed at a distance; they resounded with a shimmering noise, a brilliant sound of reproach, as it were.
Although they searched with great effort, the Asuras did not find the gods,
just as lions do not find deer that have flown up into a dense thicket of trees.
In that forest where the thickets were dense with networks of creepers and the like, [he saw] those who had flown up and then settled down. || 7 ||
When the hosts of gods had not been captured, Dāma, Vyāla,
and Kaṭa then went with joyful hearts to the Lord residing in the treasury of Pātāla.
Because it is free from latent tendencies, the state of being joyful in one's own intention is metaphorically designated as the cause for the attainment of victory. || 8 ||
Then those gods, having been defeated, became despondent; yet after consoling themselves for a moment, they went to the immeasurably powerful Brahmā in order to find a means of victory.
For the sake of the means to victory, that is, for the sake of inquiring about the means to victory. || 9 ||
To them, whose faces possessed the splendor of deep redness, Brahmā appeared,
like the moon appearing to the oceans at evening whose waters have been turned crimson.
Of those whose beauty of face was red, crimson with the blood of their own gore. || 10 ||
Having prostrated before him, those gods fully related to him the misfortune brought about by Śambara and the sequence of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa.
The desire for the activity of Śambara is the group consisting of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭaka, which is of the nature of emanation. (11)

Having heard all that and reflected upon it, Brahmā, the discerning one, spoke these words of consolation to the host of gods: tadākarṇyākhilaṃ brahmā vicārya sa vicāravit | uvācedaṃ surānīkamāśvāsanakaraṃ vacaḥ || 12 ||
Śrī Brahmā said: At the end of a hundred thousand years, Śambara must die at the hand of Hari; wait for that time. 13.
The word *tatkālam* takes the second case ending according to the rule *kālādhvanor atyantasaṃyoge*. (13)
"O best of immortals, today, while fighting these Dānavas— Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa— flee from them by means of illusory warfare."
By virtue of their practice in battle, the wondrous manifestation of egoism will enter into the hearts of these [warriors], just as a reflection enters into mirrors. (15)
The "wonder" of the ego (ahaṃkāra) is the modification of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇavṛtti) in the form of "I," characterized by the nominative case-ending. || 15 ||
"Once these gods—Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa—have taken up their latent impressions (vāsanā), they will be easy for you to conquer, like birds caught in a net. (16)
Those whose latent impressions (vāsanās) have been grasped by that mode of conduct and gradually accumulated. || 16 ||
But today, being free from latent desires and devoid of pleasure and pain, these gods have become invincible as they strike down their enemies with fortitude. (17)
"Devoid of latent impressions" (avāsanāḥ) means that their latent impressions have not manifested due to the obstruction caused by the mental construction of Śambara;

it does not mean that they are entirely without latent impressions, because the absolute eradication of latent impressions is impossible without [supreme] knowledge, and because birth is untenable for those who are entirely without latent impressions—this is how it should be understood. || 17 ||
Those who are bound by the threads of latent impressions (vāsanā) and brought under control by the snares of desire fall into subjection in this world, like birds tied with ropes. (18)

Those wise ones who have eradicated latent tendencies, whose intellects are unattached to anything, neither rejoice nor are they provoked to anger; such great-minded ones are difficult to conquer. (19)
Those whose latent impressions are shattered and whose latent impressions have perished. || 19 ||
He whose inner knots are bound by the rope of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), though he be great and possessed of vast knowledge, is overcome even by a child. (20)
One who imagines conceptual constructions such as "this is I" or "this is mine" becomes a vessel for calamities, just as the ocean is for waters. (21)
He by whom the self has been cultivated as limited to this much—even if he were omniscient—has everywhere fallen into a state of supreme wretchedness. (22)

Among all evil latent impressions (*durvāsanā*), the very impression of the delusion of limitation— consisting in the false identification of the self with the body and so forth— is the greatest misfortune, because it is the seed of great folly, wretchedness, birth, death, and the like; thus he says:
By the words "of this much" and so forth. || 22 ||
He who has conceived a limit for that which is infinite and immeasurable has, by that very act, brought his own self under control by himself. (23)
"Rendered powerless" means rendered helpless; that is to say, overwhelmed by the miseries of saṃsāra. || 23 ||
Whatever exists in the three worlds that is distinct from the self—let one's latent impression (vāsanā) be bound to that as an object of appropriation. (24)

If there were anything whatsoever distinct from the Self, then indeed there might be a latent impression (*vāsanā*) therein, either as an object to be grasped or by virtue of its suitability for being grasped; however, such a thing does not exist—this is the meaning. || 24 ||
The wise know that mere attachment is the source of infinite sufferings;
they know that mere non-attachment is the source of all-around happiness. (25)
And thus, with the intention that attachment to unreal objects must be abandoned, he says: "It is mere attachment" (verse 25).
"As long as Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa remain established in worldly existence with no detachment, we shall certainly not conquer them, just as fire cannot overcome gnats. (26)
He applies what has been said to the subject at hand: "The tether," etc. (26).
Driven by an internal latent impression that leads to wretchedness, a living being is overcome; otherwise, even a mosquito becomes like the mountain of the immortals.

The meaning is that due to the internal latent impression (*vāsanā*) which grasps at the body and so forth as "I," and the resulting apprehension of one's own destruction upon the destruction of the body and so forth, one falls into wretchedness and cowardice; otherwise,
in the absence of such an impression, even a mosquito becomes unshakable like Amarācala, Mount Meru.
Wherever a latent impression exists, there it attains growth;
for a quality increases in that which possesses the quality, as is observed in the case of what exists, not of what does not exist. (28)

For indeed, since the quality called "fatness" exists only when there is a substratum possessing qualities (guṇin), and furthermore, fatness cannot be established without accumulation, and that accumulation occurs only upon the establishment of a second constituent part; and that duality is observed in an existing substance, not in a non-existent one—this is the meaning. || 28 ||
"O Śakra, act in such a way that they cultivate within themselves the notion, 'This is he, this is I, and this is mine,' just as Dāma and the others have done. (29)

The meaning is: "Just as Dāma and the others, by whatever means they employ, conceive of this very body and so forth as the well-known 'I', and conceive of victory, defeat, honor, livelihood, and so on as 'mine', and thus become attached to them—you should likewise employ such a means. || 29 ||
Whatever misfortunes people encounter and whatever states of existence or non-existence they experience—these are the bitter yet tender blossoms of the *karañja* creeper of craving. (30)
The world, bound by the threads of latent impressions (vāsanā), revolves; when these have increased, they lead to extreme suffering, yet when they are eradicated, they lead to happiness.
The meaning is that for one who undergoes transformation, that latent impression leads to extreme suffering. || 31 ||
Though steadfast, though possessing vast knowledge, though of noble birth, and though great—a living being is bound by craving, just as a lion is bound by a chain. (32)
For this bird of the mind that dwells in the tree of the body and moves toward the abode of the heart, this craving has been fashioned as a snare. (33)
The lotus of the heart itself is the abode, the nest, for the bird of the living soul characterized by the mind that moves toward it. || 33 ||
The world, wretched with its latent impressions, is dragged away by the End-maker, like a helpless bird gasping violently, bound by a rope by a child. 34.
Like a rope with its strands. || 34 ||
Enough with the burden of weapons and the wandering about in battle;
through skillful means and effort, bring about the reversal of your enemy's latent tendencies.

Of the latent impression (*vāsanā*)—that is, the latent impression devoid of ego-inflation (*nirabhimāna*) produced by the mental construction (*saṃkalpa*) of Śambara—the "reversal" (*viparyāsa*) means its opposite; that is to say, the accumulation of ego-inflation. [This occurs] in the case of an enemy such as Dāma and others. || 35 ||
O leader of the immortals, when the enemy’s fortitude is shaken in the midst of the conflict,
neither weapons, nor missiles, nor even treatises bring victory. (36)
While the enemy’s inner fortitude remains undisturbed— this is the ellipsis— the treatises such as those of Uśanas (the science of polity),
and these [beings] Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa, by virtue of their practice in battle,
will seize that intoxicating latent impression consisting of egoism.
These [disciples] shall cast out from you the latent impression consisting of egoism through their resolve. || 37 ||
When those ignorant persons created by Śambara take recourse to latent impressions (vāsanā), then they will become conquerable.
Regarding those who know the truth, what deficiency could there be such that they would adopt [worldly] latent impressions (*vāsanā*)? To this he says:
"O immortals, let them first awaken those ignorant ones through logical debate, until they become possessed of latent impressions by the power of practice. (39)
Awaken them and make them vigilant in the affairs of worldly conduct. || 39 ||
Then those whose latent impressions are bound to you will become submissive;
their hearts will be pierced by craving in this world, and none shall remain weak.
If some, though not satiated by craving, are nonetheless not fickle-minded. (40)
This entire world, with its equal and unequal parts,
has entered into a state of stability within one's own latent impressions (*vāsanā*),
just as the mass of trembling waves rests within the ocean.
Therefore, let her very self, who has departed here, be treated. || 41 ||

Just as within a reservoir of water there exists an abundance—an excess—of various waves that are flickering and extremely restless, yet which consist essentially of water itself; so too, this world, with its even and uneven features, having attained stability and the permanence of a continuous flow, remains thus established. This is the meaning. || 41 ||

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Words of the Grandfather," in the Section on Stability within the Means to Liberation of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, which belongs to the *Ārṣa* tradition.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Words of the Grandfather," in the Sthitiprakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The twenty-eighth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having spoken thus to the gods, the Blessed One vanished right there.
Like a wave of water making a sound upon the shore of the sea. || 1 ||
The renewed battle between the gods and the dānavas, which occurred after they had rested due to the long duration of their dwelling there, is described here in detail. || 1 ||
Just as a wave of water is understood to be an ocean wave due to its proximity to the shore. || 1 ||
Having heard those words, the gods departed in their respective directions,
like breezes carrying the fragrance of lotuses and taking with them a garland of forest flowers.
"His own chosen" means the direction presided over by whichever guardian of the quarters he intends;
the term "his own chosen" is also an adjective qualifying the forest garland (*vanamālā*). || 2 ||
For some days they rested in their own lovely and ever-lustrous mansions, like bees among lotuses.
Having rested, they took their rest. || 3 ||
Having attained for a short time that auspicious state which brings about their own exaltation,
they raised a sound from their drums resembling the roar of clouds at the dissolution of the world.
Then, by those Daityas stationed in the netherworld (pātāla),
a terrible battle that caused a long delay ensued once more with me in the sky.
Then, having heard the sound of the drum, when the Daityas had armored themselves and ascended into the great void of the intermediate space (antarikṣa), || 5 ||
Multitudes of swords, arrows, spears, and mallets flew forth, along with clubs, maces, fierce axes, discs, and conchs;
as did thunderbolts, mountain rocks, fires, and trees.
And the weapons have the faces of a snake, a garuḍa, and so forth. || 6 ||
He describes nothing but the battle until the end of the creation, beginning with the words "vavau" and so forth.

*Śaṅkhāḥ* refers to specific weapons shaped like conch shells; or, because they take away the life-breath of enemies, the word *śaṅkha* may refer to weapons in general. Regarding *girayaḥ śilāḥ*: it means either mountains together with their rocks, or mountains that consist primarily of rock, or simply rocks and mountains.
Ending with trees, weapons with the faces of serpents, Garuḍas, and so forth, blew and moved through the great sky.
A great torrent of water, with weapons fashioned by magic, indeed rushed forth in every direction with rapid current;
it bore along hundreds of thousands of rocks, mountains, and trees.
The river, possessing a deep roar like a surging mass of agitated waters, [flowed] suddenly.

He describes that very [river] with the word "māyā": she whose dense torrent consists of the great waters which are indeed weapons created by Māyā; for this reason, she is called *Kṣiprāvahā* (the swift-flowing), because she brings forth those who are *kṣipra*—that is, quick-handed—for the sake of victory.
[She flows] with stones, mountains, and trees as her marks, and even with the preeminent trees among them.
The meaning is that she suddenly emerged like a river with a deep roar, its waters agitated by a flood. || 7 ||
The flood of spears, tridents, rocks, darts, swords, lances, arrows, javelins,
and mallets flowing in its current was like the Ganges, with its banks lined by celestial palaces.
By the scattering of showers of thunderbolts in all directions.

He describes that very river again with the word "madhye" (in the middle): it is like the Gaṅgā, which— by means of a siege consisting of a rain of weapons headed by thunderbolts, such as that which encircles or surrounds the abodes of the immortals (the gods) like Meru and others with its waters— is like the cutting away of a rampart.
The meaning is that it is like the Gaṅgā flowing from the ridges of Mount Meru and other mountains. || 8 ||
Even this formidable body composed of earth and other elements, like a dense mass of clouds receiving and holding forth blows,
subsides through illusion before the assembly of gods, asuras, and siddhas.
Furthermore, a form created by illusion arises, yet it is not that very same [illusion] itself.
Now, regarding the creation of various illusions for the mutual delusion of the gods and demons,
and the subsequent pacification of those by means of counter-measures— furthermore, the repeated emergence of other similar illusions and their pacification—
the author says "pṛthvyādi" (beginning with earth). "Pṛthvī" means the earth, consisting of that [earth].
From the word "etcetera," it follows that illusion consists of water, fire, air, and space. Just as this earth appears to whirl, to fall, or to obstruct;

as people appear to sink in water, to be burned by fire, to be carried away by wind, or to fall into the space of a great abyss—so too do the dreadful bodies of *rakṣas*, *piśācas*, and other such beings [appear].

As if composed of that very essence; such as those which appear to fall, to run, to fight, or to devour—consisting of a terrible physical form. It was another [battle] in which there were many instances of the giving and the seizing—that is, the grasping—of blows. It was dense, difficult for others to traverse, and had attained a state of massiveness as if it were a heaped-up pile.
That [illusion] in which the bodies of the opponents serve as the bodies of the combatants is of such a kind;
yet even when such an illusion is employed by gods, asuras, and siddhas, it is neutralized and destroyed by counter-measures,
and having subsided, a form of illusion identical to the previous one arises— is that indeed the very same one produced before?
The meaning is that it is difficult to know in reality whether it is a form created by illusion, or not, or indeed something else entirely. || 9 ||
Mountains shattered by weapons like crags,
great oceans filled with floods of blood,
and spears sprouting from the mountain-like corpses of the lords of gods and asuras—
He beheld groves of palmyra trees and the faces of the quarters of the sky.

The faces of the quarters— the cardinal directions— became like mountains marked with the characteristics of the gods and the characteristics of the lord of the asuras, upon which grew groves of *tālī* trees characterized by rows of *kunta* grass.
She who effortlessly swallows the mountains hurled by the gods and demons with her playfully brandished spears, arrows, pikes, maces, swords, and discuses;
she whose rows of teeth and the tips of her claws shine like saws.
For the creation of iron lions, endowed with life, fell down.

In that city, mountains released by the gods and Dānavas were swallowed with ease as they disgorged spears, arrows, javelins, clubs, swords, and discuses; it possessed rows of claw-tips that were the very teeth of gleaming saws used for splitting and carving,
and it was endowed with life because it seized the lives of others.
Indeed, because of their ferocity, the creation of lions—consisting of iron, being transformations of iron, and made of weapons—fell [upon them];
that is to say, they rushed forth. || 11 ||
An army of suns at the end of an eon, manifested by the mass of heat from the poisonous fire of his blazing eyes,
[and] great, long mountains flying upward—
The row of venomous serpents shone forth like the great ocean.
Now he describes the multitude of illusory serpents created by the serpent-weapon (*sarpāstra*), whose gaze is poisonous: "Ujjvālā...

etc. By the mass of heat from those fires of the poison of their eyes, which have risen up as flames, the conflagration of the quarters was displayed; [a conflagration] by which the armies of twelve suns rising simultaneously at the end of an eon were shown.
Such a line of venomous serpents shone forth, appearing like an ocean submerged and pervaded by great mountains that were lofty, long, and rising up on all sides. || 12 ||
With the mountain lords encircled by the swirling waves of the ocean agitated within by the harsh impact of the thundering vajra-makaras,
the entire world became truly constricted in its limbs.
With various whirlpools and the currents of rivers of diverse weapons.
Now he describes the encircling of the ocean by means of the illusory weapon of the ocean (*sāmudrāstra-māyā*) with the verse beginning "unnāda":

by those various streams of rivers consisting of weapons, which surround—that is, encircle—Mount Meru, the king of mountains; and by the circles of waves of the ocean, which is harsh within due to being agitated by the loud roar of diamonds and other gems, as well as by swarms of sea-monsters (*makara*).
The entire world, its limbs rendered extremely cramped by revolutions and transformations, had all its parts afflicted with pain. || 13 ||
The sky, the courtyard of the great hosts of asuras, where mountains, missiles, weapons, and Garuḍas moved like massive elephants,
became for a moment filled with oceans and for a moment ablaze with floods of fire.
For a moment it was filled with suns, and for a moment with darkness.

The atmosphere, which had become the battlefield for the great gods and asuras, was shaken by mountains uprooted and hurled with force using mountain-weapons and other weapons, as well as by illusory Garuḍas; and from that moment, the sight-poisonous serpents previously described fled, along with the lords of the waters.
For a moment it was full of masses of fire; for a moment it was full of suns;
for a moment it was full of darkness—this is a restatement of what was previously described. || 14 ||
The world became as unbearable as at the time of universal dissolution, with floods of mountain-like fires from weapons spreading through the sky, filled with the *guḍaguḍa* roar of Garuḍas.
The interior of the ground of the abode of the gods was set ablaze. || 15 ||

With Garuḍas produced from the Gāruḍa weapon, filling the sky with indistinct "guḍa-guḍa" sounds, and with floods and torrents of mountains of blazing weapons spread abroad, the interior space of the earth and the celestial abodes once again became ablaze as if it were the unbearable time of universal dissolution (kalpānta). || 15 ||
The asuras flew up from the surface of the earth into the sky like birds from a mountain slope,
while the gods fell to the ground due to their great exhaustion.
Like mountain rocks shaken at the time of universal dissolution. || 16 ||
The Asuras flew upward from the surface of the earth into the sky, while the gods fell from the upper regions down to the earth. 16.
Then, amidst the sky, the gods and demons experienced the great conflagration clinging to the forest rows of trees formed by the lofty weapons fixed upon their bodies.
possessing the beauty of a mountain shaken by the winds at the end of an eon.

In forest ranges filled with trees of towering weapons rooted in their bodies, those gods and demons— possessed by the great conflagration— attained the splendor of mountains being shaken and whirled about by the winds of the kalpa, and thus set ablaze. || 17 ||
The sky all around the mountain shone, filled with streams of blood released from the bodies of the lords of the gods and asuras, which were swirling everywhere.
O dear one, [he saw] the Gaṅgā, whose waters were diminished by the mass of twilight prayers.

The sky, acting as the hero (nāyaka)— the masculine gender being used by way of transposition— surrounding Mount Meru on all four sides, is filled with streams of blood flowing from the bodies of the great mountains characterized as gods and demons, which have been released and are wandering about on every side;
[this is compared] to the mass of rays (karaugha) of the heroine that is twilight (saṃdhyā), where the word "mass of rays" refers to a mass of fingernails (karajaugha).

They are perceived. He bore their wound; or rather, there is an option between two metaphors (*utprekṣā*): he bore the Gaṅgā filled with such streams of blood. The word *aṅga* is used for addressing. The term *pūrṇam* (filled) is an adjective qualifying both the nail-wound and the Gaṅgā, as they are feminine and neuter respectively.
By the rule "the neuter with a non-neuter" (*napuṃsakamanapuṃsakena*), there is a single-remainder compound (*ekaśeṣa*), and consequently, the treatment as a singular (*ekavadbhāva*). || 18 ||
They rained down mountains, they rained down water,
they likewise rained down various fierce weapons,
and they rained down terrible thunderbolts.
Then there was a mutual showering of fire that was equal between them. || 19 ||
The connection with what follows is that "those gods and asuras brought [them]. || 19 ||
Skilled in the paths of right and wrong conduct,
and having shattered the walls of all the great mountains,
they simultaneously created [them] on every side.
Like a shower of merit falling upon the temples of elephants. || 20 ||
During a meritorious festival, for the sake of sport, it was as if there were a raining down of liquids such as lac, saffron, and sandalwood by means of tube-machines; such is the meaning. || 20 ||
The gods and asuras, agitated by the tumult of battle, with weapons in their hands intent on crushing one another’s limbs,
crushed the broad frontal globes of the elephants of the enemy host like the young of great serpents.
Scattering their splendor, they whirled about in the sky.

The gods and asuras, casting upon one another a state of equal agitation and enthusiasm for battle, not abandoning their efforts, with limbs mangled and being distressed and frantic, and possessing hands equipped with weapons— being thus,
they [attacked] the herds of elephants belonging to the lineages of the offspring of the lords of serpents, such as Airāvata and the other elephants of the quarters.

The meaning is that the splendors— meaning the expanded beauties— of the multitude of *pṛtanās*, which are broad *pīṭhas* (seats) with backs resembling seats, scattered through the sky as if they were heavy loads filled with burdensome materials, acting like *peṣas* (grinding stones) that cause pain. || 21 ||
With severed heads, hands, arms,
and thighs wandering like ominous locusts in the expanse of the sky, the belly of the world at that time became as if filled with fierce masses of clouds.
The mass of mountains at the horizons was shrouded by the sun and moon.

The compound *ākāśakāṣṭham* refers to the collection of space (*ākāśa*), the quarters (*kāṣṭhā*), and the directions (*diś*). In that [collection], by means of locusts (*śalabhaiḥ*)—which are specific types of portentous red insects—the very sky, which has become like wood (*kāṣṭha*) because its fruits, flowers, leaves, and so forth have been entirely consumed, is [attacked] by the locusts; or alternatively, it refers to the clouds (*abhra*).

It was such that the edges of the quarters and the clusters of mountains were shrouded and covered by masses of clouds—as if by excessive loads—referred to as *abbhramaraiḥ* (in the alternative reading); even with this reading, the meaning remains "by the clouds, which are the bees (*bhramara*) of the waters. Thus, it was a state where everything up to the sun (*ābhāskaram*, i.e., as far as the sun) was veiled. || 22 ||
By the masses of sparks flashing from the blades of weapons, scattered by the slapping of the waists of shouting warriors,
and by those falling as they were struck down in mutual combat—
The earth, shattered into pieces, fell apart.

By the shouts of warriors who were correctly brandishing and striking [their weapons], by the slapping and clapping against their waist-regions, by the weapons bursting and snapping [from the impact], and likewise by the weapons falling due to being struck by one another— and thus by the fragments [of those weapons] discharged through skill in mechanical projectiles and the like— [the battlefield was darkened].

By the torrents of rocks, mountains, and so forth—the suffix *iṭ* being Vedic—the earth, having become shattered, went "piece by piece" (*dalaśaḥ*), that is, into fragments; the meaning is that it was broken apart. || 23 ||
With showers of weapons, rocks, mountains, and trees hurled at one another,
and with the friction of bodies as hard as Mount Meru,
the battle took place while the sky resounded with the crackling sound of things being shattered.
Like the end of an eon, with terrifying, heavy, and fierce roars.

The battle was like the end of the eon (kalpākṣaya), by means of those fierce roars characterized by a terrible and excessive weight produced by the rubbing together and mutual clashing of bodies and limbs as hard as Mount Meru; such is the meaning. || 24 ||
The cosmic egg— its two halves like leaves shaken by the wind of [Brahmā’s] breath, containing a vast multitude of gods and demons,
and with its walls and corners shattered— [was destroyed].
It was as terrible as the end of an eon at the time of universal destruction. || 25 ||
Where the waters and fire were agitated below by a fierce, intoxicated wind, and the sun was likewise [driven] above;
where there were two such petals; where the vast multitudes of gods and demons, increased by the power of illusion (*māyā*), were present;
and where the corner walls of the edges were shattered and torn asunder—such was it.
The universe became as terrifying and formidable as at the end of an eon occurring out of its proper time. || 25 ||

The mountain peaks, filling the horizons on all sides, were violently whirled about by the fierce winds from the high caves; struck by heavy weapons the size of their own bodies, they crashed and shrieked as if with cries of agony.
With the loud, roaring cries of lions as they charged forward. || 26 ||

He further describes what that [battle] was like at that time with the word "bhrāntaiḥ" (by those who were bewildered): by those struck by dense weapons resembling their own bodies in size; for this very reason, they were utterly bewildered. And while wandering, they were as if crying out in distress with loud, abundant sounds, echoing through the fierce caves and high winds.
The slopes of the quarters were filled with mountain peaks that stood as if crying out with the roars of lions descending upon them. || 26 ||
By illusions, rivers, oceans, armies, fires, and conflagrations;
by trees, the corpses of gods and asuras, mountains, and towering rocks;
and by whirling arrows, sharp spears, maces, missiles, and weapons—
Like forest leaves scattered by the wind, [they fell] deep within.
It continued that it was filled with arrows, swords, and other weapons whirling here and there, like leaves scattered by the wind in a forest. || 27 ||

Suddenly, there arose a wind from the falling mountain-like bodies of warriors, whose forms were as terrible and powerful as elephants with irresistible trunks, capable of shattering the very dimensions of the wings of the lord of mountains.
[He saw] the flood of the ocean's waters, which had overflowed from the city of the gods.

He describes what that [army] was like once again with the verse beginning "adrīndra": "With dimensions equal to the wings—the peripheral mountains—of Adrīndra (Meru), and therefore incapable of the movement (gama) of humans and others due to obstructing their passage; [it was composed of] those previously mentioned Durvāra elephants, possessed of great strength."
The horizon was filled with the carcasses of elephant herds; moreover,
with the falling bodies of warriors, like great mountains or celestial cities swept away by the wind,
it became like the surging flood of the full ocean.
The atmosphere was filled with a dense, humming roar, and the earth— with its mountains washed by blood—
seemed to have become a vast expanse of bloody lakes.
Then the cave of the world's expanse became agitated. || 29 ||
Furthermore, at that time, the interior caverns of the cosmic egg—the expanse of the universe—had their atmosphere filled with dense, resonant roars;
the mountains were washed by blood, as were the earth, the netherworld (pātāla), and all regions below them; it was a lake of blood.
Or, being of such a nature that it subsists on the very mode of life—the food—of those such as Rākṣasas and Piśācas, she became agitated. || 29 ||
Causing transformations that spread from infinite vision,
foretelling pleasure and pain intent upon decline and rise,
it was crowded with the friction of the gods and asuras in the act of battle.
Then, indeed, there arose here something truly characteristic of this worldly existence. || 30 ||

She causes fear and other transformations to spread among the infinite gods, such as Indra; and she causes the transformations of the world to spread within the infinite vision—the self-consciousness that is devoid of the three kinds of limitations. She indicates pleasure and pain through the reversal of those things tending toward decay and those tending toward arising.

The friction— the mutual encounter— of the Asuras, whose mental dispositions were unscriptural, the Suras, whose dispositions were scriptural, and the well-known Asuras and Suras alike, became a conflict difficult to overcome, resembling the turmoil of worldly existence (saṃsāra) such as ignorance and the rest. || 30 ||

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Renewed Battle between Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa," in the Section on Stability (Sthitiprakaraṇa) of the Holy Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa, a work of the Seers (Ārṣa). 28.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Renewed Battle between Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa," in the *Sthitiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The twenty-ninth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus, by means of such tumultuous undertakings, the life-taking asuras...
A truly great battle was commenced by those who were impetuously seized with fury. || 1 ||
The despondency of Dāma and the others—who had conceived the pride of possessing bodies—in battle with the gods is described first, followed by their flight and defeat. (1)

A truly great battle was commenced by those life-taking asuras, whose undertakings were of such a nature—consisting mostly of the types previously described—and who were agitated and largely distracted. || 1 ||
By means of illusion, as well as by dispute, alliance, and war; by flight, by fortitude, and by concealment and protection. || 2 ||

That treaty was sometimes with the gods through illusion, or through dispute, or by mere verbal combat; sometimes through means such as giving gifts and so forth, or through alliance, sometimes through war, sometimes through flight, or by remaining hidden while protecting one's own people. || 2 ||
Through wretchedness, combat with missiles, and frequent disappearances,
that war was maintained by the gods for thirty-five years.
At one time, out of miserliness, he maintained that commitment like a wretched man through such acts as seeking refuge and making supplications.
Therein, the first battle was maintained for thirty years; the second, however, was maintained for five years, eight months, and ten days; and the third was for seven and five [years].
It was held for twelve days; during that time, rains—meaning showers—fell from both armies upon trees, fires, weapons, certain chief thunderbolts, and mountain peaks. || 3 ||
For eighteen years, seven months,
and five days, trees, fire-weapon missiles, thunderbolts, and mountains rained down upon them.
After such a length of time, through the firm habituation of egoism,
Dāma and the others, their consciousnesses being swallowed up, took hold of the conviction that "I am [the body]."
"Of those whose minds are seized by latent impressions"—this is the ellipsis. || 5 ||
Just as a mirror becomes like the reflected object due to the excellence of its proximity,
so too do they attain a state of identification with the ego through the excellence of their practice.
He demonstrates, by means of an illustration, that the habitual practice of conceit is the cause of the strengthening of egoism:
"Because of proximity," [verse 6].
Just as an object situated at a great distance does not reflect in a mirror,
so too the latent impression of an object does not arise from a lack of practice.
With the intention that even a habituation (*vāsanā*) which has arisen is destroyed by abandoning it after a long period of practice, he says: "Just as...

That which has gone far away—that is, which has been abandoned for a long time—does not reflect; it departs from the state of being a reflection due to the lack of practice, that is, due to the abandonment of practice. || 7 ||
When Dāma and the others were born with the latent tendencies of egoism and self-identity, they fell into a state of wretchedness, thinking, "This is my life; this is my wealth. (8)

Those whose latent impression is that the ego itself is the self are "those with the impression of the ego as the self. Having fallen into a state of wretchedness through the hope that "may there be life for me" and "for that purpose may there be wealth—money—for me," [they remain bound]. (8)

Seized by the latent impression of worldly existence and likewise by the latent impression of delusion, they are bound by the snares of hope; consequently, they have fallen into a state of wretchedness.

From that [ignorance] arises *bhava*—the engagement in prescribed and prohibited actions; they are seized by its latent impressions (*vāsanā*), such as the delusive impression: "May my body always be free from disease, firm, and capable of enjoyment. (9)

For, like one who is deluded, the sense of "mine-ness" (mamatva) is imagined by those devoid of egoism (anahaṃkāra), just as the state of being a serpent is imagined in a rope by Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa. || 10 ||

In the reading *mugdheva hyanahaṃkāraiḥ*, the connection with what precedes is: "as if bewildered, [the mind] has fallen into a state of wretchedness. However, in the reading *śuddhairapyanahaṃkāraiḥ*, the clear meaning is that even though the servants and others are in reality pure (*śuddha*), a sense of "mine-ness" (*mamatva*) has been attributed to them. || 10 ||
"How may my body, from head to foot, become firm?"—thus did they, wretched with the thirst of "mine-ness," fall into a state of misery. (11)
The phrase "from head to foot" is an elaboration of the craving expressed as "mine. || 11 ||
