"May my body remain firm; may my wealth lead to happiness"—the fortitude of those whose minds were thus bound vanished within.
Because the bodies of the enemies of the gods possessed only slight strength and were accompanied by latent tendencies (*savāsanatva*),
their intentness upon striking was quickly wiped away as if it had been cleansed.

That previously celebrated devotion of the enemies of the gods, such as Dāma and others, to striking, became like an erased inscription—incapable of its purpose—due to their small courage and inferior strength. || 13 ||
Thinking, "How shall we exist in this world?
they became helpless and fell into a state of wretchedness, like lotuses deprived of water.
"The gods are mortal; how can we become immortal?"—with such thoughts they reflected. (14)
For those who possessed the conceit of "I," their delight in women, food, and drink became terrifying and conducive to worldly existence, rooted in the fluctuation of mental states.
Existents are the objects; their cultivation is "bhāva. Those [goddesses] abide therein; for that very reason, they have the nature of distributing—that is, bringing about—existence (bhava). || 15 ||
Then, in that battle, out of fear they became full of hesitation,
like little deer in a forest agitated by a rutting elephant.

The phrase "in living" (jīvane) is to be understood as the ellipsis for "dependence" (sāpekṣatvam). When [the elephant] is enraged and furious for the sake of battle with intoxicated elephants, [it is called] *ghana*. || 16 ||
Thinking "we shall die, we shall die," their hearts struck by anxiety,
they indeed wandered very slowly in the battle against the enraged Rāvaṇa.
Where Airāvaṇa, the elephant of the gods, was enraged. || 17 ||
For those who sought only their own bodies and were terrified even of death,
the enemy placed its foot upon their heads because of their lack of fortitude.
By others, that is, by enemies. || 18 ||
Then, their courage failing, they were unable to slay the soldier standing before them, just as fires cannot consume an oblation when their fuel is exhausted.
Having attained the state of mosquitoes while striking at the gods,
the masses of wounded and mangled common warriors stood there.
The others are common soldiers, like ordinary warriors; thus they are "common-soldiers. || 20 ||
What need is there for much speaking here? With their minds terrified by death, the Daityas fled from the field of battle toward the gods.
As they were galloping forward and charging down. || 21 ||
While those famous ones known as Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa were fleeing in terror from all sides—the Dānavas and the rest—within the abode of the gods; || 22 ||
Then that army of Daityas, having been devoured, fell scattered in flight from the sky,
like a mass of stars blown away on all sides by the wind at the end of an aeon.
From the pit, from the sky. || 23 ||
In the groves of the Immortal Mountain (Amarācala), upon the peaks of its summits, on the shores of the oceans, and amidst the masses of clouds; || 24 ||

The connection of all the locative case-words beginning with "amarācala-kuñjeṣu" (in the groves of the Immortal Mountain) is with the phrase "patitās te surārayaḥ" (those enemies of the gods fell), as indicated by the thirty-ninth verse. || 24 ||
In the whirlpools and chasms of the ocean, in ravines and rising rivers, in wildernesses, at the ends of the quarters, and in blazing forests; || 25 ||
When the rivers were rising and swelling—there is the substitution of the masculine form [for the feminine] in this *karmadhāraya* compound. || 25 ||
In villages and cities where the land was devastated by his arrows, in forests with fierce birds of prey, and in the forest fires of the desert lands; || 26 ||
When the regions of those gods and asuras had been ravaged by arrows, the territories became the domain of fierce and cruel lions, tigers, and rākṣasas.
On the mountains at the edge of the Lokāloka range and in the lakes, as well as in the cities of Andhra, Draviḍa, Kaśmīra, and Pārasīka; || 27 ||
Upon the waves of various oceans, upon the masses of Ganges water, within other continents, in nets, and upon the creepers of the Jambu region; || 28 ||

In those [rivers] whose waves exist in various oceans— which, though being a single ocean, appear as many due to the division of regions because the Gaṅgā enters the sea through a thousand mouths— and in the nets spread out for catching fish in other continents, there are the various divisions of the Jambū-khaṇḍa regions. || 28 ||
Those enemies of the gods fell from all sides like mountains, their limbs and feet shattered and their hands and arms torn asunder. || 29 ||
He specifies those very ones who have fallen by means of the passage beginning with "visphoṭitāṅga" (with limbs burst open), and so forth. || 29 ||
With entrails like strings clinging to the branches, shedding streams of blood,
their heads with crowns cast aside, they emerged with eyes full of rage.
Those by whom showers of blood were released, having stepped forth with their feet utterly cast about. || 30 ||
Armed with weapons, their armor and missiles shattered by the power of Māyā’s arrows, their various weapons and garments fell scattered as they were cast down from a great distance.
Their armor, breastplates, and weapons were shattered by forces, illusions, and arrows;
they were cast far away by the impact and their flight, falling with heaps of various weapons and garments.
Terrifying with the crackling sound of their helmets hanging from their necks,
they had hundreds of locks of hair pierced by stones and dangling from parts of their bodies.

They are fierce with the *caṭat* sounds of their helmets dangling from their necks, and they inspire intense fear. With hundreds of matted locks knotted at the tips, they are pinned to the rocks on mountain peaks; for this very reason, parts of their bodies hang down, caught in the dense thorns of the *śālmali* tree which are as sharp and hard as a violent fall.
Their heads were shattered into a hundred pieces by the impact against the surface of the beautiful stone slabs.
On the śālmalī trees, because of their thorns, there is a painful distress for those whose firm fall [upon them] is made difficult by the thorns. || 33 ||
All the lords of the asuras perished in every direction immediately upon the mere falling of all their weapons and missiles.
Like dust particles in the waters of the ocean. || 34 ||

He concludes: "All indeed. In this manner, all the lords of the asuras, at the very moment the battle began—the mere falling of all their weapons and missiles—immediately vanished from sight in every direction, just as dust particles vanish into the water of the ocean during the rainy season.
The meaning is that they go to destruction in the same way. || 34 ||
Thus ends the twenty-ninth sarga, titled "The Fall of the Asuras," in the *Dāmavyālakaṭopākhyāna* within the *Sthitiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by the Sage Vasiṣṭha.
Thus ends [the section on] "The Fall of the Asuras" in the *Sthitiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The twenty-ninth canto, titled "Nāma."
The Thirtieth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus, while the gods were being gratified and the Dānavas were being slain,

Dāma, Vyāla, Kaṭa, and the others became overwhelmed with fear. (Note: The reading "dāmavyālakaṭādīnām" as a genitive plural is found in the previously printed edition and in another manuscript; its propriety should be understood by those possessing wisdom. || 1 ||
In this [work], the succession of births in Pātāla for those consumed by Yama—from Dāma onwards, ending with Matsya of the Kāśmīra country—is proclaimed. (1)

In this manner, while the Dānavas were being slain and the gods were gratified—this should be construed according to the sequence of meaning (*arthakrama*), as it is more powerful than the sequence of the words (*pāṭhakrama*)—the [Dānavas] became dejected and despondent. || 1 ||
Enraged, Śambara—whose army had been destroyed—blazed like the fire at the end of an aeon, crying out "Where are they? as he rushed toward Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa.
Śambara, being enraged toward Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa, asked "Where are they? and thus blazed up; such is the meaning. || 2 ||
Then, out of fear of Śambara, Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa abandoned their own domain and went to the seventh netherworld (pātāla), where they remained.

He specifically distinguishes the seventh netherworld (pātāla) with the words "of Yama. To dispel the doubt as to whether there might still be fear of Śambara even there, he says "capable of terrifying Time. The meaning is that they are capable of terrifying others like Time itself—namely, Death (mṛtyu). || 4 ||
There, Yama’s servants, who are capable of terrifying even Time itself,
stand out of curiosity as the guardians of the ocean of hell.
Then those fearless ones, having instilled fear in those who had departed, gave them young maidens in succession— maidens who were like personified anxieties and possessed dense, cloud-like forms.

The ellipsis "refuge for those who have gone [to them]" is to be supplied. From the three [rivers], three young maidens—daughters whose forms were like dense clouds, standing as if they were personified anxieties—[arose]; such is the meaning. || 5 ||
Together with them, Dāma and the others brought that limit there;
it lasted for ten thousand years, until their endless evil latent impressions were exhausted.
The limit is the remainder of the lifespan. || 6 ||
"This is my beloved daughter; she is mine, for I am her master"—thus did time pass for those whose bonds of affection were deeply rooted.
One whose own latent tendencies (vāsanās) are endless elaborates [the world], thinking "this is it"—thus [ends verse 7].
Then, on one occasion, Dharmarāja arrived at that place by chance for the purpose of investigating the affairs of the great hells.
Yama is the King of Dharma. || 8 ||
Not recognizing him as the King of Dharma, three asuras did not bow down to him for their own destruction, treating him like an ordinary servant.
Because the insignia such as the parasol and fly-whisk were not seen, it was not recognized that "this is the King of the Gods. || 9 ||
Then, by Vivasvat, they were cast into these blazing, fierce realms merely by the movement of his eyebrows.

In those terrifying hell-realms such as Raurava and others which are ablaze, there are well-known features such as glowing embers reaching a depth of a hundred yojanas and rising to the height of the knees. || 10 ||
There, those cries of piteous lamentation, along with their friends, wives, and kinsmen,
were consumed like leafy branches and trees by forest winds.
Those whose branches (viṭapa) and twigs (śākhā) are merely leaves (parṇa) are "parṇaviṭapas"; that is to say, they are like children. || 11 ||
Born through their own cruel latent tendencies (vāsanā),
they again take the form of Kirātas who perform the work of bondage and serve as the king's minions.

Due to living together with executioners, prison guards, laborers, and servants, they take on the forms of those very beings through such habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*); likewise for the servants (*kiṅkara*). One should infer [the rest] in the same way hereafter. || 12 ||
Then, having abandoned that birth, they were born as crows in ravines;
at the end of that, they attained the state of vultures, and from there they went to the state of parrots.

Those of crooked intellect— [according to another reading, "those of perverted minds"]— assumed the state of pigs in Trigarta, the state of rams in the mountains, and then the state of insects in Magadha. (14)
They are tawny; the meaning is that they hold [it]. || 14 ||
Having experienced various other diverse successions of births, O Rāma, today we fish dwell in a small pond in the forest of Kaśmīra. (15)
The ellipsis "having become fish" is to be supplied. || 15 ||
Drinking water that is like thin mud boiled by a forest fire,
they neither die nor live, being worn out by the silt of old age.
In those places of decaying mud and withered mire, they are worn out and their bodies are slackened.
Having repeatedly experienced the agitation of various wombs,
they have come into being again and again, only to perish once more, like waves in the ocean.
He restates what has already been said: "Variegated," etc. (verse 17).
O Rāma, those who have entered the ocean of existence and are driven by the threads of latent impressions have long been carried away like straw by the waves in the form of bodies;
yet even now they have not attained infinite peace.
Contemplate the terrible magnitude of latent impressions (vāsanā). || 18 ||

He summarizes: "In the ocean of existence... Being driven and propelled by the threads of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), they have for a long time been carried like straw upon the waves in the form of bodies and brought to various regions; yet even now, they have not attained the infinite, indefinable fruit of tranquility (*upaśama*). The cruelty of latent impression—
Contemplate this vast destructiveness—meaning, its nature as a source of great calamity. By this very example, the meaning is that you should perceive it everywhere. || 18 ||

Thus ends the thirtieth canto, titled "The Description of the Wondrous Sequence of Births of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa," in the Section on Stability within the Means of Liberation of the Holy Vasiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa, composed by the Sage. 30.

Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Variegated Births of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa," in the Section on Stability (*sthitiprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The thirty-first canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Therefore, O high-minded Rāma, I shall speak for your enlightenment.
But [I have spoken] thus in sport, lest the logic of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa should apply to you. || 1 ||
The loss of one's purpose and the acquisition of misfortune are said here to arise from ego-inflation (ahaṃkāra);
likewise, it is the negation of the existence or non-existence of states such as self-restraint (dāma) and the like. || 1 ||
Recalling what was stated previously, he applies it to the present narrative with the words "ataḥ" (therefore). || 1 ||
Due to its persistent lack of discernment, the mind heedlessly embraces such a calamity as this,
leading to the endless sufferings of saṃsāra.
Due to the pursuit of non-discrimination and the absence of the pursuit of discrimination, such a calamity characterized by false pride [arises]. || 2 ||
Where, indeed, is the lordship over Śambara’s host that destroys the gods;
and where is the state of being a fish, worn out by a mass of mud scorched by the heat? (3)
He demonstrates the great difference in result between prior selflessness and subsequent pride by means of the verse beginning with "kva kila" (where indeed...). 3.
Where is that great fortitude capable of routing the hosts of the immortals, and where is this state of being a lowly servant to the Kirāta king? (4)
Where indeed is that noble fortitude of the pure consciousness free from egoism, and where is this wicked conceptualization of the ego arising from the influence of false latent impressions? (5)
He states the difference even in terms of their essential nature with the words "kva nāma" (where indeed...). || 5 ||
O Lord, this dense cluster of worldly existence, thick with spreading branches and shoots of egoism, rises up far-reaching.
By the word "mañjarī" (cluster), the creeper characterized primarily by it is understood. || 6 ||
O Rāma, diligently cleanse the ego within yourself;
by contemplating that "I am nothing at all," become happy.

He states the means by which that [impurity] is cleansed: "I am not anything at all. Since in all inert objects of perception (*dṛśya*) only the quality of being "this" (*idantva*) is observed, the application of "I-ness" (*ahantva*) is impossible; and since in the nature of pure consciousness—the witness of everything including the ego (*ahaṅkāra*)—the attribution of the property of identification (*abhimāna-dharmakatva*) is untenable, the application of "I-ness" is impossible. Thus, [it is established that] the Seer is not the Seer...

The meaning is: having meditated upon the reality that, because that which is non-distinct [from the self] is unreal, there is nothing whatsoever that can serve as the locus of the "I-sense" (aham). || 7 ||
The orb of the moon of ultimate reality, consisting of elixir and cool, has become invisible, shrouded by the cloud of egoism.
Having stated that egoism is the cause of misfortune, he describes its nature as an obstacle to one's welfare: "Egoism... [etc.].

It consists of elixir (*rasāyana*), having the single flavor of bliss; it is composed of nectar (*amṛta*), being cool and free from the three-fold affliction (*tāpa*). [In this context, the reading "cool and free from the three-fold affliction" is superior. 8.
Afflicted by the demon of egoism, the three— Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa—
though non-existent, attained existence as demons through the power of Māyā.
The Dānavas, such as Dāma and others, though previously non-existent there, were brought into existence within the stream of birth and death for living beings by the power of Māyā.
"O Rāma, today the fish in the great forests, lakes, groves, and ponds of Kaśmīra remain intent upon feeding on the water-moss."
They were intensely longing for, that is, possessed of great desire for, fragments of moss. || 10 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
"The non-existent has no being, and the existent has no non-being.
Tell me, how did those which are non-existent attain existence? (11)
Having heard that even non-existent things have attained existence, Rāma suspects this to be logically untenable;
thus Śrī Vasiṣṭha says: "O mighty-armed one, it is so; the non-existent never comes into being anywhere."
Sometimes even something very small becomes large, and the large becomes small.

To state his own intended distinction, Vasiṣṭha first accepts Rāma’s statement and begins his refutation with the words, "It is so. It is true that nothing whatsoever ever arises from what is non-existent;
however, that which is subtle indeed becomes vast through its manifestation.
That very origination, through its expansion, becomes subtle by means of concealment; that itself is destruction—this is the meaning. || 12 ||
Tell me, what is that which exists as non-existent, or what is that which exists as existent?
By means of correct insight alone, I shall bring about your awakening.

"Let it be so; nevertheless, since even among things that lack self-nature (*anātman*), the distinction between existence and non-existence is difficult to determine, [the author], wishing to express this, asks Rāma: 'What...? (13)
Śrī Rāma said: "O Brahmin, it is indeed true that we who are here are virtuous; yet you say that even Dāma and the others, though they are not virtuous, are established as virtuous."

The meaning is: "Is it not the case that for beings such as ourselves, existence is established by means of perception and other valid cognitions (*pramāṇa*), whereas for [beings] like Dāma and others, you yourself have stated non-existence because they are mere illusion? That being so, how can you speak of their existence again, which is contradictory? What, then, is your intention? || 14 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, just as Dāma and the others exist as composed of illusion,
they are indeed unreal, yet appear real like the flood of water in a mirage.

If you consider that the bodies of ourselves and others possess existence because they are fit for the conventional usage of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then the same applies to ropes and the like. Alternatively, if you consider them non-existent because they are sublated by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) or because their nature is difficult to define, then that too is equally applicable; thus [your position] is not tenable.
With the intention that there is a contradiction, Vasiṣṭha gives the answer beginning with "Just as" (yathā) and so forth. || 15 ||
In the very same way, we too— along with the gods, asuras, and dānavas—
are entirely unreal as we move about, go forth, and return.
Your existence is indeed false, and my existence is likewise false;
though experienced, it is unreal in nature, just like one's own death in a dream. (17)
Your state is the state of Rāma’s body; my state is the state of Vasiṣṭha’s body. || 17 ||
Just as a deceased kinsman, though experienced even in a dream, consists of unreality;
if there were such a realization that "this [person] is dead," so too would this world be.
This statement, which pertains to the utterly deluded, does not shine at all;
for [the realization] arises through practice, and there can be no denial of direct experience. (19)
For one who is utterly deluded and possesses the conviction that the world is real, this statement regarding its unreality does not shine at all with respect to him.

Why is that? He says: "By means of practice. Without the practice of investigating the reality of the ultimate truth (*paramārthatattva*), the denial—that is, the repudiation—of the experience of the world's reality does not arise. (19)
That certainty which has taken deep root within and has become established even without practice never perishes for anyone in this world at any time. (20)

Thus, he states—beginning with "certainty"—that even the destruction of previously arisen latent impressions (*duḥsaṃskāra*) does not arise without the practice of the true meaning of the scriptures. || 20 ||
He who says that this world is unreal and Brahman alone is real—
him, like one mad, even a madman laughs at excessively, as does even a fool.
For this very reason, an instruction given to one who lacks the qualification is like the prattle of a madman; [the text says]:
"Where indeed could there be identity between the ignorant and the knower of reality here?
It would be like the union of darkness and light, or of shadow and sunshine, within the consciousness of the blind and the seeing. (22)
If one who knows were to not act according to the injunctions, but instead engage in activities based on ignorance along with those ignorant ones, then he too would become ignorant;

thus, there would be identity between the ignorant and the knower. Anticipating this objection, he says: "akṣība... (not intoxicated). *Kṣība* means intoxicated by liquor; *akṣība* means sober. Where could there be identity between the two? *Andham* refers to darkness, because it blinds (*andhayati*).
Light is the sun and so forth. || 22 ||
Even with effort, an ignorant person who has experienced an object cannot deny its reality, just as one cannot step over a corpse that lies within.

For this reason as well, he states that the ignorant person is not fit for instruction with the words "by effort" (*yatnena*). Even when being awakened by great effort, the ignorant person is unable to effect the sublation— through the negation "not this, not this" (*neti neti*)— of that dualistic object which is experienced both internally and externally through the distinctions of mind, intellect, and so forth, as well as through the distinctions of form, taste, and so forth, within its true substratum.

It is not possible; just as a corpse or a rotting body is unable to perform the acts of stepping forward with its feet or moving about, so it is here. Furthermore, the meaning is that without the negation of the superimposed (adhyasta), the reality of the substrate (adhiṣṭhāna-tattva) cannot be known, and thus the instruction regarding it would be futile. || 23 ||
It is not fitting for an ignorant person to say that the entire world is Brahman;
yet, through the lack of experience in austerity and knowledge, he has experienced it as such. (24)
Regarding this very [Self], the Brāhmaṇas seek to know through the study of the Vedas, by sacrifice, by charity, by austerity, and by fasting;

since austerity, meditation, and so forth are prescribed for the sake of accomplishing the qualification for knowledge, he says "Brahman" to indicate that one who is unrefined and ignorant is not fit for instruction. For, in the absence of the experience of austerity, knowledge, and the like—

The meaning is that, in the absence of latent impressions (saṃskāra) produced by experience, that ignorant person has experienced from beginningless time only the state of being a transmigrating self consisting of the body and so forth, which is well-known to him, and never the state of being a non-transmigrating Self. || 24 ||
For this speech, O Rāma, shines forth only within the domain of the unawakened;
in the state of one who has awakened, there is indeed nothing whatsoever that can be thought "I am. || 25 ||

To the question, "Where then does the speech of instruction shine? he says: "In one who is not awakened" (*abuddhe*). The negative particle (*nañ*) is compounded here in the sense of "little," as in the expression "a girl with a small belly" (*anudarā*); thus, the meaning is "in the case of one of little intelligence. However, for the awakened one (*buddha*), who possesses perfect realization, there is nothing at all that can be grasped in the form of the ego-reflection "I am" (*asmīti*); therefore, such a person also is not a fit recipient for instruction.
This is the meaning. And thus it has been stated at the beginning: "Neither one who is utterly ignorant nor one who is [already] a knower is qualified for this scripture. || 25 ||
For the wise one who experiences, "This supreme Brahman alone is peace," how could it be appropriate for him to deny his own direct experience? (26)

Just as one who knows the meaning of the statement "I am Brahman" lacks the qualification [to practice] because of the inability to conceive "I am," so too, due to the non-establishment of a thing to be negated, he states that the knower lacks qualification even for the realization of the meaning of the negating statement "not this" (neti): "Brahman alone... (26).
Apart from the other, there is nothing whatsoever of "I" within the self;
just as a ring and so forth do not exist apart from gold, there is no distinctness in me.
One might object: "Why does the ignorant person not likewise superimpose the ego (ahaṃkāra) upon Brahman, just as one superimposes a gold ring and so forth?

To this, he says: "From the Supreme" (*parasmāt*). The meaning is that for the knower, there is nothing whatsoever in the Self that is denoted by the word "I" (*ahaṃpada*) which exists as something distinct from the Supreme, even if it were merely apparent (*prātītika*), such as a ring or the like. It is not [so].
"In me" means: since there is no distinctness in me, who am non-dual, even through delusion—such that a qualification could be negated—this is the meaning. || 27 ||
Apart from reality, there is nothing at all for the deluded person within the self;
just as gold is not present in the cognition of waves and so forth, so too ultimate reality does not exist for the knower [who perceives it as such]. 28.

With the intention that even the ultimate reality (paramārtha) appears as if extremely near through the perspective of the ignorant just as it does through the perspective of the wise, he says "bhūtatā" [in the verse], meaning that its existence cannot be made known to them.
*Bhūtatā* is the state of being essentially nothing more than the cause and effect consisting of the five elements. (28)
The fool consists of false ego, while the wise man consists of the one true Self;
indeed, these two can never be joined, for there is a denial of their respective natures.
Having already stated this, he expresses it clearly and concisely with two verses beginning with "mithyā" (29).
How can there be a denial of that which is identical with something else?
For the statement "I am a jar" on the part of a person is indeed merely the ravings of a madman. (30)
He provides an example for the point that, for one who possesses the certainty that something has a certain nature, it is useless to teach that it has a different nature: "of a person," etc. (30).
Therefore, neither we nor Dāma and the others are real anywhere;
they are unreal, and so are we, for indeed there is no origination for us.
Having concluded the introductory section, he summarizes the established subject matter with the words "Therefore":

These [beings], well-known as the bodies and selves of Vasiṣṭha, Rāma, and others perceivable through direct perception, are not real from the perspective of the scriptures; they are unreal even from the perspective of the experience of the wise; and their existence is impossible even from the perspective of logic.
The meaning is that there is no real existence. || 31 ||
Truth is pure consciousness, the stainless sky of awakening;
truth is all-pervading, peaceful, and free from rising or setting.

What, then, is the truth? He says: "The Truth. Consciousness alone is the truth from the perspective of the scriptures; it is the truth from the perspective of the experience of the wise; and it is that very same thing which exists, without setting or rising, from the perspective of logic—this is the meaning. || 32 ||
Everything is peaceful and void, existing as if it were nothing at all;
within that sky, my own innate manifestations shine forth as these creations, my dear friend.

The entire world is peaceful and ceased. One asks: "Is there a remainder of emptiness? He says, "no"—it is *niḥśūnya*, meaning emptiness has been cast out. If so, how is it peaceful? To this he says, "as if nothing at all.
It is as if everything were empty, but not actually empty; the meaning is that it abides in the state of the fullness of pure existence (*sanmātra*). These are one's own...
Appearances are manifestations in a manner other than [their true nature]. 33.
Just as the innate visual perceptions of one with cataracts appear as clusters of hairs and the like, so too do these perceptions appear therein. (34)
If it is asked, "Where has the manifestation of the existent as the form of the non-existent ever been seen?", he says: "Just as... (verse 34).
He experiences himself in an instant exactly as he conceives it;
therefore, the space of consciousness (cidākāśa) makes even the unreal appear real through its mere observation. || 35 ||
That one whose nature is Truth perceives the Self in whatever manner and by whatever means; in that very way, he experiences it in an instant.
Therefore, from that vision—by the power of seeing the True Self—even the unreal becomes as if real in an instant; this is the meaning. || 35 ||
"There is neither truth nor untruth; therefore, in the three worlds, whatever the form of consciousness perceives, that arises exactly in that way, without a doubt. (36)
If reality arises from the perception of reality by its own nature, then what is the form of the world? To this he says: "It is not real.
(36) "Just as [the illusions] such as the rope-snake and so forth arose, so have we arisen.
Whether real or unreal, my dear friend, what conceptualization can there be even with respect to them? (37)
Thus, by means of well-known forms such as Vasiṣṭha, Rāma, and so forth—those [forms] such as Dāma and the rest—the word "api" (also) has the sense of "eva" (only/just):
within this infinite, all-pervading, formless sky of consciousness, consciousness arises in whatever manner it does; in that very way, it shines forth abundantly therein. 38.
In whatever way, and in whatever form, it arises within. || 38 ||
Wherever consciousness itself manifests in the form of a rope or the like, it becomes established as such through the experience of that particular form. (39)
He demonstrates what has been stated by providing an illustration: "Where... (verse 39).
Wherever consciousness has arisen by itself in the form of ourselves and others, it has become established there in that very way, through the experience of having that specific form. (40)

The designation "world" is applied to the manifestation of one's own dream, just as the state of being a mirage is attributed to the heat of the sky, which is the void-natured expanse of consciousness.
Of the heat of the rays of the sun. || 41 ||
Where the sky of consciousness is awakened, there the designation "the visible" (dṛśya) is applied;
but where it is asleep by that very same [consciousness], there the designation "liberation" (mokṣa) is applied. || 42 ||

Wherein, with respect to the world-object, it is awakened—that is to say, watchful, consisting in the perception of external objects; wherein, in its own non-dual self-luminous Self, it is asleep—devoid of the perception of external objects—it is by that very same space of consciousness (*cidvyoman*). And thus says the Śruti: "For where there is duality, as it were, there one sees another; but where..."
When for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom could one see? Thus [it is said]. 42.
And that [consciousness] is never anywhere asleep, nor is it ever awakened;
let it be understood that the visible world is merely the sky of consciousness (cidvyoma). (43)
However, these two states have been described through a conceptualization of similarity for the sake of instruction; in the ultimate sense, he says:
"Nirvāṇa itself is the glory of creation, and the glory of creation itself is nirvāṇa.
There is no difference in meaning between these two words, just as there is none between synonyms. (44)
When the visible world is nothing but the space of consciousness alone, then the distinction between creation and liberation ceases; thus he says:
"It is indeed liberation. (44)
The ultimate reality perceives the world as its own form;
it is just as an eye affected by cataracts perceives a mass of floating hairs. 45.
He establishes what was stated by means of two verses beginning with "paramārthe": The Self, when conditioned by ignorance, is itself [the cause of error].
(45) That is not at all a mass of hair; rather, it is that vision which exists in such a way.
This visible world is nothing at all; thus the space of consciousness remains established. (46)
Everything exists everywhere, just as it has been experienced; nothing whatsoever exists here that has not been experienced.
This peaceful, singular, and all-pervading reality remains thus.
Therefore, remain here, having completely abandoned grief, fear, and the sense of duality.

In the view of superimposition (*adhyāropa*), because all things can be superimposed upon the all-pervading space of consciousness (*cidvyoman*), everything exists everywhere; however, in the view of negation (*apavāda*), nothing exists anywhere at all. Thus, in both these aforementioned ways, this world is peaceful, with all distinctions cast aside, and is therefore one, real, and pervasive—complete. Therefore, you too [should realize this].
The meaning is: "Remain full in such a way that the distinction between sorrow and fear is completely abandoned. || 47 ||
This form of the Great Consciousness is tranquil, dense like a mountain of rock, and naturally pure;
yet, in some instances, the two views of "it exists" and "it does not exist" arise.
And whatever exists is good; that alone shines forth.

Reinforcing that very point, he describes it further with the word "stone" (*śilā*): Like the interior of a crystal stone, which appears as a void yet is solid, the nature of mountains, rivers, and so forth exists there like a reflection—neither as "existent" nor as "non-existent"—and is never perceived anywhere as such; for that which exists merely as a manifestation [is thus].
The meaning is that each of those appears as such precisely because it is of the nature of consciousness itself. || 48 ||

Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Refutation of Being and Non-being," in the *Sthitiprakaraṇa* (Section on Stability) within the *Mokṣopāya* (Means to Liberation) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis. || 31 ||
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Refutation of Being and Non-being," in the Section on Stability (*sthitiprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The thirty-second canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
Like children, yakṣas, and piśācas, they behave toward both the virtuous and the wicked alike.
How can there be an end to the suffering of Dāma, Vyāla, Kaṭa, and the others? || 1 ||
Though deprived of their births as fish and cranes while in the royal palace,
they attained knowledge within the bodies of mosquitoes and other insects, and thus reached liberation.
How can there be an end to suffering—liberation—for those who, though they are actually existent, are perceived as non-existent by the intellect of the ignorant? When will this come to pass? (1)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O scion of Raghu’s line, listen to this which was spoken by Yama when he was entreated by those very servants of Yama along with the family of Dāma and Vyāla at that very moment.
Together with the families of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa, who had become his kinsmen, [he was surrounded] by the servants of Yama. || 2 ||
When Dāma and the others shall experience separation and hear their own story, they will undoubtedly become liberated. (3)

Having then realized their own true nature— the discourse on the innate state of non-dual pure consciousness, which is free from latent impressions and the sense of being a living being fabricated by Śambara’s illusion— they will undoubtedly, without any doubt, become liberated.
The meaning is that this was stated by Yama. || 3 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
O Blessed One, where, when, and how will they hear this account of your own life? Or rather, please describe it to me in due order.

Those [words] are *dāma* and so forth. The word *vā* is used in the sense of *tu* (but/rather). [The form] *kathayate* [is derived] from *kathayataḥ*; by means of a grammatical anomaly (*vyatyaya*), the dative case is used in the sense of the ablative. || 4 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
In a small pond on the shore of the Mahāpadma lake in Kaśmīra,
he experienced a succession of births as a fish again and again.
With their intentions agitated, those fickle ones will meet their end in time;
they shall become cranes in that very same lotus lake.
Those whose ponds (palvala) have their depths stirred up (ālolita)—that is, churned by buffaloes, pigs, and other such creatures during the summer—being of such a nature... || 6 ||
There, indeed, upon the rows of reeds and the clusters of lotuses, upon the excellent creepers of moss and the undulations of the waves; || 7 ||
Upon swaying swings of blossoms and upon creepers of blue lotuses, amidst streaks of clouds formed by masses of spray, and within the cool whirlpools; (8)
Having enjoyed the delights of the lake, those cranes, the ornaments of the world,
having sported for a very long time, have now arrived with their purity fully restored.
Having attained awakening, they will become liberated and separated,
just as the qualities of rajas, sattva, and tamas reach a state of separation by chance.

"Those who have attained wisdom" means those who have acquired the intellect of discernment. Just as the qualities of rajas, sattva, and tamas, when examined with the eye of discrimination, attain their distinct separation for the sake of liberation, so it is here. 10.
Within the region of Kaśmīra, there shall be a city adorned by mountains,
known by the name Adhiṣṭhāna, which will be glorious.
It was adorned with cities, trees, and mountains. || 11 ||
In its center there will be a peak named Pradyumnaśikhara,
like a small bud within the whorl of a lotus.
"Light" means fit for leaping, that is to say, easy to mount; "the circle of the treasury" is like the pericarp [of a lotus]. || 12 ||
Upon the summit of that mountain, there will be a certain king’s palace,
a great *śāla* tree reaching to the clouds, like another peak upon the peak. (13)

On the summit of that mountain, a certain person will become like a king among other houses; he will be like a sovereign. On the great peak of a *śāla* tree—which, as if scraping or piercing the clouds and the sky, is called "cloud-scratching" (*abhraṃkaṣa*)—at the tip of its middle branch, there are great, cloud-scratching halls (*śālā*).
In such a mountain peak where there were palaces, there was either a simile (upamā) or a poetic fancy (utprekṣā), namely that it was like another peak. || 13 ||
In the northeast corner of the house, within a cavity in the wall above the head,
near some grass constantly shaken by an unceasing breeze— 14.
Above the wall of the head-enclosure, there is a breach in the form of a fissure in the joints of the stones; within that [breach], there is a nest—this is the sense of the remainder. || 14 ||
In the ālaya, the demon will become a predatory beast like a kalaviṅka bird; it will be like a novice who has heard little of the scriptures and whose cries are devoid of meaning. || 15 ||

In that abode, that nest, there is a sparrow; one who has heard only a little of the scripture at first, like such a twice-born bird, whose cry is devoid of meaning—meaningless, that is to say, an indistinct warbling of "cī-cī-kū-cī. || 15 ||
At that very time, there shall be a king there named Śrī Yaśaskaradeva, like another Śakra in heaven. || 16 ||
In his house, there will be a Dānava named Dāma, who will be like a mosquito with a soft sound within a hole in the back of a large pillar. || 17 ||
At that time, within that very city called Adhiṣṭhāna,
there will also be a monastery named the Ratnāvalī-vihāra.
A "vihāra" is a pleasure-house, so called because people dwell (*viharanti*) within it. || 18 ||
In that place, a minister of that land known as Narasiṃha will reside;
having perceived bondage and liberation as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of his hand, he will dwell there.

By whom both bondage and liberation have been examined—like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand—through scripture, reasoning, the instruction of the guru, and one's own experience, and have been ascertained like the true nature of a gem. (19)
In his house there shall be a toy bird, a partridge,
which is actually the illusory demon named Kaṭa, fashioned within a royal cage.

The connection [of the words] is as follows: *krakaraḥ*—a type of śārika bird that served as a plaything (*krīḍanaḥ*) for that minister, the means of his sport (*krīḍāsādhanabhūtaḥ*)—was the illusory demon (*māyāsuraḥ*) named Kaṭa. || 20 ||
That Nṛsiṃha, together with the king’s ministers, will narrate this excellent story of Dāma, Vyāla, Kaṭa, and the others, composed in verses.
Having heard this, the cartwright Krakara will remember his former existence;
thus becoming peaceful, he will attain the supreme, great peace of final Nirvāṇa.
He by whom the Self alone is remembered everywhere and at all times is the "Self-become" (Ātmabhū), whose nature is unlimited.

That which is peaceful—wherein the form of the individual soul (jīva) fashioned by Śambara has been sublated—is likewise the Great Peace; such is the supreme liberation (mokṣa), wherein the very nature of saṃsāra is pacified from its root. || 22 ||
The kalaviṅka bird dwelling on the edge of the Pradyumna peak shall hear the discourse from those residing there and attain supreme nirvāṇa. (23)

"Vāstavya" means one who dwells on the edge of the peak of Mount Pradyumna; the suffix *tavyat* is applied to the root *vas* (to dwell) with the augment *ṇic*. "Being described by those from that place and by others"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied. "The story" refers to the narrative of Brahmā composed of his own previous history. || 23 ||
Even a mosquito, having come to dwell within a wound inside the wood of the royal palace, will attain peace by chance upon hearing [the sound]. (24)
At the end of the wood, on the back of the pillar: "Peace! Liberation! (24).
O Rāghava, the sparrow from Pradyumna’s horn, the mosquito from the royal palace, and the cricket from the monastery—all these shall attain liberation. (25)
This entire sequence of the story of Dāma and Vyāla has been told to you;
in this very way, Māyā is the void of saṃsāra, yet she is exceedingly radiant.
Due to lack of thorough understanding, one is deluded like a mirage perceived as a body of water;
likewise, even from a great state, one falls downward through the power of various forms of ignorance.
Than other words, even from a great word, [this is superior] due to the state of unripened knowledge. || 27 ||
Deluded fools fall down like Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa;
where is that power by which Meru and Mandara were crushed by a mere contraction of the eyebrows? (28)

By means of the verse beginning with "Where" (kva), he demonstrates the vast difference between the former excellence resulting from the state of being free from latent impressions (nirvāsanatva) and the subsequent birth as a dog or similar creature. || 28 ||
Where is the state of being a mosquito in a wound within a piece of wood in Rājagṛha?
Where is the power to cast down the orbs of the sun and moon with a mere slap of the hand? (29)
A *capeṭa* is a blow with the palm of the hand; by that, [it means] merely with the arm—that is to say, even without weapons. || 29 ||
Where is this state of being a bird in a hole in a wall within a house on Mount Pradyumna?
Where is this state of having Mount Meru weighed in a hand trembling with the playfulness of plucking flowers? (30)
Where is the state of those by whom Mount Meru was lifted with a hand as playful as a flower, weighing it to ascertain its exact mass? 30.
Or where, on the peak of Nṛsiṃha’s mountain, does the state of being a young partridge exist in the house?
I am the sky of consciousness alone, my luster colored by the quality of passion (rajas). (31)

These are the ministers of Nṛsiṃha. Now, by means of coloring with royal egoism, he shows the manner in which the ether of consciousness (cidākāśa) descends into the conceit of having the form of the body and so forth, beginning with the words "the ether of consciousness" (cidākāśa). || 31 ||
Without abandoning its own true nature, it perceives even that which is formless through the delusion of its own latent impressions— whether those impressions be real or unreal.
Svarūpa refers to one's own essential nature as self-luminous; virūpa refers to forms such as the ego, vital breath, body, and sense organs. || 32 ||

Just as a creature goes toward the interior [of a mirage] with the thought that it is water from a desert-thirst illusion, so too do those cross the ocean of existence by means of the very notion of their own stream [of consciousness]. 33.
The internal [mind] appears as if it undergoes a division from the nature of consciousness. Now, he states the means for crossing over that [division]: "crossing over," etc.
By "the intellect inclined toward the inner self" (svapravāhadhiyā), he means by the intellect directed inward. || 33 ||
Those who abide in nirvāṇa perceive that which is to be seen as established by the scripture;
they [reject] the various transformations of suffering, which are the doctrines of dry logic.

By means of the scripture characterized by the great sayings (*mahāvākya*) and so forth. To the question, "Why should the reliance on the great sayings not result in their determination through reasoning alone?", he says: "Not manifold... (verse 34).
They fall into the abyss [some manuscripts read *svabhram*], destroying their own gains like water;
they do so by following a path that leads according to scripture, yet is established only through their own experience. (35)
"One's own attainment" (svalābham) refers to the attainment of the supreme human goal characterized by the abiding in the ultimate self-nature.
With the intention that even direct experience (anubhūti) corroborates the path of the Upaniṣads and not that of the logicians, he says:
"by one's own experience" (svānubhūti). [This is] by means of that which proceeds through scripture, i.e., in accordance with the Śruti. || 35 ||

O noble one, there is no destruction for those who go to the supreme goal; [this is so] for one whose intellect thinks, "May this be mine, may that be mine," O Mahāmati. [In some places, "of the intellect" (*buddheḥ*) is read as "of the elders" (*vṛddhaiḥ*). 36.

The word "aṅga" is used as a form of address. By what, then, is the destruction of the human goal [brought about]? To this he says: "this," etc., referring to the person whose intellect is characterized by such [notions]. || 36 ||
Because of his own wretchedness and misfortune, not even ashes come to him;
for he who is noble-souled regards even the three worlds as a mere blade of grass.

The meaning is: "by means of the dejection brought about by misfortune. And for one who has lost the goal of human endeavor (puruṣārtha), even ashes do not remain; thus, the meaning is a state of total despair. Having thus stated that longing is useless, he says "he knows" to show that dispassion (vairāgya) brings about the cessation of all misfortunes. || 37 ||
All calamities abandon him, just as snakes cast off their worn-out skins,
whose inner being constantly vibrates with the wonder of pure goodness.

If even a fraction of knowledge belongs to one who is dispassionate, then for him the fear of calamity is far removed; on the contrary, all the gods always protect him, just as they protect their own source of sustenance and support, the universe—thus he says: "It flashes forth," etc. (38).
The lords of the world protect him as if he were an unbroken Brahma-egg;
even in the face of an endless calamity, one must never deviate from the proper course.
It is not stepped upon; thus, "akrama" refers to the wrong path. || 39 ||
Even Rāhu, though drinking the nectar in such a manner, died;
for he lacked contact with the true scriptures and the company of the virtuous, which are like the sun that grants fierce illumination.
What, then, is the path? He says: "The true scripture" (sacchāstra).
The true scripture consists of the Upaniṣads and their supporting texts (*upabṛṃhaṇa*), as well as the virtuous who are devoted to its meaning.
Contact with both of these, and constant attendance upon them—that alone is the merciless sun.

Because he brings about the complete destruction of saṃsāra, Śiva is the Supreme Self (Paramātman) who is fierce; [the mantra] bestows illumination upon him—that is, it is the cause for his direct realization—and it is an illuminator that cannot be overcome by darkness. || 40 ||
Those who take refuge [in this] do not fall again under the power of the blindness of delusion;
they inevitably attain mastery, and all calamities go to their destruction. 41.
Of the blindness characterized by delusion, which is darkness; now he praises the qualities such as detachment once more—“they are inevitable,” etc. (41).
The excellence achieved by one who has established fame through virtues becomes inexhaustible—those who have no satiety regarding virtues and whose passion is directed toward sacred learning. (42)

By that best of men, through qualities such as dispassion, tranquility, and self-control, fame was attained as being ranked foremost among the virtuous; yet there were those who felt dissatisfaction—that sense of insufficiency—regarding these aforementioned qualities, and who always possessed a longing for sacred learning, such as the repeated study and hearing of the scriptures. (42)
Those men who are devoted to truth are superior to other beings;
by the moonlight of their fame, the lakes of the hearts of living creatures are illuminated.

Those who are devoted to truth, truthful speech, and the Veda—they alone are men who have made their human birth meaningful; others, however, though they too are men, are like beasts because their birth is as useless as that of animals—the meaning is this:
for them, the hearts of living beings are not captivated by the moonlight of the moon characterized by fame.
The lake characterized by the heart has been described, illuminated by the blossoming of delightful white lotuses. || 43 ||
Hari surely resides in the very form of those oceans of milk;
everything that was to be enjoyed has been enjoyed, and all sights worth seeing have been seen.
These very oceans of milk are such that Hari-Viṣṇu, the Supreme Self, clearly resides within their form;

this is the meaning. Now, Śrī Vasiṣṭha—who desires the welfare of the world and is more trustworthy than even one's father or mother—[speaks] regarding all things experienced again and again throughout the beginningless cycle of transmigration, which result in a succession of misfortunes.

Showing that nothing new remains among sense objects or the various curiosities of the visible world, and praising steadfastness in the conduct prescribed by the scriptures on dispassion (*vairāgya*), he encourages [the listener] with the verse beginning "It has been enjoyed" (*bhuktam*): || 44 ||
What else [is needed] for the destruction of worldly existence than repeated greed for enjoyments?
[One should act] according to the sequence, according to the scriptures, according to established conduct, and according to the traditional order. (45)

Is it proper once again to be greedy for sense-objects for the sake of destruction—that is, for the ruin of one’s own self—in other existences, that is, in the succession of future births? The meaning is that it is not proper in any way. In the phrase *anyadbhave*, the vowel *du* is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*). "Respectively" (*yathākramam*) means according to their respective offices; "according to scripture" (*yathāśāstram*).

It is in accordance with the scriptures conducive to the purification of the mind and so forth for such qualified persons; therein too, it is according to practice, meaning in conformity with the tradition (saṃpradāya) initiated by successive teachers; and "according to the established state" means without overstepping the stability [of the practice] in each respective stage until its full maturation. || 45 ||
Remain steadfast; cast off the unreal web of internal enjoyments;
cultivate renown through virtues that reach unto the heavens. (46)
His reputation was established among the mouths of virtuous people through his own praise, spreading through those who travel the skies and are renowned as far as heaven itself.
For these two indeed protect from death; they are never objects of worldly enjoyment.
The beautiful women of the Siddhas sing of their fame, which is as white as the moon.
These two are intimacy and fame; the word *strīśeṣa* is Vedic, or it is neuter in the sense of a general category. || 47 ||
Through songs and the expanse of the sky, they live while others are dead;
having undertaken supreme human effort and exerting excellent energy. (48)
Regarding how fame can be achieved by those whose expansive reach is like the sky, pervading all places and times, he says: "Supreme" (paramam). || 48 ||
Who would not be a possessor of accomplishment while practicing without agitation according to the scriptures?
One who conducts oneself according to the scriptures should not harbor haste regarding accomplishments. (49)
The ellipsis is "practicing the means of accomplishment. || 49 ||
Success ripened over a long period of time becomes one that yields abundant fruit—
free from sorrow, fear, and exertion, devoid of pride, and without constraint.
"Without constraint" means being free from haste and insistence. || 50 ||
Let legal proceedings be conducted according to the scriptures; let them not perish, for the living soul has reached its end within the decaying wells of worldly existence. 51.
Now that you who were so deeply attached have been tamed by your senses, do not go from here again toward the lower, base state. 52.

The connection with the preceding verse is as follows: "O you who have many attachments, let your life not perish within the decayed blind wells characterized by worldly existence—having reached its end like death—due to the lack of restraint over the senses. (52)
Let this scripture be considered as a weapon for warding off calamities,
even in a battle where elephants are being hacked down by hundreds of rows of sharp arrows.

In such a battle where elephants and great tuskers were mangled and cut down by hundreds of rows of sharp, cold arrows— even in such a conflict— this scripture must necessarily be [studied], for it wards off immediate calamities such as fear and death, and reveals the Self which is free from old age and death, eternal, and characterized by unsurpassed bliss.
The meaning is: "Let it be investigated. || 53 ||
What is the use of the seal of life in the mud? Let the scent of worldly enjoyment be cast away. Noble ones, what is the purpose of mere wealth? Let the sacred scriptures be studied. (54)

What is this hope for life—a mere seal of living—within this saṃsāra, which is like the foul-smelling mud of a pond scorched by the heat of summer, where one dies and is revived again and again like a frog? That is to say, how utterly trivial it is. (In the reading *muhyasi*, the meaning is clear. Therefore, the "fragrance of enjoyment" refers to the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of enjoyment.
Let it be removed from your hearts. What is the use of that mere object, that trifling amount of wealth, that small fragment of material substance?
O noble ones, the meaning is: having renounced everything, let the scripture of liberation alone be contemplated. || 54 ||
"Let this be reflected upon as the truth: 'This is the reflection, this is the reflection,' by means of the intellect and through the prompting of another, just as cattle go [to water]. (55)

The reflection of the light of consciousness (cidābhāsa) mirrored in the mental modifications (vṛtti) that take on the forms of objects is the "original" (bimba) consciousness delimited by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa). However, for the reflection of the light of consciousness conditioned by the internal organ, the original is indeed the pure Brahman-consciousness itself.
The reflection and its limiting adjunct (upādhi) are unreal, whereas the original is real. In this regard, since the limiting adjunct of the internal organ is unreal—

The meaning is this: one should reflect that the difference between the consciousness of the reflected image as delimited by that [upādhi] and the Brahman-consciousness which is the original reflected image of the consciousness co-extensive with it is indeed false; thus, only the partless, true Brahman-consciousness, non-different from the inner self (pratyagātman), remains. Now, [an objection]: "But others..."

The followers of Sāṃkhya, Patañjali, Gautama, Kaṇāda, Buddha, the Arhats, and others do not accept the process of the reflection of what has been spoken; rather, describing it in various other ways, they urge people toward those very [views]. Is that urging to be accepted? No, he says—“by the intellect” (dhiyā). For just as this...

The sense is that for those who follow the authority of independent scriptural passages such as, "The self-luminous Vivasvat, though one, follows the waters divided in many ways," it is entirely improper to proceed under the impulsion of another, like a beast. || 55 ||
This deliberation, which bestows misfortune, is wretched and devoid of virtue;
let this dense, long, and great sleep be abandoned, and let one awaken.

Having thus conducted an investigation into the meaning of the scriptures, he now censures worldly concerns—such as life, wealth, cattle, and sons—as well as the investigations of other philosophical systems, in order to cause them to be abandoned: "Daurbhāgya... [He says: "In the end, it bestows misfortune; at its own time..."
Because it is caused by wretchedness, it is miserable; because its fruit is trivial, it is devoid of fruit;
because it consists solely of the entry into the thickest darkness, let this long and great sleep of wealth be abandoned. || 56 ||
Do not remain asleep like an old tortoise in a small pond;
resolve to rise up for the sake of pacifying old age and death.
The attainment of wealth leads to misfortune; a flood of enjoyments brings the disease of existence;
all prosperities are calamities; and victory everywhere consists in having no attachment.
In the first two sentence-meanings of the preceding and following halves [of the verse], the two [elements] are the primary objects to be enjoined;
in the second two sentence-meanings, it is the reverse.
For those engaged in worldly affairs, [it serves] for practical conduct through investigation according to the ways of the world;
and for the sake of fruitful action, it serves through deeds according to the conduct prescribed by the scriptures. (59)

The worldly way is the conduct of people; one should follow that [conduct] in a manner consistent with it and not in opposition to it. One should follow the scriptural rules and customary practices through such action for the sake of its fruit; thus, let the exertion for that result be accepted—this is the connection with the preceding context.

Of him whose conduct was beautiful through his proper behavior, whose life was secluded, and who was not greedy for the states of suffering that result from the pleasures of saṃsāra— [the reading *daśāsvagṛdhroḥ* appears to be more consistent with the commentary and is understood to be more correct;
otherwise...]
Otherwise, at the very root, there would result both the onset of misfortune and a lack of conformity with the commentary.
Longevity, fame, virtues, and prosperity all blossom together for the sake of good fruit, like the Mādhava creeper.
He summarizes the stated meaning in brief: "The conduct... and so forth. "Of one whose intellect is detached" means of one whose intellect possesses discernment (*viveka*).

"Of one who is not greedy" means of one who is free from desire. "They blossom" means they unfold, like *mādhava* creepers—creepers that have put forth new shoots in the springtime—for the sake of good fruit, that is, for the sake of the supreme fruit. 60.

Thus ends the thirty-second canto, titled "The Description of Right Conduct," within the *Dāmavyālakaṭopākhyāna* (The Narrative of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa), in the *Sthitiprakaraṇa* (The Section on Stability) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa*, a work of the Sage.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Description of Right Conduct," in the *Sthitiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The thirty-third canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Because of the fulfillment of all supreme excellence, everything is everywhere and at all times.
Therefore, since it is indeed possible, do not abandon your auspicious exertion.
Herein is described the majesty of auspicious exertion and the true scriptures;
and bondage arising from egoism, as well as liberation through its abandonment, is explained in detail. (1)
In order to show that for the practice of the virtuous exertion and so forth about to be described, the attainment of the fruit is inevitable when there is excellence in service,

he demonstrates a general principle with the words "sarve" (all): because there is a rule of certainty regarding the fruitfulness of all superior means (*sādhana-atiśaya*), this applies everywhere— in every means such as visible worldly service and so forth, as well as in the scriptural means for attaining liberation.
In all virtuous endeavors and the like, every result corresponding to its own nature certainly arises; there is never any fruitlessness.
Therefore, the meaning is that you too, seeking the fruit of liberation, should never abandon virtuous effort. || 1 ||
Having approached the Lord of the Lake, who bestows joy upon friends, kinsmen, and relatives, even death itself was utterly conquered.

In this regard, he briefly cites the legend of Nandīśvara and others with the verse beginning "mitra... to demonstrate that there is nothing whatsoever unattainable through auspicious effort prescribed by the scriptures. It is said that a sage named Śilāda, desiring an omniscient son, [propitiated] the Lord Rudra through ascetic penance.
He propitiated [the Lord]. Pleased by his long ascetic penance, that Blessed One, intending to grant him a boon, said:
"No one other than I is omniscient; therefore, I myself shall descend as a portion of my own self to become your son.
That son born from a portion of me shall enter the path of death at the age of fifty-six."

Having heard those words, Śilāda, unable to oppose them, sought refuge in him and consented, saying, "So be it. Then, he had an omniscient son named Nandin. Even as a child, having heard from his father about the binding of his own future death by the noose, he [sought] that very [deity] through ascetic penance.

He propitiated Rudra. Then, in his sixteenth year, while he was worshipping a linga on the bank of a lake, he was being bound with nooses by Death; thereupon, Śiva manifested right then and there, struck down Death with the tip of his left foot, severed the nooses, and made him his own attendant, free from old age and death—thus it is well known in the *Laiṅga Purāṇa*.
Even the gods, though endowed with supreme excellence, were crushed by the Dānavas—
who were rich in the wealth of the Dānavas— just as lotus-pools are trampled by elephants.
By the Dānavas, such as Bali and others; by the Dānavas who were soldiers; and by riches that were abundant, wealthy, and most excellent. || 3 ||
At the sacrifice of King Marutta, by the great seer Saṃvarta,
another creation was brought forth, including gods and asuras, like that of Brahmā himself.

Although it is well known in the Mahābhārata that at the sacrifice of Marutta, Indra— accompanied by the host of gods and desiring to create obstacles— was brought under control by Saṃvarta through his mere will, and consequently performed the duties of a sacrificial attendant along with the deities; nevertheless, in another Purāṇa, there is also an account of the commencement of the creation of gods and asuras.
In some places it is indeed heard; thus, there is no contradiction, because it belongs to the narrative of another eon (kalpa).
The status of a Brahmin, though difficult to attain, was acquired through asceticism by Viśvāmitra, who was endowed with great excellence and repeatedly applied himself to it.
For one who eats such a difficult-to-obtain water-sprinkling of flour as if it were an elixir of immortality,
even a person of ill fortune like Upamanyu obtained the Ocean of Milk.

The water for sprinkling flour— water mixed with flour— is likewise difficult to obtain because it must be acquired through such efforts as weeping and the like (the word *prāpya* is not read in some versions). Even by such an unfortunate and luckless Upamanyu, the Ocean of Milk was obtained through austerity and the grace of Śiva.
That he has attained [this state] is well known from the Mahābhārata and other sources. || 6 ||
Devouring the Trailokyamalla kings, as well as Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and the others, like blades of grass through the firmness of his supreme devotion, Kāla was himself measured out by Śveta.

"Trailokyamalla" means those renowned for their extreme strength; [the Lord] swallowed even such beings as Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and others like blades of grass. Thus, in the *Bhārgavākhyāna*, there is the speech of Kāla:
"The cycles of worldly existence have been experienced," and so forth. By Śveta—that is, by the sage named Śveta—Kāla, meaning Death, [was overcome].
"Kālita" means conquered; this is also well-known in the *Laiṅga*. || 7 ||
Having won over Yama through her affection and having established a conversation with him,
Sāvitrī brought back her husband Satyavān from the other world.

Having conquered and brought Yama under her control through the affection of the princess Sāvitrī by means of pleasing him with praises such as following her husband even unto death, she countered Yama’s statement— "Choose another boon than the life of Satyavat"— with her own request for the boon of the birth of a hundred sons from Satyavat.
"Saṃgamam" means a connection or union. The narrative of Sāvitrī is indeed well-known in the Mahābhārata as well. || 8 ||
There is no excellence in this world that does not have a manifest fruit;
one who possesses every excellence must investigate within himself what is destined to be.
"Excellence" (*atiśaya*) refers to an excellence consisting of scriptural and auspicious exertion. If that is so, since various kinds of auspicious exertions have been shown, one might ask:

"In which among them should someone like me excel? To this, he says: "One should be," and so forth. An eligible person (*adhikārī*) should not be like a fool, characterized by a meager fruit through the pursuit of insignificant results.
However, the meaning is that one should examine the gradations of results within the inner mind and, by attaining the result that surpasses all others, become preeminent above all. || 9 ||
Therefore, self-knowledge—which scrapes away the very root of all perceptions of states of pleasure and pain—must be cultivated with great intensity. (10)

The meaning is that since all excellence arises solely from the knowledge of the Self— because that [knowledge] cuts away at the very root of all states of delusion and false views such as pleasure, pain, birth, and death— one should apply oneself with the utmost effort toward that alone. || 10 ||
For one who has fallen into calamity and seeks its destruction, views such as "the seen" and so forth do not yield even a trace of untroubled happiness apart from suffering. (11)

In that regard, first, for the sake of destroying attachment to enjoyments and [wrong] views, one must seek out the perception of defects in their respective objects; thus he says, "for the destruction. The view of one who is in distress (*āpadgatārthinī*) is so called because it seeks out misfortune—such as hunger, thirst, desire, and the like—and favors it by means of the offering of sense-objects.

For the destruction of the perception of enjoyment, first the perceptions of the defects in objects—which are the opposites of that [perception]—must be sought out as things to be seen. The word *hi* (for/indeed) is intended to indicate the necessity of this. If it is objected that by seeking those [defects], one would immediately experience suffering because it results in the abandonment of sense objects, he says in response: "from suffering" (*duḥkhāt*).

Without the suffering of dispassion, practice, and so forth, can the unimpeded bliss of the abundance of consciousness (bhūmānanda) be attained? The meaning is that it certainly cannot be attained. However, if one reads the word as "kiṃcit" (something), then a change in intonation (kāku) must be understood. || 11 ||
Non-quiescence is the supreme Brahman, and quiescence is the supreme state;
even though this is so, nevertheless, know him first as Śaṅkara.

Now, even if one accepts the abandonment of suffering regarding all objects, the pacification of defects such as passion through dispassion (*vairāgya*) must necessarily be accomplished, provided that the Brahman to be attained were indeed the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) consisting solely of tranquility (*śama*). But it is not so; for tranquility itself— [The text continues: ...is also [not the ultimate goal]. Therefore, the cessation of the threefold suffering is not the supreme human goal. Rather, the supreme human goal is the attainment of the blissful Brahman, which is the very nature of the Self. Thus, the means for attaining that [Brahman] is the knowledge of the Self, which is established by the Upanishads. Therefore, the Upanishads are indeed the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for that [Brahman]. Consequently, the inquiry into Brahman must certainly be undertaken. This is the meaning. Now, the following doubt may arise: "If Brahman is the object to be known, then since it is the Self, it is already known; therefore, there is no need for an inquiry into it. To this, he says: "Indeed, it is true that Brahman is the Self, and thus it is known in its general form (*sāmānyena*). He states the reason: "For it is well known that the Self exists. He explains how it is known: "Insofar as it is the agent of the cognition 'I am,' it is known as the substrate of the notion of 'I' (*ahaṃpratyaya*). He states the reason why it is known in its general form: "Because it is not distinguished from the body, etc., in the cognition 'I am a man, I am a Brahmin, I am fair, I am dark, I am happy, I am miserable. He provides the reason for this: "For the notion of 'I' is seen to occur in relation to the body, etc. He anticipates an objection: "But if the Self is known in its general form, then what is the purpose of the inquiry? To this, he says: "However, its specific nature (*viśeṣarūpa*) is not known. He states the reason: "For it is not known whether the Self is merely of the nature of the body, etc., or whether it is something different from them. He states the reason why it is not known: "For the body, etc., are perceived as objects of the cognition 'I,' and they are also perceived as non-Self. He states the reason why they are perceived as objects of the cognition 'I': "For the cognition 'I' occurs in relation to the body, etc., which are perceived as 'this' (*idampratyaya*). He states the reason why they are perceived as non-Self: "And because they are subject to origination and destruction. He states the reason why the Self is not known in its specific nature: "Therefore, the desire to know its specific nature arises. He states the reason why that desire arises: "For the desire to know the specific nature of the Self arises from the perception of the distinction between the Self and the non-Self. He states the reason why that distinction is not perceived: "And that distinction is not perceived because of the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the nature of the non-Self upon the Self. He states the reason why that superimposition occurs: "And that superimposition occurs because of the beginningless mutual superimposition of the nature of the Seer and the Seen. He states the reason why that mutual superimposition is beginningless: "For it is beginningless, like the relationship between the seed and the sprout. He states the reason why it is like the relationship between the seed and the sprout: "For the superimposition of the nature of the non-Self upon the Self is based on the superimposition of the nature of the Self upon the non-Self. He states the reason why that is so: "For the superimposition of the nature of the non-Self upon the Self is seen in the case of the body, etc., which are perceived as 'this'. Anticipating the objection that— since the various modifications of the mind characterized by *sattva* are attributes of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and thus do not exist in the non-dual Brahman, and since anything other than Brahman, whose sole essence is bliss, is an object of perception and therefore cannot constitute the supreme human goal— he refutes it by partially conceding the point.

He demonstrates the necessity of tranquility (*śama*) with the words "aśama" (lack of tranquility). It is true that the untranquil conscious self (*cidātman*) alone is the Supreme Brahman; nevertheless, tranquility (*śama*), which consists in the cessation of the evils of transmigratory existence along with their root cause, is indeed the supreme state and the supreme human goal (*paramapuruṣārtha*). Although it might thus follow that both are equal, [the author proceeds as follows:]

Nevertheless, know him as Śaṅkara because he brings about (*karoti*) and manifests (*abhivyanakti*) this tranquility (*praśama*), which is the bliss of Brahman consisting of abundance (*bhūmānanda*). For the state of happiness that is not manifested cannot be the goal of human endeavor (*puruṣārtha*); thus, his utility is superior—this is the intended meaning. || 12 ||
Having abandoned pride and resorted to eternal tranquility, one should investigate the state of nobility with wisdom and practice the service of the virtuous. || 13 ||

Now he states the means for pacification—beginning with the words "abhimānam" (pride): having reflected upon and thoroughly cultivated one's own eternal *kaivalya* (isolation), which is unshakable, as well as one’s *āryatva* (nobility), which consists in possessing a birth and other qualities that are worthy of liberation. || 13 ||
Neither austerities, nor sacred fords, nor scriptures prevail in crossing the ocean of saṃsāra, without the service of the virtuous. (14)

With the intention that even austerities and the like, when practiced for the sake of purifying the mind, are useful for the attainment of knowledge only by way of serving the virtuous and not otherwise, he says: "Not... [and so on]. They "prevail," meaning they are capable of bringing about the arising of knowledge. || 14 ||
He whose greed, delusion, and anger diminish day by day, that virtuous person conducts himself in his respective duties according to the scriptures. (15)
Now he describes the characteristics of a virtuous person, beginning with the word "lobha" (greed). The phrase "by serving whom" is to be understood as the ellipsis. || 15 ||
Then, through association with those who know the Self,
there arises for that virtuous one the realization of the absolute non-existence of this visible world, just as it is perceived.

For one who is always devoted to serving the virtuous, there will inevitably at some point be association with those who know the Self, by which the attainment of knowledge occurs; thus he says: "Now," etc. (16).
But through the absolute non-existence of the visible, the Supreme alone remains;
by virtue of the absence of everything else, the individual soul quickly merges into that very state. (17)
He states that by means of this, even the supreme human goal (paramapuruṣārtha) is accomplished: "By seeing," etc. (verse 17).
The visible world has not arisen, nor did it ever exist, nor will it exist;
even in the present it does not exist at all, for only the Supreme, which is untouched by perception, exists.

He supports the statement that "only the Supreme remains" by establishing the absolute non-existence of the visible world, beginning with the words "And not... (na ca). "Unpierced" means that which has not been afflicted; that is to say, it is untormented. || 18 ||
Thus it has been demonstrated by a thousand arguments, and it is also seen;
it is experienced by everyone, and I shall now demonstrate it as well. (19)
Just as the impossibility of origination and so forth has been established through reasoning in the section on origination and will be established here as well, he says "thus": "In this way,
just as it is experienced by all the wise, so now for you this triple world is the sky of consciousness."
And "I shall show" is to be construed with what follows. || 19 ||
Likewise, this stainless and peaceful sky of consciousness of the three worlds—how and in what manner could there be "this reality" or "unreality" within it? (20)
He demonstrates that very point: "This is the reality. This sky of consciousness (*saṃvid-ambara*) is the reality (*tattva*) in its ultimate form.

Here, "unreality" (*atattva*) refers to *māyā*. How could the ether and so forth—which have that [māyā] as their primordial root cause—come into being? Is it from the existent (*sat*), or from the non-existent (*asat*), or from *māyā*? Since the first two are unchanging, they cannot produce [anything]; therefore, [the world] must arise from *māyā*.

Because the alternative of its non-arising due to falsity is the only one remaining; for how else could it be?
