The meaning is that it is impossible to produce even with a thousand chisels a void (ākāśa), which is by nature a cavity, within the consciousness-self (cidātman), which is flawless and immutably eternal. || 20 ||
The beautiful, flickering [consciousness] flashes forth within the motionless Self;
for by that very [consciousness], this world is understood to be that [Self] itself. (21)
If [the world] has not arisen at all, how then is it perceived as "the world" by everyone? To this he says: "Consciousness" (cid).

Consciousness, which is inherently unfluctuating, through the imagined fluctuation of Māyā reflected within it, experiences its own wonder and fashions, as it were, the state of the world; that very thing is the world, and it is perceived as such by that [consciousness] alone—this is the meaning. || 21 ||
The experience of the abundance of the three worlds is the orb of the rays of the sun of consciousness;
tell me, what distinction can there be between the rays and their source? Let that which is free from conceptual construction be described. (22)

Now, one might object: "Is this consciousness that cognizes the world not conceptual (*savikalpa*), whereas the consciousness of Brahman is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*)? Thus, for you who set out to deny the diversity of the world, a distinction would instead result within consciousness itself. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In the three worlds...
Whatever extensive experience exists throughout the three worlds, all of that is but the orb of rays of the sun of the consciousness of Brahman.
The meaning is that, in reality, there is no difference [between them], just as there is none between a mass of rays and the sun itself.

What distinction, indeed, can there be between one's own circle of rays and the possessor of those rays? The meaning is that if conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) are false, then even this abundant experience of the three worlds should be called non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*). || 22 ||
By its very nature, the opening and closing of this vision of consciousness— [if the reading is *cidvṛtteḥ*, then it would be more consistent with the commentary]—
are these two, the setting and the rising of the experience of the world-form. (23)

The opening (*unmeṣa*) of this conceptualized mental state (*savikalpā cidvṛtti*), which is the manifestation of the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*), is the arising of the experience of the world;
its closing (*nimeṣa*) is its cessation. This should be construed according to the sequence of meaning despite the inversion of the order in the text.
Alternatively, the opening of this non-conceptual mental state (*nirvikalpa-rūpā cidvṛtti*), which is the final direct realization (*caramasākṣātkāra*), is...

The setting of the experience of the world-form is its "closing of the eyes" (nimeṣa), while its non-manifestation is its "opening" (udaya); this should be understood according to the very sequence of the text. || 23 ||
The sense of "I" (ahamartha), when unrecognized, is a stain upon the sky of ultimate reality; yet the sense of "I," when fully recognized, becomes the very sky of the Supreme Self. || 24 ||

Therefore, with the intention that the very closing of the eyes (nimeṣa) of the inner self (pratīc) is the impurity of ignorance (avidyā), while its opening (unmeṣa)—characterized by purity—is liberation (mokṣa), he says: "The referent of 'I'... (verse 24).
When the sense of "I" is fully understood, the state of "I-ness" ceases entirely;
it merges with the Self of the consciousness-ether, just as water becomes one with water.

[Objection: Surely the ego (ahaṃkāra) is the object of the notion "I"; how could it, even when fully understood, be the Supreme Self, which is like the sky? To this he replies: "The object of 'I'... The meaning is that as long as it is not understood according to its true nature, it remains the ego; but once it is understood, it is no longer so. || 25 ||
The world of perception, beginning with the ego, does not exist at all in reality;
therefore, by means of inquiry into the "I," that [reality] alone necessarily remains. (26)

If it were sublated once fully understood, then what would remain? To this he says: "Necessarily indeed. That which remains—that is, what is left over—is the sky of consciousness (*cin-nabhas*). This occurs through the knowledge born from investigation preceded by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), investigating: "What could this referent of the word 'I' be? || 26 ||

Even among those of pure intellect, the notion of a ghost is suppressed when there is no ghost; how much more so for children whose inner faculties are still shrouded in darkness, who lack the capacity for discernment? (27)
The perception of a ghost in one who is not a ghost is sublated by those of pure intellect and mature understanding.

However, for those whose internal organs are clouded by darkness—those whose intellects have only slightly entered the path of inquiry—even when instructed a hundred times that "this is not a ghost," there remains only doubt through deliberation; it is not sublated. This is the meaning. || 27 ||
As long as the moonlight of consciousness remains obscured within by the thick clouds of egoism,
it cannot cause the night-lily of ultimate reality to blossom.
Just as the delusion of the ignorant obstructs awakening, so too does the conceit of the mature obstruct it; with this intention, he says: "The moonlight of consciousness" (v. 28).
When this notion of "I" has been wiped away, and one is by oneself without any self-interest, what room is there for the mere imagination of craving for hell, heaven, liberation, and the like? (29)

He says— “when wiped away”— that with the disappearance of the conceit of "I," there also disappears the thirst for hell, heaven, and liberation, which is caused by fear, passion, and the desire for liberation, and which has as its objects hatred and passion. || 29 ||
As long as the cloud of egoism expands within the heart,
so long does the cluster of blossoms of the *kuṭaja* tree of craving continue to bloom.
When consciousness is constantly overwhelmed by the cloud of egoism, only dullness persists; there is never any manifestation of light.
This ego-sense, which is non-existent and falsely imagined by itself, leads only to suffering and not to joy, like a yakṣa conjured by a child’s delusion. 32.
The deluded sense of "I," falsely imagined through ignorance, bestows an endless cycle of transmigratory existence, just as a wicked mind [perceives] a rope and other such things [as a snake]. 33.
Delusion means bewilderment; "in those of wicked minds" refers to those whose internal organs (hearts) are corrupted by pride. || 33 ||
"Whether it be 'this is I' or 'that is I,' from this vast delusion comes a darkness more profound than any other;
such a source of misfortune in saṃsāra has never existed before, nor will it ever exist again. (34)
In that regard, he states that even here, the delusion "this body is I" is the root cause of all misfortune: "This... (verse 34).
Whatever comes forth here in this world as pleasure or pain,
that is merely the unfolding of the expansion of the wheel of egoism.
The primary transformation is *pravikāra*, because all other transformations exist for its sake. (35)
The sprout of egoism, uprooted by the heart, has been transplanted; it destroys his cycle of existence—that existence which possesses a thousand branches and is difficult to sever. (36)

By him, with the very plow of a mind refined by investigation, the sprout of the wicked tree characterized by egoism was plowed; through that tilling, its roots were loosened, and having been uprooted and cast out from the field of the self,
the thousand-branched crop of knowledge— which destroys cyclic existence— was sown in its place.
When it has increased, it bears fruit; this is the ellipsis. || 36 ||
The sense of "I" is the sprout of those trees of birth that are imperishable in nature; the expansive thoughts of "this is mine" are their branches by the thousands. (37)

He states the harm that results from not cutting it off: "The sense of 'I'. This refers to those whose nature is indestructible—that is, whose essence cannot be severed without the axe of knowledge. || 37 ||
Objects such as latent impressions (vāsanā) appear like the bursting of a karatāpāta thunderbolt, yet they are like a beautiful row of waves whose sound is pleasant when investigated. 38.
And because they are to be destroyed by mere knowledge, they are utterly devoid of substance; thus he says: "Karaṭāpāta... etc.

They are called *karaṭāpātavisphoṭāḥ* because they burst apart—that is, they fall to pieces—even by the *āpāta*, the slight falling, of *karaṭas*, which are crows. It is that whose beautiful sound—the sound of bursting—is to be investigated and reflected upon.
It is like the fruit of a ripe śālmali tree and the like; the meaning is that they are as worthless and fragile as the beautiful, excellent rows of waves that break upon impact. || 38 ||
Through the conceit of "I," you appear as "you" and "I";
therefore, restrain yourself from driving the wheel of saṃsāra. (39)

In reality, however, the Self is indeed devoid of the sense of "I"; it is only due to the concealing notion of "I," which obstructs the Self, that it appears as if it were itself being carried around and wandering in the wheel of saṃsāra—this is the meaning. || 39 ||
As long as the darkness of the sense of "I" expands in the forest of worldly existence,
so long do these female demons of anxiety, intoxicated with madness, dance about.
Intoxicated by the nature of anxiety, the Piśācikās leap about and run wild. || 40 ||
For that lowest of men who is seized by the demon of egoism,
neither the scriptures nor the mantras lead to the attainment of his true nature.
The ellipsis is that they are capable of effecting the cessation of that non-existence of the demon of egoism. || 41 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
O Blessed One, by what means does the ego not increase?
O Brahman, tell that to me for the sake of pacifying the fear of saṃsāra. (42)
That means. || 42 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: When one is established in the stainless self, which has the form of the mirror of pure consciousness,
the ego does not increase through such constant contemplation.

Thus, through the continuous contemplation— that is, the constant recollection— of the nature of existence as described above, which is one's own essential self, when one remains established in the stainless state within one's own self that has the form of the mirror of pure consciousness, the ego-sense does not increase.
"This splendor of Indra’s net is false; what use have I for attachment or aversion?"—from such internal reflection, the ego-sense does not arise. (44)
Because of the internal reflection that there is no purpose whatsoever for affection and aversion apart from passion and hatred. || 44 ||
When one realizes for oneself, "I am not the self, nor do I possess the splendor of the visible world," through such peaceful conduct, egoism does not increase. (45)
That man in whose self there is no "I," no egoism, and no glories of the visible world—remaining thus, he is himself tranquil. (45)

For when the views of "rejecting" and "accepting" regarding what is called "the world" have ceased within me, and equanimity has become clear— [in some versions, it is read as "having been attained"]— the sense of "I-ness" no longer increases. (46)

When the two perceptions—the thought "I am within" and the thought "the world is without"—which serve as the basis for the worldly conventions of rejection and acceptance, have ceased, then equanimity, characterized by the absence of partiality, becomes serene. || 46 ||

When the views of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted regarding "I" and "the world" have ceased within, and equanimity has become clear— [in some versions, it is read as "has been attained"]— the sense of "I-ness" no longer increases. (47)

In the cognition of the threefold division—"I am the seer," "consciousness is the seeing," and "the world is the object seen"—even there, one must abandon the notion that "this is to be rejected as an enemy" or "this is to be accepted as a friend. When the duality of the seer has ceased, there is equanimity characterized by the realization of the Self in all things. || 47 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
O Lord, what is the form of egoism, and how is it abandoned?
Is it embodied or bodiless, and what occurs when it is relinquished? (48)

The embodied ego is that of the waking state; the disembodied [ego] is that of the dream and mental-creation states. Alternatively, the embodied [ego] is characterized by the sense of "I" pertaining solely to the physical body, while the disembodied [ego] is characterized by the sense of "I" conditioned by the intellect alone, as distinct from the body.
The meaning is that it has the characteristic of the entire sense of "I-ness. How, by what means, is it completely abandoned? || 48 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāghava, there are three kinds of egoism here in the three worlds;
two are excellent and the other is to be abandoned. Listen, for I shall tell you.
In order to abandon the non-scriptural egoism, two scriptural forms of egoism are prescribed:
that which has the subtle self as its object and that which has universal identity as its object;
for these two are not contrary to the vision of reality and are therefore appropriate for the present stage.
Its excellence lies in its being easy to abandon and in its serving as the gateway to the perception of the undivided Self;
whereas the other, consisting of the ego-sense limited to the body, is of the nature of misfortune and must therefore be abandoned—this is the meaning. || 49 ||
"I am this entire universe; I am the Supreme Self, the Infallible One;
there is nothing else"—this indeed is to be known as the supreme egoity (ahaṃkāra). 50.

"I am all this universe" refers to the effected Brahman (kārya-brahman); "I am the Supreme Self, the Infallible One" refers to the causal state (kāraṇa), or to the denoted meaning (vācyārtha) and the indicated meaning (lakṣyārtha) of the word *Tat*. The sense is that there is nothing else in the world that is not of the nature of the "I. || 50 ||
For one who is liberated while living, this [realization] leads to liberation and not to bondage;
"I am distinct from everything, as subtle as a hundredth part of the tip of a hair. (51)

Of one who is liberated while living (jīvanmukta) and established in the fourth or fifth stage; although this state also occurs for one who has merely reached the stage of practice (as indicated by the variant reading *tṛtīyā*), nevertheless, the sense is that it is "ripe" among those who are liberated while living. Of the tip of a hair—that is, the extremity of a strand of hair.

It is conceived as the hundredth part; that is to say, it is established as being without parts through the process of subtraction. This illustration refers either to the absence of grossness or to the ultimate limit of subtlety conditioned by the subtlety of the intellect, but not to the state of having an atomic dimension (*aṇu-parimāṇa*), because that is not taught in the Vedas and because it would contradict the scriptural statement, "And he is fit for infinity."
That which is to be awakened to. || 51 ||
This consciousness which is thus described is the auspicious second form of egoity;
it leads to liberation and not to bondage, for it belongs to one who is liberated while living. || 52 ||
For this very reason, he says: "of the one liberated while living" (jīvanmuktasya). The intended meaning is: "of one who abides in the sixth stage" (ṣaṣṭhabhūmikāsthasya). || 52 ||

That which is designated as "I-consciousness" (ahaṃkāra) is merely a conceptual construction and not real; this conviction that "I am this [body] consisting of hands, feet, and so forth" is what is meant. (53)

However, as for those who have ascended to the seventh stage, the notion that is postulated regarding them based on the impossibility of their being alive otherwise is not real; for there is no direct perception of such a postulator or knower. Therefore, because it is absolutely non-existent, it is called "egoism" (ahaṃkāra).
He states that because nothing remains but a mere name, it is merely the designation "I-conceit" (*ahaṃkāra-abhidhā*)—thus he says, "the designation 'I-conceit'.
He shows the third [type of identification] with the words "hands, feet, etc. This conviction that "this very body is I" is false pride (*mithyābhimāna*). || 53 ||
This third, the ego (ahaṃkāra), is merely worldly and trivial;
it is indeed to be shunned as a wicked soul, remembered as the supreme enemy—the very root of the continuity of saṃsāra. (54)
A living being struck by this powerful enemy, who inflicts various kinds of suffering, does not grow again. (55)
It does not grow, nor does it manifest with an undifferentiated nature. The mention of "grasping" (ādhi) is used as a primary illustration to indicate suffering in general. 55.
The world, its intellect rendered miserable by this long-entrenched and persistent false egoism, sinks only into calamities. (56)

From the very existence of his own nature, beginning from the long time of beginninglessness, his intellect has been made miserable by attachment; his mind is afflicted by the production of the onset of a multitude of evil latent impressions (*durvāsanā*). || 56 ||
A living being who possesses the conceit of being a refined person attains liberation through the Blessed One;
whereas one who possesses the conceit of worldly status, whose body is composed of defects, is defined by this [worldly] perspective.

By what means, then, is a person liberated from that? To this he says: "Possessing the remaining... Being one who possesses the two pure ego-senses previously mentioned, he casts away—meaning he completely cuts off—the defects such as attachment and so forth caused by the sense of "mine-ness. Thus, being one whose nature is free from defects (*doṣavapuḥ*), even with respect to this ego-sense of being the self of all (*sarvātmabhāvāhaṃkāra*), [he is liberated].

The meaning is that the Lord— whether Hiraṇyagarbha or Īśvara— having become firmly established as the "definer" (nirūpaṇa) by defining [the self] as being like the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) which identifies the body as the self— a state well-known in the world— becomes perfected through his own contemplation (bhāvanā) and attains liberation from the ego-identification with the body. || 57 ||
Having determined "I am not the body," its renunciation is the teaching of the great ones;
first, one must accept the two types of ego, including the worldly and the transcendental. (58)
He states that this very method is approved by other Brahman-realizers as well: "Not the body," and so forth.

Just as the final egoity consisting of the notion of the body as the self is most firmly established in worldly life, one first accepts the first two types of egoity; then, even while investigating "I am not the body" and reaching a firm conclusion, there is the abandonment of that [bodily] egoity.
The meaning is that it is the considered opinion even of the great ones of old that this must be done. || 58 ||
First, one should accept the two forms of ego that are non-worldly;
the third form of ego, which is worldly and brings suffering, must be abandoned. (59)
Having restated the very meaning already explained, he concludes with the words "Firstly" (prathamam). || 59 ||
"Indeed, through this wicked arrogance, Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa have reached such a state that it causes distress even in mere stories. (50)
In this regard, he states that even the aforementioned narrative serves as an illustration: "By this... (verse 60).
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahmin, having abandoned this worldly third state— the egoism from the mind— what state of being must a person attain to obtain his own welfare?

When the two questions had been resolved, Rāma, understanding that the third question— which by implication resulted in an inquiry regarding the fruit of the cessation of the third ego-sense— was now pending, asked about the various modes of existence for such a person:
Regarding the third [verse], "kiṃbhāva": what are the states (bhāva) or modes of existence (sthitiprakāra) belonging to him? He is "kiṃbhāva" (of what nature). || 61 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
This [mind], which bestows suffering, must first be abandoned;
for in whatever manner a man remains [free from it], in that same manner he attains the Supreme.

The meaning is that, in whatever manner one is able to abide— whether through the complete dissolution of the ego-sense (*sarvāhaṃbhāva*), through the pure ego-sense (*śuddhāhaṃbhāva*), through devotion to hearing [the scriptures] and serving the guru, or through the various distinctions of the seven stages— one attains the supreme state by virtue of obtaining the excellence of the manifestation of the bliss of one's own true nature (*svarūpasukha*).
O sinless one, if a person should remain contemplating these two previously mentioned views of the ego (ahaṃkāra), he attains that supreme state.
He elaborates on that very point with the words beginning "ahaṃkāra" and so forth; [these refer to] the first two mentioned previously. || 63 ||
Then, having also renounced those [objects] and being devoid of all egoism, he should remain established; thus he ascends to the exceedingly lofty state itself.
At all times and with every effort, worldly egoism must be abandoned for the sake of realizing supreme bliss, by means of this wisdom. (65)

According to the maxim that "wholesome advice should be spoken even a hundred times," he demonstrates the necessity of [this practice] by praising the virtues of abandoning the notion of the body as the self once again, beginning with the words "always" (sarvadā) and so forth. || 65 ||
The abandonment of attachment to the body, of disease, of demerit, and of evil egoism—this alone is the ultimate supreme good, this indeed is the highest state. (66)
The abandonment of that evil egoism which consists of attachment to the body, is demeritorious, and is of the nature of sin. || 66 ||
Having abandoned this gross worldly egoism born of attachment,
a man does not fall downward, whether he remains still or engages in worldly activity.
Meditation is the state of being; from that comes reflection. || 67 ||
For a person whose egoism has been completely stilled, O Great-minded One, enjoyments are like diseases;
they do not please him, just as poisonous tastes do not please one who is well-satiated.
Antidotes are those that counteract poisons; that is to say, they are things mixed with poison. || 68 ||
When enjoyments no longer provide satisfaction, the supreme good stands before a person;
for when darkness has faded, what else indeed can the mind turn toward? (69)

The ellipsis is that [the truth] becomes as if it were standing right before one due to the removal of obstacles. When the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*)—which, like darkness, is the cause of non-perception and misperception for the mind—is extinguished, what other obstacle could possibly arise to obstruct the attainment of the highest good? The meaning is: none at all. || 69 ||
O Raghava, by the mere abandonment of the pursuit of egoism and through human effort, one crosses the ocean of worldly existence.
Through human effort, fortitude, and exertion in hearing [the teachings] and so forth. || 70 ||
Thinking, "I am not [the body], nor does anything belong to me by way of it," and "everything is mine, and I am indeed all of it"—
thus one should establish this praiseworthy consciousness within the mind.
Having brought about this state, the great-souled one attains the supreme station.

First, having realized "I alone am everything," and then "everything is mine"; and then, having realized that the body and so forth are not the Self, nor is anything related to them mine; and thereby, through the destruction of all obstacles, having caused [the realization] to take firm root in the mind—thus, in the manner previously explained at length—one should worship the one worthy of praise and adoration.

Having led the pure self-consciousness and caused it to reach the state of the seven stages (bhūmikās) in succession, the great, undivided Self, being itself, attains—that is, reaches—the supreme state, which is disembodied liberation (videhakaivalya); this is the meaning. || 71 ||
Thus ends the thirty-third canto, titled "The Inquiry into Ego," in the *Dāmavyālakaṭa* episode of the *Sthitiprakaraṇa* within the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki. 33.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Investigation of Ego," in the Sthitiprakaraṇa of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The thirty-fourth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: In this regard, listen as I shall tell you what happened after Dāma and the others had departed.
Whatever occurred in the city of Śambara, which was as vast as a mountain.
Requested by the gods who had been severely wounded and cut down by Bhīma and Bhasa,
Hari slew Śambara there, and they were liberated from their exile.

In the absence of knowledge (*jñāna*) and discernment (*viveka*), even if the state of being free from latent impressions (*nirvāsanatva*) has been attained, it is destroyed by bad habits. However, when those two are firmly established, then—according to the direction stated in the Śruti: "Neither the gods nor [Mṛtyu] can master him for his lack of prosperity, for he becomes the Self of them"—it means that even the gods are not able to effect bondage again.
He begins to demonstrate the firm logic of Bhīma and Bhāsa with the words "In this," and so forth. In this matter—
referring to the subject described in the verse beginning with "Having abandoned the ego-sense due to the [transient] nature of things"— when all prosperity, which is like a mountain or Mount Meru,
has fallen from the sky and its stability is destroyed;
When Śambara’s army was destroyed, like a mass of clouds in autumn.
In the manner described; when it had fallen from the sky, having descended downward; its stability destroyed and its boundaries shattered. || 2 ||
Having spent several years with his army defeated by the gods,
that Dānava, intent on slaying the gods once again, reflected as follows.
That Dānava was Śambara. || 3 ||
But as for Dāma and the others, those demons who were created by me through my illusory power (māyā),
they conceived a false and wicked pride in battle out of their own foolishness.
He states the very manner of reflection with the words "Dāma and so forth," and so on. || 4 ||
Now I shall create other Dānavas born of my own illusory power (māyā);
I shall also make them knowers of the science of the inner self (adhyātma-śāstra) and possessed of discernment.
The syntactical connection is: "I shall make even those who know the inner science (adhyātmaśāstra) and possess discernment [into the state of being like beasts]. || 5 ||
Then, through the thorough knowledge of reality, being freed from false conceptions,
they will no longer fall into egoism and will conquer those gods.
Having reflected thus, the lord of the Daityas, by means of his intellect,
brought forth through his illusory power (māyā) such Dānavas as the ocean produces bubbles.
By means of the illusion characterized by ignorance, which has been brought under control through the power of the knowledge that attains the supreme boon. || 7 ||
The omniscient ones, who have realized what is to be known, are free from passion and devoid of sin;
they act solely according to what has been attained, being supreme beings with cultivated selves. (8)

They are omniscient because they know all cognitions through a single cognition; they possess such qualifiers as being free from passion precisely because they know the true nature of the object of knowledge.
Marked by the names Bhīma, Bhāsa, and Dṛḍha,
they possessed pure dispositions and viewed the entire world as if it were a blade of grass.
Having reached the world, those Daityas covered the sky,
roaring with weapons for lightning, like clouds in the rainy season.
"Bhuvana" means the upper world. In the alternative interpretation where "hetitaḍitaḥ" functions as a simile, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound containing the sense of "as if."
They fought equally even against the gods for many groups of years;
yet, by virtue of their discernment, they never succumbed to egoism at any time.
As long as the latent impression "this is mine" arises within them, so long will [the notions] "who is this? and "who am I? fail to reach untruth through inquiry. (12)
"O wise ones, who am I, this bodiless existence?"—from such inquiry arose their realization, and fear and other such emotions did not emerge. (13)

He says "asat" (unreal) to show that through the investigation that both that from which one should fear and that for whose sake one fears are false, fear and so forth do not arise. Both the body and the gods are unreal.
The singular form and the collective treatment [of the two] follow the rule: *napuṃsakamanapuṃsakenaikavaccāsyānyatarasyām* (Pāṇini 1.2.69). || 13 ||
"This [world] is without a physical body; it does not exist. Pure consciousness alone abides in the Self.
There is no such thing as 'I' nor any other. Having thus resolved, the Asuras departed. (14)
Then, by those who were free from ego, fearless of old age and death, accomplished in their goals, steadfast, and following the present course; || 15 ||

By those whose intellects are eternally unattached, who have destroyed all other [enemies] yet are themselves non-slayers, who are liberated from the web of latent impressions (vāsanā), and who, having accomplished their task, are non-doers. || 16 ||
Others were slain by those very same [beings], yet because they lacked the conceit of being slayers, they were not slayers. || 16 ||
"Thinking, 'This is the work of the Lord; this must be done,' they were intent upon their vow, free from passion, devoid of hatred, and always possessed of an even-minded vision. (17)

If one asks, "In that case, from where does their engagement in battle arise? he says: "By the glance of the Lord. This task is [undertaken] by the glance of the Lord Śambara; the meaning is that it is due to his command. Alternatively, because of the principle that whatever must be done for a master—whether good or bad—must necessarily be performed by those who have become his servants, they are intent on battle, and not otherwise.
The meaning is: "by means of the desire for a fruit. || 17 ||
That divine army was slain, devoured, seized, and scorched by Bhīma, Bhāsa, Dṛḍha, and the others, just as the beauty of one's own food is consumed by eaters.
"Consumed with speed" means having brought [the object] under control and enjoyed it through service and so forth. || 18 ||
Crushed by Bhīma and Bāṣpa, the army of the gods became shattered;
it fled with great speed like the Gaṅgā falling from the Himavat. || 19 ||
That army of the Asuras went for refuge to the God who reclines upon the Ocean of Milk, just as a row of clouds driven by the wind seeks a mountain for shelter.
The army of the gods is an anīkinī. || 20 ||
Hari comforted that terrified army of the gods, just as a lover consoles a solitary woman surrounded by serpents. || 21 ||
"She was forcibly surrounded by libertines acting as serpents for the sake of enjoyment"—this is also an epithet for her because she was frightened.
The "hero" (nāyaka) refers to the husband. || 21 ||
Then that celestial host dwelt in the cavern of the Milk Ocean for as long as the Blessed One did not rise up for the purpose of dispelling it.
In the hollow of the Ocean of Milk, on the White Island (Śvetadvīpa), for as long as the life-span of Śambara lasts; for the sake of that Śambara's despair, which is his death. || 22 ||
Then a terrible battle took place between Śauri and Śambara,
like the untimely dissolution of the world at the end of a kalpa, during which the great mountain ranges were cast aloft.
The battle was like the end of an aeon, even though it was not the appointed time, as the mountain ranges were tossed up into the air.
In that battle, the Daitya Śambara, along with his army and mounts, was subdued;
slain by Nārāyaṇa, he departed for the city of Viṣṇu.

He was pacified—that is to say, he died—and went to the city of Viṣṇu. "Whosoever among the Daityas were slain by the wielder of the discus, Janārdana, the Lord of the three worlds, they all went to the city of Viṣṇu, O King; for even the anger of the God is equal to a boon," according to the scriptures—this is the meaning. || 24 ||
But those [warriors], though firm as Bhīma and Bāṣpa, were brought to rest in that fierce battle by Viṣṇu alone, like lamps by the wind.
Quiescence is liberation while still embodied. || 25 ||
For when they have attained peace, being indeed devoid of mental impressions, their destination is not known, just as that of lamps which have been extinguished. (26)

He refutes the possibility of their traveling to another place—which might be suspected on the analogy of Śambara—with the words "For them... (te hi). For latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are indeed the cause of movement; as the scripture states: "Clinging to that, he goes with his karma; the subtle body (*liṅga*), whereon his mind is fixed. Since they are devoid of latent impressions, there is an absence of movement; thus, the meaning is that no movement is perceived. || 26 ||

Therefore, O Rāma, the mind bound by latent impressions is in bondage, while the mind free from latent impressions is liberated; through discernment, attain the state of being free from latent impressions.
Applying the story thus related to the present context, he concludes with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). "Bring it" (*āharasva*) means "fetch it";
that is to say, "you must certainly accomplish it. || 27 ||
Through the correct perception of the Truths, latent impressions dissolve;
and with the dissolution of latent impressions, the mind attains tranquility like a lamp [when its fuel is exhausted]. (28)
Regarding the means for its removal, he says: "By right vision" (*samyag-ālokana*).

This means by a direct realization produced through long-term reflection and meditative application, which has as its object the truth—such as reality (*satya*) and so forth—just like the direct perception of the true nature of a gem. "Ceto" refers to the mind (*manas*). "Śamam" means destruction. || 28 ||
In this world, there is not even the slightest truth; one should thoroughly cultivate the realization that no entity has real existence.
Therefore, "there is indeed no cultivation"—this is right vision. (29)

He now demonstrates the manner of right perception: "It is not real. The perfect, true being—the ultimate reality, the conscious Self (cidātman)—is that which perceives this visible world; therefore, not even the slightest part of it is real. Consequently, the contemplation of that visible world, as well as its perception, consists of forms qualified by the visible.
The meaning is that the very vision of the remaining pure self-luminous consciousness alone—realizing "it does not exist at all"—is right perception (*samyagīkṣaṇa*).
"This entire world is indeed the Self; who can imagine what, or where?
There is no such thing as 'imagination' (*bhāvanā*) at all. This is right perception. (30)

"Who should cultivate what?"—this is the negation of the triad [of subject, object, and action]. "Where?"—this is the negation of the locus. "Cultivation"—this is the negation of its mental impression (*saṃskāra*). || 30 ||
The two sounds known as *vāsanā* and *citta*, which are endowed with their respective meanings, dissolve there through the vision of truth; that is the supreme state.

The two terms "latent impression" (vāsanā) and "mind" (citta) are merely names for that [very same thing], derived from a conceptual differentiation of distinction, just like the expression "the head of Rāhu."
The mind, enveloped by latent impressions (vāsanā), attains its state here in this world; that very same mind, when liberated from them, is called "liberated. || 32 ||
It is liberated while living, because in the state of disembodied liberation (videhakaivalya) there is an absence of the mind. || 32 ||
That very mind, which has assumed the forms of various pots and cloths, must be quickly brought to stillness, like a phantom yakṣa that has arisen from delusion. (33)
A false yakṣa is like a child's phantom. || 33 ||
Just as the mind was transformed by the forms of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa,
so too, O Rāghava, your steadfastness is like the firm logic of Bhīma, Bhāsa, and Dṛḍha.

According to the maxim: "The knowledge that the body is the self is sublated by the knowledge that [the self] is not the body; he in whom this [knowledge] arises regarding the Self alone is liberated even against his will," their minds were transformed by the contemplation of Brahma as the Self, just as they had been transformed by the contemplation of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa as their own bodies.
The meaning is: "May your mountain-like [character] remain firm through the logic of Bhīma and Bhāsa. || 34 ||
O Rāghava, let not the analogy of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa be yours;
O Rāma, this was told to me long ago by my father, the lotus-born Brahmā.

In order to ensure that his own statement is received with respect, and demonstrating that he has obtained this through his father’s grace, he teaches the same point once more to stabilize it out of great affection, beginning with the words "dāma" and so forth. || 35 ||

O Rāghava, since I have spoken this to you, my most highly intelligent disciple, let there be for you no application of the analogy of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa; rather, O sinless one, may the analogy of Bhīma, Bhāsa, and Dṛḍha be yours forever.
This path of worldly existence, fraught with the dense distress of incessant pleasure and pain,
has been reached by you through the power of your worldly activity.
It perishes constantly, precisely through non-attachment. || 37 ||

Thus, when you— who conduct yourself according to the firm logic of Bhīma and Bhāsa— have attained (*yātau*), that is, reached, sovereignty (*aiśvaryam*) characterized by the ripening of the realization of reality through non-attachment toward all objects of worldly activity; |||

The path of existence—the succession of births within worldly states fraught with the peril of incessant pleasure and pain, which leads to torment through the experience of the threefold suffering—perishes only by the uprooting of its foundation, and not otherwise; this is the meaning.

Thus ends the thirty-fourth canto, titled "The Conclusion of the Narrative of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa," in the Section on Stability (Sthitiprakaraṇa) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis. 34.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Conclusion of the Narrative of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa," in the *Sthitiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The thirty-fifth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Victorious are those great heroes, the virtuous ones, by whom [the senses] have been completely conquered.
One's own mind, through the surging waves of the ocean of ignorance, is directed toward sense objects. || 1 ||
In this context, the means for the pacification of the mind is said to be the renunciation of the desire for enjoyments,
joined with the company of the virtuous, discrimination, self-knowledge, and established meditative absorption.

In this regard, with the intention that the restraint of the mind alone is the primary means while all others are for its sake, he introduces that very subject by praising it first with two verses beginning with "jayanti" (1).
For this saṃsāra, which bestows every affliction and suffering, there is only one remedy: the restraint of one's own mind. (2)
Listen to the essence of all knowledge, and having heard it, let it be firmly grasped:
bondage consists merely in the desire for enjoyment, and its renunciation is called liberation.
He says that among the means for restraining the mind, the renunciation of the desire for enjoyment is primary: "Listen! (verse 3).
What is the use of other compositions of treatises? Let this alone be done:
whatever is pleasant here, let all that be viewed as like poison or fire. (4)
And with the intention that, because one perceives the defects in those sense-objects, the means [to liberation] are loathsome, he says: "What need for others? (verse 4).
The enjoyments of sense objects are unstable; having reflected upon them again and again, one should abandon them from above, for when they are pursued [with detachment], they bring happiness.

In this regard, he says "The objects are treacherous," etc., to show that the sudden abandonment of sense-objects without reflection is indeed a source of suffering, whereas abandonment according to the sequence taught by the Guru and the scriptures, though bitter at first, results in great happiness in the end.
The phrase "the non-enjoyment of objects" implies their abandonment; the word "without reflection" is to be supplied as the remainder. Again and again...

The meaning is that, having investigated [the teachings] and abandoned the latent impressions of worldly enjoyment through the practice of endurance, these [teachings], when cultivated in due order, bring about happiness upon reaching their full maturity. || 5 ||
A mind enveloped by latent impressions (vāsanā) gives rise to expansive defects,
just as ground strewn with the seeds of thorns results in the proliferation of thorns.

If the latent impressions of enjoyment still exist, what is the loss? To this he says: "The faults," etc. It gives birth to, that is, repeatedly produces through the recollection of sense-objects, the faults such as passion and the like. [It is] that in which the seeds of thorny trees are scattered. (6)
The intellect, free from the web of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and devoid of mental proliferation, in which attachment and aversion are no longer seen, gradually attains supreme tranquility. (7)

Therefore, the meaning is that the intellect which is free from the web of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and for that very reason has not perceived passion and hatred, and for that very reason is devoid of the flow of restlessness, gradually attains tranquility. || 7 ||
It always gives birth to auspicious qualities, free from the ailments of the unwholesome,
just as the earth containing excellent seeds produces fruit-bearing sprouts at the proper time.
A pure mind, though unreal and non-existent, gives birth to such excellent qualities—

endowed with virtues like tranquility and self-restraint— as well as auspicious sprouts that yield the fruit of liberation, characterized by knowledge, meditative absorption, and rest; just as [a seed] produces rice and other crops.
The meaning is that it is ground possessing the most excellent seed. || 8 ||
Through the continuous cultivation of virtuous states, when the mind has become serene and the dense cloud of false knowledge has gradually subsided, (9)

Beginning with the practice of virtuous states such as compassion, courtesy, and forbearance, he explains in sequence the means for the mind’s repose, culminating in meditative absorption (*samādhi*), starting with the words "śubha" and so forth.
The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) of all these terms ending in the locative case denoting state (*bhāva-lakṣaṇa-saptamī*) is with the phrase: "the mind becomes free from dualities. (Verse 9)
When his benevolence increased like the moon in its bright fortnight, and when his merit spread forth like the solar radiance in the sky; (10)
In the moon, which is the boat. || 10 ||
When she had been released, as if Kīcaka had been consumed from within by his own arrogance,
she remained with her purpose fulfilled, like the moon in the springtime.
In *dhṛti*, [the qualities of] restraint of the senses and fortitude are present. Regarding *kīcaka* bamboo:

pearls are renowned in the world as being produced from elephants, clouds, boars, conchs, fish, oysters, and bamboo; yet among these eight varieties of pearls, those produced from oysters are the most abundant. Thus it is said regarding the eight types of pearls.

[The reading is *muktākareṣu*] because even bamboos are enumerated among gems in the *Ratnaśāstra*. "Abiding within the heart" means dwelling in the mind; [it refers to her] who has achieved her purpose through the attainment of self-bliss. || 11 ||
In this tree of the company of the virtuous, which bears fruit and possesses cool shade;
in this straight tree of meditative absorption, from which the nectar of bliss flows.
Association with the virtuous is meeting with the guru and others. || 12 ||
The mind becomes free from dualities, devoid of desire, and without affliction; its restlessness, misfortune, grief, delusion, fear, and disease are all stilled. (13)
Doubt regarding the meaning of the scriptures was exhausted, all curiosity had vanished,
the web of conceptual constructions was cast aside, and he was free from delusion and untainted by attachment.
Curiosity is the longing to see various objects of sense. || 14 ||
It is effortless, free from reproach, indifferent, and without excess;
it is one in whom sorrow and mist have been completely stilled, unattached, and devoid of knots.

[He avoids the charge of tautology—which might arise because "desire" (*kāma*) was mentioned in the thirteenth verse by the term "desireless" (*niṣkāma*), and here again "effortlessness" (*nirīha*) and "independence" (*nirapekṣatva*) are established—by distinguishing their meanings:

"The state of the seed" (*bījāvasthā*); "expectancy" (*apekṣā*) is the state of being oriented toward activity; "effort" (*īhā*) is the state of actual activity. Because of these distinctions, there is no repetition.
Tautology: "It becomes free from knots and attachments" is to be supplied everywhere. || 15 ||
Having destroyed the cage of his own wife along with its excessive greed and its offspring, which are the fierce sons of doubt, he accomplishes his own supreme spiritual goal.
He states what such a mind does at that time: "Doubt" (saṃdeha). What is the Self? Of what nature is it?

By what means is it to be attained—is it by ritual actions or by knowledge? And of what nature is that knowledge, and what are its means? Because various disputants describe it in diverse ways, there arise these many kinds of doubts.
One whose sons are fierce and wicked,

who is accompanied by various undertakings of desire through prominent branches, and who possesses a cage consisting of a wife characterized by craving and a coarse body— such a person [perceives] his own mind as the very nature of the Self.

The meaning is that the Lord, having destroyed [the ignorance] of His own inner self (pratyagātman), accomplishes for that which is related to it—the supreme human goal characterized by liberation while living (jīvanmukti). || 16 ||
Remembering his sovereignty over these things, he abandons the conceptual constructions that cause the body's nourishment, and casts off his own body like a blade of grass.
He explains by what sequence the mind destroys its own self, beginning with the words "The self":

first, the self abandons its own stoutness—that is, its nourishment—which is caused by the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) of enemy, friend, neutral, good, bad, and so forth. How? Within these very conceptual constructions.

The meaning is: having recollected—that is, reflected upon—his own sovereignty and capability not only in producing [the world] but also in its destruction; then he abandons his own body, his assumed form, like a blade of grass. For as long as the mind, perfumed by the ego-identification with the body, takes the form of the body, for that long...

The meaning is that [the mind] increases through thousands of conceptual constructions arising from excessive passion and aversion toward objects that are favorable or unfavorable to the body; however, when those [constructions] are exhausted, it too is exhausted. || 17 ||
The rise of the mind is its destruction; the destruction of the mind is the great awakening.
The mind of the wise man goes to destruction, while the mind of the ignorant man increases.

[Objection: But surely, since one's own destruction lacks the nature of prosperity and is, on the contrary, of the nature of misfortune, how can the mind be directed toward it? To this he says: "Of the mind" (manasaḥ). This is the intended meaning: the mind does not desire prosperity through its own independence; rather, [it desires it] because [prosperity] is its very self (ātmabhūta), and for that which is one's self...

The state of the mind is an evil; its destruction, however, is indeed an exaltation (*abhyudaya*), because it consists in the abandonment of all evils and because it leaves as a remainder the nature of unsurpassed bliss.
With the intention that the attainment of the true nature of the inner self (*pratyagātman*) is undoubtedly a great exaltation, he says:

Regarding the phrase "the destruction of the mind" (*manonāśa*): if that is so, then is it not merely the abandonment of the ego-identification with the body (*dehāhaṃkāra*) that must be accomplished; what is the use of the knowledge of the identity of Brahman and the Self (*brahmātmatājñāna*)? To this he replies: "of the knower" (*jñasya*). This refers to one who knows the oneness of Brahman and the Self. Regarding "of the ignorant" (*ajñasya*): the sense is that as long as the impurity consisting of ignorance (*ajñāna*) is not severed, the mind will surely sprout again. || 18 ||
The wheel of the world is mind alone; the circle of mountains is the mind.
The mind is the sky, the mind is the deity, the mind is the friend, and the mind is the enemy. (19)
He states what the loss would be for those things that are sprouting: "It is merely the mind. The sense is that the loss is simply the attainment of worldly misfortune. || 19 ||

That forgetfulness of the self-nature of the principle of consciousness (cittattva), which is turbid with conceptual construction, is called the "mind" (manas); it is this very thing that constitutes the latent impression (vāsanā) leading to worldly existence.
In that case, he states what the nature of that mind is, which must necessarily be eradicated: "consisting of conceptual constructions" (vikalpa), etc.
The meaning is that its very nature consists of the various latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of conceptual constructions, which are caused by the failure to reconnect with the Self (*ātman*). || 20 ||

The principle of consciousness (cittattva), which consists of pure awareness alone but is slightly turbid with conceptualization and is affected by the notions of "this" and "that," is called the individual soul (jīva).
Let it be that the mind is of such a nature; therefore, the individual soul (jīva) is bound by it. Who has said this? [The answer is: "By the object of thought" (cetya).
When the pure consciousness (cinmātra) is delimited—meaning partitioned—by the entry of the object of thought into the mind in the form of latent impressions (vāsanā), it abides therein;
thus it is "abiding" (tiṣṭhat). The suffix *śa* is used here in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) by way of grammatical transposition (*vyatyaya*).

The meaning is that Brahman itself—characterized by "stability," which is the fitness for designation, verbal expression, and conventional usage, yet slightly turbid with the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of conceptual construction—is called the *jīva*. || 21 ||

That which has fallen into the sphere of the object of thought, having acquired a fixed designation and reached a state of ignorance, is itself imagined by the internal mind to be even more devoid of essence. (22)
When that which has fallen into the object of thought— having long practiced there, its designation rooted in the conceit of selfhood—
attains such ignorance as forgetfulness of its own nature, and becomes the form of a living being (*jīva*), then,
through being deluded by thousands of conceptual constructions, it is deprived of its essential nature of bliss.
The meaning is that when there is an excess of extrusion, then, by way of its being the mind which is the instrument of the living soul, it is conceptualized as distinct.
The transmigrating person is not the self, nor is it the body, nor the blood;
everything such as the body and so forth is insentient, while the embodied one is like space, unstained.

Having thus demonstrated the living self (jīva) and its limiting adjuncts (upādhi), he shows the nature of the pure self as distinct from them with the words beginning "not" (na): the meaning is that the transmigrating person (saṃsāripuruṣa) does not, in reality, possess the nature of the individual soul (jīva). || 23 ||
When the body is cut into pieces, there is nothing else remaining apart from blood and such;
when the trunk of a plantain tree is split open, there is nothing else remaining apart from its leaves. (24)
He clarifies its very insentience with the words "in the body" (*śarīre*). "Cut" (*kṛtte*) means severed.
"From leaf" (*pallavāt*) means from the collection of bark that constitutes the nature of one leaf after another. || 24 ||
Know that the mind is the living soul, which has assumed the form of a human being;
by means of itself, it grasps its own self as it is imagined through its own conceptual constructions.
There, a person spreads out and constructs extensively from his own conceptual constructions a web for his own bondage, just like a silkworm. (26)
Having extended and manifested conceptual constructions and the latent impressions of those constructions, the person—the individual soul—[proceeds]. 26.
Having abandoned this wandering through bodies, one assumes corporeality again in another place and time, just as a sprout attains the state of a leaf. (27)
He states the reasoning for the absence of that body being the self with the words "this" (imam). "Being a body" (śarīratva) means the state of being another body.
Whatever kind of latent impression this mind possesses, such it becomes;
that mind which, having been born, sleeps, remains in the dream state during the night. (28)

He states the reasoning for the body being composed of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) with the verse beginning "yādṛg" (of whatever kind). The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: that very mind which has arisen remains, having become that [body], while sleeping in a dream. || 28 ||
A sour seed, sprinkled with sweet juice, becomes sweet;
a sweet seed, sprinkled with the paste of *prativiṣā*, becomes pungent. (29)

He provides an illustration regarding the capacity of an object to instill a latent impression (*vāsanā*): "Sour," etc. If a sour seed, such as that of the *tintiṇī* (tamarind) tree, is sprinkled with sweet juice, it becomes a tree through the sequence of sprouts and so forth;
even at the time of fruiting, having been permeated by sweetness, it produces sweet fruit. That very same seed [is the case] for every object.

The meaning is that it is well known in the world and in the treatises on gardening (*ārāmaśāstra*) that if a plant such as the *dhatura* or *karañja*—which act as substitutes for poison—is sprinkled with a paste or juice [of such substances], it will become bitter even at the time of fruiting. || 29 ||

Through a great and auspicious latent impression, the mind becomes great; a man who experiences a dream of Indra’s kingdom attains the state of Indra. (In some versions, the reading is *svapnabhāṅkuraḥ*.)
Due to a base latent impression, one perceives even a slight baseness of mind;
through the delusion of a demon, one sees demons in a dream at night.
"She sees what is delicate" is an example of ellipsis (apakarṣa). || 31 ||
In a lake of vast purity, turbidity finds no footing;
likewise, in a state of vast turbidity, clarity finds no footing. (32)
Fearing that even when purity has been attained, turbidity might recur due to the perception of duality upon rising from samādhi, he says:
"Like a lake... With the intention of showing that by this [attainment], even the possibility of remaining in a state of purity through slight discrimination and so forth is prevented, he says:
"In that very way... (32)
When there is extensive turbidity in the mind, a fruit of that same nature arises;
likewise, when there is extensive purity, a fruit of that same nature arises. || 33 ||
Even when exhausted, the noble person never abandons the sublime path, just as the moon, though waning,
never ceases its constant effort to fulfill the hope of filling itself.
Now, one might object: "In that case, if long-term meditative absorption (*samādhi*) is broken by a calamity such as a disruption of one's location, would not turbidity arise once again?

Anticipating this doubt, he says: "He abandons," and so forth. Even when "wasted"—meaning afflicted by poverty and the like—he does not abandon the "lofty peace," which is the state of mental clarity resulting from meditative absorption and similar practices. (34)

Here there is neither bondage nor liberation, nor is there non-bondage; [according to another reading, "there is no one to be bound and no binding," where in the first case, regarding "there is no state of being bound" (*na bandhatā*), the suffix *tva* is applied to the word *bandha*, meaning "the state of having bondage"]. There is no state of being bound.
This illusion is indeed arisen from falsehood, like a creeper of Indra’s net. || 35 ||

Alternatively, with the intention that because it is sublated by the awakening to reality (tattvabodha), there is no possibility of turbidity even amidst a thousand calamities, he says: "Not here" (neha). || 35 ||
It has the appearance of a city of the Gandharvas, arisen like a mirage;
it manifests as the delusion of two moons, yet is devoid of both duality and unity. (36)
He further specifies that very *māyā* with the words "gandharva... etc.; the phrase "devoid of duality and unity" connects with what follows. (36)
"All this is indeed the reality of Brahman"—this is the ultimate truth;
this world-process, being insubstantial and composed of unreality, shines forth [only as such]. (37)
What, then, is ultimate reality? He states it: "It is all. (37)
Arising from the false conviction, "I am not infinite; I am a miserable wretch," one is dissolved by the firm conviction, "I am infinite; I am the Lord. (38)
I am not infinite or unlimited; for that very reason, I am wretched and insignificant. || 38 ||
In one's own all-pervading and pure Self, the notion "this is I" is that very bondage in the world, fashioned by one's own mental constructs. (39)
This [Self] is of the measure of this body alone. || 39 ||
Devoid of the states of bondage and liberation, and free from duality and unity—this entire reality is the being of Brahman; such is the ultimate truth.
One who has attained purity through death, who is unattached to all views, and who has reached the state of mindlessness (amanastva) here, perceives Brahman; not otherwise.

One whose death—meaning one's own destruction—is imminent due to an extreme degree of purity, and who has consequently attained a state of mindlessness (*amanastva*), perceives Brahman here, in this very body of the qualified practitioner. || 41 ||
The mind, having attained purity through the waters of the auspicious continuum,
takes on the vision of Brahman, just as a white cloth takes on color.
The auspicious continuum is the accumulation of qualities produced by the practice of meditative concentration; it is characterized by the waters of those [qualities].
The "Brahmic vision" is the vision of Brahman everywhere. "Passion" is the color of a coloring substance. || 42 ||

"O sinless one, through the contemplation that 'all this indeed is my self,' when the power of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted has been exhausted, let bondage and liberation be relinquished. (43)
Let liberation also be released, since it too is dependent upon bondage. || 43 ||
For one whose mind has been purified by bodily discipline, scriptural learning, dispassion, and discernment, the world appears as a mere reflection, like the brilliance within a noble gem. (44)
If it is asked, "Could the bondage of the body and so forth not be real?", we say no;
for it is merely a modification of the mind, like a palace imagined in a dream, with this intention he says:
"of the pure one. At first, due to the conceit of being a qualified person possessing a qualified body, [one identifies] as the body... from that [arises the bondage].

Through the conceit of hearing true scripture, [the mind] becomes the nature of the scripture; through dispassion, it becomes the nature of dispassion; and thereafter, through self-awakening, it becomes the nature of awakening. Thus, for the pure mind alone—like a noble stone or a crystal—the world-process (*jagat-saṃsāra*) is merely a manifestation (*vidyuti*), meaning a diverse appearance. This is the meaning. || 44 ||
Know that the one-pointedness of the mind which arises from identifying with an object is a vision of unreal knowledge, perishing in an instant. (45)

With two verses beginning with "padārthena," he demonstrates—like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand—the attainment of bondage at the very moment of perceiving duality, and the attainment of immediate liberation at the very moment of perceiving the Self. || 45 ||
When the mind, having abandoned everything— both external and internal, as well as the entire range of the seen and the seeing— remains dissolved therein, then that supreme state has been attained.
This clear perception of the visible world is necessarily composed of unreality;
know that being composed of that [unreality] is the very nature of the mind, and nothing else. (47)
Being "consisting of that" means an abundance of the perception of the visible world. || 47 ||
Because it is perishable at its beginning and end, it is likewise unreal in the middle;
therefore, those whose minds are ignorant suffer even while [the treasure] is held in their own hands. (48)

To the question, "How can there be unreality for that which is seen through the act of seeing?", he says: "At the beginning and at the end. Because it is perishable, it is non-existent (*asat*). Thus, for one by whom the mind is known to be non-existent in this way, [the truth] is not difficult to seek out; the meaning is that it is as if already held in the hand, as if attained by the very palm. || 48 ||
Without the realization that "this world is indeed the Self," the splendor of the visible world bestows suffering; otherwise, however, it grants both enjoyment and liberation. (49)

Thus, without this state of being—that is, without awakening—the splendor of the visible world brings suffering. Otherwise, if such awakening exists, the enjoyment of sense objects does not lead to the seeds of suffering caused by the implantation of evil latent impressions (*durvāsanā*), as is the case with the enjoyments of the ignorant;
rather, it serves for the sake of the present moment. (49)

The notion that "the water is one thing and the wave another" is ignorance due to perceived multiplicity; whereas the realization that "this wave is indeed the water" is wisdom due to perceived unity. (50)
He states—“water” (verse 50)—that in this treatise, as in common worldly discourse, ignorance and knowledge are what are to be understood, not anything unprecedented.
That which consists of what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted—suffering and the illusion that it is real—is unreal;
through the knowledge of its non-existence, however, infinity alone remains. || 51 ||

From where is multiplicity to be abandoned, and from where is unity to be accepted? To this he says: "Suffering. Because that multiplicity which consists of things to be abandoned or accepted is unreal—that is, non-existent—for that reason suffering, consisting of birth, death, and so forth, arises and pursues one; therefore, it is to be abandoned. By the absence of that [multiplicity]...
Because through the knowledge of the reality of the Self, infinity—the undivided nature of the Self—remains;
therefore, that [Self] is to be accepted. This is the meaning. || 51 ||
And because it is fashioned by conceptual construction, the form of the mind consists of unreality;
tell me, O Rāghava, when that which is unreal perishes, what cause for grief can there be? (52)

Now, one might object: since the duality consisting of the beloved, the mind, the intellect, and so forth is real, and because they serve as instruments for the Self, there would surely be grief at their destruction, just like the loss of wealth and such; to this, he says: "saṃkalpa... (verse 52).
Just as a kinsman who lacks affection is perceived through a mind free from passion and hatred, so too do you perceive the reality of your own cage; behold! (53)

Furthermore, as long as passion and hatred exist, there will be sorrow due to the loss of the desired and the acquisition of the undesired; however, for one who has abandoned those two and perceives the cage of the three bodies with an impartial gaze, there is no possibility of sorrow.
With this intention, he says: "avatsalaḥ" (without affection). *Avatsala* means devoid of attachment. *Tattvam* refers to the nature of the elements, such as earth and the rest. || 53 ||
Just as one who is not affectionate toward a kinsman is not stained by that kinsman's joys and sorrows,
so too [one is not stained] by the collection of [the elements of] reality through thorough knowledge [of them] according to their true nature. (54)
From the cage of the two bodies, which consists of a mere accumulation of elements and is composed of a collection of principles (tattva). || 54 ||
That beginningless and auspicious knowledge which lies between the seer and the seen—
in that truth, the mind becomes tranquil, just as dust settles when the wind has ceased.

He describes the nature of that substratum in which the mind is dissolved with the word "that" (tat). It is auspicious (*śiva*), meaning its nature is eternal and unsurpassed bliss; it is the form of the seer (*dṛg-rūpa*) situated between the seer and the seen.
When the wind of the mind has become tranquil, the dust of the body subsides;
once again, the mist does not arise in the city of saṃsāra.

He states that even the gross body becomes non-existent upon the destruction of the mind: "When [it] has subsided," etc. Since the ignorance (avidyā), which—like mist—is an obscuring veil like mist over the Pratyagātman, the substratum of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra) which is like a city, does not function because it has been exhausted. || 56 ||

When the rainy season of latent impressions (vāsanā) has ended, when the state of stability has arrived for Rāma, when dullness has produced a trembling in the heart, and when the mud has reached desiccation; || 57 ||

He explains the very manner of that destruction by means of the verse beginning with "vāsanā" and so forth. In the word *kṣīṇe* (when [it] has perished), the neuter gender is used in a general sense according to the rule for the refinement of words (*padasaṃskāra*).

When the mind has attained—that is, reached—*rāma*, which is delight (*ramaṇa*) or sport (*vihāra*) established in its own nature (*svarūpasthiti*), the word "mind" (*manasi*) is to be supplied as the subject. In the reading *rāgam*, it refers to passion.

The meaning is "the coloring by that very nature. When the dullness—that is, the stupidity—by which a heart-tremor is produced, [or in the alternative case] when the mud in the form of coldness has reached a state of drying up. || 57 ||

When the pit of thirst has dried up, when the forest of the heart has become stilled and dull, when the clusters of the sense-faculties have withered, and when the thicket of false knowledge has been destroyed; (58)
When the thicket of passion and the like has withered; when the clusters of sense-faculties—characterized as groves of *kadamba* trees—have perished, their fruits having been exhausted. || 58 ||
The mist of delusion is dissipated like the night at dawn;
the dullness born of it vanishes somewhere, just as poison destroyed by a mantra.
On the mountain of the body, no petty streams of fear flow forth; nor do the fierce peacocks of volition, with their shimmering wings, spread their plumage.
Small streams and canals are characterized by fear; peacocks possess a collection of plumage. 60.
Moving within the sphere of the sky of consciousness, it attains supreme purity; the sun of the living soul (jīvāditya), exceedingly clear and of great exaltation, shines forth intensely. 61.
It is the object of perception, manifesting directly within the space characterized by the consciousness of one's own true nature. 61.
Freed from the heavy burden of delusion and having attained supreme solitude,
the great quarters of space shine intensely when cleansed at the proper time.

"Solitude" means being secluded, discerning, and distinct. "At the proper time" refers to the time of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and so forth, as well as the time of the rising of the sun and moon. "The quarters" are the great directions characterized by "desires"—that is, *āśā*—which are "washed," meaning untainted by the dust [of passion]. (62)
The stainless Mañjarī of Joy shines intensely, cooling the circle of the quarters like moonlight in the autumnal sky. (63)
Sympathetic joy is a mental state that rests upon the fruit of merit; it is characterized as the blossoming cluster of the sky of the mind. (63)
Through the manifestation of all perfections, which bestows supreme bliss,
the ground of discernment, when thoroughly purified, attains its full fruitfulness.

The Self is the "Illuminator of All Prosperity" (*sarvasaṃpatprakāśa*) because it manifests all prosperities—which are but fragments of the bliss of sense objects—within its own interior; this is by way of that characteristic result. Alternatively, in the case of the "crop-fruit" (*sasyaphala*) interpretation, it is to be construed as: "it manifests the future prosperity of all [beings], such as farmers and others. It is well-distinguished (*suviviktā*).
It has been thoroughly purified and divided by the demarcations of the field-terraces. || 64 ||
The interior of the world becomes exceedingly beautiful with supreme light, encompassing mountains and forests, and possesses a very clear and cool shade. (65)

The meaning is: that in which there is a shadow (*chāyā*), which is the manifestation of consciousness (*cid-ābhāsa*), cool—meaning free from the three kinds of heat—by means of the supreme light of self-luminosity as well as the light of the sun and moon; this refers to the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattva*). In the perspective of the autumn season, it is clear. 65.
It is expanded by those of excellent intelligence, made vast, and has the form of crystal.
It approaches the clear lake of the heart, which contains the lotus-bud free from dust.

It is expanded by the departure of limitations; it is broadened by the accumulation of the water born of seclusion. The lake is characterized by the heart-mind (*hṛn-manas*). It is that wherein the sheath of the heart-lotus has its quality of passion (*rajas*) departed.
In the case of the autumn season, this is clear. 66.
The restless bee of one's own egoism, soiled within the calyx of the heart-lotus, flies away somewhere beyond all hope of being seen again. (67)
He also states that it is free from passion (nīrajas) by means of its effects, beginning with the word "hṛt" [in verse 67].
He becomes free from all projection, all-pervading, and the leader of all;
devoid of latent tendencies, with a tranquil mind, he is the sovereign of the city of his own body.
He from whom all hesitation and contraction have departed; for this very reason, he is all-pervading.
Having attained the lamp of the self through investigation, the steady-minded one, as if completely free from mental fluctuations,
beholds the worldly states of existence as tasteless.
Free from the fever of worldly existence, he sports within the city of the body. || 69 ||

Having thus elaborated upon the fruits of the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanākṣaya*), he demonstrates the state of one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) by means of those very fruits, beginning with the verse "vicāraṇā": Disregarding his own faults, the wise man—being such as he is—observing the tasteless destinies, both pertaining to this world and the next, amidst deaths and births in the course of existence; *Note: The term *dhīraḥ* (wise) is glossed here as *dhīryasya tathāvidhaḥ* (one whose intellect is such).*

Having become one whose self-lamp is attained through inquiry, being liberated while living and free from fever, he sports—that is, shines brilliantly—in this city of affection, which is his own body-city. || 69 ||

Thus ends the thirty-fifth canto, titled "The Description of Tranquility," in the Section on Stability within the *Dehāpavarga* (Liberation from the Body) of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the ancient seers.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Tranquility," in the Section on Stability (*sthitiprakaraṇa*) within the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The thirty-sixth canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
"How is it that the universe exists in this manner within the conscious Self (cidātman), which transcends the universe?"
Tell me that, O Brahmin, for the further increase of my understanding.

For consciousness, which is inherently established and unattached, is said to abide everywhere; and by virtue of the abiding of consciousness, the abiding of all phenomena is not separate from it. || 1 ||

Now, desiring to know the nature of the world's maintenance, which is the primary subject of this section, Śrī Rāma asks with the words "yathā" (as): [this] being of such a kind as previously described. || 1 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Just as future waves exist in water in an unmanifest state, yet do not truly exist apart from the water itself, so too do creations exist within the nature of the mind. (2)

Desiring to resolve that the existence of the world is through the very being of Brahman alone and not separately, whereas the perception of the world’s existence as distinct from living beings is based on the failure to realize the nature of Brahman’s own existence,
Vasiṣṭha provides a corresponding illustration, beginning with the words "Just as... and so forth.
Because they are other than the Self which has the nature of reality, and because they are devoid of inherent existence, they do not abide. || 2 ||
Just as space, though all-pervading, is not perceived due to its subtlety, so too the partless nature of consciousness, though all-pervading, is not perceived. || 3 ||
If the persistence of everything depends solely upon the persistence of the Self, then why is the Self not perceived everywhere? To this he replies with the word "yathā" (just as).
The term "niraṃśaḥ" (partless) provides the logical justification for its subtlety. || 3 ||
Just as an appearance exists within a gem as if established or as if non-existent—
being neither real nor unreal— so too does this creation exist within the Self.

In the phrase "susthite nirāvaraṇasthite āsthite āvṛtasthite," *pratibhā* means a reflection. It refers to [the reflection] in a jewel, such as crystal and the like. Alternatively, it may be a qualifier of the reflection, meaning "as if well-established" or "as if situated. || 4 ||

Just as the sky is not touched by clouds that rest within it and have their own support, so too the supreme consciousness is not touched by creations that rest within it and have consciousness as their support. 5.

He provides an illustration for its state of non-attachment with the word "sva" (one's own): "Just as the fire situated within the ocean is reflected in its various receptacles due to the superimposition of mutual identity, O dear one, so indeed is consciousness perceived within the bodies, specifically within the *puryaṣṭakas*. (6)
If that is so, then [the light] would not be perceived in the body either, just as it is not perceived in a subtle jar or similar object; yet it *is* perceived there—what is the reason for this?

To this he says: "Established in water" (*jaladhiṣṭhitā*). The word "aṅga" is used as a term of address. Just as rays of light joined with water are not clearly perceived due to their being merged [with it], but are clearly perceived in the form of reflections; [so it is here].
The meaning is: likewise, in bodies consisting of the "eightfold city" (puryaṣṭaka). || 6 ||

Free from all volitional constructions and devoid of all conceptualizations, this very consciousness is the imperishable Self; it is designated by such terms as "the object of cognition" and so forth.
And because its state as a reflection consists in having name and form whose desires and volitions are dependent upon that [Supreme Self], it is not real;
thus he says, "All... Why, then, is there the designation "jīva" (individual soul) and so forth? To this he says, "That...
By the word "ādi" (and so forth), the inclusion of "ābhāsa" (reflection/appearance) is intended. || 7 ||
She is subtler than a hundredth part of space, possessing a form free from all parts,
and she perceives the single identity with the nature of the entire world, both with and without parts.

He says "ākāśa" (space), etc., based on the experience of the wise: when one reflects upon the subtlety and transparency of consciousness (*cit*), even space would appear a hundred times grosser and opaque. This is a dramatic representation of the experience of the wise, who possess the habit of perceiving that single identity wherein even the entire world-structure is without parts (*akala*) and partless (*niṣkala*).
In the reading *amalam*, the meaning is "free from the impurity of *māyā*. || 8 ||
Just as the vast diversity consisting of waves and so forth in the ocean of water does not exist apart from it, so too is the transformation of states [not distinct from consciousness].
For this very reason, he says in two verses beginning with "taraṅga" that the modifications of existence perceived there through delusion do not exist apart from it. || 9 ||
O Mother, this vast multiplicity consisting of "thou-ness" and "I-ness" exists within the ocean of consciousness;
apart from pure consciousness alone, it does not manifest at all.
It gathers the accumulated and the object of cognition; therefore, this [world] is situated within the Self.
But for the ignorant, there arises the conceptualization that "something else has come" or "something else exists. (11)

If you think that consciousness (*cit*) accumulates—that which is to be cognized (*cetya*)—by accumulating it, then consider this: consciousness accumulates only what is itself consciousness; there is no other object to be cognized. By such a thought, because it is impossible for consciousness to have an operation within its own self, the result is that this nature of consciousness remains only in itself and does not accumulate anything at all. This is the point. This very...

This is the vision of the ultimate truth (*paramārthadṛṣṭi*). The meaning is that for one who, while being ignorant, conceives "I am a knower," there arises the conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) that something other than consciousness has come into existence within the creations; or, the repetition "in each ignorant person" (*ajñe 'jñe*) is intended as an emphatic distributive sense.
