Among the ignorant, she is the womb containing the multitude of the inherently fierce cycle of existence;
among the wise, she is of the nature of pure light, the singular reality of all that exists.
Having further divided that very consciousness (citta) through the conceptualization of the knower and the ignorant, he says: "Among the ignorant," etc. (verse 12).
By virtue of being experienced, she is eternally the illuminator of the sun and other luminaries;
she is the one who tastes all beings, and she is the bringer of existence for those who enjoy worldly life.

He explains that this very consciousness (cit) is the cause for the manifestation of the world, the experience of enjoyment, and the production [of beings]—this he states with the word "anubhūti" (experience). It is the "taster" (svādinī), being the instrumental cause for the tasting of objects; and it is the "future one" (bhāvinī), being the instrumental cause for living beings who enjoy worldly existence at the beginning of birth and so forth, according to the Vedic scripture: "Verily, from bliss alone these beings are born. || 13 ||
It neither sets nor rises; it neither arises nor remains;
it neither comes nor goes; it is neither here nor not here—such is consciousness (cit).
He states that even though it serves as the cause for birth and so forth for the ignorant, from the perspective of the Knower, it remains eternally unchanging and of a single undivided nature:
"It does not set," etc. (14).
This very consciousness, whose nature is stainless, abiding by itself within itself,
O Rāghava, thus expands through the phenomenal world known as the universe.
It yawns and it revolves. || 15 ||
Just as light flashes forth through masses of light, and water through floods of water,
so does consciousness manifest through the vibrations of the delusions of creation.
With the intention that even the transformation of consciousness is, from the perspective of ultimate reality, nothing but consciousness itself, he provides an illustration, saying:
"By masses of light" (tejaḥpuñjaiḥ). || 16 ||
By its own nature, it is named Consciousness (citi), all-pervading, arisen as the Self, luminous yet non-luminous, partless yet bearing parts. || 17 ||

To show that even for that which is inherently pure, its very manifestation through the delusions of creation caused by ignorance constitutes its agency in creation—and nothing else—he states two forms relevant to that [agency]: "That" (tat), etc. By nature, it is called Consciousness (cit); conventionally, it is all-pervading; and from the perspective of ultimate reality, it is Light (prakāśa). [The thought] "I do not know" [arises].
Because it is not manifest through conventional usage; likewise in what follows as well. || 17 ||
Abandoning the infinite state through the expansion of its own mental constructs,
it gradually proceeds toward the state of pure consciousness by means of the sense of "I am."

Through its own mental construction within ignorance, by means of the manifestation of its own reflection—which has that [ignorance] as its characteristic—due to its expansive effort and its artificial guise, it abandons, as it were, the infinite state whose nature is undivided; thus, by failing to reconnect with it, it reaches the state of the ignorant known as "living-ness" (jīvatā). 18.
When this diversity has taken root within this cycle of existence from the outset, one comes to abide in the state of grasping at existence and non-existence, and of acceptance and rejection. (19)

"Existence and non-existence" refers to "this exists" and "this does not exist. "Grasping and relinquishing" refers to the acceptance of the desirable and the rejection of the undesirable, such as "this is to be grasped" and "this is to be abandoned. Their "place" or "locus" is the identification of the body with the self. (19)
Through hundreds of vibrations of the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka), it both acts and does not act;
like a cluster of sprouts within the hollow of the earth's womb, it attains its upward growth.

It does not create the world as something to be experienced through hundreds of fluctuations of the *puryaṣṭaka* (the subtle body) upon which the nature of the Self has been superimposed, nor does it not create it; rather, in reality, it unfolds the manifestation of the instruments of action in the form of various objects, beginning with the words "height" (*utsedham*). "Height" (*utsedham*) refers to elevation through accumulation. || 20 ||
The ether (vyoman) assumes the quality of vacuity, which is not in conflict with any form;
the wind possesses the single property of motion; and water exists in the form of taste.

Regarding the growth of the earth toward the nature of the sprout, he describes the performance of actions favorable to that process through the existence of other elements, beginning with the verse "vyoma" (the ether).
If the ether (*vyoma*) did not provide the cavity (*sauṣirya*), the sprout, lacking space, would not emerge.
Likewise, he says "spanda" (vibration), meaning that the wind (*vāyu*), whose nature is vibration, draws [the sprout] upward so that the sprout emerges. Thus...
With the intention that water moistens the sprout by its own essence, he says: "By essence," etc. (21).
The earth is firm, the splendor is manifest, and the worlds are established;
time abides through its creative reckoning in both prohibition and permission.
With the intention that the earth favors the sprout by granting it firmness, he says: "firm" (*dṛḍha*).

With the intention that fire manifests [the object] by granting it form, he says: "manifest" (*prakaṭa*). Likewise, with the intention that all worlds are favoring agents through the non-obstruction of the stability of their respective effects, he says—

And he says that [the Lord] is a benefactor by permitting the emergence of the barley sprout—[this is expressed in the verse] beginning with "pratibandha" (obstruction)—by means of *kalanā*, that is, by way of transformation (*pariṇāma*). || 22 ||
In flowers, fragrance gradually arises from the accumulated filaments;
on the ground, the sap rising from the hollow of a clod of earth attains the state of a tree-stump.

He says that consciousness (cit), having attained the state of prior merit and so forth, evolves in the form of fragrance and the like—this is expressed in the verse beginning with "In flowers" (puṣpeṣu).
Consciousness, having attained the state of sap within clay, reaches the condition of a trunk through the accumulation of trees, and the state of the wood at their roots. || 23 ||
Remaining at their base, these fragile traces of sap bring forth fruit;
these lines take on the form of rows of young shoots.

Having attained the state of sap residing in the root, it reaches the state of fruit. Those very saps, having entered the rows of sprouts, become lines and veins, and proceed to form the arrangement of leaves and other parts. || 24 ||
He bestows freshness through his thunderbolt and bow;
whatever favor he grants, whether by means of his form or his forest, is preceded by the production of ever-newness and occurs without ceasing. (25)
The ellipsis is to be supplied as "equal to Śakra’s bow, the rainbow. And by bringing about the "navatām"—that is, the newness—of the tree, he bestows his grace. || 25 ||
Heaps of flowers and tender shoots attend upon the spring; the riches of divine conflagration arrive as the rite of summer.
He elaborates upon her capacity to favor all effects even through the form of the seasons, beginning with the verse "Vasantam" (Spring):
the manifestations of burning from the divine solar radiance are its powers of heat. || 26 ||
The dark masses of clouds long for the rainy season, and all the heaps of fruit hasten toward autumn. (27)
In the fields, abundant heaps of grain and other fruits have come to full maturity. || 27 ||
In the winter, the ten directions become radiant with snow;
in the cold season, the chilly winds turn the water into the state of ice.
Time does not abandon its own boundary consisting of these ages;
creations pass away with the playful motion of the surging waves of a river.
And he states that she maintains the boundaries of creation and so forth through her nature as time, consisting of years, yugas, and so on, with the words "she does not abandon" (na jahāti). || 29 ||
Necessity attains stability, acting with the skill of steadfastness;
the wise, possessing the nature of supporting the earth, remain until the final dissolution.
He states that she establishes the boundaries of the world even in the form of *niyati* (destiny) and so forth, saying: "Destiny.

He demonstrates her capacity for stability and skillfulness by citing examples such as the earth: "She stands," meaning she possesses the quality of supporting all things and has the nature of being the foundation for all people. (30)
In this world-system, there are fourteen kinds of beings, possessing various modes of conduct and pastimes, and various forms of manifestation. (31)
Because they inhabit the fourteen worlds, living beings consist of fourteen kinds of elements. || 31 ||
Again and again they dissolve, and again and again they are born;
like bubbles without water, they pass away in a continuous succession.
The continuous succession of beings—the stream of the cycle of birth and death—passes away or ceases through the knowledge of reality; this is the implied meaning. || 32 ||
It comes, it goes, it remains, it wanders in play, it acquires its own purposes, and it runs through births and destructions; thus,
with its desires fixed upon the cultivation of [false] conceptions, it acts like a madman.
The wretched multitude of people is deluded and rendered helpless by destiny.

Expanding upon the very meaning already stated, he concludes with the words "it comes": "The wretched mass of people, characterized by millions of cosmic eggs and the living beings contained within them, is pitiable; thus, according to the prescribed contemplation—that is, according to the passion of their prior volitions and latent impressions—their desires are instilled and their cravings arise."
Being ignorant of any discourse concerning the investigation of its own true nature, the deluded one comes to this world from birth after birth like a madman,

goes to the next world, and remains everywhere through births as stationary beings and the like; out of a playful curiosity for experience, it acquires its own self-interests characterized by wealth, merit, and other means for worldly and otherworldly enjoyments that are exceedingly abundant.
It runs through the cycle of existence by means of births and deaths; the meaning is that it wanders in this manner. || 33 ||

Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Nature of the Sun of Consciousness," in the Section on Stability within the Means to Liberation of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Sages.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Nature of the Sun of Consciousness," in the section on Stability within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The thirty-seventh canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus, the cycles of worldly existence are on all sides of such extremely stable form.
By their very nature, all things come forth from and return again to Brahman. || 1 ||
This state of non-selfhood regarding the self is caused by ignorance, desire, and action;
from awakening, from the absence of desire, and from the state of actionlessness, there follows abiding in one's true nature.

He restates what was previously said in order to declare that the persistence of the world is nothing other than the persistence of the nature of consciousness, because consciousness itself exists in the form of the world: "In this way" (ittham). || 1 ||
All this has arisen from itself and has become the cause for one another;
perishing through mutual interaction, it dissolves back into itself alone.
This world has become mutually causal; it is born from its own foundational consciousness (svādhiṣṭhāna-caitanya) itself. The same applies hereafter as well. || 2 ||
Just as there is movement within the depths of a bottomless body of water even though it is inherently motionless,
so too is this world— both unreal and real— perceived as consciousness alone.
The meaning is that just as the movement of water within a bottomless expanse of water is actually non-movement because there is no region of space not pervaded by water, so it is here;
just as rivers appear in the formless sky due to the heat [of the sun],
even so do these perceptions of creation appear within the reality of the mind (cittattva).
Rivers are but mirages.
Just as the self, under the influence of intoxication, appears as something other than itself,
even so the element of consciousness, due to its nature as consciousness, remains that very same thing yet appears as if it were not.

That very self, though not actually reeling like others, appears as if it were reeling; it is the element of consciousness, the essence of consciousness, yet it is non-existent (asaḥ) as if it were insentient (acid). || 5 ||

And this [world] is neither existent nor non-existent, because consciousness remains as it is whether that [world] exists or does not exist; nor is it something other than consciousness, just as the nature of gold is not distinct from the bracelets and other ornaments made of it.
In order to stabilize the meaning already stated, he demonstrates the indeterminable nature (*anirvacanīyatva*) of the world with the words "na ca" (and not).

With the intention that its non-existence is difficult to assert because it assumes the form of existence, and its existence is difficult to assert because it is sublated, he says: "by its being both situated therein and not situated therein. || 6 ||
O Raghava, that by which you perceive sound, taste, form, and smell—this is the Self, the Supreme Brahman, which exists pervading everything. (7)

One might object: "Is it not heard in scripture that the world is an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*) of Brahman, and not perceived [as such] through direct experience? Anticipating this doubt, the text shows that this very [perceiver] is Brahman, by means of the verse beginning with *yena*: "By which one perceives form, taste, smell, sounds, touches, and sexual pleasures—by that very [means]; what remains here [to be known]? "This indeed is That," so says the *Kāṭhaka-śruti*.
The meaning is that this is because Brahman alone is designated as the inner self (pratyagātman). || 7 ||

Because of the non-duality of the stainless Self, which is omnipresent and transcends all distinctions of oneness and multiplicity, there exists no second conceptualization whatsoever; it is never otherwise.
Now, one might object: "Since the individual selves (*pratīcām*) are manifold and Brahman is one, how can there be identity?
Anticipating this doubt, he says—with the intention that this fault does not apply because both multiplicity and unity are illusory:
"O Rāma, other than the contemplation [of the Self], there is neither existence nor non-existence of things, whether auspicious or inauspicious. (8)
Creations are conceptualized either in what is not the self, or indeed in the self.

Since the existence, non-existence, auspiciousness, inauspiciousness, and creations of other entities are conceptualized solely through the power of mental cultivation and latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and since these— whether viewed from the perspective of illusion (*māyā*) as residing only within the illusory non-self, or from the perspective of ultimate reality (*tattva*) as being nothing but the Self— exist only in the Self, [the Self alone is real]. || 9 ||
For desire arises only when an object distinct from the self is established;
where nothing whatsoever exists apart from one's own self, what could the self possibly long for, what could it remember, toward what could it run, or what could it approach? (10)

Alternatively, he establishes through prose—beginning with "yasmāt"—the second alternative mentioned in the verse regarding the phrase "in the Self" (*ātmani*), by means of both reasoning and purpose: when the position is that the creation, which is of the nature of the Self, abides in the Self alone, then it follows as a result that there is no creation other than the Self. For creation is preceded by will.
This is based on such scriptural passages as, "He desired: 'May I be many, may I procreate,'" and so forth. For the desire [of the Self] cannot be established by the Self alone;
nor is there anything else well-established apart from the Self that the Self could desire and then proceed to create.
The intention is that one who does not first engage in activity is incapable of creating. Or rather, what is the point of running about?
What fruit shall he obtain? || 10 ||

Therefore, conceptual constructions such as "this is desired" or "this is undesired" do not touch the Self. Consequently, in the state of desirelessness, the Self does nothing at all, because of the identity of the agent, the instrument, and the object; nor does it abide anywhere, because of the identity of the support and the supported. And for the desireless Self—
Freedom from action is intended [by this], because of the absence of a second conceptualization. || 11 ||

[Objection: "Let the attainment of *naiṣkarmya* (freedom from action) be its fruit. To this, he says: "And not... (*na ca*). [The term *niriccha* appears in the root text and the commentary; in some places it is read as *aniccha*, meaning "without desire"].
With the intention that if there were no desire for the performance of action, the fruit of *naiṣkarmya* might exist, but such [desire] does not exist, he says: "Of the second... (*dvitīyāyāḥ*).
"O Rāma, you do not know this other state, which is the established order of Brahman;
being liberated from all dualities, become an agent free from the fever of worldly distress. (12)

The other—that is, any conception such as "fruitfulness" and so forth, distinct from the manner already described—is not non-existent at all; for this is indeed the state of being established in Brahman (*brahmasaṃsthiti*). If you recognize that other [state] here, then, though liberated from all dualities and free from feverish distress, become an agent; I do not forbid it—this is the sense. || 12 ||
Furthermore, O Rāghava,
having repeatedly performed this manifold deed with such vigor, tell me what is it that ought to be attained by you through the creation of living beings?
Or rather, let your conviction rest upon the fact of non-agency; as one who possesses the scriptures, remain established in yourself, pure and still like a windless ocean. 13.

Even in the state of ignorance, regarding the agency in assuming a material body, it is the elements themselves that, having produced other elements, obtain material results; it need hardly be said, then, that such agency is impossible for the Self, which is unattached and indifferent. With this intention, he suggests that no reliance should be placed on the notion of action and its fruit in that [state of awakening].

He introduces a verse to support the meaning stated in prose with the words "And furthermore" (*anyacca*). The verse is to be understood as beginning from the second occurrence of the word *punaḥ*. O Rāghava, by you, through the agency of forceful exertion (*tarasaḥ*)—that is, through the persistent attachment to being an agent (*kartṛtvābhiniveśena*)—having done it again and again, [the world] was brought into existence.

The meaning is this: what other fruit could be obtained from the nourishment of the body and such, which consists of objects of sense, that would be a fitting fruit for you, whose self is eternal and unsurpassed bliss? Therefore, abandoning the obsession with being the agent of all, let your steadfastness rest in non-agency alone, which is appropriate to your own true nature.
The word "vā" (or) is used in this sense. To establish that point, he qualifies [the subject] with a reason: "possessing scripture" (*āgamavataḥ*).

This means one who possesses self-awakening through the words of the Vedas and the guru. By the word "api" (also), the possession of the primary qualification, though not explicitly mentioned, is included.
Therefore, the meaning is: "become clear and established in yourself. || 13 ||
Thinking thus: "Even by traveling a very great distance with diligent speed, that which is here fully complete cannot be attained," do not pursue the multitude of objects with your intellect.
But you yourself are not the conscious self in the ultimate sense.

He summarizes the meaning that was explained at length with the verse beginning "Having gone": *gatvā* etc. Having reflected with your intellect and reached the firm conclusion that the means for attaining that state of fullness—which consists in the attainment of unlimited bliss and the fulfillment of all desires—is not found even by traveling to the farthest reaches of the quarters and wandering about with extreme effort, you [should act accordingly].

"Do not go even with the mind toward the multitude of external objects. Having thus caused one to abandon all activities, [the text] shows the supreme human goal (paramapuruṣārtha) in its own state: "Not you" (na tvam). The meaning is: you, whose external form has been cast aside, are yourself seen as the Supreme Person (paramapuruṣa), the self consisting of full bliss and consciousness, by way of ultimate reality. || 14 ||

Thus ends the thirty-seventh canto, titled "The Description of Tranquility," in the Section on Stability (*sthitiprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, belonging to the *Ārṣa* tradition. 37.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of Quiescence," in the Section on Stability (*sthitiprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Such being the case, this agency that is observed among those who know reality— whether in relation to pleasure and pain or in yoga and the like— is non-existent for them, but not so for the ignorant.
For one who does not recognize the unattached Self, agency arises through attachment of the mind;
for the knower, however, because there is no agency and no enjoyership, it is declared that "there is no bondage. (1)

[Objection: But surely even for those who know reality (*tattvavid*), agency is observed in worldly and scriptural actions, and that will inevitably lead to the experience of desired and undesired results; so what is the distinction between them and the ignorant? To this he says:

"Or rather, [the distinction lies] in the various stages (*bhūmikā*) resulting from the ripening of the practice of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) for those knowers of that—those who know reality."
The meaning is that this very action, though being perceived, is non-existent and simply does not exist; however, the distinction is that for the foolish, it appears to be otherwise. || 1 ||

For what is called "agency" (kartṛtva) is this: the determination of the internal mental modification, which is the conviction of its acceptability and is designated as "latent impression" (vāsanā); that is what is expressed by the term "agency. || 2 ||
In order to establish both of these points, he examines the nature of agency with the words beginning "yataḥ" (since). Regarding the phrase "yo hi":

bodily action is not agency, because in an unconscious movement, the cognition "I am doing" is not observed; rather, agency is mental, arising from a mental modification consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and passion (*rāga*), which itself originates from prior acts of agency.
The meaning is that it is called "action" (kriyā) because it has transformed into the form of a mental modification (vṛtti) whose nature is the ascertainment that "this is to be done. || 2 ||
Due to the power of activity, the person vibrates in accordance with his latent impressions (*vāsanā*) so as to become the experiencer of such a fruit;

he experiences the fruit in accordance with that vibration. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that what is called "being an experiencer of the fruit" follows from being an agent (*kartṛtva*). || 3 ||

He states that even the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) is merely a latent impression (*vāsanā*) arising from the sphere of tasting various fruits corresponding to those impressions, due to the necessity of activity dependent upon that [power]; thus he says:
"due to the necessity of activity" (*ceṣṭāvaśāt*). For it is because of this that a person vibrates in accordance with his latent impressions. (3)
And so it is said:
"Whether one acts or does not act, whether in heaven or in hell, whatever kind of latent impression (vāsanā) this mind possesses, that very thing is experienced. (4)
He cites a verse regarding the point already stated: "And likewise" (tathāca). The connection is that it is experienced [as such] both in heaven and even in hell. || 4 ||

Therefore, agency belongs to those persons who do not know reality, whether they act or do not act; it does not belong to those who have known reality, because they are free from latent impressions (vāsanā). || 5 ||

Let it be that agency and enjoyership consist merely in latent impressions (vāsanā); nevertheless, how is the distinction between the knower and the ignorant established? To this he says: "Therefore," etc. (Verse 5).
For one who has realized the truth, whose latent tendencies have become slackened, does not pursue the fruit even while acting;
moreover, with an unattached intellect, he performs only mere movement.
Although he experiences all this—the fruit of action—as being the Self alone, he acts even while not acting.
Of exalted mind. || 6 ||
He establishes the distinction regarding the knower with the words, "For one who has realized the truth...
He likewise establishes that his status as an enjoyer is also unreal with the words, "Even though it has been attained...
But the ignorant person, whose mind is submerged and whose heart is attached to enjoyment, acts even while not acting. || 6 ||
Whatever the mind does, that is done; whatever it does not do, that is not done. Therefore, the mind alone is the agent, not the body. || 7 ||

It was understood that this saṃsāra has come from mind alone, consists of mind alone, is merely mind, and resides in mind alone; and it was realized that all objects have become utterly tranquil and are nothing but latent impressions (vāsanā), and that only the Knower exists. || 8 ||

The word "previously" is to be understood as the ellipsis for "known, deliberated upon, and determined. When both the entire object and the various modifications of the mental faculty (*vṛtti*) have subsided, then only the latent impression (*vāsanā*) remains; at that time, the conscious one (*jña*), conditioned by that [impression], exists as the individual soul (*jīva*) alone. || 8 ||

For the mind of those who know the Self has attained supreme tranquility; like dewdrops vanishing in the heat of a fierce sun, or like water from a mirage when a cloud rains, it has reached and remains in the fourth state (turya).

Among those living beings, the mind of those who know the Self—having reached a state of subsidence like the water of a mirage when the rain-cloud pours in the monsoon, and having become dissolved like a drop of frost in the fierce heat—attains the fourth state (turya) and remains in that very essence; this is the distinction, such is the meaning. || 9 ||
The wise know the mind of the knower to be neither blissful nor devoid of bliss, neither moving nor unmoving, neither steady, nor existent, nor non-existent, nor yet anything between these.
He cites a verse intended to describe the state of the mind: "Neither bliss... and so forth.

It is not bliss consisting in rest in sensory objects; nor is it devoid of the bliss of one's own true nature (*svarūpānanda*). It is not immobile, meaning a state of insentience like stone and the like. Of these aforementioned states—bliss, lack of bliss, the mobile, the immobile, existence, and non-existence—[it is none].
The middle state is not of the nature of the transitional (saṃdhyavasthā) condition;
rather, by process of elimination, the meaning is that it is of the single flavor of the bliss of the Self as Pure Being (bhūmātmasukha). || 10 ||

The knower of reality does not sink into the savor of vibration consisting of latent impressions, like an elephant in a puddle; he perceives only the field of enjoyment of the mind of the fool, and not the true essence of existence.

He also states another distinction between the knower and the ignorant with the words beginning "not a latent impression" (na vāsanā). "Not reality" (na sattattva) means not the ultimate reality (paramārthatattva). || 11 ||
Likewise, there is another illustration here:

even one who does not actually fall into a pit, if his mind is permeated by the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of falling into a pit while lying on a bed or sitting in a seat, experiences the suffering of falling into that pit. On the other hand, another person, even while actually falling into a pit...
When the mind has attained supreme tranquility, it experiences the comfort of the bed and seat;

thus, between these two— the bed and seat versus falling into the abyss— one becomes the agent of falling into the abyss even though one was not its agent, while the second becomes non-agent even though he was the agent of falling into the abyss.

Because one is perfected through the power of the mind, the established conclusion is that a person becomes whatever their mind is. Having stated that for one with an ignorant mind, the dream serves as an illustration for sinking into the suffering of evil latent impressions (*durvāsanā*), he demonstrates this by saying "And thus," and so forth. Furthermore, the Śruti also says: "Now, when they seem to strike him, or seem to conquer him, or as if an elephant [were attacking]..."
"It covers [the truth], and one falls as if into a pit; whatever fear one perceives while waking, that one imagines here through ignorance.
Another, however, who knows the reality, having concluded what was said, applies it to the subject at hand: "Therefore... (12).

Therefore, let the mind there be eternally unattached, whether one is an agent or a non-agent; for there is nothing whatsoever apart from the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*) upon which attachment could be conceived. Know that whatever exists within this world is all a mere appearance, due to the purity of the mind. (13)

Let it be so; "of yours" is the ellipsis. For you who perceive reality, there exists nothing whatsoever apart from the reality of the Self (ātmatattva) with which your attachment could possibly occur. || 13 ||
And thus, for this person who has known what is to be known, when the certainty arises that the self (ātman) is not the object of pleasure and pain;
when the certainty arises that there exist no perceptions of container and contained apart from the self; and when the certainty arises:
"I am the agent and the enjoyer, distinct from all objects, even as much as a thousandth part of the tip of a hair."
When the certainty arises that "whatever exists here is all indeed myself," or when the certainty arises that "I alone abide as the illuminator of all beings and as the omnipresent one," then,
through the state of being free from feverish distress, the mental fluctuation remains in a state of effortless ease, realizing: "I am not accessible to pleasure and pain."
In legal proceedings. || 14 ||

The word "nāma" is a particle used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*). It means that once the certainty has arisen that [the Self] is indeed inaccessible to pleasure and pain, there follows the ascertainment of the non-existence of the relationship between container and contained, which serves as the basis for that certainty; and the basis for that, in turn, is either the ascertainment of the Self as being no larger than the tip of a hair and distinct from the body, or the ascertainment of the absence of the sense of "I" (*ahaṃbhāva*) in everything else.

The certainty regarding the all-pervading Self, which is the fruit resulting from that purification, arises through that means; once the previously mentioned certainty— "I am the recipient of pleasure and pain"— has arisen, the mental fluctuations, having lost the feverish anxiety of seeking the attainment of the desired and avoiding the undesired, dissolve effortlessly into the Self alone.
Manifesting her divine play for the sake of experiencing the fruits of past karma (*prārabdha*), she remains engaged in worldly affairs;
the *taṅ* (ātmanepada) ending is used here according to the rule *prakāśanastheyākhyayośca*. 14.
For one who knows that, even in the midst of adversity, there is only joy; like moonlight, it alone adorns the state of the world.

For the knower, apart from the mind, is a non-doer even while acting, because the mind leaves no stain; thus, he is not affected by the karma of actions performed with effort, such as the movement of feet and hands.
One experiences the fruit. || 15 ||
Therefore, he says that for one who knows reality, there is no experience of suffering even in times of distress; on the contrary, there is only bliss:
"Thus, the mind is the seed of all actions, all desires, all states of being, all worlds, and all destinies. When that [mind] is relinquished, all actions are relinquished."

All sufferings are exhausted and all karmas go to dissolution. Even by an action performed mentally, the Knower is not overcome, nor is he rendered helpless, nor does he undergo attachment, because [the Self] is distinct [from the mind]. 16.

Because the mind is the seed of all actions, of the mental faculty, of the intellect, of their objects, and of the movements directed toward them, it is established that by abandoning it, the relinquishment of the entire cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*) is accomplished; thus he says, "In this way. All actions—meaning all activities—and all merits and demerits, which constitute all actions, go to dissolution when performed through the mental faculty consisting of volition (*saṃkalpa*).

Since even by means of physical action the Knower is not overcome, the reason for this is that he is not brought under control. In that regard, the reason is that he does not undergo passion. For it is one who is attached to the fruit that, for the sake of his own accomplishment, brings the activity of its means under control and engages in it. And having engaged, he is overcome by the virtues and defects produced by that [action]. Why?
Because, from the perspective of ultimate reality, there is no existence of anything distinct from itself; for that which is distinct does not exist apart from it. || 16 ||
Just as a child, while mentally constructing and destroying a city, experiences that mental construction of a city as if it were effortless and uncreated,
neither regarding it as something to be grasped nor perceiving the destruction of the city as an unartificial pleasure or pain; so too [is the case for the wise].

One who perceives that which is produced by the mind as "produced" experiences even suffering as a mere play and does not perceive it as suffering; thus, although he acts from the perspective of ultimate reality, he is indeed not tainted. || 17 ||

He provides an illustration for the fact that even what has been done may be as if undone, with the words beginning "Just as" (*yathā*). "Polished" (*nirmṛṣṭa*) refers to the finishing of a constructed object. "The crushing of the city" (*nagarasya nirmathanam*) refers to the cessation resulting from the application of dissolution.
"Done" (*kṛtam*) means real. He applies this to the subject of the analogy (*dārṣṭāntika*) with the word "In this way" (*evam*). || 17 ||

Among all existing things in the world, whether they are to be abandoned or accepted, what is the cause of suffering? Furthermore, nothing that is to be accepted exists which is indestructible or distinct from the Self; therefore, this Self is neither the agent nor the enjoyer, for in reality, this so-called agency does not belong to it.
It is superimposed by one's own [mental] study. || 18 ||
Having thus examined agency, he reflects upon the cause of suffering: "In all things," and so forth.

In this world, among all things that are dealt with as either to be rejected or accepted, what is the cause of suffering? Nor is that which is to be rejected the cause of suffering, because rejection is preceded by acceptance.

Since that which is to be abandoned lacks the quality of being desirable, suffering does not arise from it; therefore, by process of elimination, it would follow that only that which is to be accepted is the cause of suffering. But even that is not possible, as he says: "Nor is it the acceptable," etc.
Is suffering [caused] by an acceptable thing that is perishable or one that is imperishable? It cannot be the first, because it is perishable.

Because that which is incapable of self-preservation cannot serve as a cause for anything else; nor is the second [alternative] possible, for in this world of things to be acquired (*upādeya*), nothing exists that is indestructible. This is because the scripture states, "Everything other than the Self is perishable" (*ato'nyad ārtam*), implying that what is to be acquired is subject to loss and acquisition due to its very nature of being perishable.

The meaning is that everything distinct from that [Self] is perishable. Thus, since no cause for the suffering to be experienced can be established, it is proven that the Self is neither an agent nor an enjoyer; this he states with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).
The particle *ca* (and) is displaced in its order. Furthermore, this agency which is experienced is not real (*atattvataḥ*).
The grammatical connection is that "it is superimposed. || 18 ||
That necessary [state] does not exist in reality due to the delusion of right vision;
because of the investigation of things as they truly are, agency and enjoyership do not exist.
Views such as aversion and desire toward the senses and their objects are seen among those who hold such views.
Not for those who do not hold that view. || 19 ||

The meaning is that it is "necessary" (āvaśyaka), meaning unavoidable for one who lives; this is according to the principle that "it is not possible for an embodied being to abandon actions entirely. To the question of why they are necessary, he says: "by the senses," etc.
[This refers to] aversion, longing, and so forth, toward the objects of the senses, and their causes.

The meaning is: "of those very ignorant ones whose intellects are afflicted by and rendered powerless by merit, demerit, and unseen forces" (this is a synonym for the word *dṛṣṭi* found in the root text).
Liberation does not exist here in this cycle of existence for those whose minds are attached to themselves; however, for those whose minds are unattached, all of this indeed exists.
For this very reason, he says "liberation" (mokṣa) to show that even the conceptualization of liberation does not exist for those who know reality—

those whose minds are fully attached to their own complete Self. However, from the perspective of those whose minds are unattached to their own self in this world, yet have reached the stage of practice (abhyāsa):
All this, including bondage, liberation, and so forth, truly exists. || 20 ||

For the knower, only the reality of the Self shines forth exactly as it is; he effects duality and unity as established by those who propound duality and unity, he effects existence and non-existence, and he demonstrates to him the state of possessing all powers, which is non-different from the web of his own powers. || 21 ||
He then states what exists for the wise person from the perspective of his vision: "as it truly is. If it is asked, "How then is his worldly transactional success established?
he replies that it is through a mere temporary acceptance of duality, unity, and so forth, as established by the perceptions of others.

Regarding the phrase "that duality and unity": that very reality of the Self (ātmatattva) itself, for the sake of establishing the worldly activities such as living and so forth for that knower of truth, produces at that time the duality and unity established by the perspectives of those who maintain the doctrines of duality and unity. || 21 ||
There is no bondage, there is no liberation; there is neither the absence of bondage nor the act of binding.
This suffering arises from lack of awakening; through awakening, it dissolves away.
He states the meaning of the commentary in verse: "There is no bondage," etc. Bondage refers to the causes of bondage, such as desire, action, and so forth. || 22 ||
The thought of liberation in this world is conceived in vain; the thought of bondage in this world is likewise conceived in vain. Abandoning everything, established in the Self without egoism—
O Rama, remain on this earth, acting with wisdom through your intellect as one who is steadfast.
Concluding the previously described state of abiding in the full Self, he instructs Rāma: "That which was intended," etc.
The meaning is clear. || 23 ||
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of Quiescence," in the *Sthitiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by Vālmīki in the tradition of the Ṛṣis. || 38 ||
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "Description of Tranquility," in the section on Stability within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The thirty-ninth canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
"O Blessed One, this being so, while the supreme Brahman alone exists, from where [does this world arise]?"
O Great-Souled One, tell me how I have come to this creation which is like a painting without a wall.
The omnipotence of Brahmā and the expansion of Rāma’s delusion are here proclaimed through the reflections of Vasiṣṭha for the sake of awakening him. (1)

Remaining within the very perspective of the ignorant, Rāma—having reflected upon the state of fullness as something entirely beyond his perception and considering it to be contradictory due to his trust in the words of his guru—raises a doubt, saying: "O Blessed One.
Thus, when the impossibility of bondage, liberation, and so forth remains established according to the manner you have described... (1)
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O Prince, this very reality of Brahman revolves; since it is the source of all power, therefore all powers are seen within Brahman. || 2 ||

To examine whether he remains in a state of contemptuous disregard or has attained some intermediate level of realization, Vasiṣṭha responds by accepting the doctrine of universal omnipotence, beginning with the words "O Prince," and so forth. He returns [to the argument].
It ceases. They are perceived through their effects and inferred by means of inferential marks. || 2 ||
Existence, non-existence, duality, unity, plurality, beginninglessness, and endlessness. || 3 ||
And thus, intending to show that contradiction applies only to those who lack power and not to the All-Powerful One, he provides an illustration:
"Existence, non-existence," and so forth. (3)
And that is not something other [than the source]; just as a body of water, by the surging and blooming of its waves, attains manifestation while displaying various forms. || 4 ||
Just as the reservoir of water in the ocean, the mass of water, blossoms—that is, becomes fully expanded—through the swelling caused by the rising of the moon which makes its appearance;

*praphulla* means "blossoming. [The root *phulla* in the sense of "to blossom" takes the suffix *kvip*; it should be understood that the intermediate *l* is elided by the rule *halo yamām* in *saṃhitā*. Being thus expanding, through *lāsa* (dancing/swelling).
By the dancing of the waves. || 4 ||

Likewise, being a mass of consciousness (*ciddhana*), it gathers, displays, sustains, generates, and dissolves all powers— whether consisting of action (*karmamayi*), latent impressions (*vāsanāmaya*), or mind (*manomaya*)— by virtue of its nature as consciousness (*cittva*). || 5 ||

The mind possesses the state of being a living soul (jīva) by virtue of its adjuncts (upādhi). This is because even that which consists of the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) possesses the nature of the mind (cittva).
It accumulates (cinoti) [karmic impressions] one by one and gathers them together. He shows the accumulated portions through their results:
it sustains [the self] with experiences (upabhoga) and then casts them away through concealment (tirobhāva). || 5 ||
The constant arising of all living beings, of all perceptions on every side, and of all objects in their entirety, proceeds from Brahman.
He cites two verses regarding the point already stated: "sarveṣām eva... (of all indeed). || 6 ||
From the world beyond they come, and because it is consciousness, they enter fully into it;
they are eternally identical with it, like waves in the ocean.
Beyond the other world, from the Supreme Self. || 7 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
"O Blessed One, this expression of yours is exceedingly profound; indeed, even now I do not comprehend the meaning of your words."

Even though he was thus consoled by the doctrine of potentiality (*śaktivāda*), Rāma, finding it inconceivable that consciousness could possess the power of inertia, as heat cannot possess the power of coldness in fire nor the power of burning in water, and that the invisible could possess the power of visibility or the eternal the power of impermanence within Brahman, raised an objection beginning with the words "O Blessed One."

The meaning is that the "mode of expression" (vacanavyakti)—which is the comprehension of the sentence-meaning—is extremely profound and difficult to achieve because of the presence of contradictions.

Where, indeed, is the reality of Brahman, whose activity transcends the six senses including the mind; and where is this fragile splendor of objects born from it? Such is the construction of these words. And if this manifestation has proceeded from Brahman, then it must necessarily be similar to Him.

He demonstrates these very contradictions with the words "kva kila" (where indeed...). The "composition of speech" is the creation of names; the "commencement" is the creation of forms. The meaning is that it ought to be consistent, not contradictory. || 9 ||
Whoever is born from something becomes exactly like that very thing. || 10 ||
The phrase "exists in the world" is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 10 ||
Just as a lamp [is lit] from a lamp, a person from a person, or grain from grain. || 11 ||
Since it has come from that which is changeless, it must itself be changeless. || 12 ||

Then, having heard that this occurrence of blemish—which is distinct from the conscious Self (cidātman) and belongs to the stainless Supreme Lord (parameśvara)—the venerable Brahmarṣi said: [In some versions, it is read as "thereafter Śrī Vasiṣṭha said. || 13 ||

The word *atha* has the sense of "if. The meaning is: "In that case, this attainment of the state of the world by the stainless Supreme Lord which you have described would be an admission of the occurrence of a stain. || 13 ||
This world exists as Brahman alone; there is no impurity here, O sinless one.
Dust does not manifest in the ocean, even amidst the multitude of its surging waves.
Seeing thus the nature of consciousness and its immutability regarding the world through the vision of reality, Vasiṣṭha composes himself, [concluding]: "This is indeed Brahman. (14)
O scion of Raghu, no second conceptualization exists here at all, other than Brahman alone, just as there is nothing other than heat alone in fire. 15.
Śrī Rāma said:
"Brahman, Brahman is free from suffering and beyond dualities, yet this world born of it is full of suffering;
O Brahman, I do not understand these words of yours, for their meaning is unclear. (16)

Rāma objects, maintaining that from the perspective of the ignorant alone, it is impossible to describe how Brahman—which is by its very nature the single essence of bliss—could possess the form of a world of suffering, which is its opposite:
"It is free from suffering. (16)
Śrī Vālmīki said: When Rāma had spoken thus, Vasiṣṭha, the tiger among sages, reflected in his mind upon how to instruct the descendant of Raghu.
Thus, Vālmīki shows his reflection on the means for awakening Rāma, who had been rendered speechless by Vasiṣṭha, with the words beginning "When this was said" (ityukte) and so forth. || 17 ||
Yet this intellect of his has not reached its highest expansion;
it has attained only a slight degree of clarity regarding this matter. (18)
For that wise one whose mind is fully developed, who has known what is to be known, and who has reached the further shore of the words concerning the means to liberation through discernment; (19)

That person whose mind is fully developed is one who, having abandoned the state of insentience of the world, is capable of perceiving it as being of the single essence of consciousness; such is the meaning. || 19 ||
No one has any fault whatsoever; for [the truth] is fully present within the self of knowledge.
O Rāghava, this [self] does not attain rest until it has been spoken. 20.
By his vision, there is no defect or contradiction whatsoever in any object;

for the world, though appearing contradictory in form, does not exist at all within the nature of Consciousness (vidyātman). Enough said—until we have fully spoken and taught, Rāghava finds no rest, nor does he attain it.
Therefore, the meaning is that he must necessarily be instructed. || 20 ||
But for one whose intellect is only half-developed, this does not appear clearly;
for he perishes while contemplating through this perception of enjoyment as if it were an object to be seen. (21)

However, for one whose vision is only half-developed, this aforementioned teaching that "all this is Brahman" is not appropriate. Why? Because this person of half-developed vision *anayati*—that is, he brings forth, presents, or gives life to—the objects of perception (*dṛśyān*). [The word *dṛśyānā* is derived from the root *an* with the suffix *kvip*, followed by the feminine suffix *ṭāp* according to the rule *āpaṃ caivaṃ halantānām*.]
Constantly perceiving objects as such through that same vision of enjoyment, he perishes;
that is to say, he falls away from the realization of reality. || 21 ||
For one who has attained the supreme vision, the desire for enjoyments does not arise;
the established conclusion that "all is Brahman" becomes appropriate for him in due time. (22)
To whom, then, is such instruction appropriate? He states this with the word "supreme" (parā). The *siddhānta* is the instruction concerning that which is fully established. || 22 ||
In the beginning, one should purify the disciple through qualities consisting primarily of tranquility and self-control;
afterwards, one should instruct him that "all this is Brahman" and "you are pure. (23)
How, then, should one who is only partially proficient be instructed? To this he says: "In the beginning," etc. (23).
He who says "everything is Brahman" to one who is ignorant or only half-awakened casts that person into the snares of great hells. (24)

For that great-souled one whose intellect is awakened, whose desire for enjoyment has perished, and who is free from expectations, it is right to say that the stain of ignorance no longer exists. (25)
And he who, being of extremely deluded intellect, instructs a disciple without first examining him, goes to hell himself until the dissolution of all beings. 26.

With the intention that one who does not know the reality (*attva*) is indeed unqualified to engage in instruction, and that for such a person—a deceiver of disciples—falling into hell is appropriate, he says: "Without examination" (*aparīkṣya*). The particle *eva* is displaced [in the verse]. He surely goes [to hell]. || 26 ||
Having reflected thus, the Blessed One, the best of sages Vasiṣṭha, who dispels the darkness of ignorance and is a sun to the earth, spoke to him.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "O sinless Rāghava, whether the attribution of a stain exists in Brahman or does not exist must be stated at the time of the final conclusion; you will know it for yourself."
"You will know it yourself. If you do not know it, then it should be stated at the time of the final conclusion, not now"—this is the meaning. || 28 ||
Brahman is all-powerful, all-pervasive, omnipresent, and "I alone am everything. || 29 ||

Now, first he teaches that which is suitable for one who is half-awakened: that Brahman possesses all powers as previously stated, and that there is the perception of the inner self (pratyak) as the "I" of all—stating, "Brahman is all-powerful. (29)

Just as you see magicians producing various actions through illusion, bringing the existent to non-existence and the non-existent to existence, even so the Self— though devoid of illusion— is like a supreme magician who, though not composed of illusion,
makes a jar into a cloth and a cloth into a jar upon a stone.

It produces a creeper upon Mount Meru’s golden slope as if it were the Nandana grove; it brings forth a stone within a creeper like a cluster of jewels upon the wish-fulfilling trees; and it projects a forest into the sky. || 30 ||

He elaborates upon how the inner self possesses all powers and universal identity through illusion alone, beginning with the words "just as by a magician," and so forth. To provide a possibility for what was previously considered impossible, he cites an example well-known in the world and in the scriptures: "on the golden shore. Just as, by divine power, even those things that are improbable...
The sense is that just as clusters of jewels from the Nandana grove and other such things are conceived [as possible], so too should [this] be conceived through one's own power. || 30 ||

In that world, it will become like a celestial garden of the Gandharvas; through mere imagination, it creates the appearance of a city in the sky and brings the surface of the earth to resemble the void, as if the shadow and collyrium had vanished. || 31 ||

With the intention that even the transposition of space and time, like the transposition of objects, must be conceived as possible through the power of *māyā* alone, he says: "It will happen in the sky. Having rendered the void (*vyoman*) devoid of shadow and collyrium—that is, having removed its blackness and soot—he leads the surface of the earth (*dharātala*), the terrestrial region, [upward] and brings it there.
The word "iti" there also serves to suggest the possibility of a thousand [instances], even though such a number is otherwise inconceivable. || 31 ||
It establishes the sky upon the surface of the earth like a multitude of women in the royal palace of a city of Gandharvas.
In that case, does the ground lead itself elsewhere in order to place the sky beneath it? He says "no":
"Like a city of Gandharvas... (verse 32).
Whatever exists, will exist, or has existed in the world— just like a reflection of the sky in red mosaic pavements— all that,
within those red mosaic floors that take the form of palaces made of rubies, is present through the redness of their foundation, like a reflection of the sky.
The meaning is that although redness is non-existent in itself, it becomes as if existent through the existence of Brahman. || 33 ||
If God, having assumed a manifest form and attained diversity, demonstrates [this world]. || 34 ||
Regarding this, he states the reason: "If [it were] God. The meaning is that he points to his own self as an example. || 34 ||
Since everything—in every way and everywhere—exists here as a single reality just as it occurs, where then, O Rāma, is there any occasion for joy, resentment, or wonder? (35)
And thus, since a single entity indeed becomes everything in every way, there is no impossibility;
moreover, joy, indignation, and so forth are appropriate. Thus he says: "Everything indeed... (verse 35).
One should always remain steadfast through equanimity alone. || 36 ||
Having thus dispelled this lack of confidence regarding Rāma, he establishes that very state of equanimity mentioned previously:
"By means of equanimity alone" (verse 36).
The knower of that reality, enveloped in equanimity, never undergoes the transformations of wonder, derision, delusion, joy, or indignation. (37)
With the intention that at that very moment there is the absolute destruction of joy and the rest, he cites the verse beginning with "vismaya": || 37 ||
For in this world, which is infinite in space and time, diverse logical arguments are indeed observed. || 38 ||
"In the endlessness of equality"—this is the ellipsis. Logical arguments, consisting of the nature of visible objects, are seen. || 38 ||
And this Self, by means of these arguments and names, diligently constructs its own manifestation and does not suppress what has arisen, just as the ocean [does not suppress] its waves. (39)

The application [of the term] "yukti" refers to the state of being endowed with the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), while "racanā" refers to the arrangement of the result; thus, the application is based on a distinction in their respective grounds for usage (*pravṛttinimitta*).
There is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) because it performs the arrangement. This Self does not disregard [this]. || 39 ||

Rather, it is as follows: just as butter exists in milk, a jar in clay, a cloth in threads, and a banyan tree in its seed, so too do the powers (śaktis) reside within the Self alone; when they reach manifestation, they are designated [as effects], being uncreated, like waves [arising from water]. // 40 //
Rather, it should somehow be construed thus: "What is being designated here are powers that have come into manifestation.
And this perspective of conventional usage is merely a conceptual construction; in the ultimate sense, however, the world is indeed uncreated. 40.
In this, there is no agent, no enjoyer, and nothing undergoes destruction. || 41 ||
The passage beginning with "nātra kartā" (there is no agent here) is clear. || 41 ||
When one remains thus, established in the pure reality of the Self—the witness, free from affliction, equal, eternal, and unagitated—then this state is attained. || 42 ||
Even though such is the ultimate reality, he introduces two verses that provide an illustration regarding the manifestation of the world: "Even while [it] exists, it manifests," etc. (42).

When existence is present, light appears like a lamp; when existence is present, the day appears like the sun; when existence is present, fragrance arises like a flower; thus the world is spontaneously accomplished. 43.
The two verses are clear. || 43 ||
This which is perceived is merely a manifestation;
it is like the movement of the wind, neither existent nor established as non-existent. (44)
"Neither existent nor non-existent"—the meaning is that it is indefinable (anirvacanīya). || 44 ||

From the perspective of ultimate reality, the Blessed One stands as if faultless regarding the views of worldly people; he is neither the creator of things destroyed nor the destroyer of things created,
appearing at times like stars that are manifest, at times slightly manifest, and at times unmanifest.
Heaps of flowers. || 45 ||

And thus, while the Self remains untainted by the defects of the world that arise merely from its own proximity, it appears as if it were the creator, the destroyer, and the controller of the world—just as the sky appears to be the locus of clusters of star-flowers.
He says this with the words beginning "as if faultless," etc.; for in the void sky alone, stars appear like clusters of flowers.
"Sometimes they become manifest in that [place]"—this is to be supplied everywhere. || 45 ||
For in this world, that object which is not one's own self perishes;
how could that object which is one's very own self ever perish? (46)

Thus, since the world is non-existent, its destruction consists in its very non-existence; its origination and persistence consist in existence itself, which is none other than the existence of Brahman. He states the conclusion regarding this distinction with the two and a half verses beginning with "naśyati" (46).
That entity which is not of the nature of the self is never born;
and that entity which is of the nature of the self is indeed born. || 47 ||
The word "is born" (jāyate) is also an indicator for "abiding" (sthitih). || 47 ||
How can that which is one's own self arise from that very same self? 48.
In that case, is the self produced? No; he says "How so? (verse 48).
Therefore, by the power of right knowledge, there is the comprehension of all categories of reality from Brahman. || 49 ||

With the intention that the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the world upon the existence of the Self constitutes the birth of the world—and not the birth of the Self—since there is no difference between them, he concludes with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).
By the power of right knowledge, that is, by the strength of the nature of consciousness which is the ultimate reality (*paramārthasatya*); *āgamaḥ* means descent, that is, origination.
...up to [verse] 49.

And for those who have entered [the path], at the very moment of their entry, ignorance arises and the knowledge of reality attains firmness; thereafter, the tree— with its hundreds of thousands of trunks, bearing a heavy burden of fruits consisting of various auspicious and inauspicious results, and possessing many branches— attains full expansion.
The tree of saṃsāra. || 50 ||

"Let there be the manifestation of categories; how is it that through them the Self attains saṃsāra? To show this, he says: "Now, for those who have not crossed over... Here, "ignorance" (avidyā) refers to the identification with that [body]. Through those two—namely, ignorance characterized by non-knowledge and identification—it reaches firmness in the course of time. || 50 ||

Having severed with the sword of discernment this tree called saṃsāra— which has the form of a cluster of hopes, which bears fruitless results through harsh sufferings, which sprouts with worldly enjoyments, which flowers with old age, and which shines with the creepers of craving— you, who were once its own shackle, are now liberated.
Roam about like a lordly elephant released from its tethering post. || 51 ||
Having thus described the tree of saṃsāra itself, he states the means for its eradication: "With hopes... and so forth.

Its form is made to blossom with clusters by means of hopes—that is, it has produced flower-clusters—and it has borne various fruits such as suffering and the like. This is according to the rule *prakṛtyādibhya upasaṃkhyānam* (Pāṇini 2.1.57), which allows for the use of the instrumental case (*āśābhiḥ*) even when there is no difference [between the instrument and the agent], as in the expression *prakṛtyā cāruḥ* ("naturally beautiful").
The third [verse]: "Climbers" refers to branches and creepers; "the self's shackle" is the place of bondage. The remainder is clear. || 51 ||

Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Exposition of Universal Unity," in the Section on Stability (*sthitiprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Sages (*ārṣa*). 39.
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Unity of All," in the *Sthitiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The Fortieth Chapter.
Śrī Rāma said: How did the birth of these living beings occur from the station of Brahmā?
O Lord, tell me in detail how much it is and of what nature it is.
Here, the origin of the various classes of living beings through their limiting adjuncts (upādhis) is described, as well as the nature of Brahman of those beings and of those adjuncts in detail. (1)

The question is clear. Although the origin of the various classes of living beings has already been described in detail in the section on origination (*utpatti-prakaraṇa*) and thus does not strictly require a further inquiry, nevertheless, the question should be understood as being asked again out of a desire for specific knowledge and to provide the occasion for the objection that is about to be raised. || 1 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Just as the various classes of beings arise from Brahman, just as they go to their destruction, and just as they indeed become liberated; || 2 ||
Therefore, Vasiṣṭha briefly declares that very samādhi with two verses beginning with "They arise" (utpadyante). || 2 ||
O sinless one of mighty arms, listen as I shall tell you in brief how they increase, how they remain, and how they disappear. (3)
The stainless power of consciousness belonging to Brahman,
possessing all powers, by its own will fashions the object of cognition, which becomes of the nature of perception.

The phrase "by chance" (*yadṛcchayā*) is used to demonstrate the indeterminate nature of the awakening of prior latent impressions (*vāsanā*), which serve as the seed for conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).
This [awakening] consists of the manifestation and grasping of the form of a future body and so forth. (4)
Having attained density through its own ideation,
whatever that [intellect] subsequently conceives, that very thing assumes the state of being called "mind" (manas).

With the intention that the very manifestation of that [Self] through the correct sense of "I" attains density, and that very density becomes the mind—the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the individual soul (jīva)—he says: "The mind. || 5 ||
By the mere volition of the mind, it instantly expands this unreal appearance like a city of the Gandharvas, as if abandoning its state of being Brahman.
Abandoning, as it were, the conception of the visible world, the ego, and so forth, [he attained] the state of Brahman, which is the nature of pure vision. || 6 ||
The nature of consciousness remains as nothingness alone;
that which exists as the visible world is indeed the visible sky itself.

Then he tells what occurred next: "The nature of consciousness" (*citsvarūpam*). Although the nature of consciousness shines forth everywhere as self-luminous, when viewed from the perspective of the external (*parāgdṛṣṭyā*), it appears as if empty, like the interior of a hollow jar. Abiding in that state, it remains of such a form.
The meaning is that what is visible to all people and well-known is called "space" (ākāśa). || 7 ||
Having formed the intention of being born from a lotus, he beholds his own form as one born from a lotus;
thereafter, he fashions the world, beginning with Prajāpati.
In that space, he demonstrates the conceptualization of the gross bodies of the four-faced Brahmā and others, as well as the worlds:
"O Rāma, this creation—resounding with the infinite multitude of fourteen kinds of living beings—has thus come into existence through the construction of the mind. (9)
Consisting of mind alone, it is empty, having a body that is mere space;
it is a city of mere imagination, existing as nothing but delusion. (10)

And since the arising of the substrate (*upādhi*) is thus false, the arising of the individual soul (*jīva*) occasioned by it is all the more false; with this intention, he says: "The mind alone," etc. (10).
In this world, some species of beings remain in a state of great delusion;
some have awakened knowledge, while others indeed falter midway.
In this context, in order to demonstrate the rarity of those qualified for the scripture, he divides living beings into three categories with the word "iha" (here).

"Iha" means in these worlds. Those whose knowledge has fully arisen are Sanaka and others. Those situated in the intermediate state are those who, although striving for liberation, repeatedly stumble due to obstacles.
The meaning is: because of the absence of firmness in dispassion. || 11 ||
Among all the classes of beings on earth that are subject to instruction, these human races attain the state of being worthy of teaching. (12)
He then states where detachment—which serves as the qualification for the study of the scripture—is easily found: "On earth" (bhuvi).
The genitive case here denotes selection from among many. These [women] are those residing in Bharatakhaṇḍa. || 12 ||
They are beset by many anxieties, filled with suffering, and afflicted by delusion, hatred, and fear;
of these, I shall first correctly describe those that are rajasic and sattvic.

He states the causes for the arising of detachment in them with the words "bahvādhayaḥ" (possessing many afflictions). Among those human races, since the tamasic ones lack the qualification for the scriptures, the rajasic and sattvic ones are suitable for instruction; these are described in the forty-second canto during the narration of the sequence of the descent of living beings.
The meaning is "I shall proclaim. || 13 ||
That which is the immortal Brahman, all-pervading and free from affliction,
is the manifestation of consciousness known as the infinite, beginningless, and devoid of delusion.
The meaning is that I shall also explain therein how that immortal Brahman, which is the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), arises in the form of the individual soul (jīva). || 14 ||
The vibration of that [Self], whose body is motionless, attains density through a portion of its existence,
just as movement appears in the calm ocean due to the movement of ripples.

The meaning is as follows: just as the movement and flickering of waves upon the calm and motionless ocean—which is a part of the existence of that Supreme Self whose body is vibrationless—attains density through the state of being a living soul (jīva), so too shall I explain that [vibration] within that very same [Self]. || 15 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
What is said to be a single portion of the infinite reality of the Self?
How could there be transformation, or how could there be the transgression of duality?

Rāma raises an objection, stating that what was said—that vibration (*spanda*) is a portion of existence (*satta*)—is incorrect; for it is impossible for there to be a "portion of existence" or "vibration" within Brahman, which is an indivisible, full existence of a single essence. He does so with the words:
"Of the infinite... (verse 16).
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "Therefore, this construction of words— 'born from that,' 'born from that'—
is for the sake of conventional usage in the scriptures, O Rāma, and not in the ultimate sense."

With the intention that this conventional usage of "origination," "part," "motion," and so forth has been devised in the scripture for the purpose of establishing the actual identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, and therefore no contradiction should be raised against it on the basis of the actual state of reality— Vasiṣṭha [says]:
He states the answer with the words "by that, it is born," and so forth. "By that" means by that cause; "from that" means from the appropriated [aggregates]. || 17 ||
Transformation, being a composite whole, existence in space, and so forth—succession is not possible in the Lord, even though it is observed [in other things] as arising. (18)

To explain why that is not so from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), he says: "Because it is subject to modification" (*vikāritā*). "Spatiality" (*deśatā*) means being located in a particular place (*ekadeśatā*).

"Those whose arising is seen" (*dṛśyamānodayāḥ*) refers to those things which, though being perceived as arising through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), [are nevertheless subject to change]. || 18 ||
Apart from that [non-conceptual cognition], there is no other conceptualization, nor will there ever be;
how then could the sequence of words and their meanings—the expressions born of worldly convention—possibly exist? (19)

If those [categories] are not possible there, then let some other root of the worlds be postulated; to this he replies with the words "without that" (*taṃ vinā*). The meaning is that even the postulation of another is impossible without the light of consciousness (*citprakāśa*). The terms "cause" and "effect," as well as the meanings of the word "sequence" and the expressions born of worldly convention, are thus rendered untenable [without it]. || 19 ||

Whatever conceptualization exists here, whatever object, whatever word, and whatever collection of speech—because they are born from that and consist of that, each is regarded as being like that very state (pada). || 20 ||

"Words" refers to names; "the collection of speech" refers to sentences. Because it consists of that [sound], and because it consists of Being (*sat*), the word becomes like the real entity (*sadvastu*) from which it is born; it is just as fire arises from fire.
The conceptualization of difference—such as "this is the produced" and "this is the producer"—is merely a mental construction. (21)
And thus, since there is no difference in existence, the cognition of difference is indeed false; so he says with the words "born from that" (tajja), etc. || 21 ||

"This has arisen from that"—this is the established order of the world; yet, regarding the capacity for action, there is either a distinction between the produced and the producer, or they are one and the same. (22)
To the question, "How then is there the conventional expression that 'this other lamp has arisen from the previous lamp'? he replies with the words "This... (ayam).

The meaning is that when a single lamp, through its power of creative manifestation (*māyā*), performs the act of fashioning its own nature in two ways, the very excellence or preeminence (*atiśaya*) therein appears as two—the produced and the producer. || 22 ||
The confusion regarding words and their meanings— thinking "this is one thing" and "that is another"—
does not exist in the case of the Lord when He is spoken of, because there is no distinction in His cognition.

One who is confused regarding the meaning of words and exhausted by the conventional usage of names and forms finds [the deity] only in speech—that is, in mere verbal expression—and not in the Lord, the Supreme Self. This is because of the Vedic scripture stating, "Modification is a mere beginning with speech; it is a name.
The meaning is that duality would exist only when there is measurement, that is, when there is a delimitation [of the object]. || 23 ||
By that very power of the mind, consciousness arises spontaneously;
therefore, through firm contemplation, the desired object is attained.

Through that very power of the mind produced by the power of action (kriyāśakti), the differentiation of names—that is, designations—proceeds spontaneously, by its own inherent nature; thus, the desired object is attained and worldly transaction (vyavahāra) is accomplished. || 24 ||
That one flame of the fire is the second, called the progenitor—this is merely a play of words; there is no truth in the matter expressed by these words. (25)
He demonstrates the very point already stated by means of an illustration: "Of fire," etc. (25).
Those expressions such as "the produced" and "the producer" do not apply to the Supreme;
for since it is one and infinite, what could produce what, and how? (26)
This is the very nature of a statement that immediately after a statement, there is another statement;
it is not appropriate [to claim] that it serves purposes such as the exclusion of a counter-correlate or the indication of number. (27)

The counter-correlate (*pratiyogī*) is that which is incompatible with identity with its own locus. Exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) is difference (*bheda*). Number (*saṃkhyā*) refers to duality and so forth. 27–28.

Just as a mass of waves is seen within the ocean, those wise ones know that very Brahman which appears in the Supreme as sound (*śabda*) in the form of the conceptualization of objects (*arthakalanākāra*).
Brahman is consciousness and Brahman is the mind; Brahman is the object of cognition and Brahman is the word. Brahman is the meaning, Brahman is the elements, and Brahman is consciousness. || 29 ||

What, then, is the established conclusion? He states it with the words beginning "Brahman": the conscious inner self (*cit-pratyagātman*) is the reality of consciousness (*vijñāna-vastu*), while the various modifications of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti-bhedāḥ*) are its manifestations. Consciousness is the Lord (*īśvara*), the witness (*sākṣin*), or the manifestation of objects (*arthaprathā*). || 29 ||
This entire universe is Brahman, and that state transcends the universe;
yet in reality, the world does not exist, for everything is solely Brahman alone. (30)

"This is one part, this is another, this is yet another"—such expressions are merely conceptualizations arising from false cognition regarding the nature of space; what truthfulness can there be here in mere words? (31)
Just as a flame arises from fire, this "flame" is the designation for the mind;
the splendor of conceptual constructions born of its restlessness does not, in reality, attain establishment.
Success is attained in the eternally perfected, immutable state.
The verbal expression of conceptual construction is indeed unreal, yet it is conceptualized as having a real nature;
this is due to the impairment of vision by darkness, like the defect of the cognition of two moons. (33)
It is conceptualized through delusion; it manifests [as such]. || 33 ||
From that all-pervading, infinite state of Brahman, nothing else whatsoever can arise; whatever emerges from it is that very same reality.
Without the reality of Brahman, nothing at all is possible here;
indeed, "all this is Brahman"—this alone is the ultimate truth. (35)
O wise one, such will be the nature of your established doctrine (siddhānta).
Within that very framework, I shall provide an exposition of the cage of words concerning the meaning of the established doctrine.
It will exist; it will be established in the Buddha. At that very place, at that very time. We shall explain this in the section on Nirvāṇa. 36.
In this world, some things such as ignorance exist, but not in any other sequence;
you will fully understand all matters when each respective ignorance has been destroyed. (37)

In this regard, within this ultimate reality, enough with the state of being the full Brahman. The repetitive expression "in the destruction of each respective ignorance" is used because one wishes to express the multiplicity of even a single ignorance along with its various types of doubt. || 37 ||
When the unreal is destroyed, the real becomes clear as it truly is, just as the visible world is seen when the darkness of night has vanished. (38)
The visible is that which is worthy of being seen by the eye, such as the world, stationary objects, and so forth. 38.
O Rāma of stainless luster, when this entire world, which has been spread out by false views, comes to rest in you who are pure and whose state is unerring, it shall become—
This is indeed unfailing; there is no doubt whatsoever in this matter. || 39 ||

He summarizes everything that has been said with the word "yat" (that which): when this entire world, which appears spread out and extended in every direction through *kudṛṣṭi*— that is, a vision corrupted by ignorance— is destroyed along with that ignorance, then [the Self] shines in the stainless supreme state, which is like a spotless mirror, non-illusory, and the ultimate reality.
That very thing will become unfailing; it shall endure. || 39 ||
