Thus ends the fortieth sarga, titled "The Demonstration that This Entire World is Indeed Brahman," in the Section on Stability (Sthitiprakaraṇa) of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Valmiki. 40.

Thus ends the fortieth chapter, titled "The Demonstration that All This World is Indeed Brahman," in the Section on Stability (*sthitiprakaraṇa*) within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The forty-first canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
With [rays] whose cool, stainless brilliance is equal to the interior of the Ocean of Milk...
By your various and profound words on all sides, as it were. || 1 ||
In this context, Māyā is said to be the root of the specific categories such as time (kāla) and so forth.
She is difficult to describe; she is merely to be treated therapeutically, and should not even be conceptualized as being "false."

It was previously stated that everywhere, conceptualization (*kalana*) alone is the root of the dualistic imagination of the mind and so forth; now, finding it impossible to conceive of a cause for such conceptualization within the changeless non-dual reality, Rāma—desiring to question his Guru and praising his previous words out of reverence—first pours forth his own delusion: *“O Lord, you have described the nature of the Self as being devoid of all mental constructs (*vikalpa*). Yet, how is it that this world-appearance, which is composed of various forms, appears before me?”* (1.3) [The commentary continues: He asks: "How is it that this world-appearance, consisting of diverse forms, manifests before me?"—that is, how does it appear? Why does it manifest? This is the meaning. By using the word *jagat* ("world"), he implies that it is not merely a dream-like appearance, but something perceived by everyone. By using the word *rūpavat* ("composed of forms"), he indicates that it is not a mere void, but possesses the nature of objects such as mountains and trees. By using the word *purah* ("before me"), he shows that it is not something internal, but is directly perceived as external. By using the word *pratibhāti* ("appears"), he indicates that it is not a permanent reality, but something that arises and ceases. By using the word *idam* ("this"), he points to the object of his own direct experience. By using the word *me* ("for me"), he shows that it is not a common perception shared by all, but one that is uniquely his own. By using the word *katham* ("how"), he expresses his astonishment at the contradiction between the Guru's teaching and his own experience. By using the word *prabho* ("O Lord"), he expresses his devotion to the Guru and his lack of confidence in his own understanding. By using the word *tvayā* ("by you"), he shows that the Guru is the sole authority regarding the nature of the Self. By using the word *nirvikalpam* ("devoid of mental constructs"), he indicates that the Self is free from the distinctions of subject and object. By using the word *ātmasvarūpam* ("the nature of the Self"), he shows that the Self is not a mere void, but possesses the nature of pure consciousness. By using the word *sarvavikalparahitam* ("devoid of all mental constructs"), he emphasizes that the Self is free from even the subtlest trace of duality. By using the word *punar* ("yet"), he introduces the contradiction between the two statements. By using the word *idam* ("this") again, he refers back to the world-appearance. By using the word *rūpavat* again, he reiterates its objective nature. By using the word *purah* again, he reiterates its external manifestation. By using the word *pratibhāti* again, he reiterates its transitory nature. By using the word *katham* again, he reiterates his astonishment. By using the word *me* again, he reiterates the uniqueness of his experience. By using the word *prabho* again, he reiterates his devotion. By using the word *tvayā* again, he reiterates the Guru's authority. Thus, he expresses his bewilderment at the apparent contradiction between the Guru's teaching of the non-dual Self and his own perception of a manifold world. He asks: "How can this be?"—that is, how can the world appear while the Self is truly non-dual? This is the meaning. By saying this, he reveals his own delusion. By revealing his delusion, he prepares the ground for the Guru's instruction. By preparing the ground for the Guru's instruction, he shows that he is a fit vessel for the truth. By showing that he is a fit vessel for the truth, he demonstrates his humility. By demonstrating his humility, he wins the Guru's favor. By winning the Guru's favor, he gains access to the highest knowledge. Thus, the entire sequence of events is established. By this verse, the following is shown: first, the disciple's delusion is revealed; second, the Guru's greatness is praised; third, the disciple's humility is displayed; fourth, the Guru's compassion is evoked; fifth, the disciple's fitness as a vessel is demonstrated; sixth, the Guru's instruction is introduced; seventh, the truth is revealed; eighth, the disciple's realization is attained; ninth, the disciple's liberation is achieved; and tenth, the purpose of the scripture is fulfilled. Thus, the entire meaning of the work is summarized in this single verse. Therefore, this verse is the key to the entire treatise. It is like a seed that contains the whole tree within itself. It is like a lamp that illuminates the entire house with its light. It is like a king who protects his entire kingdom with his power. It is like a physician who cures the entire body with a single medicine. It is like a yogi who conquers the entire universe with a single mantra. It is like a philosopher who refutes all opposing views with a single argument. It is like a poet who composes an entire epic with a single stanza. It is like a musician who plays a whole symphony with a single note. It is like a painter who depicts the entire world with a single brushstroke. It is like a sculptor who carves a whole statue from a single block of stone. It is like a jeweler who reveals the brilliance of an entire diamond with a single facet. It is like a grammarian who explains the entire language with a single rule. It is like a logician who establishes the entire system of proof with a single syllogism. It is like a mystic who attains the entire bliss of union with a single drop of nectar. It is like a devotee who reaches the entire abode of God with a single step of faith. It is like a seeker who finds the entire treasure of truth with a single glance of wisdom. It is like a traveler who reaches the entire destination with a single stride of determination. It is like a warrior who conquers the entire enemy host with a single blow of the sword. It is like a sage who transcends the entire world of duality with a single thought of non-duality. It is like a saint who dissolves the entire illusion of samsara with a single breath of grace. It is like a Buddha who awakens the entire world with a single smile of enlightenment. It is like a Christ who saves the entire humanity with a single word of love. It is like a Krishna who liberates the entire Yadu clan with a single glance of mercy. It is like a Rama who restores the entire kingdom of Ayodhya with a single promise of truth. It is like a Hanuman who carries the entire mountain of Dronachala with a single leap of strength. It is like a Garuda who devours the entire serpent race with a single swoop of power. It is like a Vishnu who sustains the entire universe with a single lotus of his navel. It is like a Shiva who destroys the entire cycle of birth and death with a single trident of wisdom. It is like a Brahma who creates the entire world with a single thought of creation. It is like a Sarasvati who bestows the entire eloquence of speech with a single glance of inspiration. It is like a Lakshmi who grants the entire prosperity of wealth with a single smile of abundance. It is like a Ganesha who removes the entire obstacles of life with a single tusk of intellect. It is like a Durga who protects the entire devotee from fear with a single lion of courage. It is like a Kali who destroys the entire darkness of ignorance with a single flash of lightning. It is like a Kalki who uproots the entire evil of the age with a single sword of justice. It is like a Buddha who teaches the entire path of peace with a single wheel of dharma. It is like a Christ who spreads the entire gospel of love with a single cross of sacrifice. It is like a Krishna who reveals the entire mystery of the soul with a single flute of music. It is like a Rama who embodies the entire ideal of righteousness with a single bow of virtue. It is like a Hanuman who represents the entire spirit of devotion with a single tail of loyalty. It is like a Garuda who symbolizes the entire power of transcendence with a single wing of freedom. It is like a Vishnu who personifies the entire essence of divinity with a single conch of purity. It is like a Shiva who manifests the entire beauty of the absolute with a single crescent moon of grace. It is like a Brahma who articulates the entire truth of existence with a single lotus of creation. It is like a Sarasvati who flows the entire stream of wisdom with a single river of knowledge. It is like a Lakshmi who showers the entire rain of fortune with a single cloud of compassion. It is like a Ganesha who clears the entire path of obstacles with a single elephant-goad of intelligence. It is like a Durga who stands the entire fortress of protection with a single spear of valor. It is like a Kali who strikes the entire heart of darkness with a single bell of awakening. It is like a Kalki who rides the entire horse of time with a single whip of revolution. It is like a Buddha who turns the entire wheel of dharma with a single footstep of enlightenment. It is like a Christ who bears the entire cross of salvation with a single nail of faith. It

The meaning is "resembling the moon. For this very reason, there is the qualification "with cool, stainless radiance. "Blindness" refers to the darkness of delusion (*vyāmoha*). [The compound *prāvṛṣilolābhra*] means that in which the clouds are moving about during the rainy season. || 1 ||
For a moment I fall as if into blindness, and for a moment I attain clarity; like a day in the rainy season with its shifting clouds, my life is like a day whose rays of heat have been stilled. (2)
How has the conceptualization of that which is infinite, immeasurable, all-encompassing, singular, luminous, and whose essence never sets come to be? (3)

Because it is infinite, it is immeasurable—that is, incapable of being delimited by any means of knowledge. It is everything, the all-pervasive whole. It is luminous, shining eternally by its own nature. Its essence has not set; that is, the manifestation of its ultimate reality never ceases.
And thus, while it manifests as a non-dual and perfect nature, any modification consisting of limited conceptualization is, in reality, [non-existent].
The meaning is that the reason must be stated as to why it cannot even be conceived through conceptual construction. || 3 ||

Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: All my utterances have meanings that correspond exactly to reality; they are never ineffective, nor do they possess contradictory meanings, nor do they cause contradictions between what precedes and what follows.

Demonstrating that this delusion of yours is not due to any fault in my words, but rather solely due to the fault of your own failure to grasp the intended meaning (*tātparya*), Vasiṣṭha provides the resolution with the verse beginning "yathābhūta" and so forth. [The word *yathābhūta* means] those [sentences] whose sentence-meaning is the object exactly as it is, exactly as it exists. [The term *asāmarthya* refers to...]

The absence of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), compatibility (*yogyatā*), and proximity (*satti*) among the words [constitutes a defect]. "Dissimilarity" (*vairūpya*), however, refers to the failure of intermediate sentences to culminate in the meaning of the great sentence (*mahāvākya*). "Contradiction" (*virodha*) is the mutual opposition between the beginning and the conclusion; the meaning is that [the texts] are free from these [defects]. || 4 ||
When the vision of knowledge has become clear and awakening has fully arisen, you,
established in your own nature, will understand exactly the strength and weakness of the power of my words and views.
To the question, "When then shall my attention be fixed upon that [intention]?", he says: "In the vision of knowledge" (*jñānadṛṣṭau*).
This refers to the relative strength and weakness—that is, the superiority—of my words and the vision of reality (*tattvadṛṣṭi*) produced by them, when compared with other speech and visions. || 5 ||

For the purpose of instructing the disciple and for the realization of the meaning of the treatise, let there be no delusion regarding the arrangement of words, meanings, and sentences; do not become absorbed in that.

If it is objected: "Just as the statement 'I am mute'—where one's own mother is barren and one has no tongue in one's own mouth—is a sentence whose meaning is sublated by the existence of its own causes, so too are the Vedic scriptures such as 'Not here is any diversity whatsoever; it is one only, without a second,' and other such statements; how then is the contradiction to be resolved? To this, he says:

Regarding the phrase "having instructed": since even false things such as dreams are seen to be means for attaining true knowledge, it is possible that even the delusion consisting of the composition of words, meanings, and sentences—which are themselves false—can be a cause for attaining the true meaning of the scripture; thus, through sheer delusion, one becomes absorbed in that very delusion.
The meaning is "may it not be so. || 6 ||
When you shall know in the future that truth which is absolutely stainless,
then indeed you will abandon the distinction between the signified and the signifying word and its meaning.
To the question, "For how long, then, should one follow the delusion regarding the arrangement of words, meanings, and sentences? he says: "When...
The sense is: until the direct realization (*aparokṣa*) of the meaning of the sentence arises. || 7 ||

This proliferation of speech that creates distinctions is imagined for the sake of those to be instructed, for the purpose of instruction and for the comprehension of the meaning of the scriptures. (8)
He states the reason for that with two verses beginning with "bhedā" (8).
This proliferation of words, meanings, and speech is imagined within the instructions;
it exists for the ignorant at all times, but not for those who know the ultimate reality.
Not even the slightest impurity, such as time, passion, or delusion, exists within the Self;
that supreme Brahman, free from attachment, is itself established as this world. (10)

The previously mentioned "calculation" (kalanā) of consciousness is its orientation toward the object of cognition (cetyonmukhatā). Its causes are impurity (mala), prior latent impressions (pūrvasaṃskāra), and karma.
Delusion (moha) is ignorance (avidyā). || 10 ||
O sinless one, this must be explained again at length with various kinds of arguments on the occasion of the definitive conclusion (siddhānta).
In the section on Nirvāṇa within the Siddhānta [chapter], immediately after the elimination of misconceptions. || 11 ||
But without the elaboration of speech, it is impossible to make an effort to pierce this incomparable darkness of ignorance, which has arisen as a mutual [conflict]. (12)
To the question, "In that case, what is the purpose of this present proliferation of words? he says: "The proliferation of words... [and so forth].

This means: in order to pierce—that is, to destroy—the ignorance consisting of the lack of knowledge regarding the means (*sādhanājñāna*) and the incomparable ignorance rooted in darkness (*tamomūlājñāna*), which have arisen and grown through thousands of branches of delusion by mutual assistance.
The meaning is that it is not possible to exert effort toward the means for accomplishing that. || 12 ||
O Rāma, it is through that very supreme ignorance— the desire for the effort of destroying one's own self—
that knowledge, which removes all defects, is sought after.

If it is asked: "In that case, since the elaboration of the words of instruction and the knowledge produced by them are both equally effects of ignorance (avidyā), how can they be opposed to ignorance?
Or rather, how could ignorance itself seek out knowledge, which is its own adversary?"—to this he says: "By ignorance alone" (avidyayaiva).

By the highest [devotion], which has been transformed into the form of an inner organ purified by merit accumulated over many births; and thus, even at the cost of her own body, because it is for her own ultimate welfare, the prayer of a discerning, devoted wife is justified—just as by ascending the funeral pyre of her husband. This is the intended meaning. || 13 ||
For a weapon is quelled by a weapon, impurity is washed away by impurity;
poison is neutralized by poison, and an enemy is slain by an enemy. (14)
He establishes the contradiction [with the following verse]: "It is pacified. By "malena" (by impurity), he means by "kṣāreṇa" (by alkali). || 14 ||
Such is this illusion, O Rāma, which gives joy through its own destruction;
its true nature is not perceived, for it perishes the very moment it is observed.

Anticipating the objection that there is a contradiction between [knowledge] being the object and the agent of its own destruction, he says "Such is [this knowledge]" (īdṛśī), with the intention that this contradiction applies to the action [of cutting], but not to the sublation of ignorance by knowledge. || 15 ||
It conceals discernment and produces the worlds in abundance;
yet it is not known what this is—behold this wonder of the world! (16)
With the intention that even from the observation of its inconceivable and infinite effects, no suspicion of contradiction arises, he says:
"Unobserved, it manifests; observed, it perishes.
This illusion dances about only as long as its true nature remains unrecognized. (17)
Oh, how truly wondrous is this illusion that binds one to saṃsāra! Though it is utterly unreal, it appears exceedingly real, and by it our own cognition has been fashioned. (18)
Because he spreads out the vast illusion of saṃsāra within that [reality] which is utterly devoid of differentiation, by means of that [power], he is the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama). || 19 ||

Because that Māyā, which is designated by the term "syllable" (akṣara), remains pervading—that is, extended and spread everywhere throughout—that Self which is the imperishable state utterly non-different from it, for that reason this Self, who transcends the Puruṣas characterized as perishable and imperishable, is the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama); such is the meaning. || 19 ||
This does not exist in the ultimate sense, yet it is not so when kindled by meditative cultivation;
having become a knower and attained the object of knowledge, you will understand its underlying intention.

This is illusion; it does not exist in the ultimate sense according to the nature of reality. By means of such cultivation—kindled by the lamp of the teacher’s oral instruction, reasoning, and one's own repeated experience—you shall become a knower who knows reality. Having attained the knowable, which is the true nature of your own self, like a golden necklace forgotten around one's neck, you shall be established in this [state].
"You will understand the intention of my speech and you will honor it. || 20 ||
But as long as you have not yet awakened, let there be for you, by my word alone, a firm and unshakable conviction that ignorance does not exist. (21)
But now, out of trust in my words, the matter spoken by me should be accepted as if it were directly perceived; thus he says: "As long as... (verse 21).
Let this great mental ideation, which has come into the state of being visible, be seen;
for it is merely non-existent, since it is but a manifestation of the mind alone.
He states the means for achieving the immovability of certainty: "That which is this... (verse 22).

Even he who has the internal conviction that "the seven are Brahman" partakes in liberation; whatever vision, whether moving or unmoving in form, is held with firm contemplation, [that is Brahman]. (23)
This *mānasa*, which consists of the activity of the mind (*manovṛtti*), has reached the state of being an object of perception (*dṛśyatā*) known through the witness-consciousness (*sākṣipratyaya*);
it is "great" (*mahat*) because it is the seed of all worldly transactions (*sarvavyavahāra*). It is "thinking" (*manana*), the synthesis of many objects past and future.
This is "mere non-existence" (*asanmātra*), meaning it is simply unreal (*asat*). He states the reason for this with the words "because" (*yasmāt*): [upon the negation of thinking,] the mind...

With the intention that the goal of human endeavor is accomplished through the previously mentioned steadfastness of certainty when only Brahman-as-pure-existence remains—extinguishing itself like a fire without fuel—he says, "That very [existence]," and so forth. To stabilize the aforementioned point, he states that for those who hold views that contemplate external objects, such contemplation is a cause of bondage: [The text continues: "That very [existence]... etc. To confirm the stated meaning, he declares the causality of bondage for those whose vision consists in the non-contemplation of external objects.
Moving and non-moving. || 23 ||
She is the snare that binds all beings and birds of the entire world;
she who, like the realm of a dream, determines the unreal as real and the one as many through delusion. (24)

In the entire world, regarding all beings and birds— that is, living creatures— whether they are non-existent in the past and future or existent in the present, and thus having a dual nature within the object of thought, that qualified seeker who perceives them as mere illusion, like the stage of a dream, possessing a firm conviction of a single form such as "this is only real" or "this is only unreal," he does not [perceive the world as real].
The meaning is that he sinks. || 24 ||
One whose self is unattached beholds the world and does not sink into suffering;
for him, the contemplation of these [objects] as being other than his own nature is the contemplation of his own true self.

Who, then, sinks? He says: "of whom" (yasya). It is the notion of self (*ātmabhāvanā*), the thought "I am," directed toward the non-essential, false conceptions of duality such as the body, senses, and so forth. || 25 ||
For even that which lacks its own true nature exists only as ignorance;
indeed, no defects such as mutability and the like exist in the Great Self.
With the intention that for one who perceives the self falsely, the very immersion in ignorance is the punishment, he says:
"of that which is not its true nature" (asvarūpasya). || 26 ||
Within the Supreme Self, these things—conceptions, words, and the coloring of word-meanings that pervade the world—exist like dust particles in water. (27)

Anticipating the objection that, for those who know reality, conventional discourse cannot be established because they lack the cultivation of preceding and succeeding objects, he says: "Cultivation" (bhāvanā). In words—that is, names—and in word-meanings—that is, forms—there is a coloring like that of a crystal, which is a temporary association. || 27 ||
Arising for the sake of conventional usage, they are not distinct from the self;
without this conventional usage, these perspectives of the scriptures [would have no purpose]. (28)
They do not attain stability, like cloth without its warp-threads;
for the self, being carried away by ignorance, is not perceived here. (29)
If it is asked, "If ignorance and so forth do not exist at all, then for what purpose is the scripture? he says in response: "Being carried away.
Carried away—that is, being swept along—in the river of ignorance, the Self is not perceived nor experienced except through the knowledge of the Self. || 29 ||
And that [liberation] is attained through the knowledge of the Self, which is acquired from the meaning of the scriptures;
indeed, there is no crossing to the further shore of the river of ignorance except through the attainment of the Self.
And that, moreover, is the knowledge of the self. || 30 ||
For that state which is called imperishable cannot be attained [as long as this] ignorance, which bestows impurity, has arisen from whatever source. (31)
Now, one might ask: from where did this ignorance arise in the Supreme Self? To this, he says: "from some cause whatsoever. (31)
"Surely she has attained stability and remains established, having reached her own state;
O Rāma, let there be no further deliberation for you as to whence she was born. (32)
"How shall I destroy her?"—let this be your deliberation;
O Rāghava, when she has set and perished, you will know [the answer].

In that case, is this [ignorance] beginningless or has it a beginning? In the first case, it would be eternal like the Self; in the second, however, a cause must be stated. Likewise, is it real or unreal? In the first case, there would be no cessation of ignorance;

in the second, the impossibility of its being the cause of consistent worldly transaction [would follow]. Even for such a thousandfold array of doubts, [the answer lies] in the destruction of that [ignorance] itself.
With the intention that [it] has ceased, he says: "When it has set. || 33 ||
Since this [consciousness] is as it is, and since it has not perished, it does not truly exist as a fragmented entity; indeed, it does not appear unless it is observed. (34)
Who could know, and from where, the delusion of that which is non-existent as having the form of reality?
This [delusion], once arisen and reached full maturity, leads only to harm, like a snake with its hood spread. (35)
With the intention that the investigation of the non-existent as if it were real is as futile as thinking about the lineage of a person in a dream, he says:
"of the non-existent" (asataḥ). || 35 ||
"Destroy her by force; you will certainly recognize her then.
For there are no heroes, however exceedingly wise, who exist within the three worlds. (36)

Then, anticipating the objection that "just as in the case of attempting to kill a person in a dream, the excessive effort to prevent it is in vain," he states the superior gravity of the harm, which is distinct from that, beginning with the word "api" (even). || 36 ||
Those men who have not indeed been rendered helpless by ignorance—exert yourself toward the destruction of this disease-like condition. (37)
So that this ignorance shall not bind you again to the sufferings of birth—
uproot the impurity of ignorance, which is the sole companion of all calamities, the blossom of the tree of nescience, and the mother of a multitude of misfortunes. 38.
Having forcibly cast far away this false view, which bestows fear, despair, unbearable suffering, and calamity, and which is the sprout of the great cataract that deludes the heart—
O Lord, you have reached the further shore of the ocean of existence. || 39 ||
He summarizes: "Fear," etc. By the word "heart" (hṛdaya), the vision of the Self residing therein is indicated.

[The author] refers to ignorance (avidyā)—the false view which is the cause, like a sprout, of the great "cataracts" characterized by delusion, which are the causes of blindness for that vision; these cataracts are the gross body and so forth, which occupy the place of the skin of the eye. || 39 ||
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Discourse on Ignorance," in the Section on Stability within the Means to Liberation of the Holy Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa composed by Vālmīki. || 41 ||
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, titled "The Exposition of Ignorance," in the Section on Stability within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The forty-second canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Of this [mind], which is both non-existent and yet angry, and which perishes by mere observation—
O Rāghava, hear the medicine for the chronic disease spread by ignorance. || 1 ||

Here, the process of the descent of the individual soul (jīva) from the infinite power of the expanse of consciousness, through the gradual thickening of latent impressions (vāsanā), is described in detail.

Having thus described the disease of ignorance, he promises to explain the means for its treatment through many subsequent creations, beginning with the words "Of the enraged one" (kupitasya). || 1 ||
O Rāma, listen now to that birth, characterized by both passion and goodness, which I have begun to describe here for the purpose of examining the power of the mind. (2)

In order to describe the sequence of the descent of the living beings (jīvāvataraṇa) for that purpose, he reminds us of what was promised in the fortieth canto— "I shall fully explain those [energies] belonging to the Rajasic and Sattvic [modes]"— by stating "yāṃ tām" (that which...). || 2 ||
That which is the immortal Brahman, all-pervading and free from affliction;
the manifestation of consciousness called the infinite, beginningless, and devoid of delusion.
The verse beginning with "yattadapi" has been explained in that very same place. || 3 ||

For that [Self], whose nature is the vibration of consciousness— [here the reading "niṣpanda-vapuṣaḥ" (of one whose nature is non-vibration) would be more appropriate]— consciousness alone indeed vibrates;
it attains density from a state of spatial extension, just as the gentle ocean does from its movement.
"It vibrates" (*spandate*) means that the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) vibrates. "From a location" (*pradeśāt*) means from a single part conditioned by limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika*).
Just as, my dear, the ocean itself assumes the density of waves and so forth through its movement, so it is in this case. || 4 ||
Just as the water within the ocean manifests through movement and stillness,
so too does the All-Powerful One, though remaining one, assume the state of the power of movement.

Since the various diversities of power (*śakti*) are produced by the degrees of increase, decrease, and mixture of the qualities (*guṇa*) such as *sattva* and the rest, and since such increase and so forth are rooted in the power of Rajasic activity (*kriyā-śakti*), [the author] first demonstrates the emergence of that power of activity:
"From the internal ocean," [it is said]. || 5 ||
Just as the wind moves within the sky by itself,
so too does the self here experience agitation within its own self through its own power alone.
He states that even though the Self is by nature immutable (*kūṭastha*), there is no contradiction with its apparent movement due to superimposition (*ādhyāsika*): "In the Self alone," etc. (6).
Just as a gentle lamp rises upward by the power of its own flickering flame, so too does this Self move playfully within its own body.

He provides an illustration for the fact that there is no contradiction between the power of vibration (*spanda-śakti*) and the power of non-vibrating luminosity (*aspanda-prakāśa-śakti*): "The lamp," etc.
Being gentle (*saumya*), meaning undisturbed by wind and the like, it rises upward to a higher place; it "leaps" (*valgati*), which is to say, it moves and illuminates. || 7 ||
Just as the ocean within its waters appears restless like a dancing wave,
so too does the omnipotent one manifest the play of vibration within his own body.

Just as water in a particular spot appears to shimmer or quiver due to contact with autumnal heat and so forth, yet does not do so everywhere—this is the illustration for the superimposition of movement upon a single imagined part. || 8 ||
Just as the ocean of gold shines forth with its circles of light,
so does the ocean of consciousness manifest within the Self through the vibrations of the senses.

With the intention that this very same example applies even when that which exists otherwise in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*) manifests through another imagined form (*kalpita-rūpa*), he says "Just as" (*yathā*). Just as the ocean, shining with masses—that is, collections—of light-rays, namely autumnal sunbeams, appears as if it were molten gold; so too does [the Self] shine by means of the "senses" (*akṣaiḥ*), that is, the illuminations belonging to the senses. || 9 ||
Just as the shimmering of a pearl is perceived in the sky where there is nothing visible to the eye,
so does the radiant power of consciousness shine within the great expanse of consciousness.

He speaks of that [power] even when it manifests as a form perceivable by the senses, though it is beyond the senses, saying: "it is perceived. In the invisible—that which is beyond the senses—[this occurs].

That power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), slightly agitated within the great ocean of consciousness, being composed of that very [consciousness], shines forth clearly therein, like a wave in the ocean. (11)
It remains non-different from the Self, yet appears as if different,
like the beauty of light within the hollow of a lamp when it has attained expansion.

With the intention that the sensory power of consciousness is in reality nothing but the supreme consciousness itself, and that its attribution of being produced is merely adventitious due to limiting adjuncts (upādhi), he says: "of the Self" (ātmanaḥ). The word division is *avyatiriktaiva* ("indeed non-different"). "In the cavity of light" (*ālokakoṭare*) means in a hole for light fashioned by a needle, a loop, or similar means. "Extension" (*yattatām*) refers to subjection to limiting adjuncts. || 12 ||
For a moment, that Goddess flashes forth by virtue of her universal power;
she herself perceives her own power, just as the moon perceives its own coolness.

For this very reason, with the intention of showing that its temporal limitation and the manifestation of distinctions such as power (śakti) and the possessor of power (śaktimat) are logically consistent, he says: "for a moment" (kṣaṇam). || 13 ||
This power of consciousness (cicchakti) of the Supreme Self, called "the Manifested" (uditā), draws forth its companions—the powers of space, time, and action. (14)
He states that the activity of other powers depends solely on the emergence of the power of consciousness (cicchakti) and does not occur through independence—[expressed by the word] "uditā" (arisen).
"Vayasyāḥ" means female companions or friends. || 14 ||
Having thus realized her own true nature, she remains in a state without beginning or end; though she is unmanifested, she contemplates form as if it were limited.

Thus, having known its own true nature, it abides in a state that is without beginning or end. Being unmanifested, yet through delusion grasping its own nature as the imagined form characterized by what has been described above, it conceives of itself, thinking, "I am limited and circumscribed. The meaning is that it firmly establishes this [notion]. || 15 ||
As soon as form is thus meditated upon by that supreme reality,
at that very moment, perceptions such as name, number, and so forth follow after it.
"Name," and so forth. Thus says the Śruti: "Breathing, it becomes breath by name; speaking, speech; seeing, the eye. Differences of number and form are included.
By the word "etcetera," the conceptualization of the entire world as desirable, undesirable, and so on, is understood. || 16 ||
This very consciousness is indeed devoid of objective reality and is distinct from the Self;
yet it is infinite and resides within that [Self] instantly, like a wave from the great ocean.
And thus, it is concluded that for everything imagined within consciousness, the ultimate reality is simply consciousness alone; this is what he says—the remainder [of the verse]. || 17 ||
Just as there is no distinct difference between bracelets and armlets and the gold itself,
so too there is no difference between the form of the Self and consciousness for one who contemplates them as being her own inherent portion.
The meaning is that the form of the entire world is partial, being dependent upon the conceptualization of parts. || 18 ||
Just as one lamp [illuminates] lamps that have arisen from itself,
so too the differentiation of the consciousness into space, time, and parts is inherent to its nature.

Space is [distinguished] by the location of its adjuncts such as a wick; time is [distinguished] by its duration through its divisions and parts; and the divisions [of time] are likewise [distinguished].

Thus, this differentiation, joined with those respective measures, does not exist in the essential nature of the lamp’s flame; similarly, for consciousness (cit) as well, [differentiation] arising from the nature of its adjuncts is not inherent. || 19 ||
Then consciousness, ignited by the power of the movement of space and time,
pursues its own volition and enters the state of conceptualization.
He establishes the example stated [in the previous verse]—namely, "deśa" (space)—as follows: || 20 ||

O mighty-armed one, the form of consciousness (cit), which assumes shapes fashioned by conceptualization and serves as the locus of space, time, and action, is called the "knower of the field" (kṣetrajña).

For this very reason, he states that the status of the consciousness as the "knower of the field" (kṣetrajña) is well-known to be dependent upon the conceptualization of the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the field: "vikalpa... (verse 21).
They say the field is the body; he knows that entire field, including both its exterior and interior, and for that reason he is called the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña). || 22 ||
Even he, while perceiving latent impressions (vāsanā), again attains the state of egoism (ahaṃkāra);
and that egoism, when it determines [objects], is called the defiled intellect (buddhi).

He shows the sequence of the conceptualization of the field with the words beginning "vāsanām" (the latent impression). The determiner is the one who makes a judgment; for this very reason, he is stained by other conceptualizations. || 23 ||
The intellect, fashioned by volitional constructs, enters the domain of the mind;
the mind, filled with dense conceptualizations, gradually attains the state of the senses. (24)
The wise know the body to consist of hands and feet, as well as the sense organs;
this body is recognized in the world as that which is born and also lives. (25)
The phrase "they go to the state of a body" is to be supplied by modifying the preceding words accordingly. || 25 ||
Thus, the individual soul (jīva), indeed ensnared by the rope of volitional tendencies (saṃkalpa-vāsanā) and its self enveloped in a web of suffering, gradually attains the state of the mind (citta).
The state of being mind means the capacity for consciousness of external objects. || 26 ||
Just as a fruit gradually attains a different state through the process of ripening,
so too does the individual soul (jīva) assume various conditions due to its impurities, and not because of its essential nature.

The fruit refers to the jujube (*badara*) and so forth; "otherness" means distinctness. This occurs solely through a change in state—namely, a transformation of qualities such as color and taste—and not by way of shape or the universal (*jāti*) such as "jujubeness.

In the same way, the living being (*jīva*), though he is the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), undergoes distinctness due to the influence of the transformation of the impurity of ignorance (*avidyā*).
The meaning is: not by way of an unchanging conscious nature. || 27 ||
The individual soul (jīva) attained the state of ego (ahaṃkāra), and that ego attained the state of intellect (buddhi);
the intellect, in turn, reached the state of mind (manas), which is ensnared by the web of volitions (saṃkalpa). || 28 ||

Having thus described the perfection of the field (*kṣetra*), he explains, in due order, the bondage of the individual soul (*jīva*)—characterized by the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of identity and association—with respect to the fields such as the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) and so forth, beginning with the words "The individual soul" (*jīva*). (28)
For the mind consists of volition and is intent upon grasping forms; it seeks even those desired objects that are real attainments distinguished from their opposites. (29)

"Configuration" (*saṃsthāna*) refers to the shape of the bodies of women, sons, and so forth; its "grasping" means its retention in the form of a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) by way of a mental modification (*vṛtti*) assuming that same form. That [cognition] is directed toward that. It is "distinguished" (*vyavacchinna*), meaning excluded, from "counter-correlates" (*pratiyogin*), that is, other objects, by means of "aims" (*īhita*)—that is, desires—which are "true," meaning fruitful, and by the word "also" (*api*), even those which are fruitless.
"Prāpti" is that by which an object is grasped; the meaning is that it becomes attached to limited and trivial objects. || 29 ||
Desire and the other powers pursue the mind, as cows pursue an intoxicated bull.

When attached to them, the mind—having fallen into the state of being an object of thought—repeatedly remembers those sense-objects and is assailed by defects such as passion and hatred; thus he says: "Desire and the others," etc. They run after and follow [the mind].
Thus, the mind, composed of creative power (śakti), having attained a state of dense egoism, enters into bondage by its own will, like a silkworm. || 31 ||
Thus, according to the sequence described, the mind— abounding in the powers of passion, hatred, and so forth—
having attained a state of dense egoism through the growth of hundreds of millions of branches of conceit,
and as if leading the body with fetters by means of its own persistent volitions; || 31 ||
Alas! Having itself come into bondage in this [body], the self suffers.

Like a fish or other creature, having approached and fallen into the snares—namely the snares of nooses, hooks, nets, and so forth—one leads one's own body to death; "self" here refers to the mind (*manas*), as it is the subject under discussion. || 32 ||

Thinking "I am bound," one gradually abandons the reality of the principle of consciousness (vidyātattva) and generates within oneself the ignorance that is like a rākṣasa lurking in the wilderness of the world.

Thinking "I am," one perceives [the ego] as the ultimate truth; abandon—that is, cast off—the reality of ignorance (*avidyā-tattva*), which is the nature of the self, until it is no longer even unconsciously entertained even in a dream. [Abandon] ignorance, which is the continuous succession of delusions such as birth and death. (33)
And dwelling within the flames produced by its own volitions, it falls into a state of supreme helplessness, like a lion bound in chains. (34)
The subtle elements (tanmātra) are the objects such as sound and so forth; the flames of passion and the like have those as their fuel; and the mind resides within them.
The word "ca" (and) serves to include the previously mentioned ignorance (avidyā) at the end of the list. || 34 ||
Under the influence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), it assumes the agency of performing diverse actions,
and likewise follows various states fashioned by its own mere will.

With effort, he assumed the agency—that is, he brought about—the performance of various actions (karmas) consisting of diverse forms of prescribed and prohibited duties; and as for the conditions (daśās)—namely, the miserable states such as various births and hells, as well as the conditions of non-remembrance and so forth to be described later—he fell into a state of helplessness following after them. This is the syntactical connection with what precedes. || 35 ||
In some places it is called the mind (manas), in some places the intellect (buddhi), in some places knowledge (jñāna), and in some places action (kriyā);
in some places this is known as the ego (ahaṃkāra), and in some places as the city of eight (puryaṣṭaka).

He states, beginning with "In some cases," that it is this very [Self] which, through the distinctions of its functions such as thinking (manana) and so forth, receives the designations of "mind" (manas) and other such terms, and not anything else. || 36 ||
In some places it is called *prakṛti*, in some it is conceived as *māyā*; in some it is declared to be *mala*, and in some it is established as *karman*.
In some places it is known as "bondage," in others it is clearly called "mind"; in some places it is declared to be "ignorance," and in others it is established as "desire. (38)
O Raghava, this very mind here is bound, suffering, overwhelmed by craving and grief, and extended toward the locus of passion. (39)
And thus, he elaborates—starting with the words "This very [state]"—that even the state of being bound belongs to that [intellect] alone, and not to the Self. || 39 ||
It is struck down by the contemplation of existence within the delusion of old age and death;
it is seized by what is desired and undesired, and stained by ignorance and passion. (40)
Its form is agitated by desire; it is the sprout of the forest of the tree of karma; it has utterly forgotten its place of origin; and it is fashioned from imagined misfortunes. (41)
By whom the state of the Supreme Self, which is the cause of his own birth, has been completely forgotten. || 41 ||
Bound like a silkworm in its cocoon, it has entered a state characterized by sorrow; it consists of a multitude of mere mental constituents and is the heat of endless hells.
Even though it is visible to oneself, this poisonous tree of saṃsāra is as terrifying in its weight as the king of mountains; it is laden with the branches of old age and death.

Although one's own self is capable of knowing even the visible world as non-self, it is terrifying due to the weight and burden of its extreme difficulty to discern— a burden as massive as the king of mountains— and it is like a poisonous, wicked tree. || 43 ||
Like a banyan seed that bears within itself a banyan tree, this entire cycle of existence— though devoid of fruit— produces within it the binding snares of hope.
Devoid of fruits, that is, the goals of human endeavor. || 44 ||
Burnt by the flames of the fire of anxiety, chewed by the python of anger,
struck by the waves of the ocean of desire, he has forgotten his own grandfather.
By whom the Grandfather, the primordial cause, has forgotten his own true nature.
Like a deer strayed from its herd, its mind overwhelmed by grief;
like a moth consumed by the flames of the fire of sensory objects. (46)
Like a lotus whose roots have been severed, it had reached a state of supreme withering;
its limbs were severed from its own place, and it was distressed by an extraordinary lack of attachment.

When one's own self is removed from its place—that is, from the specific body which serves as its dwelling—by death, it has its limbs severed through the interruption of identification with that particular body; for this very reason, it is rendered distressed due to the lack of attachment to those specific bodies. (47)
Remaining indifferent amidst sense objects and the like, and among enemies of manifold forms, it has wallowed through these endless and perilous states. (48)

The meaning is: "in those [states] whose modes have been elaborated in such a way"—that is, among enemies characterized by objects, senses, the body, and so forth, appearing in variegated forms and intent on slaying one through various diversities; and [the Self] being situated in their midst, out of misplaced trust in them. || 48 ||
The world has fallen into terrible suffering, like a bird in the ocean,
trapped in its own bonds within the net of existence, as empty as a city of Gandharvas.
That [mind] which possesses *āsthā*—an excessive attachment—to one's own bondage, to the causes of bondage, and to the body and so forth which are the instruments for that [bondage].

O you who resemble an immortal (*amara*), rescue my mind—which is being carried away in the ocean of *anāsthā* (disregard) and is distracted by sense objects—from it, just as one might rescue an elephant from the mud. (49–50)

Lift up the mind that is being carried away and floating in the ocean of that very form— namely, lack of interest and disregard for the knowledge of reality and its means— by strengthening that very disregard.
O Rāma, forcibly pull out my mind, which is submerged like a bull in the pond of passion and whose limbs are torn and shattered. (51)

When the merit accumulated through long engagement in the enjoyment of sense objects is exhausted, there is an absence of the means for proceeding to the next world; thus, one's limbs, such as the feet, are mostly severed and shattered. This is clear in the case of the ox. || 51 ||

O friend, he in whose mind no distress arises here— though his form is struck down by the expansion of the auspicious and inauspicious, and though he is fainting from the sorrow of blazing old age and death— [is truly wise].
O Rāma, that Rākṣasa in human form dwells in this world. || 52 ||

He concludes the previously mentioned lack of reliance by means of censuring others with the words "śubhāśubha" (good and evil). [It refers to] one whose form is struck down and defiled by the expansions of auspicious acts—meaning meritorious deeds performed for the sake of desire—and inauspicious acts—meaning prohibited actions; and who is thus rendered unconscious by the blazing miseries of old age and death. In such a state...

The meaning is that he who experiences distress when there is suffering in his own mind, yet feels no pain from the anxiety of considering how to rescue [the other], is a Rākṣasa indeed, merely disguised in human form. || 52 ||
Thus ends the forty-second canto, titled "The Descent of the Living Being," in the *Sthitiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by Vālmīki in the tradition of the Ṛṣis. 42.
Thus ends the forty-second chapter, titled "The Descent of the Living Being," in the *Sthitiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The forty-third canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus, the living beings are manifestations of consciousness, nourished by the mental impressions of worldly existence.
Even from hundreds of thousands or tens of millions of imagined forms of Brahmā. || 1 ||

In this work, the destinies of living beings resulting from their karma are explained in detail; it is also shown how liberation occurs for some due to the extreme difficulty of attaining discernment and other such means. || 1 ||

Having thus described the manner in which the mind acts as its own binder, [the author] now reiterates the previously mentioned birth of the individual soul (jīva) through its various modes, in order to demonstrate the connection for describing the diversity of the ways in which the souls— whose nature is consciousness conditioned by that mind— remain in the cycle of transmigratory existence until liberation.

By the words "evam" and so forth: the states (*bhāva*) of consciousness (*citaḥ*), which are adventitious (*aupādhika*) and of the nature of differentiation (*vibhāvarūpa*), are the individual souls (*jīva*). They are "impelled" (*ūhita*)—the form *iṭ* is Vedic—meaning they are set in motion by the "contemplation of existence" (*bhavabhāvanā*), that is, by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of saṃsāra. The connection with the subsequent [text] is as follows: they are born from Brahman, whose forms are imagined according to prior latent impressions (*pūrvavāsanā*). || 1 ||
O sir, countless [beings] have been born in the past, they are being born even now, and they will continue to be born, like a torrent of water droplets from a mountain cascade. (2)
They are born right now, this very day. "O! is an address to Rāma. || 2 ||

Overcome by the influence of their own latent impressions, they have fallen into a state of helplessness regarding their hopes; with their intentions bound of their own accord, they remain within these most diverse conditions of existence.
Without ceasing, in every direction, in every land, upon water and on dry ground,
beings are born or die like bubbles in water.
"Anārataṃ" means constantly. The two words beginning with "vā" are synonyms. || 4 ||
Some have had only one birth; some more than a hundred births;
some an incalculable number of births; and some are within two or three lifetimes [of liberation]. || 5 ||
Those who have their first birth in this kalpa have attained only one birth. Those for whom no number of births exists are "those whose number of births is non-existent" (ajanmasaṃkhyākāḥ). || 5 ||
Some belong to future births, some have arisen from past existences; some belong to the present life, while others have gone to the state of non-existence.

Those for whom birth—that is, future rebirth—exists are "those whose birth is yet to come" (*bhaviṣyajjātayaḥ*); the meaning is that they have not yet arisen even now in this *kalpa*. Those who have "come into being" (*bhūta*) are those who have passed away; those for whom there is no further arising of existence are, in other words, the "liberated while living" (*jīvanmukta*). [The verse speaks of] the liberation from the body (*videhamukti*) for those who are no longer subject to becoming (*abhavatām*). || 6 ||
Some, being born again and again for thousands of kalpas,
remain within a single womb, while others have resorted to different wombs.
The womb, that is, the birth from a body. || 7 ||
Some endure great suffering, while others remain with little prosperity; some are exceedingly joyful, and others have arisen like the sun and other luminaries.
The denizens of hell endure great suffering; mortals experience little arising and little happiness; the gods are exceedingly joyful;
and those who go to Satyaloka are like the sun and other luminaries that have arisen.
Some were kinnaras, gandharvas, vidyādharas, and mahoragas; some were Arka, Indra, Varuṇa, the Three-eyed One, Adhokṣaja, and the Lotus-born.
The mention of "the three-eyed one" and so forth refers to those living beings who have attained a resemblance to the three-eyed deity and others.
Some were kūśmāṇḍas, vetālas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas;
some remained as brahmins, kings, and groups of vaiśyas and śūdras. || 10 ||
Some were dog-cookers, Cāṇḍālas, Kirātas, Āveśas, and Puṣkasas;
some were grasses and herbs, and some were fruits, roots, and moths. || 11 ||
Those very beings who have entered the womb of Kirātas are "possessed by Kirātas. The dual number in "tṛṇauṣadhī" (grass and herbs) refers to the two classes [of species].
The mention of "fruits and roots" is intended to include the living beings existing in the state of seeds contained within them. || 11 ||
Some appeared everywhere like variegated creepers, shrubs, grass, and stones;
others were like kadamba, jambīra, śāla, tāla, and tamāla trees.

The mention of "grass" once again is for the purpose of illustrating the diversity of its intermediate species. Those who perceive a stone as their own body are called "stone-seers," such as mountains and the like. || 12 ||
Some were ministers, vassals, and regional lords within the cycle of worldly existence;
others, clothed in bark garments, had attained the silence of sages.

They are called "wandering through the cycle of existence" (vibhava-saṃsāra) because they wander and transmigrate through various states of being; or they are so called because they are clothed in rags for the sake of asceticism, due to the difficulty of obtaining fine garments. || 13 ||
Some were serpents, pythons, worms, insects, and ants; others were lions, buffaloes, deer, goats, yaks, and antelopes. (14)
Gonāsas are pythons. || 14 ||
Some became cranes, ruddy geese, herons, cormorants, and cuckoos;
others took on the form of lotuses, white water-lilies, night-blooming lilies, and blue lotuses. (15)
Some were young elephants, great elephants, boars, bulls, and donkeys; others were bees, mosquitoes, gnats, and those born from stinging insects.
*Kalabha* means a young elephant; *puttikā* means a small fly. || 16 ||
Some are overcome by the force of calamity, some have attained prosperity;
some reside in the city of heaven, while others are situated in hell.
Some were situated upon the circle of stars; others had entered into the hollows of trees;
some remained as if they had become wind, while others were stationed in the realm of space.

The "bear-circle" (ṛkṣacakra) is the circle of constellations; those situated therein have become like the wind, having attained mastery over the winds such as the Āvaha and Pravaha. In the "station of space" (vyomapada), that is, in the domain of the ether. || 18 ||
Some abide in the rays of the sun; some abide in the rays of the moon;
and some abide in the sweet essences of grasses, creepers, and shrubs.
In the rays of the sun, there is the authority for the extraction of sap; in the rays of the moon, there is the authority for the nourishment of plants and the like.
Wherein lies the sweet essence of grass and other such things—meaning, that which is fit for animals and the like, and characterized by a craving for sense objects. || 19 ||
Some here wander as liberated while living (jīvanmukta), vessels of auspiciousness;
some remain as those long-liberated; others are surely fully matured.
Others, having merged into the Supreme Self and attained that very state, are liberated while in the disembodied state (videhamukta). || 20 ||
Some will become auspiciously liberated after a long period of time; others, being of the nature of consciousness, hate their own state of isolation (kaivalya).
Living beings, being of the nature of consciousness yet greedy for enjoyment, hate the state of the Kevalin, which is liberation. || 21 ||
Some were vast quarters of the sky, some were rivers of great velocity,
some were women with lovely eyes, and some were eunuchs and neuter beings.
The quarters are the deities of the directions. || 22 ||
Some possess awakened intellects, while others have extremely dull dispositions;
some are instructors of knowledge, and others have attained meditative absorption.

All these [misfortunes] arise solely from the latent impressions (vāsanā) of the evils of saṃsāra; therefore, with the intention that those very impressions must be eradicated along with their roots, he concludes with the verse beginning "jīvāḥ.
The repetition "in each of these" (etāsvetāsu) is used for the purpose of including everything mentioned and everything not yet mentioned. || 24 ||
Living beings, rendered helpless by the onset of their own latent impressions (vāsanās),
remain in these various states with their mental dispositions firmly bound.
They dwell upon the earth, they fall into hell, and they soar up to heaven; for this very reason, they are like balls.
Some beings dwell, some fall, and others leap up;
incessantly struck by Death as if by a hand, they are like balls. (25)
They dwell upon the earth, they fall into hell, and they rise up into heaven; for this very reason, they are like balls. 25.
Bound by hundreds of snares of hope and bearing the latent impressions of their past states, they pass from body to body like birds flying from tree to tree. (26)
Those whose nature is such that they maintain entities in the form of latent impressions (vāsanā), such as future bodies and so forth. || 26 ||
By means of the illusion that produces the conceptualization of infinite and endless volitions,
she spreads out this great world-enchantment consisting of the universe.
By means of ignorance (*avidyā*), which is illusion (*māyā*) acting as the cause for producing infinite conceptualizations and imaginings regarding infinite objects.
Fools wander in saṃsāra like masses of whirlpools in water for as long as they do not perceive their own blameless Self. 28.
The phrase "like whirlpools and depths" is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 28 ||
Having seen the Self and abandoned the unreal, having attained true consciousness and reached the supreme state in due time, they are not born here again.
He states what the benefit is for the discerning ones from the vision of the Self: "Having seen," etc. By means of time, through the sequence of the consolidation of the stages (bhūmikās). || 29 ||
Having experienced thousands of births, some who are ignorant fall once again into the perils of saṃsāra, even after attaining discernment.
He describes the destination of those who have fallen away from discernment with the words beginning "Having enjoyed... (verse 30).
Some, even after attaining a high state of power, return again to the condition of animals due to their base intellect,
and from the state of animals they fall even into the hells.
"Power" (*śaktatva*) refers to being endowed with excellence such as a praiseworthy birth, place, time, intelligence, humility, and association with the virtuous.

"High status" (*uccaiḥ*) consists of the form of supreme prosperity, such as that of the gods, *gandharvas*, and *brāhmaṇas*. "By his own intellect alone" means by means of a mind that is trivial and obsessed with trivial objects. In the reading *śakratvam*, it refers to Nahuṣa.
This is to be cited as an example. || 31 ||
Some, being of great intelligence, having arisen from the state of Brahmā,
immediately upon that very birth, swiftly and completely enter back into that same place.
The high-minded ones, Sanaka and the others; at that very time, in that very kalpa; there, in the state of Brahman known as liberation.
In other cosmic eggs, there are different multitudes of living beings;
some attain the state of being born from a lotus (Brahmā), while others even attain the state of being Hara (Śiva).
In other Brahmāṇḍas where they themselves were born, just like the followers of Indu; in those Brahmāṇḍas which are their own places of birth, let them attain the same form as Hara. || 33 ||
Some go to the state of animals, others even to the state of gods;
others too, O Rāma, reach the human world, just as they do here.
Whether moving like serpents or moving like living beings; the implication is that just as it is here in this universe, so it is likewise in other universes as well. || 34 ||
Just as this vast universe exists, so too do other universes exist;
many have passed away, and many more will come to be.
This world is the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa); worlds are cosmic eggs. 35.
Through various diverse sequences and by different causes, their manifold creations arise and fall away. (36)
They descend and manifest, and they fall and disappear. || 36 ||
One becomes a Gandharva, another goes to the state of a Yakṣa; one attains the state of a Suras, and another comes to the state of a Daitya. || 37 ||
With the intention that even within this very universe, the course of the individual soul is diverse due to the variety of karma, he says: "Someone... (verse 37).
By the very same conventions by which people abide in this cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa),
they likewise abide in others, though differing in their specific arrangements.

They are distinguished solely by their specific conventions suitable for humans and so forth, and by differences in their configuration and physical form, like the inhabitants of other continents. (38)
Through the mutual friction resulting from the influence of their own respective natures, creations revolve like the waves of a river. (39)

Let it be so; nevertheless, how does the cycle of creation proceed through their mutual affection, opposition, and the like, according to their status as superior, inferior, and so forth? To this he says: "By virtue of their respective natures," etc.
It proceeds from the engagement in activities corresponding to each [nature], by the power of their respective natures—such as *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and *tāmasa*.
The meaning is that the revolution of creation occurs through the mutual friction of thoughts competing for a single object.
Through manifestations and disappearances, through emergences and submergences, creations revolve like the waves of a river. (40)

Regarding that as well, he says "manifestation" (*āvirbhāva*) and so forth. When *rajas* manifests, there is the emergence of creation and the submergence of *sattva* and *tamas*; when *tamas* manifests and *rajas* is concealed, there is the submergence of creation;
and when *sattva* manifests in the interval, there is preservation for that duration—thus [the functions] revolve according to the shifting of their causes.
The meaning is that they revolve. || 40 ||
From that Supreme [Self], the multitudes of individual souls emerge incessantly;
indescribable and self-cognizable, they flash forth rapidly right there.

With the intention that the emergence of the individual soul (jīva) as conditioned by those [attributes] is well-known through the creation of the internal organ and so forth—which are dependent on the qualities—he says: "They emerge" (niryānti). Therein, in that Supreme [Self] alone, they manifest clearly and function. || 41 ||
Like light from a lamp, like rays from the sun, like sparks from heated iron, or like scintillations from a fire. (42)
In this regard, he states an example well-known from scripture and other sources: "From a lamp," etc. (42).
The various manifestations of time and so forth are like the diverse fragrances from flowers, like the coolness resulting from a shower of rain, or like the waves of the ocean. || 43 ||
They are cool, like snowflakes. || 43 ||
Having experienced a succession of bodies over time through repeated births,
the multitudes of living beings naturally attain their final rest in the supreme state.
In the state of dissolution, which is peaceful and serves as the seed, [he attains] a dwelling, that is, a state of absorption. || 44 ||
This delusive illusion (*māyā*) that constructs the three worlds is incessantly spread abroad; thus, it rises high, perishes, and grows again— all in vain.
In the supreme state, like a wave in the ocean. || 45 ||
He concludes the brief exposition on the creation of the living world with the words "uninterrupted" (*aviratam*).

This Māyā, characterized by the delusion of the construction of the three worlds, has been spread forth in vain within the Supreme State (*paramapada*)—continually and incessantly; thus it expands through creation, and likewise it rises high, undergoes transformation, and perishes.
The analogy "like a wave in the ocean" is cited regarding the state of being in vain. || 45 ||

Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Abode of the Multitude of Living Beings," in the Section on Stability (*sthitiprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Valmiki, within the *Divya Mokṣopāya*.
Thus ends the forty-third chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Abode of the Multitude of Living Beings," in the *Sthitiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The forty-fourth canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
By this sequence, by which the soul attains its own state of existence...
O Blessed One, how does he compose his body, this cage of bones? || 1 ||
Although liberation and dissolution are similar, a distinction between them is proclaimed here;
likewise is the sequence of the assumption of a body by the soul of Viriñci.

Regarding what was stated—that at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), the multitudes of individual souls (*jīva-rāśi*) dissolve by themselves within the [supreme] space—Rāma raises a doubt with the word "gradually" (*krameṇa*). By this, he refers to the sequence you described: "having been born again and again, and having experienced a succession of bodies over time. He asks: which soul, having attained its own abiding in the supreme state at the time of dissolution through that very process, [remains there]?

If he is already liberated, why does he take on a body again? For if there were a return for one who has attained the supreme state, it would follow that there is no confidence even in liberation. Nor can there be a distinction made by the state of being a seed for one still shrouded in ignorance; for one who is without a seed [of rebirth], there is no such thing.
The meaning is that, because a stone fragment or similar object is not seen to possess the nature of a seed for sprouts and so forth merely due to being obscured by ignorance. || 1 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāma, I have already told you this; why do you not understand?
Where has your discernment, which ought to consider what precedes and what follows, gone?

Even though a rope or similar object is not seen to be the cause (bīja) of a snake or the like that possesses the same ontological status as itself, it is observed to be the cause of a snake or such things that possess the same ontological status as the obscuration; therefore, you can infer by your own intellect—even without it being explicitly stated—that the status of being a false cause is produced solely by the obscuration. Thus, there is no fault.
With the intention that this is worthy of inquiry, he states the answer: "Precisely previously," etc. (2).
For this world, consisting of bodies and so forth, both stationary and moving, is merely an appearance, arisen like an unreal dream. (3)
Appearance is transformation; it is merely that much.
O sinless Rāma, this is indeed a long dream that appears as something entirely false—
like the illusion of two moons, or like mountains seen within a delusion.
To the question of how things that endure for a long time—such as the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) and the worlds—are merely appearances, he says: "Long... (verse 4).
But he whose sleep of ignorance has been stilled, whose mental constructions have dissolved, and whose mind is awakened, does not perceive the dream of saṃsāra even while seeing it. || 5 ||

With the intention that even when the dream of saṃsāra appears, it does not affect the knower because the state of being a seed for the self of ignorance has ceased, he says: "tranquil," etc. Though seeing what is fit for the conduct of one liberated while living, he does not see it from the perspective of ultimate reality. || 5 ||
O Rāma, for all living beings, this world-process indeed exists within the self at all times until the attainment of the state of liberation; it is imagined as having an intrinsic nature.

With the intention that rebirth occurs because the nature of the self, which has become a seed, exists in a subtle form within future saṃsāra until liberation, he says: "By its own nature," etc. (verse 6).
The body of the living being is as flickering as a whirlpool in water;
it is like the swelling sprout within a seed, or like the leaf within its own sprout.
There are such analogies as: "The body is flickering within the living being, just as a whirlpool is within water," and so forth. (7)
Just as a flower is within its bud and fruit is within the calyx, so too does that body, which is of the nature of mental construction, exist within the mind. (8)
He states the reason why the body exists within the living being with the words "yataḥ" (since). "Antare" means in the middle. || 8 ||
O Rāma, because it possesses manifold forms, that which is clearly one among them arises indeed as the very manifestation of this mind.
Regarding how a body can even be conceived there, he says: "by way of manifold form.
The meaning is that since the mind is well known to be manifold in form, a body-form is also possible there in the nature of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
If it is asked why many bodies are not produced simultaneously, he says: "because... [in] many...

The meaning is that among those [latent impressions] which exist in the form of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), whichever one alone is made manifest—clearly revealed—by fully ripened karmas, that very appearance generally arises for him at that time, and not all of them. || 9 ||
That very [consciousness] quickly becomes this body, like a lump of clay becoming a jar;
in the primordial creation, it was formerly the supreme manifestation of this [being].

This mind itself becomes that body. In this regard, he demonstrates—starting from the initial creation—that when there is the ripening of superior karma, a superior body alone comes into being, by saying "at the initial creation" (ādisarge). || 10 ||
Since this all-pervading Brahmā was situated within the interior of the lotus-bud,
it therefore attained its existence solely through the process of his volition.
"Thus, creation is infinite, like an illusion produced by a dense delusion.
Śrī Rāma said:
"The individual soul (jīva), having attained the state of mind (manas), reaches the station of Brahmā (vairiñca). (12)
"O Brahman, tell me everything in detail exactly as it is; speak to me quickly.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
"O mighty-armed Brahman, listen to the sequence of taking on a body."
By that very illustration, you shall understand the state of the world:
the reality of the Self, which is unconditioned by space, time, and the like, [manifests] through its own power.

When he assumes, as if in mere play, a body defined by space and time, at that very moment it becomes a manifestation of the individual soul (jīva), intent upon the penetration of latent impressions (vāsanā).
The mind becomes restless, intent upon the process of conceptualization;
the power of the mind, beginning its purification, first brings about [this state] in an instant.

He explains what was stated as "intent upon both manifestation and non-manifestation" with the passage beginning "kalayantī" (manifesting): the mind, which in the previous creation was refined by the practice of identifying with Hiraṇyagarbha—who had emerged in the sequence starting from space—and which thus dissolved back into the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*), is called *śakti*; that [power] [emerges] again in that very same sequence.
The meaning is: being such that she imagines her own manifestation. || 16 ||
Then, from that mental state which is as pure as the contemplation of space and oriented toward the essence of the seed-syllable of sound,
the mind attains density through the process of dense vibration.

The seed of sounds is the subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātra), and their essence is the sense of hearing; having attained that state of meditative cultivation upon such space, the mind reaches a state of density and accumulation. (17)
With the eye of the mind, he contemplates the movement of the wind, which is oriented toward the moisture of the seed of touch, through those two— the ether and the wind— which are invisible.

"By means of the nature of air" refers to slight vibration or movement. "The seed of touch," and so forth, is as explained previously. Because it is extremely subtle due to being unquintuplicated (*apañcīkṛta*), it is perceived by the mind—by the individual soul (*jīva*) whose nature is consciousness delimited by the mind—through the two [factors of] unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*). || 18 ||
Fire is produced from the combination of the natures of sound and touch;
the mind, having reached that state, then brings it forth in an instant.
From aggregation, from accumulation, and from impact, fire consists of the essence of the seeds of form. (19)
Through that light, the stainless illumination of luminosity increases;
meanwhile, the mind, having attained its qualities, experiences the subtle element of taste.
"Attaining such a quality" means having reached an accumulation—a multiplication—by those same number of spaces, winds, and fires. || 20 ||
Within half a moment, however, the coldness of the water arises from the perception of the water;
thereafter, the mind, having attained such qualities, contemplates that very state in an instant. (21)

The meaning is that the coldness of water, having attained the subtle element of taste (*rasatanmātra*), becomes perceived as "water"; that is to say, it becomes fit for the cognition of consciousness. Such [subtle elements], having reached the state of a composite aggregate of these four qualities mentioned above, [become gross matter]. || 21 ||
Its own form will be gross and fragrant, by which the earth shall emerge;
then, having been enveloped by such subtle elements (tanmātras), it shall abandon its state of subtlety.
The use of the *lṛṭ* (future tense) in "it will arise" (*udeṣyati*) is intended to express futurity with reference to the time of birth of the preceding elements.
This group of five, when combined and enveloped by the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), abandons its state of being a body—that is, it relinquishes its subtlety (*saukṣmya*).
One perceives a body in the form of sparks of fire flashing in the sky, joined with a portion of egoism and endowed with the seed of the intellect. (23)
The grammatical connection is: that body which one perceives is called the *liṅga*, namely the "city of eight" (*puryaṣṭaka*). || 23 ||
That is called the "City of Eight" (puryaṣṭaka), a bee within the lotus of the heart of beings;
by means of intense spiritual fervor, one should contemplate its radiant form therein.

The groups of organs of action and knowledge, the elements, the vital breaths, and the mind, along with ignorance, desire, and karma—these, by their marks (*liṅga*), are known as the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*). For, through the process of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*) of this very subtle body (*liṅga*), its density results in the manifestation of the gross body; this is what he states by means of the forthcoming contemplation of the body: [The text continues: "By the process of quintuplication of this very subtle body (*liṅga*), its density results in the manifestation of the gross body; this is what he states by means of the forthcoming contemplation of the body."
"But in that case," [it is said]. || 24 ||
Through this maturation, the mind attains solidity like a wood-apple fruit;
it shines in the stainless sky, possessing the luster of molten gold within a crucible.

That light—the agent—assumes the form of a *liṅga*, which is like a lump of clay containing within it a crucible in the shape of a mold; it is like molten gold poured inside that [clay], appearing gross and radiant on the outside while being subtle and radiant within, conjoined with the gross body, and possessing the configuration to be described hereafter. || 25 ||
That fire assumes a configuration according to its own inherent nature;
and within that configuration, which consists of a mass of fire, [the mind (or "manas" is also a reading)]...
Regarding that, he says "in that [mind]" and so forth, stating that the mind is a mass of branches and sub-branches consisting of the conceptualization and adherence to distinctions. || 26 ||
He cultivates an expansive, certain, and vast meditation,
which consists of the seat of the head above and likewise the feet below.

"Ātatāmbarām" means having pervaded the sky—that is, having extended as far as the limitless space. Regarding that, he describes the conceptualization of the parts, beginning with the head, in sequence, starting with the word "ūrdhvam" (above). || 27 ||
With hands positioned at his sides and a belly in the middle,
the child’s limbs were clearly manifest, and his form was pure with garlands of flames.
With its limbs made manifest through the completion of the fingers and other parts. || 28 ||
Then, by the power of his mental resolve, he remains with a body assumed [therein];
thus, through the influence of his own latent impressions (vāsanā), the sage of the mind (manomuni) has fashioned his limbs.
He is Brahmā; the sage is one whose nature is to reflect upon the manner in which he previously practiced worship. || 29 ||
