Just as the season brings its own inherent nature to fullness, it causes the body to reach growth;
in time, it attains clarity and becomes a stainless form. (30)
Established in the power of intellect, goodness, strength, energy, discernment, and sovereignty, he alone is the Blessed Lord Brahmā, the grandfather of all the worlds. || 31 ||

He demonstrates the attainment of those attributes well-known from the Smṛtis— namely that "the Lord of the World possesses incomparable knowledge, dispassion, sovereignty, and righteousness as a fourfold set established by nature"—
with the words: "Resembling molten gold, born from the supreme ether."
Just as he abides in the supreme ether, possessing no other form. || 32 ||

The meaning is this: just as that [Self] exists in the supreme ether (paramākāśa) which is Brahman by means of its own being (svasattā), so too, by means of a being capable of empirical transaction (vyavahārakṣamasattā) of exactly that same kind, it produces for itself delusion—which is indeed ignorance (ajñāna)—through the play of the mind (cittalīlā) in the form of the gross five-fold ether and so forth, which will be described later. || 32 ||
By the play of the mind, it sometimes produces within itself a delusion regarding its own nature—
[perceiving] as mere space that which is supreme and devoid of limits.

He shows the various kinds of conceptualizations regarding that [space] according to the difference in time, beginning with "kadācit" (sometimes). The meaning is that he imagines a mere void (*kevalaṃ vyoma*) which lacks a limit on this side (*pāra*), a limit on the other side (*parāvadhi*), a starting point (*ādi*), a limit at the end (*paryanta*), and a limit on the sides (*pārśvato'vadhi*); thus, it is devoid of even a middle limit. || 33 ||
Without beginning, middle, or end, it is sometimes pure water,
and sometimes a mass of light shining with the flames of the fire at the end of an aeon.
At the time of the daily dissolution, however, he fashions only pure water; sometimes at the end of a kalpa, during the time of universal conflagration;
sometimes a forest, sometimes blackness, sometimes Time, or a lotus bud—the Lord is the limit of every birth, manifesting various and manifold forms. || 34–35 ||

At one time, following the creation of the earth and prior to the creation of living beings, he beheld the entire forest—the whole earth covered with trees—as being "kārṣṇya," meaning black; here the suffix *ṣyañ* is used in the sense of the base word itself (*svārthe*), as in the term *cāturvarṇya*. At another time, during the Padma Kalpa...

Because he has the nature of a dark-blue lotus, he fashioned Time as a dark lotus bud arising from the navel of Viṣṇu; and fashioning various other manifold forms and configurations such as the worlds, the oceans, and living beings, he himself protects them in the form of Viṣṇu and others.
He effortlessly creates and protects these various forms;
therein, by virtue of being the very first, he [proceeds] from the station of Brahmā.

Beginning from the first kalpa, he demonstrates the process of conceptualizing one's own body for one who has just awakened from sleep, starting with the words "tatra" (therein). Since all cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍas*) and the Brahmās who preside over them manifest from the very state of Brahman, which is not limited by time, there is no sequence of priority or posteriority from that perspective.
Intending "precisely the state of being first," it is said "as being for the very first time. || 36 ||
Then, having descended from that state due to ignorance, he likewise remains in a blissful state of non-recollection;
upon the cessation of the sleep of the womb, he beholds his radiant body.

From the moment he entered [the womb], whether within the interior of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) or within the belly of Viṣṇu, he remained in a state of deep sleep—characterized by the bliss of sound sleep, devoid of memory, and consisting in the non-recollection of his former real form, bodily functions, and so forth; this is the sense of the verse. || 37 ||
Rich with the flow of prāṇa and apāna, as if constructed from material substances,
it is covered with millions of pores and endowed with thirty-two teeth.
By means of substances consisting of the pure portions of the five elements. || 38 ||
It has three pillars, five deities, and is marked at the bottom by feet;
it consists of five parts, possesses nine gates, and its limbs are made smooth with a coating of skin.
It has three pillars formed by the bones of the thighs and the back; it has five divine supports consisting of the five vital breaths;
and it has five parts consisting of the hands, feet, head, chest, and belly.
It was appropriately twenty finger-breadths in length, marked by twenty nails;
it had two arms, two breasts, and two eyes, yet also possessed many eyes and many arms.
By his will, he may at times even possess many eyes and arms.
It is the nest of the bird of the mind, the lair of the serpent of passion,
the abode of the demoness of craving, and the cave of the lion of life.
Then Brahmā, having observed his own most excellent and lovely body—which was a tethering post for the elephant of pride and adorned with the lotus of his mind—[became enamored]. (42)
The Blessed One, whose vision is stainless regarding the three periods of time, reflected upon this vast expanse of space, marked by bees.
By the word "madhupa" (bee), a similar blackness is indicated; [the moon] is marked by that. || 43 ||
Having just been born, Brahmā, whose vision perceives the stainless Self, thought: "In this [universe] whose further limit is unseen, what was there in the beginning? (44)

"First" means prior to my birth. The two occurrences of the word "iti" are used for emphasis (*vīpsā*) in order to include the consideration of all preceding particulars. He is one whose self-vision (*ātmadṛk*) is stainless—due to its purity—and capable of perceiving the past and the future. || 44 ||
He beheld the numerous multitudes of creations that had passed away many times over;
then, he recalled all the various groups of dharmas in their proper sequence.
Then, immediately after reflecting upon that cause; "all" means including the limbs and sub-limbs;
the mention of the "multitude of dharmas" is also an elliptical indication for non-dharmas. || 45 ||
Like the spring season taking up flowers, he took the well-praised Vedas and effortlessly fashioned creatures born of his wondrous resolve.
For this very reason, with the intention that even his subsequent creation became easily accomplished precisely according to the sequence prescribed in the Vedas, he says:
"by play" (līlayā). || 46 ||

[This was spoken] regarding their various conducts and observances, which are like a city of the Gandharvas, for the sake of their attainment of heaven and liberation, and for the accomplishment of dharma, desire, and wealth. (47)
He composed infinite and diverse treatises;
thus, O Rāma, this very vision has come to abide within this creation,
like the beauty of flowers from the mind of Viriñci, as from the springtime.
He concludes by summarizing that the proposition—that the entire creation proceeds from the mind alone—has been established in this manner:
"The vision... (verse 48).
O son of Raghu, she was led away by the mind alone— which had assumed the form of the lotus-born Brahmā— through various compositions and playful acts of creation.
The glory of creation here in this world has attained incomparable stability. || 49 ||

The meaning is that the splendor of creation, as it was being manifested in the lineage of the Raghus— that son of Raghu— was brought by him to a state of incomparable and peerless stability through his mind alone, which took the form of a lotus-born [Brahmā], because that state was characterized by a reality distinct from the insubstantial. || 49 ||

Thus ends the forty-fourth canto, titled "The Instruction on the Exposition of the Descent into Saṃsāra," in the Section on Stability (*sthitiprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, the Great Epic of Vasiṣṭha. 44.
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Exposition of the Descent into Saṃsāra," in the *Sthitiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The forty-fifth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
This world is indeed already accomplished; nothing at all remains to be accomplished.
And it remains as mere appearance, empty and a play of the mind. || 1 ||
Since it is observed in dreams and the like, the mind is the effect [of the cause], and nothing exists as real anywhere;
therefore, the form of the world is unreal, while the Real is described as being only the Existent (Sat). || 1 ||

Though it appears complete and fully established, nothing at all has been accomplished; for everything that is a play of the mind remains as mere appearance and mere manifestation. The meaning is that apart from that, it is simply empty;
space and time are not situated as something enveloped by this cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
Even by one who possesses a great form, though that form is as subtle as space, not even slightly [is it affected].
Furthermore, from what [source] could there be emptiness of that [universe] apart from its appearance? To this he says: "No.

Because the space and time of appearance are not covered—that is, not pervaded—by this delimited universe, even for the millions of universes situated outside in the past and future, just as [the space] within a mote of dust is [not covered] by sunlight.

Because its throbbing is seen within appearances. To say more: even by space (*ākāśa*), the first element, which is established as being of the nature of great form and possessing supreme magnitude, those two [the heart and the self] are not pervaded.
For according to the Vedic scripture, "He is greater than space," there is no evidence for His greatness if space were not itself manifest.
It should be understood that since its manifestation must necessarily be described as occurring within another appearance,

the phrase "even slightly" (*manāgapi*) is used to indicate that its pervasiveness across space and time— characteristic of that which is one among the infinite varieties of appearing objects— is refuted. || 2 ||
Consisting of mere volition, like a city seen in a dream, wherever it may be, that [world] is empty; there remains only the absolute void.

Let it be granted that there is no pervasion of prior or posterior space and time; however, even regarding the space and time belonging to its own substratum (*svāśraya*), there is no possibility of pervasion by the appearance because the superimposed object does not touch the substratum. With this intention, he says: "This [is so]. In whatever space and time the world appears in Consciousness (*cit*), in that very same space and time is its substratum, Consciousness.
The meaning is that the world is empty, existing as nothing but space alone. || 3 ||
Even that which is not made of clay is seen as a painting without attachment to a wall; this wonderful, variegated picture exists in the sky, uncreated yet appearing as created.
For this very reason, it was stated previously that "this is like a painting in a city of Gandharvas"; thus he says: "without a wall" (abhitti). || 4 ||
Everything from the body to the three worlds is imagined by the mind;
this is the cause for their manifestation, just as the eye is the cause for the perception of light.

Furthermore, since the mind is the cause of mere recollection (*smṛti*), this [mental construction] is composed of that and is thus equivalent to recollection; it does not exist as a real object at its own time. To this he says: "By the mind" (*manasā*). This refers to the mind. (5)
For the world is a mere appearance, revolving through the delusions of jars, huts, and cloths;
it does not exist as something separate from the nature of reality, nor do walls and such things stand apart from it.
He states that because it is impossible to show the world—such as walls and so forth—as something distinct from what exists, it is non-existent apart from existence: "Ābhāsa... (verse 6).
For this body has been fashioned by the mind for the sake of latent impressions (vāsanā),
just as a silkworm creates its own cocoon within itself.

Just as one fashions a cocoon for oneself out of one's own substance, even so this body is fashioned as a nest for the sake of its own latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and for its maintenance, in the manner of a silkworm’s cocoon; such is the meaning. (7) And there is nothing whatsoever that is not the mental resolve of the consciousness, like the sky.
He performs no action and attains nothing, even that which is difficult or exceedingly hard to achieve.

He states "na tat" (not that) because the logical consistency of the aforementioned point is established by the well-known fact that the power to acquire even non-existent things exists through the mere volition of the mind.

The word "yat" is neuter in gender, used in a general sense. The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: "That which does not create—that is, does not attain—the sky, which is empty of objects, and which consists of volition. [The phrase] "durgam" means difficult to reach. || 8 ||
In the case of the God who possesses all powers, what indeed are those powers that do not exist [independently], yet by which the inner caves of the mind are resorted to? (9)

The syntactical connection is as follows: those powers by which the cave of the mind is not pervaded within—even in the case of the Lord of the Universe, the Divine, what powers whatsoever could possibly exist? || 9 ||
For indeed, O mighty-armed one, the existence and non-existence of all things at all times occur only when the omnipresent, all-powerful Lord exists.

If the world is always non-existent and Brahman is always existent, and if there is always no contact between the two, then how can there be occasional existence and non-existence in the world? To this he says: "Existence and non-existence. These are not occasional, but rather eternal. The conceptualization of their alternating entry through mutual suppression is indeed inconceivable.
The sense is that it is produced by the power of illusion (māyā-śakti). || 10 ||
Behold, O son, how by means of meditative cultivation (bhāvanā) one attains a body through the mind alone;
therefore, O Rāma, they know that mental ideation (kalanā) to be endowed with all powers.
He says, "Behold," so that this sovereign power of all capacities may be seen directly within one's own mind.
He further states that even the powers of the various objects in the world arise solely from the mental construction of the omnipotent mind:
"All [beings], such as gods, asuras, and humans, are created by one's own volition."
When one's own volitions are stilled, they extinguish like a lamp without oil.
For this very reason, with the intention that liberation cannot be obstructed even by the powers of the gods and others, he says: "By one's own volition... (verse 12).
O one of great intelligence, behold the entire world as being like space, a manifestation of mere mental construction, arisen like a very long dream. (13)
Nothing whatsoever is born or dies here at any time; according to the ultimate truth, O wise one, everything that appears exists only as a false illusion. (14)
That which neither increases nor decreases and is never anything at all—what could possibly be minute therein, and for whom, indeed, could there be any destruction? (15)

But it has not been diminished by fragmentation; for there is no possibility of defining that which is indivisible without fragmentation, nor is fragmentation itself possible—this is the meaning. || 15 ||
O Rāghava, not seeing with your skillful vision that which has become the ground and has arisen from your own body, why do you, like an ignorant man, become deluded within yourself? 16.
The state of being much is "plentitude" (bhūmā); it is thus [described as] such. That is to say, it is unlimited.
Seeing that which has arisen from your own body as distinct [from it], like a blade of grass from a clump of munja grass, why do you become deluded by a limited perception of the self? || 16 ||
Just as a mirage appears due to heat, so too do all these beings, from Brahmā downwards, appear as if they were real through the mental determination of the mind, though they are non-existent. 17.
From heat—that is, from the rays of the sun; from certainty—that is, from volitional resolve. || 17 ||
All the multitudes of forms in this world are like the illusion of two moons, arisen like a daydream, and are dense masses of false cognition. (18)
The "masses of forms" are the collections of visible forms. (18)
Just as the perception of a stationary post as moving by one traveling in a boat is false,
so too this constant succession of forms has arisen as something unreal.
Know this to be a magical illusion, a cage constructed by *māyā*; it is a creation of the mind's own reflections, existing as if neither real nor unreal. (20)
It is as if non-existent, yet as if real. || 20 ||
This entire world is indeed Brahman; how, then, can there be any otherness?
What occasion for it could there be, what would it be like, where would it reside, or where does it exist? (21)

Of otherness (*anyatā*), that is, of difference (*bheda*). By four interrogative particles (*kiṃvṛtta*), there is a negation of its means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), its modes (*prakāra*), its essential nature (*svarūpa*), and its substratum (*ādhāra*). That is otherness. || 21 ||
"This is a mountain, this is a post"—such is the delusion of grandeur;
through the firmness of mental cultivation, that which is non-existent appears as if it were existent. (22)
The mountain is the limit of increase, and the pillar is the limit of decrease; by these two, all the delusive displays of intermediate distinctions are likewise characterized. || 22 ||

O Rāma, this world is the beginning of a descent into conceptual proliferation for one who is heedless; abandon the mental preoccupation with desire and craving, and contemplate that which is other. 23.

For a man who is heedless and devoid of discernment, this world—which consists of the gratification of desires and cravings—initiates a fall into the manifold expansion (*prapañca*) of births as gods, denizens of hell, animals, and so forth; thus, the remainder of the meaning is that "the commencement of falling into the manifold expansion occurs.
Therefore, having abandoned the world through discernment, [seek] the other: the Self, which is free from the manifold expansion (*niṣprapañca*).
The meaning is "one should cultivate. || 23 ||
Just as a dream with its great undertakings is merely an illusion and not a reality, know that this long dream is likewise produced by the mind. (24)
Abandon this ostentation of saṃsāra, which appears as great enjoyment yet is grasped as something devoid of substance—the treasury of the serpents of hope. (25)
Though appearing in a state of great enjoyment, vast, and as if delightful,

it is "substantialless" (avastuka) and "trivial" (tuccha), because only a few among them can actually be grasped, and even when grasped, they are enjoyed by someone at some time only, and perish in the very next moment.
In objects previously seen and those not yet seen, which remain unenjoyed, it stands like an anthill—the nest of the serpents of hope, whose venom of craving is fierce. (25)
Knowing that this is unreal, do not fix your mind upon it;
for the wise man, having recognized a mirage, does not run after it. (26)
Regarding how it should be abandoned, he says: "asat" (unreal). "Bhāvam" means attachment (rāga). || 26 ||
That deluded soul who pursues prosperity consisting of mere mental constructs, rich in its own conceptualization but devoid of true essence, becomes a vessel for nothing but suffering. (27)
He states the disadvantage in pursuing that [object] with the words: "By one's own volition," etc. (27).
If this world does not exist as a real entity, let it go as something unreal at will;
but he who abandons the real and pursues the unreal perishes.

It is said that for him there is not only the attainment of misfortune, but also the loss of his goal; thus [the author] says: "But he who... He perishes, meaning he falls away from the supreme human goal. || 28 ||
This world is merely a delusion of the mind, like the fear of a snake in a rope; through the diversity of mental cultivation alone, it revolves for a long time. (29)
One is deceived here only by a fool through entities that arise from the non-existent and are as unstable as the moon reflected in water; one such as you, who knows reality, is not so deceived.
That fool who, while cultivating this collection of qualities, desires happiness, merely rubs away his own dullness by means of his own cultivation of fire. (31)

Contemplating the aggregate of qualities such as sound and so forth—which constitutes the body and other such things—one conceives of them as "I" and "mine. "Dullness" means cold; [it is overcome] by the contemplation of fire, that is to say, by a fire imagined through the power of the mind. || 31 ||
This entire world, though non-existent, appears as a captivating snare of water, like a city conjured by the mind’s own thinking within the heart.
The "water-cage" refers to the body and so forth, which have become a collection of inert matter due to the non-difference between *la* and *ḍa*. || 32 ||
This arises by the will of the mind and dissolves by its lack of will;
thus it is falsely perceived as vast, like a city of Gandharvas.
If this [world] has arisen by the power of a voluntary mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*), then why does it not cease simply through a voluntary resolve for cessation?
To this he says: "It dissolves" (*līyate*). This occurs through the mere destruction of passion (*rāga*) without [any further] desire on the part of that painting.
Such a thing is seen as purely false in the world; the mention of a "city of Gandharvas" (*gandharvanagara*) is used as an illustration.
This is an illustration of a city imagined by the mind. || 33 ||
O Rāma, when this world perishes, nothing at all perishes;
and even when this world is joined [with existence], nothing at all is joined. (34)
Therefore, with the intention that one should not experience grief at his loss nor joy at his prosperity, he says "O Rāma," and so forth. "Yukte" means when there is prosperity. || 34 ||
When the city of the heart, constructed by the mind, is broken and yet has grown into a vast expanse, tell me: what has increased, and what of whom has been diminished? (35)
Just as a mental representation arises for children for the sake of play,
so too does this world arise incessantly through the mind.

The remaining sense is that one does not grieve when living for the sake of play with dolls and the like, or when imagining the semblance of worldly dealings such as children, cattle, and so forth. || 36 ||
Nothing belonging to anyone is truly lost, just as in the waters of a magical illusion; likewise, when this saṃsāra—which has arisen falsely—is cast off or perishes, nothing is lost.
If that which is non-existent remains non-existent, then what loss has indeed occurred to whom?
Consequently, there would be no basis at all for joy or sorrow within this cycle of existence.
If that which is unreal and false were indeed non-existent and absent, what would be lost for whom? The sense is: "nothing at all.

Alternatively, the negative particle *na* may be used in the sense of "as if" (*iva*). Therefore, the syntactical connection is: in this saṃsāra, there is nothing whatsoever that serves as the locus for joy or sorrow. (38)
Since that which is absolutely non-existent does not exist at all, what indeed can perish? For in the absence of destruction, O Mahāmati, what occasion is there for suffering? (39)

Having thus stated the undesirability of grief by accepting [the reality of] destruction, he declares that in truth there is no destruction of anything at all: "It is simply non-existent," etc. Since it is simply non-existent, therefore [there is no grief]. (39)
Or rather, what indeed can perish of that which is eternally existent? This entire world is Brahman alone; how then could pleasure and pain arise? (40)

Having established the impossibility of destruction from the perspective of superimposition (*adhyasta-dṛṣṭi*), he establishes it even from the perspective of the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna-dṛṣṭi*) with the words "sadeva" (only Being). [The question is: "What cause has given rise to pleasure and pain?"—the meaning is that they have not arisen at all. Furthermore, what kind of growth could there be for that which is absolutely non-existent?
O high-minded one, in the absence of growth, what occasion is there for joy? (41)

Since origination has already been refuted, modifications such as growth and so forth are likewise refuted; therefore, he states that joy caused by them is also improper—[the reading is "pyuktatā"]—with the words "asat" (non-existent), etc.
The particle "vā" is used in the sense of restriction (avadhāraṇe). || 41 ||
In this entire cycle of existence, which is unreal and exclusively productive of conceptual proliferation, what is there for a wise person to accept that they might desire? (42)
For joy would arise upon the attainment of what is desired; yet he says that in that which consists of illusion, there is no such thing as "desired" at all—thus: "everywhere. (42)

Since this entire triple world consists of the reality of Brahman and is everywhere truly existent, what could there be that is to be abandoned? Let the wise discern that which should be relinquished. (43)
Thus, for one who perceives everything as being of a single flavor with bliss (ānanda), there is nothing to be abandoned; this is stated in the word "sarvatra" (everywhere).
[The phrase] "brahmatattvamaye" means consisting of the essence of Brahman; the suffix *mayaṭ* is used here in its own sense (svārthe). [The command] "pariharantu" means "let them abandon. || 43 ||
Whether the world exists or does not exist, he is inaccessible to both pleasure and pain;
yet the fool is distressed by its destruction. (44)
In both cases, he is pained by the destruction—imagined through his own delusion—of his son, friends, and others, who are themselves incapable of perishing. (44)
That which did not exist in the beginning and at the end likewise does not exist in the present;
O Rama, for one who desires what is non-existent, only non-existence is perceived.
Now, he demonstrates the logical proof for both the positions of "non-existence" and "existence" by means of two verses beginning with "In the beginning":

through such scriptural passages as "In the beginning, this was non-existent," and "In the beginning, there was nothing whatsoever here," it is heard that the sky, the wind, the worlds, and so forth, are non-existent at both their beginning and end.

Furthermore, the direct perception of a jar or similar object is experienced for a long duration; moreover, its non-existence at both [prior and subsequent] times and its existence for a short time are well-established in each individual instance. And these two—existence and non-existence—which are by nature mutually exclusive, cannot reside in a single entity without the abandonment of one or the other.
Thus, since one of the two [extremes] must necessarily be abandoned,

and because non-existence has been established for a much longer duration at the beginning and the end, all individual manifestations must likewise be non-existent even during their present state; therefore, by one who desires the position of non-existence, non-existence alone is perceived through scripture, reasoning, and experience.
This is the meaning. || 45 ||
That which is real in the beginning and at the end is indeed real in the present as well;
for one for whom everything is indeed real, only reality itself is perceived.

"Existence alone, my dear, this was in the beginning; how could the existent be born from the non-existent? and so forth—by such scriptural passages, because all things are experienced as "existent, existent" at the time of the operation of the means of valid cognition, even by merely postulating the non-manifestation of existence at the initial stage and its concealment at the final stage, [the opponent might argue that] "this was indeed non-existence in the beginning."
Because of the validity of such scriptural citations and logical arguments, and because the scriptural and logical proofs for existence cannot be explained otherwise,
it is logical that the existence of all things— which is eternal and universal— is one and the same due to parsimony (*lāghava*). Once this oneness of existence is established,
since everything is real at the beginning and at the end by virtue of the very existence of the causal Brahman, it must be so during the present time as well.
The meaning is that, according to the proponent of the true doctrine, the undivided existence of Brahman alone is perceived everywhere. || 46 ||
Only the ignorant, not the superior ones, long for such unreal things as the moon within the water or the surface of the sky, which serve only to delude the mind. (47)

With the intention that "the conceptualization of existence as delimited by space and time is excluded from both alternatives [of being and non-being], contradicts all scripture and logic, is imagined through a blind tradition by thousands of fools, and causes all manner of misfortune; thus, it is appropriate only for those fools and not for you," he says:
By the words "unreal" and so forth. || 47 ||
For the fool, through purposes that are empty of substance despite their expansive forms, attains satisfaction that leads to endless suffering and not to happiness. (48)
By means of purposes that are devoid of substance, empty of meaning, and mere semblances of pleasure. || 48 ||
Therefore, O lotus-eyed Rāma, do not be a fool;
perceiving that which is imperishable here, take refuge in that which is eternal and steadfast. (49)
"Mā bhavaḥ" means "do not be. In this context, the *laṅ* [aorist] has been used by way of substitution (*vyatyaya*) for the *luṅ* [aorist]. || 49 ||
Do not fall into despondency by calculating that all this, including myself, is non-existent;
for here, indeed, everything, including myself, is existent.
And seeing this, let there be no despondency in you. || 50 ||

Now, demonstrating the synthesis of the two positions— existence and non-existence— which have been presented through their different approaches and which ultimately lead to a single purpose, he concludes with the words "asat" (non-existent): "Having realized that this entire world, accompanied by the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) imagined as the Self by those deluded by Māyā, is indeed non-existent..."

Having ascertained through scripture, the teacher’s instruction, reasoning, and one's own experience that there is dejection (*viṣāditā*)—which is sorrow (*śoka*)—upon the loss of sons, friends, wealth, and so forth;

and that "one whose nature (*śīla*) is to eat (*attuṃ*)" or consume—that is, to enjoy (*bhoktuṃ*)—objects of sense which grant suffering in their ultimate result is a "dejected one" (*viṣādī*), meaning one possessed by passion (*rāgī*);
let there be no such state of dejection or passion. And thus, by means of the removal of sorrow, passion, and the like—
The sense is that the doctrine of the non-existence of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is useful for the realization of the oneness of the Self (*aikātmyadarśana*).

Thus, by means of this introduction to the theory of non-existence for another purpose, one should not think that the world is devoid of reality (*nistattva*); rather, everything is indeed real (*sat*). For if existence itself were unestablished, then non-existence—which is its negation—could not be established either.

Furthermore, since non-existence is rejected by that very [existence] when it is established, its non-existence is not proven. Thus, in every case, non-existence—which is rejected by existence—is rendered baseless and is incapable of delimiting anything anywhere.
When the state of being exclusively one with the undelimited existent is established, [the form that delimits jars, cloths, and so forth...]

Having perceived that which is indeed Being— the undivided unity— conjoined with the inner Self (pratyak) by Me, who am the pure essence of consciousness alone, purified and free from all distinctions and remnants, as "I am the Infinite" (bhūman); for you who are thus established in your own Self, let there be no further despondency, nor the attainment of the sorrow of worldly birth, death, and so forth, even throughout the three periods of time.
The meaning is "esteemed. || 50 ||
Śrī Vālmīki said:
When the sage had thus spoken, the day passed away, and the sun went to its setting for the performance of the evening rites.
Having offered salutations, the assembly departed to bathe;
and at the end of night, it returned together with the rays of the sun.
Thus ends the forty-fifth canto, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of Reality as It Is," in the *Sthitiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki.

Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, titled "Instruction on the Yoga of Things as They Truly Are," in the Section on Stability (*sthitiprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, within the *Tātparyaprakāśa* commentary. || 45 ||
The Ninth Day.
The Forty-Sixth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: "In wealth, wives, and the like—which are delightful—there is indeed an occasion for sorrow; what occasion, then, could there be for joy?"

The reading [is as follows]. Furthermore, in the *Ṭīkā*, immediately after the phrase "connected with both," there is an additional reading found in some manuscripts: "When [the world] consisting of wife and so forth—which is like a magical illusion—is seen to be wicked for even a moment, what occasion is there for joy? Or, when it has perished, what cause is there for lamentation? This is the connection [of the words]. Indeed, [the word] "kaḥ" [is used here].
When that which was seen through the sight of Indra’s net has vanished, what cause for lamentation is there? || 1 ||
Even while dwelling in saṃsāra, those qualities by which one does not sink are here proclaimed for Rāma, who abides among those liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 1 ||

In this context, wishing first to teach the two qualities characterized by indifference toward what is lost and lack of longing for what is yet to come— due to non-attachment toward all things— the author says "ramye" and so forth, in order to demonstrate the utility of the preceding introduction.
In the view that the word *ramye* undergoes grammatical refinement (*pada-saṃskāra*), it is in the singular number.
By the grammatical rule that "the word *vacana* is a universal noun," it is in the singular number; through repetition, it connects with both [terms]. || 1 ||

Whether it be for the sake of a city of Gandharvas, or for that which is defiled or adorned, or for the portion of ignorance such as a son and so forth—what sequence of pleasure and pain can there be? (2)
Kramaṇa means stepping, gait, or spreading. || 2 ||
What occasion indeed is there for joy in pleasant wealth, wives, and the like? When the mirage has vanished, can those seeking water find any delight? (3)
And when wealth, wife, and so forth are abundant—the word "being" (satī) being understood as the remainder—is there not an abundance of joy, such as the pleasure of water-sports and the like?
When wealth, wife, and elders have perished, there is only suffering and no contentment;
since one has grown old in the midst of delusion and illusion, who here can find any consolation? (4)

He says—beginning with the verse "dhanaiḥ"—that since the increase of those [wealth and status] leads to the probable increase of the disease of saṃsāra, it is only appropriate to feel sorrow and not joy. || 4 ||
By those very same objects of enjoyment which produce passion in the fool due to his excessive attachment, detachment arises in the wise man. (5)
By those who have attained an increase and further growth. || 5 ||
When wealth, wife, and so forth are lost, what occasion indeed remains for joy?
But virtuous men, looking toward the further shore, attain detachment through these very things.
When that which is perishable by nature has perished, those who look toward the beyond perceive the bitterness of the future,
seeing that perishability is the cause for hell and other such states.
Therefore, O Raghava, you who know the truth regarding the worldly affairs of saṃsāra,
disregard what is lost as lost, and accept what is obtained as obtained.
He shows the purpose for which this discussion was undertaken with the words "ataḥ" (therefore). "Upāhara" means employ.
Since its utility is already established by the attainment of the object, it is not a quality subject to injunction. || 7 ||
Not desiring future enjoyments and experiencing those that have arrived without artifice—this is the characteristic of a wise person. (8)
He states another quality [of the past and future]: "Of those that are not yet come" (anāgatānām) || 8 ||
In this turmoil of saṃsāra, while the self is concealed like an assassin,
conduct yourself as a fully awakened one, so that you do not fall into delusion.
He teaches another quality characterized by heedfulness—beginning with the words "In saṃsāra..."—as follows:

that which causes one to wander in *saṃsāra* is *saṃsārasaṃbhrama*, namely desire (*kāma*). One who approaches (*upaiti*) with the intent to kill (*jighāṃsayā*) the concealed self (*channātmani*) by means of poison, weapons, fire, and so forth, when it is hidden, is an *ātatāyin*.

The enemy is therein. As it has been said: "One with a raised sword, one with poison or fire, one with a hand raised for a curse, an assassin using Atharvanic rites, a slanderer in royal courts, and one who violates his wife—one should know these to be the seven *ātatayin* (assassins). Being fully awakened means being vigilant in enlightenment. 9.
Those of perverted intellect who do not perceive this process of the world’s grand display as being free from conceptual proliferation through right knowledge are destroyed. 10.

That which is stepped upon in that which is devoid of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is "the step" (*krama*), namely the supreme state (*paramapada*). Even those who possess perfect knowledge of it, if through negligence they do not perceive the deception of this ostentation of saṃsāra, are of evil intellect;
the meaning is that they are destroyed by negligence. Alternatively, [it refers to] Brahman, which is devoid of conceptual proliferation.

Those who possess right knowledge regarding the sequence of acquiring virtues such as discernment (*viveka*), dispassion (*vairāgya*), awakening (*prabodha*), and vigilance (*apramāda*) do not perceive this grand display of worldly existence; the genitive case here is used because it is intended to express that [this display] is merely a remnant of *karman*. However, those of evil intellect who are devoid of the aforementioned virtues are ruined.
This is the meaning. || 10 ||
By whatever means possible, if one’s attachment to the visible world and such has departed,
that pure intellect of his does not sink anywhere.

He teaches another quality, characterized by the absence of delight in the seen and the seeing, with the words "by which": by whatever reasoning that establishes any one of the following— falsity, being a cause of misfortune such as hell, and the nature of causing the loss of one's true self through the depositing of dualistic impressions that delight the mind— the attachment (*āsthā*) has departed, having ceased.
The stainless and sinless intellect, which is intent upon the ultimate truth, does not sink into the ocean of delusion. || 11 ||
For one whose conviction that "this is real" has ceased regarding all things,
unreal ignorance does not embrace that omniscient one.

With the intention that the abandonment of attachment to external objects is likewise a virtue, he says: "Of whom... The ellipsis is to be supplied as "by the certainty that 'this is unreal'. *Āsthā* means attachment. (12)
He whose intellect is established in the realization that "I and this entire world are one," having abandoned both attachment and aversion, does not sink.

He states that even the vision of the identity of the self is a quality: "I am [the Self]... [and so forth]. It consists of the relinquishing of attachment and following whatever has been obtained as it comes. || 13 ||
Having supported yourself with the intellect upon the pure state that lies between being and non-being,
neither grasp nor release the visible world, whether external or internal.
He explains what has already been stated with the word "pure" (śuddham). It is that which follows as the middle between the existent and non-existent, the manifest and the unmanifest.
"Pure" means pure being (sattāmātra). Taking that very state (padam) as the inner self (pratyagātman), [one attains it]. || 14 ||
Utterly detached, established in your own self, and free from all attachments, remain like the sky, O Rāma, devoid of passion even while engaged in your duties. 15.
He teaches the qualities of being a non-abode for contentment through cessation and being unattached: "Exceedingly... (verse 15).
For the wise man who stands firm in action, there is neither desire nor aversion;
his discernment is not defiled, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
To the question of how one might become free from passion or free from attachment, he says: "Of whom... (verse 16).
Whether your senses and mind perform acts such as seeing and touching or refrain from them, you remain indifferent; being a master of yourself, you are free from desire.

Since it is secondary because it is merely a persistence of what has been sublated, let your mind, together with the senses, perform acts such as seeing or not perform them; it is figurative [only]. || 17 ||

Let not the mind, which conceives of the objects of the senses as "this is mine"—though that is unreal—sink into them; whether it acts or does not act, let it not be submerged once it has already been immersed.
Teaching the quality characterized by the renunciation of possessiveness toward the objects of the senses, he establishes non-attachment—beginning with the word "mine.

In the phrase "being unmagned," the masculine form is a Vedic usage (chāndasa). However, if the reading is "tvam ajñaḥ san" (being ignorant), the meaning is: "O mind, do not cause me to sink. || 18 ||
O Raghava, when the splendor of the objects of the senses no longer pleases your heart,
then you have realized true knowledge and have crossed over the ocean of worldly existence.
He states the sign for the conviction of having attained liberation while living (*jīvanmuktatā*) with the words "When... (verse 19). "It does not please him" (*na svadate*):
even without reflecting on it, it does not find favor by itself because it is recognized as a cause of misfortune.
For you, whether possessing a body or being bodiless, liberation has been achieved by the power of the object itself, even though you had no desire for it while tasting the objects of the senses.

The word *āsvāditā* is to be analyzed as *ā-asvāditā*. It refers to that wise person (*dhīra*) for whom all sensory objects—both those of this world and those of the next—have been thoroughly (*ā*) tasted and found to be objects of distaste. This applies both to one who possesses a body during emergence from meditation (*satanoḥ vyutthāne*), and to one who is bodiless (*atanoḥ*) due to being devoid of it through meditative absorption (*samādhinā*). By virtue of the sense of the context, this means "without effort" (*anāyāsena*).
O Rāma, by means of supreme wisdom, separate the mind from the multitude of latent impressions for the sake of the highest state, just as one extracts noble fragrance from a flower.

Regarding that liberation while living (jīvanmukti), he states that the primary means is the extraction of the mind from its latent impressions (vāsanās) by saying "for the high station" (uccaiḥpadāya). The mind (cetas) is the internal organ (manas) which has become sublime (udāra), meaning preeminent through discernment (viveka) and dispassion (vairāgya). || 21 ||
In this ocean of saṃsāra, flooded with the waters of latent impressions (vāsanā), those who have boarded the boat of wisdom have crossed over, while others have drowned. 22.
Bruḍitāḥ means submerged or sunk. || 22 ||
Having investigated the reality of the self with an intellect that is as sharp as a razor’s edge and supremely steadfast, you shall then enter your own state.
He shows what that boat of wisdom (*prajñānaus*) is like: "sharpened as a razor's edge" (*kṣuradhārā*);

the meaning is that it has been made keen by discernment (*viveka*), dispassion (*vairāgya*), and so forth. It is "steadfast" (*dhīrā*), meaning endowed with fortitude in enduring the pairs of opposites (*dvandva*). || 23 ||
O Rāma, one should conduct oneself just as those wise ones who know reality do— their minds nourished by knowledge— and not like a fool.

The great-souled ones who are liberated while living, ever-contented and possessed of supreme intelligence, are to be followed by their conduct; not the deceitful who are wretched in their pursuit of enjoyments.
The deceitful are those who deceive both themselves and others. || 25 ||
They neither abandon nor desire worldly activity;
those people who know both the near and the far shore conform to everything.
The knowers of that [reality] regard the far shore as the principle of Brahman and the near shore as the principle of the world.
Those great ones who perceive reality never become wretched in this world on account of their power, pride, virtues, fame, or fortune. (27)
One might object: "Could there not be miserliness even in the wise at times? To this he says: "Of power," and so forth.
*Prabhāva* is the excellence of knowledge, austerity, prowess, and the like; *guṇas* are skill, noble lineage, character, and so on; *śriyas* are riches or prosperity.
For it is well known in the world that miserliness occurs in regard to these things. [But this is not the case] for one who perceives reality (*tattvadarśin*).
Because [the world] consists of power and so forth, it is seen by those who perceive it as not being for the sake of the person (apuruṣārtha) that it is subject to mutual contradiction. || 27 ||
Even in utter solitude they do not feel distressed, for they are unattached even in the celestial gardens;
like the suns, the great ones never abandon their destined course.

Even in total emptiness, even in the destruction of all things, and even in the celestial gardens such as Nandana where every desire is fulfilled, they are not attached—that is, they have no clinging. They do not transgress *niyati*, the boundary established by the scriptures. In the case of the Sun (*bhāskara*), "in total emptiness" refers to the sky;
"their own course" refers to the boundary of his path. || 28 ||
Free from desire and following conventional usage as it has been attained, they move about exalted, established in their own state while situated in the chariot of the body. (29)
Those who are fully prepared with the means prescribed in such scriptural passages as, "The man for whom consciousness is the charioteer and the mind is the reins," and so forth. 29.
O Rama, you too have attained this expansive discernment;
by the power of this wisdom, O handsome one, you are established in knowledge.
He consoles Rāma, who is anxious and hesitant as to whether those virtues exist in him or not, with the words: "You too..."
Firmly maintaining a clear vision, free from pride and devoid of envy, dwell upon this seat of the earth; you shall attain supreme perfection.
Established in yourself, having renounced all that is beneficial [to worldly ends], and desiring the vision from afar, wander, O sinless one, having taken up supreme inner coolness.
"Śrī Vālmīki said"— the meaning is that he spoke while being one whose desire to see the wonders of the objects of perception at a distance was aroused;
thus, with these pure words, [he spoke] to the one of pure intention.
Rāma immediately appeared as if cleansed by the sage;
his inner self, radiant and filled with the sweet nectar of knowledge, attained a coolness like that of the full moon. || 33 ||

Vālmīki describes the manifestation of Rāma through the awakening within him of the secrets of the meaning thus taught: "In this manner," etc. By the speech of the sage Vasiṣṭha, spoken in the aforementioned way, Rāma—whose disposition was pure—shone forth, polished and cleansed like a mirror, by the nectar of knowledge.
With his inner being illuminated, he—[the reading is "sampūrṇaḥ"] being full—attained, like the full moon, a state of coolness, which is the cessation of the threefold suffering. || 33 ||

Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Qualities of One Established in Jīvanmukti," in the Section on Stability (*sthitiprakaraṇa*) within the Means to Liberation (*mokṣopāya*) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki according to the Seer’s tradition.
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Qualities of One Established in Jīvanmukti," in the Sthitiprakaraṇa of the Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa, within the Tātparyaprakāśa.
The forty-seventh canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
"O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, you who have reached the further shore of all the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (vedāṅgas). [Note: The text repeats "vedavedāṅgapāraga" for emphasis.]
I stand as if refreshed by your pure words. || 1 ||
The past and future existing Brahmās, as well as millions of cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍa*), and the gods and others herein described, follow both fixed and unfixed sequences. (1)
He was comforted, like a man whose burden has been removed and whose fatigue from the road and hunger has vanished.
I do not reach satiety in hearing your words as you speak—words that are noble, secluded, refined, and sublime. (2)

They are sublime, bestowing vast and supreme wealth; they are distinct, being clearly articulated through the differentiation of phonemes, words, sentences, and chapters; they are elegant, being skilled in the composition of diverse narratives and logical arguments; and they are exalted, by virtue of illuminating the reality of the self.
And because they cause the lotus of the heart to blossom, they have arisen like the sun and other luminaries. || 2 ||
In the course of another occasion for discourse, you have described the birth of the lotus-born Brahmā according to the scriptures, as being of a rajasa-sattvika nature. (3)

Having thus encouraged the Guru with praise, he asks— beginning with the words "By birth"— desiring to know the incidental truth concerning the sovereignty of the deities such as Brahmā and others: "On the occasion of your speaking of the 'birth' of the living beings, which is of a *rājasa-sāttvika* nature..."

By means of the scriptures—namely the various authoritative sources such as the Śrutis and Purāṇas that expound upon creation—describe clearly the birth of the Lotus-born (Brahmā) which has been mentioned and introduced; this is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 3 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāghava, many hundreds of thousands of Brahmās, hundreds of Śivas and Indras, and thousands of Nārāyaṇas have already passed away.
Because the word "many" (bahūni) is connected to every instance, even terms such as "hundred thousand" and so forth refer to the infinite.
And in many other diverse cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas),
they sport by the thousands, engaging in various modes of conduct and pastimes.
In other cosmic eggs, as well as in this one, there are bodies of gods, demons, and others, characterized by various modes of conduct and pastimes; this is the sense. || 5 ||
Simultaneously, and throughout infinite worlds existing at other times, many others will likewise arise in great numbers.
O mighty-armed one, the births of those dwellers of heaven, such as the lotus-born Brahmā and others, within the cosmic eggs appeared like various and wondrous manifestations.
They appeared as if arisen from a manifold magical illusion.
Sometimes these creations belong to Śarva, sometimes they originate from the Lotus-born [Brahmā],
sometimes they belong to Viṣṇu, and sometimes they are fashioned by the Sages.

The *śārvya* [powers] are those preceded by Rudra; they are those whose origin is from the one born first from the Lotus-born (Brahmā). The *vaiṣṇavya* [powers] are those preceded by Viṣṇu. Thus it is said in the Purāṇa: "Having gratified the Lord through austerity, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara were born from one another, each desiring victory over the others."
The phrase "created by the Sage" refers to the intention of an intermediate creation.
Sometimes Brahmā is born from a lotus, sometimes he is born from the waters;
sometimes he is born from an egg, and sometimes he is born from the sky.
He states that even the places of manifestation for Brahmā and the others are indefinite with the words "kadācit" (at times).
In the Pādma-kalpa, the lotus-born one is well known as being born from the water, called Āpa, and born from the cosmic egg (*aṇḍodbhava*). Regarding the phrase "from the sky" (*ambarāt*):
likewise, it is stated in the earlier Rāmāyaṇa, in the account of the Solar dynasty and so forth, that "Brahmā has his origin in space (*ākāśa*). || 9 ||
In one staff there was the three-eyed Śiva, in another the Sun, in another Indra, in another the lotus-eyed Viṣṇu, and indeed in yet another the three-eyed Śiva himself.

Thus, he states that there is no fixed rule even regarding those authorized for the positions of the Sun and other deities, saying "in some [person]": by the force of the word "only" (*eva*), it is understood that the Three-Eyed One alone [is authorized] in all offices of the deities. The word "for" (*hi*) is intended to illuminate that it is he alone—and not anyone else—who may be conceived as having the nature of another deity even in other contexts. || 10 ||
In one creation, the earth was densely crowded with trees;
in another, it was packed with men; and in yet another, it was covered by mountains.
"Thickly crowded with dense trees"—this phrase is to be understood as a supplement in every instance. || 11 ||
One was made of earth, another was made of stone;
one was made of gold, and likewise another was made of copper.
The suffix *mayaṭ* is used in the sense of abundance.
Right here, some other worlds appear in various ways;
some are distinct from one another, and some are even devoid of light.

In this very universe (brahmāṇḍa), what and how many wonders and marvels exist? Furthermore, there are other worlds and universes as well; "otherwise" means in other ways. The meaning is that they possess many marvels.
In each of these, every single world is an illumination consisting of light, like the sun and other luminaries, while those [other worlds] are devoid of splendor and without light.
In this great sky of the reality of Brahman, infinite worlds sink down and emerge like the waters of the waves of the ocean.
They sink down; they dissolve. || 14 ||
Just as waves are in the ocean, as a mirage is in the desert,
and as flowers are on the mango tree, so too are the glories of the universe in the Supreme.
The motes of dust in the rays of the sun may be counted;
but the multitudes of worlds, with their flickering forms, cannot be numbered in truth by Brahman.
And those with restless bodies are fickle. || 16 ||
Just as swarms of mosquitoes become agitated during the rainy season and perish again and again as they arise, so too do these creations of the world.
Nor is it known from what time these successions of creations have come forth; they are characterized by a constant flux of coming and going. (18)

He states that the stream of those creations is beginningless with the words "And not... and so forth: "The coming and going, the manifestation and disappearance, are eternal; they are devoted to that. (18)
Beginningless and incessant, they flash forth like waves; indeed, each preceding one arose from the one before it, just as that which preceded it arose from its own predecessor. (19)
Having come into being again and again, all classes of beings—including gods, asuras, and humans—dissolve away, just like the breaking of waves upon a river. (20)
In the manner or style of the breaking of waves upon the river. || 20 ||
Just as this egg of Brahmā exists, so too do the series of cosmic eggs,
thousands of which have perished like the channels [of time] within years.
Thousands upon thousands; nāḍikās and ghaṭikās. || 21 ||
Others currently exist, possessing present bodies,
at the edge of this city of Brahmā, in the vast realm of Brahman.
He states that all cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍas*) are imagined within Brahman itself, situated in the space of the heart, according to the method described in the *Līlopākhyāna*—namely, "others":

other series of cosmic eggs. Even now, at this very moment, they exist on the periphery of this body, which is called the "city of Brahman" (*brahmapura*) because it is the locus for the realization of Brahman.

In the region of the heart-lotus, situated in the vast and exceedingly expansive abode of Brahman, there exist the Satyas, whose bodies abide in Brahman and whose forms are ever-shifting; for the Śruti declares, "In this [abode], heaven and earth are contained within. This is the intended meaning. || 22 ||
There will be others who are devoted to Brahman, possessing the splendor of the city of Brahmā;
yet they too will perish again and again, just like spoken words.

The series of Brahma-eggs, created by Brahmā, are the very ornaments of the splendor of the space within the heart, which is characterized as the city of Brahmā; just as various sounds, having arisen in the sky, perish after they have come into being, so it is with them. (23)
Other successions of creations, destined to exist within Brahman,
remain as if pots reside in a heap of clay, or as sprouts do within a seed.
He states what was already said for the purpose of providing another illustration: "In Brahman," etc. (24).
Just as within the space of consciousness up to the realm of Brahmā, the splendors of the three worlds—
though rich with vast forms and transformations— are seen to be nothing at all when scrutinized.
The meaning is that as long as they are examined by the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna), there will be a sublation (bādha) to the effect that "nothing exists at all. || 25 ||
Emerging and submerging, these fortunes are neither real nor unreal;
like wickedness, they expand through their dull undertakings.
Inert undertakings, superimposed by fools, spread out like the creepers of the sky that expand through wickedness.
Possessing the nature of waves, their bodies appearing and vanishing, all these streams of creation exhibit diverse forms and activities. (27)

The "creations" (sṛṣṭayaḥ) are the manifold activities and the movements of the living beings contained within them—referring to those whose very nature consists of the diverse creations of universes (brahmāṇḍas), which themselves constitute the collective totality (samaṣṭi) of the creations within their own selves. || 27 ||
Indeed, all creations possess diverse forms and transformations, yet all perceptions of creation are not distinct from [the Creator]. (28)

The connection with the subsequent clause is as follows: all the perceptions of creation belonging to all the cosmic eggs (*brahmāṇḍa*) are not distinct from the object of the knower of reality, just as raindrops are not distinct from the water. || 28 ||
O Rāma, emanations flow toward one who knows reality as rain from water, or as rain from a cloud from the Lord. || 29 ||
But from the perspective of one who does not know reality, [these powers] come from the Lord as a detached sovereign, just as rains come from a cloud. || 29 ||
The perceptions of creation for all beings are not entirely distinct from one another,
just as the fluids, the ocean, and the swallows are not distinct from the Śālmalī tree itself.
In the ultimate sense, however, they are not distinct from anyone—whether ignorant or knowers of reality.
The "liquid oceans" (*dravāmbhodhi*) are the veins that sustain the waters of the earth, which are uprooted and liquid in form;
these are one's own (*svāḥ*), belonging to oneself, as are the bark, *kināṭa*, leaves, and so forth, as well as the knots such as the *aṣṭhīla* and wooden seeds.
Just as [the branches] are not distinct from the śālmali tree, so it is in that case.
O Rāghava, here in these creations— whether flourishing or degraded—
the garland of impurities consisting of the subtle elements (tanmātra) arises from the supreme ether (paramān-bhas).

In the gross bodies and so forth, which are nourished and composed of gross elements, and in the subtle senses and so forth, which are inferior and composed of subtle elements— these have arisen from the supreme ether, the unmanifest space (*avyākṛtākāśa*),
which is characterized by the five *tanmātras* known as the subtle elements, the impurity of *māyā*, and which serves as the thread-like substratum.
The meaning is that all states of being are like garlands strung with crystal rudrākṣa beads. || 31 ||
Sometimes he first attains the state of abiding in the ether;
from that, this Prajāpati Brahmā, born of the ether, is produced.

Regarding what was stated previously—that Brahmā is sometimes born from a lotus—the author explains, with the words beginning "kadācit," that the regulating factor there is the sequence of the first manifestation of the gross ether and so forth, which occurs subsequent to the process of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*). "Pratiṣṭhām" refers to their existence in a gross state. This applies everywhere in the same manner.
Sometimes first the wind attains a foundation;
from that, Brahmā is born—this Prajāpati who is born of the wind.
Sometimes first the fiery energy attains a firm foundation;
from that, this Prajāpati, the creator of the fiery energy, is born.
Sometimes, first the water attains stability;
from that, Brahmā is born—that Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) who is born from the waters. || 35 ||
Sometimes first the earth attains expansion;
from that, Brahmā is born, he who is the earthly Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati). || 36 ||
When this fifth [element] increases by compressing these four, then,
having arisen from that very [state], it performs the activities of the world.
Now, he states the reasoning for the initial manifestation of each individual element, such as space (*vyoman*), beginning with the words "this" (*idam*).

This [world], which is distinct from one's own self, consists of the fourfold aggregate of elements; having compressed it and rendered it as if latent through the expansion of its own parts, when whichever fifth element increases, then this [universe] is born from that alone.
The meaning is that Brahmā performs the activity of the subsequent creation and so forth of the world. || 37 ||
Sometimes, within water, or air, or even in a vast expanse of fire,
a person who is conditioned by primordial nature (prakṛti) suddenly manifests of his own accord.

If it is asked: "Since all things consist of the five elements as their effects and are thus composed of those five, how can Prajāpati, who arises from them, be designated as being born from each one individually? [The author] replies: "By virtue of predominance" (*vaiśeṣyāt*), according to the [Vaiśeṣika] principle. He says: "Sometimes," etc.
When [the primordial matter] is highly expanded—that is, when a particular portion is predominant—the person (puruṣa) who has that as his limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is Prajāpati, by nature.

The meaning is that one who has been cultivated and perfumed by a nature following the sequence of prior worship spontaneously becomes, all at once, of the form of the elemental air-born, the fire-born, and so forth. || 38 ||
Then, at times a sound was produced from his mouth;
sometimes from his feet, sometimes from his back, and sometimes from his eyes or his hands. (39)
He shows the commencement of creation from the limbs of that [Being] with the words "tasya" (of him). "Then" (atha) means immediately thereafter.

The word "name" (śabda) is also an indicator for both name and form (*nāmarūpa*). Thus, from the limbs such as the mouth, the names "Brāhmaṇa" and so forth arise together with their respective objects, as appropriate. "The Brāhmaṇa was his mouth."
The meaning is according to such scriptural passages as these. "From the front part" means from the forward portion; "from the back" means from the rear portion. || 39 ||
At one time, a lotus is produced from the navel of this Puruṣa;
within it Brahmā grows, and he is celebrated as the "Lotus-born. (40)
This refers to that very person named Nārāyaṇa. Regarding him, he says "in that [lotus]" (tasmin), because of his birth from that very lotus, he is called Padmaja (the Lotus-born). || 40 ||
This is an illusion, a delusion like a dream, a circle falsely constructed; it is like a kingdom of the mind, as beautiful as a whirlpool in restless water. (41)

To Rāma, who was questioning how the birth of that [Self] which is already existent could possibly be established, he replied: "Tell me, how can this [birth] occur here in this consciousness? This inquiry is like the daydreams of a child. (42)

If birth in one's own navel-lotus is not possible for an existent person (puruṣa), then how could that second form—the world—be possible for you in this Brahman, which is non-attached and non-dual consciousness?
And in what manner would it be possible? The meaning is: "just like that. Thus, your objection is [inapplicable].
He says that this is equivalent to the inquiry into the kingdom of a child's imagination—“In some cases,” etc.; it is an interrogative intonation (kāku). || 42 ||
Sometimes, within the pure ether, due to the coloring of the principle of the mind (manas-tattva),
the golden cosmic egg containing Brahman manifests of its own accord.
He supports the arising of [beings] from space by relying on the mind’s power of inconceivable construction, just like the arising of the lotus-born [Brahmā], stating: "Sometimes... (verse 43).
At some time, this person indeed creates vigor within the water;
from that, either a lotus or the great cosmic egg is born. (44)
The lotus is the earth-lotus. || 44 ||
From him Brahmā is born; at times he is the Sun, at times Varuṇa, at times Brahmā, and at times Vāyu, the egg-born.
Bhāskara, who occupied the office of the Sun in the previous kalpa, becomes Brahmā in this kalpa;
likewise it is with Varuṇa and the others as well. || 45 ||
Thus, O Rāma, within these various creations that have been successively lost, manifold and diverse origins of Brahmā have come to pass.

When the internal, inward-facing selves have become non-existent and perished, the various emanations of Brahmā—the Hiraṇyagarbha under discussion—have likewise passed away. The reading "brahmāṇaḥ" (the Brahmas) is clear. || 46 ||
This origin has been told to you for the sake of illustration regarding the creation of me alone, the Prajāpati; there is no fixed rule in that matter whatsoever.

He says "nidarśana" (illustration) to indicate that this description of one [case] is for the purpose of illustrating others as well, according to the maxim of the grain from the cooking pot (*sthālīpulākanyāya*). || 47 ||
This which is commonly regarded as saṃsāra is merely the manifestation of the mind; this sequence of creation has been described for the sake of awakening you. (48)
The established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is that which is universally accepted; it is for the sake of correctly awakening others to that [doctrine]. 48.
The various castes, beginning with the *sāttvika*, which have thus come into being—this sequence of creation has been described to you for the sake of explanation. (49)
He states that even the previously described distinctions among the classes of living beings are for the sake of illustration alone—namely, "the *sāttvikī* [creation].
He further states that the description of the sequence of creation is also for this very purpose—namely, "thus" (*iti*). || 49 ||
Again creation, again destruction; again suffering, again happiness; again the ignorant, again the knower of that [reality]; and again the perspectives of bondage and liberation. (50)

He shows that as long as this mind is not uprooted along with its very root, the succession of saṃsāra will never cease— by means of the verse beginning with "punaḥ sṛṣṭiḥ" (creation again), etc., and ending with "mokṣadṛśo mokṣāstitvakalpanāḥ" (the views of liberation are merely conceptualizations of the existence of liberation). || 50 ||
Furthermore, those who perform creation, whose vision is free from both attachment and aversion, like lamps that have shed their light, repeatedly subside and arise again. (51)
There are glances of affection toward those who are not yet departed—those dear ones present and yet to come—and toward those who have already departed—those dear ones of the past. || 51 ||
In the arising and destruction of both lamps and Brahmas, once their superiority in duration has been relinquished by time, there is no difference whatsoever in their destruction. (52)

[Objection: But surely lamps last only a short time; how can they serve as a comparison for the bodies of Brahmā and others, whose lifespan lasts for two *parārdhas*? To this he says: "At the arising of the body. In the case of the lamp, the "arising of the body" refers to the completion of its form and configuration, shaped like a campaka bud. [This refers to] both arising and destruction.

The transformation of existence consists in the momentary nature of its beginning and end; however, destruction is the non-existence of that which has no beginning or end during the preceding and succeeding times—thus there is no tautology. || 52 ||
Again there is Kṛta, again Tretā, again that Dvāpara and Kali;
the entire world revolves once more like the turning of a wheel. (53)
Because it revolved like a wheel, it was called *cakrāvarta*; by virtue of that state [he became so]. 53.
Again the commencements of Manvantaras, again the successions of Kalpas,
and again and again the states of activity, like day after day at dawn.
The interior of this world, fashioned by the divisions of light and darkness and the movements of time, is repeatedly perceived as this entire universe; yet again and again, it is nothing at all.

In which [all] internal objects are delimited by the calculations of the life-span of living beings, composed of the divisions of time consisting of days and nights (the light and dark halves), the thirty *kalās*, the *muhūrta* consisting of thirty *kāṣṭhās*, and the thirtieth part of a *kṣaṇa*, which is one-twelfth of a *muhūrta*. || 55 ||
Like sparks from fire on a heated iron ball, these states of being always abide by their very nature within the space of consciousness. 56.
In the unstruck [sound], which is free from obstacles such as stones; by its very nature, that is, by virtue of having the nature of the seed-syllable of illusion (māyā). || 56 ||
Sometimes unmanifest and sometimes having attained manifestation,
all this exists within the Supreme Reality like the seasonal growth on a tree.
The menstrual flow (ārtava) arises according to each respective season, just like fruits, flowers, and so forth. || 57 ||
The vibration of consciousness alone is the self of all, always possessing such a form;
from it arises creation, just as the state of duality arises from the eye.
The vibration of consciousness (citspanda) is a transformation (vivarta) of consciousness; the state of "two moons" (dvindutva) is the appearance of two moons. 58.
All continuous perceptions of creation flow together into the consciousness;
though they reside within it, they appear as if not residing there, like rays from the moon.
O Rāma, this saṃsāra is indeed never truly real;
for within the all-powerful [Reality], there exists the power of non-saṃsāra.

The state of having no power of saṃsāra, the state of having no nature of saṃsāra—that is to say, the state of having a nature that is unattached and non-dual—exists from the perspective of ultimate reality; this is the remainder [of the sense]. || 60 ||
And yet, O virtuous one, this world has never been otherwise at any time;
for within the power of all, the power of saṃsāra exists.
The power of saṃsāra is the boundary of the seed of the world. || 61 ||
Due to the impetus of transmigratory existence over time extending for the duration of a great aeon (mahākalpa),
it is logical that the cycle of rebirth will no longer exist from this point forward.

The construction is as follows: characterized by the power (*ṛddhi*), the consciousness that presides (*adhiṣṭhāna-caitanya*), the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāritā*), and time, there exists a cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) which is a great aeon (*mahākalpa*);

this is the dissolution known as liberation (*mokṣa*) belonging to the realm of pure knowledge (*vaijñānika*). The conventional usage—that "it has reached its limit and will not exist hereafter"—is appropriate at this present moment.
O Great-minded One, through the vision of knowledge that "all this is indeed Brahman," it follows logically that there is no such thing as saṃsāra. (63)

Anticipating the objection that there is a contradiction between the non-existence of sentient beings and their existence in saṃsāra, he states the contradiction from the perspective of different viewpoints, beginning with "jñadṛṣṭyā" (from the perspective of the wise). || 63 ||

However, from the perspective of the ignorant, because cyclic existence is uninterrupted, this illusion of saṃsāra is constant; thus, even though it is false, it is established as such in this world. (64)
And because it has been meditated upon again and again, it has never been otherwise;
thus it has been said, "The world is not such [as it appears]," O descendant of Raghu—this is not false.

For this very reason, the Mīmāṃsakas who follow the path of ritual action (karmamīmāṃsakāḥ) maintain that the world has never been otherwise than it is now; thus, their conventional usage of the world as being "eternal by way of its stream" (jagatpravāhanitya) is also justified. He says "again" (punar) [to indicate this]. By this view, [the world] is not false; the meaning is that it serves to establish the authority of the Karmakāṇḍa, which is desired by them. || 65 ||
The quarters of space, seen as constantly falling away in form and subject to destruction—how is it not established that this entire world is perishable? (66)

Because the views of the ignorant are diverse, even the conventional designations of momentary atoms and so forth—imagined by the Buddhas and others to establish their own respective systems—are indeed consistent with those very views; thus he says:
"anārata... Lightning and other phenomena arising in various directions are constantly falling, appearing at all times.
The meaning is that they are observed to have a nature that perishes in an instant; it is precisely thus [that things are perceived] everywhere due to conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). Why?
This is the interrogative particle (*kāku*). 66.
The quarters of the sky were seen with the sun and moon risen everywhere, and the mountains appeared as stable and immovable;
likewise, the thought that "the entire world is indestructible" was an unerring analogy.

Thus, since the stability of mountains, lands, and oceans is observed in all directions filled with the abundant light of the moon, sun, and so forth, the conceptualization of the Sāṃkhya school and others—that the world is eternally existent by its own very nature—is indeed tenable; thus he says: "everywhere" (sarvatra). || 67 ||
There is nothing that does not exist within that one, all-pervasive Self;
for the web of mental constructs and conceptualizations cannot possibly arise within that which is ineffable. 68.

And thus, in Brahman, there is nothing whatsoever that is impossible regarding those objects conceived by its will; rather, it is only the web of conceptualization itself that is not ultimately established. Thus he says: "There is no such thing" (na tadasti). || 68 ||
Again and again all this occurs; again and again there is death and birth; again and again there is pleasure and pain; again and again there are the instruments and actions. (69)
Having established that everything arises as a matter of course, he describes the actual subject at hand—the recurrence of creation—beginning with the word "again" (punaḥ). || 69 ||
Again the quarters, again the sky, again the oceans and the mountains;
creation arises once more, just as the radiance of the sun returns to the sky.
Just as the single light of the sun appears in various ways through houses possessing windows and lattice openings,
so too do the Daityas arise again, the gods again, the successions of other worlds again,
the abodes of heaven and liberation again, Indra again, and the moon again. (71)
Again there was the god Nārāyaṇa, again the sons of Danu and the rest;
again there were the beautiful Candra, Ārka, Varuṇa, and Anila, moving through the quarters [the reading "āśāścalat" is found].
Adorned with Sumeru as its pericarp and graced by the filaments of the Sahya mountains, [the earth shone forth].
The full-blown lotus, with its swollen belly, rises once again toward the two worlds.

Filled with the fragrance of the merit of living beings and swollen with the nectar of enjoyments, she whose belly is vast and whose womb is wide is a lotus-pond characterized by heaven and earth, the two worlds.
Having ascended the forest of the sky and leaping with the multitude of his rays as claws,
the lion of the sun comes forth again to shatter the herd of elephants that is the darkness.
It moves and rises up. || 74 ||
Furthermore, the moon, with rays as beautiful as swaying, clear blossoms, creates a delightful nectar that adorns the faces of the women of the quarters. (75)
It is delightful, brings happiness to all living beings, and produces and accumulates nectar. || 75 ||

Furthermore, the heaps of flowers belonging to those who have performed meritorious deeds fall here upon the earth, their limbs shattered, driven by the wind of the exhaustion of merit from the tree of heaven.
They cut away merits; they sever [them] through enjoyments—thus are the "merit-makers," the inhabitants of heaven, who are characterized by those [lotuses] as heaps of flowers.
Furthermore, having made some sort of rustling sound through the various modes of activity and action known as the commencement of saṃsāra,
the partridge of time departs.

Having made the sound *paṭapaṭa*. [Objection: Since it is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) and not ending in a verb root (*anitipara*), it receives the designation *gati* by the rule *anukaraṇaṃ cānitiparam*; consequently, by the rule *kugatiprādayaḥ*, it ought to be invariably compounded with *lyap*. [Response: True. However, because of the observation of the qualifier "something" (*kiṃcit*), there is no compound, in accordance with the statement in the *Mahābhāṣya*: "There is no formation of a compound for those that have qualifiers. Thus, no compound occurs here.
Time is the period of creation; Kapiñjala is a specific type of bird characterized by that [time]. || 77 ||
Furthermore, when Indra and the others have departed,
