the bee that is another lord of gods, having mounted his chariot alone, approaches the lotus of heaven.

When the minor bee-like Indra, who possessed the characteristics of the former Indra, had departed and his office was terminated, another host of deities authorized for that particular Manvantara arrived, fully prepared and mounted upon Airāvata and other [elephants].
(In the reading "rājyam," this is clear: it was merely empty of the previous host of gods. || 78 ||
Furthermore, the Kali age defiles even that time which has been purified by compassion—
just as a violent wind of refuse defiles the ocean, even though it possesses the discus-bearing Lord Viṣṇu.

The Kṛta age is filled with purity on all sides; Kali is unrighteousness (*adharma*). "Accompanied by Cakra" means together with Viṣṇu who lies within his heart. "Avalaka" refers to the wind that scatters dust, namely the wind of universal dissolution (*pralaya-vāyu*).
Furthermore, it is like a vessel for living beings fashioned by the potter that is Time.
The wheel called "conceptualization" revolves incessantly with great speed.
In which [place] vessels for living beings have been prepared. || 80 ||
The world, its auspicious state destroyed, returns once more to a state of saplessness,
like a forest that has become parched through the habitual persistence of its own volitions.

"Aridity" means the lack of the flavor of the Dharma. "One whose volitions have become habitual" refers to that person in whom volitions have become conformable to whatever object was previously practiced. || 81 ||
Furthermore, when the solar cycles have passed, the world— its infinite bodies consumed by fire and filled with the bones of all beings— attains the state of a cremation ground.

Furthermore, with the downpours of the Puṣkarāvarta clouds, which take the form of the boundary mountains, the world— possessing the great foam of the dancing cycle of existence— returns to the state of a single ocean.
Bhava, who is Saṃhārarudra himself, is dancing; she is so called because of the large foam [of his matted hair] which is white. || 83 ||
Furthermore, when wind and water have subsided and it is devoid of all material things, the world returns to emptiness, like that unprecedented space. (84)
Furthermore, having spent several years with an equanimous disposition toward the flavors of worldly existence,
one dissolves back into one's own self through the body of the aged.
Having lived and experienced life. || 85 ||
Again, at another time, it likewise expands the multitudes of worlds within the void,
just like a city of Gandharvas.
Furthermore, O Rāma, the undertaking of all merit results in the manifestation of everything at the time of dissolution;
indeed, all this revolves again like a wheel. (87)

Furthermore, when dissolution occurs, there is the commencement of creation [the reading "the commencement of all things" (sarvasamārambhaḥ) also exists]. O Rāma, in this grand display of great illusion, which is like a long-lasting cloud-bank, what that is spoken of here— whether it be true or false— must be determined.

In this long-extended delusion, what is there to be determined? The meaning is that when one investigates in this manner, there is nothing at all to be ascertained. In the reading "nirṇayam," the meaning is "that which is devoid of logical justification. || 88 ||
O Rāma, this wheel of saṃsāra is like the story of Dāśūra;
its form is constructed by imagination, devoid of reality, and not real in fact. (89)
With the intention of illustrating the stated point by means of the narrative of Dāśūra, he says: "Dāśūra... (verse 89).

This [world] is spread out without interval by conceptual constructions that, though arisen from the unreal, are like the vision of two moons; it is fashioned by the unreal and possesses a truth that is logically untenable.
Why, then, has such delusion arisen here in this world because of him? 90.
By that cause through which this world has been spread out— dense with conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) arisen from the ignorance of the unreal, and with a continuous, uninterrupted flow—
just so has it been fashioned by an unreal, non-existent agent; and by that [cause] through which the unarisen, underlying *Brahman* is the truth, such being the case, by that [cause].

From what cause does your delusion arise, and from what sign has it been born? That for which you perceive a sign does not exist at all; that which exists in the ultimate sense is Brahman alone, which is fearless. Therefore, this causeless delusion of yours is not logical—this is the conclusion. || 90 ||

Thus ends the forty-seventh canto, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga for Determining the World's Latent Impressions," in the *Sthitiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by Vālmīki in the *Ārṣa* tradition. 47.
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga for Determining the World-Desire," in the *Sthitiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The forty-eighth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Those whose intentions are destroyed by enjoyments and power are full of various ritual activities.
When the deceitful do not regard the truth, it is because they do not see it.

Herein is described Dāśūra’s desire for enjoyments and the like, his contempt, and his subsequent birth; and from the propitiated Fire, the attainment of boons is narrated up to its conclusion. [The reading "prāptyartham" is also found.]

If this wheel of saṃsāra is merely a mental construction, and if Brahman alone exists in reality, then why is it that no one perceives it—even among great persons endowed with intelligence, genius, and skill? If one asks what the cause of this is, he says: the cause is disregard for that [Brahman] and attachment to enjoyments, power, and so forth, which are contrary to it.

Regarding the phrase "by specific actions": those who have accumulated desires through various worldly and Vedic specific actions—which serve as the means for attaining enjoyments and sovereignty in this world and the next—are deceitful and deceivers of both themselves and others. || 1 ||
But those who have gone beyond the intellect and are not enslaved by the senses,
they behold this worldly illusion as clearly as a wood-apple fruit in the palm of their hand.
To whom, then, do they appear? He says: "But those who... The mention of *māyā* (illusion) is also indicative of *satya* (reality).
Having seen that worldly *māyā* to be insubstantial, the discerning individual soul casts off the *māyā* consisting of egoism, just as a snake sheds its skin. (3)
The external world, consisting of the notion "mine," which is the cause of attachment; and the internal one, consisting of the ego-sense, which is the cause of the attachment "I. (3)
Then, having attained non-attachment, O Rāma, one is not born again, even while remaining for a long time in the fields [of rebirth], like a seed burnt by fire. || 4 ||
Fools strive for the benefit of the body— which is beset by mental and physical ailments and destined for destruction tomorrow morning— but not for the sake of the self.

Seeing that one who is deeply attached to enjoyments and power exerts effort for the sake of protecting the body—which is like strengthening a prison—and thus engages in futile misfortune while neglecting the supreme goal of man (puruṣārtha), which is utterly improper, [the author] laments for him with the verse beginning "ādhī-":
"perishable either tomorrow or today. The fourth case ending here is used in the sense of "for the sake of that" (*tadarthārtha*).
The dative case is used in connection with the word *hita*.
Do not, like an ignorant man, fulfill the desires of this ignorant body for the sake of suffering; rather, be solely devoted to the Self, which is your true nature.
Śrī Rāma said: "O Lord, is this wheel of the cycle of existence— which is like the story of Dāśūra— merely a form constructed by imagination, devoid of any real substance?"
Rāma, desiring to hear the story of Dāśūra which was previously introduced, asks: "Dāśūra...
[The meaning is: "What is that which you have said—that the wheel of saṃsāra, for the sake of sensual pleasure, is devoid of substance?
Describe it in such a manner as it truly is. || 7 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, listen as I relate the narrative of Dāśūra, which is told by way of describing the true nature of the world-illusion (jaganmāyā).
"By way of designation through description"; that is to say, by way of illustration. || 8 ||
On this surface of the earth, there is a great and glorious region known as Māgadha, famous for its trees bearing variegated flowers.
The country inhabited by the Magadhas is Māgadha. The suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "the place of their residence. (Pāṇini 4.2.81)
Its forests were graced by the playful expansion of kadamba groves, and it was enchanting with every wonder due to the flocks of various birds. || 10 ||
Its boundaries were crowded with grain, it was adorned with city groves,
and the banks of all its rivers were filled with lotuses, water-lilies, and white lilies.
In which the boundaries of the villages, extending to the limits of the fields, were crowded and densely packed with crops.
There was the humming of songs sung by women sporting on garden swings; the ground of the paths was dense with flowers gathered during the night.

In which [place] the earth was such that its paths were densely covered with flowers—discarded after being enjoyed by night—that had become withered; it was as if those very arrows of the God of Love remained there. 12.
There, on a certain mountain slope thick with *karṇikāra* flowers,
it was adorned with dense groves of plantains and clusters of *nīpa* trees.
There, in that region, it was resplendent with *nīpa* and *kadamba* trees, as well as other shrubs.
In that place where the wind was shimmering with a flood of flowers and reddened by the pollen of filaments, where the kāraṇḍava birds raised their cries and the cranes warbled melodiously; (14)
In which [place] the winds resounded and roared with floods and currents of flowers;
in which the impassioned cranes, full of affection, were crying out.
In that meritorious, excellent mountain, where the trees were filled with various birds,
there lived a certain sage of supreme righteousness and great ascetic power.
Named Dāśūra, he was endowed with great ascetic power;
residing on the slopes of Mount Kadamba, he was free from passion and possessed of great intelligence.
By means of yoga accompanied by austerity. He is called *vāstavya* because he dwells (*vasati*) upon the top of a *kadamba* tree, that is, at its summit;
for there is an injunction stating: "The suffix *tavyat* is applied after the root *vas*, and [the prefix] *ṇi* is added when it denotes the agent. || 16 ||
Śrī Rāma said:
O Blessed One, for what reason did that ascetic dwell in the forest, and how was it that he lived upon the back of the great Kadamba tree? (17)
How, by what power, and in what manner? || 17 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
His father was renowned as Śaraloman;
like a second Brahmā to Rāma, he dwelt upon that very mountain.
He had an only son named Kaca, who was like the preceptor of the gods;
together with that son, he spent his life in the forest.
He brought his life and lifespan to an end. || 19 ||
Then, having eaten only śaraloma, he went through a multitude of ages;
casting off his body, he went to the abode of the gods like a bird that has abandoned its nest.

Having experienced—that is, having undergone—the multitude of ages (yuga), the multitude of years consisting of pairs of solstices (ayanayugala), or the multitude of dualities such as pleasure and pain. || 20 ||
In that forest, Dāśūra alone wept piteously like a kurara bird whose father has been snatched away by fate. (21)

By the statement "only one," it is understood that he followed his mother and father. One whose father was removed by fate (*daśā*)—that is, by the final stage of existence or by a particular planetary period (*graha-daśā-viśeṣa*)—or one from whose body the father has departed with ten vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and been led to the other world. *Kurara* is a species of bird. (21)
With his heart tormented by grief due to the separation from his parents,
he surely fell into a state of withering, like a lotus in the winter season.
O Rāma, that boy, whose soul was exceedingly distressed, was thus consoled in the forest by a forest deity whose body remained invisible.
"In this manner" means by the method that is about to be described; "by her whose body was invisible" means by her who had become hidden. || 23 ||
O son of a seer, possessed of great wisdom, why do you weep like one ignorant?
Why do you not understand the flickering nature of this saṃsāra? (24)
It is flickering and impermanent. || 24 ||
O virtuous one, such is the nature of the world at all times; in this cycle of existence, the course of life is unstable.
One is born, lives, and thereafter inevitably perishes. (25)
"Jīvyate" means "he lives. The transposition of the suffix and the word is a Vedic (chāndasa) usage. || 25 ||
O Sage, whatever is seen within this vision—from Brahmā downwards—all of that must come to an end; of this there is no doubt.
In the conventional view of the seen and the seer, whatever is well-known—this is the remainder [of the sense]. It is that which is to be gone to, that which is to be attained. || 26 ||
Therefore, do not indulge in useless despair over the death of your father;
the setting of one who has been born is inevitable, like that of the sun.

For that purpose, for that reason: *aharpateḥ* means of the Sun (*sūrya*). According to the rule "the substitution of *r* should be stated for words beginning with *ahar* when followed by words beginning with *pati*," the substitution of *r* occurs. || 27 ||
Hearing the voice saying "I am bodiless," Śikhaṇḍin, his eyes bloodshot with rage,
regained his composure as if from the sound of thunder.
From "stanita," meaning from the thundering of clouds. || 28 ||
Having risen and performed his necessary duties, he then, out of respect for his father,
formed a firm resolve for asceticism for the sake of attaining the highest perfection.
A son must necessarily perform the funeral rites for his father as an obligatory duty.
Through his brahminical deeds while practicing austerities in the forest,
he attained the status of a Vedic scholar characterized by infinite resolve.
The state of being a *śrotriya* consists of being composed of endless intentions, abounding in numerous conceptualizations regarding purity, impurity, and so forth;
it is the state of being devoted to the study of the Vedas, the investigation of their meaning, and the performance of the prescribed rites. (30)
Though he was a master of the Vedas, his mind found no rest even upon the sacred surface of the earth, for his intellect remained intent on objects yet unknown.
He whose intellect is such that it does not know Brahman—which must necessarily be known—is [deficient] by virtue of that very conceptualization of purity, impurity, and so forth. || 31 ||
Seeing even this entire surface of the earth— which was in fact completely pure— as if it were impure, he did not find delight anywhere at all.
The particle *eva* is used in the sense of "only" even in the phrase *kvacideva*.
Then, by his own volition alone, he resolved:
"The very tip of a tree is utterly pure; there my dwelling is appropriate."
Therefore, I shall now perform such austerity by which I may attain a state like that of my own self among the branches, as well as among the twigs and the leaves. (34)
That is for that purpose. Like a bird (khaga), like a winged creature (pakṣin), or like a god (deva), there is the capacity for stability, that is, for remaining [there]. || 34 ||
Having reflected thus, he kindled a most brilliant fire and,
having carved flesh from the surface of his own shoulder, offered it as an oblation into it.

From the observation of the resolve, "I shall perform austerity," it is understood that this undertaking of thousands of oblations follows immediately after austerity, since success was not seen to occur quickly thereafter. || 35 ||
Now, let not the entire throats of the host of gods pass through my mouth and be reduced to ashes by the flesh of a brahmin. (36)

Then the Blessed One [acted] after thinking thus: "I am Saptārchi" (the seven-flamed one); this is the connection with what follows. He shows the very manner of his thought with the words beginning "of the host of gods" (*gīrvāṇavṛndasya*). "By my mouth" means by the mouth of Agni, for according to the Vedic revelation (*śruti*), "The gods indeed have Agni as their mouth. All the surfaces of the throat-regions were smeared by having eaten the flesh of the Brahmin.
The grammatical connection is: "Thinking, 'May they not go to the state of ashes; may they not attain it. || 36 ||
Having reflected thus, the Lord Saptārchi, whose rays were blazing like those of the sun, appeared before that deity as if he were Vākpati himself.
He possessed blazing rays and radiant splendor, like the sun, the lord of light, or like Bṛhaspati, the lord of speech.

He spoke these firm words regarding the boon desired by the prince: [The reading *dhīram* (firm) is correct, as the commentator accepts *dhīra* in the place of the second singular vocative, which provides better euphony. "O wise one, [grant] the boon favored by the prince."
"O virtuous one, take this which has been placed [here], like a jewel from the space within a treasure chest. || 38 ||
"O Dhīrā"—this is an address appropriate to her courage. "That which was established by the fulfillment of your resolve is already situated within you;
take it, just as the owner takes a gem from the interior of its own sheath. (38)
Having spoken thus, the young Brahmin, having honored the Fire-god with a beautiful flower for the guest-offering (arghya) and with words of praise, spoke.
"O Blessed One, I do not obtain the sanctifying circle of the earth that was once filled with living beings; therefore, let my station be upon the tops of trees. (40)
It was filled with those who defile purity—such as Śūdras, Cāṇḍālas, dogs, cats, and the like.
A purifying circle is a sacred place. 40.
When the son of the sage had spoken thus, the Lord Śikhin (Agni), the mouth of all the gods, said,
"So be it for you," and vanished from sight.
Śikhin is the deity of fire. || 41 ||
When that god had vanished like twilight from a lotus in an instant,
Kumāra, his desires fulfilled, shone like the full moon.
Filled with joy, he laughed at the moon, which had attained its full orb yet was surrounded by its digits, as if it were a lotus that had attained the splendor of the faces of its beloveds.
And it was blossomed by the beauty of his white smile. || 43 ||

He describes the very splendor of his face: "Adhigatena" and so forth. The poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) is that Dāśūra laughed at the moon and the lotus because of the abundance of radiance from the circle of his face, which was employed through the attainment of the desired boon. || 43 ||

Thus ends the forty-eighth sarga, titled "The Description of the Bestowing of Boons upon Dāśūra," in the Section on Stability (*sthitiprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrī-Vāsiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa*, within the *Vālmīki-Devarāja-Mokṣopāya*.
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Bestowal of Boons upon Dāśūra," in the Section on Stability (*sthitiprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The forty-ninth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, [he beheld] that which stood in the midst of the forest, kissing the circle of the clouds.
The circle of his shoulders was attended by the horses of the sun, exhausted at midday. || 1 ||
Here, the Kadamba tree—charming with its branches, sprouts, abundance of flowers, fruits, and birds—is described through poetic ornaments such as *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) and others. || 1 ||
Whose shoulders were frequented by the horses of the sun at midday, as if they were weary. || 1 ||
With his branch-arms, he was like a canopy stretching across the belly of the quarters;
with his eyes of blossoming flowers, he was gazing upon the directions.
The ellipsis is "acting like a canopy. He was looking all around the quarters of the sky to see whether there remained any other spot not covered by the canopy of branches. || 2 ||
With his hair-like bees fluttering in no small measure, dusted by the wind,
he was as if wiping the faces of the quarters with his hands of tender sprouts.

He whose abundant locks of hair—consisting of wandering bees rendered devoid of pollen by the winds—are shaken about; [he who is the lord] of the quarters, the beautiful women of the directions. || 3 ||
The forest garlands seemed to laugh with their mouths— the dense clusters of bright guḍūcī blossoms on the kaccha shrubs— which appeared like betel-filled lips.
The *kacchās* are the regions of sprouts that cover the frosty water by dividing it into droplets;

with those large, clear clusters of blossoms belonging to the *guḍucchā*—a specific kind of creeper—which stand like rows of teeth and are filled with filaments (*kañjara*), they are *kesaritaiḥ*. || 4 ||
With the playful splendors of creepers and the pollen of flower filaments, it formed a circular expanse like the full moon with its radiance. || 5 ||

By whom a circular arrangement has been formed through the playful movements—the extraordinary beauty—of the creepers, which are radiant with blossoms and whose pollen is settled upon the filaments. || 5 ||
The world was encompassed by its great height, as if by a path of the Siddhas hidden by a thicket of creepers where cakora birds warbled.
In which [forest], in bowers—regions covered by creepers—chakora birds were warbling;
which was crowded and dense with rows of branches and twigs;
and which, due to its height, was like the path of the Siddhas (Svātīpathavīthī), veiled by the celestial chariots of the planets, lunar mansions, and stars.
The meaning is that it stands supported by its upper portion, like the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa). || 6 ||
The sky was adorned by the hanging peacock plumages of those seated upon the pedestals of the *skandhas*, appearing like clouds accompanied by rainbows.
With the plumage—the tail feathers—of *kalāpins*, which are peacocks. || 7 ||
It was filled with white yak-tails (*camara*) resting upon every shoulder, rising and sinking as they moved,
appearing and disappearing again and again like moons throughout a year.

They were resting, having taken refuge in the hollows of each individual trunk; some were submerged with half their bodies inside, while others were emerging with half their bodies outside, some having entered and others remaining on the exterior.
For this very reason:

By means of the *camara* deer—varieties of deer that are seen and then lost, or seen and not seen—the great size of the shoulders and their contact with the ground are understood from this. In the case of the moon, they are "sunk and emerged," or set and risen; for this very reason, they are "seen and lost. (8)
With the warbling of flocks of francolin partridges, the sweet cooing of cuckoos, and the cries of pheasants,
it seemed as if the mountain were singing aloud with its lofty peaks.
The jīvañjīvas and cakoras [are birds]. || 9 ||
It was as if the world were covered by flocks of *kādamba* geese sporting in their nests and by *siddhas* resting in the hollows of heaven.
With kadamba ducks and kalahamsa swans, and with perfected beings (siddhas) sporting and playing in their nests and dwellings, it stood like the entire universe (brahmāṇḍa). || 10 ||
It was resorted to on all sides by clusters of blossoms with hands of trembling young shoots and eyes of bees, like heaven inhabited by celestial nymphs.

In the verse beginning with "pravāla" (coral), the qualifiers should be applied as common to both the celestial nymphs (*apsarases*) and the flower-clusters (*mañjaryaḥ*) through the device of *śleṣa* (paronomasia). || 11 ||
With the pollen from clusters of night-lilies, shimmering like the play of Indra’s bow,
it was dark-hued and tawny with blossoms, like a cloud accompanied by lightning.
The mention of "kumuda" (white water-lilies) is an indicative term for various colored creeper flowers similar to the kumuda, nīlotpala, kokanada, and so forth. For this very reason,
it is characterized by their pollen accompanied by the play of Indra’s bow (the rainbow), and is tawny with its own clusters of blossoms.
"Dark on all sides with leaves"; in the word *vidyutvantam*, because it is a *bha*-stem by the rule *tasau matvarthe*, the substitution of *jaś* does not occur. 12.
Rich with a thousand branching arms, filling the hollow of the sky,
it was like the Cosmic Form (Viśvarūpa) dancing, with the moon and sun serving as its earrings.

The meaning is that he was standing like Viṣṇu, displaying his own universal form (viśvarūpa); or alternatively, the meaning is that he was standing as if he were the very nature of the universe. || 13 ||
Seated upon that lord of serpents, it was like another celestial sphere in the midst of the sky, crowded with hosts of stars and composed of creepers and flowers. (14)

The "orb of the earth" (khamaṇḍala) is the space within the interior of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa). For that [space] also is one in which the lords of serpents, such as Śeṣa, and the elephants of the quarters are seated—that is, settled—beneath the surface of the earth. The rest is clear. || 14 ||
Like the Grandfather (Brahmā) adorned with all the mountains and forests,
he was like a single treasury of fruits, shoots, and flowers upon the earth.
In the case of Pitāmaha (Brahmā), it means shining with all the creatures, mountains, and forests created by himself;
in the case of Kadamba, the meaning is shining with all the forests of the mountain.
It bore a mass of buds veiled by the pollen of flowers,
like the sky at its edges where the net of stars is obscured by the rays of the sun.
In the marshes mentioned previously, it bore a mass of buds—a cluster of flower-buds—covered and overspread with the pollen of flowers. || 16 ||
The surface of the earth was covered in the world by tree trunks filled with flocks of nests and swarming with restless birds, as if it were filled with inhabited districts.
Valitam means pervaded. || 17 ||
Abounding with flower-clusters and beautiful banners, adorned with circles of creepers, white with *maṅkola* flowers, and strewn with heaps of blossoms. || 18 ||
He describes the similarity to the inner apartments with three verses beginning with "mañjarī":
[The palace] was filled with the sound of cooing cakoras, bees, parrots, cuckoos, and sārikās; its fierce windows were like deep caverns covered by thick clusters of blossoms. (19)

In the case of the inner apartments (*antaḥpura*), the windows and inner chambers (*gavākṣāḥ kuḍyāpavarakāṇi*) are formidable and unassailable because their cavities are covered with thick clusters of many jewels and the like, their interiors are filled [with valuables], and they are protected by iron bolts and eunuchs (*varṣavara*). In the case of the trees, they are formidable because they contain serpents within them. (19)
Abounding with birds in flight and having hollows where people moved slowly,
it was like the supreme inner apartment of all the forest goddesses.
In the case of the tree, its hollow was stirred up at its base by people seeking shelter in the shade.
It shone with swarms of bees on its banks and rows of flower filaments falling like rivers descending upon a mountain. || 21 ||
Its trunk was covered by swarms of flower petals wandering about, playfully tossed by the gentle breeze,
increasing like white clouds covering a mountain.
By means of the "Vardhamāna" [vessels], which increase and accumulate day by day. || 22 ||
With her broad hips rubbed by the flanks of an elephant and her knees firmly planted,
she stood with fixed steps like a young woman against a great mountain.
Now he describes the *mūlabandha* (the root-lock): "By the elephant... and so forth.
By the phrase "rubbed by the temples of an elephant," the height of the *mūlabandha* is indicated.
It is [performed] with the knees raised and fixed like a pedestal (*pīṭhinā*), extended like a seat (*pīṭhavat-prasṛtena*), and expansive (*ābhoginā*) or wide.

With its foundations secured by the *mūlabandha* (foundation-binding), it was a firmly established site; with young trees, it was filled with groves of trees growing on the foothills (*upatyakā*). || 23 ||
It was surrounded by a multitude of birds with variegated-colored wings that moved within the hollows of its trunks,
like Śārṅgin (Viṣṇu) surrounded by a host of living beings.
As if with a multitude of his attendant spirits. || 24 ||
With his trembling web of fingers formed by clusters of blossoms, he seemed to be demonstrating the art of dramatic gesture for the forest creepers dancing in the woodland breezes. (25)
Abhinayas are specific gestures of the hands, eyes, and so forth, well-known from the *Nāṭyaśāstra*, which manifest internal emotions;
[he was] as if instructing or teaching the manner of performing—that is, the method of accomplishing—those gestures. || 25 ||
Thinking with satisfaction, "This alone shall be my dwelling for those who seek me," it seemed to dance as if through the swaying of its many richly adorned creeper-circles.

Among the regions of my roots, hollows, trunk, branches, leaves, flowers, and so forth, there is not even a single spot that is exclusively for the dwelling of those who seek me—such as humans, deer, birds, and others. At any given time, every other part may be utilized as a dwelling, leaving perhaps only one remaining. Oh, how great is my service to others!
"By reason of satisfaction and the overpowering intensity of joy, [he thought] that all his limbs had become fruitful. (26)
Because it was the sole beloved of the creeper, it was overflowing with the sentiment of love (śṛṅgāra-rasa),
as if singing in a low, sweet tone (kākali) through the humming of intoxicated bees.
Because he was the sole beloved among many lovely women characterized as creepers;
[he sang] with a *kākali*, a sweet-toned sound. || 27 ||
It seemed to offer a welcome, as it were, to the sky-dwelling Siddhas with flowers cast down in reverence, through the warbling of cuckoos and the humming of swarms of bees.
In such a way that it would be like a flower released with great reverence. || 28 ||
With the splendor of the flowers and fruits of the five trees at its edge,
it seemed to be smiling with the brilliant luster of its flower buds.

It was as if laughing with the splendor of creepers and other plants, [situated near] the five auspicious trees— known as the banyan (*vaṭa*), the udumbara, the *plakṣa*, the mango (*āmra*), and the *palāśa*— which stand at the edge, or perhaps the five celestial wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpataru*) such as the *mandāra*, which stand at the northern edge. || 29 ||
With its neck held high, it seemed to flee through the midst of the sky as if to conquer the *pārijāta* tree, pursued by swarms of birds soaring above.
It was as if it were running through the midst of the sky, with its neck excessively raised and its head held high. || 30 ||
With dense rows of clusters, their lofty centers shimmering with bees,
it seemed as though it were striving to surpass Indra, who possesses a thousand eyes, by means of its incomparable beauty.

"By dense rows," meaning by thick lines; "having attained the state of having a thousand eyes," meaning the state of having innumerable eyes—this is the remainder of the sentence (the reading *prāptaiḥ* being understood). "Incomparable," because they surpass Indra's eyes in both splendor and number, they are impossible to equalize. || 31 ||
In some places, covered by a multitude of jewel-encrusted hoods as clear as clusters of blossoms, it was like the serpent Śeṣa risen from the netherworld with a desire to behold the sky.
With his clear-jewel hoods resembling clusters of flowers and marked by the characteristics of flower-bunches, he stood like Śeṣa risen from the netherworld out of a desire to behold the sky;
with his form covered in dust, he appeared like a second Śaṅkara.
[He was] like a tree bearing fruit through its shade, bringing welfare to all people.
The Blessed One, Śaṅkara, is indeed the benefactor of his devotees alone; however, this one is the benefactor of all people—this is the distinction.
The Kadamba tree in the sky, like a city, was filled with new pavilions of flowering creepers whose buds were burst open by the dense mass of their petals.
He beheld it teeming with flocks of birds and throngs of serpents.

It was constructed with new pavilions of flowering creepers, consisting of clusters of dense petals— blossoms whose buds had opened by the bursting of their sheaths— which, through the parting of those thick masses of leaves, assumed various distinct shapes; and it was frequented by city-dwellers who bore the characteristics of flocks of birds.

The meaning is that he beheld the *kadamba* tree standing like a city constructed and situated in the sky, densely crowded [with birds]. (34) Thus ends the forty-ninth canto, titled "Description of the *Kadamba* Tree at Dāśūra," in the Section on Stability (*sthitiprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by Vālmīki and belonging to the Divine Sage (*ārṣa*). (49)
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Daśūrka Tribe," in the Sthitiprakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
Fifty-fifth Sarga.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Then he [the sage] beheld him thus, resplendent with the blossoming sprouts of the fruit of his intellect.
With a mind slow with bliss, he was like a mountain composed of flowers. || 1 ||
Observed here by Dāśūra, who was stationed at the tip of that Kadamba tree, the quarters of the sky, appearing in the form of women, are described through an expansion of their qualities. (1)
This one is Dāśūra; likewise, he is one who possesses the aforementioned kind of notion regarding the impurity of the ground. (1)
Śauri ascended the kadamba tree standing in the forest, which acted as a pillar for heaven and earth,
just as [Viṣṇu] ascended the lofty banyan tree situated in the single ocean.
Like a pillar standing between the two worlds, heaven and earth, as if fixed in a forest. || 2 ||
There, upon the tip of a leaf at the end of a branch reaching toward the sky,
he entered with freedom from fear and established himself in one-pointed ascetic practice.
In such a way that there may be freedom from the apprehension of impurity and distraction. || 3 ||
Then, having sat down upon a soft seat of fresh sprouts,
he gazed for a moment at the directions with eyes flickering with curiosity.
Upon a seat fashioned from fresh sprouts, she sat with her restless, tremulous eyes moving about out of curiosity. || 4 ||
Beautiful with single-strand pearl necklaces, they have the great mountains for their budding breasts;
the stainless sky is their braid of hair, and the swaying dark clouds are their locks.

In all these cases, the qualifiers are to be applied to both [the women and the rivers]. They are beautiful with single-string necklaces (*ekāvalī*), which are varieties of pearl necklaces characterized by their flowing lines. || 5 ||
Clad in garments of blue shoots, adorned with ear-ornaments of abundant flowers,
holding full jars of the ocean, and richly decorated with many ornaments.
Possessing many ornaments, they have numerous adornments. || 6 ||
They bear blossoming lotuses, their breath is fragrant,
their low humming is like the warbling of cuckoos, and the sound of their waterfalls serves as their tinkling anklets.
Those [women] whose sweet, indistinct speech consists of the very humming sounds of blue bees, cuckoos, and other such creatures. || 7 ||
The mountains have the sky for their heads, the earth for their feet, rows of forests for their lines of body hair,
jungles for their thighs, and the moon and sun for their earrings.
The fields of the saṃsāra of Śāligrāma are provided with sandalwood planters;
they are draped in the white cloud-garments of snow clinging to the peaks of their breasts.
Whose fields were the various worlds, quivering with the tremors of crops such as rice; whose portions were the constituent parts of the warrior class (*kṣatra*);
who were endowed with foreheads marked by bees resting upon sandalwood trees;
and who, like snow, were clinging everywhere to their breasts characterized by mountain peaks.
Whose garments of cloud are bright white.
They are mirrors adorned by the full expanse of the waters of the great ocean;
they possess the horripilation of the heat of the multitude of stars; and they are the inner apartments within the universe.
The floods of water in the great oceans were themselves the mirrors for beholding their fresh adornments;
and the hosts of stars, the clusters of constellations, were themselves the drops of perspiration upon their skin.
Wearing garments dyed with safflower, adorned with saffron and the rays of the sun, they were endowed with various flowers and anointed with sandalwood as white as moonbeams. || 11 ||
Their bodices were made of seasonal materials—namely, flowers and sprouts produced in their respective seasons—by which they supported their breasts. || 11 ||
Seated upon a leaf of a creeper suspended in the sky,
he joyfully beheld the women of the three worlds, who appeared like a spreading flood of water from the forest-land of the earth.
The ten directions were adorned without interruption by flowers.

Seated upon the leaves of a branch of a creeper situated in the sky, he beheld the ten directions (*daśa āśāḥ*), which are the quarters of space; these are like women of the three worlds (*tribhuvanavanitāḥ*) because they are enjoyed by the people residing in the three worlds, and whose garments (*veṣāḥ*) consist of spreading, extensive forests, valleys, and clouds, as well as artificial distinctions of form and ornaments.
The meaning is that he saw. || 12 ||

Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "The Survey of the Directions by Dāśūra," in the Section on Stability (*sthitiprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, belonging to the Holy Tradition (*ārṣa*). 50.
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, titled "The Survey of the Directions by Dāśūra," in the Section on Stability (*sthitiprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
Fifty-first canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
From that time forth, he became renowned there in the hermitage of ascetics.
Kadambadāśūra was a hero in fierce asceticism. || 1 ||
The awakening of the Self through mental sacrifices, the birth of a son from the forest goddess, and the bestowing of knowledge upon the son of Dāśūra are celebrated here. (1)
In severe austerity, the hero was not averse; that is to say, he was intent upon it. || 1 ||
Therefore, having stood upon the leaf of the creeper and gazed at the quarters for a moment,
he assumed the firm lotus posture (padmāsana) with his mind withdrawn from the directions.
The quarters, the directions; by one who has withdrawn his self, that is, turned it back. || 2 ||
Not knowing the ultimate truth, abiding in mere ritual action,
and with a mind joined by the meanness of desiring results, he performed that sacrifice.
With his inner self situated within the leaves of the creeper in the sky,
he performed all the sacrificial rites in their proper sequence with that very mind of his.
By him, while staying upon the leaves of a branch of a creeper reaching toward the sky, [all rites] beginning with the *ādhāna* and ending with the *aśvamedha* were performed. || 4 ||
There, for ten years, he worshipped the gods with his mind alone through sacrifices such as those involving cows, horses, and human beings, accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
When his expansive mind had attained purity over time,
knowledge born of self-serenity descended within him by its own power.

"Purity" means being devoid of defects such as passion (*rāga*) and the like. Thus, when obstacles have been destroyed, [this occurs] by the force of the awakening of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) from hearing [the teachings] performed in previous births. (6)
Then, with his veils shattered and the impurity of latent impressions washed away,
he once beheld her standing before him within that creeper.

Then, through that knowledge, his veil of ignorance is shattered; and by its repeated practice, he becomes one whose impurities of latent tendencies have dissolved—meaning he is liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 7 ||
[He saw] the forest goddess, large-eyed, with flowers for her garments and light for her ornaments;
a lovely woman with a beautiful face, her eyes rolling with intoxication.
To her, whose limbs were faultless and who was exceedingly captivating with the fragrance of blue lotuses, that sage spoke as she stood with her face cast down.
With faces bowed down by the shame of prostrating in devotion. || 9 ||
"O lotus-petal-eyed one, who are you—like a forest creeper filled with *kokilā* flowers, you who agitate the God of Love with your splendor? (10)
She was bowed down by cuckoos and by floods of flowers.
"Why do you stand there like a flowering creeper, as if you were a female friend?"—when she was thus addressed, the fawn-eyed woman with her fair and full breasts [remained silent]. (11)
"Having grasped a creeper"—this is the ellipsis. || 11 ||
He spoke these charming words in an innocent tone to the sage:
"Whatever things there are on the surface of the earth that are difficult to obtain and desired," (12)
Those [fruits] are quickly obtained through the very supplication of the great.
I am here in this place thick with creepers and adorned by your kadamba trees. (13)
By means of begging and supplication. || 13 ||
O Brahmin, in the forest that is the abode of the playful charms of Lakṣmī, there dwells a forest deity;
and on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, during the festival of Smara, [she appears].

She whose dwellings for her pastimes are indeed the bowers of creepers. Having given the answer to the question "Who are you?", she states the purpose of her arrival with the words beginning with "He who... [and so forth].
[This refers to] a festival consisting of song, instrumental music, dance, offerings, food, and so on, which was undertaken for the propitiation of Smara (Kāmadeva). 14.
A gathering of forest goddesses took place in the Nandana grove;
there, O Lord, I went to that assembly of the beauties of the three worlds.
The assembly was a gathering of forest goddesses, the most beautiful women in the three worlds. || 15 ||
There, at the festival of love, I saw all my friends accompanied by their sons;
because I am childless, I was therefore deeply distressed. (16)
By that state of being sonless. || 16 ||
O Protector, while you—the great wish-granting tree—stand as the caravan leader for the multitude of all goals, how is it that I, like one without a protector and childless, must indeed grieve? (17)
Of all objects and human goals, it refers to the caravan, that is, the community; the word "caravan" (sārtha) is used figuratively for a community that does not consist of living beings. || 17 ||
"Give me your son, O Blessed One; do not give him here to the fire.
O son, I shall offer you as an oblation for the sake of pacifying the burning pain of my grief. (18)

The phrase "for the sake of allaying the burning" refers to the burning of the body in comparison with the burning of the mind; the sense is that the bodily burning is easy to endure, as indicated by the reading "the suffering of burning is slight. || 18 ||
Having spoken thus to that slender woman, the eminent sage, filled with compassion, smiled and said to her while giving her the flower held in his hand.
The meaning is that he is endowed with compassion, but has not fallen away from fortitude. || 19 ||
"Go, O slender-limbed one; in a month you shall give birth to a lovely son whose eyes are free of impurity—one worthy of worship—just as a fine creeper brings forth its blossom. (20)
Worthy of worship, adored by the world. || 20 ||
However, this son of ours was requested by you while you were overcome by the impulse of death; having undergone great hardship, he will therefore become a knower [of the truth].

Having encountered a hardship—a life-threatening crisis—he formed the intention of suicide due to the onset of death; because he was entreated by you, who had come along with him, for that reason he became known as a knower of reality (*tattvajña*).
The meaning is that he is not like the son of another forest goddess, who is merely greedy for sensual enjoyments. || 21 ||
Having spoken thus to the slender maiden, whose countenance was bright with joy and who was eager with the prayer, "I shall perform service for you," that sage dismissed her.
Service consists of attendance, association, worship, and other such offerings. || 22 ||
She went to her own abode, and he remained with his own self;
time passed in due order, marked by seasons and years.
"With his own self" means "without assistance"; he "carried away," that is, he overcame. || 23 ||
Then, after a long time, that very same lotus-eyed woman approached the sage, bringing with her her twelve-year-old son.
Having prostrated and sat before the sage whose face was like the moon,
she spoke with a gentle voice, like a female bee to a mango tree.
Alinī means a female bee. || 25 ||
"O Blessed One, this is that son of ours, the prince who is worthy [of his station]. Indeed, I have made him an expert in all the arts. (26)
Of the arts, that is, of all sciences beginning with the Vedas. || 26 ||
O Lord, he has not attained that auspicious knowledge alone by which one is no longer tormented within this wheel of saṃsāra. (27)
Knowledge is the science of Brahman. || 27 ||
O Lord, out of compassion, please instruct me now in this very knowledge yourself; for who indeed would consign a son born into a noble family to the state of ignorance? (28)

Regarding the phrase "by folly": since other forms of knowledge have as their object that which is not the ultimate reality, they are indeed merely ignorance; thus, the sense is that there can be no deliverance from folly by means of them. || 28 ||
To her who was speaking thus, that sage said, "O powerless one, establish this son right here," and having spoken, he dismissed her.
He was a true disciple, endowed with the qualities of a most excellent disciple. || 29 ||
When she had departed, that wise man remained self-restrained in the presence of his father, like Aruṇa before the sun.
Being self-restrained through the vow of serving his teacher as a resident disciple, and being firm in his observances, Aruṇa, the elder brother of Garuḍa, [set out]. || 30 ||
Having attained this realization, the sage then instructed his son there for a long time with various eloquent expressions.

"Having been made wretched"—meaning, having been tormented by the hardships of service, the observance of vows, and so forth—he remained after attaining "knowledge," which refers to the indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*) produced by the scriptures that serve as a means; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
Then, immediately thereafter, he enlightened that son for a long time.

The meaning is that he instructed him so that [the truth] might become directly perceived (*aparokṣībhāva*). Alternatively, the meaning is that the father, having previously been tormented by austerity and having attained realization, taught it himself so that his son might not likewise be so tormented.
By means of hundreds of narratives and legends, through illustrations devised from experience, as well as through historical accounts and the definitive conclusions of the Vedas and Vedānta; || 32 ||
*Ākhyāyikās* are compositions consisting of narratives concerning events experienced by the author himself; *ākhyānas* are compositions consisting of narratives such as the accounts of others.

By means of hundreds of these—decisions [or conclusions] based on doctrines imagined through the perception of similarities, namely, those well-known historical episodes from the *Mahābhārata* and other sources.
By means of established doctrines. || 32 ||
Through constant and detailed discourses that inspire no weariness,
and by means of experiences brought to fruition, may [this devotion] attain firm establishment in me.

The connection with the preceding verse is as follows: he enlightened [his son] through historical examples and other means, so that the son might attain—through his intellect—a firm mastery, that is, a deep-rooted understanding, of me, the inner Self (pratyagātman). || 33 ||
The Great-Souled One, through the power of his own experience, has had enough of the multitude of words whose meanings are merely conventional and devoid of aesthetic flavor;
like a cloud [refreshing] a peacock standing before him, he [delights the one before him].
The great sage awakened his son in the sky.

By means of those multitudes of words whose meaning is such that it is "experienced"—meaning the wonder of self-realization—and by virtue of which they are "surpassing," that is, superior to all other aesthetic flavors (*rasas*);
"fitting," because its nature is the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*) and thus it must necessarily be understood; [and] in the case of the cloud, by virtue of experience, merely upon hearing [them].

By means of such multitudes of thundering words— which generate joy for the peacocks (*śikhaṇḍin*), which abound in other aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*), and which are appropriate for the purpose of dancing together with the peahens (*śikhaṇḍinī*)— [the sky] resounded in the atmosphere, at the tops of trees, and in the firmament. Thus, in the *Ārṣa* (Sage-authored) *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by Vālmīki, within the *Mokṣopāya* section, in the *Sthitiprakaraṇa*.
The fifty-first canto, titled "The Awakening of the Sons of Daśūra," from the [Daśūra] section. 51.
Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, titled "The Instruction of the Son of Dāśūra," in the Section on Stability (*sthitiprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The fifty-second canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: Then, at one time, by that path, [he went] to her who dwells on Kailāsa.
I went to bathe, having become invisible and traveling through the path of the sky.
The life story of King Khottha is here fashioned and described with the intention of showing that the universe, being constructed by mental conception, is indeed false. (1)
By that path characterized by the cluster of Dāśūrakas; [she went] to the Mandākinī residing on Kailāsa—this is the ellipsis.
Having emerged from the hollow of the circle of the seven sages in the sky, O wise one,
I arrived at night at the lofty Dāśūra tree— [according to the reading "mūlataḥ," the suffix -tasi is used here in the sense of all case endings]. || 2 ||
From such a sky—that is, from the space of the celestial realm (dyuloka)—which had the circle of the seven sages as a cavity in one part.
As I heard from the hollow of a tree-branch in the forest a voice, like the sound of a bee clinging to a lotus bud. (3)
The particle *yāvat* is used here as an indeclinable (*nipāta*) in the sense of totality (*sākalya*). || 3 ||
Listen, O son of great intelligence, to this truly marvelous narrative; I shall relate to you this one extraordinary story. (4)
He speaks that very speech which was heard, beginning with "Listen, my son," and so forth; [he describes] the equal likeness of this saṃsāra. || 4 ||
There is a king of great heroism, renowned throughout the three worlds,
named the illustrious Khottha, who is capable of subduing the world.
"From the void" means from the indeterminate space (*avyākṛtākāśa*), or from the space of Brahman (*brahmākāśa*) which is empty of the world even throughout the three periods of time; it "arose.
Since the explanation of this [term] in the context of the subsequent creation is clear in the root text, it is not explained here in detail. || 5 ||
The leaders in all the worlds bear his instruction upon their heads with great reverence, like seekers carrying a crest-jewel.
The leaders are even the lords such as Brahmā and others; the seekers are those who possess wealth. || 6 ||
This great-souled one, who delights solely in daring feats and dwells in various wonders, has not been brought under control by anyone in the three worlds.
Who is able to count its thousands of undertakings, which bestow both pleasure and pain, any more than one can count the waves of the ocean? (8)
The prowess of that one of great valor has not been overcome by anyone in the world, whether by weapons or by fires, just as the sky cannot be grasped with a fist.
It is that which has been traversed, overcome, or followed. || 9 ||
Even Śakra, Upendra, and Hara do not in the slightest degree emulate her playful grace, which is expansive in its undertaking and radiant with creative manifestation.

Even when the purpose is small, they are capable of following— that is, they are able to imitate— a [work] that is expansive in its undertaking due to being crowded with thousands of manifold conceptualizations, and which is radiant through the creation of dreams, daydreams, and the like.
O mighty-armed one, he has three bodies capable of moving about;
having pervaded the world, they remain as the superior, the inferior, and the middling.
Due to the distinctions of sattva, rajas, and tamas, there are three types [of beings];
they are capable of wandering and competent in the play of all worldly activities. || 11 ||
Born within that very vast expanse of space, he became possessed of three bodies;
and there alone he maintained his station, moving like a bird at the fall of a sound.
In the sky— that is, in the unmanifest space— just as a bird,
consisting of the three bodies composed of the egg-mass and its wings, having been born sequentially in the sky itself,
fearing defeat from all sides and greedy for the taste of sapless fruits such as the *pippala*, flies up from the mere sound.

The meaning is that, just like that [child], this one too— possessing the three bodies consisting of the gross, subtle, and causal— having been born in the sky of Brahman, wanders about, terrified on all sides, attached to worthless objects, and following the words of injunctions and prohibitions, without reflecting upon the reality of the ultimate truth. || 12 ||
Right there in the boundless sky, he created a city with fourteen great streets, adorned with three divisions.

The city has the form of the universe; it possesses great thoroughfares consisting of the fourteen worlds, and it is divided by streets and paths consisting of the fourteen branches of knowledge. Thus, it is adorned by the threefold division according to action (karma), instrument (karaṇa), and proficiency (vyutpatti), as well as by the nature of the three worlds and the nature of the three Vedas.

Abounding in rows of groves and pleasure gardens, beautiful with its playful peaks, and adorned by seven ponds encircled by strings of pearls (or, according to another reading, overflowing with them). 14.
Of the groves, such as Nandana and others; by the peaked mountains, such as Meru and others; and the seven ponds are the oceans. 14.
It was illuminated by two inexhaustible lamps consisting of cold and heat,
and it was crowded with the paths of merchants in the form of upward and downward movement.
The two lamps are the moon and the sun; upward movement is by means of scriptural actions, and downward movement is by means of non-scriptural actions—such is their nature. (15)
In that very same exceedingly vast city, by that king, groups of worldly beings were fashioned as charming apartments. (16)
Those who transmigrate are the moving beings. "Deluded" means bewildered by sense objects;
because they delimit the space of the Self like a small room (*apavarakavat*), the multitudes of bodies—gods, humans, and so forth—are called "rooms.
16. Some are stationed above, some below, and some in the middle.
Some perish after a long time, while others are subject to swift destruction. || 17 ||
Covered with black awnings, adorned with nine gates, with winds blowing incessantly, and provided with many windows; || 18 ||
They are covered with dark coverings and with hair-grass; they have many windows and upward openings.
Illuminated by five lamps, they have three pillars made of white wood;
they are smooth, plastered, and soft, crowded with the arms of the city gateways.
With the five lamps of the sense organs, they are luminous and radiant— those whose three pillars and beams are the thighs and the *kaserukā* (the spinal bone),
and in which the white bones themselves serve as the bamboo and timber, being smooth.
The city was crowded with arms resembling its main streets and thoroughfares— arms that were like moist ointments and clay, and which served as its leather shields.
By that high-souled king, great yakṣas who were constantly afraid of the light were created through his illusory power (māyā) and stationed as guardians within them.

The yakṣas who guard those inner apartments out of conceit are those who are to be honored through their activities, who have become masters, and who are characterized by egoism (ahaṃkāra). They are afraid of light—that is, of the discernment of the Self (ātma-viveka). Therefore, the meaning is that they perish upon its destruction.
Then, as the throngs of inner apartments moved about, that lord of the earth engaged in various diversions, like a bird in its nests.
While worldly affairs were proceeding, that lord of the earth was the living soul whose nature consists of volition.
O son, having dwelt at will for three hundred lifetimes within those [beings] together with those yakṣas, he emerges again and departs.

"By means of his divine sports (līlābhiḥ), he dwells and departs in such a way that he is 'involuntary' (avaśam) and 'not under his own control' (asvādhīnam); this applies to both [dwelling and departing].
(22) O child, at times a firm desire arises in him, whose mind is fickle: 'I shall go to construct some city that is yet to be. (23)"

The world of dreams and so forth is a future manifestation that does not exist; yet, as long as its experience lasts, it remains motionless and stable, like one possessed by a spirit who, out of agitation, rises up and runs, and then reaches that city, just as if with the Gandharvas. (Note: The reading "tadāyam āpnoti" is found in some versions.)
An emanation. || 24 ||

Rising up from the onset of sleep due to agitation, having abandoned the identification with the waking body and so forth, he runs; for there is the Śruti: "Having enjoyed himself and wandered about there in the world of dreams, and having seen both merit and evil, he hastens back again according to the rule and according to his source, toward the end of dream-sleep alone," [referring to] a city constructed by Gandharvas.
The meaning is that it is false, like a city of Gandharvas. || 24 ||
O son, a desire sometimes arises in that one of unsteady mind, "I shall bring about his destruction," and by that [thought], he quickly perishes. (25)

Dissolution is the state of the subsidence of mental constructs, which is deep sleep. It perishes within the causal ignorance (avidyā), dissolving like a lotus-stalk, leaving behind only the latent impressions of the seeds of karma. || 25 ||
It arises again swiftly— [the reading is *pūrṇam*]—
like a wave from its own self within the water;
it expands worldly activity intensely, yet remains sluggish in its renewed undertaking.

"By its own self" means by its very prior nature; the sense is that this is because of the experience of recognition by one who has awakened from deep sleep, thinking, "I am that very same person. || 26 ||
Then, by that very same worldly activity, one is sometimes humiliated;
one grieves, thinking, "I am a servant, I am ignorant, I am miserable. (27)
One is humiliated by enemies, diseases, poverty, and so forth. || 27 ||
Having attained joy at one time, it itself returns to a state of wretchedness,
like the current of a river that swells with the exuberant floods of the rainy season.
Having attained, transcended, or recollected the joy of previously experienced pleasure. || 28 ||
Victorious is that lord of the earth, possessed of great majesty; he triumphs, moves, leaps, yawns, throbs, shines, and yet does not shine, radiant as he is.
Like the lord of waters agitated by the force of the wind. || 29 ||
That high-souled king previously mentioned, though possessing the capacity to overcome others, approaches and conquers his enemies;

yet having attained prosperity, he yawns, quivers, trembles, and shines when awake or dreaming, but does not shine during deep sleep, dissolution, meditative absorption, or liberation. He is radiant because of the inner light of the Self; for this very reason—
Possessing great majesty, he is like the ocean, the lord of the waters. || 29 ||

Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Wealth Arising from the Daśūra Ocean," in the Section on Stability (*sthitiprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, belonging to the *Ārṣa* tradition. 52.

Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Manifestation Arising from One's Own Self," in the Section on Stability (*sthitiprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The fifty-third canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Then, there in Jambūdvīpa during the dead of night, the son asked:
He saw his father, whose mind was purified, standing at the top of a Kadamba tree with a crest-jewel upon his head.
The essential meaning of the Khotthākhyāna is here described in detail;
it serves as an illustration for the stated point that the universe is said to be a mental construction (saṃkalpa). || 1 ||
"Standing like an ear-ornament upon the top of a Kadamba tree"—this is an *upamita-samāsa* (compound of comparison). || 1 ||
The son said: "Who was this king known as Khottha, whose form was like that of my father? And what was it that you told me? Tell me this according to the truth. (2)
Where will the manifestation be? Where can one go while it is present?
Because your words contradict both purposes, they lead only to my confusion.
If you ask, "How do you know that the intended meaning (tātparya) does not lie in the literal sense as heard, but elsewhere?"— [we reply:

because in statements such as "I am going to build a city" or "I am stationary," there would be a lack of syntactic coherence due to the contradiction between future-ness and present-ness occurring simultaneously.
Dāśūra said:
Listen, my son; I shall tell you this exactly as it is, so that you may realize the true nature of this wheel of saṃsāra.
You have awakened; you will awaken. || 4 ||
Thus have I described this structure of saṃsāra, which, though non-existent, is vast, composed of unsubstantial things, and characterized by rising and beginning.

From that very ignorance which is non-existent—devoid of ultimate reality—arises the undertaking [of worldly activity]; for this reason, *māyā* is a non-entity consisting of that [ignorance]. Thus, for the sake of making this matter understood, it has been described and explained indirectly. (5)
Volition, born from the supreme ether, is said to arise from the void;
it is born by itself and dissolves by itself.

"Saṃkalpa" means the mind whose primary function is volition. By the etymological derivation that it "arises from Kha" (the unmanifest ether) through the unification of the collective and individual minds, it is called "khottha" (arisen from Kha). It is born by itself solely from the emergence of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of activity produced by its own volitions, and [it ceases] through the strengthening of the latent impressions of cessation.
The meaning is that it dissolves by itself. || 6 ||
This entire expansive universe exists as that very nature;
it is born when that is born, and when that is destroyed, it perishes.
Its nature is its transformation. He confirms the stated meaning by demonstrating its conformity with presence and absence (anvaya-vyatireka), saying: "It is born," etc. (Verse 7).
They know Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, Rudra, and the others to be merely his limbs,
like the branches of a tree or the peaks of a mountain.

[Objection: But it is heard in scripture that the world was produced from Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others; how then can it be said to have arisen from another? To this he says: "Brahmā," etc. [The word] *viṭapān* means branches; *skandhān* means trunks. || 8 ||
In that empty sky, this city of the three worlds was created by him;
having attained the state of Viriñci through the mere persistence of appearance.

If it is asked, "How can this insentient [matter] possess the power of creation within the void of Brahman, which is empty and devoid of the world throughout the three periods of time? [the author] replies with the word *pratibhāsa* (manifestation), stating that it attains the form of the sentient Viriñci through the grace of the presiding consciousness. || 9 ||
In this [world] are spread out the fourteen world-enclosures with their vast expanses of light,
where there are rows of forests and groves, and successions of pleasure gardens.

He states that this very city of the three worlds is as previously described, beginning with the words "where," and so forth. "Vitatalokāḥ" means illuminated by the radiance of the sun and other luminaries. The meaning is that in this place, a series of gardens and groves—well-known as "vanopavana-mālā"—has been described. || 10 ||
Where the Sahya, Mandara, and Meru mountains serve as pleasure peaks;
where the moon and sun, with their cool and fiery splendors, are like lamps in the form of fire.
They were shaped like fire and blazing; if the reading is *anilākṣatau*, it is clear [that they were shaped like wind]. || 11 ||
There, the rivers bear moving strings of excellent pearls, which are like lofty pearls upon waves as tremulous as the rays of the sun.

He explains the meaning of the statement, "adorned with seven ponds encircled by strings of pearls" (noting that "vigalita" is the reading), with the words beginning "sūrya": the justification for the comparison of the waves to pearls is their shimmering, swaying nature like the rays of the sun. || 12 ||
Where the seven great oceans are like ponds whose waters consist of sugarcane juice, milk, and other liquids, and which contain sprouts of jewels and gems, as well as the submarine fire and lotuses.
In that city, the lotus stalks were indeed excellent jewels, and the lotuses were indeed the submarine fires (aurvānalas). // 13 //
Furthermore, in the vast expanse above and below, within the void, there exist the wealth and splendor of merit and demerit for men,
gods, and kirātas, wherein buying and selling take place.
Regarding what was said—that [the path] is crowded with the merchant’s route consisting of upward and downward movement—he states its meaning as follows:

"Below," etc. By this [path], which nourishes the gods—namely those noble men and immortals who are entitled to ritual action (*karma*) and meditation (*upāsana*, and possess wealth and prosperity consisting of merits, demerits, and sins)—those gods...
According to the principle stated by the Blessed One, "May you cultivate [virtue]," there are the buying and selling of merit and its fruits. For the *kirātas*—
those dwelling in border regions who are excluded from the authority to perform [Vedic] rites—
the buying and selling of sin and its fruits should be understood as occurring through the extensive mutual assistance between them and stationary beings, animals, and so forth.
In this very world, within this city, various chamber-like bodies have been fashioned by the mountain of volition for its own sport. (15)

He states the intended meaning of the statement, "The hosts of transmigrating beings are fashioned like the rooms of a deluded person," with the words beginning "In that very [state]," etc. (verse 15).
Some, known by the names of gods (gīrvāṇas), were appointed only above;
some, such as humans and nāgas, were appointed only below. || 16 ||
Moving by the flow of wind-machines, they were composed of flesh and clay, with white bones made of wood; they were variegated, smooth with a coating of skin, and stainless.

The vital breaths are the wind-machines by their flow; the flesh itself is the clay and its various modifications; the white bones are the wood upon which they rest; and those oils, ointments, and so forth with which the skin is smeared are the skin-pastes, by means of which it becomes smooth, glossy, and stainless. 17.
Some perish after a long time, while others are subject to swift destruction;
some possess the beauty of a covering fashioned from the lush growth of hair-like grass.

This is an explanation of the phrase "covered with dark coverings," meaning those whose beauty of covering is fashioned by the lush growth of *ulapa* grasses, which are characterized by their hair-like appearance. || 18 ||
Endowed with nine openings, foremost among which are the ears, eyes, and nose,
they [the breaths] are hot and cold, driven by the life-force wind (prāṇapavana) that flows without ceasing.

He explains the statement "adorned with nine gates" with the words beginning "karṇa-". He explains the statement "with winds blowing incessantly" with the words beginning "anārata-". The heat of the *prāṇa* and the coldness of the *apāna* are established through direct perception. || 19 ||
Equipped with a multitude of windows such as the ears, nose, mouth, and palate;
possessing the side-streets of the arms and other limbs; and having the five sense-faculties as its small lamps. || 20 ||
He explains the passage beginning with "provided with many windows" and so forth by means of the verse beginning with "ear-nose" and so forth.

By the explanation of the term *kudīpaka*, the intended meaning is indicated that in the compound *dīpapañcaka*, the suffix *kan* is used in the sense of a collection (*saṃgha*), and through its inherent capacity (*tantra*), it also suggests contempt (*kutsā*). || 20 ||
O Great-minded One, within those [realms] fashioned by illusion,
there are great yakṣas of egoism created by mental construction, who are utterly terrified of the supreme light.

He explains this [verse]—"the great yakṣas who are protectors"—with the words "by means of illusion" (māyayā). Regarding the phrase "those who are terrified of the supreme light," the intended meaning is as follows: since there is a scriptural teaching that the knot of the heart, which consists of egoism, is destroyed by the vision of the Supreme Self, they are "terrified" (bibhyataḥ), meaning they fear the sight of the Supreme. || 21 ||
Within the chambers of the body, he constantly sports excessively with the great yakṣas of egoism that arise from what is unreal.
Just as a cat is in a granary, as a snake is in a bellows, and as a pearl is within bamboo, so is the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) within the body. 23.
Is it not the case that the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) is nothing other than the body itself? No; he says "as follows" (yathā). || 23 ||
In the houses of the body, the waves of volition rise for a moment and subside for a moment like lamps, or like waves upon the oceans. (24)
He describes the manner of his sporting: "For a moment," etc. The waves of volition are its mental modifications (*vṛtti*). (24)
He then pervades that city with a newly created manifestation when he perceives the intended object in an instant. (25)
He explains the purport of the passage beginning with "the desire for that arises," by resolving the contradiction stated by the son: "The future," etc. (25).
By mere non-mental-construction, it perishes quickly by itself;
for its very destruction leads to its attainment of supreme well-being. (26)
He states the intended meaning of the phrase "therefore it quickly perishes" as follows: "by non-conceptualization.

Having experienced the supreme—that is, the extreme—exertion caused by wandering during the states of waking and dreaming, one attains dissolution as "perishing" in deep sleep through mere non-conceptualization for the sake of the highest good, which is the bliss of rest.

The meaning is that "existence" (sattā) refers to arising by virtue of the mere presence of ignorance as its cause. Alternatively, when—after becoming weary through the power of destiny over many millions of births—one attains the direct realization of the reality of the Self (ātmatattva) through the strength of the scriptures, the teacher, the practice of meditative absorption, and so forth; [then...]

By the mere absence of volitional construction (*asaṃkalpana*), resulting from the very uprooting of the root that is volitional construction (*saṃkalpa*), there arises well-being— that is, liberation (*mokṣa*). However, according to the reading *paramāyāsya*, the arising— meaning the manifestation— of this [state] through the destruction of volitional construction, by way of the state of emptiness (*śūnyabhāva*) brought about by the exhaustion of latent impressions (*vāsanākṣaya*), leads to the highest well-being.
The word "it occurs" (*bhavati*) is to be supplied as a remainder in every instance. || 26 ||
It arises by itself as a mere mental construction, like a ghost imagined by a child; it leads only to endless personal suffering and never to bliss. (27)
He states the intended meaning of the statement "it arises again" with the word "svayam" (itself). || 27 ||
This pervasive suffering of the world expands through the existence of the self;
through its non-existence, it destroys it, just as dense darkness is dispelled by light.
He weeps because of his own actions that bring him suffering,
like the monkey who pulled out the wedge while his testicles were pinned between two pieces of wood.

He states the seed for the expression of grief beginning with "What shall I do? with the words "by herself": [it refers to] that which causes suffering, consisting of the conceit of performing prohibited acts and so forth. "Fixed upon a piece of wood" has been explained in the section on [her] birth. || 29 ||
He stands with his neck upraised, like an elephant that has suddenly fallen upon a drop of honey, merely to taste a tiny fragment of the bliss he had imagined.

*Karabha* means a donkey. By this, it is suggested that even the pleasure of sense-objects is as difficult to obtain for one who licks honey as it is for a donkey, let alone the bliss of liberation. || 30 ||
For a moment it attains detachment, for a moment it attains passion of its own accord,
and for a moment it undergoes transformation through mere conceptualization, like a child.
Having diligently uprooted this [mind] from all objective existents, O son, act in such a way that the intellect enters the inner state. 32.
He states the purpose of describing this narrative: "enam" (this).

Having turned away from all existents—that is, from all external objects—and having rendered ignorance, along with its latent impressions (*vāsanā*), rootless through the practice of *samādhi* and the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), the intellect [realizes] the inner state, which is Brahman as the inward-facing self (*pratyagbhūta*). As...
The meaning is: "He goes, he rests while leaning [on it]; act in that same manner. || 32 ||
That Mother has three bodies—inferior, superior, and intermediate—which are designated as Tamas, Sattva, and Rajas; they are the cause for the existence of the world. (33)
He elaborates upon the three bodies previously mentioned with the words "The three": [referring to] the mind (*mati*), which consists of volition (*saṃkalpa*). || 33 ||
For volition, being of the nature of darkness (tamas), through constant worldly activity,
falls into supreme wretchedness and descends to the state of worms and insects.
Through natural behavior—that is, through innate inclination—one attains the well-known state of extreme wretchedness in the hells;
the mention of "worms and insects" is an elliptical expression intended to include stationary beings (*sthāvara*) and others as well. (34)
For volition, whose nature is pure being and which is devoted to the knowledge of reality, presides over its own sovereignty, from which the state of absolute liberation is not far removed. || 35 ||

Knowledge here means worship, which is to say the observance of scriptural activity; it leads to a state not distant from oneness with the Absolute (kevalībhāva), to liberation at hand, to self-sovereignty (svārājya), and to the station of the deity that culminates in the state of Hiraṇyagarbha. || 35 ||
For volition, which is of the nature of passion, exists within worldly activity;
it persists in saṃsāra, enamored with sons and wife. (36)
Worldly convention consists of human birth; it is that which possesses the appropriate conduct for such a state.
But having abandoned these three kinds of form, O Mahāmati, conceptualization reaches the supreme state upon the exhaustion of the self. (37)
The supreme state is liberation; this occurs upon the destruction of the self, that is, when there is the absolute eradication of all volitional constructs. || 37 ||
Having abandoned all views and restrained the mind with the mind, bring about the destruction of all conceptualization regarding internal and external objects. (38)

If so, what is the means for the destruction of volitional construction (saṃkalpa)? He states it: "All," etc. That is to say, one should restrain the "views"—meaning the perceptions of external objects or the external sense organs—through dispassion (vairāgya). || 38 ||
Even if you perform severe austerities for thousands of years, or even if you completely grind yourself to dust upon a stone, (you will not attain it). 39.

[Objection: "Is it not difficult to destroy volitional thought (*saṃkalpa*)? Please teach some other means for the sake of liberation. [Reply: No, he says— "Whether you enter fire, or even the submarine fire (*vaḍavāgni*), or whether you fall into a chasm, or likewise upon the edge of a sword's blade; (40)"
Whether it be Hara who is your instructor, or Hari, or even the Lotus-born Brahmā, or perhaps the ascetic Lord of the World who is overcome with supreme compassion; (41)

The "ascetic" (yati) who, being overcome by extreme compassion, would be the instructor— be it the Lord of the World Śrī Dattātreya or Durvāsas— or else, by the force of the adjective "overcome by extreme compassion," the ascetic here is the Buddha, the instructor of absolute non-violence; his inclusion here is because [his teachings] exist even among non-Vedic paths.
This is for the purpose of removing the hope for liberation. || 41 ||
Whether you are situated in the netherworld (pātāla), on earth, or even in heaven,
there is no other means for that [liberation] than the cessation of mental constructs (saṃkalpa).
Exert yourself to the utmost through human effort toward the cessation of mental constructs, which is unobstructed, changeless, supremely purifying, and blissful. (43)
With the intention that this cessation of conceptualization (*saṃkalpa*) is indeed the very nature of Brahman, he qualifies it with the words "unassailable" (*anābādha*), and so forth.
"Supreme effort" refers to the fourfold means consisting of the attainment of the four qualifications, hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*). || 43 ||
O sinless one, it is said that all states of being are woven upon the thread of volition;
