when that thread is severed, I know not where those fragile things go.

Now, one might ask: "How can the cessation of all worldly bondage occur merely through the destruction of volitional constructs (*saṃkalpa*)? To this he says: "Volitional construct" (*saṃkalpa*). Then, one might ask: "Where do those destroyed entities go? To this he says: "I do not know.
This refers to the sublation (*bādha*) of superimposed entities within their substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*); in some places, the reading is "upon realization elsewhere" (*anyatra bodhe*).
The meaning is that going is not established. || 44 ||
Everything—whether non-existent, existent, or both existent and non-existent—arises from volition alone and not from anything else.
Since volition itself is thus both existent and non-existent, what can be called "real" in this world? (45)
Now, is this cessation of all mental constructs such as volition non-existent, existent, or both existent and non-existent?

In the first case, liberation is not established; in the second, duality would result even in liberation; and in the third, there is no prevention of either occasional bondage or duality—thus, there is no liberation.

He dispels the multitude of faults, such as the "establishment of flawlessness" (*nirvraṇatāsiddhi*), by means of various statements beginning with the word "non-existent" (*asad*). All conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) such as existence and non-existence arise from volition (*saṃkalpa*) along with its concomitants; they are unable to conceive of volition itself as either existent or non-existent. In this regard, what [faults] can touch the Brahman whose volition is the ultimate reality (*paramārthasatya*)? What is there to be gained or lost? What is there to fear? What is there to delude? Thus, he concludes that all these faults are merely imagined. Therefore, it is established that Brahman is free from all defects. || 17 || |||I hope this is correct. O knower of reality, never conceptualize anything at all.

The meaning is that one experiences this worldly suffering in vain; it is neither fitting nor appropriate for oneself, for one's own self. || 48 ||
Therefore, O sinless one, what is the use of your death which leads to great suffering?
The wise in this world resort only to that which results in no suffering, and nothing else. (49)
What fruit is there for you in being born through various wombs by means of that cause, and in dying again and again for the sake of suffering, with death resulting only in further suffering? (49)
Having attained the ultimate reality and having forcefully cast aside the web of conceptual constructions,
realize that peerless state.
The mental fluctuations are in a state of deep sleep for the sake of pervasive bliss. || 50 ||

To the question "What, then, is my duty in this regard?", he says: "Having attained... You, having attained—that is, having reached—the state of having realized the ultimate truth (*paramārthatā*), which is the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñatā*), and having forcefully cast away the web of conceptual constructions (*vikalpajāla*) by means of uprooting it at its source, [should strive] for that non-dual state called liberation (*mokṣa*) for the sake of expansive bliss, that is, for the attainment of unsurpassed bliss (*niratiśayānanda*).

Thus ends the fifty-third canto, titled "The Investigation into the Yoga of Conceptualizing the City of Saṃsāra," in the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa* of Valmīki, belonging to the *Divya Mokṣa Sthiti* section of the *Dāśūra* cycle. || 53 ||
Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, titled "An Investigation into the Yoga of Conceptualizing the City of Saṃsāra," in the *Sthitiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
Fifty-fourth canto.
The son said:
"O Father, what is the nature of that resolve (saṃkalpa), and how does it arise, O Lord?"
And how does it attain growth, and how does it perish? (1)
How volition arises, what its nature is, how it becomes solidified,
and by what means it is eradicated— all this is proclaimed here.
The question is clear. || 1 ||
Dāśūra said:

They know that the mind's orientation toward an object of cognition—which belongs to the infinite reality of the self, whose nature is universal existence—is the sprout of volitional construction (*saṃkalpa*). (2)
Having acquired its existence even in a subtle degree, that very [ignorance] gradually attains density,
filling the sky of the mind like a cloud for the sake of solidifying its dullness.
The meaning is that what was previously explained as "the mind" (*manas*)— its state of being directed toward objects of thought—

is known as the first sprout of the wish-fulfilling tree of volition (*saṃkalpa*), arising from the seed of ignorance (*avidyā*). Having completely filled that very "space of the mind" (*cittakha*), the space of consciousness, on all sides...

Having pervaded [the substrate], it serves to produce a state of firm insentience; that is to say, by concealing the conscious nature of the consciousness of the substrate, it brings about the manifestation of the form of the insentient phenomenal world. || 3 ||
The consciousness, while contemplating the object of thought as if it were distinct from itself,
attains the state of volition, just as a seed reaches the state of a sprout.

Having thus described the emergence of the world from the collective volition (*samaṣṭi-saṃkalpa*), he likewise describes the arising of the individual volitions (*vyaṣṭi-saṃkalpa*) that take the form of the intellect, ego, vital breath, senses, body, and so forth, with the words: "They conceive... (verse 4).
For by means of volition, volition itself is produced;
it grows by itself quickly, leading only to suffering and not to happiness.
Then, he describes the growth ending in suffering through a succession of conceptualizations of the forms of external objects, like the growth of branch-sprouts from a root-sprout, with the words:
"by conceptualization" (saṃkalpena). || 5 ||
For the world is merely a mental construction, just as the ocean is merely water;
apart from such a construction, you have no other worldly suffering.
Indeed, it has arisen in vain through a mere coincidence, like a mirage or the appearance of two moons; though unreal, it increases.
Now, one might ask: "How can the world arise without a seed from a reality that is changeless and non-dual? To this he replies: "It is like the 'crow-and-palm' (coincidental) occurrence.

With the intention that this objection should be resolved by resorting to the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivarta-vāda*), he says: "Just as for one who has swallowed a citron, there arises the perception of gold [in its place], so too is the world perceived in the Unborn."
Thus, that unreal mental construction within your heart has come forth by itself.
With the intention that the delusion of the world is to be abandoned through the awakening of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of objects previously experienced, he says: "Swallowed," etc.
A *mātuliṅga* is a particular kind of fruit; for when seen, it intensifies the bile and produces the illusion of yellow in what is white. (8)
You were born as nothing but unreality, and you exist as nothing but unreality;
yet when this knowledge is realized, unreality indeed dissolves away.
In this treatise consisting of my instruction, it is "vijñāna" because it is understood (*vijñāyate*) by means of it. (9)
"That person was I; these various states consisting of pleasure and pain are mine"—thinking thus that it is all in vain, you burn within with diverse anxieties. (10)
That Perfect Self who is well-known in the Vedāntas—that very one am I; these states of mine consisting of birth and so forth, composed of pleasure and pain, are useless and merely false.
You are tormented by that ignorance which is the cause of this lack of conviction; since that ignorance does not exist, why do you suffer? 10.
Though unborn, you appear to be born; from where does this play of birth arise?
You are deluded in vain by your own power of volition.
This birth and so forth, which belongs to you, was never actually existent at any time; it has arisen through delusion.
As for its manifestation, how could there be any birth from your own radiance, which is characterized by ultimate, absolute fullness?
Do not form a conceptualization; do not dwell upon existence in its state of persistence.
By this much alone, through such a disposition, one becomes fit for the sake of ultimate well-being.
He states the means for the cessation of this delusion: "Do not will" (*mā saṃkalpaya*).
Do not contemplate—that is, do not remember—the previously experienced states of pleasure, pain, and so forth, in your present condition.
For the underlying idea is that if memory of the past exists, there will inevitably arise the volitions (*saṃkalpa*) to acquire or abandon those objects.
By the effort to destroy conceptualization, one does not follow after fears;
by the mere absence of mental cultivation, conceptualization itself perishes of its own accord.

And thus, from the destruction of mental constructs (*saṃkalpa*) comes the destruction of all fear; and from the non-contemplation of prior states comes the destruction of mental constructs—such is the established sequence, as he says: "Mental constructs... (verse 13).
In the crushing of a *sumanaḥ* blossom, there might be some slight contact;
it is easily accomplished by mere presence of mind, but not in the destruction of one's mental constructs (*saṃkalpa*).

He praises this means as being extremely easy to perform with the words beginning "sumanasām": "The slight exertion (*kiṃcid-vyatikara*) consisting of the crushing of the sprouts—that is, the petals—of *sumanas* flowers such as the *śirīṣa*, might indeed be easily accomplished (*susādhya*) and feasible; however, [this is not the case]."

The meaning is that non-existence is the contemplation of non-existence; when the destruction of conceptual construction is to be accomplished by that alone, it is the possibility of that [contemplation]. || 14 ||
The effort of moving the hand when picking flowers is useful for the son;
yet even that [effort] assists in this [state] once conceptual construction has ceased.
He explains what has already been stated with the words "puṣpa" (flower) etc. That too—meaning even that, and moreover to that extent—does not assist [the purpose]. || 15 ||
By that [means] through which conceptual construction is to be destroyed, it is effortlessly destroyed even in half a moment, through the reversal of mental states. (16)
Existence is the cultivation of mindfulness; its opposite is non-remembrance. || 16 ||
O dear one, when one has attained stability within one's own self, which is perfected as mere being, what impossible thing could there be that is not accomplished for you? 17.

Now, one might ask: even if suffering is destroyed through the cessation of mental constructs (*saṃkalpa*), by what means is the attainment of unsurpassed bliss (*niratiśayānanda*) to be accomplished?
To this, he says: "bhāva... etc. *Bhāva* means *bhāvanā*—the continuous contemplation of one's own nature as the fullness of bliss.
When stability has been attained—that is, when one has reached one's own self and does not fall away from its true nature—merely by that [contemplation].
Even that which is unattainable is attained. Now, one might object that to say "the unattainable is attained" is a contradiction;

to this he replies with the word "of whom. With the intention that what is self-established does not depart [from its nature], it is said that it "would be attainable," but not with the intention that it is produced. For the disappearance of entities is twofold: either by being taken away by another, or...

Or [what would happen] upon destruction or the attainment of another state? O dear one, whose would your self be if it were being carried away by another? For no other [self] than the non-dual Self is established. Or, if it were perishing, what indeed would it become? For a jar, when perishing, becomes shards; but as for the Self, what could it become? Whatever it might become, that cannot be seen by means of what has perished.

It is possible [to perceive this], yet there is no seer other than the self. Therefore, the destruction of the self cannot be established as being without a witness; thus, the meaning is that liberation, which is of the nature of the self, being self-evident, shall not perish. || 17 ||
O sage, having severed thought with thought and your own mind with the mind within your very self, remain established in the Self; what is difficult in this? (18)
By means of the very resolve of non-resolution—that is, by the mind itself in the form of reflection upon the reality of the Self—one cuts off all volitions; this is the meaning. || 18 ||
For when volitional thought is stilled, O Great-Minded One, all this suffering of saṃsāra becomes stilled even from its very root. (19)
The meaning is that when [the cause] has been pacified even from its root by means of the two aforementioned methods, suffering also becomes pacified from its root. || 19 ||

For volition, mind, the individual soul, consciousness, and intellect along with its latent impressions—these differ only in name, not in their actual meaning, O best of those who know the truth. (20)
Now, one might object: "Even when conceptualization (*saṃkalpa*) has subsided, suffering will surely still arise due to the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the living mind.
Anticipating this doubt, he states that these [other factors] are included within conceptualization: "Conceptualization... (verse 20).
Apart from conceptual construction (saṃkalpa), nothing whatsoever exists anywhere here;
cut that very thing out from your heart—why do you grieve over this? [The reading "what else" (kim anyat) is an alternative.]
Just as this sky is empty, so indeed is the world empty; for both of these are extended from conceptual constructions consisting of the non-existent. (22)

Now, one might object: "If the world and the individual soul (jīva) are of the very nature of volition (saṃkalpa), then upon the cessation of that volition, would there not result a void characterized by selflessness (nairātmya-śūnyatā)?

For there is no so-called 'Self' other than the individual soul. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Just as... Just as the desert land does not become a void even when the mirage is cut off, such is this illustration.

Even when there is the sublation of everything perceived, such as the world and living beings, the Self, whose nature is seeing, does not become void; both this mirage and the world are equally extended, being merely expansions of superimposition.
All of this has been proven by that which is itself unproven; since the world arises through mere conceptualization, where could mental cultivation possibly find a firm footing? (23)
Anticipating the objection that "even what has been sublated might arise again through mental cultivation (bhāvanā)," he says: "unestablished.
The meaning is that when an object has been sublated, mental cultivation itself does not even occur. || 23 ||

If there were no conviction in reality, on what basis would latent impressions (*vāsanā*) be established? Through the exhaustion of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), perfection is attained; consequently, nothing remains to be acquired.
Therefore, one should disregard all this which is unreal as something to be known by means of meditation.

Therefore, with the intention that one who desires the destruction of mental impressions (*bhāvanā*) must first accomplish the vision of the world's falsity, he says: "By *bhāvanā*... [and so on]. By means of *iddhi*—that is, by that which has been made firm through repeated practice—and by means of *helā*—that is, by the disregard for the visible world. || 24 ||
By that cultivation of the body's attenuation, one is no longer smeared by pleasures and pains;
and having determined that it is not a real substance, attachment and longing do not arise.

The meaning is that, through this disregard for the visible world, through the contemplation of the body as insubstantial, and through the recognition of the identity of the self with the body, one realizes—by means of the previously mentioned pleasures and pains—that even sons, friends, and others connected to the body are non-substantial; thus, no attachment or reliance toward them arises. || 25 ||
When attachment is exhausted, joy and resentment, as well as existence and non-existence, do not arise.
Therefore, all this is unreal, consisting of the delusions of pleasure, pain, and the like. (26)
The mind, as the living soul, vibrates intensely; it is the mental city that constitutes the world, revolving through the future, the present, and the past. (27)

The meaning is that the mind itself, being the individual soul (jīva) through the reflection of consciousness, manifests as it revolves, constructs, transforms, and destroys the mental city characterized by the world. || 27 ||
Enveloped by latent impressions (vāsanā) and abiding in the world with its power manifesting, the mind— turbid and flickering— establishes this order according to its own disposition.
To the question of why it vibrates while thus undergoing such transformations, he says: "Because of latent impressions" (*vāsanā*).

Since this [mind], through its connection with objects of the mind, is enveloped by various latent impressions and is connected to the consciousness that is the substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna-cit*), it effects the aforementioned arrangement and so forth; this is the meaning. || 28 ||
The living being, like a monkey in the forest of the heart, performs play that resembles its own nature;
assuming a long form, it becomes short again in the blink of an eye.
Why then does he not do only what is desired, and why does he do what is undesired? To this, he says: "Of the self," [verse 29].
The waves of the water of conceptualization cannot be grasped;
when seen even slightly, they swell and diminish along with their entire retinue. (30)
To the question of how its increase and decrease occur, he says: "In order to grasp... This means "in order to restrain.
"Observed" means awakened by the sight of objects. However, when there is the abandonment of the sight and remembrance of objects, [the afflictions], along with their retinue, diminish. || 30 ||
Even by a mere blade of grass, intentions blaze up like the remnants of a fire;
though their form is unmanifest in the world, they are ignited and perish in an instant. (31)

"By even a mere blade of grass" means by even a small object similar to a blade of grass; "a remnant of fire" refers to a spark of fire. The words "the world," and so forth, connect with the subsequent portion [of the verse]. || 31 ||
O son, these volitions— which cause delusion, which consist of dull matter, and which are like fires of lightning—
must be quickly treated with that very medicine which is their own nature.

Causing delusion— being the causes of errors such as mistaking a post for a person— and having their configuration within dull objects, such as clouds and water (the *la* and *ḍa* sounds being interchangeable), [these are the sense-objects]. Having thus described the answers to questions such as "Father, what kind of thing is volition (*saṃkalpa*)?", [he now explains] how this [volition] perishes.

Desiring to state the answer to the final question, he speaks of the ease with which the aforementioned mental construction (*saṃkalpa*) can be cured, beginning with the words "yadeva" (whatever...). It is "consisting of the unreal" (*asanmaya*), meaning it is a transformation of false ignorance. || 32 ||
There is no doubt in this matter: that which is non-existent never becomes existent anywhere.
If a mental construction (saṃkalpa) remains established, it would be difficult to cure by its own nature.
"It can be known" is the ellipsis; [this applies] if it were established as being of the nature of ultimate reality. || 33 ||
However, this [defilement] would be easily curable only if it were unreal;
for if the impurity of saṃsāra were innate, like the blackness of charcoal, [it could not be removed]. (34)

But on the view that the world is real, since the Self is not distinct from the world, it would follow that the Self possesses a defiled nature; thus, the removal of reality through knowledge—which contradicts all means of valid cognition—would result in the impossibility of liberation.
Even if one were to accept such a contradiction, it would be like the blackness of charcoal which persists even after being washed with soap.

With the intention that the "remainder" (pariśeṣa) refers to the human goal (puruṣārtha) remaining after the complete washing away [of all else]—just as in the expression "the remainder is zero" (śūnyāvasānatā)—he says: "uncreated" (akṛtrima). "Created" (kṛtrima) means that which is produced by *kṛti*, i.e., false conceptualization; that which is different from that is "uncreated," meaning real (*satya*). || 34 ||
O virtuous one, what evil-minded person would proceed to wash this away?
For it remains within the very grains of rice, like the husk. (35)
Just as the husk, which is not actually rice, is cast off from the grain, so too that which is unreal is cast off from the Real; such is the meaning. || 35 ||
For this reason, O son, even that which is obtained naturally may be utterly destroyed again through human effort applied from here and there. (36)

*Kṛti* means the operation of a cause; that which is produced (*nirvṛtta*) by that is *kṛtrima*. The meaning is that it is distinct from that [natural state], being beginningless (*anādibhūta*). According to the rule *ḍukṛño ṅvitaḥ kriḥ*, the suffix *kri* is applied after the root *kṛ*; then, by the rule *kremamnityam*, the suffix *map* is added in the sense of "produced" (*nirvṛtta*). 36.
For the knower, the pervasive impurity of saṃsāra is easily eradicated, just as the husk is from rice or the blackness from copper. (37)

The meaning is that for the knower who knows reality, [this ignorance] is "extended" (ātata)— that is, vast— yet it is capable of being severed with ease, without effort; for it is observed that the extremely extensive delusions of silver, dreams, and so forth, which arise from beginningless ignorance, are severed by mere awakening.

However, with the intention that the impurities such as lack of conviction and contrary cultivation are destroyed even by human effort characterized by the practice of the stages of knowledge (*jñānabhūmikā*),
he says "of the rice," and so forth. || 37 ||
O son, just as a man's impurity is destroyed by action, so too [this] is surely destroyed;
there is no doubt. Therefore, be one who exerts effort. 38.
Since this saṃsāra has not been conquered in vain by these false conceptualizations, it will quickly dissolve with little effort; for where can a non-existent thing endure for long? (39)

The meaning is this: that you have not conquered this saṃsāra—which is characterized by conceptual constructions based on what is unreal—for so long a time, has been entirely in vain due to your lack of knowledge regarding the proper means. || 39 ||
When one investigates its own nature, this cycle of existence (saṃsāra) is found to be non-existent,
just as the appearance of two moons vanishes for one who has examined his vision after being deceived by the light of a lamp and the like.

When one's own established position—that is, one's own conclusion—is non-existent, it is like the blindness of a blind man when a lamp is lit, even though his vision has been obscured by darkness; this is the implied meaning. || 40 ||
He does not belong to you, nor do you belong to him; O son, abandon this delusion!
Do not harbor such a conception regarding that which is seen as unreal, yet appears as real. (41)

This is saṃsāra. For (hi), since when that which is unreal is seen as if it were real, such a thing—namely, the cultivation (bhāvanā) or further reflection upon it—is indeed not proper; this is the implied sense. || 41 ||
Let there be no vain delusion within you that "my master's splendors are radiant with grace"; for you,
too, possess extensive graces of your own.
All this shines forth as that very essence of the Self. || 42 ||
Let there be no delusion in you that these enjoyments and pleasures— resplendent and shining with great wealth and prosperity from my worldly nature— are real and eternal;
for although you are a transmigrating being, those pleasures— and by the word "and," everything else as well, such as birth, death, and so forth— are merely appearances.
The meaning is that it is the reality of the Self alone that shines forth in such a manner, and there is no other existent thing in the form of an object of perception. || 42 ||

Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Volition," in the *Daśūra* section of the *Sthitiprakaraṇa*, within the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis. || 54 ||
Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Treatment of Volitional Conception," in the Sthitiprakaraṇa of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The fifty-fifth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having thus heard that conversation between the two there at night, [he remained silent].
O descendant of Raghu, moon in the sky of the Raghu clan! || 1 ||
The mutual conversation between Dāśūra and the honored Vasiṣṭha, the observation of the beauty of the Kadamba trees, and the departure in the morning are described here. || 1 ||
Addressing is clear conversation. || 1 ||
He fell with a thud upon the top of a kadamba tree, thickly laden with leaves, flowers, and fruit; silent, his soul released from the rain, like a cloud resting upon a mountain peak.
He descended silently and noiselessly; by that cloud, the self was caused to descend below, released from the guise of rainwater through the act of raining. || 2 ||
There I beheld Dāśūra, a hero in the restraint of his senses,
endowed with supreme austerity and like a sacrificial fire in its brilliance.
With his splendors issuing forth from his body, he was heating that region and making the earth golden, like the sun heating the world.
Scorching, illuminating, [or, according to another reading, terrifying]... || 4 ||
Seeing that I had arrived,
the fisherman honored me with the ritual offering of water (argha) and worshipped me by providing a seat and honoring me with leaves.
To him for whom a *viṣṭara*—that is, a seat—has been offered; the mention of "leaves" (*patra*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) that includes flowers, fruits, and so forth as well. || 5 ||
Then, together with that radiant Dāśūra, he related former stories intended to awaken his sons,
which were capable of enabling them to cross over saṃsāra.
"Pūrvakathāḥ" refers to ancient narratives concerning the discussions of Brahman that were previously initiated. "Tanayasaṃbodhāḥ" means those which properly awaken the son;

the suffix *aṇ* is applied here in the sense of an action (*karmaṇi*). According to the rule "gatikārakopapadānāṃ kṛdbhiḥ saha samāsavacane," when a compound with a *kṛt*-suffix is prescribed, it includes cases where the *kṛt*-suffix is preceded by a *gati* (preverb); thus, a compound is formed with the preverb (*upa*) as well.
I saw that tree,
its hollows filled with buds, frequented by all the herds of deer who were moving with effort at the will of Dāśūra.
"By those who do not cause distress," that is to say, by those who do not cause agitation. || 7 ||
Like a forest being enjoyed, adorned with circles of creepers,
it seemed to bloom with a smile, its petals quivering with breath.
He describes that *kadamba* tree, dressed in the fine attire of a bridegroom embraced by his bride, with the words beginning "with a smile" (*smitena*).
Since its hollows are filled with buds and its shoots quiver in the breeze, it stands as if manifesting a smile.
With chowries as beautiful as the moon, whirling at the tips of the creepers,
it was covered like the autumn sky by clusters of fragments of white clouds.
With chowries—tails of the yak—mounted upon the tips of branches at the ends of millions of creepers.
Adorned with a pearl necklace in the form of a succession of frost-drops,
every limb was completely filled with an abundance of clear blossoms.
The ellipsis is to be supplied as "pervading all the limbs. || 10 ||
It was anointed with applications of saffron and sandalwood paste, unblemished,
and adorned with a vast covering of pure, expansive, and deep red garments.

*Samālabdham* means smeared. He is one whose garments and coverings—namely his lower garment, upper robe, tunic, turban, and so forth—are vast, red, and crimson due to the expanse of his own foliage-like shoots (*pallava*). || 11 ||
It was compared to a city-dweller who, out of a desire for marriage, has donned the attire of a woman, being excessively burdened by a weight of flowers and clinging to a creeper.
Adorned with creeper-arbors in the shape of huts built by sages, and joined with flower-clusters as banners during the great festival of the city; 13.
It was adorned with creeper-arbors whose form resembled the appearance of huts built by sages;

it was joined with banners during a great festival—by implication, "like a city" is understood [to complete the comparison]. The reading "puramivotsave" (like a city during a festival) is the correct one. || 13 ||
Dusty with the pollen of flowers shaken off by deer scratching themselves,
it stood like a bull-fighter who has driven away those nearby in the forest.

By whom the forest at its edge was rendered grey by the pollen of flowers—scattered and fallen through the shaking of deer scratching themselves—and which, having been exalted by his own excellence, was now cast into insignificance; [he approached] the bull-like champion, the best of bulls. 14.
With its peaks made crimson by the pollen exhaled from the flowers of the *barhī* trees,
the mountain appeared as if it had cast down a young sprout of twilight clouds.

With peacocks as its *barhi* grass, and with mountains as the deposits—meaning they were cast down and established as such—it was as if its own hair, characterized by the pale clouds of twilight, had been placed there; this is a poetic conceit (*utprekṣā*). || 15 ||
With a hand as red as coral, beautified by a smile of flowers, reeling with intoxication, and possessing the luster of horripilation at its edge; || 16 ||

Now, with the common epithets beginning with "with eyes like lotuses" (*alinetreṇa*) and ending with "shining" (*bhāsinā*), he describes that Kadamba tree as the abode of either a sporting man or a host of forest goddesses dwelling there;
he does so by means of the description starting with "sprouts" (*pravāla*), etc. In that regard, according to the first interpretation, [it is] "by himself" or "by his own body."

The object of the description (*viśeṣya*) is to be supplied at the end [of the verse]. "With honey" (*madhunā*) implies, through double entendre (*śleṣa*), both with nectar and with wine; "as if with intoxication" (*madeneva*) refers to being reeling;
"by the edge" (*prāntena*) implies, by extension, being filled with filaments; and "possessing the beauty of horripilation" (*pulakaśobhāvatā*) serves as the reason. || 16 ||
With eyes in the form of buds ready to sleep, stirred by forest breezes, and bearing breasts in the form of flower-clusters, [the forest] was filled with flowers packed without any gaps.

[He was] being touched by [the tree], which was completely filled with flowers without any gaps, possessing breasts in the form of clusters of creepers, and having hands in the form of tender shoots. || 17 ||
Clad in garments as reddish as saffron from heaps of pollen from clusters of flowers,
he leaned against the window of his dwelling, which was a canopy formed by spreading creepers.
In the windows— the latticed openings of the palaces— of dwellings characterized by canopies fashioned from creepers, he was accompanied by his beloved, who carried a quiver.
With playful grace, it performed a dance upon swings of blue-flowered creepers,
having constructed its abode everywhere from the tips of its feet to the ends of its head.

By him who had become a playful man amidst the forest goddesses—who were surrounded by a host [of them] characterized by the warbling of cuckoos; [and] who was engaged in the sport of graceful dancing and the curious swinging upon creeper-pendulums with glossy green foliage amidst blue [trees]. One of these two readings, or a supplement to them, should be supplied: "by such a self."

In the first [interpretation], it refers to Him by whom all the limbs have been fashioned everywhere from the very top of the head down to the tips of the feet as abodes, serving as the support for ornaments such as flowers, fruits, and birds. In the second, the phrase "in every limb" should be connected with the meaning that an abode has been fashioned at all times and in every way by Madhu—that is, by Spring—possessing the aforementioned collection of attributes. In the third [interpretation] as well, [the same applies].
It should be connected with the following [phrase]: "a dwelling constructed on all sides by a multitude of forest goddesses possessing the aforementioned collection of qualities. || 19 ||
He was accompanied by a multitude of forest goddesses who were skilled in the warbling of cuckoos,
radiant with eyes like bees amidst a cluster of blossoming flower-stalks.

The meaning is that because the bees sit upon the clusters of *kadamba* blossoms in succession, they become the object of doubt as to whether these are the eyes of the creepers or the eyes of the *kadamba* trees— thus being possessed of a multitude of blossoms. Alternatively,
it means that by the swarm of bees resembling the eyes of the forest goddesses, one wonders whether these are the eyes of the forest goddesses or [the eyes of the bees].
"Clusters of blossoms filled with bees"—this should be construed as "a network of blossoms that is ambiguous. || 20 ||
Their fatigue from passion was allayed by the dew, they were languid with intoxication,
smeared with the pollen of flowers, and closely embraced one another.

Anointed with the pollen of flowers and smeared with them, they were closely embraced with one another in secret; surrounded by pairs of clear, intoxicated bees humming all around within the inner apartments of the flowers, they performed something befitting their love. || 22 ||
The interior of the flower is itself the inner apartment (antaḥpura), filled with pairs of intoxicated bees. || 22 ||

For a moment, with its ears pricked up from a desire to hear the humming sounds from the city on the edge of the forest, it was filled with the beautiful warbling and cries of birds from all directions.

For a moment, he desired to hear the tumultuous clamor of wild beasts and birds at the edge of the forest— the very outskirts of his own city— announced by the charming and sweet *ṭāṃ* sounds of blue flies, which act as heralds amidst the regions of the quarters that were not yet stilled.
The meaning is that it stood as if with its ears pricked up and raised. || 23 ||
For a moment,
they gazed at the ocean-girdled earth, which resembled the moon’s silken garment, as its exceedingly lovely crest rested upon the tips of the lotus petals.

By virtue of their heads— which were exceedingly beautiful and utterly charming, resting for a moment upon the tips of the leaves and sprouts that served as pillows due to the onset of sleep and their restlessness—
the entire network of limbs belonging to the forest and other regions was covered by the moon with its silken garments of rays.

The interior of whose forest floor was filled with auspicious deer within leaf-cups— appearing like the personified principles of policy (naya) that are the offspring of the forest regions, standing there waiting for the departure of night upon this earth girt by the ocean— [he entered]. 25.

The forest regions were radiant and rendered meaningful by their "essences"— the deer, monkeys, and other forest-dwellers— who, through the power of the sages, had assumed embodied forms as if they were the very principles of policy and discipline (naya and vinaya) personified; these creatures remained within the leaf-cups— the interiors of the web of foliage— hidden from view, while the lower ground beneath them was filled with their presence.
And him whose limbs are the branches and so forth. || 25 ||
In its nests, birds were sleeping with full confidence;
around the edges of the trees, circles of tree-spirits clung to the fruits that had fallen during ripening.

In that place where birds, breathing in their nests, were merely asleep— utterly trusting because they were fearless due to the power of the sage; that is to say, they were unobserved because of their sleep— there, upon fruits that had previously been swarmed by bees and which had by chance fallen to the ground due to ripening...

The compound is to be construed with the following [verse]: he whose [palace] was filled on all sides by circles of bees—beings such as deer situated nearby—who were silent out of fear and apprehensive of being eaten or crushed, like those within a cloak. || 26 ||
With clusters of flowers serving as rosaries for worship, it was filled with bees that were silent with doubt;
its borders were darkened by nests adorned with tender sprouts.

By the word "worship" (pūjā), the recitation at that time is indicated. In that regard, he is one by whom the entire forest is made fragrant with rosaries fashioned from hanging clusters of creepers. (27)
The entire forest was made fragrant, the sky was turned into a mass of flowers,
and the ground below was variegated with *kadamba* pollen and covered with an abundance of fruit.
Its root-ground was covered and overspread with masses of fruit variegated by clusters of *dhūlīkadamba* flowers. || 28 ||
What is the use of saying more here? There is not even a single leaf on that tree where it neither grows nor is it joined. (29)

On whichever tree and on whichever leaf there exists not even a single leaf that is not inhabited by living beings, nor is not joined with them, or is not utilized by them—what then need be said of its branches, fruits, flowers, and so forth? Oh, how the purpose of its birth is rendered meaningful in every way through its service to others! Such is the intended meaning. || 29 ||
In every leaf the deer slept, at every step they rested,
and in every thicket the birds were nestled within that king of trees.

"Patre patre" means in all the petals that have drooped downward. "Kaccha" refers to the lower part of the petals and so forth; it is that which "cuts" (chinatti) the dew-water (avaśyāya-jala). This is derived from the root *cho* (in the sense of cutting), with the suffix *ka* added according to the rule *āto 'nupasarge kaḥ*.
As I gazed upon him, distinguished by such qualities, that night became like a great festival for me. (31)

For one who beholds with divine vision: "The dark night" (tamasvinī). Although it was previously stated that [the sky] is "filled with a web like moonbeams," and thus it is indeed possessed of moonlight, it is nevertheless described in this way with the intention of expressing merely its nature as night. || 31 ||
Then, by means of delightful stories that were beautiful with the light of higher knowledge, I led his son once again to the supreme awakening.
There, that night passed for us as we conversed with one another in various stories, like a mere moment for a pair of lovers.

The word "āvayoḥ" (of us two) is the remainder of the word "asmad" (we), according to the rule: "tyadādīni sarvair nityam" (words beginning with *tyad* are always [retained] when combined with all other pronouns). || 33 ||
At dawn, as the dense mass of flowers gradually spread far and wide,
the cluster of stars, resembling the limbs of celestial nymphs, slowly faded away.
In the phrase "puṣparddhighanajālapratikṛtau," the suffix *kan* is applied in the sense of "resembling" (*pratikṛti*), as in "tārakānikare iva pratikṛtau. || 34 ||
Having sent away my son along with the fisherman toward the path leading to the region of the sky filled with kadamba trees, I then went to the celestial river. (35)
"Having followed him as he approached"—according to the Smṛti: "One should follow a dear traveler as far as the edge of water. Thus, having sent him back toward home, she turned him away. || 35 ||
Having reached that desired place and ascended to the vault of the sky,
he entered the space in the midst of the sages and remained there as if established in his own self.
O delight of the Raghus, this story of Dāśūra has been told to you;
it is like a reflection of the world, appearing real in form yet composed of unreality.
O Rāghava, I have related this story of Dāśūra to you for the sake of your awakening in the investigation of the nature of the world. (38)
He recalls the previously mentioned connection of the narrative with the words "dāśūra" (38).
Therefore, having abandoned both unreal and even real attachment, remain always noble and self-possessed through the vision of the Dāśūra Siddhānta. 39.
According to the perspective of the established doctrine taught by Dāśūra. || 39 ||
Therefore, having shaken off the impurity of conceptual construction from yourself, behold the stainless reality of the Self;
you shall attain that state before long.
By which you shall become worthy of worship among the worlds.
Having shaken off conceptual construction, the mind that possesses those qualities, its cause, impurity, and ignorance—
by means of this attainment, you will become one who is to be sacrificed to and worthy of worship.
Thus ends the fifty-fifth sarga, titled "The Meeting of Vasiṣṭha and Dāśūra," in the *Moḥa-sthitiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by the sage Vālmīki. 55.

Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Meeting of Vasiṣṭha and Dāśūra," in the Section on Stability (*sthitiprakaraṇa*) within the *Tātparyaprakāśa* commentary on the glorious *Vāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa*. || 55 ||
The narrative of Dāśūra is concluded.
The fifty-sixth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having determined with certainty that "this does not exist," abandon attachment toward everything;
for what reliance can there be here, for those who investigate, upon that which does not exist? (1)

Having reflected in every way upon the existence and non-existence of being and non-being, as well as the agency and non-agency of the insentient and the consciousness here, attachment to the visible world is entirely warded off. (1)

This world is inert. It is an attachment characterized by the superimposition of association and identity in the form of "mine" and "I. [This applies] to those who investigate, that is, to the discerning. || 1 ||
If this which is being perceived exists and has attained reality, then remain in your own self; why indeed do you falsely attribute the nature of a self to it? (2)

Is the visible object existent, or both existent and non-existent, or even non-existent? To the [objection] that in all three of these positions it is not fitting for there to be attachment to the ego and so forth, he says—by means of three verses—beginning with "That which is being seen": "If you think that this body and so forth exists as having attained an existence independent of your own existence, then you too [must exist] independently of its existence..."

"Abide in your own Self, which is of the nature of consciousness, unattached and indifferent. Why do you falsely attribute the nature of the Self to this body and so forth, which are devoid of selfhood? It is not fitting for you to do so. Alternatively, if the reading is *tiṣṭhatvātmani*, the meaning is: "If it has attained existence, then let it indeed abide in the Self—that is, in its own inert nature."
"Thou art here," and so forth, as before. || 2 ||
Even if you possess the certainty that "this exists" or "this does not exist," how can attachment to mental cultivation be appropriate for one who is both moving and unmoving? (3)

Attachment to cultivation refers to the superimposition previously mentioned. It is "unstable" because it is of an indeterminate nature, consisting of the mutual destruction of existence and non-existence. || 3 ||
This world does not exist, O Rāma; it is not yours, O high-minded one.
It is merely the pure Self itself, thus extended and measured in such a manner.
Now, the word "atha cet" (if, however) is drawn forward [from the previous verse]. If this world does not exist, then there is no bondage for you at all;
rather, the reality of the Self alone is thus spread out—extended on all sides and measured—as meaning that there is no room for any other coloring. || 4 ||
This is not created by an agent, nor does it follow a sequence produced by an agent;
yet, having reached the state of being both agent and non-agent, this manifests of its own accord.

Furthermore, is this world possessed of a creator, or devoid of a creator, or common to both creator and non-creator—having its very nature obtained merely through the proximity of an indifferent Self? In all three of these positions, your attachment to it is not appropriate;
thus he says with two verses beginning with "This is not... (5).
Whether the web of the world be without a creator or with a creator,
do not remain with a mind clouded by such dualistic notions.

Contemplating the variegated [universe] as having attained a state of oneness through the superimposition of mutual identity, and perceiving the body and so forth as the Self, do not remain—do not abide—in the limitation of the mental adjunct of the intellect; this is the meaning. || 6 ||

Deprived of all senses, that self is like an insentient object, as if it were an agent; yet I consider it then to be a non-agent, and the world to arise by mere chance, like the "crow-and-the-palm-fruit" coincidence.

One might object: "How has this position of non-agency arisen, which contradicts such scriptural passages as 'From whom indeed these beings are born' and 'The maker of the universe, the protector of the world,' and for what purpose have you presented it? To this, he says: "All... [and so forth].

"That which is invisible, ungraspable, without color, without eyes or ears, without hands or feet, eternal, all-pervading, omnipresent, and extremely subtle—that imperishable source of all beings which they behold," according to such scriptural passages; because of its non-attachment and indifference, the Self is like a mountain or a block of wood, yet [the text continues]: "Mount Meru [does not obstruct] the sun..."

Just as in the expression "he causes [the wheel] to revolve," the agent is used figuratively for the sake of establishing the falsity of the world; the meaning is: "when the inner intent of all those scriptural passages that establish that everything has an agent has been understood. || 7 ||
Whatever occurs by way of a chance coincidence like the "crow-and-the-palm-fruit" event,
it is only the fool— and no one else— who attaches his thoughts to that occurrence.
Whatever it may be, it is indeed indefinable. "Bhāva" refers to the conceit of "I-ness" (ahaṃtā) and so forth;
by that, there is repeated mental engagement, which is remembrance. "Bāla" means a fool. || 8 ||
O Rāma, this world is never at peace, nor is it subject to destruction;
for it is perceived incessantly and because it manifests again and again.
He demonstrates its very indeterminability through reasoning with the words beginning "no," and so forth:
it is not of the nature of emptiness consisting of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), nor is it of the nature of emptiness resulting from destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*). Of emptiness...

The meaning is: because the world is never perceived as a static whole, because it is always seen in the form of a continuous flux, because there is a contradiction in the arising of what has already been destroyed, and because the world arises again and again. || 9 ||
This world, O Rāma, never exists, nor does it perish;
for by inference, it is because it is constantly perishing and because it lacks existence.

In that case, let it always have the nature of being real like the Self, or let it have the nature of momentary existence; to this he replies: "No. It cannot have the nature of eternal existence, nor can it have the nature of perishable, momentary existence. In the first case, there would be a contradiction with experience, because one perceives a state of wasting away through a difference in transformation at every moment. In the second case...

The meaning is that because it does not exist in the prior and subsequent times—which are beginningless and endless—it cannot possibly possess existence even in the moment intended to be its present; therefore, its non-existence is inferred. || 10 ||
When the agent here has transcended the sphere of all the senses and is free from fever, he never experiences weariness while acting at all times. || 11 ||
Or rather, let his status as the creator at the beginning of creation consist merely in his proximity, impelled by destiny;
nevertheless, it is not fitting for him to feel distress there due to the conceit of being the creator. Thus he says with two verses beginning with "sarvendriya-": || 11 ||
Therefore, this mature destiny, consisting of states of existence and non-existence, is seen to be just such—stable, long-lasting, and yet arisen from falsehood. (12)
Why does he pursue for even a single hundred-year portion of that infinite time—that which is so exceedingly marvelous? (13)

A hundred autumns is the ultimate limit of time for living in a human body; since neither the beginningless past nor the endless future has ever existed [for this body], it is a great and most firm marvel characterized by the identity of the human body with the self—a marvel so utterly improbable that it lasts for only such a brief duration. Being of such a nature...
Why does that Self, which transcends the domain of all the senses, run after this? The meaning is that, in every respect, this is improper.
If the entities of the worlds were eternal by their very nature, then attachment [to them] would not be fitting;
for how indeed could there be a mutual union between the insentient and the sentient? (14)

Now, he states that even if one accepts permanence in the view that there is no agent, reliance [on such a self] is not appropriate—saying "sthirā" (permanent). The meaning is that because of its very nature of permanence, it is unfit for abandonment or acquisition. With the intention that reliance on it is also inappropriate because of the impossibility of a connection with an insentient object due to its being unattached (*asaṅga*), he asks "how? (verse 14).
If the phenomena of the world are unstable, then even that [desire for them] is not fitting;
for this [instability], which is as transient as water-foam, will bring you suffering at its end. (15)
Now, he states that even in the view that things are non-agents and impermanent, reliance [upon them] is not appropriate—saying, "They are impermanent.

Because you bind your reliance upon those which are unstable, this reliance, having become attached even to the end—the destruction—of something as unstable as the froth on milk, results in suffering;
that is to say, it leads to the infliction of pain. And thus, by relying on the froth of milk...
The meaning is: if grief is appropriate at the destruction of that [body], then it would also be appropriate at the destruction of the body and so forth, since they are held in such regard. || 15 ||

O mighty-armed one, the binding attachment to the world as being the very nature of the self does not shine forth, whether toward the stable or the unstable, just like [the comparison] between foam and a mountain.

The state of the self being the world, and the world having the nature of the self—meaning, having the nature of birth, destruction, and so forth—is nothing other than the bond of attachment characterized by the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of mutual identity and relation; it cannot be defined as anything else. And that [bond] does not shine—that is, it does not appear beautiful—in the investigation of reality (*tattvavimarśa*), for neither of the two positions, whether [the self is] stable or unstable.

This is the meaning. Alternatively, the meaning is that the bond of attachment characterized by identity between the self and the world—whether stable or unstable—does not shine, just as it does not shine between a mountain of foam and a [real] mountain. || 16 ||
Although it is the creator of all, the Self does nothing at all, as if it were not the agent;
thus it remains indifferent, like a lamp in relation to its light.
Now, one might ask: "If [the Self] is the agent, how is its state of non-existence (anāsthā) possible? To this he says: "All... etc. It is a non-agent, like a mountain;
this is an illustration regarding its aspect of indifference (*audāsīnya*). However, it is called an "agent" because of the accomplishment of effects;
he states this with an illustration by saying "it stands," and so forth. || 17 ||
Doing nothing, he does everything, like the sun performing its daily work; moving, he does not move, remaining established in his own self like the sun stationed in its own place.
The "divine duty" (divākārya) is the fulfillment of all the daily tasks of every living being. || 18 ||
From some unknown source, this world appears as if it has come into being,
spreading out like the whirlpools in a flood of water on the banks of the Aruṇā.

Now, one might object that the sun is merely the instrumental cause for the activities of the day, whereas people are seen to be its distinct agents; however, in the creation of the world, there are no other agents. Anticipating this disparity, he says: "Aruṇā...
The river named Aruṇā has a bank that is naturally rugged with rocks and indifferent [to the flow]. Even the flood of water...

The nature of water is to flow downward; it does not create irregularity in its current. Since a whirlpool arises when those two [water and a vessel] are in proximity, it occurs quite spontaneously from some cause or other. Likewise, the world arises in the proximity of consciousness and the insentient.
The point is that, therefore, the burden of being its creator cannot be placed upon the head of anyone.

The first [type of *vat* suffix] occurs after a word ending in the locative case in the sense of "like" (*iva*), while the second occurs after a word ending in the instrumental case in the sense of "equal to that" (*tena tulyam*). (19)
If this has been determined by you with such skill, O Rāma, it has not been investigated with a mind purified by valid means of knowledge. (20)
He says that, upon such reflection, attachment to the world is even more utterly inappropriate—by means of the three verses beginning with "iti. (20)
Nevertheless, O virtuous one, you ought not to cultivate a conceptualization regarding an object;
for what kind of cultivation can there be for a firebrand-circle, a dream, or an illusion? (21)
A person who arrives unexpectedly is not a fit vessel for affection;
this web of the world arises from delusion, so do not rely upon it as a vessel for such feelings.
Of affection and friendliness. || 22 ||
Just as you do not conceive of reality in heat, in the moon, in the cool sun, or likewise in the water of a mirage, so too should you not conceive of reality in this world.

And because it is unreal, reliance upon it is not appropriate; thus he says, "auṣṇya" (heat), etc. Just as one afflicted by cold does not place reliance on the moon perceived through the delusion of heat, nor one afflicted by heat on the sun made cool by delusion, nor one afflicted by thirst on the water of a mirage—so too is it with the existence of the world. This is the meaning. || 23 ||
Just as you perceive the delusions of a person created by thought, a person in a dream, or a second moon,
so too should you view this entire collection of existing things.
Having abandoned all intermediate states consisting of the cultivation of the glory of worldly existence, O sinless one, remain as you truly are and sport here in this world with ease.
Bhāvaśrī is the beauty of objects such as women; [it is that which is abundant with the contemplation thereof]. (25)
Having drunk the state of non-agency, even while acting, and having drunk away desire as well—of that Self which abides within all beings and yet transcends all. || 26 ||

"Having drunk"—that is, having swallowed—the state of non-agency and its corresponding desire, as well as the state of agency and its corresponding desire (due to the word "api"), that which remains as the residue, you are that; this is the connection with the preceding [verse]. He explains what was said [in the previous verse], namely, "sport playfully":
"the state of non-agency," etc. [This refers to] remaining indifferent toward worldly activity while acting.
By your mere presence, though you are the agent, destiny unfolds itself entirely without desire;
that is to say, it manifests in the form of worldly transaction. || 26 ||
This destiny unfolds merely through proximity;
it shines forth without any desire of its own, just as light appears merely through the presence of a lamp.
Regarding this, he states the illustrations—beginning with "the lamp"—and adds that the light shines without any desire; this is the implied meaning. || 27 ||
Just as *kuṭaja* trees [blossom] by the mere proximity of a cloud, so too do the three worlds [arise] by the mere proximity of the Self. 28.
*Kuṭajāni* means *kuṭaja* flowers; the word "grow" (*jāyante*) is to be supplied in both cases. || 28 ||
Just as the sun remains in the sky devoid of all desire,
so too does activity arise when the Lord exists, even though He is free from all longing.
In the god, the Supreme Self. || 29 ||
Just as light proceeds from a jewel that remains without desire,
so too does this multitude of worlds proceed from the Lord by His mere existence alone.
Therefore, both agency and non-agency reside within its own self;
because it is devoid of desire, it is a non-agent, yet it is an agent by virtue of its mere presence.
Showing the seed for the statements regarding agency and non-agency, he concludes with the words "ataḥ" (therefore). || 31 ||
Because he transcends all the senses and so forth, the one consisting of pure being (sanmaya) is neither agent nor enjoyer;
however, because he is present within the senses, he alone is indeed the agent and the enjoyer.
And he shows this in another verse with the word "all": the meaning is that he is stated to be both the agent and the enjoyer, not the non-agent and the non-enjoyer. || 32 ||
O sinless one, these two views exist: agency and non-agency.
Relying upon whichever you perceive as the better, remain steadfast.
The words "agency" and "non-agency" are to be supplied [as the subjects]. || 33 ||
By means of this firm conviction, "I am all-pervading and a non-doer," one is not tainted even while performing actions that have come into the current of worldly flow.
He demonstrates the superiority of each of the two [methods] individually with the words beginning "sarvastha" (abiding in all). || 34 ||
A living being falls into a state of despondency due to the lack of mental engagement when he reaches the firm conviction: "I do not perform even the slightest action here in this world. (35)
He explains how one is not stained by saying "it goes": [it goes] to a state of saplessness, which is dispassion (virāga). || 35 ||
In that state, who would desire a flood of enjoyments, or who would even renounce them?
Therefore, one should cultivate with fervor the realization: "I am eternally a non-doer. (36)
That which is called supreme nectar remains as equanimity alone;
then, by means of that [equanimity], through the state of being the great agent, one thinks, "I do everything. (37)
He shows the superiority of the second kalpa as well, beginning with the words "atha" and so forth. || 37 ||
If you desire stability, O Rāma, they know that even this is considered supreme;
alas, that I do not bring this entire worldly delusion to an end! (38)
He demonstrates that even in such a state, there is no possibility of attachment, aversion, and so forth during the first kalpa:
"How could there be a sequence of attachment and aversion there, since another is utterly impossible?
For one body is burned by one [person], while it is cherished by another. (39)

How could there be any possibility for me? The meaning is that it would belong to someone other than me, since [such a thing] is absolutely impossible for anyone else. However, if the reading is *anyasaṃbhavāt*, the meaning is:

because of the possibility of another—namely, another agent who is not the [intended] agent, such as passion (*rāga*) and so forth. Even in the second alternative, there is no such application [of the objection].
He shows this with the words: "That which... (39).

Therefore, since this [world] is merely my own undertaking, what sequence can there be for weariness or delight in the expansion of my own pleasure and pain, or in the destruction and arising of the web of the world? (40)

Our undertaking is indeed performed by us alone; therefore, I am the agent in the destruction and arising of the web of the world, which consists of the sorrow and joy of weariness and exultation. (40)
Thinking "I am the doer," what room is there within for the sequence of sorrow and joy?
For in the play of sorrow and joy, one acts through this very sense of being the self as the agent. (41)
The phrase "of one who remains [in that state]" is to be understood as the ellipsis. Even if this be so, how is the attainment of equanimity achieved? To this he says: "Sweat... (verse 41).
When [the mind] has itself gone to dissolution, only equanimity remains;
that which is equanimity toward all beings is the true, supreme state. (42)
"When they had gone to dissolution"—the use of the singular number [for the plural] is a Vedic anomaly (chāndasa). || 42 ||
The mind established in that state does not undergo birth even in the slightest degree;
or rather, O Rāghava, it possesses both universal agency and non-agency.
Having established two views corresponding to practice, he demonstrates the perfected view with the words "Alternatively" (athavā). || 43 ||
Having renounced everything and drunk in the mind, remain firm as to who you are;
"I am He, I am He; this is not I, nor do I do this or that."
Through this perspective, he demonstrates the inferiority of the two previous views with the words "this" (*ayam*).

This *haṃsa*, well-known in this body, is the form of the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) consisting of all bodies; thus, in the second alternative (*kalpa*), there is incompleteness because the limitation of the collective totality and the conceit of agency have not departed. However, in the first alternative...

Although there is a purification of the referent of the term *tvaṃ* (the "thou") by means of the elimination of the sense of agency and so forth— through the realization that "I am not this body, senses, and so on, and therefore I do not perform even the slightest action"—
it remains incomplete because the purification of the referent of the term *tat* (the "that") and the establishment of the meaning of the sentence as a whole have not yet been attained.
The meaning is that even these two views do not lead to contentment. || 44 ||
Thus, this vision consisting of the contemplation of [transient] entities does not lead to contentment;
it is the path to the Kālasūtra hell and the snare of the Mahāvīci hell.
If it is asked, "If these do not bring you satisfaction, for what purpose were they presented?"—
the intention is that they were presented as means for liberation from the sense of "I" (ahaṃbhāva) regarding the body, which is the root of all misfortune. With this in mind,
he demonstrates that the identification with the body is of the nature of misfortune and must be abandoned in every way:
By the words beginning with "seti" [it is meant]: Kālasūtra and others are specific types of hells, such as the Forest of Sword-leaves (Asipatravana).
The grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is due to the superimposition of non-difference between cause and effect, as in the expression "clarified butter is life. || 45 ||
That state of "I am the body," which is like a row of sword-leaf forests,
must be abandoned with every effort, even if total destruction is imminent.
She was not to be touched by a noble man, like a Puṣkasī woman with dog-meat;
she was utterly abandoned by that film-like streak which had appeared before his eyes.

"Accompanied by dog-meat" (*saśvamāṃsā*) means together with dog-meat; the sense is that even the notion of "I am the body" is defiled by impurities such as desire, which are like dog-meat. In the vision of the pure Self, it acts as a cause for obscuration and distraction, like a film over the eye in the region of the *svādhiṣṭhāna*. || 47 ||
The supreme vision arises like moonlight when the clouds have vanished;
O Rāma, once it has dawned, the ocean of worldly existence is crossed by its means.
Having clearly realized within oneself that "I am not the doer, nor am I that [agent]," or else having reached the certainty that "I am the doer, and I am all that," [one attains liberation].

Or else, having resolved that "I am indeed nothing at all," remain established in your own true state, which is the most supreme, where the virtuous who know the path abide as the highest of beings. (49)

Now, having summarized the three views, he concludes by teaching the non-volitional state appropriate to one’s own authority among them, beginning with the word "kartā" (the agent): "I am not that [agent] which is the body and so forth, the instigator of agency. The word "samagram" (entirely) is used twice—once in the accusative and once in the nominative—by means of *tantra* (repetition), according to the maxim of the lamp on the threshold (*dehalī-dīpa-nyāya*).
This connects with what precedes and follows. Thus, the meaning is: "I alone am the entire whole";

that is, I alone am even that cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) which constitutes the totality of all things. In this way, I am not anything whatsoever in the form of the well-known visible world, but rather I am someone [ineffable].

The meaning is: "I am the Self whose nature is full bliss and consciousness, distinct from the self that is insentient, of the nature of suffering, limited, and well-known in the world. By the word "having ascertained," it is implied that this [realization] must necessarily be the ultimate conclusion of even the two previous views. For those who know the words...
The knowers of Brahman. || 49 ||

Thus ends the fifty-sixth canto, titled "The Instruction on the Yoga of Contemplating Agency," in the Section on Stability (*sthitiprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa*, the Great Epic of Vasiṣṭha, composed by the Sage (*ārṣa*). Canto 56.
Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Union with Agency," in the section on Stability within the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The fifty-seventh canto.
Śrī Rāma said:
"O Brahman, what you have spoken is true and beautiful in its expression."
For the Self is indeed a non-doer yet the doer, and the creator of beings is a non-enjoyer yet the enjoyer.
The occasion for Rāma’s questions, the sequence for abandoning latent impressions (vāsanā), and the detailed praise of those who have attained success through that sole means are presented here. (1)

Desiring to ask the questions that will be stated hereafter, Rāma demonstrates his own comprehension of the previously mentioned topics through a summary and praise of them, beginning with the words "It is true. By the same logic, he also [demonstrates his understanding of] this [subject], namely his non-enjoyership and his being the enjoyer of all, which were not explicitly stated.
He indicates that "I am the one who causes [them] to eat" by using the word "bhoktā" (the enjoyer). || 1 ||
The Lord of all, omnipresent, pure consciousness alone is the stainless state;
He is the abode on earth, the divine form, dwelling within all beings. (2)

A "station" (sthāna) is so called because all beings abide within it. This should somehow be construed by supplying the word "just as": just as the body—the physical form of the fourfold collection of beings—abides upon the earth, so too [does He]. And He Himself abides within all beings. (2)
O All-pervading Lord, my Brahman has now reached the state of being heart-pleasing through your words, just as a mountain is relieved of its distress by showers from the ocean.

And thus, because I have understood through the very same reasoning the meaning declared by the Śruti— namely, "Beholding the Self in all beings and all beings in the Self, one attains the Supreme Brahman, and not by any other means"— Brahman has ascended to the level of my direct experience; so he says:

Regarding the phrase "reaching the heart": the ellipsis is that just as a mountain of earth remains unperturbed by torrents of rain and is freed from the heat of summer, so too do I now remain by means of your words. || 3 ||
Due to indifference and lack of desire, he neither enjoys nor acts;
yet, because he brings about the welfare of the entire world, the Lord both enjoys and acts.

He shows that even if there is no contradiction between being an enjoyer and not being an enjoyer, the reasoning you have stated applies equally [to both cases], by saying: "Because of indifference" (audāsīnyāt) || 4 ||
However, O Blessed One, this vast doubt remains in my heart;
O Brahmin, sever it with your words, as the moon dispels darkness with its rays.
This is of the manner that will be described [in the following]. || 5 ||
"This is existent, this is non-existent; this is he, I am this, yet not this;
this is one, this is a second"—such is the nature of the world, consisting of the conceptualization of "I" and "mine. (6)

Having restated the two positions regarding the existence and non-existence of the world mentioned in the previous creation—namely, the perspective of the individual ego (*vyaṣṭy-ahaṃtā*) and the perspective of the universal collective identity (*samaṣṭy-ahaṃbhāva*)—he asks [the question] with a view toward its utility for inquiry:
"Is this... and so forth. Is this world real or is it unreal, according to the direction you have stated? This is the well-known [question].

"I am indeed the totality (samaṣṭi), and not merely this individual body (vyaṣṭideha)"— or rather, "this phenomenal world (prapañca) is one from the perspective of the totality, but dual or manifold from the perspective of the individual. Such conceptualizations of indefinite, manifold forms exist within that which is a single, fixed, and unitary nature at the end of the path.

Since it is self-luminous, how could that which is opposed to it— like mist to the sun— now exist within the Self, which is pure, stainless, and has by its very nature dispelled the darkness of delusion? If you should say that this [world] first resided within the womb of Brahman as variegated by *māyā* and is now manifested, even in that case:
I ask: how could this have existed even for the very first time? The meaning is that the contradiction remains the same even then. || 6 ||
Just as mist does not exist within the sun,
how could this [world] be situated within the pure Self from the very beginning?
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said: O Rāma, at the very time of the final conclusion, I shall give you a firm answer to this inquiry, by which you will know it according to reality.

By the power of Rāma’s words alone, Rāma attained the vision of his own self-luminous inner Self, the realization of the oneness of that Self in all bodies, and the understanding of the world's indeterminability; yet,
due to the absence of the destruction of latent impressions (vāsanā), he did not effect the eradication of ignorance, which is the root of all doubt.

Having determined that the undivided experience characterized by the identity of the inner self (*pratyagātman*) and Brahman has not yet occurred, Vasiṣṭha— desiring to explain the means for the eradication of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) as a means toward that end—
declares that this is not the occasion to state the answer, beginning with the words "In the Siddhānta" (*siddhānte*). In the Siddhānta...
In the latter half of the Nirvāṇa-prakaraṇa, beginning with the story of the stone (pāṣāṇākhyāyikā) and so forth. || 8 ||
O Rāghava, until you have attained the definitive conclusion regarding the means to liberation,
you will not be sufficiently qualified to hear these questions and answers.
The final conclusion of the instruction on the means to liberation, which consists of the perfected state of non-dual cognition. || 9 ||
O Rāma, just as a youth is the recipient of the songs of beloved women, so too is the doer of merit the recipient of questions and sublime utterances. (10)
With the intention that even what is being said now will not take root in your mind, he says "Kāntā":
one who has performed meritorious deeds, one who has reached the culmination of the fruits of all actions, and one who possesses self-knowledge. || 10 ||
Just as a discourse filled with passion is in vain among the foolish, so too a discourse of noble inspiration is useless for those of meager understanding. 11.
That from whose presence arises noble prosperity and the highest good. || 11 ||
At a particular time, something shines forth for a person;
the fruit of a tree appears only in autumn, not in the month of Mādhava.
With the intention that this question also shines forth at that very time, he says: "In a certain... [referring to] a tree such as an orange, betel-nut, or citron tree. || 12 ||
The words of instruction take hold in an elder, as dye does on a clean cloth;
and the discourse on sublime wisdom takes hold in one who has realized the Self.
The meaning is that the words of instruction—namely, instructions on dispassion—take root in one who is aged, meaning advanced in knowledge and discerning, but not in one who is passionate. || 13 ||
The answer to this question was previously stated by me in brief; because it was not given in detail, it has not been clearly understood by you. (14)

He states— “of the question”— that even though the latter part of this [work] had been commenced previously at the end of the Bhārgava-episode, it was nonetheless set aside upon observing that [the interlocutor] lacked the requisite qualification. || 14 ||
If you yourself perceive the Self by means of the self, then you will rightly know the answer to this question; of this there is no doubt.
He says: "Once the knowledge of the indivisible reality has arisen, you will understand the answer yourself even without my words":
"But when you stand with realization attained at the time of the final conclusion, O virtuous one, the sequence of questions and answers must be explained by me in full detail. (16)
"In that case, will you remain indifferent? To this he replies: "By me," [verse 16].
The self alone knows the self; indeed, the self is made by the self alone.
Being perfectly serene, the self attains the self.

My instruction is merely the pointing out of the door; however, with the intention that "you must see the Self by yourself through self-concentration," he says: "He knows. Even the transmigrating self is known only by the Self itself.
For, because of the lack of grace toward the Self, the Self has been made such [as it appears].
The meaning is that, through the awakening to the Self, the Self itself, being perfectly serene, realizes its own true, full nature. || 17 ||
Thus, O Rāma, has this investigation into the agent and the non-agent been told;
however, due to ignorance of it, one whose latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are not yet exhausted remains bound. (18)
Even this investigation into the nature of the agent and the non-agent was spoken by me solely with the aim of awakening you to that very indivisible Brahman.

Although it has been explained, because you have not known that state of the indivisible Self due to ignorance, you must surely still possess unextinguished latent impressions (*vāsanā*). The use of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) here indicates possibility. Your latent impressions have not yet been destroyed.
The meaning is: "I consider him to have been born. || 18 ||
For one is bound by being bound to latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and liberation is the destruction of latent impressions.
Having abandoned latent impressions, abandon even the desire for liberation. (19)
Now, demonstrating the secret of bondage and liberation, he describes the sequence of means for severing latent impressions (vāsanā) with the verse beginning "baddha" (bound), etc. (19).
Having first abandoned the tamasic tendencies perfumed by sense objects, take up the pure tendency known as the cultivation of friendliness and the other [divine attitudes]. (20)
Regarding the first section on the destruction of latent impressions (*vāsanākṣaya*), he says "the tamasic ones" to indicate the firmness of dispassion (*vairāgyadārḍhya*).
"Tamasic" means those that lead to rebirths such as the animal realm, which are dominated by *tamas*;
this is also an elliptical expression for those that grant birth as humans and so forth, which are dominated by *rajas*. "Perfumed by objects" means infused with them.

Loving-kindness (maitrī), compassion (karuṇā), sympathetic joy (muditā), and equanimity (upekṣā) are called "the cultivation of loving-kindness and the rest. Accordingly, the Patañjala Sūtra states: "The clarification of the mind arises from the cultivation of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity toward those who experience happiness, suffering, merit, and demerit as their fruits. [20]
Having renounced even that internally, though engaging with those [objects] outwardly,
remain with all internal attachment stilled, possessing only the latent impression of pure consciousness.
Seeing that even friendliness and the other virtues do not exist apart from the inner pure consciousness alone,

remain one whose latent impressions are strengthened by the practice of *samprajñāta-samādhi*, thinking "I am indeed pure consciousness alone," even while outwardly engaging in those practices such as friendliness. 21.
Then, having abandoned even that [mind] together with the intellect, remain in the remainder with steady concentration; abandon that by which you abandon.

The mention of "mind and intellect" (*manobuddhi*) is also an elliptical indication for the mind (*citta*) and its modifications (*vṛtti*). Regarding the remainder, because it is the very nature of the Self (*ātmatva*), it cannot be abandoned; thus, one whose steady concentration and rest reside in that which necessarily remains—the state of inwardness (*pratyaktattva*)—is meant. That is to say, one who has come to rest in *asaṃprajñāta-samādhi*. By whom...
You abandon everything previously mentioned by means of that which is called *kalana*—the ego (*ahaṃkāra*), which serves as the foundational pillar for the conceptualization of duality;
abandon even that. For the abandonment of everything consists precisely in the relinquishing of the conceit of "I" and "mine" in each respective instance.
And that [relinquishing] occurs even regarding the ego through the vision of the Self as the full, non-ego state, whose nature is pure consciousness alone.
