The sense is that because it arises by itself through the eradication of root-ignorance, there is no dependence on any other cause therein, and thus there is no infinite regress. || 22 ||
Consisting of pure consciousness, [it perceives] the time of mental construction, light and darkness,
as well as the latent impression and the one who possesses it, preceded by the vibration of the vital breath.

Having uprooted—along with the ego—the vibration of the vital breath (*prāṇa-spandana*), the conceptualization of time, light and darkness, latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the impressioner, the objects of sense, and by the force of the word "and" (*ca*), the senses which are their gateways, as well as the ego together with its very root;
she becomes like the sky: gentle, stainless, with distractions stilled, and possessing the single undivided form of the Self that is Brahman.

The connection with the subsequent part of the verse is as follows: "He who, being of such a nature—that is, you who consist of consciousness (*cinmaya*)—becomes or attains that very state, you are indeed the one whose form is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). He is "honored" (*satkṛta*), meaning worshipped by all. || 23 ||
O one of noble intellect, may you—who have completely renounced even the very roots [of worldly existence] and whose mind is as serene and tranquil as the sky—be honored by all. 24.
Having completely renounced everything from the heart, he who remains free from agitation is liberated and is the Supreme Lord. || 25 ||

He demonstrates the very venerability of one who has attained such a state through the praise beginning with "the sun of the heart" and so forth: "one whose agitation—the cause of all distractions—has departed from the heart. (25)
Whether he practices meditative concentration or performs actions— or whether he does not— such a person,
having cast aside all mental objects through the heart and possessing the highest disposition, is indeed liberated.

Thus, for one who has ascended to the seventh stage through the ripening of practice and has attained perfection, there is indeed the state of having accomplished all that was to be done, with no further task remaining; thus he says: "Samādhim" (concentration). He is one by whom all "āsthās"—the aforementioned forms of conceit and false attribution—have been cast out and eliminated. || 26 ||

For one whose mind is free from latent impressions (vāsanā), there is no need for inaction (naiṣkarmya), nor is there any need for ritual actions; nor is there any need for meditative absorption (samādhi) or the chanting of prayers (jāpya). || 27 ||
The scriptures have been sufficiently investigated and long debated among one another;
yet there is no higher state than the silence that arises from the abandonment of all latent impressions (vāsanā). 28.

To prevent a reversal [of understanding] arising from the delusion of having accomplished all that was to be done even before the dissolution of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—which occurs through *śravaṇa*, *manana*, and *dhyāna* practiced for only a short time—he says: "It has been investigated. This means it has been firmly established through mutual discussion with learned men, such that it is capable of being presented [as a settled conclusion].

It has been accomplished. The meaning is that, through great effort and with the consensus of all learned scholars, it has been determined that this alone is the secret of the scriptures on liberation (*mokṣa-śāstra*).
From silence—namely, from the previously mentioned non-conceptual [state] produced by the maturation of hearing and reflection, which are denoted by the terms "childhood" and "scholarship"—...

The meaning is that it has been determined that there is no state beyond that of a sage (*muni*), which culminates in the ripening of *asaṃprajñāta-samādhi*, and which is called the "Brahmin state" (*brāhmaṇa*) characterized by the final establishment of the knowledge of reality. Thus says the Śruti: "Therefore, having become disillusioned with scholarship, a Brahmin should abide in childlike simplicity; and [having become disillusioned with] childlike simplicity..."

"Having become disillusioned with scholarship, one becomes a sage; then, having become disillusioned with both non-silence and silence, one becomes a Brahmin. And: "This is the eternal glory of a Brahmin. (28)
Having wandered repeatedly through the ten directions, everything that is to be seen has been seen;
yet only a few people perceive things as they truly are. (29)
For this very reason, he says that those who know reality are rare and difficult to find: "It is seen," etc. (29).
Whatever is perceived, none of it exists;
apart from the desirable and the undesirable, people do not strive for anything else therein.

Because all people are outward-turned, they perceive only what is desirable or undesirable in the external world; thus, it is observed that their inclination is solely toward the means for attaining or avoiding those objects, rather than toward the Self. To this he says: "Whatever is perceived"—whatever is seen at all does not exist apart from the desirable and the undesirable.

But as for that other reality of the Self which is beyond the scope [of the senses], no person at all exerts effort toward it; rather, they strive only for what is desired and undesired—this is the meaning. || 30 ||
Whatever undertakings there may be, whatever sequences of actions people perform—all those are solely for the sake of the body; they are not at all for the sake of the Self.
And with the intention that this effort regarding the non-self, because it serves only the purpose of the non-self body, is indeed the cause of the repeated commencement of bodies, he says:
"Whatever [undertakings]... Undertakings (*samārambhāḥ*) refer to worldly objects such as houses, palaces, and so forth; they are sequences of actions (*kriyākramāḥ*).
Vedic sacrifices and so forth. || 31 ||
In the netherworld, in the world of Brahmā, in heaven, and on the surface of the earth,
as well as in the sky, only a few are seen whose vision has been witnessed.
In the sky, that is, in the world of the intermediate space; those persons by whom Brahman, which is of the single essence of consciousness, has been seen—[they have seen it]. 32.
That wise man for whom the certainties— "this is to be abandoned" and "this is to be accepted"— have dissolved as they arise from the unreal, is exceedingly rare to find.
Arising from the non-existent means arising from ignorance of one's own self. || 33 ||
Let it rule the world, or let it enter the ocean or its waters;
yet no living being attains rest except through the attainment of the Self. (34)

One might object: "Is not a state of rest seen even within saṃsāra upon attaining high positions such as supreme sovereignty? What is the use of the vision of the Self? To this he says: "Let [it] do... Let the cloud enter into the authority over rain through the attainment of Indra's station;
or let the water enter everywhere through the attainment of Varuṇa's station, or through the mastery of the elements by means of yogic powers. || 34 ||
Those of great intelligence who are virtuous and heroes against the enemies of the senses—
they, the high-minded ones, should be venerated for the sake of destroying the fever of rebirth.
In that case, who are those to be worshipped by one seeking rest? He states [the answer] with the words "ye" (those who...). || 35 ||
Everywhere there are the five elements; nothing else exists as a sixth.
Where, then, can one of steady intellect find delight—in the underworld, on the earth, or in heaven? (36)
To the question, "Even when the knowledge of reality arises through that worship, by what can one's attachment to the planes of enjoyment be prevented? he says:

"In all [cases]. According to the direction stated in the Śruti—"The fire-nature of fire has departed; the three forms alone are the truth"—there is the realization of the falsity characterized by the mere nature of the elements (bhūtamātratā) in all elemental things; regarding those [things],...
The meaning is: "because of the non-arising of passion. || 36 ||
For the wise one who acts with reason, saṃsāra is like the footprint of a cow;
but for one who has utterly abandoned reason, it is like a vast, intoxicated ocean.

If it is argued that, since only the remaining elements remain, they are infinite and thus impossible to cross over, this is true for those who lack knowledge; however, for those who know reality, [the crossing is possible] through the vision of Brahman as the substrate of all, according to the reasoning shown in the scripture: "O dear one, by means of food as the sprout, seek water as the root."
With the intention that crossing over [the ocean] is indeed easy because even for living beings there is the certainty of its unreality, he says:
"by means of reasoning" (yuktyā). The "intoxicated ocean" (mattārṇava) is the ocean of dissolution (pralayārṇava). || 37 ||
For one whose consciousness is expansive, the entire universe is equal to a *kadamba* flower bud;
even when this whole world is attained, what does he give away, and what does he enjoy? (38)

Furthermore, because one perceives the universe as exceedingly small through the vision of the bliss of the undivided Self, there arises no attachment to the desire for giving, enjoyment, and so forth regarding trivial things such as wealth and wives—things comparable to the enjoyments of a mosquito on a *kadamba* flower-bud. Thus he says: "The *kadamba*... (verse 38).
For this reason, O Rāma, I consider those great acts of war undertaken by the ignorant to be censurable, as they bring about the destruction of the two hundred thousand [warriors] in battle.

The knower of reality who is compassionate must indeed despise, and never honor, the happiness of sovereignty and the like, because it brings about the destruction of hundreds of thousands of warriors through calamities such as battle; this is what he says with the words "for this purpose" (*etadartham*). The word "this" (*etat*) refers back to the meaning of the relative pronoun "that" (*yat*).
[It is for the sake of] the ignorant, the deluded; the phrase "that happiness of sovereignty" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sense. (39)
Within the extremely fragile interior of that [body], which lasts for only a single kalpa,
there occurs indeed that destruction which is the supreme affliction for those of great intelligence.
One might object: "Could he not find delight in the state of Brahmā, which is to be enjoyed for a long duration until the end of a great aeon (mahākalpa)? To this, he says:

"Kalpa... Because it withers away even in a time limited to the end of a great aeon—lasting two parārdhas—that state, too, has an interior that is exceedingly fragile; [thus, there is no delight] in that state for any living beings.

Because it is the cause of dissolution, destruction—which is the cause of mental anguish—is desirable only for those of small intellect, the deluded; it is not for the knowers of reality. This is the meaning. || 40 ||
Since not even the slightest [notion] of creation and so forth has arisen for the wise Self, even when those three worlds are attained, how could the Self become subject to anything? (41)

Furthermore, from the perspective of the knower who realizes the truth, the three worlds have not arisen even slightly— not produced at all— by means of creation and so forth, according to such scriptural passages as, "There is neither destruction nor origination. When that trifling world, which is like the son of a barren woman, has been realized as such, how could the conscious Self be powerful or strong therein, by virtue of which [it would act] there?
The meaning is that there would be passion (rāga). || 41 ||
On one side this earth is covered by hundreds of mountains, and likewise on the other by masses of water;
how small is its body, that it might fill [the vessel] so magnificently?

With the intention that the position of a universal monarch (*sārvabhauma*) and the like is not to be desired because it abounds in insubstantiality and contains only a small portion of what is truly useful, he says "from this": "noble" (*udāram*), meaning one whose vast disposition is empty through the renunciation of everything. (42)

There is nothing in this world—including the netherworld and the abode of the gods—that could be considered more worthy of being accomplished for a self-possessed and wise person than that [liberation]. (43)
It is more urgent, that is to say, it must necessarily be performed, because one has already accomplished all that was to be done through the attainment of all desires. || 43 ||
For the wise one who has attained oneness, who is as pervasive as space, who is self-abiding, possessed of the Self, established in the Self, and free from the fluctuations of the mind; || 44 ||

Just as a mirage, being established in dependence upon the light of the sun, depends upon the sun, whereas the sun— though it serves as the cause of the mirage— does not depend upon it; so too, the world, which is established in dependence upon the light of consciousness for one who knows reality, must instead depend upon that knower of reality.
The knower of reality, whose delight is in full bliss (*pūrṇānanda*), does not look upon the world even with a sidelong glance; far less does he have any desire for it.

With this intention, the author says "oneness," etc. For one who is self-possessed, devoid of consciousness—that is, without a mind—the vast riverbank of the mirage characterized by the three worlds [is no more].

The meaning is that she, being auspiciously beautiful yet with all saṃsāra stilled, is like the hollow of emptiness or like the interior of space; she does not exist in a formal, material form. To explain how the appearance continues even for those things that are non-existent—by means of the persistence of what has been sublated until the exhaustion of *prārabdha* karma—he specifies her as "the mist of the web of bodies. (44)
The vast bank of the three worlds is grey with the misty net of bodies, its hollows empty, and beautiful through the cessation of saṃsāra. (45)
All the great mountain ranges are but foam upon the vast and pure ocean of Brahman;
they possess the splendor of the mirage-water within the great radiance of the sun of consciousness.

He elaborates upon the dependence on the light of the Self by one who knows the reality of the world, beginning with the words "sphāra" and so forth. The "glories of water" refer to rivers, oceans, and the like. (46)
The successions of creations are the waves of the great ocean of the reality of the Self;
the perspectives of the scriptures are the rains from the cloud of the unsurpassed state. (47)
The "scriptural visions" (*śāstradṛṣṭayaḥ*) are the manifestations of the reality of *dharma*, *brahman*, and so forth, as revealed by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*.

Although even ordinary worldly perceptions, such as visual perception, are indeed like rain from the ocean of Brahman because they are of the nature of light, nevertheless—just as rain falling on fertile soil is most beneficial—the scriptural visions alone are useful for the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*). Therefore, [the text] refers to those [specifically].
Thus they are appropriated. || 47 ||
The lights of the moon, fire, and sun are like a jar, wood, and so forth;
likewise, the rays of the nature of consciousness are the particles of impurity that are to be illuminated.

Having stated that [the Self] is required as the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), he states that it is also required for the manifestation (*prakāśa*) of insentient things, beginning with the word "candra" (moon):

"When even the pure sun and others require its light, then what need be said of the earthly elements and so forth, which are extremely impure and consist mostly of particles of impurity? Thus he asks.
With the intention that this must be stated, it was said: "and likewise the specks of impurity. || 48 ||
Men, gods, and asuras dwell as their own selves, wandering in the forest of saṃsāra like deer seeking mouthfuls of grass in the form of sensual enjoyments. (49)

Based on the Vedic scripture, "Other beings subsist on a mere portion of this very bliss," he states that even for the sake of the bliss of objects—which is the cause of life for all living beings—there is a dependence upon that [bliss], saying: "They sport.
That which is measured, delimited, experienced, or indeed harmed by one's own body as its self—that is [the object].

The ellipsis is to be supplied as follows: those who are like deer—characterized by the enjoyment of desires—become like deer in devouring the *ulapa* grasses, which have for their soul a dream of that very kind. 49.

The bodies of the world are like coffins with bones for their door-bolts, skulls for their lids, and sinews for their chains; they are the repositories of the blood and flesh of decaying living beings. (50)

In the forest, deer possess independence; however, for humans, gods, and asuras, because they are confined within the cage of the body, there is only the suffering of absolute dependence—with this intention, he says: "The bones... [referring to] the bodies of all beings in the world—humans, gods, asuras, and so forth—which belong to living beings worn out in the beginningless wilderness of saṃsāra.

In another sense, the words refer to the meaning of "bondage": caskets (*samudgaka*) and boxes (*saṃpuṭaka*) constructed from blood and flesh—meaning cages, as it were—made by the Dhātṛ; this is the ellipsis. He describes the very components of the cage with the word "bones" (*asthi*):
those whose crossbars and supporting beams (*viṣkambhadāru*) are merely fragments of bone; [and] the head itself...
Those whose upper planks serve as covers; those whose sinews, veins, and chains serve as iron fetters. 50.
Innocent forest deer were made to move about and stand still during their processions through the city; likewise, leather dolls were employed for the amusement of those with childish intellects. (51)

The meaning is this: thus, these leather dolls inhabited by living beings (jīva) are themselves the deer of the forest-garland of saṃsāra; being deluded and devoid of discrimination regarding the body, they have been placed by the Creator in various cities characterized as fields of enjoyment, for the amusement of the children that are their own respective intellects, through the consumption of the leafy sprouts of various enjoyments. || 51 ||
A high-minded person of great intelligence who possesses such a noble mind does not waver even slightly before floods of enjoyments, just as a mountain does not move before gentle breezes.
Since even one who knows the truth perceives a body, does he too act in that same way? He says "no": "not such a one.
One whose mind is noble, who has renounced everything, and who possesses the aforementioned great intelligence—such a person is not like this even in the slightest degree.
(The sandhi *yalopa* is not established here; thus the elision is an archaic Vedic usage. One whose mind is fixed upon "wives," meaning upon enjoyments characterized by wives.
Or, "Is it not of such a kind? || 52 ||
O Rāma, it is said that in that most supreme state dwells the Knower,
in which even the region of the moon and sun remains as if situated in the netherworld.

Even the region of the orbs of the moon and sun, though devoid of light, does not remain as if it were the netherworld (pātāla); how much more so, then, can it be said that [the world] which is luminous does not remain? Alternatively, even the vast space where the moon and sun move, though it is the sky, does not remain as the netherworld—a cavity in the earth—even in its state of being small; such is the case in that great state.
The meaning is: for one who abides in states delimited by a single portion within the belly of space, what craving could there be? || 53 ||
By whose light the world-protectors become clearly visible and well-informed,
they guard their bodies as if seeing [him] before them, though they are deluded in the ocean of worldly existence.
By the light of that Knower of Reality— the radiance of consciousness— the world-protectors, Brahmā and the others, become fully illuminated;

though their light is common to the entire universe, they become excellent perceivers through the eyes and other senses, as well as through the internal intellect, possessing a perfect awareness suited for worldly transaction, even while [the ignorant] remain in the ocean of night, the sea of ignorance.

Even though they see the great [truth], they are deluded; even though they perceive their own self as bodiless after having discriminated it, being deluded, they protect—that is, they guard—the body with the notion that "the body is the self," just like ignorant people.

This is because of the power of the *prārabdha* karma pertaining to their specific office (*adhikārika*), which is accompanied by the deeply ingrained latent impressions (*vāsanā*) for enjoyment. || 54 ||
None of these worldly phenomena can delight one who knows reality, even when they are encountered through habitual practice; they are like clouds to the vast sky of his heart.

But for one who knows reality, whose heart has expanded through the firmness of dispassion and the exhaustion of the latent impressions of enjoyment, and whose internal organ is pure and free from impressions— even these worldly states such as sovereignty over the three worlds, which are enjoyed by the world-protectors, do not [bind him], even when they come before him repeatedly through practice and are cultivated again and again.
The meaning is "they cause delight. || 55 ||
None of these worldly phenomena can delight one who knows reality, just as dancing monkeys cannot please Hara, who seeks the dance of Gaurī.
None of these worldly phenomena can please one who knows reality,
just as a jewel placed inside a jar does not reflect the beauty of its former reflections.
The former beauty of the reflections of pillars, walls, and so forth, which was visible within the jewels during the state of remaining outside the jar. || 57 ||
Beholding it as being like a reflection cast upon a diamond, as insubstantial as a bubble of water, and as fleeting as a towering wave that forms a transient image,
one does not find delight in the pleasures sought by such fickle desires.
One who knows that [truth] is like a royal swan amidst bits of kusha grass and water-moss. || 58 ||
He summarizes the very point already stated in brief: "The Vajra. One who knows that is a knower of reality (*tattvavid*).

The entire splendor of the world, extending as far as the realm of Brahmā, is like a diamond (*vajra*) because it is exceedingly difficult to pierce for one with an ignorant vision. For one with the vision of discernment (*viveka*), however, it is like the play of water within the ripples of a stream.

Having perceived with the vision of reality that which is high and elevated— like the reflection of the moon and other objects cast upon its own surface by a wave— as indescribable, unstable, composed of unreality, and trivial, one does not,
like an ignorant person, develop a longing or restless attachment for the pleasures sought therein.
The meaning is that, in the same way, a royal swan finds no pleasure in the wretched fragments of moss that are the domain of common water-fowl. || 58 ||

Thus ends the fifty-seventh canto, titled "The Description of the Nature of the Fulfilled Will," in the section on Stability within the Means to Liberation, in the glorious Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa composed by Vālmīki, which belongs to the Ṛṣis.
Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Nature of the Perfect Will," in the Section on Stability (*sthitiprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
Fifty-eighth canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O Rāghava, listen to the account of the ancestors who arose concerning this very matter.
The purifying verses sung by Kaca, the son of Bṛhaspati, [were recited]. || 1 ||
Here, for Rāma who has ascended to the full state, Vasiṣṭha teaches the Kaca-gāthā, which awakens the realization of abiding in the universal self.

Regarding this very subject matter mentioned previously, the ancestors—those who lived in former times—[spoke] by means of Bārhaspatya, the son of Bṛhaspati. The suffix *ṇya* is applied here because it follows a word ending in *pati* when referring to the immediate offspring. || 1 ||
Once, while staying in a certain thicket of Mount Meru, the son of the preceptor of the gods attained rest within his own self through the power of practice.
By the power of practice, this refers to the reflection upon the heard knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā), which results from the maturation of meditation (nididhyāsana).
His mind, filled with the nectar of right knowledge,
found no delight in this contemptible, visible world, which consists of the five elements and possesses a fragile nature.
In the word *amānya*, it refers to one who is unworthy of respect. || 3 ||
Despondent as it were because he saw no state other than that of the eternal Self, he spoke these words alone with a faltering voice: || 4 ||

Because he was always delighting in that which is visible [the Self], and seeing no other state or object apart from that eternal oneness— being as if despondent due to the fact that nothing remained but the One— he spoke these following words with a voice faltering with joy. (4)
What shall I do? Where shall I go? What shall I take up? What shall I abandon?
The entire universe is filled by the Self, just as it is by the waters at the end of a great aeon.
What he said, he expresses with the words beginning "What shall I do? and so forth. || 5 ||
Suffering, the self, and happiness—through the vastness of space and hope—I have realized that everything consists of the self; thus, by means of the self, I am one whose afflictions are destroyed.
If it is argued: "Perform those means of happiness that belong to the individual soul (jīvātman); go to where they are obtained;

take up that happiness and its means, and abandon suffering and the means of suffering," to this he replies with the word "suffering" (duḥkham). Suffering is the individual soul who experiences it, and happiness is that which is desired by it.

All this world, beginning with "that which is perceived" (cetyādi), when its root is investigated, is found to be merely the void, the empty sky; it is composed of the self (ātmamaya) because of its extreme greatness compared to the quarters (sadāśābhyo digbhyo) and mental desires (manorathebhyaḥ). The suffix *mayaṭ* is used here in its own sense (svārthe mayaṭ).
Since it is known that "it is indeed the Self," one thinks: "By means of that very Self, whose sole essence is bliss, I am one whose all suffering has perished. Thus [it is not so].
The meaning is that there exists a purpose for relinquishing and acquiring. || 6 ||
Within the body, both externally and internally, below and above, and in all directions—the Self is here and the Self is there; nowhere does anything exist that is not composed of the Self.

The meaning is that within the body— which is accompanied by external afflictions such as fear and the like, as well as internal, spiritual ones, and which serves as the cause for the distinction between the two— and when the directions such as below, above, east, and so forth are perceived in their true nature, the Self alone is everything. And thus says the Śruti:
The Self alone is below, the Self is above, the Self is behind, the Self is in front, the Self is to the south, the Self is to the north; the Self indeed is all this. || 7 ||
For the Self indeed abides everywhere, and everything exists as consisting of the Self;
all this is the Self alone, and thus I exist within the Self alone.
In every case, I abide as the underlying substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) when viewing the imagined transformations that consist of illusory appearances;

yet, upon seeing the reality (*tattva*), everything is of the nature of the Self, and indeed, everything is the Self alone. Thus, from this perspective, the meaning is that I am always, at all times, present within the ultimate Self (*paramārthātman*). || 8 ||
Whatever is indeed called "name," all that is entirely my own inner self;
filling the boundless sky, I abide everywhere as pure existence.

The meaning is: "whatever is known as conscious" and "whatever is known as unconscious"—all that [is He]. "Consisting of Being" (sanmaya) means that because the aspect of Being (sadaṃśa) is all-pervasive, it is the substratum of everything. || 9 ||
"I remain full, my soul rejoicing, like a single ocean of bliss"—
thus he meditated there in that bower of the Golden Mountain.
The explanation of "modātmā" (the self of joy) is "sukham" (happiness), and so forth. || 10 ||
Uttering the syllable *oṃ* in succession like the sound of a bell—
one that is as subtle as a fraction of the *oṃ-kāra*, as delicate as a child's hair—
neither dwelling within nor without, one should contemplate it in the supreme heart.
By what means was this seen by him? To that he says: "while uttering. And so the Śruti says:

"The Praṇava is the bow, the Self is the arrow, and Brahman is said to be its target; it must be pierced with undistracted mind, and like the arrow, one becomes absorbed in That. Since the vowels *a*, *u*, and *m* within the syllable *Oṃ* denote Virāṭ and the other states, [the result is] the Fourth (*turīya*).
He explains by what part that [reality] is seen: "Of the syllable Om.

Having dissolved each preceding element—such as the *mātrās*, Virāṭ, and so forth—along with their respective objects into each subsequent one, like a hair on the head of a child, [one perceives] that which is subtle and tender, observed at the head of the syllable Om.
Meditating upon the western half-measure, known as the mere *kalā*,

which is characterized by the fourth state (*turīya*) that serves as the ultimate limit of the dissolution of all things— and perceiving it through the very nature of the Fourth— one becomes absorbed in that state and does not abide in any internal cause.
And "established in external activity" means situated in the manner that will be described hereafter. || 11 ||
Pure, with the stain of temporal succession removed,
with the fluctuations of the vital breath dissolved within the heart,
he is comparable to the autumnal sky when the clouds have vanished.
Thus stood Kaca, O Rāma, singing. || 12 ||
Demonstrating that very state, he concludes with the words "vyapagata" (dispelled): "vātavṛttiḥ" refers to the movement of the vital breath (prāṇa).
The sense is that this mental activity (*kalanā*) vanishes of its own accord upon cessation. The meaning is that he remains like the autumnal sky, from which the thick clouds have departed.

Thus ends the fifty-eighth canto, titled "The Verses of Kaca," in the Section on Stability (*sthitiprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the Ṛṣis.
Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Song of Kaca," in the Section on Stability (*sthitiprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
Fifty-ninth Sarga:
Apart from food, drink, and the company of women, there is nothing else here.
Saying "May it be auspicious," what indeed would a great man desire? (1)

The worthlessness of sense-objects, the conceptualization of the universe from the Brahma-vow, the Creator’s repose in detachment, and the creation of the scriptures are proclaimed [in this work]. (1)
Having concluded the incidental verse concerning hair, Vasiṣṭha continues with the demonstration that the various kinds of enjoyments are unfit for the desire of one who knows reality;
for the purpose of instructing in dispassion (*vairāgya*), he elaborates upon the worthlessness of sense objects, beginning with the words "food and drink," and so forth. Here:

Having ascertained— so that it may be consistent with what is heard in the scriptures, remembered in the traditional codes, taught by authoritative persons, and confirmed by direct experience— that there is no auspicious goal of human endeavor other than that which exists apart from attachment to the objects characterized by food, drink, and women, which provoke the tongue, the genitals, and other senses within saṃsāra;
The Great One, having ascended to the supreme state, what indeed could he desire among these enjoyments? The meaning is that there is nothing here worthy of his desire. || 1 ||

Those who are like animals, beasts, and fools—those wicked ones who are not satisfied with enjoyments that constitute the entire wealth of the wretched, and which are fragile in their beginning, middle, and end. (2)

Now, as for those who claim that desire (kāma) is indeed a human goal (puruṣārtha) just like liberation (mokṣa), and therefore must be desired by all, he addresses them with the words beginning "the animals" (tiryañca). || 2 ||
Those who place their trust in this world are like human donkeys;
for this body of a woman consists of hair on one side and blood on the other.
By this [offering], dogs find satisfaction, but not human beings;
for bodies, though composed of flesh, are merely made of clay, earth, trees, and wood.
Saramā is the divine dog; those born of her lineage are the *sārameyas*, the dogs. All the earth is merely clay; all trees are merely wood; and all bodies are merely composed of flesh. || 4 ||
The earth is below and the sky is behind; what unprecedented thing is there for the sake of happiness?
Sensations following from contact with objects perish at every step through discernment. (5)

In the back—that is, in the upper part—is the sky itself, the void. What unprecedented essence exists therein that could lead to happiness? This is the meaning. "Mātrās" are the sense organs because they measure (minvanti) objects; they follow after contact with those objects.
In the state, the place, or the reality of discernment (viveka), they are fragile—that is, subject to being sublated. || 5 ||
All worldly perceptions remain entirely untouched by delusion;
even at the ultimate limit of everything, they abide within the hope for happiness.

Untouched [by ultimate reality], worldly understandings—the conventional dealings of people—are delightful only so long as they are not investigated. At the end, for everyone, every hope for happiness—whether through the acquisition or the non-acquisition of objects—is stained; that is, it is defiled by sin, the objects of sense, and the like, and likewise involves suffering induced by separation, despair, and so forth. "Ca" has the sense of "and. Thus [it is].
"It remains just like the end of present happiness"—this is its connection with what follows. (6)
Thus, impurity and suffering are like soot from a flame;
the activities of the six senses, with the mind as the sixth, are impermanent, arising and passing away. (7)

With the intention that the loss of enjoyment necessarily follows either from the exhaustion of the power of the senses or from the exhaustion of the excellence of objects, he says: "Āgama... (verse 7).
Creeper-like women, crushed by the lord of serpents—wealth—do not hold fast;
yet they regard this beloved one with respect, thinking, "She is made of blood and flesh."
Prosperities—the prosperities of the sense objects—though constantly enjoyed, are like creepers trampled by a lordly elephant;

they do not endure, meaning they perish. Not only are they impermanent, but that which is to be enjoyed, such as beloved women and the like, is also impure and of the nature of hell; thus he says, "putrikā" (a doll), referring to a heap of bones.

This doll, made of blood and flesh, is embraced with affection by a man using his own body as its name, under the delusion that "this is my beloved. This, it means, is the method of Māhaka, the god of love. || 8 ||

Through the name of one's own body, the process of delusion clings to the heap of bones— [in some places it is read as "for the sake of its stability," but that is understood to be inconsistent with the context].
O Rāma, all this is true, yet it is for the satisfaction of the ignorant man alone.
For this very reason, he says "all" [in verse 9] to show that enjoyment leads to satisfaction only for the ignorant, not for the wise.
O Rāma, the instability and unreality of the world bring no satisfaction to the wise man;
it is like the sensation of poison even before one has eaten it, which brings on the fainting fit of that very poison.

Instability is indeed nothing but lack of steadiness. This thirst for enjoyment, which exists even when one has not enjoyed—that is, even in the absence of experience—is "poison" (the word *viṣa* meaning that it destroys, like poison);
it brings about a stupor like that of poison. What need is there to mention its effect when enjoyment has actually occurred? || 10 ||
Abandoning that attachment to enjoyments, resort to the state of oneness with your own Self.
When the mind attains stability through the realization that it is not composed of the non-Self,
then this unreal web of the world is seen as unborn.

The meaning is: when the mind has attained stability through the very latent impression of enjoyment—that is, through the identification with the non-self body and so forth as being the self. || 11 ||
By the power of latent impressions, a body is imagined by the mind of Brahmā,
just as the self appears golden when its radiance rests upon a wall.

An objection is raised: "Since the world, consisting of the body and so forth, arises in accordance with the stability of our own mind, how can it be said that it follows the mind of Viriñca, given that it is more appropriate for what is born from Viriñca’s volition to follow his mind alone?

Anticipating this, he says: "Vāsanā... [The world] arises through the mind of Brahmā Viriñca, following precisely that [our own state] due to the power of our latent impressions (*vāsanā*), karma, and so forth.
The meaning is that the body of the world is imagined from volitional construction (saṃkalpa). || 12 ||
Śrī Rāma said: O Brahmin of great intelligence, having attained the state of Vairiñca,
how does the mind gradually bring this world to a state of extreme density?
He provides an illustration for the conceptualization of one thing as having the form of another, stating: "by light" (*tejasā*).

The meaning is that just as by light—such as the radiance of the sun and so forth—which relies upon a wall made of gold, silver, sapphire, and other materials, the respective forms corresponding to those [materials] are conceptually constructed, so it is here. Incidentally, [the author] describes the process of Rāma’s conceptualization of the world from the mind of Viriñci.

He asks: "Vairiñca. Having cast off the former individual identification (*vyaṣṭy-abhimāna*) of the mind of the previous worshiper through the ripening of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the accumulation of the contemplation of the universal self (*samaṣṭy-ātmatā*), and having attained the station of Vairiñca—which is characterized by manifestation as the universal self—he becomes the *kārya-brahman*.
How did this existing world gradually attain its state of solid density and its crowding with the fourfold collection of living beings?
This question concerns the intermediate creation (*avāntarasarga*), since the sequence of the primary creation (*ādyasarga*) has already been explained many times before. || 13 ||
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
Having arisen from his bed in the womb, the first child, the lotus-born, uttered the word "Brahman"; therefore he is called Brahmā.

The "womb" (garbha) refers to the interior of the lotus-bud because it possesses those characteristics; the "web of volitions" (saṃkalpajāla) is the collective totality of the mind whose nature is volition, belonging to that [Brahman] which, by its own mind, has assumed the form of the four-faced [Brahmā]. || 14 ||
Then, for him whose form was a web of volitions and whose shape was fashioned by the mind,
Saṃkalpalakṣmī established her abode in the northern quarter.
Then, immediately after the conceptualization of awakening characterized by rising, he made a firm resolve toward the subsequent creation; thereafter, he first willed forth a light of great splendor,
which, at the end of autumn, formed a circle of creepers that encircled the quarters of space.

Since all worldly transactions depend upon light such as that of the sun, the author, desiring first to describe the creation of the sun, speaks of the creation of the light that pervades the entire sky—which serves as its material cause—and then describes that very light with the words beginning "Then... [tataḥ]. At the end of the autumn season, it was encircled by masses of frost-white creepers, as if by a circle of vines.
By whom the intermediate space of the quarters [was pervaded]. || 16 ||
With its wings sewn together by karma that is exceedingly virtuous and imperishable,
its extremities tawny with masses [of merit], it possesses a garment resembling the golden sky of primordial wisdom.

By whom [the sky] was made like a pair of wings spread out, resembling the wings of a bird on both sides; by means of the work of sewing—the continuous application of threads—it became as if exceedingly virtuous and composed of many threads; that which is imperishable, devoid of the nature of decay, and whose essence is emptiness, namely space (ākāśa).

By him, the quarters of space, extending to their very limits, were turned tawny by the spreading masses of his radiance as it struck the peaks of the Cakravāla mountains at the horizon with their various mineral ores; he was like gold, radiant, unobstructed,
and of a single essence consisting of undivided light, resembling the knowledge of Brahman.
And by which the sky, that is, space, [is pervaded]. || 17 ||
His own abode was dense with a network of golden creepers like lattices, and it was adorned with earrings in the form of shimmering, spreading gardens. 18.

By whom his own abode was made dense with filaments— resplendent like golden creepers fashioned within the lattices of the windows— as rays of light entered the hollows of the petals for their expansion; and which [abode] shone, gleaming through the reflections of the waves of the single vast ocean.
And it was adorned with earrings that took the form of spreading gardens and groves, with the swirling patterns of their rays. || 18 ||
He fashioned that body within that radiant light so that it took on the very form of the Self, shining with its own luminous nature.
Regarding that fire, he describes the entry [of the Self] by means of the conceptualization of another form similar to itself:
"The mind, previously mentioned, fashioned within that fire a luminous, light-filled form identical in shape to the Self, as is well known from the Purāṇas and other sources. (19)
From that splendor, the sun rises,
situated in the midst of a circle of rays, with his blazing golden earrings.
From that mass of radiance, that god, becoming the Sun (Divākara), even today rises visibly, situated in the center of a halo consisting of a web of light;
he whose earrings of gold are blazing. Alternatively, he is situated in the center of the circle of women characterized by the network of the quarters, common to all, and shining.
The meaning is that he is shining, having become a golden earring. || 20 ||
Bearing a mass of blazing matted hair with flames flickering at its edges,
his limbs were vast with tongues of fire, filling the entire circle of the sky.
Whose blazing mass of matted hair bears flames, and whose edges are spread wide with fires that hold the fire itself.
Then the highly intelligent Brahmā, having protected those other portions of his splendor, cast them aside like the ocean casts its waves.
Immediately following that, he describes the creation of the Prajāpatis, beginning with Marīci, starting with the word "atha.

Brahmā—the creator of the universe, the one of great intellect, the omniscient one, or the self consisting of the universal intellect—is the four-faced one. And those other portions of light remaining after the fashioning of Āditya were set aside (apālya), having been excluded.
That is to say, having divided [it] into nine parts and cast it forth as non-existent,

those fragments of fire— by the mere power of his volition, having attained all perfections and possessing powers equal to his own— became Prajāpatis; and seeing the object exactly as he had willed it appear before them in an instant, they attained [their goal].

The connection with the subsequent verse is "they attained. [The form] *apālāḥ* is derived from the root *al-* preceded by *apa-*—which signifies ornamenting, sufficiency, capability, warding off, or prohibition—followed by the suffix *lyap*. [The form] *asrāk* is derived from the root *asu* (meaning "to cast") with the suffix *aṅ* according to the rule *ūdito vā*; the absence of *āṭ* and *thuk* is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*). || 22 ||
They too, having attained their perfections through mere volition and possessing equal powers,
beheld the object exactly as they had intended it appear before them in an instant.
Forming various intentions, they created many diverse hosts of beings—
some among other beings, others among those, and yet others of various kinds.
He states that from them proceeds the evolution of the creation of gods, dānavas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, humans, and so forth, in the words:

"They willed" (saṃkalpayantaḥ). Those Prajāpatis [willed] those many hosts of beings—diverse in kind through the various species such as gods and dānavas, and diverse in individual manifestation through the succession of sons and grandsons.

Forming various intentions, they became those very waters; this is what follows. He shows the commencement of the creation through sexual union among those beings in the verse beginning with "bhūteṣu" (among the beings). || 24 ||
Having recollected the Vedas and subsequently the many qualities of the sacrificial rites,
Brahmā established the boundaries for the world, the house, and other domains.
The phrase "conceiving [the waters]" (saṃkalpayanta āpaḥ) also carries over here. Thereafter, he shows the engagement in sacrificial activity:
"Assuming a Brahman-form, the great body named Mind spreads out this vision, which is crowded with the succession of beings. (26)
[She is] rich with oceans, mountains, and trees, having performed a world-transcending course;
her circular interior is a thicket of matted locks consisting of Mount Meru, the surface of the earth, and the forest groves of the cardinal directions. || 27 ||
[She is] characterized by pleasure, pain, old age, birth, and death;
agitated by passion and hatred; and composed of the three qualities (guṇas). || 28 ||

She was taught that this cycle of existence (saṃsāra) is to be abandoned in every way, due to its physical states— happiness, suffering, old age, birth, and death— as well as its own mental afflictions.
Whatever was fashioned of old by the hands of Manu arising from Viriñca, all that is seen even today through Māyā exactly as it was ordained.

Now, if all worldly activity (*vyavahāra*) is encompassed by the mental fluctuations (*manovṛtti*) of Viriñci, what is the reason for the established distinction that sacrifices and the like are bodily while meditations and the like are mental?
He states that [reason]: "by the hands of the mind" (*manohastaiḥ*). Whatever object is to be seen in whatever manner by means of the hands—which are the mental fluctuations—arising from Viriñci...

And that which is fit to be attained, having been determined in a prior kalpa, is seen to remain exactly so even today and is indeed attained; the meaning is that the determination of the conceptualizations of others also follows precisely according to that [prior] determination. || 29 ||
Thus, whether among all beings or only some of them, he conceives of saṃsāra; yet he perceives that which is situated as the supreme consciousness.

Whether from the perspective of the universal whole (*samaṣṭi*) existing in all beings, or from the perspective of the individual (*vyaṣṭi*) or the doctrine of a single soul (*ekajīva*) existing in some, it is the mind that wills while consciousness (*cit*) perceives; or rather, it is the mind itself, abiding within consciousness, that wills and perceives the Supreme. || 30 ||
Delusion itself, consisting of this [world], has falsely attained stability in the world;
it was fashioned by its own volition through the mind, and thus came into being in an instant.
Thus, in the manner described, it was resolved very quickly, that is, immediately. || 31 ||
By the power of volition, all the activities of the world arise;
by the power of volition, the gods emerge, established in their fixed order.
O Lord of Creatures, this powerful Brahmā, born from the lineage of the Creator of the World, sits upon his lotus-throne and reflects deeply while you are enraged.

Having thus elaborated upon the expansion of creation, he establishes the introductory framework (*pīṭhikā*) to state the reason for its cessation and the composition of the scripture, beginning with the words "of her who was provoked to anger. This refers to [the Goddess] being incited by Indra, Virocana, and other lords of gods and asuras for their respective superiority, and for the increase of dharma and adharma among the human and other species.

He is "Kulodbhava" (the source of lineages) because all families of beings arise from him; he is despondent toward the creation of the world, which is provoked and excessively tormented by thousands of afflictions such as death, bondage, birth, old age, and disease, due to its being forcibly impelled by those striving within the modes of sattva, rajas, and tamas.
The meaning is that this aforementioned Brahmā contemplates in the manner that will be described hereafter. || 33 ||

Through the mere vibration of the mind, the wondrous consciousness arises—whether as creation, as the enjoyer, as the expansive, or as that which undergoes transformation through worldly activity. (34)

By the mere vibration of the mind, that which has become the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the individual soul (*jīva*), for the sake of its experience, arises as the expansive and vast creation of worlds and so forth; the connection with the subsequent clause is: "All this is merely the net of my own volitions, spread out immeasurably by me. (34)
It is filled with Rudra, Upendra, Mahendra, and others— [the reading "mahendrāḍhyā" is also found]— and crowded with mountains and oceans;
its hollows are the constricted pathways to Pātāla, the earth, the quarters, and heaven.
This entire web of mental constructs has been spread out by me on all sides;
now I have desisted from this process of the proliferation of conceptual fluctuations.
Having thus resolved, he desists from the perilous web of conceptual constructions and,
by means of the self, remembers the self as the beginningless, supreme Brahman.
"Virata" means having attained tranquility. || 37 ||
Having attained that state which shines with its own luster, the tranquil-minded one, with a mind dissolved [in it], dwells in bliss like a weary man resting upon a couch. (38)

The meaning is that, having approached—that is, attained—that Supreme Self merely by means of mindfulness, one dwells happily in that very state, which shines forth on all sides; such is the state where the mind has dissolved, characterized as the seventh stage (bhūmikā), specifically upon a prepared couch in a lower, enclosed chamber—in other words, in a secret place. || 38 ||
Free from the sense of "mine" and free from egoism, having attained supreme peace, he remains within himself by means of the self, like an undisturbed ocean. (39)
Sometimes the Lord himself desists from meditation,
just as the ocean ceases from the flow of its waters due to its inherent tranquility.
From meditation (dhyāna), which is characterized by the persistent application of one-pointed mental activity (ekākāravṛtti) through the binding [of the mind]. || 40 ||
He contemplates saṃsāra, which is endowed with pleasure and pain, bound by hundreds of snares of hope, and afflicted by passion, hatred, and fear. (41)
Then, his mind overcome with compassion for the sake of the manifestation of reality, he composes here various treatises of great significance.
The Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, which contain the womb of inner knowledge, as well as the Purāṇas and other texts, lead to the liberation of all embodied beings. (43)
Again, having taken hold of that very same state, he emerges from the supreme calamity;
with a tranquil soul, he remains established in his own nature, like the ocean when Mount Mandara has ceased its churning.
That aforementioned supreme state, characterized by the seventh stage,
has emerged from the calamities characterized by the distractions of emanation.
Having observed the activities of the world and having established the boundaries of conduct,
Brahmā, seated upon his lotus throne, abides once more within his own self.
Sometimes, being free from all conceptual constructions,
he remains as if following the course of the world, acting by chance for the sake of bestowing grace.
The meaning is that it is solely for the purpose of bestowing grace. || 46 ||
In this [reality], there is neither rectitude nor renunciation, neither the body nor its grasping;
there is neither diversity nor consciousness, neither stability nor instability established here.
In that case, during his state of meditative absorption (samādhi), there is straightforwardness; but at the time of creation, dissolution, and so forth, there is renunciation,

the grasping of a body and the like, multiplicity in the form of creation, consciousness during the period of emergence (vyutthāna), abiding in the lotus [of the heart] and non-abiding elsewhere— thus, amidst these undertakings of various states and fluctuations of the mind, he is just like one who lacks knowledge (ajña).
Anticipating the objection that an inconsistency has arisen, he refutes it in due order, beginning with the words "not straightforwardness" (nārjavam) and so forth. || 47 ||
The undertaking of all states of being is equal in all modes of conduct;
like the form of a full ocean, it remains free from any remainder. 48.
Sometimes, being entirely devoid of all conceptual constructions, he awakens by chance for the sake of bestowing grace upon the worlds. (49)
O Mahāmati, this meritorious state of Brahmā which I have described is that same sattvic state which the hosts of gods and asuras have attained. (50)
He summarizes: "This... Now follows the mental creation of the Prajāpatis;

for they possess accomplishments attained through mere volition (*saṃkalpa*), and their knowledge, yoga, and sovereignty are self-evident. This is the first class of creators. Even in the case of sexual reproduction, there are gods, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and so forth.

Having kept in mind the division of the three armies— wherein the celestial army (*surānīka*) is middling because, being characterized by *sattva*, it possesses knowledge and sovereignty attained through a single instruction;
whereas the human army (*narānīka*) is inferior because, being overwhelmed by *rajas* and *tamas*, its knowledge and sovereignty must be achieved through thousands of efforts— for those [beings]:

He demonstrates the attainment of Brahman by distinguishing it through the arising of knowledge corresponding to the purity of mind acquired from its own causes, beginning with the words "yātām" and so forth: "May even the two armies of the gods attain— that is, reach— this aforementioned state of being (brāhmī sthiti), which is characterized by goodness (sāttvikī) and is to be reached through the excellence of sattva."
In the space where the creation of consciousness has ceased, that which arises as the first fruit of Brahman’s mind— that alone attains the state of Brahmanhood.

In that regard, because the first army (*anīka*) is the fruit of mental worship (*mānasopāsanā*), it is subtle by virtue of being produced by the mind alone; therefore, he states the distinction regarding its attainment: "In the *citsarga*," etc.
Since the first army exists within the *cidrūpa* (the form of consciousness), which is the cessation of all creation and the universal space of Brahman (*sarvabrahmākāśa*), [it resides] in Brahman...
The *manasphala* (the fruit of the mind) first arises as if it were a fruit imagined by the mind of Viriñca; therefore, she alone is that [Viriñca] and he alone is she.

There is the elision of the *su* suffix according to the rule *soci lope cet pādapūraṇam*. The meaning is that she is first correctly understood and heard through self-established knowledge and sovereignty. || 51 ||
But when the state of persistence has occurred during the creation, another conceptualization arises;
that, having resorted to space and wind, enters into medicinal herbs and sprouts. (52)

He demonstrates the distinction— namely, that the attainment of Brahman occurs by depending merely on instruction because [the second army] is a grosser transformation than the ordinary, being the fruit of rites accomplished with herbs, sprouts, soma, clarified butter, and milk— as follows, beginning with the words "In the creation," etc.

When the creation and maintenance of the Prajāpatis and the herbs and other beings has been accomplished, another secondary manifestation (*kalpanā*)— inferior to the first— arises in the form of the host of gods (*surānīka*). This [manifestation], first taking the form of the lunar digits (*candrakalā*),
resorts to the ether and wind, enters the sprouts of the herbs, and exists in the fire in the form of Soma, clarified butter, and milk.

The connection with the subsequent [verse] is as follows: being offered into the solar orb, it transforms into the form of nectar; consumed by Prajāpati and others, it transforms into the form of their semen and, through the gateway of sexual union, attains the state of being Indra and other gods, as well as birth in the divine species of Kubera and other Yakṣas. || 52 ||
One attains the state of a god, another attains the state of a yakṣa;
first she arises as this very [power], and then she fully partakes in the state of Brahman. (53)

Because of its sattvic nature, this very [state] first arises among the Prajāpatis through their favor, instruction, and so forth, as well as their abundance of knowledge and sovereignty—compared to humans and others. Therefore, the meaning is that it attains the state of Brahman at the very outset. || 53 ||
Whatever being a particular entity is associated with, that very entity quickly arises for it. Once born, by virtue of association with that very same birth,
it is either bound or liberated through its own subsequent engagement.

If so, is there no liberation for all the gods? He says "yet": among gods or humans, whatever individual being—whether endowed with knowledge and dispassion or greedy for enjoyment—is accompanied by friendliness and other virtues, that being quickly becomes like that through such association; the meaning is that it comes to possess those very qualities.
The meaning is that by the power of association with those greedy for enjoyments, one becomes likewise and is bound;

whereas through association with the opposite, one becomes endowed with knowledge and dispassion oneself and is liberated. If that is so, what is the purpose of the third group? To this he says: "oneself... Therefore, regarding bondage and liberation...

Because it conforms to one's attachments, one should personally, through human effort, undertake the means for conquering the senses and the mind—such as the company of the virtuous and the hearing of sacred scriptures—and practice them until the fruit arises; this is the meaning. || 54 ||
O Rāmabhadra, such indeed is the nature of this creation, acquired through clearly manifest and perilous karma;
it shall emerge as the burden of various swift movements and activities.
She is held within the state of conceptualization, which contains the essence of agitation.

He summarizes everything that has been said in brief with the word "ittham" (thus): by means of those various causes obtained in succession—namely, *sphuṭāni* (clear) practices consisting largely of illumination; *prakaṭāni* (manifest) rites such as sacrifices well-known to all people; and *saṃkaṭāni* (perilous) actions mixed with prohibited ones which result in misfortune.
Held and obstructed by the momentum of past actions (*prārabdha*), by the weight of worldly distractions, by playful curiosities filled with agitation,

and by activities fueled by anger and greed— while Brahman remains poised toward creation at the stage of manifestation— it has thus proceeded solely through the aforementioned construction of mental volition (*saṃkalpa*).
The meaning is that this creation, consisting of the three armies, manifests in such a way that it has attained its established existence (*sattā*). || 55 ||
Thus ends the fifty-ninth sarga, titled "Description of the Conduct of the Lotus-Born," in the Section on Stability (Sthitiprakaraṇa) of the Holy Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa composed by Vālmīki.
Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Conduct of the Lotus-born," in the *Sthitiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
The Sixtieth Chapter.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
O Brahman, when this Blessed One had taken up his fickle station, [the world was transformed].
O mighty-armed one, when the Grandfather had established the order of creation. || 1 ||

The process by which living beings, having arisen from Brahman, take on bodies here [in this world]—specifically that of those characterized by sattva and possessing enlightenment—is now described. (1)

She prepares the introductory stage (*bhūmikā*) to describe in detail the previously mentioned creation of the three armies (*tryanīka*), by expanding upon the sequence stated in brief, beginning with the words "In this," and so forth. [The word] "Brahman" refers to Brahmā, the Grandfather (*pitāmaha*). The locative case ending is elided according to the rule *supāṃ suluk* (Pāṇini 7.1.39).
By the rule *ṅisaṃbuddhyoḥ*, there is a prohibition against the elision of the nasal (*n*). A "fickle state" refers to emerging from meditative absorption (*samādhi*). || 1 ||
In this world, which is like a dilapidated water-wheel, life flows by its own mechanism,
using as its rope the thirst for existence and the buckets consisting of the bodies of living beings.
In the water-wheel (*āraghaṭṭa*) of worldly existence, by means of the rope-string of the *ghaṭī*—

which is characterized by a continuous succession (*samūha-lakṣaṇā*) of transmigrated beings (*vipreta-bhūta*) who are like jars (*ghaṭā*), or rather, where the transmigrated beings themselves are the jars— there is "life," which consists of both the grasping of a body again and the water [of existence], driven by the thirst for its objects.
It carries [the breath] as it revolves through ascending and descending movements. || 2 ||
And while the beings, having arisen from Brahman, were entering the cage of worldly existence—
whirling within the eddies that revolve in the midst of the space of the Lord and the individual soul.

While other minds were revolving—that is, tending toward wandering—within the midst of that ether which is the first-born son of the Lord, who is Brahman variegated by Māyā, [the Lord remained unmoved]. || 3 ||
In other minds, like grains of dust tossed by the wind at the edge of a forest, some depart incessantly while others enter from all sides in the same manner. (4)

O Rāma, some multitudes of living beings emerge incessantly and perpetually from Brahman—due to the departure of their limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)—like sparks from a fire; while others enter it for the sake of rest, like those who fall asleep upon the dissolution of their adjuncts. This is the meaning. || 4 ||
O Rāma, the multitudes of living beings are like waves in the ocean within Brahman;
born from the state that is without beginning or end, they have fallen into the condition of conceptualization.
The explanation of the term "arisen" is that they have reached the state of conceptual construction. || 5 ||
These multitudes of individual souls enter the elemental ether, like a mass of smoke entering a cloud; they attain oneness with Brahman through the spaces and winds.

Therein, he first elaborates upon the sequence of the emergence of the third army, which was not mentioned in the previous creation, beginning with the words "the elemental ether" (bhūtākāśam). Together with the ether and wind superimposed upon Brahman, they attain oneness like milk and water. || 6 ||
Just as the gods are assailed by a fierce host of demons, so too [the senses] are overcome by that wind alone, through its nature as the vital breath (prāṇa). || 7 ||
Then, once the emergence of fire, water, and earth has occurred,

they are pervaded by the previously mentioned air— now accompanied by the subtle elements (tanmātra) characterized as sound, touch, form, taste, and smell— and likewise by the nature of the two types of vital breaths (prāṇa), both primary and secondary, which serve as the instruments for their experience.
They are brought under control. || 7 ||
By means of that wind which carries the elements and vital breaths, and by that bearer of fragrance,
living beings enter into bodies and attain vitality.

Thus, having attained the state of the subtle body (liṅgadeha), they enter into bodies by means of that vital breath (prāṇa), that carrier of fragrance (gandhavāha)— the wind accompanied by the subtle elements (tanmātra) of the elements— and through the medium of food, water, and so forth; they reach the vital air of the fourfold classes of beings, which consumes the morsels of food, and enter [the bodies] via the specific function of the downward breath (apāna).
In the word *nerviśaḥ*, the absence of the suffix *taṅ* (the middle voice) is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*). "Let it enter" means let it become semen (*retas*). || 8 ||
From that, O Rāma, living beings are born in the world and become unmanifest; there is another succession of souls produced from smoke and the other [stages].

"Unmanifest" means that their knowledge and sovereign powers (*jñāna-aiśvarya*) have not been fully revealed. Having described the sequence of creation for the third group, he states it for the second group with the words "others. For this group as well, the sequence up until the attainment of the subtle body (*liṅgadeha*) is exactly as previously described; they are offered into the fire through the transformation of milk, clarified butter, and so forth, by entering into herbs and trees.
The oblation, having reached the solar orb by way of smoke, either enters the moon by means of the sun's rays or—

according to the principle of the "substratum" (adhikaraṇa)— the life-breaths of the sacrificer enveloped by the waters of the oblation enter the lunar orb via the path beginning with smoke; thus, it has come to the path of smoke and so forth.
They have entered. || 9 ||
In the hollow of the sky, which is filled with those very subtle elements and not yet empty,
the Blessed Moon rises with its full, radiant orb.

She too, having attained the nature of a digit of the moon (*candrakalā*), enters into the fruits of the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*) by way of their essence; then, through the transformation of the vital potency (*vīrya*) of those who consume them, she is born as a divine embryo (*devagarbha*).
With this sequence in mind, he says: "possessing the subtle elements" (*tanmātravatī*), and so forth.
In that which possesses the subtle body (*liṅgadeha*) consisting of the *tanmātras* as previously described, the Lord Moon— possessing a vast orb and full— rises,
illuminating the world with his rays; for as many as those rays he rises with,
so many flickering, pale-colored rays fill [the space], making it non-empty and full, and thus serving as the receptacle within the ocean of milk.
Or rather, she remains within the hollow of the garment acting as her representative; this is the remainder of the sense. || 10 ||
The world was then flooded by those exceedingly beautiful moonbeams, which fell like the shimmering, pale rays from the ocean of milk.
Thereafter, as those moonbeams were flying toward the Nandana and other groves—
here the *sup* case-ending is elided by Vedic license (*chāndasa*)— the female servant (a maidservant) flying along with the rays entered that grove;
like one eager and busy with domestic duties within the inner apartments, she, being mostly composed of birds, made her entrance.
The remainder. || 11 ||
The restless female bird makes [the fruits] in the forest as if she were a servant among others;
yet even from those, they attain fullness by their own inherent nature alone.

Then, in that forest, the fruits— by their very own nature— gradually attain fullness, growth, and even sweetness, caused by those moonbeams and, as implied by the word "also" (api), by the sunbeams as well.
Struck by the rays of the moon, the row of living beings (jīvālī) sets foot upon those fruits,
as if upon the mother’s breasts filled with milk.
In this manner, the previously mentioned series of living beings (jīvālī), when diminished by the rays of the moon and divided among those [planetary] results which are full of essence (rasa),
establishes its position— that is, it takes its place— just as a child places its feet upon the fullness of its mother’s breasts.
Those circles of fruits will ripen by the rays [of the sun];
having attained potency within those very [seeds], they remain there until awakening is reached. (14)

By the rays—that is, the sunbeams—when those very fruits had been consumed by Kaśyapa and others, their potency (vīrya) reached its peak; yet they remained unawakened, as if in a state of swoon. || 14 ||
The glory of the seed presides over the cage of the womb, which contains the living force of the network of dormant latent impressions (vāsanā),
just as a banyan tree with its leaves still folded rests upon its seed.
He provides an illustration for those whose life-force is dormant yet who remain within the womb of awakened parents:

"The glory of the seed," and so forth. Just as the glory of the *vaṭa* seed—whose leaves are dormant and whose sprouts, branches, and foliage have not yet appeared—remains presiding over the *vaṭa* tree once its branches, sprouts, leaves, and fruit have manifested.
The meaning is "in that same way. || 15 ||
Just as fire resides within wood and as pots reside within clay,
so too [all things] have come forth from Maheśvara through the application of various successive stages.
It is not only in the case of those who have fainted that the state of being hidden occurs by depending on another;

rather, it also occurs when, at the time of dissolution, one has departed from the Unmanifest (avyakta) attained through the dissolution of limiting adjuncts (upādhi) in the presence of Maheśvara, and having emerged [from it], exists in the state of ether and so forth, at the time of the commencement of the subtle body (liṅga), and at the time of entering the rays of the moon and other such phenomena.
The meaning is that, just as there is activity through the application of various successive stages, so too is there stability. || 16 ||
He who does not boast and whose excellence of body is unseen by others—he indeed would be of noble birth and possessed of magnanimous conduct. (17)

Thus, he demonstrates the distinction for those who have entered the womb based on the difference in their causes for birth, beginning with the words "adṛṣṭa" and so forth: one who, having not seen the splendor of another's body—such as that of a woman or a son—in a previous birth, remains thus detached from everything and passes through the time until death; and [the other] who...

Though urged toward worldly and Vedic actions— which are the means for attaining enjoyments in this life and the next— by numerous passions such as attachment and by various scriptures such as the ritual sections (Karmakāṇḍa),
he neither impels himself nor engages in them; for he is indeed a steadfast man, the foremost among men.

The meaning is that one who is born from the womb of a deity according to the previously mentioned sequence, being of an extremely pure (sāttvika) nature, shall attain knowledge therein and become possessed of the noble conduct appropriate for one liberated while living (jīvanmukta). || 17 ||
If one becomes a partaker of liberation through that very birth, then that is *sāttvika*;
but if, having attained this womb, one undergoes a succession of births, [that is *tāmasa*]. (18)
Regarding those who perform the practice of ritual service (*upāsanā*) as a means to attain the office of a deity, he says: "Now" (*atha*).

Having reached this "divine womb" (*devayoni*), even though one is capable of cutting through the succession of births—which are like a magical spell (*kṛtyā*)—if one does not cut them due to a craving for enjoyment, and is thus born again solely for the sake of protecting the enjoyment of one's own office; if that is the case...
"Endowed with darkness" (tamoyukta) means characterized by both passion and goodness (rājasasāttvika). || 18 ||
O Rāma, I shall now describe how a person, having attained birth for the sake of protection, may be characterized by the qualities of tamas, rajas, or sattva through their subsequent birth.
Now, he describes the purely *sāttvika* nature and the state of non-rebirth for those born in the first army:

"By the last," etc. By means of his final birth, which—relative to the armies of men and gods—is preeminent due to its status as a *prājāpatya* office, one who has entered the cycle of existence as a purely *sāttvika* member of Vidhi’s army is liberated.
The syntactical connection is: "I shall speak thus. || 19 ||
Primarily, as for how one has come into this cycle of existence, that is the *sāttvika* type;
such a person, O sinless one, never at any time becomes anything other than what they are. (20)
That first-born person never arises again at any time; the meaning is that he is indeed liberated. || 20 ||
O Rāma, men of both rajasic and sāttvika natures arise here in this world;
having investigated them thoroughly, one should reflect upon them with an intelligent mind.

He states who, then, are those who are possible [to attain liberation]—namely, "those who are possible. He states what the reason is for the absence of rebirth for one who possesses pure *sattva* alone: "having investigated," etc. Because they, even in a previous birth, having investigated the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*) by means of hearing and other methods, [performed] that which is appropriate for the destruction of mere obstacles.

Having attained a birth characterized by *sattva*, even in this present life, the reality of the Self alone must always be contemplated by their intellect and cultivated through reflection; such is the meaning. || 21 ||
O Rāma, those men who have emerged preeminently from the Supreme Self are endowed with great qualities and are difficult to find.
For this very reason, he says that they are difficult to obtain: "by way of predominance. || 22 ||
And as for those others who are various kinds of fools, mute, and of a tamasic nature—those who are equal to immobile beings—what indeed, O Rāma, can be deliberated regarding them? (23)

As for those others—besides the hosts of gods and men—who are Rākṣasas, Piśācas, and so forth, as well as animals, since they are equal to stationary objects (plants and minerals), they lack even the fitness to be considered in the discussion regarding the qualification for knowledge; thus he says, "And those others," [to indicate] that they are mentioned for that reason. || 23 ||
A few humans and gods have not yet reached the contemplation of existence (*bhavabhāvanā*) within this natural cycle of birth;
like me, they lack the fitness for profound investigation.
Is not one who has attained humanity indeed both rajasic and sattvic? || 24 ||

Demonstrating the very rarity of the truth, he concludes with the words "only a few": although an excellent birth has been attained through the sequential process described, only a few men and gods have not fallen into *bhavabhāvanā*—that is, a craving for worldly enjoyments. Thus, the meaning is that dispassion (*vairāgya*) itself is exceedingly difficult to find.

What need is there for much? The word *nanu* is used here in the sense of "even. Among them, although I too—like them—had attained from birth onwards a preeminent fitness for self-investigation through the perfection of all virtues such as tranquility (*śama*) and self-restraint (*dama*), I was nonetheless [prevented] by the force of *prārabdha-karma*, which had brought about my appointment to the office of domestic priest (*purohita*) at the royal court—an obstacle to the bliss of uninterrupted meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

The term "non-sāttvika" refers to one who is merely sāttvika with a slight admixture of rajas, rather than being purely sāttvika; this is a hyperbolic expression (atiśayokti) used to highlight extreme rarity, arising from the absence of pride. || 24 ||
Since you remain thus for so long without investigating the Great State, you should investigate it directly this very day; here there is no duality.

Just as it is for me, so too for you there is indeed the full perfection of detachment, tranquility, self-restraint, and the like; however, because you remain in a state of non-investigation—failing to investigate the supreme state of the Great Self—this aforementioned delusion of saṃsāra has become long-lasting and extensive. Therefore, that very state, right here before me, this very day, may be attained directly and swiftly.

Reflect! By the mere act of reflecting, you yourself here become directly manifest; the meaning is that you are that supreme state which is neither duality nor non-duality. Or, it may be construed as: "The great calamity that was coming upon you has arrived" (*āyatā* or *āyātā*). || 25 ||

Thus ends the sixtieth chapter, titled "The Descent of the Living Being through Instruction on the Determination of the Person of Contemplation," in the *Vasiṣṭha-mahārāmāyaṇa* composed by Vālmīki, within the section on the Inquiry into the State [of Liberation].

Thus ends the sixtieth chapter, titled "The Descent of the Living Being through Instruction on the Occasion of Determining the Person of Inquiry," in the *Sthitiprakaraṇa* of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa Tātparyaprakāśa*.
The sixty-first canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
"Those who are born on earth with great qualities through the *rājasa-sāttvika* [nature],"
They were eternally joyful and radiant, like moons in their own right.
People who are rajasic-sattvic are praised as being fit for liberation;
their gradual process of discernment and dispassion is taught here.

Those persons who have attained the fitness for discernment were born on earth through their past karma and spiritual practice characterized by the qualities of passion (rājasika) and goodness (sāttvika). || 1 ||
They do not succumb to weariness, just as a portion of the sky does not become soiled;
they do not wither through misfortune, just as a golden lotus does not close at night.
Mental exhaustion is mental suffering; dejection is physical suffering. || 2 ||
