They do not desire anything other than their own nature, nor do they stand as anything else, just like stationary objects; they delight in their own proper conduct, just as trees delight in their own purposes.

Just as an immobile entity such as a tree does not strive for anything other than the enjoyment of its *prārabdha* (past karma), so too those established in knowledge and the means thereto do not strive for anything other than their own purposes— the causes consisting of their own flowers, fruits, and so forth. || 3 ||

O Rāma, just as the moon-like beautiful woman reaches a state of being eternally filled with nectar when she possesses the qualities of passion (rājasa) and goodness (sāttvika), so too does she attain liberation.

The intellect of the person described as being of rajasic temperament, when nourished by the nectar of tranquility and other virtues, reaches a state of fullness and further growth; for this very reason, it becomes beautiful like the moon in the bright fortnight. (4)
Even in adversity they do not abandon [their nature], remaining cool like the moon;
by their very nature, they shine with the beauty of virtues such as loving-kindness.
Like the moon, they do not abandon their gentleness, which remains as constant as coolness.
Like forest trees with creepers that will soon bear new clusters of blossoms,
truly virtuous people are always even-minded, equanimous, and gentle.

The connection with the preceding verse is as follows: [he was] "constantly embraced by Guṇakāntā," who, like a creeper, possessed clusters of blossoms resembling her breasts and was full of love for him; those who are virtuous even toward the virtuous. || 6 ||
Those who maintain their boundaries like the ocean become equal to you;
therefore, O mighty-armed one, their station is free from the taint of calamity.

Since they are endowed with such qualities, that state which is the non-abiding and non-contentious cessation of those calamities—that very state must be reached; and thus, in this world, one should move about with an undaunted mind—this is the connection with what follows.
That state must be constantly sought, it must be reached, not within the ocean of calamity.
In this world, one should conduct oneself in such a manner as to remain free from weariness.
And one's own spiritual advancements flourish,
becoming free from passion and characterized by purity of mind, as one repeatedly reflects upon the true scripture through its inconceivable course.

The meaning is as follows: just as those who are sattvic—free from passion (arājasā), endowed with the destruction of passion (rajaḥkṣayopetāḥ), characterized by the awakening of the Self (ātmodayāḥ), and having attained their own bliss (svānandalābhāḥ)—thrive, so too, through an inconceivable process (acintyagatyā), by abandoning the pursuit of objects fit for the thoughts of the deluded, one must repeatedly investigate the true scripture (sacchāstra). || 9 ||

One should quickly contemplate with one's own mind the various forms of impermanence, as well as that activity which exists throughout the three worlds and persists constantly from beginning to end. (10)

Thus, by means of such devotion and extreme earnestness, even the impermanence of all things— which is established through various and manifold signs— becomes quickly investigated and is thereby transformed [into realization]. Having instructed Rāma on his virtuous qualities for so long by way of noble praise, he now instructs him directly, beginning with the words "In the beginning," and so forth.

Thus reflecting on impermanence, the wise one of purified intellect considers both worldly activity— which is employed for enjoyment in this life— and transworldly activity— which is employed after death in the next life— as well as all things existing within the three worlds that constitute the fruits of such activity, namely cattle, children, wealth, celestial chariots, apsarases, and so forth.
One should contemplate that adversity itself is this prosperity; the connection with the subsequent [verse] is that one should not contemplate anything else as being prosperity. || 10 ||
The wise man should quickly contemplate the categories of reality and nothing else;
having abandoned improper views, he should cast off the useless succession of ignorance. (11)
This infinite knowledge of reality must indeed be rightly contemplated:
"Who am I? How has this grand spectacle of saṃsāra arisen, O All-pervading Lord? (12)

This knowledge, consisting of inquiry in the manner about to be described, is for the purpose of attaining infinite reality—this is the ellipsis. Having been propitiated by means of service and other efforts through diligent practice together with virtuous fellow-students who have approached him according to rule, the wise Guru [should be addressed] by one who asks with humility, beginning with the words, "O Lord, who am I? and so forth.
The connection is that one should reflect [on this] before it is to be remembered. || 12 ||
Having investigated with effort together with wise and virtuous men,
one should not plunge headlong into actions, nor should one dwell with that which is harmful.
He declares the renunciation of action as an auxiliary to hearing with the words "And not... (na ca). "Maṅktavyam" means that which is to be immersed (*majjanīyam*).
The suffix *tavya* is applied to the root *masj* in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*), according to the rule *masjinaśor jhali*. || 13 ||
One should always observe the total cessation of everything that follows the cycle of existence;
one should follow only what is wholesome, just as a peacock follows a rain cloud. 14.
It should be understood that the separation from everything dear is inevitable. || 14 ||
Having adorned oneself with self-inquiry regarding the ego, the body, and this raftless cycle of existence, one should behold reality alone. (15)

Having made one's own inquiry—which serves as a boat—sufficient for reaching the culmination of full realization, [one crosses] the three oceans of worldly existence: first the internal ego, then the external body, and further beyond that, the cycle of worldly life consisting of sons, friends, and so forth, which is like a vast ocean. || 15 ||
Having completely abandoned the body, though it be unstable and possessed of great splendor— like a thread from which a string of pearls has been removed— one should behold pure consciousness alone.
Regarding what was stated—that one should perceive only the Truth—he states the means for doing so: "The body," etc.

By the use of the word "api" (also), it is implied that one should also completely abandon the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*). The use of the suffix *-lyap* is Vedic. "Ghana-śobhanam" means exceedingly beautiful. "Vītā-muktāvalī" refers to that by which a string of pearls is pervaded or spread.
Due to its Vedic character (*chāndasatva*), there is no shortening of the subordinate member (*upasarjana*). In the reading *bhūta*, the meaning is clear.
The sense is that it is the internal pure consciousness (*sākṣicinmātra*) common to the ego-sense of all bodies, like the thread contained within them. || 16 ||
In that state, which is eternally extended, all-pervading, and permeated by all things—
within that auspicious one, this entire universe is strung together like clusters of gems upon a thread.
He demonstrates the similarity of the illustration with the words "In that," and so forth. || 17 ||
That very same consciousness which exists in the sun, the ornament of the sky that encompasses all worlds,
exists likewise within the belly of an insect dwelling in a hollow of the earth.
Just as there is no difference between jars and space in the ultimate sense here, O sinless one, so too there is no difference among those situated in bodies within consciousness. 19.

He dispels the suspicion of a difference within consciousness with the verse beginning "kumbha": [it refers] to the individual souls residing in bodies; "in consciousness" means in the absolute Consciousness (citau). || 19 ||
For all beings who experience bitter, pungent, and other such tastes,
there is indeed only a slight difference from one another due to the unity of experience. (20)

Just as there is no difference in experience despite the variety of tastes such as bitter and pungent belonging to a single person, so it is even with respect to the differences of bodies and so forth; with this intention, he says: "Of all... (verse 20).
While the reality that is pure existence alone remains eternally established, your intellect here [in this world] conceives: "This has arisen," and "This has perished. (21)

With the intention that there is no difference in the true nature (*satsvarūpa*) among all existing things, just as there is no difference in consciousness (*cidbheda*) among sentient beings, he says:

"In one... This refers to those things such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth; the meaning is that your intellect (*dhī*) regarding these, which is well-known here among the ignorant, is not in accordance with the scriptures. || 21 ||
And there is no such thing as a real entity that, having come into being, is utterly dissolved;
this is merely an appearance, O Raghava, neither existent nor non-existent.
What, then, is the scriptural cognition? He states it with the words "And not... (na ca). || 22 ||
With a mind that has arisen and is not yet tranquil, it remains for a moment;
there is no end to delusion here until liberation, for this which exists is not an unreal thing.

He establishes the statement "neither existent nor non-existent" with the words "by that which has arisen": because it is clearly perceived by a mind that has arisen, manifested, and not yet subsided from the beginning until liberation (*āmokṣāt*), and because it exists at its own time, it is therefore not non-existent. However, when delusion (*moha*) ceases—that is, upon its cessation—at the end [of samsara], until liberation is well-established here...
The meaning is that since this does not exist in the prior time and exists even less so at the time of liberation, it is a non-entity and therefore not real even while existing. || 23 ||
Why indeed does Rāma remain idle here and abandon the snare of delusion?
For whatever arises from attachment to association is truly a cause for further delusion.

Even when considering the efficacy of knowledge (*jñāna*), it is difficult to say whether delusion (*moha*) and the like exist or are absolutely non-existent; thus, their very indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatā*) follows as the conclusion. He states this with the words "What indeed" (*kiṃ kila*): if the web of delusion were absolutely non-existent, what indeed would knowledge dispel or cast out? For if there is nothing to be dispelled, it is impossible for the dispeller to be efficacious.
Thus, if [the world] were absolutely real, what could knowledge abandon? For it is never observed that reality is to be dispelled by knowledge.

Therefore, whatever that attachment may be—whatever attachment is the indefinable superimposition (anirvacanīyādhyāsa)—by means of that connection characterized as such, it is like [the perception of] a snake in a rope and so forth.
The meaning is that, by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), it is established that the entire range of perceptible phenomena is the cause of delusion. || 24 ||
If delusion does not exist in the world, what indeed is it here?
And if it does exist, my dear friend, what is the cause of that delusion?
"Therefore, amidst the conditions of birth and death, remain forever as utterly equanimous as the sky and perpetually tranquil.
Thus ends the section on "Stability" within the Means to Liberation in the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, the work of Vālmīki, according to the tradition of the sages.
The sixty-first canto, titled "The State of Birth and Death."

Thus ends the sixty-first chapter, titled "The State of Birth and Death," in the Section on Stability (*sthitiprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, in its exposition of the essential meaning (*tātparyaprakāśa*).
The sixty-second canto.
Śrī Vasiṣṭha said:
A steadfast person, possessing discernment and great intelligence, from the very beginning...
A learned person should examine a treatise with the aid of another treatise, and a virtuous person should deliberate upon it with the help of a virtuous person.
The complete perfection of all qualities as taught in every scripture is attributed to Rāma;
yet even for one who is inferior, the state of excellence can be attained through association with the virtuous and through personal effort. (1)

It was stated previously that "the true scripture should be investigated again and again through an inconceivable process"; as to how it is to be investigated, he says: "The steadfast one. The steadfast one (*dhīra*) is one who endures the dualities of the external and internal worlds. The discerning one (*vicāravān*) is one skilled in reasoning and refutation (*ūhāpoha*). For the sake of directly realizing that [truth] by himself, he...

The meaning is that, having approached a teacher with fuel in hand, as prescribed by such scriptural injunctions, one should first investigate the scripture together with a learned and virtuous teacher who is patient with the student's transgressions. || 1 ||
Having deliberated together with a virtuous, dispassionate, wise, and great person through the practice of supreme yoga, the highest state is attained.
By a virtuous person of noble lineage; from great yoga, that is, from the samādhi culminating in the dissolution of the mind. || 2 ||
A person who is refined by study of the scriptures, association with virtuous people, detachment, and practice shines like you, becoming a vessel for innate wisdom. (3)

A person who has been refined and purified by the constant practice of the meanings of the scriptures— including other treatises useful for Vedānta— as well as virtuous actions, noble conduct, association with good people, detachment, and so forth,
shines like you; such a person, upon hearing this present scripture, [attains] his own...
The meaning is that he is a vessel for his own self-knowledge, which has the inner reality (pratyaktattva) as its object. Alternatively, the construction is:
having been honored by the scriptures of spiritual science (adhyātmaśāstra) and so forth, he has become a vessel for his own self-knowledge and thus shines like you. || 3 ||
You, whose own conduct is noble, steadfast, and a mine of a multitude of virtues,
abide free from suffering, with the impurities of the mind removed through the cessation of worldly existence.
He says that the aforementioned qualities indeed exist in you: "Thou... (verse 4).
Surely you have become like the autumnal sky from which the clouds have been released;
be free from worldly attachment through contemplation and remain united with supreme consciousness.

Now, anticipating Rāma’s state of liberation while living (*jīvanmuktatā*) through his awakening, he says with the words beginning "surely" (*nūnam*): "Surely, the mind of Kalāvatī, who is free from anxiety, remains in a state of liberated imagination; and since it is free from all divisions, it is undoubtedly liberated indeed. (6)
He states the characteristic of one whose mind is liberated— the seed for the possibility of that state— in the word "cintā" (thought).
This refers to the liberation from all thoughts of external objects, and through internal unification with the Supreme Self like milk and water,
it possesses the skill characterized by the transformation into the form of Brahman, as established by the experience of the liberated ones.
The mind that abides free from conceptual construction is indeed liberated; there is no doubt in this—this is the meaning. || 6 ||
Now, on this earth, people will follow the conduct of your supreme majesty, which is free from passion and hatred.

Thus, when your mind is liberated, those previously mentioned who are liberated while living will follow your conduct by means of the aforementioned mental disposition, which is free from attachment and aversion. || 7 ||
Those wise people who conduct themselves according to the customs appropriate for the world outside [the monastery] will cross the ocean of existence, like those equipped with a boat.
The children, equipped with the raft of knowledge, [crossed over]. || 8 ||
That virtuous person who possesses a mind equal to yours and has an even vision is fit for the insights of knowledge described by me; he is one who possesses true vision.
As long as the body lasts, remain with a mind free from passion and hatred; outwardly, observe conduct appropriate for the world, while inwardly, having abandoned all desires. (10)

Rather, [the author] says "as long as the body" (yāvaddeham) to show that for me, who am liberated while living (jīvanmukta), there should be neither the abandonment of the body nor acting according to one's own whims. He is one whose conduct follows the dharma scriptures and the excellent traditions appropriate for the world. 10.
Attain supreme peace, just as other virtuous ones do;
for those who are not free from deliberation here are like jackals in their nature. (11)
Those whose nature is like that of jackals deceive others through skill in self-interest; those whose nature is like that of children act according to their whims and are deluded. (11)
By cultivating those inherent natures which belong to great-souled men born with a virtuous disposition, a person attains the status of one who will have a noble birth in the future.

The meaning is that even an ordinary person, by cultivating and acquiring those natural qualities such as tranquility and self-restraint— which are the inherent characteristics of those born of pure *sattva* who are liberated while living— gradually attains knowledge and subsequently achieves the state of a noble birth, namely, the final body of one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*). || 12 ||
Whatever caste and qualities one constantly cultivates here, even if born into another caste, one assumes that very caste in an instant. (13)

To explain why that is so, he says: "yāneva... (whichever...). The meaning is that there is a fixed rule: by serving those of superior birth and qualities, one obtains birth in a superior caste; by serving those of inferior birth and qualities, one obtains an inferior [birth]. || 13 ||
All previous states of being follow one who has fallen under the power of karma;
yet even great mountain ranges are overcome by human effort.
"Those from previous lives" means according to the principle: "Whatever state one remembers at the time of death, that very state one attains.

With the intention that even by one who is most debased, an effort must certainly be made for liberation alone—since for one who does not desist from human exertion (*pauruṣa*), the attainment of the fruit is inevitable—he says: "by human exertion. Dharādharā...
In this world, kings, mountains, their great lineages, and forest armies are all subdued through prowess guided by the science of ethics (nītiśāstra) and by means such as cutting them down. || 14 ||
With fortitude, one should uplift the intellect from [the lower states], as one would rescue a bewildered cow from the mud—
even if one has resorted to a tamasic or rajasic birth, or any other such state.

One should uplift [the self] by turning it away from the objects of the senses. A person who has resorted to—that is, attained—any birth or womb, whether tāmasī (in the form of demons, piśācas, śūdras, and so forth), rājasī (in the form of kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, and so forth), or any other mixed with both *sattva* and *tamas* (such as the species of serpents and the like). || 15 ||
By the power of their own discernment, the virtuous attain the state of sattvic birth;
therefore, O Rāghava, that which is directed toward the clear jewel of the mind— || 16 ||

He elaborates on what has already been stated with the words beginning "svaviveka" (one's own discrimination) and so forth: "In the mind-jewel," that is, in the crystal of the mind; "is employed," meaning it is attached. || 16 ||
Thus, being absorbed in that, one manifests accordingly; therefore, through human effort, one comes to possess highly precious qualities. (17)
Those of later auspicious birth become seekers of liberation here;
there is nothing on earth, or in heaven among the gods, anywhere at all [that can compare]. (18)
Though endowed with virtues, even through human effort,
celibacy, fortitude, and the force of valor and dispassion,
you do not attain that desired goal without being joined by the proper means. (19)
Having established the reality of the self through wisdom as the welfare of great beings, become free from sorrow; then, by your very example, these people—
Then he will become liberated and free from sorrow. || 20 ||
He summarizes what has been said concisely with the word "beneficial" (*hitam*).

Having established [the means] as one's own self through an intellect characterized by the aspiration for the means of accumulating the quality of pure *sattva*— which consists of unsurpassed bliss characterized by the absolute cessation of suffering for all living beings— ...

"Having become firm [in this state], be free from sorrow"—this is both the instruction and the blessing. The meaning is that by the sequence taught to you, other qualified persons as well shall become liberated. || 20 ||
O Rāmabhadra, in this final birth, endowed with the great majesty of discernment and delightful through the manifestation of all virtues,
establish yourself in action rooted in purity.
Let her not entertain thoughts deluded by attachment to worldly existence. || 21 ||

O Rāmabhadra, now that you have attained this final birth— which is delightful due to all the virtues such as tranquility and self-restraint that have blossomed forth through the great majesty of your discernment—
take your place, that is, establish your station, in the activity of those established in *sattva*, the *jīvanmuktas*, which is characterized by the seventh stage (*bhūmikā*). This...

The meaning is: may that reflection on the delusion of attachment to worldly existence—which was described in the section on dispassion (*vairāgya*) and is well-known to all people—not find a place or footing within you. || 21 ||

Thus ends the sixty-second canto, titled "The Section on Stability," within the "Means to Liberation" of the *Śrī Vāsiṣṭha Mahārāmāyaṇa*, composed by Vālmīki, spoken by the Divine Messenger, in the collection consisting of thirty-two thousand verses. 62.
Thus ends the sixty-second canto in the Section on Stability (*sthitiprakaraṇa*) within the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.

Thus [ends the work] composed by the mendicant named Śrīmad Ānandabodhendrasarasvatī, disciple of the venerable feet of Śrīmad Gaṅgādharendrasarasvatī, who was himself the disciple of the illustrious Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Śrīmat Sarvajñasarasvatī.
The section on "Stability" (Sthitiprakaraṇa) is completed in the *Śrīvāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇatātparyaprakāśa*.
This chapter on stability is completed.
